en: Preface to the Annotated *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

Now, this single scripture, the *Lotus Sūtra*, stands alone at the head of all scriptures; it directly imparts the teaching to all capacities of beings, culminating only in the attainment of Buddhahood.

The Sūtra says: "To reveal, instruct, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. How sublime! This is what is called the "one great causal event" (*ekamahā-karaṇīya-dharmahetupratyaya*).
When the Great Master Zhiwei read the Sūtra, he reached the passage: "This is called true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering."

He realized that the assembly on Mount Lingyan was still present, as if it had never dispersed. He consulted Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue, who said: "It is not that you have not awakened; it is not that I do not recognize you.
Among the Dharma masters of letters, none can equal you. Thereupon, he expounded the profound meanings (*xuan-yi*) and provided commentaries on the titles.

He further explained the textual phrases (*wen-ju*) to interpret the sutra. The Venerable Zhanran of Zhang'an recorded these in notebooks that formed complete volumes. Subsequently, various masters wrote commentaries upon them.
The commentaries differ in their brevity and detail, and their fundamental tenets are not uniform. Like those who divide a river to drink from it, they do not emerge from the great ocean.
A śramaṇa named Shou-lun of Mount Ke in the Song dynasty—who devoted himself to supporting his parents and took refuge in the forests and springs—annotated this sutra;
it was only after more than twenty years that he completed the work. He followed the Tiantai school’s system for dividing the text into sections and segments, based on two...
In ten fascicles, those who enter the Tiantai school will see everything clearly at a single glance; it is not difficult to penetrate its depths.
My late teacher Ousheng once obtained an ancient manuscript of this work and treasured it like a supreme jewel, keeping it within his chest.

In the Wuli year of the Earth-Mouse cycle (1608), while he was expounding it to the assembly beneath the Daibi Pavilion at Shunqing Temple in Tongyi County, one page of the manuscript happened to be missing. My late teacher then made a vow and prayed in silence.

Regarding the King of Samantabhadra’s Vows: once, there was a monk who brought this sutra, which also lacked one leaf; by successively supplementing it with the missing portion, they fulfilled the supreme cause.
This is its verification. When my late master passed away, I, the unwise one, wished to once again collate and re-carve it for circulation, but the necessary conditions did not coincide.
On the Buddha’s birthday in the Dingmao year of the Tianqi era, my disciple Faji suddenly said to me:
I said, "The Master previously used Master Shou-lun’s commentary on the *Sūtra*, but he found the explanations of characters too prolix and wished to revise and edit them further.
This aspiration remains unfulfilled; would it be acceptable for me now to complete it on his behalf? I gave my approval. Just then, the layman Gu Zheng-xun arrived.
When [Master] Chi heard of this matter, he said with joy, "I, your disciple, have a vow to carve the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Now that you, Master, are carving it, I wish to serve as its patron.
On the day of the *Ullambana* feast, he attended the invitation for the offering of food by Mr. Kāizhào of Wuxing and mentioned the matter again. Mr.
Kāizhào was likewise filled with exuberant joy and immediately granted permission to carve ten fascicles; furthermore, he exhorted others to provide donations and verses of praise.
It is accomplished. That which is called the causal conditions of the Buddha-dharma cannot be forced. Were it not for those present at the single assembly on Vulture Peak, how could this exist?
May those who read and study these commentaries in the future take care not to obscure the single-minded devotion of Master Lun;

may they cause all sentient beings with the capacity for awakening to immediately attain the opening, showing, entering, and realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As one lamp transmits to another, their merit shall be inexhaustible.
How inconceivable! This preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
annotated by Shengxing of Yuxi Bodhi Hermitage, was composed on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the first year of the Chongzhen era, the Wuchen year (1638).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shou-lun of Qiyun, Keshan, Jinxian, Song Dynasty.
The Lotus Sūtra is the ultimate teaching of the Tathāgata, a sublime and heroic exposition of the Dharma. It is the fundamental means for sentient beings to restore their true nature;
its merit exceeds all other transformations, and its virtue surpasses those of the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching]. Now, I shall expound it, as all other sūtras unanimously extol it.
All Buddhas of the past, present, and future have taken this as their primary cause. It is like the finest gold among jewels, like the vast ocean of the great river.
How magnificent is the profound teaching—subtle, wondrous, and empty! How expansive is the True Vehicle—deep, firm, and far-reaching!

Those with the karmic affinity encounter it, like the *tāpa* flower blooming once in a thousand years; it gathers in all dharmas without exception, like the great earth which provides sustenance to all equally.

Moistened by a single rain, the "withered seeds" of the śrāvakas receive their prediction of enlightenment; the "withered wood" returns to spring. Even animals and dragon-girls transcend and ascend, and cold ashes flare up again.
The crest-jewel is bestowed equally, and the royal feast provides universal sustenance. Encompassing the boundaries of the entire dharma-realm, one governs the vast estate of wealth and nobility.
Through opening, showing, awakening, and entering, the single path is pure; through person, principle, teaching, and practice—

The four dharmas are perfectly integrated, and the Great Matter reaches its ultimate consummation; thus, his original intention is fully realized. Although the underlying principle is a single thread, why is it that the sutra has three versions?
These shall not be detailed here, as they are already set forth in the Prolegomenon (*Yuanxu*).

Moreover, since the phrasing is vast and extensive and the purport is profound and subtle, were it not for one of great wisdom and great eloquence, who could penetrate this Dharma that is so difficult to believe and difficult to understand? It is said: "There is..."
The Wise One manifested his traces at Tai and Heng; he attained awakening through this very sutra and received its seal at Nan Yue.

There, he realized the samādhi of *dhāraṇī* and the purification of the six sense faculties. He elucidated the title of the sutra through five layers of profound meaning (*xuan-yi*) and analyzed the text into three sections.

Without lingering on names or appearances, he freely expounded and propagated [the teaching]. At that time, there were disciples such as the Venerable Guanding, who humbled himself for the sake of the末代 (final age).

Collected and compiled into this book, the language is concise yet the meaning is rich; the events are harmonized and the principles are radiant. Although this literature was composed by humans, some may still remain confused.

During the Tang Dynasty, Jingxi [Zhiyi] further augmented it with the *Ji* (Records) and *Chao* (Excerpts), examining the subtle details with thorough scrutiny so that they might circulate alongside the *Shu* (Commentary).
This is like Mencius assisting Confucius, or Yunmen drawing upon Shaoshi; thus, its literary excellence flourished to such a degree that it nearly rivaled the contents of the Tripitaka itself.
Wherever it is proclaimed, it is only as a partial teaching; the secular world has no means to investigate the ancestral Way, and it cannot be fully elucidated.
How tragic, how lamentable! Truly, it is a matter for deep sighs. A fine jade is hidden within dark stones, and excellent timber grows upon distant peaks;
if people remain unaware of them, who shall employ them? I humbly reflect that the scriptures were opened for the fourfold assembly, for the Buddhas and Patriarchs bestowed them universally.

Fearing that the teachings on the mind might be restricted to a single corner and that lay practitioners would have no way to enter the Path, I, though lacking in talent, have ventured to provide these explanations.
I follow the pure regulations of our ancestral predecessors to broaden the wholesome karma of future generations.

My intent in adding these annotations is for them to circulate widely, so that upon opening this scroll one may dispel doubts and encounter the text without obstruction, thereby allowing the Sky of Meaning— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
With a mind as clear and calm as a moon shining in a solitary sky, he shattered the weariness of worldly toil and suddenly awakened from the dream of the Yellow Millet.

Having opened wide the path of the profound mystery, he steadily rides the white bull; within the lands of even a single mote of dust, he universally manifests the Samādhi of the Form Body, and enters among the various species of animals to practice the four methods of integration.
Thus, both self and other, enemies and kin alike, all arrive at the state of non-abiding.

Returning to the fundamental ground, both self and others—ordinary and sagely alike—are perfected; through the harmonious fusion of the perfect causes gathered without exception, I respectfully offer these auspicious wishes for the present Emperor, Your Majesty:

may you govern with the Golden Wheel over ten billion Mount Sumerus, and may your sagely lifespan extend beyond the celestial kalpas of the immortals, so that the Buddha-Dharma may find its reliance and the teachings of the religious schools remain free from demonic interference.

Abiding in his position, he exhorted and praised the circulation [of the teachings], such that his virtue equaled that of Śakra and Brahmā; year after year, military force and penal law were not employed, and his transformation followed the legacy of the Tang and Yu dynasties.
Under his rule, the worthy officials of civil and military ranks all attained a hundred blessings, and the six armies and the myriad people were preserved in great harmony.

Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* Compiled by the Layman Min Mengde of Pingcheng, Wuxing Part One:
The Preface Section Section Eight: Initial Preface Subsection One:
The Title of the Preface *Preface to the Propagation of the Lotus Sutra* (Miaofa Lianhuajing Hongchuan Xu)

The profound meaning of the Dharma is summarized as follows in the subsequent text; that which has not yet been fully analyzed here is what the "propagator" (弘傳者) shall proclaim, disseminate, and extol.
This means ensuring that this Way flows forth and spreads universally without obstruction. It is said: "People can propagate the Way, but the Way relies on people for its propagation.
Regarding the term *xu* (序), the *Erya* states: "The walls on the east and west are called *xu*"; Guo Pu [comments]...

The phrase "Cloud Preface" distinguishes between the internal and external. Now it is said that once one has ascended the wall and reached the sequence (*xu*), one must enter the hall and the inner sanctum (*ào*);
the origin of the term "sequence" lies precisely here. △ Second, the designation of the author.
Composed by Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
Zhongnan Mountain lies several tens of *li* south of the city of Chang’an; it connects to Hanzhong to the south and serves as a guardian peak (*zhenshan*) within the Guannei region.
This preface concerns the Master, who habitually practiced the Way and resided here, thereby marking the mountain as his place of reliance.
"Śākya" is the clan name; fully explained, it is *Śākya*, which means "Straight Forest" (*ṛju-vana*) or "Capable Sage" (*śakya*).

Because the distant ancestor of the Tathāgata, King Amṛta, banished his four sons from the palace to dwell in the Straight Forest at the foot of the Snowy Mountains, they established a residence there for several years.
Their virtue attracted followers like a marketplace, and they grew into a powerful nation under their father.
Reflecting on his past summons and the transgressions he had committed, he did not return; thus the Father-King sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses such capability.

From that time forward, he took "Forest of Rectitude" (Zhí-lín) as his surname, or alternatively, the surname "Capable One" (Néng-rén). Now, since those of the Southern Mountains have taken the Buddha as their teacher, they consequently adopt the name "Śākya.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "When the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer retain their original names; likewise, when the four castes leave the household life, they are all the same."
That he was called Shi (of the Śākya clan) is the proof of this; Daoxuan is his given name, his courtesy name is Fabian, and his surname is Qian.
He was a native of Changcheng in Lake District. His father, Shen, served the Chen dynasty as Minister of Personnel (*Libu Shangshu*). The Master was the eldest son of Shen;

his mother, Lady Yao, dreamed that a white moon pierced her womb, and she subsequently conceived him. He remained in the womb for a full year, during the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the [blank] year, he was already widely versed in the classics and histories by the age of nine.

At twelve, he was skilled in literary composition, earning the respectful admiration of all men. At fifteen, weary of worldly life, he followed Master Ying of Riyen Temple to take the tonsure and enter the monastic order;
all the affairs of the Buddhist gate were mastered by him without formal study. At seventeen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination, and his conduct was as pure as ice.
His resolve was as firm as metal and stone; though clad in coarse hempen robes through spring and autumn, winter and summer, he sustained himself on but a single meal.
Following the Venerable Zhishou, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka, penetrating its profound mysteries and subtle nuances until his reputation for excellence surpassed that of his teacher.

As his virtue spread, both monastics and laypeople praised him; he resided at Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan, where he practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, during which auspicious and miraculous signs were exceedingly numerous.

There was a dragon who transformed himself into human form and visited the Master to request the Dharma; he was accompanied by celestial beings who offered incense, flowers, and ambrosia (amṛta), which became his regular practice.
The Master, regarding life lightly and the Dharma as paramount, disregarded his physical body until he gradually developed a chronic illness.
Moved by this, the Northern Heavenly King bestowed upon him an excellent remedy for restoring the heart; the medicine was divinely efficacious, capable of rejuvenating the youth and prolonging life.
While the Master was practicing the Way one night, his foot stumbled; suddenly, a divine being supported him.
The Master looked back and asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am the swift messenger beneath the seat of the Southern Heavenly King.
The Master further asked who were at his side, and they replied, "This is the Prince Nātha of the North, who, by the command of his royal father, constantly comes to attend upon you."
Later, during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Wei dynasty, a celestial being came to inform the Master, saying:
"The ancient sacred site of Jingye Monastery in Qinggong Village is suitable for establishing the Dharma banner; you should grant this request.

Accordingly, in the second year of the Qianfeng era, he constructed a single *śīla-maṇḍala*. At its completion, he was moved by the appearance of the Long-Browed Arhat (*Dīrghanakha*) and the Venerable Piṇḍola.
As he was about to descend, he followed [the Master] with sincerity for many days, engaging in extensive discussions on the characteristics of the Vinaya and the conduct of masters.

Since the Master’s reputation for practice had already become established, he was frequently moved by the protection of devas and humans. One day, as someone stepped outside his room, making a sound, the Master asked, "Where is the donor?
The person replied, "I am a disciple named Zhang Qiong, the fifteenth son of the Southern Heavenly King. The King has ninety..."

The sons were both heroic and divine, each possessing martial strategy as they defended their respective provinces and capitals, upholding the orthodox teachings. When asked who had come with the Master, he replied:
"This is my third elder brother, named Yu. He held the Buddhist gate in high esteem and personally compiled the *Tujing* (Illustrated Scripture) of Jiyuan Temple in one hundred fascicles;
I obtained the upper and lower volumes by recording his oral instructions. Furthermore, there was a celestial being."
His surname was Wei and his name was Kun; he was none other than General Wei, one of the eight great generals of the Southern Heavenly King.
Among the thirty-two generals of the Four Heavenly Kings, Wei Kui is the foremost.

Because he possesses the body of a *kumārabhūta* (a youthful or celibate being), all the other celestial hosts revere and submit to him. He constantly guards and protects the Master, for the Master possesses the Vinaya.
Regarding matters of institutional regulations, ritual procedures, measurements, and the weighing of offenses where there was some uncertainty, he sought clarification and resolution;

consequently, he compiled the spiritual traces of this master as well as the sacred sites of the West, totaling three thousand eight hundred entries, which were organized into ten fascicles titled the *Gantong ji* (Records of Resonance and Response).
Later, in the spring of the second year of the Qianfeng era, a celestial being suddenly came to inform him, saying:
"The Master’s allotted lifespan has now reached its end; he shall be reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita.
Having said this, he then gave a bundle of incense, saying, "This is the true product of the Thorny Forest (Khadira-vana), possessed by all the devas.
After another ten days, the Master told his disciples, "I am about to pass away. You may move my remains to the stone chamber at Tangu Valley. Shortly thereafter, the assembly...
He beheld banners and precious canopies spread like clouds and arrayed like stars coming to welcome him as he returned to the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Master’s worldly age was seventy-two, and his years of wisdom were fifty-two; this was on the third day of the tenth month of the year Dingmao.
The above is a brief selection of the general outline of the Great Master’s auspicious manifestations and noble conduct during his final incarnation. The Master, by...

His long-standing vows were ever more profound; across three successive lifetimes, he appeared as a human and a celestial eye. His first birth was during the Qi dynasty, when he was known as the monk Senghu.
He resided at Yinyue Temple on Mount Shicheng in Shanxi, Yuezhou, where he made a vow to carve a one-hundred-foot stone image of Maitreya;
this site is present-day Xinchang. His second birth was during the Liang period, when he was titled the monk Sengyou and resided at Zhongling Temple in Jinling.

The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) in ten fascicles, compiled by Shan Dinglin Temple, along with the biographies of various masters and disciples, have both circulated in the world.

Now, observing that the Great Master’s virtue and conduct were most flourishing and that devas and humans looked up to him in reverence; that he followed the tracks and regulations of the former sages and expounded the essential principles of the *Vinaya*;

that his merit surpassed that of dragons and elephants, and his Way rescued those in the dark realms; and that he appeared as a succession of three births, extending his compassion to all—[it is clear that he was a great being].
Among the multitudes of beings, he was none other than a Great Being who has ascended the stages, or perhaps an emanation of Upāli.

As for being a vessel and a sail for the ocean of suffering, the sun and moon of the Dharma-realm, a virtuous guide on perilous paths, or a divine physician for the sick—who else could it be but the Master?
Thus, his noble conduct and magnificent deeds, which look up to the Sage and transmit his instructions, are fully recorded in the monastic histories; I shall not cite them here at length.
Zheng Kangcheng said that it "explains its meaning. The *Yueli* says, "The creator is called a sage; the transmitter is called enlightened.
The saying "I transmit but do not create" is all phrasing used for self-effacement. △ Third, indicating the source and cause.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas manifest their spiritual power.
This serves as the basis for the general title of the present scripture and provides the foundation for this preface. "To unify" (*tǒng*) means to encompass and include;
it encompasses the ten directions and includes the three periods of time. Does not the Scripture itself say: "The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods"?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that [the Buddha] appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-karaṇa-artha-hetu*).
"Appearing in the world" refers to his descent of the spirit. "Fundamental aim" refers to his original vow.

One should know that all Tathāgatas, the guides of the ten directions, have simultaneously transcended the two deaths and fully manifested the three virtues; they abide in the principle of the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (tranquil light) realm.
The wondrous body that realizes the dharmatā of the earth is pure, unconditioned, serene, and eternally abiding;

yet, because his compassion has not ceased, he regards his vows with ever-increasing intensity. Establishing sublime plans for expedient means and deploying excellent strategies of skillful artifice, he entices the ignorant and childish—though the chariot was originally no chariot—and guides the common folk who are lost and forgetful.

How could there be a teaching that does not have a reason for its manifestation? Out of compassion for the five turbidities, he expediently expounded the Three Vehicles so that all those lost in delusion might reach the ultimate One Vehicle.
Yet these profound and mysterious secret words cannot be set forth without being revealed; this sublime Dharma and heroic exposition can only be brought forward once the assembly has gathered.
Thus his original intent is fully expressed and the Great Matter is clearly manifested—a task not undertaken by a single Buddha alone.
Indeed, this has been the case throughout the three periods of time. Fourth, clarifying how the scripture was transmitted to both lands:
its essence was formed in the Great House (India) over a thousand years ago, and it was transmitted eastward to China for more than three hundred years.
"Accumulation" (*piṇḍa*) means gathering together. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Brahma-sound was no longer heard;

this Great Teaching was entrusted to Ānanda. Because it was received through hearing, it was "accumulated"; because it was accumulated, it was "bound," so that it might be universally inscribed upon palm leaves (*pustaka*).
"Great Hall" (*mahā-śālā*) is a magnificent designation for the West; "hall" (*śālā*) is the same as "summer" (*śarad*). It is also... [text ends]
This refers to what are called the magnificent palatial residences of the capital cities. The *Baitu tong* (White Tiger General Explanation) states:
"In the Xia dynasty it was called Xiayì; in the Yin dynasty it was called Shangyì; and in the Zhou dynasty it was called Jīngshī. Furthermore, "Xià" means great, and "huá" means flourishing.

The *Fuyixing* (Commentary on the Subcommentary) says: "To the left of the Iron Pass are all Hu regions; to the west of the Pamir Mountains are all of the Brahmanic stock. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
The land of the Hu was a place for miscellaneous precepts, while the land of the Fan was exclusively the capital of true sages.
South of the Snow Mountains, extending three directions to the sea with a circumference of ninety thousand *li*, it was named Daxia. The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* states:

"Observing the arrival of the scriptures in previous dynasties, those transcribed by men of virtue and wisdom all claimed to have translated the Hu language into Han. Furthermore, throughout the Nine Provinces..."
Regarding the designation of the western region as "Tianzhu" (India), this is the general name for that country, though it is also called "Shendu," "Yintu," and so forth.
As for the term "Zhina" used by those in the west to refer to the Nine Provinces, this is likely the common appellation for our own land, though it is also known as "Zhen dan" or "Zhendan.
Now, what is called "Hu" refers to the frontier customs of the west, whereas "Fan" refers to the central region of India.
How could the Prefect have regarded Buddhist scriptures as "barbarian" (Hu) speech? To fail to investigate their origins and flow is the height of disparagement.

I send these words to future worthies: should there be those who consider the scriptures to be the language of the Hu, or those who refer to the Buddha as the "Old Hu," I hope they will reform this by means of the Sanskrit (Fan).
If this is done, one will not only avoid falling into the ridicule of those with clear discernment.
This may perhaps serve to avoid the fault of slanderous calumny. Master An styled himself "The Heaven-Pervading One" (Mitiān) and yet still spoke of translating from the Hu to the Han;
how much more so for those who are merely ordinary? This is like a single flaw in a fine jade.

As for what is called "Fan," it descended from the Brahmā Heaven to the human realm at the beginning of the kalpa, giving rise to the present generations; thus, these various lineages essentially retain that original nature.

Regarding the name: since the Buddha appeared in the generation of King Zhao of the Ji Zhou dynasty and the scriptures arrived during the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Han, one can know that a thousand years have passed.
As for the "Eastern Transmission": it is said that the Buddha emerged from the land of Zhutu (India) and his teachings spread to Shenzhou (China);
thus, he is described as flowing from the West to the East. As for *Zhendan*, some call it *Zhandan*; however, the meaning of these names is difficult to ascertain.
The phrase "for over three hundred years" refers to the Han and Jin dynasties. This is because the subsequent passage regarding "over six hundred years" states that it was "from the Han to the Tang.
Thus, the contrast between the distant and the near makes the meaning of the text even more evident.
However, this section should logically be divided into two parts; first, according to the structural outline (*ke*), and second, the detailed explanation.

The meaning begins with the symbolic expressions of the texts; if it were not so now, I fear that matters would become overly complex and cluttered, which would not be conducive to a dignified appearance.

While the wording may appear to be conflated, the underlying intent is not confused; readers should grasp the meaning through their own insight. The subsequent passages may be understood by applying this same principle.
△ Fifth, regarding the translations, there are three types of revisions.

During the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin dynasty, the Dharma-protector from Dunhuang, the Bodhisattva Zhu Fahu, first translated this sutra, naming it the *Zhengfahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).

Later, during the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Śramaṇa Kumārajīva of the Later Qin—under the reign title Hongshi—subsequently translated this sutra, naming it the *Miaofa Lianhua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka). During the Sui dynasty...

[the reign title] Ren... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end; the standard historical record indicates that the Sui dynasty's relevant period for this scripture is the Kaihuang era.)
The version translated later by the Śramaṇa from North India, Jñānagupta, at Daxingshan Temple during the Kaihuang era bears the same title, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
During the Western Jin dynasty, the capital was located in Luoyang; Emperor Hui (Emperor Xiaohui), whose personal name was Zhong and whose surname was Sima, reigned there.
He was the second son of Emperor Wu of Jin. He ascended the throne in the fourth month of the gengxu year, the first year of Taixi, and changed the era name to Yongxi.
In the second year of Yongxi, he changed it to Yongping; in the ninth year of Yongping, in the gengshen year, he changed it to Yongkang.
However, as the two emperors Hui and An resided in different capitals, they were subsequently distinguished by the designations "East" and "West."
This is similar to how China is designated as "East" and "West," or how the Qi state was referred to as "North" and "South.
Regarding Chang'an, the *Hanshu* states that its original name was Xianyang. When the Han Founder first pacified the empire, he intended to establish his capital at Luoyi;

however, following the remonstrance of Lou Jing, the Emperor sighed, saying, "I shall remain permanently (*chang*) secure here (*an*). His descendants took this as the name for the city, which became known as Qingmen (the Green Gate).
The *Lunheng* states that to the southeast of the city of Chang’an there was a gate named Bāchéng;
because its color was blue, it was popularly designated as such. "Dunhuang" is the name of a commandery. The *Jiuyuzhi* states that it was formerly the region of Shazhou.
As for "Bodhisattva," this is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in full, it is called *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*.

This refers to "Accomplishing Sentient Beings through the Great Bodhicitta": by expounding the Four Great Vows to benefit all beings and practicing compassion through the Six Perfections, one is said to "accomplish sentient beings through the Great Bodhicitta.
Regarding Zhu Fahu, tradition states that he was originally a man from the Yuezhi kingdom;
his name was Dharmarakṣa, which translates as "Dharma-Protected," and his original surname was Zhi. He was thirty years old [when he arrived].
The *Liù guó yǔ* (The Speeches of the Six Kingdoms) places him next after Dūnhuáng, where he was styled Zhú Shì.
He subsequently returned to Cháng'ān, where he established a monastery outside the Qīngmén Gate and practiced the Way with extraordinary diligence.

Regarding this scripture, although there had previously been three translations, Dharmarakṣa was the first to produce it; this is why it is so described. The sūtra consists of ten fascicles; its title lacks the word "Miaolián" (Wondrous Lotus), but...

It is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [was translated during the reign of] Emperor An of the Eastern Jin, whose personal name was Dezong and who was the grandson of Emperor Jianwen and son of Emperor Xiaowu;
he ascended the throne in the ninth month of the twenty-first year of Taiyuan, the Bingshen year, and changed the era name to Long’an.

As for the Later Qin, there were four dynasties with the name "Qin": first, the Qin; second, the Former Qin; third, the Later Qin; and fourth... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The fourth was Western Qin, also known as Qifu Qin; Shi Gong’s arrival occurred precisely in the third year of the Hongshi era of Later Qin.
The ruler of Qin was named Xing, with the courtesy name Zilüe, and belonged to the Yao clan.

However, this single passage is somewhat disjointed, likely because during the eras of the Qin and Jin dynasties, military blades were crossed in combat and usurpers and pretenders carved out territories, with shifting and unstable hegemonies.
It was for this reason that it came to be so. "Qiuci" (Kucha) is the foreign name; Master Shi was born there.

Its original script reads "Jiuji," which is simply pronounced "Qiuci. This is similar to how "Wanhou" (Ten Thousand Marquisates) is pronounced "Mohu," or "Yechi" (the consort of a king) is pronounced "Yanzi.
"Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term; *śramaṇa* here translates as "diligent rest," meaning one who diligently cultivates goodness.
"Karma" refers to the cessation of all unwholesome conduct. The *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states: "Because one is free from the accumulation of all fetters, one is called a śramaṇa.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "When the mind is free from attachment and one has no desire for anything, seeking liberation from all greed—this is called being a śramaṇa.
The *Mahāvyūha Śāstra* states: "One who has transcended all attachments is called a śramaṇa."
The *Śramaṇapuṣpaśīrṣa-sūtra* states: "Just as space is unimpeded and smoke and dust cannot defile it, so too I say that the Dharma of the śramaṇa is unstained;
it is likewise. The *Lalitavistara-sūtra* states: "The triple world is tumultuous, and the six realms of existence are shrouded in darkness.
One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa; this is the origin of the title 'śramaṇa'."
How easily can such a person be found? Upon seeing the worthy, one should think of emulating them, so as not to disgrace their name or reality.

"Kumārajīva" is said in full to be Kumārajīva; because his father’s name was Kumārayana and his mother’s name was Jīvā—she being the younger sister of King Kaniṣka—he was given this title by his parents.
"Ji" (童) means "child," and "Shou" (壽) means "longevity"; this [name] was established according to this Dharma.
The Master was profoundly skilled in the literary compositions and phrasing of this land; as he rendered both the Chinese and Indic texts together, he was called Kumārajīva.
His flourishing virtue and fragrant legacy shall be seen subsequently in the following translations.

As for the reason it says "translated after the Western Jin," it is because the term "Miaolian" (Wondrous Lotus) was added later. The Sui dynasty had its capital at Chang'an; the ruler of Sui was Emperor Wen.
The Emperor’s posthumous name was Jiān and his surname was Yáng; he was the eighth-generation descendant of Yáng Zhèn, the Grand Marshal of Guānxī under the Hàn dynasty.
In the second month of the first year of Dàdìng (the Gēnzí year), he received the abdication from the Zhōu dynasty and ascended the throne, changing the era name to Kāihuáng.
In the twentieth year of Kāihuáng, it was changed to Rénshòu. In the fourth year of Rénshòu, Emperor Yáng ascended the throne and subsequently changed it to Dàyè. It was also known as Dàxīng.
The "Good" (Śan) refers to the capital city. At that time, the Buddha-dharma was flourishing, with monasteries standing shoulder-to-shoulder and their names intermingling;

therefore, they were distinguished by the terms "small" and "large. This is also like the case of the *Zhuāngyán* and *Zhāotí* [monasteries], all of which have "small" and "large" counterparts even today.
As for the character for "temple" (*sì*), its etymological explanation is "succession" (*sì*); it means that those who manage the affairs succeed one another therein.
In the past, the Son of Heaven had nine monasteries (*si*). In the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the year Dingmao, the Buddha-dharma first arrived.
Two monks from India, Mokṣala and Dharmaratna, brought scriptures and images on white horses and reached Luoyang;
by imperial decree, they were accommodated at the Honglu Monastery. In the eleventh year, the year Wuchen, furthermore—

An imperial edict was issued to construct a separate monastery outside the Yong Gate, which was named after the White Horse; thus, the reason why Buddhist monasteries (*fan-chà*) are all called "temples" (*sì*) today originates from this.
Regarding North India, the *Xiyu ji* states that "Tianzhu" is a Sanskrit term for which the Chinese translation is "Moon.
This means that once the Sun of the Buddha has set, the Sages and Worthies arise in succession, and the teachings are like the moon. Furthermore—

It is said that the five regions of India are collectively called *Bhāratavarṣa* (印土), measuring ninety thousand *li* in circumference. It is bordered by the great ocean on three sides and backed by the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) to the north;
it is narrow in the south and broad in the north, shaped like a half-moon. Its fields are demarcated and divided into more than seventy kingdoms.
Some texts refer to it as "India" (*Yindu*), which means "Sun and Moon" (*Sūryacandramas*); this is because the sun and moon have a thousand names, and this is one of them.
First, because those sages and saints appeared in the world to guide the multitudes of sentient beings, they are like the moon shining down upon the earth.
Some say that names such as Shendu (身毒) and Xian dou (賢豆) are merely different transcriptions of the same Indic sound.
As for Śīlagupta, one phrase contains two individuals; the *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* states: "The first is Śīlagupta, which is translated as 'Arrival' (至)."
De also states that [the former] was a person from North India whose name, Buddhadeva, means "Buddha's Virtue.
The second was Dharmagupta, which is translated as "Dharma-Confidential" (Famì) or "Dharma-Treasury" (Fáng); he was a person from South India. The *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) states:
"The two Dharma Masters Dharmagupta and Jñānagupta arrived at Daxingshan Temple in the first year of the Renshou era, the year of Xīyǒu (601 CE)."

This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with added chapters (*Xiānpǐn Fǎhuá jīng*). As for the version translated later, it is called the "later translation" because it was produced after the earlier Qin translation.
The general table of contents for the sūtras translated by these two Dharma Masters does not differ from the Qin version;

however, there are differences in the specific wording, consisting of additions, deletions, and transpositions. Therefore, it is commonly known in the world as the *Xiānpǐn Fǎhuá*. (From the *Nèidiǎn*).
The *Yinshu* (Commentary on Sounds) states: "Although this version has been augmented, it is cumbersome and a confused mixture; the wise must understand what has been added.
Specifically, regarding the two versions of the Qin and Jin scriptures, there are six instances where the text was augmented, combined, or modified:

first, the addition of the verses following the 'Universal Door' chapter (*Pumenpin*) from the Qin and Jin editions; second, the supplementation of the 'Simile of the Sunlight' (*Riguangyu*) in its entirety within the Qin translation."

1. The "Chapter on Medicinal Herbs" (*Bhaiṣajyavastuka*) is moved to after the "Chapter on the Three Kāśyapas" (*Tri-kāśyapa-parivarta*). 2. The "Chapter on the Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) is moved to the end of the sutra. 3.
The "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*) is moved to after the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Rddhy-abhisamskāra-parivarta*).

4. The "Chapter on Returning to One's Original State" (*Prakṛti-sthiti-parivarta*) is changed to read: "He then returned and went back to his original person. 5. However, the single "Chapter on the Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) is not [moved].
It would be appropriate to move [this section] to the end of the sutra; following the translation by Kumārajīva will be in deep accord with the intent of the scripture.
△ Sixth, showing that the textual aims differ:
the three sutras overlap, and their textual aims are presented alternately.
Regarding the three scriptures that are repeated, it can be seen that the first and last three translations overlap; their mutual references and differences are as follows.
△ Seventh, demonstrating the excellence of the Qin edition alone.
At that time, those whom people revered and followed all propagated the Qin edition.
As for "those whom people revered and followed," everyone looked up to them; those whom the world revered were in elegant accord with the needs of the times, and all held Kumārajīva in high esteem.
△ Eighth, concluding the brief summary and pointing toward the extensive [text].

As for the remaining verses from other chapters and sections, they are not without their own tradition; as they are fully detailed in the *Xùlì* (Chronicle of the Preface), they are not recounted here.

"The remaining chapters and sections" refers to the various divisions of the text, the categories of which are indeed numerous; it would certainly be difficult to describe them exhaustively, as they are complete within the *Xùlì*.
II. The Main Body (*Zhèngzōngfēn*), Part 14: First, clarifying the appearance [of the Buddha] and his guidance.
Now, as for the phrase "the numinous mountain descending its spirit," were it not for a Great Sage, there would be no means by which transformation could be brought about.
Regarding the terminology, "Numinous Mountain" refers to Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Yet, since the Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, why is it here called the "Numinous Mountain"?
This is because it takes up the present sutra’s revelation of the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world, thereby fully elucidating it.
I do not think so; could it not be that the mountains and peaks concentrate their excellence to give birth to sages and worthies, and that this is merely a conventional way of speaking?
A poem says: "The mountains have sent down their spirit to produce Fu and Shen. This is an analogy for the descent of the divine spirit, which refers to the manifestation of its traces.
To examine the descent of the Tathāgata’s spirit in detail, according to the *Lunheng* (Treatise on Weighing Matters) by Wang Chong of the Han dynasty: [it concerns] the House of Ji...
In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin, on the eighth day of the fourth month, the rivers, streams, springs, and wells overflowed;
mountains, rivers, palaces, and halls shook; the fixed stars disappeared; and five-colored lights pierced through the Taiwei Palace.
When the King questioned his ministers, the Grand Astrologer Suyou reported: "This is because there is a Great Sage in the West."
A thousand years after his birth, the teachings shall flow to this land; by imperial decree, they were engraved upon stone and buried in the southern suburb to record this auspicious response.
The *Sūtra on Auspicious Responses* states: "When the months of Queen Māyā’s pregnancy were nearly complete, she desired to visit the Lumbinī Garden.
Upon arriving, she raised her right hand to grasp a branch of an *aśoka* tree and gave birth from her right side."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wrapped his hands in celestial, exquisite garments and received [the Prince] in them;
a celestial being held a golden-handled parasol over him, while the various devas scattered fragrant flowers and the dragon deities played music.
The great earth in the ten directions trembled, and there were thirty-two auspicious omens, though many of the texts have not been recorded here. Or there were...
The text states that during the era of King Ji of Zhou, the month in which the *jianzi* (the first solar term of the year) occurred was established as the first month;

thus, what was called the "fourth month" corresponds to the second month of the present calendar. However, since the Tathāgata’s manifestation in the world has long since occurred, and because the sages and philosophers of preceding dynasties have all followed this precedent until now, it is difficult to propose a reform.
Furthermore, if one considers that the Supreme Being is fundamentally not subject to birth...
If one were to extinguish [the notion of] his descent, what harm would there be in [accepting] the two or four [aspects]? One should know that the Tathāgata has long been free from birth and death;
he merely manifests these shadow-like events within a heart of great compassion. Why is this? The *Nirākāra-sūtra* states:
"If one says that the Tathāgata was truly born in the royal palace and so forth, up to the accomplishment of the eight signs of enlightenment, then one slanders the Buddha. It is for this reason.
How could such knowledge be made manifest were it not for the Great Sage? This is especially true for those who are like the blind, long asleep, and the ignorant young and childlike;
were it not for the Sage’s compassionate grace, who else would provide guidance? △ Second, pointing to the conditions upon which the transformation is based.
That which is reached through appropriate transformation cannot be guided by the mind without past conditions.
One should know that what is reached through appropriate transformation arises because the teaching relies on conditions due to the resonance of spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

Were it not for these causes from the past and the present, how could the relationship of father and son be established? "Appropriate" (*shi*) means "to please"; it refers to unfolding [the teaching] in accordance with the prevailing emotional dispositions of the capacity.
This is merely an instruction. △ Third, revealing the differences in spiritual capacities.
This is why, when the "Grove of the Immortals" was completed, the distinction between small and great capacities was differentiated.

Regarding the completion of the "Grove of the Immortals": the "Grove of the Immortals" is also called the "Deer Park. As for the "Grove of the Immortals," in ancient times there were immortals (ṛṣis).
Dwelling here in the Deer Park, the Tathāgata was once a king of deer during his causal stage;
one should know that this is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and not the site of the final attainment of enlightenment. Now, "final attainment" refers to the realization of the Way.
Why is this? According to the *Record of the Western Regions*, ten *li* to the southwest of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Magadha, there is a tree named...
Beneath Bodhi is a precious adamantine terrace where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment;

thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that this seat is named as such because it connects downward to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakra*). All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have attained perfect awakening upon this very spot.
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara-sūtra* (or *Pusa benxing ji jing*) states that when the Bodhisattva was about to reach that place, his physical...
The gods of the various realms previously hung celestial silk banners and canopies upon the trees as markers;

now, by illuminating these records, one sees even more clearly the clarity of the fulfillment of the prophecy. As for the distinction between small and great capacities, this difference between small and great has not arisen only recently;
it has existed ever since the Tathāgata descended from the Suyāma Heaven into his mother’s womb.
There are those of great vision who see it as a sandalwood pavilion, while those of lesser insight perceive it as piercing the brilliance of the sun or as a white elephant.
Question: Since you previously stated that the Immortal Garden (Xianyuan) was not the site where [the Buddha] attained realization, how is it now different?
Answer: For instance, the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Way occurred beneath the Bodhi tree; in Sanskrit, *bodhi* means...
The Way should be called the "Way-tree" (bodhi-vṛkṣa), and its fulfillment should be celebrated as auspicious.

If this is so, it not only accords perfectly with the ritual of transformation, but also deeply accords with the profound meaning of the scriptures. One should know that our Buddha, at nineteen, left the city;
after five years of wandering and six years of ascetic practice, he reached the age of thirty. On the eighth day of the second month, when the morning star appeared, he—
He attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree. △ Fourth, it is said that the teachings differ.
At the Golden River, he gave his final charge; the path distinguishes between the stages of the Half-Teaching and the Full-Teaching.
"Golden River" (Jinhé) is in Sanskrit *Hiraṇyavatī*, or it is erroneously abbreviated as *Vatī*; this is translated as:
There is a Golden River (*Suvarṇanadī*), the source of Jāmbūnada gold; in its purity, nothing can compare to it.
Therefore, the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* here. Master Zong of the Liang dynasty said: "That the Tathāgata entered *parinirvāṇa* here was not without its significance.
Furthermore, the rushing flow of the river's current is a metaphor for the swiftness of birth and death, while the immobility of the golden sand serves as a simile for [the state of liberation]."
The permanence of the Buddha-nature is like that of the Tathāgata in his causal stage, who, through these six acts of relinquishment, gave up his wheel-turning king’s body and life;
thus he now comes to this world to repay the debt of gratitude for the land.

As for the "bequeathed charge," it refers to the Tathāgata’s final day and night, when he expounded the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, teaching three provisional means to support one perfect reality, thereby redeeming the life of wisdom of all sentient beings.
This means that the Tathāgata, by means of this teaching, entrusts his disciples with the charge to propagate it so as to benefit future generations and ensure its continuity.
That the paths differ is truly due to the distinction between small and great capacities, which results in the divergence between the Half-Teachings and the Full-Teachings.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The half-syllables are the basis for the discourse of afflictions; they are of provisional meaning."
The "full characters" (*pūrṇākṣara*) are the basis for the verbal expression of wholesome dharmas; they are the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Tiantai says that the "half characters" (*ardhākṣara*) refer to the ninefold canon of the Hīnayāna, while the "full characters" refer to the twelvefold canon of the Mahāyāna. One should know that the essence of the Dharma is eternally one, yet the capacities of sentient beings naturally vary;
thus, beauty and ugliness manifest of their own accord, and the mirror does not determine whether it is beautiful or ugly. △ Fifth, attributing the fault to the capacity of the recipient.
Is it not the case that when the teaching covers those who ride the vehicle (*yāna*), there is no means to fully scrutinize their ultimate convergence?
"Is it not" (*qǐfēi*) is equivalent to saying "is it not so? "The teaching covers" (*jiàobèi*) refers to the Tathāgata expounding the Dharma according to the capacities of beings;

"when the time [of the vehicle] arrives" (*chéngshí*) refers to sentient beings attaining understanding according to their respective types. "No means to" (*wúzú*) means they are not yet capable; "scrutinize" (*hé*) refers to investigating and exhausting the depths of the matter.
"Opening and revealing" refers to the seat of the present sutra. To transcend the eight teachings and go beyond the four periods—how lofty this is!
Furthermore, that the "lofty assembly" has not yet been revealed is because sentient beings' capacities have not yet been sufficient to receive it.

Though the brilliant sun shines upon the heavens, what can it do for the blind? Although the text does not manifest [these truths], their meaning is indeed fully contained within it; thus, one should not cast blame [upon the teaching].
Thus, it is clear that their faith was sincere and not deceptive. △ Sixth, regarding the statement that those who withdrew from their seats should find further benefit:
We know that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats were a group whose pride had increased;
yet, the greater benefit for those who withdrew lay in the assembly at the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, for the Buddha feared they might slander the Dharma and fall into suffering. Therefore—

By the power of the dark [protection], you were driven to avoid falling into the great pit; yet even having heard this brief exposition, you have not realized the One Truth, yet you falsely claim the rank of the Four Fruits.
You boast of your own arrogance, your mind is crooked and insincere, and you dwell therein—this can only lead to harm.
It would be better to retreat than to advance; "advancing" here refers to being spurred on. Since manifest benefit lies in the present, you must increasingly advance in secret.
"Chou" (儔) refers to a group or cohort. △ Seventh, recording the past karmic conditions of the original text:
the traces of five hundred [disciples] receiving predictions and collectively honoring the esoteric transformation.
Regarding the "five hundred predictions": in the past, when the Tathāgata was... [the five hundred śrāvakas obtained their subsequent predictions].
When the Prince delivered his supplementary lectures, he expounded the True Vehicle that unfolds the Buddha’s wisdom, serving as the perfect seed for all disciples.
Although he occasionally set aside the fundamental and employed the minor [teachings] for guidance, today we have been able to hear them;
thus, by drawing from the current, the source remains distant. It may be said that while concealing the lofty foundation, he manifested humble and accessible traces to benefit all beings. △
The eightfold array now serves as the path and support.
Thus, he emits light and manifests auspicious omens to open up the source of the teachings for the request [of the Dharma].
As for the manifestation of these omens, one should know that the light from his brow shines universally upon the Eastern Land and the eight thousand four-petaled lotuses tremble.
As the fragrant wind wafts, the six auspicious omens manifest, startling all sentient beings; Maitreya thereby gives rise to doubts, while Mañjuśrī accordingly provides clarification.
By citing the past Lamp-Light Tathāgata, he validates the present Śākya Tamer;

as that Tathāgata arose from meditative absorption to proclaim the wondrous Dharma, so too does this manifestation of omens inevitably herald the revelation of the Lotus Sūtra. Thus, the request is presented in accordance with its original intent.
Regarding the resolution of doubts through questions and answers, it is precisely here that the manifestation of auspicious omens serves to inspire and prompt the inquiry.
△ Ninth, the description of the Tathāgata’s revelation:
emerging from meditative concentration, he extols his virtues and elucidates the grand outline of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding "Emerging from Samādhi to Proclaim Virtue": The Tathāgata arose serenely from samādhi and extolled the gateway of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—stating that only a Buddha can know it while other vehicles cannot fathom it.

Although Śāriputra was earnest and persistent in his request, the Benevolent One (the Buddha) responded to his plea to proclaim and reveal this profound discourse on the stages of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering. Herein, the teachings for practitioners are suddenly manifested.

The subtle meaning of this principle is now clearly manifested; it is like the bright sun traversing the sky, where there is no hidden place it does not illuminate, or like the *tāpa* flower standing out in its excellence, which all who behold it rejoice in.

This is the reason why the Tathāgatas of the three periods and the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions appear in the world during the five turbidities—it is none other than for this great cause and condition. △ Ten: Citing four metaphors as proof.
The "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) provides the textual framework for universal entry into the Great [Vehicle]; the "City of Illusion" (Gandharvanagara) ensures that past karmic conditions do not fall away;

the "Tied Jewel" clarifies that the rational nature (dharmatā) is eternally present; and the "Well-digging" demonstrates the manifold methods of awakening. The phrasing and meaning are perfectly complete, and these metaphors are presented with profound depth.
The three realms offer no peace, like a burning house; yet because that which is not truly real is taken as real, it is called a dilapidated dwelling.
The parable of the illusory city and the jewel kept within one’s robe illustrates how past seeds persist;

the analogy of digging a well to seek water shows how one attains awakening through the sutras, just as one sees the moon by following the pointing finger. If one shakes the tree to teach about the wind, the underlying intent lies therein.
This is why it is said: the power of the Great Sage’s skillful means, as well as the merit of the latent capacities planted by the various beings in their past lives, are at work here.
Yet that parable of the tied jewel refers to the five hundred śrāvakas of the latter period who received their predictions and attained realization;

it describes how they had previously heard [the teaching] from Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and had expounded it repeatedly, thereby planting the seeds within their nature. Due to delusion, however, they were unaware of it, like a jewel hidden within one's clothing.

"Now, having received your instruction, I have obtained the pearl for trade and attained great wealth. Regarding this parable, if one speaks of it in terms of the categories of nature according to the Tiantai school, it corresponds to the category of "seed" (*gotra*). Question: Since this refers to the category of seeds for cultivated virtue, why does the preface employ the metaphor of "tying the pearl" to represent the rational nature? Answer: This is likely not the case. Why? It should rather be stated as follows: [The text continues: "I was once a poor man who had lost his way... and so forth. This is because the meaning of the parable is that the "poor man" represents sentient beings, while the "pearl" represents the Buddha-nature. The "tying of the pearl" signifies that although the Buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, they do not realize it; thus, it is called "tying. Furthermore, the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) here refers to the nature of the Dharma-body, which is the essence of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is appropriate to use the metaphor of "tying the pearl" to illustrate the rational nature. As for the statement "obtaining the pearl through trade," this refers to the cultivation of practice based on the principle of the nature. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the seed of all Buddhas. This is precisely what is meant by the "category of seed. The *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* also says: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of the three bodies. This is also the meaning of the "category of seed. Therefore, the metaphor of the "tying of the pearl" is used to illustrate both the rational nature and the category of seed. There is no error here. It is simply that the preface, in order to clarify the meaning of the sutra, employs various metaphors such as "tying the pearl" and "obtaining the pearl through trade" to explain the relationship between the rational nature and the category of seed. One should not, however, take these as definitive explanations of the essential meaning of the Tathāgata-garbha. If one were to say that the "tying of the pearl" illustrates the rational nature and the "obtaining of the pearl through trade" illustrates the category of seed, this would be a misinterpretation. Why? Because the "tying of the pearl" already implies the existence of the pearl within the garment; it is not the case that the pearl is first tied and only later found. Therefore, the metaphor of "tying the pearl" primarily illustrates the rational nature, while the subsequent "obtaining of the pearl through trade" illustrates the manifestation of that nature through the cultivation of practice. Thus, the two are mutually inclusive. This is the intended meaning. If one insists that the "tying of the pearl" alone illustrates the rational nature, then one must also admit that the "obtaining of the pearl through trade" illustrates the category of seed. Otherwise, the meaning of the parable would remain incomplete. Therefore, one should understand that the "tying of the pearl" illustrates the rational nature, and the "obtaining of the pearl through trade" illustrates the category of seed. This is the correct interpretation. If one interprets it otherwise, one will fail to grasp the profound intent of the Great Master. This is the conclusion. As for the phrase "fearing it might not be so," this expresses the author's humility in acknowledging the difficulty of the matter and his desire to avoid error. It serves to encourage others to investigate the meaning with care. This is the purpose of the preface. Thus ends the discussion.
The "Tying the Jewel" illustrates that the seeds planted in former lives are ever-present; this is truly the mark of a master.

through the realization of the essence, one attains the thesis; based on the thesis, there is the function; and furthermore, one must distinguish them by means of the teaching-aspect to prevent confusion with the Lesser Vehicle.

Now, the title designates the "Sublime Dharma," which transcends the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching].

This wondrous metaphor of the lotus surpasses all that has been taught in a single lifetime; for the advent of a Tathāgata is the very source through which sentient beings may restore their original nature.

△ Second, the identification of the translator:

A "Dharma Master" is one who transmits, translates, and widely propagates the teachings. Kumārajīva—whose name is translated and explained in detail as in the preceding preface—was the son of Dharmanandin.
His ancestors were from India, and his family had served as prime ministers for generations; he was exceptionally brilliant and stood out from his peers. Kumārajīva’s father...
Named Kumārajīva, he was exceptionally intelligent, brilliant, and outstanding; declining the position of state minister and renouncing worldly glory, he went forth as a monk.
Thereupon, he traveled east across the Pamir Mountains. When the King of Kucha heard of him, he held him in the highest esteem.

The king had a younger sister, twenty years of age, whose literary talent was extraordinary; he consequently gave her in marriage to him. Thereupon, Śrīmitra and Puṣyadeva were born, and Śrīmitra himself—
At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk; by the end of each day, he could recite thirty-two thousand words. At nine, he went with his mother to the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There was a Dharma Master there named Bandhudatta, who had a thorough mastery of the Tripiṭaka and the nine divisions of the scriptures.
From dawn until noon, he would transcribe a thousand verses by hand, and from noon until dusk, he would orally recite a thousand verses. Kumārajīva subsequently followed this master as his teacher.
When he reached the age of twelve, they went together to the Northern Mountains of the Yuezhi. There was an arhat there who, upon seeing him, said:
"You must diligently protect this young śrāmaṇera; his character and demeanor are extraordinary.

This is precisely what is meant. I humbly reflect that whenever our Patriarch Tiantai explained a single passage, he invariably employed the four methods of interpretation:

"I have heard. "I have heard" is Ānanda’s own self-designation; alternatively, it is said that "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) reflects differences in the versions of the sūtra, with either the beginning or the end being cited.

If you wish to hear, you shall hear; when asked, one should simply say "I hear. Why then do you say "I hear"? The answer is:

△ Fourth, the place where [the Dharma] was heard and upheld: The Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

"Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; its Chinese translation is "Awakened One" (*jue*). This means one who has attained ultimate awakening and realization that all phenomena are nothing other than mind itself.
A person who has awakened in this manner is called a Buddha. Furthermore, there are three meanings to "awakening," namely the perfection of oneself and others;
it is for this reason that [the Buddha] differs from those such as non-Buddhists, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas. Tiantai says: "Buddha."
He who is called the Awakened One and the Knower, beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, realized the general and specific characteristics of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
His realization of the mundane world was the suffering and its origin; his realization of the supramundane world was the Path and its cessation. He was also able to awaken others.

Standing six feet tall, with a lifespan of eighty years, appearing as an aged bhikṣu, he attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree through thirty-four moments of mind, having fully mastered both the active defilements and their latent tendencies.
The Buddha of the Tripitaka, who has exhausted both [defilements and karmic traces], awakens himself and awakens others while manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu yet appearing with a sublime body;

the Buddha of the Shared Vehicle, who has severed the remaining residual habits through a single thought-moment of correspondence under a tree, awakens himself and awakens others while manifesting solely in a sublime form seated upon a lotus pedestal to receive the office of a Buddha; and the Buddha of the Distinct Vehicle, who awakens himself and awakens others.
The preceding three marks are concealed; they merely demonstrate the inconceivable mark that is like empty space, which is precisely the Perfect Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "I see the Tathāgata’s body as sixteen feet tall, or see it as a small body or a large body;
or see him seated upon a lotus pedestal, preaching the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for hundreds of thousands of Śākyamunis; or I see..."
That "the body is identical to empty space, pervading the Dharma-realm without distinction" is precisely this meaning. I, being ignorant, reflect upon this:
the Teacher of the present sutra cannot be equated with the Buddhas of the former Tripitaka, Shared, or Distinct Teachings.

Furthermore, since Tiantai has already explained that the Teacher of the present sutra refers exclusively to the final, Perfect Buddha who awakens himself and awakens others, one should discuss him solely in those terms.
If the meaning is already sufficient, why list all four teachings? Might it not be overly prolix to do so regarding the Buddha of the fruit? Answer:

One must understand that because this present sūtra belongs to the stage of "opening and revealing" (kaixian), it is necessary to contrast the past with the present to demonstrate its supreme excellence.

One should know that without the lower there is no way to manifest the high; without the inferior there is no way to distinguish the superior. If one relies on the perspective of the Ultimate Person (zhiren)...
The essence is fundamentally without distinction of superior or inferior; yet, in response to the various capacities of sentient beings, it manifests the forms of the Small and Great Vehicles.

This is like a precious mirror placed upon a stand: the beauty and ugliness [reflected] are revealed of themselves, yet this is not the fault of the mirror. One must know that the Buddha-body is originally one, appearing as two only because it accords with conditions.
Therefore, while the three were separated in the past, they are now unified; one must not abandon the three in order to seek the one.
First, one must know that the one is precisely the three. What were called the "three" in the past are like extending a fist to form fingers;
what is now called the "one" is like closing the fingers to form a fist. Although their essence and function differ, in reality they are one.

One should know that where there is one, there are always three, and where there are three, there is always one. It is neither one nor three, yet it is precisely three and precisely one. This is why it is recorded thus.
It is said that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the three Buddhas were separated from clarity and obstructed by the partial and the small;
therefore, they have come to this sutra to distinguish the superior from the inferior, realizing that the three are one—this is the proof.

One must understand that what Tiantai refers to as "concealing the three previous aspects and manifesting only the inconceivable aspect like empty space" clarifies that the Teacher is already Perfect (Yuan).
The Buddha’s excellence is likened to the perfect fusion and sovereign freedom of space; from the outset, it is without obstruction and pervades all things.
This is because it is designated as "space-like" according to what it represents. One should know that, like space, it encompasses and contains everything without exception;
its myriad characteristics are brilliantly manifest and omnipresent, appearing in response to the capacities of sentient beings. It must not be called a mere void.

However, it is not that there is no Buddha; why is this so? A record states: "If one conceals the previous three marks and speaks according to what is preeminent, this does not mean that the great void is called the Perfect Buddha. This is the clear evidence.

One should know that since this present sutra speaks of the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle, the current Teacher must certainly be the Honored and Most Preeminent Body abiding [in this world].
As for the Buddha dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha: in the Sanskrit language, it is *Rājagṛha*.
*Rāja* means "king" (*rājā*), and *gṛha* means "city" (*nagara*) or "dwelling.

Furthermore, it is said that because the common people of that land had built their dwellings seven times among the five mountains and were burned down seven times, the people deliberated [and named it accordingly].
My merit is meager, and thus my house frequently meets with destruction by fire; yet by the power of the King’s merit, his palace remains unburnt.

From this time forward, let all my dwellings be cleared away to make way for the King’s residence, so that they may be spared from burning. For this reason, it is called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence). The *Xiyu ji* states:
"The city of Rājagṛha is surrounded on all sides by lofty mountains, which serve as its outer wall; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north."
One hundred and fifty *li* [to the north] is the inner city, thirty *li* in extent; the northern gate of the palace is the place where Devadatta released the intoxicated elephant.
To the northeast is the place where Śāriputra met Aśvajit and attained the first fruit of the path.

Further northeast, fourteen or fifteen *li*, one reaches Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata*), the place where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached. The record states that the Tathāgata originally resided in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
The city of the three virtues of samādhi is merely a trace located within the royal city of this Sahā world.
Regarding Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, it is translated here as "Numinous Vulture Peak," also called "Vulture Head" or "Wolf’s Trace. There are three meanings for the term "Numinous Vulture":
first, the shape of the mountain peak resembles that of a vulture; second, to the south of the mountain lies the Śītavana (Cemetery) forest.
Because vultures eat corpses and then perch upon them, people of that time called it Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
Third, Buddhas of the past and Buddhas of the future all dwell on this mountain; after a Buddha has passed away, Arhats reside there; after the Arhats have passed away, Pratyekabuddhas reside there;
and if there are no Pratyekabuddhas, then spirits and deities reside there. Since it is a dwelling place for such holy beings, there are three reasons [for its name].
It is called Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. The *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 31, states: "The Buddha was at Vulture Peak and addressed the bhikṣus:
'This mountain has been known by the same name, Gṛdhrakūṭa, for a long time. Do you know its other names?

It is also called the Mountain of Universal Extensiveness (*Vipula*), the Mountain of Bearing Heavy Burdens, and the Mountain of the Cave of the Rishis. Arhats and Bodhisattvas who have attained the Way always dwell here.'"
Furthermore, this is the dwelling place of various ṛṣis endowed with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), where five hundred pratyekabuddhas also reside.
When the Tathāgata wished to descend, he first commanded the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven to come here and issue a decree to purify this land. Two years later, the Buddha appeared in this region.
Upon hearing this, the pratyekabuddhas entered parinirvāṇa by means of self-immolation. Why is this? Because there are not two Buddhas in the world, nor can they coexist in a single realm.
