"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus.
"Accompanied by" means together with them; they are all of the same class as great bhikṣus, like a multitude where the noble and the humble each have their respective ranks.
Now, these bhikṣus are all well-known to the assembly, being of high renown and great virtue. "Great" refers to the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).

"Great" (mahā) means great in terms of capacity, numerous, and superior. It is called "great" because his vessel-like measure is so venerable that he is revered by great beings such as the heavenly kings.
It is called "superior" because he has transcended the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths.
It is called "numerous" because he possesses comprehensive knowledge of both internal and external scriptures; furthermore, the number [of his followers] reaches twelve thousand.
Therefore, it is said "many" because there are the Great Path, the Great Function, and the Great Knowledge;
it is said "Great Path" because [the Path] is superior, the Function is superior, and the Knowledge is superior; it is said "many" because there are many Paths, many Functions, and many Knowledges.
Furthermore, "Great" means that [the Buddha] is revered by all the great Bodhisattvas; "many" means that he is able to know all the immeasurable phenomena of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Victor" (*jina*) refers to one who has triumphed over all bodhisattvas; this is an explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Regarding "Bhikṣu," Master Zhaō says that in the Qin language it means "pure livelihood. Begging for food, destroying afflictions, purely maintaining the precepts, and terrifying Māra—these are four meanings contained within a single name in India.
Because there was no corresponding term in the Qin language to translate it, the original designation was retained. Master Śīkṣānanda says it begins with...
Having departed from the household of wife and children, one should sustain oneself through alms-seeking and maintain a pure livelihood;
only by ultimately departing from the household of the triple world—necessarily breaking the afflictions (*kleśa*), upholding the precepts, and guarding oneself—does one fulfill these two meanings.

Therefore, the celestial Māras fear that he is leaving their realm. The *Śāstra* states: "Fearing the Māras, destroying evil, and being a seeker of alms (*bhikṣu*). This is truly because Māra delights in birth and death.
Having already left the household life, he further transforms others so that they all depart from the three realms, thereby contravening the will of Māra.
Although Māra uses his power to restrain him, binding him with the five fetters, Māra can do nothing but grieve and loathe him; for this reason, he is called "Terrifier of Māra" (*bhayabherava*).

Furthermore, because those who leave the household life must destroy the evils of the seven branches of body and speech, he is said to "Destroy Evil. As for those remaining in the household life, there are four types who act in accordance with the Dharma: first, the official.

The second [class] are farmers, the third artisans, and the fourth merchants; these sustain their own lives. As for those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit this [mode of livelihood];

rather, they support themselves solely through alms so that their persons may be at peace and the Path may endure, thereby benefiting the donors (dānapati). Because these three principles mutually support one another, it is called the meaning of *bhikṣu*.
Regarding the term "community" (*yìzhòng*): the Sanskrit word is *saṃgha*, which translates as "harmonious assembly. A single person is not called a harmonious assembly.
With four or more persons, it is called a "harmonious assembly" (saṃgha); this means there is no separate group and no discordant dharma, and thus no discordant principle.
△ Next, the number is shown:
together with twelve thousand people.
Regarding the twelve thousand people, they were originally twelve thousand bodhisattvas who manifested as twelve thousand śrāvakas.
The *Jiwen* (Recorded Questions) asks: "Why is it that whenever there is an assembly of followers or those who have attained the Way, their number is invariably complete without any deficiency?

The answer is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which, in its commentary on the section concerning the great number of five thousand, states: "Whether exceeding or falling short [of the standard number], all..."
The preservation of the "great number" means that the present figure of twelve thousand is likewise intended to preserve that great number.
△ Third, the manifestation of their stages: they are all Arhats.

Regarding the term "all are arhats," the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* (A-yin jing) calls them "responding-to-truth" (*yingzhen*), while the *Ruiying jing* (Rui-ying jing) calls them "true persons" (*zhiren*; *satpuruṣa*).
These are all explanations based on the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Alternatively, it is said that there is no direct Sanskrit equivalent for this name, as it contains three meanings:

first, because the husks of ignorance have been shed, one does not receive the retribution of birth and death within the field of future lives; therefore, it is called "non-arising. Second... [text continues].

The exhaustion of the ninety-eight *anuśaya* afflictions is called "slaying the thief. Third, possessing both the virtues of wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), one is worthy of being a field of merit for humans and devas;

this is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*). This is the meaning according to the *Vaipulya* (Shared) and *Āgama* (Distinct) teachings. However, if explained according to the *Bhūmi* (Distinct) and *Vimalakīrti* (Perfect) teachings, the meaning is not so:
it is not merely slaying the thief, but slaying even that which is not a thief; it is not merely non-arising, but non-arising within non-arising.
Furthermore, "not merely being worthy of offerings, but also able to provide offerings" praises the merits of those dwelling on the stages of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

Moreover, for one who practices through contemplative understanding, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional also possesses three meanings, up to the Middle Way contemplation which slays the thief of ignorance and prevents the arising of the mind of the Two Vehicles;
one can make offerings to such a person as if making offerings to the World-Honored One.
The *Vaipulya* [sūtras] state that making offerings to the Buddha and to Mañjuśrī is not as meritorious as practicing the *Vaipulya*; it says that a single meal sufficient for the body is enough.

Furthermore, the text below states that while the offenses and blessings of slandering or praising the Buddha are light, the offenses and blessings of slandering or praising one who upholds this sūtra are grave.

This is truly because the Buddha has no thought of food, having long since departed from the eight winds [of worldly influence], and thus neither gains nor loses anything; yet, to bestow upon those who uphold this sūtra is to give completely.
It is beneficial because it sustains the physical body and prolongs life, thereby increasing the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya*.
If one destroys it, one will experience sorrow, affliction, and regret; thus, contrary to its superior benefits, one will inevitably incur great harm. △ Fourth, praising its virtues.

Tanyun said: "Leakage (āsrava) causes one to fall into birth and death; yet, although the terminology of the Abhidharma and the Vinaya differs, their meaning is the same.

To clarify the meaning of 'leakage' is truly because of the thief of deception who loses the treasure of principle. Becoming impoverished and destitute, one commits various evil karmas, resulting in the suffering of birth and death.

To lose the Dharma-body, to forfeit the life of wisdom, and to lose these precious treasures—all these constitute the meaning of the 'thief. The afflictions (kleśa) are precisely the ninety-eight latent tendencies (anuśaya)."

The outflows (*āsrava*), yokes (*yoga*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) merely oppress and afflict the practitioner; however, these afflictions are that which moisten, while the outflowing karma is that which is moistened.

When both the "moistener" and the "moistened" are exhausted, this is precisely what is meant by "slaying the thief" and "attaining one's own benefit. Thus, it is in praise of the Worthy One (*arhat*):
for all causes and effects within the three realms are termed "the other," while the merit of wisdom and abandonment are termed "one's own benefit. One's own refers to oneself.
"Because he is endowed with benefit, he has become one worthy of offerings who has exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava*)";
this is a praise of non-arising. "Existence" refers to the twenty-five places of birth; "fetters" refers to the twenty-five causes of birth.

Since the cause is exhausted, the fruit perishes—this clearly praises non-arising. "One who has attained mastery over the mind" means that he is endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*); hence the name.

Being endowed with mastery over the mind through wisdom is called "mastery of wisdom. Mastery of wisdom does not necessarily entail mastery of the mind, whereas mastery of the mind necessarily entails mastery of wisdom. △ Fifth, listing the names.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa.

Each presides over a single dharma to guide those with various inclinations. Tiantai said: "If one wishes to eliminate names, one must understand their underlying practice;

when titles are established based on virtue, there is nothing to which they do not apply. Kauṇḍinya is his clan name; this is translated as "Fire-Vessel. He was originally of the Brāhmaṇa caste, and because his ancestors served fire, he was named after that lineage.

Kāśyapa declined, saying, "I have no lodging. The Buddha pointed to the dragon’s hall, saying, "You may stay in this place. Kāśyapa immediately replied, "The nature of dragons is violent and evil; I fear they might harm you, O Benevolent One.
The Buddha said, "Fear not," and immediately gathered his robes, entered, and sat down. When night fell, the dragon returned and saw [him].
The Buddha then became enraged and emitted fire to burn the Buddha; however, the Buddha entered the *ābhāsvara-samādhi*, and the entire realm became brilliantly illuminated.
The dragon fled, having nowhere to hide, until it saw only the pure alms bowl, whereupon it leapt into its midst.

Having realized that all phenomena are entirely without attachment, they are most excellent at skillfully teaching and transforming others;
namely, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Ānanda, and Kapphiṇa.
Śāriputra is fully called Śāriputra; this translates as "Seed-pearl" (Zhūzi) or alternatively "Body-son" (Shenzi).

He walked alone through the royal city, challenging others to debate while beating a drum, yet no one could defeat him. He was the nephew of [the aforementioned] maternal uncle.

This wise man entrusted his eloquence to his mother’s mouth; if such was the case even while still in the womb, how much more so after he had emerged from it?

Once, in the past, during a year of abundant harvests in Rājagṛha, the King, together with his ministers and the common people, established a great assembly and prepared three high seats.

Feeling ashamed that his own arguments were not permitted, he said to his peers: "I am inferior to this child; there is nothing worthy of praise in my victory.

The king, his ministers, and the common people celebrated boundlessly, each saying to one another: "The kingdom..."
The Wise Man of the Great Peace appeared; at the age of sixteen, he had thoroughly mastered the classics and was proficient in every matter.

Having extensively read the past and present, he expounded upon the profound and abstruse. In debate among the sixteen great nations, he was peerless, being the foremost in all of the five regions of India.
Later, on one occasion while walking along a road, he beheld the majestic presence of the bhikṣu Aśvajit.
With dignified decorum, he then questioned him, saying, "Who is your teacher? He replied, "Gautama. He asked again, "What Dharma does your teacher teach?
He answered, "All phenomena arise from conditions; therefore it is said that they have causes and conditions. This is the cessation of phenomena and their conditions—this is how my teacher teaches.
Upon hearing this once, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit [of the path]. He then went to the Buddha’s presence, arriving after seven days.
Within this interval, he thoroughly mastered the Buddha-dharma; regarding a single phrase spoken by the Buddha, Śāriputra produced a lion’s roar for seven days and seven nights.
He was even able to produce further nuances of meaning from that single phrase such that they were inexhaustible—how much more so when the Buddha spoke extensively?
How could the wisdom and eloquence of Śāriputra ever be exhausted? As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana, his clan name is translated as "Praised Recitation," and Mañjuśrī is [the one who]... [text ends].

*Kolita* is simply the name of a tree. Because the parents prayed to the tree deity and obtained a son, they named him after it.

In the past, five hundred followers of a non-Buddhist teacher used incantations to attempt to move a mountain for an entire month;

although the mountain had already begun to shake, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "If this mountain moves, it will cause great harm," and he immediately sat cross-legged in the air above the summit of the mountain, whereupon the mountain ceased its movement.
The non-Buddhists said to one another, "We believed our incantations could move the mountain."

Furthermore, the two nāgas Nanda and Upananda dwell on the edge of the ocean at the side of Mount Sumeru; the Buddha constantly flies through the air to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for their sake.
When his mother preached the Dharma, that dragon became enraged and harbored resentment, thinking to himself: "How can this shaven-headed man pass over me?
Later, when the Buddha wished to ascend to heaven, the dragon spat forth black clouds and dark mists to obscure the three luminaries.
All the bhikṣus desired to subdue him, but the Buddha did not permit it. Maudgalyāyana said, "I am able to subdue him," and the Buddha said to him: "You..."
"How should Maudgalyāyana respond? [The Buddha asked. He replied, "First, I shall terrify him with my massive body; next, I shall bore into and gnaw at him with my small body;

When Maudgalyāyana flew there, Śakra took him to view the hall, but all the celestial maidens were ashamed to be seen by Maudgalyāyana and hid themselves, refusing to come out.
Maudgalyāyana thought that Śakra was attached to pleasure and did not cultivate the root of the Path, so he immediately transformed his supernatural powers and burned down the Vaijayanta Palace.
The hall suddenly collapsed in a blaze; Śakra then preached extensively on impermanence for the Emperor. Śakra rejoiced, and the hall was restored to its former state, free from smoke and ash.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers, able to travel light and swift to the ten directions;
Mahākātyāyana—translated as 'Fan-sheng' (Fanning the Cord)—is also [foremost in eloquence]."
*Koḷa-koḷa* is translated here as "thought-victory" (*sīsa-vāda*). Regarding the term "fanning-rope" (*vījanī-yotta*):

the Venerable One [the Elder] explained that at the time of this child's birth, his father had already passed away; because this boy obstructed his mother from remarrying—just as a fan tied with a rope cannot be separated—he was called "fanning-rope.

As for "thought-victory": "thought" (*sīsa*) refers to the mental factor of wisdom (*paññā*), which is so powerful in its capacity for debate and deliberation that it earns the name "thought-victory. This is from the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
The *Shanhai jing* states that there were non-Buddhists who clung to the view of annihilationism, asserting that there is no future life. There are ten rounds of questions and answers regarding this;
those non-Buddhists say, "There is no future life. The response is: "Are the sun and moon of today celestial beings or humans?
Are they of this world or of another world? If there were no other world, there would be no tomorrow. Furthermore, it asks: "I see people die..."
[The opponent asks: "Since it is said that the Non-returner (anāgāmin) undergoes suffering, we know there is no other world.

[The respondent answers: "Is a criminal who has been detained able to return [to his former life]? [The opponent asks again: "If one is born in heaven, why does one not return? Therefore, we know there is no other world. [The respondent answers:
"Would a person who has fallen into a latrine and escaped ever willingly enter that latrine again? Furthermore, one day in heaven is equivalent to a hundred years here."

[The opponent says: "A person who has died for three or five days has not yet had the leisure to return [to their body]. Even if there were one who did return, since you have already passed away, how could they know it?
Furthermore, when I observe a cauldron boiling a sinner with its lid tightly sealed, I do not see the spirit emerge;
therefore, I know there is no other world. [The Master replies: "When you sleep during the day, people standing by your side see your spirit emerge."
Again he asked me: "I flayed the skin of a dead man, cut his flesh into pieces, and crushed his bones to seek the spirit, yet I could not find it;
therefore, I know there is no other world. I replied: "It is like a child who breaks firewood into inch-long splinters seeking fire;

how could he possibly obtain it? Again he asked me: "When weighing a dead man, he was the heaviest. If that spirit had departed, he should have been light; if the spirit had not departed, then there would be no other world."
The World-Honored One replied: "It is like iron combined with fire; when the iron is separated from the fire, it becomes light, but when it regains the fire, it becomes heavy.

When a person is born, they possess a spirit (*ātman*); while alive, they are light, but upon death, having lost the spirit, they become heavy. He asked again: "I have seen those facing death who turn back to seek their spirits, yet do not find them.
Therefore, I know there is no other world. The World-Honored One replied: "It is like a person turning back to seek the sound of a conch shell; how could one possibly obtain that sound?"
Furthermore, [the opponent] says: "Although you have refuted my attachment to the self (*ātma-grāha*) in various ways, it has persisted for a very long time and cannot be abandoned.

[The Master] answers: "It is like a person gathering *snuhi* seeds: first they see the hemp, take the hemp, and then discard it; next they take the inner bark of the hemp and discard the hemp; next they take the fibers and discard the inner bark;
next they take the cloth and discard the fibers; next they discard the cloth and take the silk; next they discard the silk and take silver; and finally they discard the silver..."
"Taking silver and discarding gold, taking the inferior and discarding the superior"—how is it that you cannot abandon such [views]?

Thus, as he analyzed and deconstructed these points one by one, extensively expounding upon their various meanings, the non-Buddhists were subdued and praised him, saying: "The previous discourse on the sun and moon we have already understood;
now we wish to hear your skillful discernment. Therefore, as he took up each point of difficulty, they exclaimed: "Excellent! This wondrous exposition is inconceivable! (Aṅguttara Nikāya)
It is said that among those who skillfully discern meanings and expound the teachings of the Buddha, Kātyāyana is the foremost.

Aniruddha—also called Anāyuṣ or Āniruddha—all of which are transcriptions of the Sanskrit sound with varying nuances—is translated here as "Free from Poverty," "As One Wishes," or "Without Hunt. Regarding the name "Free from Poverty": in the past, during a time of famine...
Because he offered wild rice gruel to a Pratyekabuddha, he obtained the retribution of sufficiency for ninety-one kalpas; therefore, he was named Abhijāta (The One Free from Poverty).
The *Xianyu jing* (Sutra on the Wise and the Foolish) states: During the period of the final dharma of Buddha Puṣya, there was a famine in the world.
A Pratyekabuddha named Liṭa went begging but returned with an empty bowl, having obtained nothing. A poor man saw him and, moved by compassion, addressed him, saying: "O Noble One..."
He was able to accept the millet and immediately offered what he had eaten to him. After the meal, [the Buddha] performed eighteen miraculous transformations.

Later, as he went to gather more millet, a rabbit leaped up and embraced his back; it then transformed into a dead man. Having no companion, [the Buddha] waited for darkness to return home and cast it to the ground, where it immediately became a golden man.
When he pulled out its fingers, they grew back accordingly; when he used his feet to step on it, it emerged again, inexhaustible. [The Buddha] felt aversion toward it.
When people detested the king and came to seize it, they saw only a corpse; yet what they beheld was entirely gold and jewels.
Because the retribution for ninety-one kalpas had been fully exhausted, he was named "The Indigent-Free" (Aparājita).

As for his being called "Wish-Fulfilling" (Cintāmaṇi), from the time of his birth, his family wealth was overflowing and increased day and night, and beneath his gate there were always ten thousand people daily.
Two thousand people took six thousand in debt and returned six thousand in payment;
after he had gone forth, wherever he went, people saw him with joy, and whatever they required was no different than if it were their own home.
It should be known that Aniruddha was the nephew of King Śuddhodana, the second son of King Droṇodana, and the cousin of the World-Honored One.
Nan’s elder brother, Luo Yun’s uncle, was no ordinary man; he was truly like the Duke of Zhou, who sighed, saying:
"I am the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the uncle of King Cheng.

In the world, I am no lowly person, yet I have been summoned three times and dismissed three times. If even one who honors the worthy is treated thus, how much more so should others be? This increases [the value of such conduct].
One account states: "In my Buddha-dharma, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost among those with the divine eye that penetrates all sights;

Kapphiṇa [is foremost] among those who dwell in their own abodes. *Kapphiṇa* is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (*Fángxiù*). His parents prayed to the lunar mansion (the Pleiades), and because they were blessed with a son through this, he was named accordingly.

Furthermore, it is said that the lunar mansion refers to this bhikṣu, who shared a room with the Buddha; because he obtained an audience with the Dharma-body while dwelling in that same room, he received his name from this.
The *Āgama* (42) states: The Buddha was traveling through Magadha and arrived at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the house of a potter and said to him, "I wish to stay overnight;
will you grant me your permission? The potter replied, "I have no objection; however, there is already a bhikṣu who has been here first. If he permits it, you may stay."
At that opportune time, the bhikṣu Vakkula was already inside the potter’s house.
The Blessed One said to him, “I wish to stay overnight; will you grant me permission? The bhikṣu replied, “You may do as you please;
how would I dare to oppose you? Since the grass mat has already been spread in this potter’s house, you may stay there as you wish.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spread his *niṣīdana* upon the grass seat and sat cross-legged;

throughout the night he remained in profound stillness, and the bhikṣu did likewise. Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought silently to himself, "This bhikṣu is truly extraordinary," and asked him, "Who is your teacher? He replied, "Gautama, the Unsurpassed Awakened One."
"This is my teacher," [he said]. He asked him again, "Have you ever seen your teacher? He replied, "I have not.
He asked once more, "If you had seen your teacher, would you have recognized him? He replied, "Even if I had seen him, I would not have recognized him;
I merely heard that he was endowed with the ten epithets, and so I went forth under him. The World-Honored One said, "I shall now briefly explain the Dharma for you."
"Listen attentively," [the Buddha] said. The bhikṣu replied, "I wish to hear it with joy. The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"A person consists of an aggregate of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four abodes.

As for the aggregate of six elements, it refers to earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. Because of these six, there are the six bases of contact; that is to say, visual contact perceives forms."
Up to the mind-contact that cognizes mental phenomena—because of these six, there are eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*):

namely, seeing a form with the eye, one dwells contemplating it with joy; one dwells contemplating it with grief; one dwells contemplating it with equanimity. This applies likewise to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Because of this, there are four stations (*vihāra*), namely: the station of the Noble Truths and the station of wisdom.
Regarding the dwelling-place of giving and the dwelling-place of resting, it is for this reason that non-negligence and wisdom are taught.

If a bhikṣu analyzes the element of the body, he reflects: "In this body of mine there is the internal earth element, which undergoes birth—namely, hair, body hair, nails, teeth—and likewise the external earth element;
none of these are mine, nor do I belong to them, nor are they the self."
In this way, observing with wisdom is called the heedfulness-wisdom of a bhikṣu.

Thus, one proceeds through earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, examining each internally and externally. Having explained this Dharma, the bhikṣu becomes free from dust and defilement, immediately attaining the noble fruit.
Tiantai says: "This bhikṣu is skilled in divining the stars and planets and clearly understands diagrams."
Regarding those who are designated by their specific attainments, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, Kapphiṇa is foremost among those who well know the stars and constellations;
Gavāmpati, Revata, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, Bakkula, and Mahākoṣṭhila [are foremost among those possessing various other qualities]."
Nanda, Gavāmpati—here translated as "the Cow-Chewer"—is called "King of Cows" in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and "Cow’s Footprint" in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
In five hundred past lives, he was constantly the king of oxen; because oxen always emit a hollow belch after eating, this was his residual karmic retribution.
When he was constantly chewing with his mouth open as if never finished eating, people called him "the ox-chewer" (*gomayūka*).

In a past life, he had been a bhikṣu who, while plucking a stalk of grain, caused several grains to fall to the ground; consequently, for five hundred subsequent lifetimes, he was born as an ox to repay that debt.

Although he has now realized the state of an Arhat, he still retains this residual habit. Tiantai said: "People merely observe his outward form and fail to recognize his virtue; they would laugh at the Arhat."
This constitutes an offense; however, because he avoids the laughter of others, he constantly dwells in the heavens. The devas know that he possesses virtue, which is why they do not laugh.

It is also said that when the Buddha was formerly in the world, he once spent a summer retreat at the invitation of King Ajātaśatru, where he and five hundred bhikṣus all ate horse fodder, while Gavāmpati alone remained in the heavens in the Śirīṣa Garden.
Receiving the offerings of the Heavenly King is due to the merit of five hundred geese from the past;
among them, one goose constantly offered flowers and fruit to the Goose King, and it is by the power of that merit that he now enjoys celestial bliss. Regarding the increase of one [verse]:

"One who delights in dwelling in the heavens and does not delight in the human realm" refers to the Bhikṣu Goṭīrṇa (also called Līpida). He was foremost in [the practice of] *viveka* (seclusion). Līpida is also translated as Li.
Beyond this, some translate it as the *Nakṣatra* (Constellation) or the *Kṛttikā* (Pleiades). In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is called "Constantly Making Sound.
His parents sought a son from the celestial bodies; having obtained him through such a response, they named him after the star.

Although he left the household life, he still retained his original name. Regarding the term "provisional combination" (*prajñapti-saṃghāta*), some cite the *Śāstra* (Treatise), which states that he stayed overnight in an empty pavilion.
This is based on the account of two ghosts contending over a corpse. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states:

"If a person travels far and stays alone in an empty pavilion, and during the night a ghost carries a dead corpse and places it before him, another ghost comes from behind and angrily reviles the first ghost, saying: 'This is my corpse; why have you carried it here?'"
The first ghost spoke again, saying, "This was originally my property. The two ghosts each contended for it, and the first ghost said, "We may ask this man.
The second ghost then asked him, "Whose corpse is this? Who brought it here?
The man reflected, "These two ghosts both possess great power; whether my words are true or false, neither will spare me from harm. I must answer truthfully."
Upon hearing this, the former ghost replied, "I brought it here. The latter ghost became greatly enraged and tore away its hands and feet, casting them onto the ground.
The former ghost was ashamed and took the corpse to replace them;
he then attached the arms and feet, and as the entire body was thus exchanged, both ghosts together ate the limbs of the living man they had replaced, each wiping their mouth as they finished.
They parted ways and departed. The man reflected: "My parents gave birth to this body, yet my eyes have seen it consumed entirely.
Now this body of mine is entirely the flesh of others; does it exist, or does it not? When dawn broke, he sought his path and encountered a community of monks.
He immediately asked them, "Does this body of mine now exist, or does it not? The assembly [of monks] said: [It does not.]
The monk replied, "Your body has been fundamentally non-existent from the beginning; it is merely formed through the combination of the four great elements.
Because of this, he awakened to the Way and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was an Arhat named Revata who sat in meditation in the mountains. A certain person lost his ox and, following its tracks, arrived at that place."
At that time, while Li Yue was boiling grass to dye it, the grass suddenly transformed into beef.
The vessel he held turned into a cow’s head. When the owner of the cattle saw this, he seized him and brought him before the king.

The king cast him into prison, where he remained for twelve years constantly serving as a jailer, drinking the horses’ water and clearing away their dung. However, those who were disciples of Li Yue and had attained Arhatship...
Seeking his teacher, he could not find him, as his karmic conditions were about to end; subsequently, he saw him in a prison in Kaśmīra.

He went immediately to the king’s presence and related the aforementioned matter in detail. The king then issued a decree to pardon him and release him from prison. As soon as he leaped into the air, he performed the eighteen transformations.
When the king saw this, he sought his mercy and repented his transgressions. The king asked again: "By what causes and conditions did this occur?"
When this matter was reported, Li Yue replied: "In the past, I also once lost my oxen. Following their tracks to the mountains, I saw a Pratyekabuddha sitting alone in meditation;
I immediately slandered him, and for one day and one night because of these causes and conditions, I fell into the three miserable realms.
Although the remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, I have now become an Arhat, yet I am still subjected to slander. (From the *Ekottarika Āgama*)
It is said that while sitting in meditation and entering *samādhi*, his mind was not distracted or confused, yet he transgressed the first precept.
Piṅgala-bāśpa (畢陵迦婆蹉) means "residual habit" (*vāsanā*). In the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he had been a Brahmin, and his habitual tendencies remained lofty.
Once, when the Buddha was formerly his servant, they encountered the Ganges River; because the current was swift and difficult to cross, he exclaimed, "You little slave! Stop the flow!"
The goddess Gaṅgā divided her stream into two branches and went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha instructed her to offer an apology; she then joined her palms, saying, "Little maid, do not be angry.

The great assembly laughed at her. Having apologized, she continued to scold him. The Buddha said, "This is merely my habitual practice; truly, I have no prideful heart. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"He sat in painful meditation under trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain. Vatsa was foremost [in patience], and Bakula was foremost [in long life]."
"Luó" (羅) is translated here as "excellent countenance" (*śubha-vaktra*) or "noble form," because his physical appearance was upright and handsome; thus he is called "Excellent Countenance.
He lived for one hundred and sixty years, free from illness and untimely death, possessing the five rewards of non-death. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the son of an elder who gave birth to a son. At that time, due to a great assembly, [the father] went to the Great..."
The mother by the river was not steadfast and lost her son as he fell into the water; yet because the child possessed merit, he did not die.
At that time, there was a fish in the water that swallowed the boy; though he was inside the fish's belly, he still did not die.
Later, a man caught this fish and, cutting open its belly, saw the boy therein. He rejoiced immeasurably. At that time, the two fathers...
When the mother heard of this matter, she went to demand the child back; as the dispute continued without end, they went before the king and presented their case in full.
The king told them, "The two elder brothers should not be partial in their recognition of this child.

At that time, each of the two elder brothers took a wife for him and provided him with fields and a home. Later, the boy grew weary of worldly life and requested to leave the household to become a renunciant.
The Buddha called out, "Welcome," and he immediately became an Arhat. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What is the cause and condition for this?

The Buddha said, "In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was an elder who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, received the Three Refuges and observed the precept against killing.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he now receives this retribution. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya Piṭaka* (or *Dharmakośa Sūtra*) states regarding Bakula: [text continues].
When he was young, seeing his stepmother making cakes, he asked his mother for some. His mother, out of resentment, seized him and threw him onto a griddle;
though the griddle was glowing hot, it could not burn or harm him. She then threw him into a cauldron, yet again he was not harmed.
She finally cast him into the water, where he was swallowed by a fish, but still did not die. Later, when people were fishing and cutting open the fish with knives, [he emerged unharmed].
Furthermore, because his belly was not injured, Bakkula [possessed this quality]. The *Pinimu jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of the Five Kinds of Immortality) states:

"In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was an elder of a naturally kind and humble disposition who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for ninety days of offerings during the four seasons.
A certain bhikṣu came to him seeking medicine, and the elder asked him:"

"What is your ailment? he asked. He replied, "I have a headache. The elder reflected, "This must be water accumulated above the diaphragm attacking his head from below," and immediately had him take a *harītakī* fruit. The illness was instantly cured.
At that time, the elder was none other than the present Bakkula; according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, his lifespan was exceedingly long, and he never met with an untimely death.
Bakkula was foremost among those who delighted in living in seclusion and avoided the company of crowds. Mahākoṭṭhila—translated as "Great Knee"—was skilled in debate;
he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. Whenever they debated, the uncle would always prevail over his sister.
However, once she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her in discussion. He realized that the one she carried must surely be a wise man who had lent his eloquence to his mother.

"If even while still in the womb his mouth was already like this, how much more so once he has left it? Thereupon, he abandoned his home and studies to travel to South India to read the eighteen scriptures.
People of the time ridiculed him, saying, "It will be difficult to master them in many lifetimes; one lifetime is not enough to hope for such a feat.
He, however, sighed deeply and said, "At home I was surpassed by my sister; on the road I am slighted by others. I swear that I shall not stop until I have finished reading them."
Because he had no time to clip his nails, people called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail). Having completed his studies, he returned home and asked his nephew where he was.

People told him that the boy had become a disciple of the Buddha. At this, he became greatly arrogant and thought, "My nephew has been a prodigy since the age of eight, his fame shaking the Five Indies;
what kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to have seduced my sister’s son? He then went straight to where the Buddha was staying to deliberate upon the matter.
Having long been unable to find a single dharma that entered his mind, he spoke to the Buddha, saying: "I do not endure any dharma; 'endurance' (kṣānti) means the sense of being at peace.
This means that regarding all dharmas, I am able to destroy them so that they cannot attain peace; therefore, I say I do not endure any dharma.
The Buddha asked: "Do you perceive this endurance? This would result in a double defeat: if I were to perceive endurance...

Previously, he could not endure anything; because he could not endure the view of a self, he was unable to surpass the Buddha. He immediately lowered his head and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Among those who are able to answer difficult questions, Kaccāyana is foremost. Nanda—this refers to the cowherd Nanda—is translated as "Good Joy" or "Delight."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*), he instructed his cowherds to stay nearby so that they might deliver milk and curd daily until the end of the three months. The king was deeply moved by this and ordered him to have an audience with the Buddha.
He consulted with his peers, saying, "I have heard that the All-Knowing One is indeed pure."
The Prince of Food was born in the royal palace; did he know anything of tending cattle? He then entered the bamboo grove and sat upright to question the Buddha.
The Buddha explained eleven matters for him, whereby he resolved his mind on leaving the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

Because he was named after his original occupation, he is called "Tending Cattle. Regarding "Good Joy" (*Sukha-nandi*), the record states that he was named after his initial aspiration for the Way, meaning "rejoicing."
"Joy" (*prīti*) is another name for wholesome gladness (*saumanasya*).
[The disciples are] Sundarananda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Ānanda,
and Rāhula.
Sundarananda: *Sundara* means "lovely" or "handsome"; *Nanda* refers to his clan, as explained in the section on Aniruddha.
He was named after his wife. He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha (one finger-width being four *cun*).
His appearance was exceptionally distinguished and far surpassed that of ordinary people; even when he entered a crowd, there were those who did not recognize him.
This refers to saying that the Buddha has come. Why? Because Nanda was the Buddha’s own younger brother.
One should know that the ancestral lineage of the Tathāgata traces back to King Siṃhahanu (Lion Cheek). That king had four sons: first, King Śuddhodana;
second, King Śuklodana; third, King Droṇodana; and fourth, King Amṛtodana. Of these, King Śuddhodana initially had two sons: first, Siddhārtha; and second, Nanda.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra had two sons: first, Devadatta, and second, Ānanda. Triśaṅku had two sons:
first, Mahānāman, and second, Aniruddha. Amṛtodana had two sons: first, Śānta, and second, Bhadrika.

The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha) states that Devadatta was born on the seventh day of the fourth month, while the Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month.
Nanda was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; Ānanda was born on the tenth day of the fourth month.

His wife, Sundarī, was of such exquisite beauty that they were never apart even for a meal or a breath. Once, as the Buddha and Ānanda were walking along the road begging for alms, they arrived at his door.
At that moment, Nanda had risen to welcome the Buddha, while his wife remained atop a high tower eating and drinking with him.
Nanda said to the Buddha, "I must wait until you have returned before we may eat together. Nanda asked, "How can one born of the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King humiliate himself thus?
He immediately took the Buddha’s bowl and fetched the food. The Buddha then returned to the Nyagrodha Grove and said to Ānanda, "Have Nanda deliver this food.
When Ānanda conveyed this command, Nanda brought it at once. The Buddha then ordered him to shave his head; Nanda then clenched his fist.
He said to the barber, "Do not bring your razor near the crown of King Jambū’s head; even if the Buddha urges you, do not stop him, but shave him completely.
The next day, the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus arrived at the request to stay and maintain the monastery. Intending to flee, the king ordered his chambers locked and the floor swept.
He closed the doors to the north and south and opened them to sweep this side and that, yet he was defiled by filth and feared the Buddha’s return.
He immediately fled back home, but on the road he encountered the Buddha. He hid his body behind a tree, but the tree rose high into the air.

Seeing this, the Buddha called out to him and brought him back, asking, "For what reason did you leave? He replied, "Yesterday I parted from my wife; I was waiting for her return before eating, and so I left because I missed her.
The Buddha had him grasp the corner of his robe and led him to travel to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, reaching the Garden of Joy.
As he looked among the various court ladies, there was one place where he saw only celestial maidens (*devakanyā*) without their husbands.

He then questioned the Buddha, who instructed him to ask the celestial maiden herself. She replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda, having strictly maintained the prohibitive precepts, shall be born in this heaven as my husband.
The Buddha then asked Nanda, "Compared to the celestial maiden here, how does Sundarī compare?"
If asked which was superior or inferior, he replied: "If one were to compare them with a celestial maiden, this Sundarī would be like a blind monkey.
The Buddha then returned with him to the Jeta Grove. Nanda, longing for rebirth in heaven, redoubled his diligent efforts and constantly practiced virtuous deeds.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "O Bhikṣus, you must not associate with that Nanda."
They lived together, even in matters such as sitting, rising, and conversation. He thought to himself, "Ānanda is my younger brother;
he will surely not disdain me," and so he went to sit with him. Ānanda immediately rose and asked him, "Younger brother, why do you abandon your elder brother?
Ānanda replied, "Venerable sir, your conduct is different, which is why we have parted ways. Why is this? You delight in being born in the heavens."
I wish for parinirvāṇa. Having heard this, Nanda felt distress in his heart. The Buddha asked again, “Do you see the hells?
He replied, “I have not yet seen them. The Buddha then had him grasp the corner of His robe and led him to tour the hells.
They saw that in all the various hells there were wardens, but one particular hell was empty. Nanda then questioned the Buddha, who instructed him to ask the hell-warden himself.
He replied: "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda practiced for the sake of being born in heaven;
though he was born there for a time, he will inevitably fall back into this world and undergo various sufferings. Nanda was filled with anxiety and fear, his tears flowing freely.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereby he attained awakening and realized the fruit of sainthood. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra—Pūrṇa.
*Pūrṇamitrā* is translated as "Fulfilling the Vow. *Maitrānī* means "Compassionate One" (*maitrī*) and refers to a woman; her father prayed to Brahmā at the Pūrṇa River for a son.
It happened that the river was full at that time, and he further dreamed that a vessel made of the seven treasures, filled with jewels, entered his wife's womb.
Because the father’s vow was fulfilled once she had conceived the child, she received this name. *Maitrānī* is translated here as "Compassion."
Regarding his conduct, it is also said that among the four Vedas of the non-Buddhist scriptures there is this one chapter; because his mother recited it, he was named after it.
"Ni" (尼) is a general term for an ordained woman, while "Na" (那) is a general name for men in Western India (Sindh).
Since he was born from Maitrāyaṇī, he is called the Son of Maitrāyaṇī. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "My father’s name is Pūraṇa, and my mother’s name is..."

The compassionate fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; they also say that I am foremost among those who are well able to extensively explain and analyze the principles and meanings, and that I am the most excellent of those who fulfill vows.

At a later time, when I wished to return to my native land to benefit sentient beings, the Buddha said, "That country is corrupt and evil; how will you transform them? I replied, "I shall practice patience. If...
"If I am insulted, I shall consider myself fortunate that I am not struck with fists; if I am struck with fists, I shall consider myself fortunate that I am not struck with wooden staves;
if I am struck with wooden staves, I shall consider myself fortunate that I am not struck with blades;

if I am struck with blades, I shall consider myself fortunate to have escaped the poisonous vessel of the five aggregates. The Buddha said, "Excellent! You may now go and convert them. As stated in the *Saptasārathi-sūtra*: "For the sake of..."
The fellow practitioners of the holy life whom the Great Wise Śāriputra has praised shall all wrap their robes around their heads and honor you;
whoever beholds you will obtain great benefit. Subhūti—here translated as "Empty Birth"—was so named because at the time of his birth, the storehouses and utensils in his home were all empty;
the diviners declared this auspicious, and thus he was named for being born from emptiness.
He is called Śūnyatā-ja (Born of Emptiness) because he was born from the auspicious signs of the environment; since both his primary and secondary retributions are auspicious, he is named Śūnyatā-ja.
He constantly delights in dwelling in secluded forests, stone caves, and places of stillness, making emptiness the foundation of his practiced path.
He frequently enters the samādhi of emptiness, abides in the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention), and joyfully proclaims the Dharma of emptiness whenever he has something to declare.

His discernment is entirely the differentiation of emptiness; he protects sentient beings so as not to allow them to give rise to obstacles, aversion, or attachment. When they dwell in aversion, he practices; when he dwells in practice, he remains.
Furthermore, it is said that because he constantly practices the conduct of emptiness, he is called "Virtuous" (Śubha). Because making offerings yields a reward, he is called "Auspicious" (Kalyāṇa).
That which is referred to as "Virtuous and Auspicious" (Śubhakalyāṇa) in various texts is precisely this meaning. Ānanda is here translated as "Joyful."
It is also said that in the past, King Śuddhodana hoped his crown prince would become a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin) to rule over his realm;
however, the prince suddenly abandoned his kingdom and renounced his glory, leaving the king in a state of near-despair. Mara came to deceive him, saying, "Your son is already dead.

The king remarked, "The words of Asita were already false, and these auspicious signs have likewise proven unverified. Furthermore, another deity came to inform him, saying, "Your son has attained Buddhahood."

The King’s doubts remained unresolved for a moment when a messenger arrived with news that the night before, heaven and earth had shaken violently; the King rejoiced greatly at the news that the Prince had attained Buddhahood.
King Śuklodana further reported the birth of the Prince, and the entire kingdom was filled with joy. Consequently, an auspicious name was established.
The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle seven, states that Ānanda served the Buddha for twenty-five years and heard eighty thousand [teachings].
The *Khandakas* (translated here as "Dharma-aggregates") were all recited without omission, nor was there any need for further questioning.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, while on the lion throne, Kāśyapa and the great assembly praised him, saying: "His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses.
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flows into Ānanda’s heart. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "He knows the proper time and clearly understands the nature of things."

Ānanda has reached the stage of being free from doubt; he remembers everything without forgetting, his learning is vast and far-reaching, and he is capable of upholding the teachings—thus he is foremost among the disciples.
Rāhula, which is translated here as "The Obstructor," was the Buddha’s legitimate son. Formerly, when the Prince sought to leave the household life, his father the King would not permit it.
Because the Prince was persistent and did not cease his entreaties, the King said: "If you have a son, I shall allow you to leave the household life. The Prince [then agreed].

He raised his hand and pointed to his consort’s belly, saying, "Six years from now you shall give birth to a son. Because he had been in the womb for six years, it was said that he "obscured the True Truth" (*tattva*).
The Tripitaka Master [Amoghavajra] stated that Rāhu’s original name was Asura, who was capable of obstructing the sun and moon;
however, it should specifically be said that he obstructed the moon. The Buddha said, "My Dharma is like the moon; this child obstructs me, so I shall not leave the household life immediately."
Because he was able to renounce the world, the self, and the worldly life that obstructed him, it is said that he had already concealed his intent to leave the household life.
While Yaśodharā was pregnant, all the Śākyas were enraged; for what reason did this happen? They wished to punish and kill her, and evil rumors filled the roads.
The noble woman Gopī testified on her behalf, and the slander subsided slightly. Then, before the fire-pit of Brahmā, she made a great vow: "If I..."
"If it is not so, that both mother and child perish together, and if Heaven shall bear witness to this true body, then I will take my son and cast him into a pit.
She then took her son and threw him into a pit, which transformed into a pond where lotus flowers supported his body. Only then did the King and the people cease their doubts.

Later, when the Buddha returned to the kingdom, Yaśodharā was commanded to offer him joy; though she was but nine years old and still very young, she directly held up [the bowl] amidst the great assembly.
The Buddha Yaśodharā thereby silenced the slander; thus, although King Śuddhodana was grieved at having lost his son, he rejoiced at having gained his grandson.
"Though I have lost my son, I have gained his descendant as a Golden-Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*); what cause for regret could there be?

I only hoped that as he grew up, the divine treasures would arrive, yet the Buddha sought to renounce the world and the Father-King did not permit it. Later, when Yaśodharā was ascending a high tower, Maudgalyāyana flew through the air [to meet her].
He came from emptiness to take him; the Buddha ordained him as a renunciant and gave him as a disciple to Śāriputra. △ Sixth, the summary:
Such great arhats, well-known to all, and so forth.

Among those who know [the Master], some say that "knowing" (zhi) is simply consciousness (shi), while others say that hearing the name is "knowledge" (zhi) and seeing the form is "consciousness" (shi);
they may also say that seeing the form is "knowledge" (zhi) and perceiving the mind is "consciousness" (shi). Dharma Master Zhao said:

"When a Great Being dwells in the world, it is like the sun and moon rising in the sky; among those with eyes, who would not know and recognize him? Now, this refers to understanding the Buddha’s correct view.
It is said that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to knowing how to stop on the wrong paths; this is what is meant by "discernment. △ Second, listing those of limited knowledge:
there were further two thousand persons, both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The term "those of limited knowledge" merely cites their status to clarify the number and does not praise their virtues; they are called "limited" only in this sense.

Moreover, the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person is absolute and cannot be divided by degree; yet, for those who aspire to the lofty and admire the distant, one leads them by means of extensive knowledge.
For those who conceal their virtue and hide their names, one guides them even with limited knowledge. Because this follows the capacities of sentient beings, there appear to be degrees of depth;
however, one must not perceive these traces and thereby forget the fundamental source. This is as in the eighteen [divisions] within the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding the nine grades of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the nine grades of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), all five stages are called "in training," while the sixth stage is called "beyond training.
Furthermore, according to the [Shared Teaching], all nine stages are called "in training," and the Buddha-stage is "beyond training.

Alternatively, the distinction between the Separate and Perfect Teachings (*pratyeka-pūrṇa-yāna*) clarifies "in training" and "beyond training" based on whether they possess effort (*sābhoga*) or lack effort (*anābhoga*), and whether the qualities are complete or incomplete. The present text contains both of these meanings. Now...
This is explained in one section. △ Second, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, consisting of two parts:
first Mahāprajāpatī, then Yaśodharā (Rāhula’s mother).
Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī was accompanied by her retinue of six thousand, including Rāhula’s mother.
The bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā was also there together with her retinue.
Pajāpatī—this is translated as "Mahāmāyā" (Great Love-Path)—is also called Gautamī, which is translated as "Sattvā" (Sentient Being).

"Ni" is the general designation for women who have left the household life in the Western lands; this is because she fundamentally dwells in the dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom).

In her manifested form (*vyañjana*), she is the mother of the thousand Buddhas who nurtures and protects the Teacher. Mahāprajāpatī is so named because her Middle Way (*madhyama-pratipad*) is vast and extensive;

she is called "Great" (*mahā*) because of the power of her unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*). She is called "Way" (*pratipad*) because the principle of her love is empty and all-pervading.

The number "six thousand" refers to the gate of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*): when one contemplates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), each is endowed with a thousand merits, even in the case of the eye.

There were eight hundred ears and one thousand two hundred eyes; with the many supplementing the few, they total six thousand, representing the meaning of this fundamental Dharma-gate and the intent of contemplative practice. Yaśodharā means "Flower-Colored" or "Renowned";
she is called the mother of Rāhula because the son is used to designate the mother. Nevertheless, she was endowed with the virtues of gentleness, kindness, propriety, and frugality.
When the Crown Prince was at home, he served as a spiritual friend to the wives of bodhisattvas and to devas and humans;
when he left the household life, he became the leader of the community of nuns and attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). How could he not have been renowned among the masses?
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* mentions three consorts: first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā. Furthermore, there are accounts of unprecedented wonders.
The *Śrīvyūha-sūtra* (瑞應) states in all cases that Rāhula was the son of Gopī; however, both the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* state that he was the son of Yaśodharā.
What do you think? Perhaps those other sūtras mention the mother (*mātṛ*), while this one mentions the one who gave birth (*janitrī*).
The *Śāstra* clarifies that Gopīdhā was a "precious woman" (*ratnastri*) who was barren; she is indeed Gopī, which translates as "Bright Woman" (*Vimalā*).
Therefore, we know she is certainly the daughter of Yaśodharā. The *Beihua jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) states that she made a vow to become the wife of the Buddha Ratnapuṣpa;

how could one from the common world be the wife of a Prince? Thus, we know she fundamentally dwells in the subtle joy of the Dharma within meditative concentration, appearing in the traces of being a Buddha’s wife.
△ Second, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, in six parts: first, clarifying their types.
Regarding "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva":
if one were to retain it in its entirety, it should be called *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*. Master Shi [Xuanzang] disliked its prolixity and thus omitted the two characters *ti* and *tuo*.
*Bodhi* is translated as "Enlightenment" (*dao*), *sattva* as "Sentient Being" (*xin*), and *mahā* as "Great. This...
All these people seek the vast and great Way and are also able to bring sentient beings to maturity;
they are thus of the same kind as those who possess the spirit of the Great Bodhicitta. △ Second, showing their number.
"Eighty thousand people.
This "eighty thousand" is a numerical figure; however, since the assemblies in other sūtras are far more numerous, why are those in this sūtra so few?

It may be that this refers only to a general estimate, or it may be like a king discussing secret matters—how could he involve the entire realm in the conspiracy? If one were to... [the text ends here].

Regarding the "Explanation by Contemplating the Mind": one contemplates that a single wholesome mind possesses the ten dharma-realms; as these ten realms intersect with one another, they possess one hundred dharma-realms and a thousand natures and characteristics.
Thus, the ten wholesome acts comprise ten thousand dharmas, and in terms of the Eightfold Noble Path, they comprise eighty thousand dharma-gates.
△ Third, the Manifestation of the Stages.

All have become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. *Anuttara* is translated here as "unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*); *samyak* as "right" (*zheng*); and *saṃ* as "equal" (*deng*). *Bodhi* is translated as "awakening" (*jue*). Regarding "non-retrogression," it is discussed in terms of their stage, practice, and mindfulness. To explain this in detail: [The term] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* refers to the supreme, perfect, and complete awakening. "Non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) signifies that one will not fall back from that state. This is analyzed according to three aspects: first, non-retrogression in terms of the stage (*bhūmi*); second, non-retrogression in terms of practice (*caryā*); and third, non-retrogression in terms of mindfulness (*smṛti*). To elaborate: 1.

**Non-retrogression in terms of stage** refers to the point at which a bodhisattva has entered the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), such as the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) or higher, where they are no longer subject to falling back due to the power of their realization. 2. **Non-retrogression in terms of practice** refers to the firmness of one's cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and other bodhisattva deeds, ensuring that one does not regress despite obstacles or adverse conditions. 3. **Non-retrogression in terms of mindfulness** refers to the constant maintenance of right mindfulness and wisdom, whereby one remains undeluded and does not lose the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*). Thus, these bodhisattvas are all established in the state of being irreversible from the attainment of unsurpassed, right, and complete awakening.

One should examine the four teachings, each of which possesses its own three [stages], yet they differ one from another. Now, in explaining this sutra, we discuss only the stages, practices, and mindfulness of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).

This is as clarified in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: that upon attaining the first stage (prathama-bhūmi), one obtains the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies, endowed with the three non-regressions (tri-avaivartika).
This is the reality of the "one true thing," which is precisely the non-regression of the Perfect Teaching. However, it is not...
As for those who regress, their intent encompasses both directions; however, for the sake of harmonizing the text, we shall follow the interpretation from above.
This sentence should be understood as extending through the subsequent passages. △ Fourth, praising their virtues:
they have all attained *dhāraṇī*, the eloquence of joyful speech, and the power to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma, making offerings to immeasurable hundreds [of buddhas].
Having planted the roots of all virtues in the presence of thousands of Buddhas, they are constantly praised by those Buddhas.
Cultivating their bodies with loving-kindness, they skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom, penetrate great knowledge, and reach the further shore.
Their fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and they are able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
These thirteen phrases are interpreted through two approaches: vertical and horizontal. First, the vertical approach accords with the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
second, the horizontal approach accords with the meaning of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). Regarding "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*): establishing it as preceding clarifies the stage itself;
establishing it as subsequent praises its virtues. This corresponds to the first stage, which is named "Joyful" (*pramuditā*), because one rejoices in not falling back.
"Entering from the extremes into the Middle Way and attaining the three non-regressions" refers to praising the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
"All having attained *dhāraṇī*" praises the second stage, the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*);

this stage is named "Vimalā" because it is free from the obstruction of all evils and possesses the maintenance of all virtues, which is precisely the meaning of *dhāraṇī*. "Eloquence in joyful speech" praises... [the third stage].
The third is the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). This is because once internal wisdom is clear, external exposition becomes eloquent;
that is to say, if one wishes to know where wisdom resides, it resides in speech, and among the various forms of eloquence, the most supreme is *pratibhāna* (joyful eloquence).

"Turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma" praises the fourth stage, the Stage of Blazing Fire (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). This is because fire can dispel darkness and also burn the wick; thus, "turning the wheel of Dharma" [is likened to this].
"Thus, destroying one's own delusions is like burning away a wick; dispelling the confusion of others is like removing darkness.
"Making offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" praises the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*).

On this stage, one attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) that are difficult to surpass or equal; in a single moment, one reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings.
"Those who nourish all Buddhas and plant the roots of various virtues under the presence of all Buddhas"—this praises the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Because they have attained profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they are able to make offerings to all Buddhas; sustained by this merit, the seeds of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) manifest.
This wisdom that manifests is the root of virtue, just as planting a seed in the earth. They are constantly attended by all Buddhas.

"Praising" refers to this praise of the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*). In this stage, the two types of wisdom and skillful means transcend all [lower stages] through extensive cultivation of benefit, and they accord with the Buddha-mind.
"Cultivating the body with loving-kindness" praises the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā*).
Because right knowledge is immovable, one does not emerge from the triple world; yet, perfuming the body with loving-kindness, one should enter the five [pure abodes].
To permeate the mouth with the Way is to preach the Dharma; to permeate the mind is to establish skillful means.

This is precisely the meaning of what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to as "thoroughly permeating the three karmas. "Skillfully entering the Buddha-wisdom" praises the ninth stage, the Stage of Good Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

This is because one has profoundly entered the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and wondrously penetrated the fundamental source; thus it is said that "the Buddha-wisdom thoroughly penetrates great knowledge."

This praises the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Its *dharmakāya* is like empty space, its meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like a great cloud, and its wisdom (*prajñā*) is like a heavy rain.
Skillfully entering the Buddha-dharma is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*), while skillfully applying the Buddha-dharma is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
these are mentioned interchangeably here. "Reaching the other shore" praises the internal virtues within the ten stages; it refers to reaching the "other shore" of the three truths.
"This shore" refers to explaining the fruit within the context of the cause; furthermore, it indicates that before long, one's fame will be universally heard.

This praises the external virtues beyond the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). It means that because internal virtues are profound and vast, they cause one's reputation to spread everywhere, such that the internal and external correspond to one another.
If one were to open up the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), these two phrases may be applied to it, for it can deliver hundreds of thousands.
Regarding "sentient beings," those who deliver people in other stages, or from one realm up to nine realms, are not called "able to deliver" because the Ten Stages are superior to what precedes them;
thus they are designated as "able to deliver. However, each of these stages individually possesses the many aforementioned merits.

The reason for providing this explanation of their emergence and disappearance now is that people’s dispositions favor variety, and it is also for the sake of making the established doctrine easier to understand.

Next, regarding the praise from the perspective of horizontal progression: this refers specifically to the single stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*); the subsequent stages are to be understood by analogy.

What is meant is that in the first dwelling of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one arouses all [virtues] at once, transcending the two extremes, transforming the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and surpassing the sages, entering the Middle Way.
Because the mind is quiescent and flows moment by moment into the ocean of *sarvajñatā*, it is said that "attainment" occurs.

It is non-retrogression; furthermore, because the first stage (bhūmi) obstructs and distances one from the hindrances of grasping at signs, ignorance, and nescience, and sustains the virtues of prajñā, liberation, and the dharma-body, it is said that one "attains dhāraṇī.

If even those at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), whose understanding is merely semblance-like, can already use a single wondrous voice to pervade the three thousandfold world-system, how much more so for the true understanding of the mouth-secrecy (*mukha-guhya*) of the first stage?
Because of these merits, it is called the "eloquence of joyful exposition. In the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one is able to manifest as a Buddha in a hundred worlds;

yet in reality, the number of such manifestations is immeasurable and boundless. Because one is able to act as a Buddha, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings, it is said that one can "turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, having attained inconceivable spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) in the first stage, one is universally able to serve and attend upon [the Buddhas].

Because the Buddhas of the Dharma-realm [are his teachers], it is said that he makes offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Having attained the reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*), he is thus able to plant all manner of virtues.

Furthermore, because he opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*) at the first stage, knowing that his own dharma is identical to that of all Buddhas, it is said that he is constantly praised by all Buddhas. Moreover, at the first stage, by means of the objectless [compassion]...
Because the Universal Manifestation Body of Compassion responds throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it is said that "one cultivates the body through compassion.

Furthermore, because one enters the Secret Treasury at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), it is said that "one skillfully enters the Buddha-wisdom. Moreover, because the threefold wisdom within a single mind is unimpeded at the first stage, it is said that "one penetrates great wisdom.
Additionally, because the ultimate distinction between phenomena and principle is realized at the first stage, it is said that "one arrives at..."
Furthermore, because the true perfection of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) accords with its name, it is said that "its fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds.

Moreover, because the first stage can serve as the support for the ten realms of existence (*dharmadhātu*), establishing and protecting them, it is said that "it can deliver hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the first stage possesses immeasurable and boundless [qualities] beyond these.

The inconceivable varieties of merit can be briefly summarized in thirteen phrases; from the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is likewise so.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The first letter-gateway 'A' possesses the merit of forty-one letters, and the final letter 'Ḍha' likewise possesses the merit of all letters;
the same applies to those in between. Thus, the letters are equal, and the words are equal in their merit.
Their virtues are also equal. △ Fifth, the listing of their names:

They are named Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, and Bodhisattva Śūradatta.
The Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Anantavikrama, the Bodhisattva Trailokyavikrama, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Ratnākara, and the Bodhisattva Nāyaka.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) and the Great Name (Mahānāman) may derive from a dharma-gate, from conduct and virtue, or from original vows;
though they share a single name, they encompass immeasurable meanings. Now, relying on the sutras and based on contemplation, we shall explain the names of the eighteen bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). As the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states: "To see the Buddha-nature clearly is to be equal to Mañjuśrī."
The *Meghasūtra* says: "Pūrṇa-megha-śrī. The *Samantabhadrotsāhana-sūtra* says: "Mañjuśrī. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"Although he preaches all dharmas, he gives rise neither to the mark of dharmas nor to the mark of non-dharmas; therefore, he is named 'Wondrous Virtue' (*Guṇākara*). The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"May it be my vow that while I practice the bodhisattva path, all sentient beings whom I transform shall first attain perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions, so that my divine eye [may see them]."
All shall behold my land, where all are bodhisattvas in their final birth; I cause them all to follow me and resolve upon the path of enlightenment.
In my practice of the bodhisattva path, there is no limit. The Buddha Baozang said: "The merit you have cultivated is exceedingly profound and deep.
I pray that you take up a wondrous land; for this reason, I now name you Mañjuśrī. He resides in the north.
In the world named *Prāmodya*, he acts as a Buddha named *Ratnakūṭaprāmodyagarbha-maṇi*;
he is still present now, and hearing his name extinguishes the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*). He appears as the image and shadow of Śākyamuni for the sake of bodhisattvas.
The new translation renders *Mañjuśrī* as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*). The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that when this bodhisattva was born, there was...
The ten kinds of auspicious omens were: first, a single radiance filled the chamber; second, ambrosia overflowed the courtyard; third, seven treasures surged from the pond;
fourth, spirits opened the hidden treasury; fifth, a rooster gave birth to a phoenix chick; sixth, a pig brought forth a dragon-pig;

seventh, a horse produced a qilin; eighth, an ox gave birth to a baize; ninth, the granaries transformed into golden millet; tenth, an elephant was endowed with six tusks—these arose from such extraordinary causes.
Because of these auspicious signs, he is named "Auspicious" (Śrī). In India, he is called *Bhalaṅkateśvara*. In the *Sukhavihāra-sūtra*, it is said:
"If sentient beings see him, they will immediately and certainly attain Bodhi; those who call upon his name shall be liberated from all sufferings.
Therefore, he is named "Avalokiteśvara. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings suffering who call upon his name and mind me..."
"By what I have seen with my divine eye and heard with my divine ear, none can escape suffering; I shall not attain perfect awakening.
Treasure Store Buddha said, "Observe all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion; from now on, I shall name you Avalokiteśvara (Guan Shiyin).
Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "Wherever I set foot, the three-thousandfold world system trembles."
Because his world and the palace of Māra are equal, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"I vow that my world shall be no different from that of Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"Because you have taken a vow to encompass a great trichiliocosm, I now name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Ever-Vigilant. The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva..."

Because he pursues even a single sentient being through immeasurable kalpas without ever abandoning them, and because he does not relinquish them for even a single thought-moment despite their failure to be transformed, he is named "Ever-Vigorous.
Regarding his lack of rest, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*) states: "A period of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitutes one day and night;
thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year. Thus, after passing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas..."

Having encountered one Buddha, and likewise encountered Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, practicing all forms of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and cultivating meritorious virtues, one subsequently receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because the mind does not cease, it is called the "prediction of non-ceasing.
It is said that "non-ceasing" and "constant diligence" are roughly identical in meaning and intent; however, to distinguish them, entering [the path] without interruption is termed "diligence."
That which is practiced for a long duration without cessation is called "uninterrupted"; this is now said to be merely a distinction between self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
As for the "Jewel Hand," the *Puchao* (Universal Transcendence) Sūtra says: "Donning the armor of supreme virtue, such that even unto Buddhahood none can obstruct or defeat it;
one shall uphold the Mahāyāna. Even in dreams, one does not set one's mind upon the two vehicles, but always maintains a sincere heart and a mind of all-encompassing supernatural wisdom."

Because he preached and proclaimed for others while his mind was free from greed or attachment toward all precious jewels, he was named Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Palm). Regarding the King of Medicine, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"I vow that when the first one thousand four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa attain initial enlightenment, I shall make offerings to all those Buddhas;
when they enter parinirvāṇa, I shall erect stupas for them; and when the kalpa ends and there is suffering and affliction, I shall rescue and protect them from the calamities of weapons and disease."
