After acting as the Great King of Physicians during an epidemic, he then became the Buddha Ratnagarbha. The Buddha said: "I shall now name you 'Agniviśuddhi Bhaiṣajyarāja' (Fire-Purified Medicine King).
In the future, you shall become a Buddha, namely the Tathāgata Rocana. This prediction states that "Fire-Purified" (Agniviśuddhi) was established as his name because he burned his own body.
In this text, from "Vīradatta" to "Transcending the Three Realms," these seven bodhisattvas are referred to in the commentary as lacking an explanation.
The preface states: "I, being ignorant, have hastily formulated regulations based on the ancestral instructions and provided a rough commentary on the fragrant legacy.

As for those details that remain unclear, I await future sages to supplement them. 'Viryadatta' (Brave Giver) refers to one who is able to give universally all the internal and external worldly wealth, as well as the unsurpassed supramundane Dharma-wealth;
who is courageous and fearless, and possesses no stinginess. 'Ratnacandra' (Jewel Moon) refers to—"
The three virtues are partially realized as noble and precious, like the seed of wisdom; their perfection, clarity, and coolness are like the moon.

Regarding the "moonlight," the moon has the meaning of waning and waxing, as well as dispelling darkness; this is used as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva, whose original nature is full while his manifested traces appear to wane.
Alternatively, it is said that the light of the middle-way wisdom partially realized by the Bodhisattva can suddenly shatter the dark obscurity of the afflictions of the ten realms.
"Brilliant full moon" means that because this Bodhisattva is fully adorned with the hundred merits, his wondrous marks are perfectly clear and bright, like the full moon.
"Great power" means that the object and wisdom are merged in profound stillness; he uproots suffering and bestows happiness, surpassing all partial and inferior [vehicles].

"Immeasurable power" means that his original nature is lofty while his traces appear humble; his power is great and his function is deep, universally rescuing and liberating all beings. "Transcending the three realms" means...

He has attained wondrous awakening to the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*) and thoroughly dispelled the hundred negations; because he transcends both the mundane and the supramundane, he receives this name.

Bhadrapāla means "Good Guardian" (*śubha-rakṣa*) or "Worthy Guardian. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadrotsāhana-parivarta* states that if sentient beings hear his name, they will certainly attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), and for this reason he is named "Good Guardian.
The *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecy) states that this Bodhisattva’s name also appears in the *Pratyutpanna-buddha-sammukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra*.

The name "Bhadrapāla" (Worthy Protector) signifies that he is virtuous; it means he skillfully protects others so that they do not regress. As for "Maitreya," this is translated as "Maitreya" (The Compassionate One).
Regarding "Siyi" (Thought-Benefit), it is said that if sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the *maitrī-citta-samādhi* (samādhi of the compassionate mind);
therefore, he is named Maitreya. This Bodhisattva currently resides in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven, and will emerge in the future to appear in the Sahā World.
In the place where Śākyamuni was born, the World-Honored One Maitreya shall attain perfect enlightenment beneath the Nāgapuṣpa tree within the Puṣpavana Garden.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), fascicle 34, states: "At the first assembly of the Nāgapuṣpa [tree], he will deliver ninety-nine billion śrāvakas;
at the second assembly, ninety-six billion śrāvakas; and at the third assembly, ninety-three billion."
The *Śrāvaka-koṭi-sūtra* states that the auspicious signs and sublime conduct of this Bodhisattva are explained in detail elsewhere. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"I vow to protect sentient beings amidst the kalpas of swords and fire. Regarding "Ratnakūṭa" (Treasure Accumulation), it refers to one who has partially realized the threefold noble virtues (*triratna*), which are as precious as jewels;

because these three virtues are perfectly integrated and subtle, they are called "Kūṭa" (Accumulation). Regarding the "Guide," the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says: "Regarding those who have fallen into error..."
Because he gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, leads them into the Right Path, and does not seek any reward for his kindness, he is called the "Guide.
△ Six: Conclusion.
Thus, there were eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas together with him.

The phrase "such as these" is a term for a general summary. The *Ji* (Record) states that among the various great bodhisattvas within the teachings of this one lifetime, those who received predictions based on their past conditions are mostly found in the second fascicle of the *Beihua jing* (Sutra of the Lotus of Compassion). Thus, that sutra says:
"There was a bodhisattva named Jiyi (Śāntamati) who addressed the Buddha, saying: 'All Buddhas possess pure lands; why is it that the Tathāgata alone has taken [one]? "
Regarding this defiled land, the Buddha said: "By virtue of my original vow, I have taken [birth here].
In the past, during incalculable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a world named Sālendrarāja and an eon named Susthita.
At that time, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Araṇemin who ruled over the four continents; he had a thousand sons and a great minister named the Brahmacārin Ratnasāgara."
He had an only son who possessed the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
constantly, various devas came to make offerings to him, for which reason he was given the name Ratnagarbha. Upon leaving the household life and attaining the Way, he was also called Ratnagarbha.
He preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, their number being immeasurable. After his thousand sons had each made offerings to him for three months, the King [desired]—
He entered a samādhi first and manifested the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, gathering all the bodhisattvas there.
He first bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon those in the ten directions who had been taught by Ratnasāgara;

then he bestowed the predictions upon the thousand sons of the Wheel-Turning King. Regarding the eldest son, he said: "Observe the six realms of existence and give rise to great compassion; sever all..."
"Since you cause sentient beings afflicted by defilements to dwell in peace and happiness, I shall now name you Avalokiteśvara.
After Amitābha Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, during the first watch of the night when the True Dharma has perished after two asaṃkhyeya kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and during the final watch of the night, that land shall change its name to 'Accomplished of All Precious Jewels,' and all its adornments..."

In a single thought-moment, he attained perfect awakening within the realm of Exalted and Peaceful Bliss, receiving the name King of Mountains of All Merits, with a lifespan of ninety-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
The second prince was named Mahāsthāmaprāpta (as explained above); the third was named Mañjuśrī (also as explained above); and the fourth was named Samantabhadra.
In the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Ganges-sands, there is a world named Animiṣa, continuing in this sequence up to the ninth, named Akṣobhya.
Among these thousand princes thus successively prophesied, there is one who, out of great compassion, vows to attain Buddhahood in the five turbidities;
his land is named Sahā. Why is this? Because the sentient beings therein endure [the afflictions].
Because it can endure these evils—the three poisons and all afflictions—it is called the "Land of Endurance" (Sahā).
Among these thousand people, with the exception of one, all shall attain Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa. △ Third, the miscellaneous assembly, part eight:
first, the devas of the desire realm.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was present together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras, including the devaputra Candrama, the devaputra Samantagandha, and the devaputra Ratnaprabha;
the Four Great Kings were also present with their retinues of ten thousand devaputras;
and Īśvara and Maheśvara were present with their retinues of thirty thousand devaputras.
Regarding the term "various assemblies" (*miśra-parṣad*): the old translations rendered this as "the assembly of ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*), yet within it there are noble ones (*ārya*);

they translated it as "the assembly of the laity" (*gṛhastha*), yet within it there are those who have attained the Path; they translated it as "the assembly of devas and humans," yet within it there are *nāgas* and *pretas*. These meanings are all inconvenient;

therefore, we now use the term "various assemblies," which encompasses all these senses—namely, the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), the two realms (*dvi-dhātu*), and so forth. Now, observing this passage, there is...

In these eight sections, Śakra is first designated, followed by the listing of the Four Heavenly Kings; because dragons appear before birds and ghosts and spirits are listed twice, this is termed "miscellaneous" (*miśra*).
Within this, there are those who have attained the Path and those who have not; their karmic fruits and physical appearances are mixed.
Furthermore, there are those who have attained the paths of the Two Vehicles, wherein untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) coexist without distinction.

It is explained that "mixed" refers to those who have attained the path of a bodhisattva being mixed with various capacities (sattvas), and those who have attained the path of a Buddha being mixed [with them], because a single dharma contains all dharmas;
thus, the meaning of "mixed" is as such. How could it be judged by the physical forms of ordinary beings?
Nor can it be judged by the five classes of beings, humans, or devas; therefore, it is called "mixed. At that time...
This refers to that very time. Śakra Devānām Indra is sometimes called Indara or Candira;
this translates as "Capable of Acting" (Nengzuo) or "Capable Heavenly Lord. It means he is the one capable of acting as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Trāyastriṃśa translates as "Thirty-three. This is because Mount Sumeru has four sides, each...
There are eight cities on each face, which together with the city of Sudarśana (Joyful to Behold) constitute the Heaven of the Thirty-three who dwell together upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
"Sumeru" is translated here as "Anming" (Peaceful Brilliance) or "Miaogao" (Sublime Height).

This mountain is composed of four precious substances and is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li* in height and breadth. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the Sublime Height has four terraces, each separated from the next by...

Extending ten thousand [yojanas] outward, the sixteen thousand, eight thousand, four thousand, and two thousand [yojanas] in measure, the Kings Sthiraśiras, Mālādhara, Sadāmatta, and Mahārāja dwell respectively on the four tiers;
they likewise reside on the other seven mountains. On the summit of Mount Meru, eighty thousand [yojanas high], dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
At its four corners are four peaks inhabited by the Vajraśiras; in the center is the palace named Sudarśana.
Beyond ten thousand *yojanas*, there are four gardens adorned with the [heavens of] Saṃtarpita, Audārika, Praharṣaṇa, and Nirmita. The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Because this is the lord of the desire-realm devas, it is listed first. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* (40) records that a bhikṣu asked the Buddha, "For what reason is he named Śakra Devānām Indra?
The Buddha replied, "In his former life as a human, he practiced immediate giving and was capable of performing [great deeds]."

Because he is the lord, he is named Śakra Devānām Indra. The *Prajñāpāramitā* states that after two thousand twenty-four kalpas beyond the Bhadrakalpa, he will become a Buddha named the World-Honored One "The Unattached" (*Asaṅga*), with the name "Universal Fragrance of Moon-like Jewel Light.

As for the "Three Sons of Heaven," these are the inner ministers of Śakra, similar to the high ministers and counselors of the world; some say they are simply the "Three Radiant Sons of Heaven. The Four Great [Kings]...
The Heavenly King (Devarāja) is like a high-ranking external minister or general to Śakra; he resides on Mount Caturmahārājakāyika, halfway up Mount Sumeru.
The *Ratnakoṭi-sūtra* states that it is 240,000 li wide. To the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Holder of the Nation" or "Abider of the People.
He dwells upon a mountain range of golden peaks and commands two types of spirits: first, the Gandharvas, and second, the Kumbhāṇḍas.
*Virūḍhaka* (Nan-pi-liu-le-cha) means "Increase" (*vṛddhi*) or "Liberation" (*vimukti*). He dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads two classes of spirits:
first, *piśācas*; second, *kumbhāṇḍas*. *Virūpākṣa* (Pi-liu-bo-cha) means "Non-beautiful Retribution," "Evil Eyes," or "Mixed Speech.
He dwells on Mount Rūpya and leads two classes of spirits: first, venomous dragons (*nāgas*).
The second is the *piśāca* Vaiśravaṇa, which is translated here as "Various Hearings" (*zhǒngzhǒng wén*) and also as "Much Hearing" (*duōwén*).

He dwells on the Crystal Mountain and presides over two classes of spirits: first, the *rākṣasa*, and second, the *yakṣa*. Each of these Four Heavenly Kings presides over two types of spirits to prevent them from harassing human beings;
therefore, they are called the "World Protectors. Next, above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the Yāma Heaven, which is translated here as "Well-Held" (*shànchí*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that [the Heaven of] "Exquisite Goodness" (*Sudṛśa*) is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li* from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
"Well-Sustained" (*Sudharman*) is above that, and it is translated as "Exquisite Feet" (*Suyāma*), also called "Contentment" (*Tuṣita*) or "Joyful Contentment.

It is as far from the Yāma Heaven as the earth is distant [from the heavens]. Those not listed here now are omitted for brevity. "Mastery" (*Vaśavartin*) refers to the fifth heaven, Nirmāṇarati. Furthermore, "Great Mastery" (*Mahāvaśavartin*)...
Those present were the sixth [heaven], the Paranirmita-vaśavartin. △ Second, the gods of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu):
Śikhin Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, Prabhāsa Mahābrahmā, and others, together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.

*Saha* is translated here as "Endurance" (*kṣānti*). Because the sentient beings of this land dwell complacently in the ten non-virtues and are unwilling to renounce them, the land is named after its inhabitants and thus called "Endurance.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* asks: "Why is it called Saha? It is because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions;
therefore, it is called the Land of Endurance. It is also called "Mixed," for it is a mixture of the nine realms of existence.
This is because they dwell together. "Brahmā" (梵) here means "free from desire" (*vītarāga*) and is also called "supremely pure. "Śikhin" (尸棄) here means "topknot" (*śikhā*).

This is likely because foreign lands refer to fire as *jyotiṣ* (which resembles *druma*, tree); Śikhin was originally named after his virtue, having cultivated the *ābhāsvara-samādhi* (fire-light concentration) and thereby destroyed the afflictions of the desire realm.
However, since the sutra designates him as the Brahmā King and further mentions Śikhin, it appears [to be a distinction].

Just as with two people, according to the *Śāstra* (Śīlaskandha-śāstra), Śikhin is correctly identified as the king; however, since this sutra mentions his rank to reveal his name, it likely refers to one specific individual.

One who dwells in the intermediate dhyāna, possesses vitarka and vicāra internally, and engages in verbal expression externally, attaining the status of a leader as a king, is a Brahmā-purohita when practicing dhyāna alone.
When he adds the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), he becomes a Mahābrahmā. This refers to the first dhyāna.
There are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā heavens; now, by citing the King [Mahābrahmā], one encompasses all the luminous realms, which constitute the Second Dhyāna.
In the Third Dhyāna, there are the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara heavens. In the Fourth Dhyāna, there are the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens.
In the [fifth] stage, there are the Guhyaka (also called Anāvaraṇa) and the Apramāṇaguhyaka (also called Puṇyaprasava).
They are also called the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) and the Unconscious (*Asaṃjñin*). There are also the five *anāgāmins*:
the Untroubled (*Avṛha*), the Heatless (*Atapa*), the Well-Appearing (*Sudṛśa*), and the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), also called the Great Sovereign (*Maheśvara*), that is, Maheśvara.
The scriptural texts omit details and do not list them exhaustively, merely stating "and so forth" (*ādi*) to refer to these various devas. △ Third, the Dragon Kings (*nāgarāja*).
There were eight dragon kings— Nanda the Dragon King, Upananda the Dragon King,
Sāgara the Dragon King, Vāsuki the Dragon King, Takṣaka the Dragon King, Anavatapta the Dragon King, Mānasa the Dragon King,
and Utpala the Dragon King— each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Nanda is named "Joy" and Upananda is named "Good"; these two brothers constantly protect Magadha so that rain falls at the proper time and the land knows no years of famine.
King Bimbisāra held an assembly once every year, and when the common people heard of it, they all rejoiced;

from this, [the place] received its name. This dragon is the very one who was subdued by Maudgalyāyana. His dwelling is in the midst of the ocean; his fundamental and manifested traces are explained herein.
This one originally dwells on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); his trace-abode is within the great ocean. As for *Sāgara*, he derives his name from dwelling in the sea;
this is as described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The old translation says he is named after the country he originates from;

his original abode is the great ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, while his trace-abode is the vast blue sea. As for *Hayaśrī* (Andhaka), this is translated as "Many Heads" or also as "Jewel Renown"; he dwells in...
The one who originally dwells within the water and universally manifests the form-body through the *samādhi* of "traces," and displays the virtue of having many heads, is called *Dhṛtarāṣṭra*.

This is translated as "Manifesting Poison" (*Xiandu*), also as "Many-Tongued" (*Duoshel*), or sometimes as "Double-Tongued. Originally he dwelt in the joy of unhindered eloquence in preaching the Dharma;
his traces manifest as being many-tongued. *Anavatapta* is named after its lake; this is translated as "Heatless" (*Wure*).
Regarding the Anavatapta Lake, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18, states: "At the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a lake named Anavatapta;
within it is a hall with five pillars, which takes its name from the lake. A nāga king constantly dwells therein.
Now, the nāgas of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions: first, hot winds and hot sands strike their bodies, burning their skin, flesh, and marrow."

First, two evil winds of suffering and affliction arise and blow upon their palaces, causing them to lose their precious ornaments, garments, and the like, so that their dragon bodies manifest in their true form, leading to suffering and affliction;

second, when the dragons are enjoying themselves, the King of the Garuḍas enters the palace, seizing and devouring newborn dragon offspring, which causes them fear, dread, and burning anguish; now, this pond is free from those things.
Regarding the three calamities: if a bird conceives the desire to go there, its life immediately ends; therefore, it is called the Lake of No Heat-Affliction (*Anavatapta*).
Its original abode is Cool, Constant Bliss, Self, and Purity, and its trace-locus is the Cool Lake. *Mānasa* means "Great Body," or alternatively "Great Mind" or "Great Power.
When the asuras pushed back the ocean to submerge the City of Joyful Sight (*Sudarśana*), this dragon coiled its body [around the city].
The method of dwelling in the ocean of the sea, which is the trace of the Dharma-gate of the Boundless Body (Anantagātra), constitutes its great essence.
"Utpala" here means the dark-colored lotus; the dragon dwells in this lotus pond and is named after it. It dwells in accordance with the Lotus Samādhi (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi).
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the dragon protects the realm for the various devas against the asuras.
He raised an army and first fought with the dragon; thus it was known that he was under the jurisdiction of Heaven.

△ Fourth, the Kiṃnaras: there were four Kiṃnara kings—the Dharma Kiṃnara King, the Sublime Dharma Kiṃnara King, the Great Dharma Kiṃnara King, and the Upholder of Dharma Kiṃnara King—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The Kiṃnara is also called the Caṇḍāla; this is translated as "Doubtful Spirit. They resemble humans but possess a single horn, hence they are termed "Non-Humans" (amanuṣya).
They are the deities of the celestial music of the Lord of Devas. They dwell on the Ten Jewel Mountains and possess extraordinary physical characteristics.
Whenever the Buddha ascends to play music or preaches the Dharma, the various devas provide stringed songs and perform the pañcaśīrṣa lute while chanting verses on the Dharma-gates.

Regarding "Original and Traces": the Original dwells in the inconceivable, neither arising nor ceasing from meditative concentration, joining palms in dhyāna and praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses;
the Trace is manifested through lutes, pipes, songs, and chants of the Ten Powers. As for the "Contemplative Understanding":
observing that sounds and voices are themselves empty, provisional, and middle, thereby acceding to the Three Truths—this is precisely the praise of the Buddha. △ Fifth, the Gandharvas.
There were four gandharva kings— Gandharvarāja, Gandharvasvara, Gandharvarājasvara,
and Gandharvasusvara— each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

Gandharva is translated here as "Fragrance-Olfactory" (xiu xiang), for they take fragrance as their food; it is also called "Fragrant Aggregate" (xiang yin) because fragrance issues from their bodies.
These are the deities of the secular music of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. "Music" (*nṛtya*) refers to the performance of dancers and acrobats;

"musical sound" (*gīta*) refers to drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments. "Beautiful" (*śobhana*) refers to the excellence among dancers and acrobats; "beautiful sound" (*svara*) refers to the excellence among strings and wind instruments.
The record states that "dharma" (幢) refers to the *yuan-chong* (緣橦), which is a wooden pole; "inversion" (倒) refers to being thrown down.
The *Ahan Yin Yi* (阿含音義) explains that "climbing the *yuan-chong*" means using one's hands to climb up an object; it is the soft pole used in the performance arena.
△ Sixth, the Asuras.
There were four asura kings— Asurinda the asura king, Kharaskandha the asura king,
Vemacitra the asura king, and Rāhu the asura king— each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Asura is translated here as "No Wine" (Madyarahita). In the past, they gathered flowers from the four continents and fermented them in the great ocean;
however, due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor did not change. Because they vowed to renounce wine out of anger and jealousy, they are called "No Wine.

They are also called "Not Upright" because their forms are coarse and their appearances are ugly, while their mental conduct is crooked and deceitful. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states regarding the Asuras: [text follows].
Among the four types, first, there are those in the realm of hungry ghosts who, through the power of protective mantras (*dhāraṇī*), attain supernatural powers and enter the sky;

these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*). Second, there are those in the heavens who have descended due to the loss of their merit and fallen;
their dwellings are adjacent to the sun and moon; these asuras are born from the womb and are categorized within the destiny of humans (*manuṣya-gati*). Third...
First, those who possess the power of the world, are thoroughly fearless, and are able to contend for authority with Brahmā and Śakra;

these asuras are born from transformation and are included within the celestial realms. Second, there is a separate class of inferior asuras who dwell in the heart of the great ocean, roaming to the mouths of their caves in the morning and returning to sleep in the water at night; these asuras are born from moisture and are classified among the animals.
The *Shengjie sheshu* (Commentary on the Compendium of Births) states: "Bāzhì" means "bound," or it refers to being tied around the neck by five evil objects so that one cannot attain liberation;

hence it is called "bound. It is also said that there is bondage because one is bound by Śakra, and that the original capacity for the five fetters binds the traces of Māra—this is merely the representation of this image.
The *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) says: "The Most Victorious Observer [uses] three..."
The wisdom of contemplation binds the afflictions of the five abodes and enters into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
*Kharaskandha*—translated here as "Broad Shoulders" (*guǎngjiānjiè*) or "Evil Aggregate" (*èyīn*)—is described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhèngfǎhuá) as "Jeweled Brocade.

Because he fundamentally abides in the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real (*upāya* and *prajñā*), and because he compassionately bears the burden of sentient beings, he manifests in the trace [body] with broad shoulders. *Vemacitra*—this...
Cloud-Pure Mind is also called the Sea of Various Doubt-Waves; he who emerges from it and utters sound is named Vemacitra, the father of Śacī.
Rāhu is translated here as "Obstructing-Holder," meaning one who obstructs and holds the sun and moon.
He belongs to the species of beasts, his body is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length, his mouth is one thousand yojanas wide, and he is adorned with precious jewels.
Furthermore, his body daily emits light such that the eyes cannot behold it; therefore, he raises his hand to block the sun, which everyone universally calls a solar eclipse.
It is the same when he eclipses the moon. Or, when he makes a great sound, people say it is the "roar of a celestial beast," but these are all false doctrines.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states: "When Rāhu desires to devour the moon, the Moon Devaputra is struck with terror and hurries away."
He ran to the Buddha and spoke in verse: "O Buddha, World-Honored One of great wisdom and diligence, I now take refuge in you and pay homage with my head bowed.
Rāhu has tormented me; may the Buddha, out of compassion, grant me protection.
The Buddha spoke in verse to Rāhu: "The moon can illuminate the darkness and is cool and refreshing; it is the great lamp of brightness within the void of space."
Its color is pure white and it possesses a thousand rays; do not swallow the moon, release it quickly!
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that on Mount Vajra in Jambudvīpa there is a palace of the asuras, its governed domain being six thousand yojanas wide, complete with railings and rows of trees.
Yet, three times every day and night, instruments of suffering come of their own accord to enter it, causing them to experience pain.
That the imperial palace belongs to the four evil destinies is indeed for a specific reason. Within this matter, there are both provisional and ultimate aspects;
one must investigate their root. Perhaps they are originally high-ranking Bodhisattvas manifesting themselves to protect the Dharma. △ Seventh, the Garuḍas.
There were four Garuḍa kings— the Garuḍa King Mahātejas, the Garuḍa King Mahākāya, the Garuḍa King Mahāpūrṇa,
and the Garuḍa King Manojña— each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
*Kalaviṅka* (迦樓羅) is translated here as "Golden-Winged" (*jīngì*). Its wings and feathers are golden in color, and it dwells atop a great tree spanning the four continents;
the distance between its two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*. Some call it the "Great Peng" (*péng*).

Regarding its "great majestic power" (*dà wēidé*), its majesty surpasses all its peers and strikes terror into all the *nāgas*. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that it is "endowed with a massive body. "Great" refers to its vast physical scale.

The term "Greatly Satisfied" (*Mahāpūrṇa*) refers to his filling his own desires by devouring dragons. As for "Wish-Fulfilling" (*Cintāmaṇi*), he receives this name because he possesses this jewel on his neck.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls him "Immovable," while the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states that his correct name is Garuḍa.
On one day in the east, he devours one dragon king and five hundred small dragons; the same occurs in the other three directions.

Thus it revolved again and again for eight thousand years. At the end of its life, it lost its momentum; wishing to devour the dragon’s son, the mother dragon cried out in distress, unable to catch its prey.
She then gave rise to anger and, from Mount Vajra, she leapt through the ocean, piercing the earth-wheel and the wind-wheel, attempting to spring past [the child], but she could not.
Returning once more through the same opening, she reached Mount Vajra; thus she repeated this seven times.
Returning to the mountain peak, his life came to an end; his flesh split open and fire erupted, about to consume Mount Ratnaparvata. The Nanda Dragon sent down rain to extinguish it;
as his flesh decayed, his heart pierced through the wind-circle and fell back onto the mountain peak seven times, where it became a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
The dragon obtained it and immediately became its king. Human kings, too, have had experiences with this jewel. As stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18: [text follows].

To the north of the great ocean there is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
To the east of the tree is the palace of the egg-born nāgas, and also the palace of the egg-born garuḍas;
to the south is that of the womb-born, to the west that of the moisture-born, and to the north that of the transformation-born—each having its respective nāga and bird palaces.
The palace has seven tiers of surrounding trees where various birds sing in harmony. When seizing dragons, those born from eggs strike the sea water with their wings for two hundred *yojanas*;
those born from the womb for four hundred; those born from moisture for eight hundred; and those born by transformation for one thousand six hundred.
Those born from the womb, egg, moisture, and transformation respectively devour one, two, three, and four dragons. 8. Aṣṭaka.
World-Honored One, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of attendants—
*Vaidehī* being translated as "Reflection" (i.e., the mother of King Ajātaśatru), and *Ajātaśatru* being translated as "Unborn"— [approached].
The enemy is sometimes called *Vairocana*, which means "Fingerless. Those who attend him protectively call him "Sudarśana" (Good Vision);
this is his original name, while the title "Fingerless" expresses his outward manifestation. A great sūtra states:
"The term *a-jāta* means 'unborn,' and in the world it is called 'enemy. Because the Buddha-nature is unborn, afflictions are therefore the enemy."
Because the enemy of afflictions has arisen, one does not see the Buddha-nature; by not giving rise to afflictions, one sees the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, "Ajāta" means "unborn," while "Śatru" (in worldly terms) refers to the worldly dharmas;
because he is not defiled by the eight worldly winds, he is named Ajātaśatru—this is the fundamental meaning. Puchao says that Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī.
Having attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), at the end of his life he entered the Piṇḍala Hell;
upon entering, he was immediately reborn in an upper buddha-field where he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When Maitreya appears, he will return to this realm as the Bodhisattva Acala, and later he shall become a Buddha named Śuddhaloka Tathāgata. Since his traces are thus [inconceivable], how could his original nature be measured? He preached the Dharma in this manner.
When the flowers bloom, they first join the pure assembly; when Nirvana arrives, they lead those who have committed the five grave offenses.
One should know that it is impossible to be deluded by the traces while remaining confused about the source. Regarding "several" (若干): this refers to a certain number.
Thus, whether it be thousands or tens of thousands, they cannot be listed exhaustively, but only their general magnitude is preserved. △ Second, the summary.
Each bowed at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew, and sat to one side.
Having withdrawn and sat to one side, they collectively concluded the assembly, paid their respects, and sat back to listen to the Dharma. The Commentary asks:
"The Buddha is preaching the Dharma among humans; why is the number of people listed here so small? The answer is that the text is abbreviated and does not record the actual number of people present.
Not a few [beings] are mentioned as follows in the text, including various minor kings and wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin*);
furthermore, in the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, four types of wheel-turning kings are listed—kings, ministers, citizens, and men and women—and their assembly is vast. Again, it is asked:
gods, humans, dragons, and ghosts all see the Buddha and hear the sutra; why is it that those in the single path of hell and the single realm of formlessness do not?
The meaning of not including [this] in the answer shall now be clarified. Among the various paths, there is ascent and descent depending on whether the precepts are maintained or violated;

there is seeing the Buddha or not seeing the Buddha depending on whether the vehicle is swift or slow. However, because the maintenance of precepts has degrees of coarseness and subtlety, the resulting retribution has distinctions of excellence and inferiority;
because the vehicles have distinctions of smallness and greatness, the seeing of the Buddha has aspects of provisional and real. △ Next, the fivefold separate introduction.
First, the assembly gathers; second, auspicious omens appear; third, doubts arise; fourth, questions are posed; fifth, the questions are answered. Now, for the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, revered, honored, respected, and praised him.
The "separate preface" (bie xu) receives its name by extension from the general title. "At that time" (er shi) refers to the moment when the six auspicious omens were about to manifest;
generally, whenever "at that time" is mentioned, it points to the conclusion of a preceding matter and the beginning of a subsequent one—all other cases may be understood accordingly.
This, then, refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the six omens, at the very moment the great assembly had first gathered to hear the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra*. Worldly... [text ends]

The Venerable One is endowed with both merit and wisdom, having perfected the myriad practices; among those honored in both the mundane and supramundane realms, none surpass him. Regarding the "Fourfold Assembly" (catur-parṣad):

the old interpretation refers to the two groups of renunciants and the two groups of householders, totaling four assemblies. While this name is precise, its scope is limited and does not encompass the full meaning. Here, we shall define a single assembly and further divide it into four, namely:

those who initiate the teaching, those who are the appropriate recipients (*sannipāta*), those who act as influences (*prabhāva*), and those who form karmic connections (*praṇidhāna*). Thus it is said:

The "Initiator" (Prasthāpaka) possesses skillful means, wisdom, and discernment; knowing the opportune moment and the proper time, he strikes, raises, and mobilizes [the assembly] to accomplish and fulfill their benefit.
Just as a great elephant knocks down a tree so that its young may eat to their fill, the Initiator causes them to gather.

From the auspicious signs of initiation up to the questions and answers, all such instances are termed the "Assembly of the Initiator. As for the "Those Who Are Appropriate for the Occasion" (Tatkālina), they have planted [roots of merit] in past lives...
When the conditions for the roots of virtue converge and ripen—like an abscess ready to burst—one hears of the path attained without rising from one's seat;

this is called "responding to the occasion" (*kālacitta*). As for those who are like shadows or echoes: these are the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas of the Buddhas of antiquity who conceal their perfect and ultimate nature to assist the Dharma King, like the myriad stars surrounding the moon.
Though they perform no deliberate action, they bring immense benefit; this is called... [the name of this category].

As for those who influence the multitude through the formation of karmic connections, they lack the power to lead them forward or stir their awakening; their virtue lacks the function of subduing things or imposing solemnity.
Because their past roots were shallow, being shrouded by outflows and defilements, the three types of wisdom did not arise.

Although they may see the Buddha and hear the Dharma in the present life, they derive no benefit from the four *siddhāntas*; rather, this serves only as a causal condition for attaining liberation in the future.
They are called the "assembly for establishing karmic connections. Just as it is with the assembly of bhikṣus, so it is with the other three assemblies;
thus, taken together, they constitute sixteen assemblies. Regarding those who surround [the Buddha]: when the Buddha first appeared in the world, people did not yet know the Dharma.

A being from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven transformed himself into a human form, arrived, circumambulated the Buddha to the right, paid homage, and, having prostrated, wished to sit and listen to the Dharma. Therefore...

To revere the heavens and take humans as models is the explanation through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, "circumambulation" refers to the dignified deportment of walking in a circle;

it symbolizes that when the mechanisms of the four gates move, the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) is seen simultaneously. To correlate the perfect with the partial involves four meanings, which is the explanation according to the teachings (*yathā-śāsana*).
Moreover, the Buddha’s body is surrounded by the adornments of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); gazing up at these from all four directions increases [one's faith].

The meditative concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) is the interpretation of contemplating the mind; if one contemplates the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) and thereby perceives the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this is the interpretation of the fundamental and the manifested.
Regarding "making offerings" (*pūjā*): generally speaking, all three types of action (*trikarma*) constitute offering;

specifically, humble and reverent prostration is called "respectful reverence" (*gaurava*), focused and concentrated mindfulness is called "veneration" (*satkāra*), and speaking words of praise is called "eulogy" (*stuti*).
To praise the basis upon which giving relies is called "offering"; this text provides a brief account as explained at length in the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
The celestial kitchens, celestial incense, celestial bowls, and so forth are the offerings.

The Great Ornament Bodhisattva and the eighty thousand great beings joining their palms and clasping their hands constitute "reverence. Beholding with single-mindedness constitutes "veneration. Thus it is said.
The seven-syllable verse is a hymn of praise. Regarding the reference to that passage concerning the assembly in the present treatise:
when the assembly gathered for that sutra had finished hearing the Dharma and remained solemnly without dispersing, they continued to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* from their very seats.

Thus, we know that the offerings of the three karmas must not differ; therefore, the extensive account from that [sutra] is used to explain this concise one. △ Second, the manifestation of auspicious signs (has two parts).
First, regarding the six auspicious omens in this land, the first was the preaching of the Dharma:
for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings," which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken for the sake of all bodhisattvas, the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* (or *Bhadraśīla-sūtra*) sets forth seven forms of greatness: 1. **Greatness of the Dharma**:

This refers to the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*), specifically the Vaipulya. 2. **Greatness of Mind**: This refers to seeking after Bodhi. 3. **Greatness of Understanding**:
This refers to understanding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. 4. **Greatness of Purity**: This refers to the purification of the mind upon seeing the Path (*darśanamārga*). 5. **Greatness of Ornamentation**.
This refers to the greatness of merit and wisdom; the sixth is the greatness of the six periods, meaning the practice of deeds throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;

the seventh is the greatness of fulfillment, meaning that one attains *bodhi* by adorning oneself with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). The sixth is the greatness of the cause, and the seventh is the greatness of the fruit;
because these great causes and great fruits are combined, they constitute the Mahāyāna Sūtra. As for its being named "The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings," it is as stated in that sūtra.
It is said that all arises from a single dharma; this "single dharma" refers to the signless (*animitta*).
That which is signless and non-characterizing is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). From this true mark, immeasurable dharmas arise—namely, the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits.
Now, following that sūtra, I shall explain this meaning: "signless" means being devoid of the marks of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); it is non-characterizing.

This is the characteristic of non-nirvāṇa; since nirvāṇa itself is also non-existent, it is said that "non-characteristic" and "absence of characteristic" refer precisely to the Middle Way and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

The "two dharmas" refer to the sudden and the gradual: the sudden refers to all dharmas within the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, while the gradual refers to all dharmas within the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā. The "three paths" refer to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Furthermore, the four fruits are the Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha. These various dharmas are called "immeasurable," which refers to the ultimate reality (dharmatā) as their locus of meaning.
From this single locus of meaning, immeasurable dharmas emerge; thus they are called "immeasurable dharmas.
Entering into this one locus of meaning serves as the introduction, just as a mathematician derives all calculations from the number one.
To eliminate various calculations and return them to a single calculation is the sequence of elimination, wherein one eliminates the lower by means of the lower.
To derive all from one branch and consolidate all into one is the sequence of inclusion; it is likewise so. Therefore, it is called the "Infinite Meanings" (Ananta-artha).
Regarding "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas," the locus of infinite meanings is employed to teach Bodhisattvas. This "locus of meaning" refers to the principle of truth (tattva). Below...
"May I cause all sentient beings to likewise attain this path"—this is precisely the meaning of "if I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way.

As for being "protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha," it is because [the teaching] originates from the *Ananta-artha-sthāna* (The Place of Infinite Meanings), which is what the Buddha himself has realized.
Therefore, it is that which the Tathāgata protects through his mindfulness; as the subsequent passage states, "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna."
This is so; although he wished to reveal it to the assembly, because their faculties were dull, he remained silent for a long time, not seeking to speak hastily.
Therefore, it is said that he "protected and remembered" [the teaching]. △ Second, entering meditative concentration:
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meaning, his body and mind being...
Movement.

After the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings; because the characteristics of wisdom and concentration are mutually perfected, we know that there is no meditation without wisdom and no wisdom without meditation.
Therefore, he first entered concentration, and because there is no meditation without wisdom, he first preached the Dharma—this is wisdom within concentration.

Regarding those who harbor doubts because they think that if the Buddha had already entered this samādhi while possessing both concentration and wisdom—without any obstruction or interval between their prior emergence and subsequent entry—then why would he enter samādhi after having preached this sūtra? The explanation is as follows: He first entered this samādhi and subsequently preached this sūtra; the meaning of this can be explained. That he enters samādhi again after having finished preaching this sūtra is for the following reason: [the sūtra continues: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom is profound and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to fathom. This is because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable and boundless, and his eloquence is likewise immeasurable and boundless. Furthermore, it is because the Tathāgata wishes to manifest the power of his supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and to cause sentient beings to generate great reverence and respect. It is also because he wishes to demonstrate that the Dharma he has preached is not in vain, and to show that the Tathāgata’s words are true and not false. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is immeasurable and that the Dharma he has preached is eternal and inexhaustible. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible and that the Tathāgata’s mind is unshakeable. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s power is supreme and that the Tathāgata’s merit is unsurpassed. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s compassion is vast and that the Tathāgata’s kindness is deep. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s vows are fulfilled and that the Tathāgata’s work of salvation is accomplished. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is definitive and that the Tathāgata’s liberation is final. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s realm is pure and that the Tathāgata’s field is adorned. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s light is infinite and that the Tathāgata’s sound is pervasive. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s name is honored by all worlds and that the Tathāgata’s fame is celebrated by all gods and humans. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s presence is always near and that the Tathāgata’s protection is never absent. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s grace is constant and that the Tathāgata’s benefit is enduring. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the ultimate truth and that the Tathāgata’s path is the only way. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is peerless and that the Tathāgata’s power is invincible. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s merit is inexhaustible and that the Tathāgata’s virtue is boundless. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s compassion is impartial and that the Tathāgata’s love is universal. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s vows are firm and that the Tathāgata’s resolve is steadfast. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the source of all dharmas and that the Tathāgata’s liberation is the gate to all peace. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s body is the embodiment of all virtues and that the Tathāgata’s mind is the treasury of all wisdom. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s speech is the manifestation of all truths and that the Tathāgata’s deeds are the fulfillment of all vows. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s presence is the refuge of all beings and that the Tathāgata’s protection is the shelter of all worlds. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the medicine for all afflictions and that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the light that dispels all darkness. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s power is the sword that cuts through all delusions and that the Tathāgata’s strength is the armor that protects against all evils. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s compassion is the rain that nourishes all roots of goodness and that the Tathāgata’s kindness is the wind that sweeps away all defilements. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s vows are the earth that supports all beings and that the Tathāgata’s resolve is the mountain that cannot be shaken. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the ocean that contains all dharmas and that the Tathāgata’s liberation is the moon that cools all hearts. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s body is the sun that illuminates all worlds and that the Tathāgata’s mind is the space that encompasses all things. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s speech is the drum that awakens all sleepers and that the Tathāgata’s deeds are the bridge that leads all across the sea of suffering. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s presence is the jewel that fulfills all desires and that the Tathāgata’s protection is the fortress that wards off all dangers. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the fire that burns away all ignorance and that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the water that washes away all stains. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s power is the king that rules over all dharmas and that the Tathāgata’s strength is the minister that assists in all tasks. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s compassion is the mother who gives birth to all bodhisattvas and that the Tathāgata’s kindness is the father who raises all disciples. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s vows are the path that leads to the city of nirvana and that the Tathāgata’s resolve is the vehicle that carries all to the shore of safety. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the lamp that dispels the darkness of the three realms and that the Tathāgata’s liberation is the medicine that cures the disease of birth and death. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s body is the tree of enlightenment that bears the fruit of all virtues and that the Tathāgata’s mind is the flower garden where all wisdom blooms. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s speech is the melody that harmonizes all beings and that the Tathāgata’s deeds are the dance that delights all hearts. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s presence is the mirror that reflects all forms and that the Tathāgata’s protection is the shield that defends against all calamities. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s teaching is the boat that ferries all across the river of desire and that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the oar that propels all forward. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s power is the steed that gallops through the wilderness of saṃsāra and that the Tathāgata’s strength is the bow that shoots down all demons. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s compassion is the net that gathers in all straying beings and that the Tathāgata’s kindness is the hook that draws out all submerged souls. It is also because he wishes to cause sentient beings to know that the Tathāgata’s vows are the ladder that ascends to the palace of the Dharma and that the Tathāgata’s resolve is the stairway that reaches the peak of liberation.
