The *Lotus Sūtra* merely serves as a preface. Why is this? If one does not first open [the way], there will be nothing with which to harmonize later.
Therefore, entering the "Opening" (Kai) and "Determining" (Jō) first is established as the preface; it is called a "portentous sign" (sui-sō), and this is precisely that meaning.
If one were to explain the sequence, one would first enter the *Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings*, and then one should enter the *Samādhi of the Lotus*. If one clarifies...
When these words were proclaimed, the assembly understood at once; there was no need to wait for Maitreya’s earnestness or Mañjuśrī’s reticence.
Thus we know that by composing this preface, its meaning becomes even more clear. That body and mind are unmoving is because they correspond to the locus of their objects.
Yet the source of the body is profoundly still like empty space, and the nature and principle of the mind are ultimately and eternally quiescent. Great!
The body, hands, and feet of the Buddha, the Supreme One of Penetrating Wisdom, are tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving;
his mind is always serene and never distracted. His body is like a vajra, incapable of being shaken, and his mind is like the great void, free from discrimination.
Because he maintains both body and mind through the dharma of the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, he remains unshakable.
That which is now called "Immeasurable" is a samādhi that is tranquil yet constantly illuminating; it is able to know that from this one dharma, immeasurable dharmas emerge.
If one interprets this as the meaning of a "preface": the essence of the body-dharma is movement and activity, which is now rendered non-moving and non-active;
the essence of the mind-dharma is discrimination, which is now rendered non-discriminating. This inquiry into auspicious signs is truly marvelous according to the original treatise.
Question: It is the constant practice of the Buddha to preach the Dharma and enter meditative absorption; how can this be considered an auspicious omen? Answer:

Although the preaching of the Dharma has concluded, the assembly does not disperse because they are solemnly awaiting something. Thus we know that the previous preaching of the Dharma was for the purpose of gathering the entire multitude to await what would follow.
This matter is extraordinary and differs from ordinary preaching; why then would it not be an auspicious omen? Although he entered meditative absorption, his intention remained [open].
Why is it that this entering into meditative concentration differs from ordinary entry into concentration? What is the meaning of its not being a "sign" (*prātihārya*)?
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī cites that among the six signs of the ancient Buddhas, all included this very event. If in the past it was not a sign, how could it serve as proof for the present?
Since the past and the present are identical in this regard, how can one reject it based on mundane sentiments? △ Third, the raining of flowers.
At that time, the heavens rained down māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers,
and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.

Heaven rains four kinds of flowers— formerly called "small white," "large white," "small red," and "large red"— which the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to as "intention flowers" (*manojña-puṣpa*) and "great intention flowers" (*mahā-manojña-puṣpa*),

as well as "fragrant flowers" (*gandha-puṣpa*) and "great fragrant flowers" (*mahā-gandha-puṣpa*). The *Śāstra* (Treatise) states in section 99 that the most exquisite heavenly flowers are named *māndārava*,
and in section 79 it says that in the buddha-fields of eight hundred bhikṣus who have attained enlightenment, there is a constant rain [of these flowers].

Regarding the five-colored *manḍārava* flowers—formerly [the tradition] held that white and large represented the two groups of householders (small and great), while red and small represented the two groups of renunciants (small and great)—this was intended to symbolize those who, though having long since set out on the path, had not yet achieved their goal. Now, it is said that this interpretation is narrow and inappropriate;
for if one were to discuss the fourfold assembly directly, it would still fail to encompass even the sixteen assemblies found within the Tripiṭaka, let alone others.
Furthermore, the previous forty-eight assemblies were therefore narrow; the present mention of the rain of flowers clarifies that these were causes from the past, yet not the causes for Buddhahood.

Among them, the causes within the Tripiṭaka are the causes of the Two Vehicles; the causes within the Shared [Teaching] are common causes; and the causes within the Distinct [Teaching] are the causes of Bodhisattvas—none of these are the cause for Buddhahood.
Today, the heavens rain flowers as a retribution for the fact that he shall attain the cause of Buddhahood. As for this "cause of Buddhahood":

This refers to the causes of the four wheels: thus, the small white [circle] symbolizes the copper wheel, representing the stage of the nature-seed (śīla-bīja) and the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), wherein the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened;
the large white [circle] symbolizes the silver wheel, representing the nature-seed stage and the ten practices (*caryā*), wherein the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are revealed;

the small red [circle] symbolizes the gold wheel, representing the path-seed stage and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), wherein the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are realized; and the large red [circle] symbolizes the lapis lazuli wheel...
The wheel of lapis lazuli represents the lineage of the noble ones (*āryagotra*) and the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Now, these four wheels are all alike causes arising from within; thus, they fall as rain from the heavens. Because they belong to the stage of cause, they are symbolized by flowers.
Yet, because there is the principle of the cause leading toward the fruit, they are scattered upon the Buddha. Who, then, could have elicited such a cause and fruit?
Since [the Buddha] was merely addressing the assembly gathered at this very meeting, he spoke of "all the great assemblies.
△ Fourth, the earthquake: the worlds of all Buddhas shook in six ways.
Now, the earth shakes in six ways; this signifies that within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), there are six stages of breaking through ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because the massive boulders of ignorance have never before been invaded or destroyed, they are now about to be shattered; thus, the shaking of the earth is used to symbolize this. When ignorance is transformed, it immediately becomes clarity (*vidyā*);
therefore, throughout all Buddha-worlds, there is a sixfold earthquake. These six modes symbolize the stages of abiding and practice (*zhuxing*).
This is the sixth section concerning the earth and other phenomena. The *Upāsaka-śuddhacaryā-sūtra* states: "When the Bodhisattva was born, the earth shook;

this demonstrates that his births have been exhausted and he is no longer subject to afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, because the afflictions of all sentient beings who are destined to attain the Way are about to be extinguished, the earth shakes.
This is precisely that meaning. Regarding the "sixfold shaking," it refers to shaking, rising, and surging.

The "thundering roar" refers to the fact that within each [of these] there are further three types: namely, shaking (*calana*), pervasive shaking (*vicālana*), and universal pervasive shaking (*samantavicālana*).

If it shakes directly, it is "shaking"; if it shakes the four continents, it is "pervasive shaking"; if it shakes the trichiliocosm, it is "universal pervasive shaking. The same applies to the remaining five [elements].
Thus, combined, they constitute eighteen kinds of shaking, which symbolize the purification of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). The Record states:
Regarding these six matters, the new and old commentaries differ from one another. The new [commentary] says: "moving, leaping, shaking, striking, roaring, and bursting.
For now, we shall follow the old [commentary], which states: "swaying and being unsettled is called 'moving' (*iṅgita*); rising from below to a higher level is called 'arising' (*utthāna*);

having uneven mounds and hollows is called 'leaping' (*valgana*); making a deep, rumbling sound is called 'shaking' (*prakaṃpana*); emitting a crashing resonance is called 'roaring' (*nirghoṣa*); and causing objects..."
Awakening is called *jue* (awakening); the new translation says it is like striking a firecracker, such as the sound of a firecracker exploding. △ Five:
The Assembly Rejoices. At that time, among the assembly were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas... [and so forth].
The gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all the minor kings and universal monarchs—
this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
The assembly, seeing the rain of flowers and the shaking of the earth, knew that the nectar of the Dharma was about to descend;

thus, their hearts were filled with joy, manifesting that their great spiritual capacity was about to be awakened and would move the Supreme Response. Question: Joy and anger are the common emotions of human beings; how can they constitute an auspicious omen? Answer:
The celestial flowers delight the eyes, and the shaking of the earth vibrates the heart. As a Great Sūtra says: "When it shakes, it is able to cause the hearts of the multitude to shake."
One should know that the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth are external auspicious signs, while the joy of the great assembly is an internal auspicious sign.

This is indeed an extraordinary joy; although such things have occurred before, they did not move the minds of those present. Now, being able to contemplate the Buddha with single-mindedness, how could this not be an auspicious sign?
If joy were to agitate the mind of the aggregates (*skandha*), that would merely be the principle of gods and humans. If [joy]...

To move the mind of the true reality (bhūtārtha) and the untainted (anāsrava) is the meaning of the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings. If one delights in moving the provisional mind (*prajñapti-citta*), this is the meaning of the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching.
If one delights in moving the mind of the true aspect (*dharmatā-svabhāva*), this is the meaning of the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching. *Bhikṣu* is translated here as "male one who eliminates hunger";
*bhikṣuṇī* is translated as "female one who eliminates hunger. *Upāsaka* is translated as "male of pure faith"; *upāsikā* is translated as "female of pure faith."
This [term] is translated as "pure-faith woman" (*upāsikā*). *Mahoraga* is translated as "great-bellied crawler";
this refers to the *mǎngshén* (serpent deity). It may be a human or a non-human; alternatively, it is said to be a collective summary of the aforementioned eight classes.
Or perhaps it refers to those led by the four *kiṃnara* kings, appearing separately from them. Why? Because all such beings have forms that resemble humans.
It is for this reason that it is called "having one horn. If this is the case, then there is merely a distinction between the principal and its attendants;
the remaining names and meanings have already been explained above and will not be repeated here. They may be understood by applying the same principle. △ Six: Emitting Light.
At that time, the Buddha emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a light that illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction,
pervading them all without exception, reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The Buddha emits rays of light as an auspicious omen to manifest teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, thereby shattering delusions and removing doubts.
Furthermore, that *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) possesses various merits; as stated in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sūtra*: "When the Buddha was first born, the tuft was five feet long;
by the time he practiced austerities, it was fourteen feet long; and upon attaining Buddhahood, it was fifteen feet long. Such is that tuft.
Both its interior and exterior are empty, resembling a cylinder of white lapis lazuli, pure within and without.
All the various manifestations of the practices performed from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta through to the entry into nirvana—all these merits appear within the *ūrṇā*.
This *ūrṇā* is situated between the two eyebrows and represents the permanence of the Middle Way. Its appearance is soft and supple, signifying...

Joyfulness signifies mastery over contraction and expansion, representing the self. White represents purity. The emission of light to shatter darkness represents the arising of the light of wisdom from the Middle Way.
Illuminating this land and other lands represents both self-awakening and awakening others.
Furthermore, although those of the Two Vehicles have attained the Two Truths, they do not know the Middle Way; it is as if they have two eyebrows but lack the white tuft of hair between them.
Although the teachings acknowledge the three truths, they cannot manifest all phenomena within a single hair-tip;

one should know that the fact that all matters within the dharma-realm, from beginning to end, appear within a single hair-tip expresses the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Furthermore, it is said:

"If a Buddha of sixteen feet height emits light, this is the meaning of the Tripitaka (Sanzang); if a Mahāpuruṣa (Zun-te) Buddha and a Buddha of sixteen feet height emit light together," [this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching].
"Light" is the meaning of penetration; if the Buddha of Solemn Form alone emits light, it is the meaning of distinction.
If the sixteen-foot Buddha—that is, the Dharma-body Vairocana—emits light, it is the meaning of perfection.

As for "illuminating the eastern direction," the east is the beginning of the directions, signifying that the Ten Abodes are the beginning of the stages; thus, the teaching of the Trace Gate is produced.
The Bodhisattva of the Body clearly perceives the principle and enters the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

Since one knows the middle and the end by grasping the beginning, it is said that there is nothing to which he does not pervade. One should know that this is likewise true for all directions and likewise for all stages.

If we consider the assembly of Buddhas from the four directions as described in the teaching of the "Root Gate" (*mūlaparivarta*), it symbolizes the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who gather for the teaching of the Root Gate.
The four stages of increase—namely, the increase of merit (*puṇya*), the increase of the path (*mārga*), the decrease of birth (*janman*), and the increase of birth—are as follows:

from the Avīci Hell (also called Abi, which means "uninterrupted" because it is located beneath the earth, hence "earth-hell") up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (which means "ultimate limit of materiality," i.e., the Akaniṣṭha Heaven). From the Avīci Hell upwards...

The "Summit of Existence" (*bhavāgra*) refers to the six dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, because one sees the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and so forth, the ten realms are fully present;
thus, the text states that there is "nothing that is not universally pervaded," which is precisely this meaning. △ Second, the six auspicious omens in other lands.
First, seeing the six destinies.
Within this world, one sees all the sentient beings of the six destinies in those lands.
Next, to briefly explain the six auspicious signs of the light illuminating other lands: first, seeing the six destinies;

second, seeing the various Buddhas—this constitutes one pair, comprising both the supreme sages above and the ordinary beings below; third, hearing the Buddhas preach the Dharma; fourth, seeing the fourfold assembly attain [realization].
The Way and the person constitute one pair; the five views are the Bodhisattva’s practice, while the six views are the Buddha’s Nirvana—these constitute another pair of beginning and end.
Since there are sentient beings who can be transformed, there must be a Buddha who can transform them. Where there is a Buddha, there is the teaching of the Dharma;
where there is the teaching of the Dharma, there are disciples. Disciples are the beginning of practice, and the beginning of practice necessarily...
The conclusion is as follows: the six auspicious omens of this land collectively signify that sentient beings shall attain self-awakening;

the six auspicious omens of that land collectively signify that sentient beings shall awaken others. Furthermore, these six omens of this and that land represent that the paths of the Buddhas of this and that land are identical.
From the observation of the six realms of existence in that land down to those who practice the bodhisattva path, it is all thus.

Having manifested that land as being identical to this one, the passage from "he again sees the various Buddhas" down to "the seven-jeweled stūpa" manifests that this land shall likewise be identical to that one.

The further detailed explanation, beginning from "he again sees the sentient beings of the six destinies," manifests that those Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). △ Second, seeing the various Buddhas.
Furthermore, one sees the Buddhas currently residing in those lands;
this Buddha is likewise so, clearly demonstrating that the intent of these two lands regarding the appearance in the world is identical. △ Third, hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, hearing the sutras and teachings expounded by those Buddhas is manifested as the Buddhas' initial teaching of the single dharma of formlessness; it is not gradual, yet it is sudden, and its intent is the same as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* first taught in this land.
△ Fourth, seeing the fourfold assembly attain the Way.
Furthermore, they see those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have attained the Way through their practice.
This manifestation of that Buddha is gradual, just as the Buddhas of this land gradually teach the Three Piṭakas; the intent is the same. △
He saw the practices of the bodhisattvas;
furthermore, he saw various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path through various causes and conditions, various modes of conviction, and various characteristics.
This indicates that the teaching of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā and other sūtras after the Tripiṭaka of that Buddha is identical in intent to the teaching after the Tripiṭaka of this land’s Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the various causes and conditions: past goodness serves as the cause, while the present teaching serves as the condition.
Moreover, to speak of them separately, these precisely clarify the common and uncommon Prajñā following the Tripiṭaka.

Taking the factors of the path—such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—as causes, and taking conditions as they relate to the three types of persons, there arise various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the various causes, conditions, and characteristics of both common and uncommon persons:
for each of the four gates of the common and uncommon, there are again immeasurable characteristics, such as the five hundred bhikṣus each describing their own bodies.

"Condition" (*hetu*) is precisely its meaning. Since this is also the case for the four gates of non-commonality, one knows that the characteristics and varieties of conditions and causes are immeasurable;

yet all of these are the same as "that" and "this. When "that" clarifies "this," the characteristics and appearances of conditions and causes return to being one cause, one condition, one characteristic, and one appearance. One should know that this land is likewise the same as that. △ Six: Seeing.
The Buddha entered parinirvāṇa;
furthermore, they saw various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa, and after those Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, they saw stūpas made of the seven precious gems being erected for their relics.
This manifests the Prajñā of that Buddha; thereafter, he reveals the provisional to manifest the real, gathering immeasurable dharmas back into the single dharma.

He proclaims his entry into Nirvāṇa, ceasing his transformative activity and causing stupas to arise; thus the light illuminates that land from beginning to end, reaching its ultimate conclusion with such brilliance that it appears clearly before one's eyes.
One should know that in this land, the emergence of the immeasurable from the one is neither sudden nor gradual, yet it is both sudden and gradual.
As the gradual unfolding of these matters reaches its conclusion, one must inevitably gather the immeasurable teachings and return them into the single Dharma;

by opening up the provisional to reveal the real and ceasing the transformation to return to the True, it shall be identical to that [of the previous Buddhas]. △ Third, the doubts and reflections, in two parts: First, Maitreya’s doubts and reflections;
third, the six portents of right mindfulness.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests these signs of supernatural transformation;
by what causes and conditions does such an auspicious omen exist?

As for 'supernatural transformation' (ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā), 'supernatural' (ṛddhi) refers to the internal, while 'transformation' (vikurvaṇā) refers to the external. 'Supernatural' (ṛddhi) is called the Heavenly Mind; it is innate wisdom."
The transformation and movement are the manifestation of the six auspicious omens externally. △ Second, the thought of questioning whom:
"Now that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered samādhi, this is an inconceivable and rare occurrence;
to whom should I ask? Who is able to answer?"
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "The Buddha abides in the non-dual Dharma and is able to manifest supernatural powers; as a Dharma King, his power surpasses and covers all things.

Maitreya cannot fathom his external transformations, nor does he know his internal wisdom; thus he gives rise to thoughts that reach this point. As for those who are mediocre, they do not understand skillful means;
those who are scattered, they do not understand meditative concentration; ordinary people do not understand the sages; and lesser sages do not [understand the Great Sage].
Śāriputra does not know the Bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattvas do not know those in their final birth (caryā-bhūmi), and those in their final birth do not know the Most Honored One;

this refers to the fact that even at the highest level, they do not know. Yet, since Maitreya has encountered Buddhas and planted many roots of goodness, how could he possibly fail to have some general understanding?
It must be that he spoke of "not knowing" as a skillful means, concealing what is manifest and revealing what is obscure. △
He thought three times of Mañjuśrī, further reflecting: "This is the son of the Dharma King Mañjuśrī, who has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
he must surely perceive this rare and wondrous sign, and I shall now question him."
Question: The sutras state that Mañjuśrī is a son of the Dharma-king; among these bodhisattvas, who is not a son of the Dharma-king?
Answer: There are two reasons for this: first, among the sons of the king, Mañjuśrī is extolled for his supreme virtue;
second, in various sutras, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is consistently designated as the foremost leader. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states:

The Buddha is the King of Dharma; from the time Bodhisattvas enter the correct position of the Dharma up to the tenth stage, they are all called "Dharma-Prince Sons" and are all capable of becoming Buddhas—how much more so Mañjuśrī?
II. The Doubts and Reflections of the Great Assembly. A. First, the Six Auspicious Omens as the Correct Reflection.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, all formed this thought:
"This is the mark of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal power."
△ Second, the two thoughts regarding whom to question:
"Whom should I now question?
The great assembly has two thoughts: first, the right mindfulness regarding the six auspicious omens; second, the thought regarding whom to question, which anticipates the following verse.

This also allows for three contemplations. A verse says: "The fourfold assembly looks up with joy toward both you and me; there is no third. What is the purpose of looking toward you when this [third] is absent? It is because one wishes to push Mañjuśrī aside so that Maitreya may occupy the foremost position as the Regent (Upapadya). Question: The virtues and ranks of Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are nearly equal; why is it that one asks and the other answers? Answer: This is because the capacity of the audience has its own specific focus. There is no [third party] present. Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the two Bodhisattvas, the former is the teacher and the latter is the disciple. Thus, the former asks and the latter answers. Moreover, Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom of the past, while Maitreya represents the wisdom of the future. Since the present is the time when the teaching is being expounded, the one who answers must be the representative of the present. Therefore, Maitreya answers. Finally, Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the Dharma, while Maitreya is the recipient of the Dharma. Hence, the teacher asks and the recipient answers. These are the reasons. Although their status is equal, the proprieties of host and guest differ; the Sage responds to the occasion, for one who does not inquire cannot be answered.

Furthermore, within the Dharma-gates there are the provisional and the real: that which is provisional requires inquiry, while that which is real requires response. Moreover, there are long and short traces:
it is simply that the inquiry is recent while the response is from long ago. Also, names are used for convenience; Maitreya’s name is "Compassion," and compassion is for the sake of sentient beings.
One must ask about Mañjuśrī’s name, "Wondrous Virtue," and he should answer this; these are the four ways of interpreting the meaning of the text.
The Record states: "This great assembly together beheld the six auspicious omens.

Since entering their respective stages, they have attended many assemblies and have long known that Mañjuśrī’s spiritual efficacy is unfathomable; thus, when Maitreya gave rise to his thought, the assembly was also refined."
Because he was truly focused on Wondrous Virtue (Guṇākara), when Maitreya was about to pose his question, he first observed the great assembly;
only then did he proclaim his firm doubts, clearly knowing that Mañjuśrī was the ground for resolving them. △ Fourth, the posing of the question, in two parts: First, the prose section, in two parts:
First, the narration by the sūtra compiler, in two parts: First, the narration of his own doubt.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva wished to resolve his own doubts.
From the passage "At that time, Maitreya wished to resolve his own doubts" down to the verses constitutes the introduction to the inquiry;
the text is divided into two parts: first, the prose (long-xing), and second, the verse (gāthā). Within the prose, the scribe describes both his own doubts and those of others.
The text is clear. △ Second, stating the doubts of others:
Furthermore, he observed the minds of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the assemblies of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth.
△ Second, the posing of questions. First, the question concerning this land.
He addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared, emitting such great radiance?"
△ Second, questioning regarding other lands.
Shining upon eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, he saw all the adornments of those Buddha-fields.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, questioned him with verses:

Regarding the term "verse" (*gāthā*), the *Nāgārjuna-vibhāṣā* states: first, according to the customs of the land, in India there are the traditions of "scattered flowers" and "strung flowers," which correspond here to the preface and the postscript, respectively; second, according to differing inclinations, some prefer the scattered exposition while others prefer formal verses;
third, according to differing ways of attaining understanding, some attain realization through the scattered exposition while others [attain it through verses].

The commentary and verses provide understanding through four aspects of following [the capacity of] sharp or dull faculties: those with sharp faculties awaken upon hearing once, while those with dull faculties awaken only after a second explanation;
furthermore, they manifest the Buddha’s earnestness in repeating the teaching, and they serve to assemble the multitude at both the beginning and the end, which is why there are verses.

△ Second, the verses in praise, in two parts: first, praising the preceding questions; second, praising the six auspicious omens of this land. First, praising the six auspicious omens of this land, in five parts; first, the question regarding the preaching.

1. Question on Entering the Dharma-concentration (the light emitted from between the eyebrows); 2. Question on the Rain of Flowers (the rain of *māndārava* flowers); 3. Question on the Trembling of the Earth (and this);
4. Question on the Joy of the Multitude (at that time).

“Why, O Guide Mañjuśrī, does the great white tuft of hair between your brows radiate light everywhere, raining down *māndārava* and *mañjūṣaka* flowers, while a sandalwood-scented breeze gladdens the hearts of the multitude?

By these causes and conditions, the earth is entirely adorned and purified, and this world quakes in six ways; at that time, the fourfold assembly is filled with joy, their bodies and minds feeling sublime.”
"An unprecedented attainment!

This single verse consists of sixty-two lines of prose. It is divided into two parts: the first fifty-four lines constitute the verses of the initial inquiry, and the final eight lines constitute the request for an answer.
Within the inquiry, there are two further divisions: the first four lines inquire about this land, and the subsequent fifty lines inquire about that land."

Question: In the prose section of the verses concerning the six auspicious omens of this land, there is mention of fragrant winds and the purification of the earth, yet there is no mention of preaching the Dharma or entering meditative concentration.
One should know that the two characters "Teacher" (Nāyaka) refer to these very acts;
for since preaching the Dharma and entering concentration can guide others, the title "Teacher" itself constitutes a question regarding preaching and meditative absorption.
Regarding the sandalwood-scented wind, one must know that the wind itself originally has no fragrance; it is the fragrance that is extraordinary, and thus it constitutes an auspicious omen.

Yet, as for the celestial flowers, how could they be so wondrously sublime and yet possess color without fragrance? This symbolizes that as the causal stage proceeds toward the fruit, it is like flowers possessing fragrance.
Just as when the wind gathers the flowers, the ground becomes adorned and pure; so too, if the cause tends toward the fruit, the fruit becomes adorned and pure.
Because the cloud of light gathers to adorn the Buddha-body with merit, these two matters manifest and establish the four flowers.

Regarding *candana* (sandalwood), some say it is not translated because it does not exist in this region; others say it is translated according to its meaning as "medicine," for it can eliminate all diseases—this should be understood.
As for the term *geya* (verse), it refers to verses that restate the prose (*gadya*); if one were to produce further [verses], then...

For the following sections on "proliferation" (*prapañca*), all should be understood according to this principle; they can be grasped through the meaning. Furthermore, in the verse text, whenever the term "practitioner" (*yogin*) is used, it follows the pattern of four lines.
△ Second, the six inquiries regarding the six auspicious omens in other lands. Part one: the inquiry concerning the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, making them all appear like gold.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, within all these worlds, the destinies of birth and death for sentient beings of the six realms,
as well as their good and evil karmic conditions and the resulting beauty or ugliness of their retributions, were all clearly visible therein.

These three lines pose questions regarding the six destinies; by examining them through this, one knows that the preceding passage on the light shining toward the east signifies the general illumination of other lands.
This verse summarizes the aforementioned general inquiry concerning sentient beings of the six destinies:

those who transmigrate are the "beings," birth and death are the "places" to which they go, karmic conditions of good and evil are the "causes" for their transmigration, and beauty and ugliness are the results.
This is the attainment of the fruit. △ Second, the inquiry regarding seeing the Buddhas preach the Dharma:
Furthermore, one beholds the various Buddhas, the holy lords and lion-like teachers, expounding the sutras which are subtle and supreme;
their voices are pure, emitting soft sounds that teach countless billions of bodhisattvas with profound and wondrous Brahma-voices, causing all to delight in hearing them.
In each world, they preach the True Dharma through various causes and conditions, illuminating the Buddha-dharma with immeasurable parables to awaken sentient beings.
These four lines of inquiry reveal that while previously one saw those Buddhas directly and saw them preaching the Dharma, this section now extensively clarifies their preaching of the Dharma.
They said to one another: "The Holy Lord, the Lion, who teaches the Sudden Teaching to suit those of great capacity, has manifested here in this land as the image of Vairocana.
He expounds the Dharma of the sutras, subtle and supreme, which is precisely like the manifestation of the *Avataṃsaka* teachings upon the High Mountain in this land.
He instructs all bodhisattvas, just as in this land there were the seven assemblies and other such gatherings, yet without sound."
"A man of learning who illuminates the Buddha-dharma and awakens sentient beings; thus, for the first time in this land, he has beheld the Buddha-body and entered the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
△ Third, the question to the fourfold assembly.
If there are people who encounter suffering and weary of old age, illness, and death, he preaches for them the nirvāṇa that brings an end to all suffering.

If there are people with merit who have previously made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to the supreme Dharma, he preaches for them the path of the pratyekabuddha. If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices seeking unsurpassed wisdom, he preaches for them the pure path.
These three lines of inquiry concerning the fourfold assembly of that land clarify the Sūtra-piṭaka teaching immediately following the sudden teaching.
The phrase "if a person encounters suffering" opens the way for the Śrāvaka-yāna. This verse fully elucidates the Four Noble Truths;

specifically, "if a person encounters suffering," one should know that "suffering" encompasses both cause and effect, which are the two truths of Suffering and its Origin (duḥkha-satya and samudaya-satya). [The subsequent line] expresses weariness with old age and illness.
Death is the Truth of the Path; it is taught that Nirvana is the Truth of Cessation.

If a person encounters suffering yet commits unwholesome karma, such that they do not reach exhaustion [of suffering], they are like the lowest of beings. If a person encounters suffering yet performs wholesome karma, their suffering will likewise not be exhausted;
they loathe the lower and grasp for the higher, as when Nanda observed the precepts for the sake of desire, and so forth.

Furthermore, if a person encounters suffering while seeking liberation within the teachings of non-Buddhist paths, their views will only increase and their errors will grow, such that their suffering will never be exhausted.
If a person encounters suffering and becomes weary of its accumulation, and further grows weary of the fruits upon which it depends, the Buddha speaks of *nirvāṇa* for them;
such a person is then able to reach the ultimate end of all suffering. Therefore, this vehicle is also opened in other lands. If a person possesses merit...
The next line opens the discussion on the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*). If one makes offerings to the Buddha sparingly, one may encounter suffering and distress;

if one makes offerings to the Buddha extensively, although one may encounter suffering, it results in merit. Therefore, it is said that *śrāvakas* plant the seeds of merit over three lifetimes, while *pratyekabuddhas* plant the seeds of merit over a hundred kalpas.
Because this refers to those *śrāvakas*, it is said they possess merit. Those who "seek the supreme Dharma" are the *śrāvakas*.

Those who weary of suffering and practice the path of the Pratyekabuddha, seeking the Way by deeply investigating the profound and subtle principle of dependent origination, are those for whom the Middle Vehicle is revealed in other lands.
The passage beginning with "If there are sons of the Buddha" below reveals the Mahāyāna of the Six Perfections;

because they can carry forth true compassion and succeed the lineage of the Buddhas, they are called "sons of the Buddha. Because they cultivate the Six Perfections, it is said that they [practice] "various" [virtues].

Because one practices with the resolve to seek to become a Buddha, it is called "unsurpassed wisdom. Among the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), there are no six obscurations (ṣaḍ-āvaraṇa), just as there is no disease within medicine;

thus, it is called the "pure path," yet it is not ultimate purity. Furthermore, while Śrāvakas take the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) as their gate of contemplation and Pratyekabuddhas take the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) as their gate, the Bodhisattvas of the six perfections take the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) as their gate; therefore, it is so called.
The Path of Purity. △ Fourth, concluding the preceding and opening the subsequent:
"Mañjuśrī, I abide here and have seen and heard such things as these, as well as thousands of billions of other matters; though they are thus numerous, I shall now speak of them briefly."
Within these one and a half verses, "seeing and hearing such as this" concludes what precedes, while "in this manner, so many" opens up what follows.
△ Fifth, the question regarding the Bodhisattva’s cultivation, in three parts: first, the general inquiry.
"I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.

This first general question is easily understood. △ Second, the sequential questions consist of six parts; first, the question on *dāna* (giving), which has three sub-sections, beginning with the question on the relinquishing of wealth.
There are those who practice giving by joyfully bestowing gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels, conch shells, agate, diamonds, and various treasures;
as well as male and female servants, vehicles, precious ornaments, and palanquins, dedicating these gifts toward the Buddha-way with the vow:

"May I obtain this vehicle, the foremost in the three realms, praised by all Buddhas. Or there are bodhisattvas who possess precious chariots drawn by four horses, complete with railings and flowered canopies.
The eaves were adorned with offerings.

Regarding these six types of practice, when one asks about *dāna* (generosity) in terms of precious jewels, male and female slaves, and so forth, both the noble and the humble are capable of such giving;

however, as for the gift of four-horse chariots and precious carriages, these fall within the domain of what the wealthy and heroic bestow. As for gold, silver, coral, and the like, [this is according to] the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It is said that gold comes from the sands, stones, and red copper within mountains, while silver comes from scorched stones. Furthermore, the *Erya* states: "White metal is called silver.
Among the treasures of Mount Zhong, there is "silver-candle" (*yin-zhu*), which refers merely to its brilliant luster being like that of a candle.
As for coral, it is like stone yet grows in clusters. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it is produced in the sea and is red in color; the *Guangya* [describes it similarly].

As for coral, it is a pearl. Regarding *māṇi* pearls, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that pearls are produced from within the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, and from within the brains of snakes.
*Māṇi* is also called *maṇi*; this translates as "free from defilement" (*vimala*), which is simply the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
As for *śukti* (conch) and *musāragalva* (agate), the color of *śukti* is bluish-white, while the colors of *musāragalva* include...
The red [gems], or perhaps white vajras and various precious vajras, are the most refined among metals; they cannot be melted even after a hundred smeltings, and thus they can cut jade.
"Various precious gems" refers collectively to all such jewels. As for carriages, these were first created in this region by Xi Zhong of the Xia Hou clan;
this is the original name for the construction of chariots and wheels. The precious-decorated litters and carriages were adorned with various rare treasures.
Because it is adorned, it is called "jeweled ornamentation" (*ratnabhūṣaṇa*); this refers to that which decorates palanquins and carriages. Regarding the *lian* (palanquin):
the *Shuowen* states it is a "drawn carriage," so named because people pull it from the front. In antiquity, it was the vehicle used by high officials (*qingdafu*);
since the Han dynasty, the Son of Heaven has used it. A carriage used by the Son of Heaven is called a *lian*. Regarding the *yu* (carriage body): the *Shuowen* states—
Regarding carriages: those with wheels are called *chē* (chariots), while those without wheels are called *yǔ* (litters). "Railing" refers to vertical bars and horizontal rails.
A "canopy" (*huā-gài*) is of the same category as the precious canopies used here in this region;
for example, when the Yellow Emperor fought against Chiyou on the plains of Zhuolu, five-colored cloud-gas with golden branches and jade leaves settled above the Emperor, forming floral blossoms.
The image of this [canopy] was subsequently styled by the world as the "Flower Canopy" (*huágài*). This is simply because various flowers and miscellaneous jewels were interlaced to form a canopy.
As for "ornamenting the carriage" (*xuánshì*), *xuán* also refers to a chariot; it is adorned and embellished with precious flowers.
Because one practices *dāna* (generosity) by means of this, it is called "bestowing gifts. △ Second, the question on sacrificing the body.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas giving their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children in pursuit of the Unsurpassed Way.
Wives and children are the external body; flesh and so forth are the internal body. △ Third, the question regarding the relinquishing of life.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas joyfully giving away their heads, eyes, and bodies in pursuit of the wisdom of a Buddha.

One should know that the relinquishing of head and eyes is equivalent to relinquishing life; yet, the fact that the gift of Dharma is not mentioned is because it is deferred to the subsequent *prajñā*.
Moreover, by regarding body, life, and wealth as equal to the future limit of birth and death, one attains the indestructible and eternally abiding state.
Because this is a gift of the Dharma, it is not explained separately. △ Second, the inquiry regarding the precepts.
Mañjuśrī said: "I have seen various kings go to the Buddha's dwelling and inquire about the unsurpassed path;
they then abandon their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and concubines, shave off their hair and beards, and don the dharma robes."
These two lines of inquiry concern the precepts as discussed in relation to bhikṣus. For those who maintain the precepts, giving is easy while the precepts are difficult for laypeople;
conversely, giving is difficult while the precepts are easy for renunciants. The record states that "going to visit" and so forth indicates that one must go to him and not elsewhere;
thus it refers to the Buddha’s abode. Since that which is questioned is the most supreme, it is called the "Unsurpassed Way. Since what is abandoned is not treated lightly, it is called "joy."
Because the body and mind are both detached from the earth, it is said they are "shaved off," as stated in the *Pañcarāja-sūtra*:

"In the past, there were five kings whose neighboring countries did not compete with one another, and who were mutual friends. One great king was named Puhuan (Universal Peace); he practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Because the four remaining kings were full of intense wrong views, Puhuan took pity on them, summoned them to his palace, and for seven days and seven..."
While they were enjoying themselves at night, the Four Great Kings said, "Our state affairs are many; we request to return home.
The King accompanied them with his attendants, escorting them for half the journey, where he asked them, "What do you each desire now?
One replied, "I wish for a spring day to roam the wilds. Another replied, "I wish to always be a king."
Adorned with various ornaments and attended by a retinue of people, everyone along the road turned their eyes toward him. One said, "May I obtain a fine wife and sons who are peerlessly handsome.
Another said, "May my parents live long, may I have many brothers, and may we enjoy ourselves together with fine food and music.
After each had spoken thus, they turned to address the Great King: "What is Your Majesty’s wish? He replied: "I—"
First, let us speak of your aspirations: they will not endure long. If you delight in spring excursions, you will first wither and decay in winter;
if you delight in being a king, your merit will be exhausted and others will strike you down; if you delight in wife and children, one day they may fall ill, and you will suffer immeasurable pain;
if you delight in your parents remaining forever with you, one day when misfortune strikes, they may be seized by others. The Four Kings asked the Great King again: "As for..."

"What is it that you delight in? they asked. He replied, "That which I delight in is neither arising nor ceasing, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither hunger nor thirst, neither cold nor heat; it is the mastery over existence and non-existence.
The Four Kings asked, "Where does such joy exist? The Teacher replied, "My teacher is named Buddha; he is nearby at Jetavana. The kings rejoiced and each went there.
The Buddha withdrew to sit to one side and spoke to himself in self-reproach. The Buddha then taught the Eight Sufferings;

the King and his retinue of hundreds of thousands of myriads of people attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and abandoned their kingdoms to enter the Way. A sutra states that those who don the Dharma robes are like those described in the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra on the Necklaces):
"If the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings engage in strife, they should contemplate this *kāṣāya*, giving rise to a mind of compassion."
It causes the bhikṣus to be peaceful and content, and it also inspires these worldly beings with admiration and joy.
Thus, when a dragon obtains a single thread [of the robe], the golden-winged bird (garuḍa) does not swallow him; that which the King admires is essentially the same as this.

Herein, one should simply clarify the meaning of what is perceived, using the preface to manifest the correct principle. However, the characteristics, merits, and such things as the *kāṣāya* of the various *pāramitā* practices are merely...
This is merely offered as a general clarification. △ Third, the inquiry regarding patience (*kṣānti*).
Suppose one sees a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.
This single line of inquiry concerns patience; there are three types of patience: first, patience toward wild forests, deep valleys, wicked people, and ferocious beasts.
Enduring without anger is the patience toward living beings (*sattvākṣānti*); restraining oneself and maintaining one's resolve is the patience toward suffering (*duḥkhākṣānti*);

and seeking the Buddha-way is the patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthākṣānti*). Furthermore, becoming a bhikṣu is the patience toward suffering; dwelling alone in seclusion is the patience toward living beings;
and delighting in reciting the sūtras is the patience regarding the ultimate truth. As it says in the Āgamas, the Buddha said:
In Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin who came to where the Buddha was and reviled and harassed the Buddha in various ways.
The Buddha said to the brahmin: "Suppose you were to offer various kinds of food and drink to a king and send some to his kinsmen, but they did not accept them;
to whom would those things then belong? The brahmin replied, "They would belong to me. The Buddha said, "This case is exactly like that."
Since I have not accepted it, it still belongs to you; therefore, this non-acceptance is also the meaning of the patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*).
△ Fourth, the inquiry regarding progress:
Furthermore, one sees a bodhisattva who, with courageous vigor, enters deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
This single line of inquiry concerns diligence (*vīrya*); one should know that it is so named because it is pure and thus unmixed, and because it is non-retrogressive.
This is truly because deep mountains are fearsome and are not the dwelling place of the indolent or the timid; only those who advance with courage can find peace therein.

Regarding all things as if they did not exist, they contemplate the cultivation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), never ceasing for a moment, and advancing in their quest for the Buddha-way. △ Fifth Inquiry.
Dhyāna. Furthermore, he saw those who, having detached from desire and constantly dwelling in seclusion, deeply cultivated meditative concentration and attained the five supernormal powers;
he also saw Bodhisattvas, settled in dhyāna with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses.
These two lines pose general questions regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which contain two intentions:

the first line asks about the cultivation of fundamental dhyāna, while the second line asks about the cultivation of supramundane and superior-to-the-world dhyāna. Generally, all [practitioners] may attain the cultivation of the fundamental [dhyānas].

As for those who have abandoned desire (*vairāgya*), if they attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), this refers to the concentration of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇanaya*). Furthermore, one cultivates the fundamental [dhyānas].

Detachment through renunciation (*vairāgya-vairāgya*) also involves the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and other methods for detachment; these are distinct teachings that simultaneously involve detachment from the desires of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Within this, the Middle Way further involves detachment from the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path (*mārgānulomika-dharma-tṛṣṇā*). For those who deeply cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the first dhyāna arises as a single grade (*ekaprakāra*);

as this concentration becomes deeper, it proceeds through up to nine grades (*navaprakāra*), each successive stage becoming increasingly profound. Furthermore, there are the nine stages of renunciation (*navavimokṣa*), the eight stages of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten [stages of totality] (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).

The successive transmissions of the *sarvāyatana* (all-entrances) and so forth are profound; through mastery in the transformation of this samādhi, one can manifest the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

While ordinary beings possess only five supernormal powers and those of the Two Vehicles possess six, the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching yield to the Buddha regarding the presence or absence of the untainted (*anāsrava*) powers, and thus they too are said to possess only five.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), both the beginning and the end possess all six supernormal powers. Regarding the verse of praise for peaceful meditation (*anadhyāna*):

This is because the distinct and perfect [teachings] possess the highest levels of meditative stillness and mental dispersion, which do not obstruct one another; thus, one does not arise from the samādhi of cessation yet manifests various dignified postures.
It is like the lute of the asuras, which produces harmonious tones without being struck and manifests its form through resonance despite the absence of intentional thought.
Therefore, one is able to dwell in dhyāna while praising the Buddha. △ Sixth, the inquiry regarding wisdom, part two: first, self-cultivation.
Furthermore, one sees that the Bodhisattvas possess profound wisdom and firm resolve, such that they are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
Regarding these three modes of inquiry, there are two intentions for wisdom: the first mode concerns their own practice.
"Profound wisdom" means that their insight exhausts the fundamental principle; "firm resolve" means that their vows are vast and great. These constitute the two kinds of adornment.
Question: This refers to what is called "being able to uphold. △ Second, transforming others:

Furthermore, seeing sons of the Buddha endowed with concentration and wisdom, who expound the Dharma for the masses using immeasurable metaphors, who delight in preaching the Dharma to transform all bodhisattvas, and who shatter the hosts of Māra while beating the Dharma drum.
The next two lines concern the intention to transform others: wisdom is predominant before reaching [the higher stages], while formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are predominant;

in the four *dhyānas* and so forth, liberation-wisdom (*vimokṣa-jñāna*) is predominant; among the nine concentrations (*navasamādhi*), concentration is predominant; and among the ten all-encompassing bases (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), both are equal. Furthermore, regarding the destruction of Māra’s armies:
the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) destroys the four Māras, and the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) follows.

Third, the sequential questioning regarding the seven [aspects] within the section on "Thoroughly Destroying the Eight Māras": first, the question concerning *dhyāna*; second, the question concerning relinquishing *dhyāna*. Regarding the "one who beats the drum against the eight māras, the ten māras, and all māras" within the thorough destruction of the eight māras:

upon the initial stage of resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one immediately attains perfect enlightenment and acts as a Buddha in a hundred buddha-worlds, thoroughly beating the Dharma-drum of the Brahma-wheel.
△ Third, the non-sequential questioning regarding the seven [aspects], beginning with the question concerning *dhyāna*. First, the question concerning relinquishing *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, seeing that the Bodhisattva remained in silent composure while devas and nāgas paid him homage, he felt no joy.

As before, having sequentially inquired about the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), he had already personally gathered and completed the myriad practices (*sahasrapratipatti*). Why then does he inquire further?
One should know that this sequential questioning is merely one path of gradual self-cultivation; it is not that there is no [other] sequential questioning.
Regarding the fixed single path: since the preceding text speaks of "various characteristics," how could it refer to only two paths?

However, the two sequences—the sequential and the non-sequential—of the six perfections are intended for the other land; they are taught after opening the Tripitaka and expounding the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya sutras.
The characteristics of the six perfections therein are no different from those here. Now, within these two modes themselves, there are two [further aspects].
The first line of the mind asks about entering the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*); the self-practice commentary states that "dhyāna of equanimity" refers to the fourth dhyāna.
Alternatively, it may refer to the equanimity of forgetting the mind in the Separate and Perfect [teachings], which is called "equanimity" because one forgets that dhyāna itself.
△ Second, the question regarding the dhyāna of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas dwelling in forests emitting light to relieve the sufferings of those in the hells and lead them into the Buddha-way.

Next, one again sees Bodhisattvas descending to inquire after others and enter the meditative concentration of compassion; this is precisely the transformation of others. Thus, when Bodhisattvas enter samādhi and emit light, they bring about various benefits.
This is fully set forth in the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saṃantabhadra’s Questions*, and the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka*, which also describes the emission of light.
He emits a light named Non-Miserliness; that light awakens those who harbor greed and stinginess.

He also emits a light named Refreshing Coolness; that light awakens those who violate the precepts. He also emits a light named Adorned with Patience; that light awakens those who harbor anger and hatred.
He also emits a light named Transcendent Victory; that light awakens those who are indolent. He also emits a light...
The light named "Tranquility" awakens those with distracted minds; furthermore, the light named "Adornment of Wisdom" awakens those who are deluded.

Moreover, in the first section of the second fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-sūtra*, it is stated that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emits a light that universally illuminates incalculable lands in the ten directions, such that all illnesses and all afflictions encounter this light and attain peace and happiness.
...up until the Buddha himself emits the light of the six perfections, whereby those touched receive benefit. Regarding the practitioner of compassion (*karuṇā*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"It is easy to cultivate compassion in the first dhyāna, joy (*muditā*) in the second dhyāna, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the third dhyāna, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the fourth dhyāna.
What is referred to as the cultivation of compassion and so forth consists of these four dharmas: loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; these four are named [the Brahma-vihāras].
The four immeasurable minds are also called the four boundless minds; these are precisely the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the inquiry regarding progress:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, but practice walking meditation in groves, diligently seeking the path of the Buddha.
This single line of inquiry concerns diligence (*vīrya*), which is precisely the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Banzhou) and other such dharma-gates.
Herein, because one seeks only the Buddha-way on a grand scale, the *Pratyutpanna* is cited as the model for practice. *Pratyutpanna* is translated as "the Buddha standing";
this is raised because it is practiced constantly throughout ninety days, serving as the most effective means for removing sleep. Regarding sleep, the *Zhi guan* (Contemplation) states: "The mind..."
When the spirit is dark and obscured, it is called sleep; when the six consciousnesses are blocked and the four elements are relaxed and abandoned, it is called slumber.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it deceives and robs one of clarity.
It is like standing amidst white blades on a battlefield, or sleeping in the same room as a venomous snake. △ Third, the inquiry regarding precepts.
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts and whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is flawless and pure like a precious gem as they seek the path of the Buddha.
This single line of inquiry regarding the precepts states that "majestic deportment is flawless," which refers to the first, the precept of non-deficiency;
and "pure like a precious gem," which refers to the tenth, the ultimate precept. One should know that "non-deficiency" and "ultimacy" are cited here from among the ten precepts.
These ten names for the precepts appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the ten kinds of precepts are:
first, unimpaired; second, unbroken; third, unpierced; fourth, unmixed; fifth, conforming to the Path;
sixth, unattached; seventh, praised by the wise; eighth, sovereign; ninth, conforming to meditative concentration; and tenth, complete. Among these, "unimpaired" refers to this:
The nature of the four *pārājika* offenses is grave; not violating them is "unbroken. The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are "unpierced. The *pāyattika* and other offenses are "unmixed.
These constitute the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*). Following the Path means conforming to principle and seeing the truth without attachment.

This is the praise of wisdom that is untainted by the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), established according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As for the perfection of concentration, this pertains to the Middle Way.

This is because it is clarified [in other sources]. Furthermore, within the Great Sūtra (*Mahā-sūtra*), ten kinds of precepts are also clarified, namely: first, restraint (*saṃvara*); second, purity (*viśuddhi*); third, goodness (*kuśala*);

fourth, non-deficiency (*anupahata*); fifth, non-fracture (*asaṃbheda*); sixth, Mahāyāna (*mahāyāna*); seventh, non-retrogression (*avivartana*); eighth, conformity (*anuloma*); ninth, ultimate (*atyanta*);
and tenth, fulfillment (*paripūrṇa*) of all *pāramitās*. Although the names given in the Sūtra and the Śāstra differ, their meaning is the same.
The same. △ Fourth, the inquiry regarding patience:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who, abiding in the power of patience, are able to endure all the insults and beatings of arrogant people in their quest for the path to Buddhahood.
This one and a half lines inquire about the patience that arises from the Dharma; the power of these two types of patience is as stated in the Āgamas:
"There are six kinds of power: first, the power of a child’s crying; second, the power of a woman’s anger; third, the power of a king’s arrogance;
fourth, the power of an Arhat’s progress; fifth, the power of the Buddhas’ compassion; and sixth, the power of a bhikṣu’s patience. △
Fifth, he asked about dhyāna.
Furthermore, he saw bodhisattvas who had distanced themselves from all frivolous laughter and foolish companions, and who associated with the wise;
with single-mindedness, they eliminated distraction and concentrated their mindfulness in mountain forests for hundreds of thousands of millions of years in order to seek the path of the Buddha.

These two lines further inquire about how meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) abandons frivolous laughter, thereby removing the hindrance of restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*); how it abandons the associates of delusion (*moha*), thereby removing the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*);

how it stays close to the wise, thereby removing the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*); how single-mindedness removes distraction, thereby removing the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*);

and how gathering mindfulness in mountain forests removes the hindrance of torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*). As for what is stated here regarding "abandoning deluded frivolous laughter," it is as described in the *Ratnakūṭa*.
In the Sūtra, Kāśyapa says that because there are four things, one must flee swiftly and abandon them at a distance of more than a hundred yojanas.
What are these four things? First, gain and offerings; second, evil friends; third, evil assemblies;

and fourth, dwelling together with those who engage in much laughter and jesting, or those who are prone to anger and strife. Furthermore, it says that even if one were to strike or cut down all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm...

The offense is still light; however, if one with an evil mind disturbs and confuses a person who has generated the bodhicitta, the transgression of that sin is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater.
△ Six: Question on Dāna (Giving), Part One: Initial Question on Almsgiving.
Or they see Bodhisattvas bestowing a hundred kinds of fine foods, delicacies, and medicinal decoctions upon the Buddha and the Sangha;
giving robes of renowned quality and superior garments worth tens of millions, or even priceless robes, to the Buddha and the Sangha;

and offering billions of varieties of sandalwood jewel pavilions, exquisite bedding, pure gardens with flourishing flowers and fruits, and flowing springs and bathing pools to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Giving to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Regarding these five lines of inquiry on *dāna* (generosity), the first four lines clarify the giving of the four requisites.

As for these four requisites, the first three lines correctly enumerate them; the first line refers to two items, namely food, drink, and medicinal decoctions. The next line clarifies... [text continues]
Regarding clothing, secondly bedding, dwellings, and various items taught in the scriptures— such as bridges, fine wells, gardens, and bathing pools—
if there are currently no bridges and the like, there may instead be pickled vegetables; "fine food" refers to delicacies,
while "named garments" and so forth may be like Kāśyapa’s *kāṣāya* robe in this land, worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, or perhaps like those seen within the Golden Light.

This Āgama states that when Mahākāśyapa wished to renounce the household life, he selected the lowest garment from among those in his home and obtained a tattered robe whose value was still worth one hundred thousand *liang* of gold; he immediately took it to make a *saṃghāṭī*.
At that time, in the center of the great earth of Rājagṛha, there was a *rallaka-kaṇṭhara-rallaka*.
In the interim, there was the Many-Sons Stūpa; it was here that Kāśyapa encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and sought to leave the household life.
He took this very robe and used it as a seat, offering it to the Buddha, who then accepted it. △ Second, the conclusion.
In this way, through such various kinds of giving, they experience subtle and wondrous joy without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
The final line constitutes the conclusion of the intent behind the giving. △ Seventh: Inquiry regarding Prajñā.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescence, instructing and transforming countless sentient beings;

or one may see a bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, like empty space; or one may see a son of the Buddha whose mind is free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
Regarding these three lines of inquiry concerning Prajñā: the first line concerns explaining Prajñā which is inexpressible;

the second line concerns observing Prajñā which is unobservable; and the third line concerns that which is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—this is to discuss Prajñā by explaining the inexpressible and observing the unobservable. △ Sixth, the question regarding the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to the relics and see sons of the Buddha constructing countless *tathāgata*-stūpas—
more numerous than the sands of the Ganges— adorned throughout the realms, with these precious stūpas being five thousand *yojanas* in height and exquisite beauty.
Measuring exactly two thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, each stupa and temple was adorned with a thousand banners and streamers, and draped with jeweled lattices and canopies;
precious bells chimed in harmony as devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly made offerings of incense, flowers, and music.
Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddhas honored the relics and adorned these stupas and temples, such that the entire realm became spontaneously magnificent.
Exquisite and wondrously beautiful, like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.
These seven lines clarify that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas are erected from his relics;

they correctly praise the emergence of Buddhas in other lands during the five turbidities, who, through the single dharma of formlessness, open the gradual and sudden teachings—hence there are two dharmas and three paths of seeds.
The various types of practices and their characteristics differ as seen above.
Now, seeing that the Buddha in another land has entered parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-sons, longing for his virtue, erect trees and build stupas; this signifies the infinite [returning] to the one.
Each emergence from the one signifies the infinite, while the very entry into nirvāṇa is precisely the infinite returning to the one. Thus it is stated in the text.
The first line of the six stanzas provides a general heading concerning the construction of stupas after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
the second line clarifies the number of those stupas; the third line clarifies the dimensions of the stupas;
the fourth line clarifies the characteristics of each stupa; and [the fifth line concerns] the devas and nāgas.
The first line of the fifth section, "The Descent of the Deity," clarifies the offering; the sixth section, beginning with "Mañjuśrī," concludes the intent in two lines.
*Stūpa* is here translated as "square mound" (*fangfen*), similar to the tombs and graveyards of this land. *Mahābhiṣeka* is translated as "grave";
the new [translation] calls it *suduopo*, which means "highly manifest. Furthermore, some say it refers to a "temple. The term "square mound" is established based on its meaning.

This refers to the place where the bodily relics are enshrined. As for the description of the halls, palaces, and sacred edifices—wherein lofty terraces and steep staircases support dew-receptacles that touch the clouds, and tall pillars mark the pure realm for the sake of directing the heart toward the Supreme Sage—and regarding the King of Trees, namely the Pārijātaka tree, which is worshipped with music by devas, nāgas, and spirits:
it is precisely because the *dhātu* (relics) are enshrined within the stūpa that those who make offerings thereby gain merit.

Regarding the layout and arrangement of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Hall, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu Brahmamā stood before him holding a fan to fan the Buddha.
The Buddha then dismissed him, not allowing him to stand in front. Ānanda thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has constantly attended upon the Buddha and provided for his needs without weariness; now, at this final moment, he must [be present]."
"Why have you dismissed those attendants? The Buddha told Ānanda, "Now, within twelve yojanas of Kuśinagara, the devas are so densely packed that they resent this bhikṣu standing before me.
At this final hour, all the devas wish to make offerings, yet this bhikṣu possesses great majesty and radiance."
"It outshines others so that they cannot approach; for this reason, it causes them to retreat. Ānanda asked, "By what causes and conditions does this bodily radiance exist?
The Buddha said, "During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, with a heart of joy, you held a torch in your hand to illuminate that Buddha’s stūpa.
By virtue of this meritorious retribution, your radiance is thus. Even the bodily radiance of the various devas cannot surpass it."
When its fire was lit and it shone in this manner, the rest may be understood by analogy. *Śarīra* is also called *śarīraka*;

this is translated as "bone-body. Furthermore, a *stūpa* is sometimes called *sūdupa*, or *tāpa*, or *dūpa*, or *thūpa*, or *suthūpa*, or *jitedudou*, or *futu*, or *caitya*, or "great mound" (*mahācaya*).
The various distinct names such as *saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*, *brahma-puṣpa*, and others appearing in the sūtras and śāstras are not without basis.
"Equal in length and breadth" means that what is long is considered horizontal; the south and north are called "length" (*dīrgha*), while the east and west are called "breadth" (*vistara*).

"Jeweled lattice curtains" (*maṇi-jāla-vidhāna*) refers to precious jewels interlaced to cover and shield the area above; "curtains" (*vidhāna*) are a type of canopy. Those on the sides are called "screens" (*parikarṣaka*).
The Emperor said: "The precious bells on the carriage canopy chime in harmony; this is what is meant by the musical harmony of the *shijing* (Odes), which says:
'The tinkling bells ring out harmoniously. The *Zuozhuan* states: 'The *xi*, *luan*, *he*, and *ling* bells manifest their sounds. [Section] Two: Requesting an Answer. [Subsection] One:
Raising Doubts and Submitting a Request. [Part] One: Citing What Was Seen in This Land.
When the Buddha emitted a single ray of light, I and the assembled multitude beheld this world-system in its various and wondrous splendors.
First, regarding the vision of the events within this land, it is said that "the white tuft [of hair between the eyebrows] is the basis," hence it is mentioned first;
and because one beholds various phenomena, it is described as "various. △ Second, regarding the vision of events in other lands.
The spiritual power and wisdom of all Buddhas are rare and marvelous; they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.
Next, following the spiritual power of the Buddhas, the events observed in other lands are presented;
this takes the Buddhas as the foundation, thereby subsuming the remaining five [aspects]. △ Third, the request for an answer.
"We have seen this which we have never before encountered; O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.

The phrase "next, for our sake" expresses the intent of the request for an answer. △ Second, the explanation of the anticipated objection, in two parts: first, the direct explanation of the objection.
The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy and reverence; why, O World-Honored One, do you emit this radiance?
Son of the Buddha, please answer now to resolve our doubts and bring us joy. For what benefit do you manifest this light?

Is it because you wish to proclaim the wondrous Dharma attained while seated at the site of enlightenment, or will you bestow predictions of future Buddhahood, reveal the various Buddha-lands adorned with myriad jewels, and allow us to behold the Buddhas?
This is no small matter.
These four lines of text serve to resolve potential objections. Regarding the resolution of objections: within his mind, Mañjuśrī formulates a difficulty and is unwilling to answer immediately;
his intention is threefold: first, this auspicious omen is rare and extraordinary, and it cannot be treated with haste or superficiality.

There is a judgment that these two wisdoms are like the ocean and the humble light; by yielding and elevating, they restrain and solidify, causing those who come before to retreat and giving rise to a multitude of yearning.

Therefore, the hidden objections are rejected by remaining submerged (the term "submerged" means to lie latent). Their meaning is darkly present beneath the text and can be sought through intention; since the objections are met with the convergence of speech, they are called "submerged.

One should know that Mañjuśrī remains darkly and secretly submerged while Maitreya explains with manifest clarity. Regarding the four submerged doubts in the following text, their meaning follows this same principle. Maitreya explains with manifest clarity.
The intent of the objection is threefold: first, the omen is great and the doubt is great; if it is not explained, anxiety will remain in the breast, hindering the hearing of the true teaching.
Second, the assembly is as vast as the ocean, and many have the capacity for understanding in the Benevolent One. Third, the entire multitude gazes upon the Benevolent One;

thus we know that their focused sincerity is profound and earnest, which is why they speak out to resolve the difficulty and request an immediate response. It should be understood that this is a submission to the objection.
This cause arises from a formal request, which says: "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly.
Mañjuśrī then initiates the first refutation of this objection: "You say there are doubts in the assembly, yet the assembly has never doubted;
if they were in doubt, they would ask. Since the assembly does not now doubt, what is there for me to resolve? Maitreya then explains with the first verse: "The fourfold assembly rejoices..."
Looking up in reverence, he said, "May you extend your kindness to me and those like me; may you allow me to question you, O Benevolent One, so that I may obtain your answer.

Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised a second challenge, as there were doubts shared by the assembly that were not easily resolved, awaiting the Buddha’s emergence from meditative absorption before they could be settled.
Maitreya then used the second verse to explain: "If there are doubts lingering in the heart..."
Fearing that the rhinoceros-like [obstinacy] would not be resolved, he responded with a timely reply so that it might be known when the Tathāgata would arise from meditative absorption;
thus he said, "O Son of the Buddha, answer in a timely manner to resolve doubts and bring joy. Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised a third challenge, saying:
"I and you both dwell on the stage of training; we wish to fathom the subtle intent of the Buddha and his lifespan together, yet you alone have been made to answer me."
