The principle was not yet resolved, so Maitreya explained it with the third verse: "I too, with a subtle mind, pondered and hesitated between the two pillars as to whether he would preach the wondrous Dharma or bestow a prediction.

Thus it is said that the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while sitting at the site of enlightenment—would he now preach this, or would he bestow a prediction? Based on this, Mañjuśrī raised the fourth objection. If...
"If it is as you have said, this already resolves the doubt; why trouble me with an answer? Maitreya then explained with the fourth verse, saying:
"How could one use a mind of hesitation to judge such a great matter? To say 'he shows the various Buddha-lands' implies this is no small cause.
Thus, when Mañjuśrī’s challenges were exhausted, his humble radiance also ceased. It is said:
These four "concealed difficulties" (fu-nan) were received by Guangzhai from his predecessor, and his predecessor received them from Master Zhao of the North of the River.
Since these were the ingenious insights of former sages beyond the literal text, they are employed here. △ Second, the conclusion and request.
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are looking toward you, waiting for you to speak on what [the Dharma is].
This is the formal request for instruction, as can be seen in the text. △ Fifth, the answer to the question, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
Regarding the first part, there are four sections; first, the answer through reflection."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and the other great beings, sons of good family, saying: "As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
now intends to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the rain of the Great Dharma,
to blow the conch shell of the Great Dharma, to beat the drum of the Great Dharma, and to expound the meaning of the Great Dharma."

"Vimṛśati" means to contemplate; "vicārayati" means to deliberate. Contemplating the present as it was in the past, and deliberating the past as it is in the present, he intends to preach the Great Dharma—this answers the auspicious sign of preaching the Dharma.

He rains down the rain of the Great Dharma—this answers the auspicious sign of raining flowers. He blows the conch shell of the Great Dharma—this answers the auspicious sign of the great assembly’s joy.
He beats the drum of the Great Dharma—this answers the auspicious sign of the earth’s trembling. He expounds the Great Dharma...
The meaning of the answer is that this is an auspicious omen of the emission of light.

Those who wish to preach the Great Dharma—just as in the past all Buddhas preached immeasurable meanings and subsequently opened up the provisional to reveal the real, gathering the immeasurable back into the One—the present Buddha, having already preached the Dharma, likewise opens up the provisional to reveal the real and unites the immeasurable to return it to the One. That "One" is precisely the Great Dharma; hence the rain of the Great [Dharma].

Regarding the "rain of Dharma," in the past, after the Buddhas rained down the four kinds of flowers from heaven, beings universally entered the causes of perfect enlightenment through the stages of abiding, practicing, and advancing;

since the present Buddha’s raining of flowers likewise constitutes the causes for all to become Buddhas through the stages of abiding, practicing, and advancing, it is said that he rains the great rain of Dharma.
Regarding the "blowing of the great Dharma conch," in the past, the fourfold assembly saw the auspicious omen and rejoiced.
Having attained what was never before attained, obstructions were removed and their spiritual capacities were stirred; they immediately reformed their persons, teachings, practices, and principles.

Considering that the assembly is now joyful, it must also be that obstructions have been removed and their capacities stirred, leading them to reform their persons, teachings, practices, and principles. Since that which has been reformed is profound, it is said that "the great Dharma-conch is blown.
As for "beating the great Dharma-drum," previously, after the earth shook, there were six occasions on which the [obstructions] were destroyed.
The wise thief reflects that after the Buddha’s ground has now shaken in six ways, he too shall likewise shatter the delusions of ignorance;

because his voice and teaching are supremely wondrous, it is said that he "beats the great Dharma drum. As for the "expounding of the great Dharma meaning," it is simply that just as the Buddhas of the past emitted light from the white tuft between their brows before preaching the Lotus Sūtra—wherein the path of this and that is identical—the present Buddha, having likewise emitted light, [acts in the same way].
Later, the five Buddhas’ paths are explained in detail; since these are all Buddha-paths, it is said that they "expound the great Dharma-meaning.
Thus, these five phrases are entirely [based on] judging the present by the past and inferring the present by the past, where the text is harmonized with the meaning.

Only the single auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is slightly lacking; as for the rain of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emission of light, these all occur because of entering concentration—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, there is no need for further doubt. Now, let us provide a further analysis: the first line is the general [statement], while the subsequent four lines are the specific [explanations].
The "Great Dharma" (*mahādharma*) is the general; "rain," "blowing," "striking," "spreading," "opening," "showing," "awakening," and "entering" are the specifics.
It is like the sky, which is neither small nor large, and neither red nor white, yet rains down flowers that are both red and white—just as with the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).
It is not that one attains "opening, showing, awakening, and entry" merely upon seeing this principle; rather, it is like a seed that sprouts when it receives rain.

Now, having heard the great rain of the Dharma, the seeds of the *dharmatā* are moistened, the husks of ignorance are shattered, and the Buddha-knowledge and vision of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are opened.
It is like blowing a conch shell to signal a change of era; what is now and what was before are already [one].
Having attained the Ten Abodes, one now hears the Dharma from the perspective of the Ten Abodes and transforms this to enter the Ten Practices, thereby manifesting the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

It is like beating a drum to signal the soldiers; what was previously in the Ten Practices is now, through hearing the Dharma from the Ten Practices, signaled to enter the Ten Transferences and awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To "expound" means to spread it out horizontally and broaden it, while to "unfurl" means to extend it vertically and deepen it.

This is indeed an exposition of the meaning: what was previously in the Ten Stages of Devotion (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*) is now, from the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), entering the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), exhausting the source and reaching the limit, profound, vast, and fully complete.

Just as after the six omens of old, there was the opening, showing, awakening, and entering, one should infer that after the present omen, it should likewise be so. △ Second, a brief account of what was previously seen.
He replied:
"Good sons, in the past I have witnessed this omen among the Buddhas of the past; having emitted such light, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so, desiring that all sentient beings may attain it."
This auspicious sign was manifested because he has heard and known the Dharma that is difficult for all the worlds to believe.
Previously, he reflected upon it through his own wisdom; now, having briefly experienced it, it is somewhat clearer than before.
This is raised to answer the question regarding other lands. The five auspicious signs of this land do not extend to other lands; there is only the single sign of emitting light.

Because it illuminates the eastern direction, we know that this is a brief response based on what was previously seen; since it specifically answers regarding the emission of light, we know it is an answer to the question concerning other lands.
Seeing now as one saw in the past, and the past being exactly like the present, [the Buddha] desires to cause all sentient beings to hear and know this.
Thus, the two wisdoms of hearing and contemplation, as well as the two practices of faith and Dharma, encompass the immeasurable and unify the three.

Based on the sixfold refutation of ignorance and so forth through the principles of the teachings, and because all Buddhas equally reveal, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is said that "this is a dharma difficult for all the world to believe. △ Third, the detailed answer concerning what was previously seen, in three parts:
first, citing the same account from one Buddha; first, clarifying the time period.

"O sons of good family, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, I previously gave a detailed answer that was even more distinct than this brief one. This detailed response addresses the questions concerning this world and other worlds.
Maitreya, by means of the light, saw horizontally toward the east and thus formulated his question; Mañjuśrī, by citing the past, saw vertically and thus provided the answer."
Whether read horizontally or vertically, this reveals that the paths of all Buddhas are identical. In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Subhūti asks the Buddha:

"What is the distinction between the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and the boundless (*ananta*? The Buddha replied: "The 'incalculable' refers to that which does not fall within the realm of calculation;
it does not fall among either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) natures. As for the 'immeasurable,' its measure cannot be..."
Whether measured in the past, the future, or the present, all are immeasurable and boundless; the limits and depths of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Since they are said to be immeasurable and boundless, they are thus inconceivable, beyond comparison, and difficult to describe.
The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* translates here as "an incalculable period of time."
Section Two: Identical in Name.

At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

There is a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp-Bright). This refers to the identity of their designated names; if one asks about their general titles, they may be considered identical. How are their specific names the same?
The answer is that this should be explained by the principle that while the names differ, the meanings are the same.

Why is this so? Because "sun" represents wisdom (*prajñā*) and "moon" represents concentration (*samādhi*); concentration and wisdom are the virtues of one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti-guṇa*), while "lamp-bright" represents the virtue of transforming others (*parārtha-guṇa*). Through these, [the Buddha's qualities] are fully expressed.

The Capable Sage (Nengren) possesses both meditative concentration and wisdom, and is further capable of benefiting both himself and others; he is also like the sun, moon, and lamp—these are the three types of wisdom. Now, the Buddha likewise possesses these three types of wisdom.
While their designations differ according to conditions, their essential meaning is not distinct; therefore, it is said that their names are the same. The Record states:

"Regarding the 'universal title,' since the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) possesses all ten titles, it is called 'universal. From the perspective of the dharma-body (dharmakāya), it may also be established as such based on its meaning in relation to the response-body. I [the author] say: so it is.

Since this present body is itself the Dharma-body, one should know that its title ought to be "the One who is the Dharma" (Jífǎ). However, in establishing the title "Dharma," it must be derived from the Dharma itself.
As the second fascicle of the *Zhíguān* commentary states: "Because one comes by means of non-dual wisdom to accord with the true realm, one is called 'Tathāgata' (Thus-Come-One).
Because one universally enters all dharmas through the principle of non-duality, one is named 'Arhat' (Worthy of Offerings), having realized non-duality."
The essence of wisdom is impartial, thus it is called "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).

Knowing that non-dual dharmas interpenetrate the dharma-realm, and though there is no coming or going, penetrating throughout the three periods of time, it is called "One Endowed with Clarity and Conduct" (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*). The non-dual nature of reality is darkly harmonized with the three virtues, thus it is called "Well-Gone" (*sugata*).
Its principle pervades all things and possesses the understanding of the three worlds; because one understands this principle, it is called "Knower of the World" (*loka-vid*). It is capable of...

To understand this principle without anything surpassing it is called being a "Supreme Being" (Anuttara-puruṣa). To understand this principle and be able to tame those difficult to tame—taming the ten dharma realms—is called being a "Tamer" (Vināyaka).
To realize the dharmas of the dharma realm is called being a "Great Man" (Mahāpuruṣa). Because one accords with this principle, all honor and look up to one;
because one transcends the three teachings and the realms of humans and devas, one is called a "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām). Because one awakens to this principle...
He is named "Buddha" because he has realized this principle; thus, he is the one venerated by the three periods of time and is called the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*).
Because his wisdom accords with the Dharma-body and he possesses the title of the Dharma-realm, he is able to manifest the ten titles of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

One should know that the ten titles of the Dharma-body and the response-body are of one essence and not two. △ Third, the commonality of the preaching of the Dharma, part three: first, clarifying the initial teaching of the sudden [Dharma].

Likewise, he expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated,
and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life of Brahma-faring.
To expound the True Dharma that is good in the beginning, middle, and end is precisely the initial opening of the Sudden Teaching’s seven excellences (*saptasu-kalyāṇa*).

While the term "seven excellences" applies generally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, according to the present text, it refers specifically to the Mahāyāna seven excellences. Regarding "good in the beginning, middle, and end":

the introduction, main body, and conclusion of the Sudden Teaching are called the excellence of timing (*kāla-sauṣṭhava*) because their significance is profound and far-reaching. As for "its meaning is profound and far-reaching," it is...
This is the principle of the definitive meaning of the sudden teaching; because the two vehicles cannot fathom its limits or depths, it is called "profound and far-reaching.

This is what is meant by "excellence of meaning. Its phrasing is skillful and subtle, being that which issues from the eightfold voice of the sudden teaching. It directly explains the realization of the principle and delights the minds of Bodhisattvas;
thus, the text of the sudden teaching is called "excellence of expression. It is pure and without admixture, not [to be confused with]...

The shared practice of the two vehicles constitutes the Sudden Teaching; that which is uniquely and fully endowed with goodness is the Sudden Teaching of the complete *maṃtra* (full-syllable) dharmas within and beyond the realms.
That which is perfectly pure and wholesome is free from the defilements of the two extremes;
this is the Sudden Teaching of harmonious flexibility. Master Nanyue said: "This is the excellence of practice, the characteristic of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."

"Brahmā" refers to the无缘 (unconditioned) benevolence and compassion of the Sudden Teaching; furthermore, the interpretations of "goodness in the beginning, middle, and end" differ. Here, we follow one particular tradition:
in the Hīnayāna, the three goodnesses are defined as precept, concentration, and wisdom; in the Mahāyāna, they are defined as the good mind in the beginning, middle, and end.
Moreover, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light Most Victorious King Sutra), fascicle four, states: "The former mind is the Tathāgata..."
In the midst of the inconceivable, the Tathāgata’s various adornments follow the Tathāgata’s indestructible mind;

this is also the meaning of the three virtues. Mañjuśrī cites the sudden teaching of the seven virtues of the ancient Buddhas, which is identical to the seven virtues suddenly taught by the present Buddha, and also identical to the initial sudden teaching in other lands; for this reason, he uses this as his answer.

This refers to the response given by Maitreya above; according to the *Guang*, he cross-examined regarding the Buddhas of other lands, saying that the Holy King Siṃha’s exposition of the Dharma is subtle and supreme.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī cited his past [encounter] as an answer. This is identical to the first Buddha’s teaching of the sudden Dharma (*dunfa*).
△ Second, clarifying the identity in the opening of the gradual Dharma (*kaijian tong*).
For those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Four Noble Truths for the purpose of crossing over birth, old age, sickness, and death to ultimate nirvāṇa;

for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for all bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Six Pāramitās.

To those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka who should be taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, it is identical to the gradual teaching opened after the initial sudden teaching by the Buddhas of antiquity.

Therefore, since the previous question asked how one should speak of Nirvāṇa to those who encounter suffering, I now cite the Buddhas of antiquity who likewise opened this gradual teaching to answer that question. To those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, one should speak of the Ten [Stages].

The second section, on the Dharma of Dependent Origination, answers the question regarding those with merit who seek the supreme Dharma by explaining that one should practice the six *pāramitās* for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
it answers the question regarding the Buddha-sons practicing various deeds by citing the gradual teachings opened by past buddhas;
and it answers the question regarding seeing other lands by extensively citing those who have previously seen such buddhas. These are explained as they correspond [to the questions].

This refers to the principle that the Dharma corresponds to the capacity [of the recipient], and the capacity accords with the Dharma. △ Third, the clarification that the Sudden and the Gradual are identical:
it causes [beings] to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
"Causing them to attain *sambodhi* and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)":
this clarifies that after the ancient Buddhas had taught the sudden and gradual [approaches], they immediately revealed the teaching of the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

This is merely an answer to Maitreya’s question regarding the construction of stupas after witnessing the parinirvāṇa of Buddhas in other lands. By citing the ancient Buddhas’ preaching up to the six *pāramitās*, it clarifies the present [teaching].
The Buddha has already been identical to those of the past; having attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he now proceeds toward the light. Thus, the present Buddha shall be identical to those of the past.
2. Citing the Identity of Twenty Thousand Buddhas:
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa; next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Thus, these twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa, and the same clan name, Bharadvāja. Maitreya,
you should know that from the first Buddha to the last, they were all identical in name as Candrasūryapradīpa,
fully endowed with the ten titles, and the Dharma they taught was excellent in its beginning, middle, and end.
Next, he cites the names of twenty thousand Buddhas; their preaching of the Dharma is entirely the same as that of the first cited Buddha.

While the initial citation of one Buddha fully enumerates both sudden and gradual teachings, the subsequent enumeration of twenty thousand Buddhas mentions only the sudden teaching. Thus, it is said to be "good in the beginning, middle, and end.
Later, when citing one Buddha, he mentions only the opening of the gradual teaching. These are mutual citations; the former can be understood by referring back [to the latter], and vice versa.
The reason for not citing the twenty thousand Buddhas of the past is that they all taught the Dharma using names;
since this present case relies on the meaning for convenience, it is so stated. *Phalada* translates as "swift," "sharp-witted" (*tīkṣṇendriya*), or "full speech.

Furthermore, according to the *Benxing ji jing* (Sūtra on the Collection of Past Deeds), it is translated as "Heavy Banner," which is one of the eighteen clans of the Brahmins. △ Third, citing the final [Buddha].
The first Buddha was identical to the three [subsequent ones] in his initial experiences, which were the same as those of the present.

When that last Buddha had not yet left the household life, there were eight princes: the first was named Meaningful Intent (*Cittamati*), the second Good Intent (*Sucittamati*), the third Immeasurable Intent (*Apramāṇacittamati*), the fourth Jewel Intent (*Ratnacittamati*), the fifth Increasing Intent (*Vardhamānacittamati*), the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Intent (*Vimativinodacittamati*), and the seventh...
Ghoṣamati was the eighth; these eight princes possessed majestic power and sovereignty, each ruling over four continents.

When these princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal thrones and likewise followed him into the homeless life.
They resolved upon the Mahāyāna, constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and all became Dharma-preachers. Having already [passed] a thousand...
The roots of all virtues were planted by ten thousand Buddhas;
the last of these Buddhas had eight princes, which is a matter witnessed in the past that is identical to the present.
Although the number of sons differs—the former Buddha had eight while the present Buddha has one—they both emerged from and dwell within the same land. As for that land:

There are two views: one holds that both [the birth of] a son and the matter of having a son signify the same thing; the other holds that they respond to different conditions and thus signify different things.

The birth of one son signifies the purity of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), while the birth of eight sons signifies the Eightfold Noble Path. Although their numbers differ, their underlying meaning is the same;
here, we take the sense of "having a son" as being identical. Furthermore, in the past, the sons of the Buddha left the household life and resolved upon the Mahāyāna. Now...

The Buddha’s disciples abide in the fruits of the Small Vehicle; how can this be the same as those of the past? Because the Buddha’s transformative path was already completed, he manifested his original state to reveal his fundamental reality;
thus it is said that they have now resolved their minds on the Great Vehicle. Previously, their true origins were not revealed, so they were still called Arhats.

When their original nature is later revealed in the text below, they are shown to be Bodhisattvas; the meaning is then identical. △ Second, the events witnessed in the past compared with the present. Now...
The first two points regarding the initial manifestation of signs are identical; the first two points clarifying the six auspicious omens in this land are likewise identical.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Ananta-artha*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he immediately sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered into the state of immeasurable [samādhi].

In this samādhi of the locus of meaning, his body and mind were unmoving. At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways. At that time, among those in the assembly were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [upāsikās, and devas].
The upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all the minor kings, universal monarchs (cakravartin), and other such great assemblies, having attained what they had never experienced before,
rejoiced with palms joined and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion. At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The light of these marks illuminated the eighteen thousand Buddha-lands of the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.

The six auspicious omens that previously appeared in the Buddha’s own land were entirely identical to those of the present, following the same sequence as described in the text. △ Second, clarifying that the six auspicious omens in other lands are the same.
"What we see now are these Buddha-lands.

By stating that the six auspicious omens in other lands were "just as what is seen now," one knows that the six auspicious omens in other lands during the time of past Buddhas were likewise identical to those of the present.
△ Second, resolving doubts through commonality.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time there were twenty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly who desired to hear this Dharma.

When these bodhisattvas saw this light universally illuminating the Buddha-land, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the causes and conditions for the purpose of this light.

However, in the ancient *Mingbie xu* (Preface on Clarifying the Distinctions), there are only two sections—the "Manifestation of Signs" (*xiànxiàng*) and the "Suspending Doubts" (*huáiyí*—the same as the *Tóng*).

It lacks the three sections consisting of the "Gathering of the Assembly," "Posing Questions," and "Providing Answers. By logical inference, these must exist: since it mentions preaching the Dharma, we know the assembly must have gathered;

since it speaks of suspending doubts, we know there must have been questions; and if questions are answered, the other two [sections] must necessarily be present. Thus, the three sections are identical in both cases.
Furthermore, if one were to recount the former response, there would be no need for Mañjuśrī to expend further words;

since neither the answer nor the question was explicitly stated, the meaning is readily understandable. Nevertheless, this single passage contains three distinct meanings, which I shall now explain as a single section.
To clarify their sequence, please refer to the previous outline. △ Third: Past Experiences Are Identical to the Present.
Sixth, first clarifying the similarity of the causes:
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples.

Just as the former Buddha attained enlightenment through the preaching of the sutra by Wonderful Light, so too did the present Buddha attain enlightenment through the preaching of the sutra by Śāriputra. This is the point of similarity.
How should one understand this similarity? One should know that the past cause was Subhūti and the present cause is Śāriputra; these are precisely the persons through whom [the Dharma] is received.

Furthermore, in the past, when the Buddha’s eight sons studied under the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, the Buddha arose from meditative concentration and addressed Prabhāsa, as well as entrusting him with the teachings.
Now, the Buddha’s son Rāhula also studies under Śāriputra; the Buddha likewise arises from meditative concentration and addresses him.
When the section on the Trace Gate (Ji-men) concludes, [the Buddha] again entrusts [the Dharma] to Śāriputra. Whether ancient or modern, who could surpass this?
Yet, to abandon Śāriputra in favor of Bhaiṣajyarāja seems remote; those who doubt say that while Miaoguang was a bodhisattva and Śāriputra was a śrāvaka, how can they be the same?
Their past deeds were already manifest when he was discussed as a bodhisattva, but his present state has not yet been revealed.
To set forth the Way is the voice of a *śrāvaka*, yet to reveal one’s true station (*yíjí*), Śāriputra is a great *bodhisattva*—how could he be otherwise?

As for what was called "the former manifestation of Prabhāsa," why must he not have acted as a *śrāvaka*? This is merely Mañjuśrī’s skillful use of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*), concealing and manifesting himself at will.
Regarding the term "disciple" (*dìzǐ*), the *Jìngmíng shū* states: "The teacher possesses the capacity to mold and perfect; the learner..."
There is the virtue of being a *zī* (disciple) and a *bǐng* (recipient). As for being a *zī*, one leaves one's father to follow a teacher, revering the teacher as one would a father;
the teacher’s humility and yielding toward the *zī* are like those of an elder brother toward a younger brother. △ Second, the names of the teachings are identical.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi and, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Meghasvararāja, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
which teaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
The names of the teachings are identical and can be understood according to the text. However, previously, when Maitreya saw other lands, he first saw them suddenly and then gradually;
later, he saw various modes of practice, followed by the absence of objects, and finally the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
Now, in this passage, Mañjuśrī answers that he has seen the Buddha: first suddenly, then gradually, and finally through various modes of practice, at which point he sees [the truth].
After the six auspicious omens of this and that [land] in the Lotus Sūtra, the Dharma of the Lotus was preached; immediately following the preaching of the Lotus, he entered nirvana.
This clearly and definitively answers the question regarding other lands. △ Third, the identity of the time periods.
For sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat, and those in the assembly who were listening likewise sat in one place for sixty minor kalpas with body and mind unmoving,
listening to the Buddha’s discourse as if it were the duration of a single meal; at that time,
there was not a single person among the multitude whose body or mind experienced weariness or fatigue.
Regarding the identity of their time periods, as stated in the following text: "fifty minor kalpas are said to be like half a day," this refers to their being identical.
The *Ji* (Commentary) states that "sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal";

although sixty and fifty, or the duration of a meal and half a day, seem slightly different in number, they are all instances of the long appearing as the short, and thus they are called "identical. Master Sengsheng asked: "How can it be..."

In reality, because he intended to emphasize the gravity of the Dharma, he merely used the expression "borrowing time" as a metaphor. If one were to say he was borrowing time, it should have been stated as "like sixty minor kalpas";
how could he simply say "sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal"? This is merely a matter of conventional perception;
it is not that the time is actually short. △ Fourth, the same applies to the proclamation of his passing into extinction.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he then declared these words before the assembly of Brahmās,
Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras: "This very day, at midnight,
the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."

Regarding those who proclaim the entry into extinction: in the past, when he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he likewise proclaimed his entry into extinction, just as Kāśyapa Buddha did (and so forth).
Now, in the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*), it is clarified that the Tathāgata will before long enter *nirvāṇa*, for his work of transformation and guidance is complete;

thus, the matter of proclaiming extinction is identical. The record states that "Brahmā, Māra, and others": Brahmā is the lord of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and also the lord of the three realms.
Māra is the lord of desire; "śramaṇa" (沙門) is translated here as "diligent in cessation," meaning one who diligently ceases evil. "Brāhmaṇa" (婆羅門) is translated as "pure conduct.
Among non-Buddhists, those who have left the household life are called "those of pure conduct. Here, first, the two lords—form and desire—are mentioned;

the four castes are cited to represent excellence; and the six realms are designated to signify goodness. Furthermore, among these, the superior ones are mentioned while the remaining evil realms are omitted for brevity.
It is easy for all to enter the Buddha-dharma; as it was in ancient times, so it is now with the present Buddha. As the sutra below states:
"At that moment, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernatural powers, received the great assembly and placed them all in space, and with a great voice he addressed the assembly:
'Who among you is able to extensively expound this [teaching] in this Sahā world?'"
The present moment is precisely that time; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa. However, although the Buddha now proclaims his extinction, he does not immediately pass away;

thus it is said he will "not be long" [in this world]. This is because, while in this defiled land, he must preach the "ransom for life" in order to gather in [sentient beings], and he upholds the Vinaya and discusses the eternal to cause him to abide long, employing provisional means as well.

Because the provisional clarifies the real and assists in the manifestation of the real, it possesses the utility of the real; because the power of the provisional is revealed through the power of the real, it transcends both permanence and impermanence;

because the beginning and end are one, the form-body and the eternal body are without birth or extinction; thus, although these aspects differ, the proclamation of nirvana and other such matters are identical.
△ Fifth, the prophecy is the same.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This Bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a Buddha, and his name shall be Viśuddhakāya Tathāgata, Arhat..."
"Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha. To bestow a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is what the holy words describe as "granting the fruit"; to record the aspiration of the mind is called a "prediction.

When one considers that the Buddha previously bestowed a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Guṇasaṃbhava, whereas this present sutra bestows a prediction upon the Śrāvaka Śāriputra, how could these two be the same? One must know that in the past...

Since the task has been accomplished, the statement that the Bodhisattva is given a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is precisely the point where the three [vehicles] are unified and the Śrāvakas obtain their prediction.
If one were to say that the prediction for the Śrāvakas was granted in the past, what further discourse would there be once the Buddha has arisen from his meditative concentration?
It is simply that Mañjuśrī’s skillful discourse does not reveal his true origins. *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*). *Arhat*... [text fragment ends]
"Ho" (Arhat) is translated here as "Worthy of Offerings"; "Samyak-saṃbuddha" is translated here as "Perfectly All-Knowing. These are simply three of the ten titles [of a Buddha].
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: "If I were to analyze the meaning of these three phrases, I would not finish even at the end of an eon."
△ Sixth, after the extinction [of the Buddha], the sutra is transmitted, identical to the first five [sections]. First, it clarifies the time:
after the Buddha had given his prediction, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at midnight.
This passage has three parts: first, the time, which refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. △ Second, it identifies the person.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhāpāla) upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The second appearance of this person was none other than Wonderful Light himself. △ Third, clarifying the duration and proximity [of his lifespans].
He preached for humans for a full eighty minor kalpas.

"Three times, long and short" refers precisely to these eighty minor kalpas. △ Fourth, clarifying the assembly of those transformed; this has two parts, the first of which clarifies those who were already established as disciples.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all became disciples of Prabhāsa; Prabhāsa taught and transformed them, causing them to become firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha.
The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.

Those who have already attained perfection are the eight sons who achieved their practice long ago and have already become Buddhas. △ Second, clarifying those who shall attain perfection as disciples:
Among the eight hundred disciples, there was one named *Yaśaskāma* (Seeker of Fame), who was greedily attached to gain and offerings.
Although he recited many sutras, he did not master them and forgot much; therefore, he was called "Seeker of Fame. This person also planted various [roots of merit]...

By virtue of the causes and conditions of his roots of goodness, he encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them.

Furthermore, "fang" (方) means "esoteric," and "bian" (便) means "subtle"; thus, subtle penetration into the esoteric is precisely the true secret point within the garment.
The priceless jewel and the single jewel upon the king’s head are non-dual and indistinguishable;
the hired laborer and the son of the elder are likewise non-dual and indistinguishable. Such words are secret and sublime, as the sutra says:
"Only I know this mark, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak of my Dharma."

Because it is wondrous and inconceivable, it is explained through the "secret" (mi); and because it is explained through the "wondrous" (miao), this precisely accords with the intent of the present chapter;
thus, it is called the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) Chapter. Regarding the ten pairs of the provisional and the real: first, phenomenon and principle;

second, principle and teaching; third, teaching and practice; fourth, bondage and liberation; fifth, cause and fruit; sixth, essence and function; seventh, gradual and sudden; eighth, opening and closing; ninth, general and particular.
Regarding these ten *siddhāntas*, they are further explained in detail through eight perspectives— such as the sequence of arising, the provisional and the real,
and the fundamental and the manifested— yet they do not transcend the meaning of the causes and effects of one’s own practice, and the subject and object of transforming others.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text has two parts: first, a brief opening of the three to reveal the one; second, an extensive opening of the three to reveal the one.

The first part [the brief opening] further has two sections: first, a brief opening of the three to reveal the one; second, the movement of attachments and the arising of doubt. The first of these [the brief opening] further has two sections:

first, praising the two wisdoms through words; second, praising them beyond words. The first of these [praising through words] further has two sections: first, praising the two wisdoms by way of metaphorical expression; second, praising them beyond words.
The first section of the "Two Wisdoms" (Erzhi) also has two parts: first, praising the provisional and real [wisdom] of all Buddhas; second, praising the provisional and real [wisdom] of Śākyamuni.
The first of these [two praises] further has three parts: first, a double praise; first, the narrative by the Sūtra compiler.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Mañjuśrī had finished answering the questions. He asked: "The Buddha is constantly in meditative concentration;
for what reason do you say he 'arises'? He replied: "This is for the sake of instruction. When the Buddhas of antiquity preached this sūtra, they would invariably first enter [samādhi]."

The meaning of "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is that the Buddha is likewise now in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), entering it to take the principle as his object and settle his mind in the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

Upon emerging from concentration, he causes others to likewise settle their minds in the true reality; because he first establishes himself in the true reality before arising to transform others, it is said that he "arises with composure.
He addresses Śāriputra because, among those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), he is foremost in wisdom, and [the Buddha] intends to refute [his views] by means of him.
Because the small wisdom reveals the great wisdom, he first informs them to stir the multitude. △ Second, the formal praise of the two wisdoms;
first, the praise of the wisdom of reality:
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable."
True wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is precisely the wisdom of all Buddhas; it is not the provisional or ultimate [wisdom] used by the three types of teachers to transform others.

Therefore, "all Buddhas" is said to manifest their own practice of realization, while "wisdom" is said to clarify the essence of that realization. The substance of this wisdom is the one mind and threefold wisdom (*tri-jñāna*), which is profoundly deep and immeasurable—this is a term of praise.

It clarifies that the Buddha’s true wisdom penetrates vertically to the very bottom of the principle of reality (*tathatā*); therefore, it is said: [The passage continues: "...it is called... (as per the original fragment).
Because it is profoundly deep and extends horizontally to the very limits of the *dharmadhātu*, it is called "immeasurable. This immeasurable profundity is high vertically and broad horizontally;

just as deep roots result in luxuriant branches and a distant source results in a long-flowing stream, so it is with real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is likewise. 2. Praising Expedient Wisdom.
This gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know.

This gate of wisdom is precisely a praise of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). It is called a "gate" because it serves as a preliminary skillful means (*pūrvayoga*) for one’s own practice, possessing the power of progressive advancement.
By entering through this gate, one arrives at the Way; within the Way, it is termed the "Way of Reality" (*bhūtārtha-mārga*).

The preceding passage—describing the provisional [teachings] as difficult to understand and difficult to enter—is an expression of praise for the provisional; it means that they are realized without deliberation and constitute a boundlessly great function (*mahāprayoga*) that cannot be fathomed by the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).
One understands them only upon beginning the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*) and entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

thus, one may know that while the beginning and the end are mentioned, the intermediate stages are difficult to demonstrate and difficult to awaken to. Furthermore, it specifically mentions those things which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to attain.

It is known that because their attachments were so heavy, they were specifically refuted; for the original intent of the Dharmakāya was to employ provisional and ultimate teachings for one's own practice, yet as they lacked the capacity to respond, they fled, and thus it is said they "did not know.
Because the *Avataṃsaka* provides sudden illumination, those who are deaf, mute, and blind cannot perceive it, and thus it is said they "did not know.

Because the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) employs censure and rebuke, they remained in their thatched huts, and thus it is said they "did not know. Finally, when the *Prajñā* was used to convert others through teaching, [they likewise did not know].
Because they lack the intention to seek even a single morsel of food, it is said that they do not know. Now, as the great capacity is awakened, light is emitted and the earth shakes;
since the paths of the Buddhas of this and other ages are identical, yet they still harbor doubts, it is said that they do not know.

Those bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who can understand according to their respective stages do so, while those of dull faculties who are equal to the two vehicles likewise do not know. △ Second, the dual explanation.
Second, first explaining true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Why is this? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas and has fully practiced the immeasurable path-dharmas of all those Buddhas.
Why is this so? This is the phrase that introduces the dual crowning of the two types of wisdom.

That "the Buddha once drew near to and exhausted the practice of the Dharma" explains the reason for the true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) of all Buddhas. Because he encountered Buddhas externally and received many essential teachings, his true wisdom is profoundly deep;
this is truly due to the purity and thickness of his internal practice and his exhaustion of the path of the Dharma. Therefore, it is true wisdom.
"Immeasurable and immeasurable" explains the horizontal breadth; "profound" explains the vertical height. △ Second, the explanation of expedient wisdom:
"Valiant and diligent, his fame is heard everywhere."
"His courageous diligence and fame are heard everywhere" means that these are the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas;
the gate of his wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. It is precisely because of his courageous diligence that he is able to enter this gate so difficult to enter.

Having entered the gate, his benefits spread throughout the infinite [world], and because beings revere his supreme virtue, his fame is heard everywhere. This may also be explained by dividing the phrases.
That "valiant diligence can enter the Dharma-gate" explains the profundity of the provisional wisdom; that "its profound fame is universally heard" explains the vastness of the provisional wisdom.
Although the provisional text contains no explicit words regarding profundity and vastness, this meaning can be established by analogy with the true wisdom.
△ Third, the double conclusion: first, concluding the true wisdom.
He has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas.

Because he has reached the ultimate limit in accordance with principle, it is said that he has "accomplished" them; because he has reached the bottom of the other shore, it is said that they are "profound.
This concludes the establishment of true wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). △ Second, the conclusion of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
The intended meaning of what is taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.

Because it accords with capacities and meets [the needs of beings], it is said to be "according to what is appropriate"; because it is not known by those at the stage of the seven expedients (*saptopāya*), it is said to be "difficult to understand.
This concludes the establishment of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). △ Second, explaining the provisional and the real of Śākyamuni. Part one: first, a double eulogy. First, the eulogy.
True Wisdom. Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have praised true wisdom;
for if true wisdom were not perfected, the Way of the Buddha could not be accomplished.
Since it is said that "attaining Buddhahood once is to attain all," this is a praise of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). △ Second, a praise of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*):

Through various causes and conditions and various parables, he extensively expounds the verbal teachings; by means of countless skillful means, he guides sentient beings and causes them to leave behind all attachments.
The following section on "various causes and conditions" is a praise of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). For more than forty years, [the Buddha] has transformed others through three modes;
because he adapts both the provisional and the real to meet the needs of sentient beings, he speaks of "various causes and conditions and parables. Regarding these parables:

the Hīnayāna takes the plantain tree and water bubbles as metaphors, while the Mahāyāna takes the city of the *gandharva* and mirror-illusions as metaphors. According to various sūtras and śāstras, this refers to the Hīnayāna.
The vehicle is likened to milk, while the Mahāyāna is likened to the clarified butter (ghṛta).

The "extensive exposition" refers to the ability to derive immeasurable meanings from a single dharma through innumerable skillful means—namely, the seven kinds of skillful means. It guides sentient beings to cause them to leave behind all attachments:

it teaches the ten wholesome actions in their dispersed form to lead them away from attachment to the three miserable realms; it teaches the ten wholesome actions in their concentrated form to lead them away from attachment to the desire realm; and it teaches the three [vehicles].

The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is taught to be free from attachment to views and thoughts; the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is taught to be free from attachment to *nirvāṇa*; and the Buddha-Dharma is taught to be free from attachment to the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path. △ Second, the dual explanation:
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the *pāramitās* of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.

This pair explains the two wisdoms: "Tathāgata" (Thus Come One) explains the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), meaning that because he attains the Buddha-way by emerging from the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*), he is called Tathāgata;

"expedient means" (*upāya*) explains the wisdom of skillful means (*prajñā-upāya-jñāna*), meaning that due to his skillful expediency, he is able to teach through various causes and conditions. "Knowledge and vision of the *pāramitā*" refers to...

This pair [of terms] refers to the knowledge and vision of both the provisional and the real: "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called "real knowledge," and the "Buddha-eye" is called "real vision";

"knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*) is called "provisional knowledge," and the "Dharma-eye" is called "provisional vision. Because they have all reached the ultimate limit of both phenomena and principle, they are all termed *pāramitās*.
To say that "all are already perfected" means that both the provisional and the real are fully consummated. △ Third, the pair.
The first part of the summary: the summary of the wisdom of reality.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is vast and profound.

This pair of summaries for the two types of wisdom—the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—was already clarified in the preceding text; here, by saying "vast," it clarifies the horizontal [comprehensiveness].
Profound, far-reaching, luminous, and vertical—such true wisdom is neither horizontal nor vertical; it is expressed through words as a tribute to its excellence.
Discussing its horizontality and verticality, its illumination is boundless and infinite, like a large box requiring a large lid. △ Second, the conclusion on provisional wisdom.

With immeasurable, unimpeded powers, fearlessnesses, meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis, he penetrates the boundless and accomplishes all unprecedented dharmas.

"Immeasurable and unimpeded" below immediately concludes the provisional wisdom; this refers to the skillful means of the provisional path as practiced by himself, specifically regarding the preliminary preparations (*pūrvayoga*).
Because all dharmas are gateways, one knows that this is the manifestation of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); one should know that true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) has no diversity.
"Immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) of the Buddha-ground; "unimpeded" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) of the Buddha-ground.

Being able to produce from a single word or a single meaning an immeasurable flow of eloquence without exhaustion—when compared to other bodhisattvas who have attained penetration—it is like a fingernail.
"Superior earth" corresponds to the power of the earth; "power" refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*); "fearlessness" refers to the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*);
"dhyāna" refers to the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of dhyāna; "samādhi" refers to the Śūraṅgama-samādhi; and "samāpatti" refers to the King Samādhi.
"Entering deeply into the boundless" concludes the vertical depth, while "accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas" concludes the horizontal breadth.
△ Second, praising the two wisdoms beyond words. 2. First, presenting the reason for praising them beyond words. 2.1. First, presenting the reason for praising them beyond words:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and explain all dharmas with supple and gentle speech that is pleasing and agreeable."
The minds of the assembly.
To raise again the distinction between the provisional and the ultimate as the basis for words that transcend speech is to express profound earnestness; it signifies great solicitude.
That the Tathāgata is able to skillfully discern and eloquently expound all dharmas refers to the raising of the provisional; his speech is gentle and soft, pleasing to the multitude.
The term "mind" (*citta*) refers to the actual reality, as stated in the preceding passage where, upon seeing the other lands, it says: "Its sound is pure, emitting soft and gentle tones.
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage where Śāriputra expresses his realization, he says: "I have heard the Buddha’s soft and gentle voice, profound and most subtle.
Based on these two preceding and following passages, we know that this refers to the actual wisdom. Question: In the previous section of praise, was it not already the actual [reality]?

Question: Why is it that the provisional comes first and the real comes later? Answer: It is clarified that previously, because he wished to employ provisional words, he extended the provisional from the real;
now, because he wishes to cut off all words, he must roll the provisional back into the real. △ Second, pointing to the realm where words are cut off.
Śāriputra, to speak of it in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
To say "to speak of it in brief" refers to the realm of reality (*tattvārtha*); "in brief" means nothing surpasses the reality itself.

"Immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas" refers to the realm of expedient means (*upāya*). Furthermore, citing what is essential marks the beginning of the initial indication; as for "immeasurable," [it continues] without limit.
"Expedient means" refers to the provisional, while "unprecedented dharma" refers to the real. The Buddha has fully accomplished these two dharmas through the attainment of the path of cultivation;
therefore, how could they be described? If one were to clarify only a single matter, one should not say "fully";

only when pointing to both the provisional and the real is the meaning made clear. △ Second, the formal expression of ineffability in praise, which has two parts: first, the formal expression of ineffability in praise.
"Stop, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further.
Master Yin (Yin Shi) said: "He wished to stop [the discourse] because it gave rise to doubt and a desire for inquiry. Master Guan (Guan Shi) said:

"Because the true Dharma is difficult to know, he first suppressed [further speech] to startle common understanding; now he clarifies that this Dharma is profoundly quiescent, beyond the path of language, and its essence [is such]."

Because it is ineffable, [the Buddha] desisted and praised it; he established compassion and intended to explain it, yet because those who heard it could not understand and this would damage their roots of goodness, he therefore desisted.

△ Second, explaining the intent behind the desisting and praising, in two parts: first, clarifying that the Buddha is the supreme person who has cultivated and attained the supreme Dharma, and thus it is ineffable;
second, clarifying the provisional and ultimate [teachings] of the supreme person. First, clarifying the supreme person’s provisional and ultimate [teachings] horizontally...
It is "full" in an ineffable manner.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has accomplished the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.

This explanation serves to clarify the intent of the preceding praise; it first elucidates how the provisional and the real are horizontally pervasive in an ineffable way, and then addresses the accomplishment [of that Dharma].
The non-attainment of what is difficult to understand, as opposed to what is not difficult to understand, is explained horizontally as the attainment through the cultivation of the path;
therefore, it cannot be described. △ Second, the explanation of the supreme person’s provisional and ultimate [teachings], which are vertically profound and thus ineffable.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it.

Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it; those who have attained the initial and middle stages have not yet reached its source, like the moonlight on the fourteenth day, which has not yet reached its full extent.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas reach the ultimate limit, like the moon on the fifteenth day.

The substance of this moon is nowhere not perfect and its light is nowhere not pervasive; it is because one attains this through practicing the Way in such profound verticality that it cannot be described.
△ Second, clarifying the profoundly deep realm, in two parts: first, a brief indication of the provisional and the real chapters.

The true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is their provisional nature; the true mark is their reality. This single phrase is the general indication of the provisional and the real. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of the provisional and the real.
That which is called all dharmas having such characteristics, such natures, such essences, such powers,
such functions, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, such retributions, and such ultimate equality from beginning to end.
Regarding these ten phrases, beginning with "all dharmas have such characteristics as these," there are now four ways of explaining them:
first, by way of the ten realms; second, by way of the Buddha-realm; third, by way of their separation and combination; and fourth, by way of the stages.
Because the sutra says "all dharmas," they are explained by means of the ten realms; and because it says "the foremost and most rare dharma accomplished by the Buddha," the Buddha-realm is employed.
In explaining the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is further stated: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.

This employs the method of analysis and synthesis (*li-he shi*). It is also stated: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it," which employs the method of defining by stage (*yue-wei shi*).
First, regarding the ten realms (*shi-jie*), this refers to the ten dharmas consisting of the six paths and the four classes of noble beings. Although these dharmas are immeasurable in number...
Although there are many branches within each of the eleven realms, they do not exceed ten.

This is because, within the realm of hell itself, its own characteristics, nature, beginning, and end are fully present, including the characteristics, nature, beginning, and end of the animal realm, and so on, up to the characteristics, nature, beginning, and end of the Buddha-realm, without any deficiency.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states regarding the earth: [text follows].
That the hells achieve the dharmas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is an illustration of this;
one should know that it is the same for the other nine dharma-realms. Within each single realm, there are all nine realms and ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).

When these nine realms and ten suchnesses within their own respective positions are illuminated, they are called "provisional" (*upāya*); when the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm within its own position are illuminated, they are called "real. Each one contains all.
Within the immeasurable and immeasurable, there is that which contains the one; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.

If it illuminates the six realms of existence and the three types of sages as the five suchnesses, this is the provisional; if it illuminates the Buddha-realm as the four suchnesses, this is the real.

When each part is clearly distinct, this can be explained and demonstrated—why wait for the "cease, cease" [of the Lotus Sūtra] and the exhaustion of words through praise? Thus, within the one, there are the immeasurable. All...

Now, although ordinary people possess principle, they are cut off from it; though deluded by emotions, they seek liberation. Although those of the Two Vehicles possess renunciation, they seek only escape.

Although Bodhisattvas possess illumination, it is not all-encompassing; thus, these are called "not yet clear. The Tathāgata, however, penetrates and surveys both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, being fully endowed with this alone.
He is personally and solely enlightened, while others do not see it; it cannot be proclaimed or shown. Cease, cease! It is here that words are utterly exhausted. Thus it is.
Second, regarding the explanation based on the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*): the Buddha-realm is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks, yet it is designated as having "such marks.
This refers to the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) of myriad virtues; as the subsequent text states, "adorned with various jewels" is precisely this meaning.

The Buddha-fruition (*buddhaphala*) is neither a nature (*svabhāva*) nor non-nature, yet it is designated as having "such a nature. This refers to the revealing cause (*vidyā-hetu*) of wisdom; as the subsequent text states: [the passage concerning]...
There is a great white ox; the Buddha-realm is neither a substance nor a non-substance, yet it is designated as such a substance.

This refers to the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and the primary cause (*hetu*), for the subsequent text states: "The chariot is high and wide; the Buddha-realm is neither power nor lack of power, yet it is designated as such power.
This refers to the power of the bodhicitta, the roots of goodness of compassion, and so forth, for the subsequent text states: [and so on].
Furthermore, upon it, canopies and awnings are spread; the Buddha-realm is neither created nor uncreated, yet it is designated as "thus created.
This refers to the spontaneous path of effortless exertion (*anābhoga-mārga*), for the subsequent text states: "Its swiftness is like the wind.
The Buddha-realm is neither caused nor uncaused, yet it is designated as "thus caused. This refers to the forty-one stages (*ekacatvāriṃśat-pada*), for the subsequent text...

It is said that one "rides this precious vehicle to travel through the Buddha-fields of the four quarters. These are not conditions, yet they are not non-conditions; thus they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*).
This refers to all the factors that assist the path to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). As the text below states: "Furthermore, he is attended and guarded by many servants.
These are not fruits, yet they are not non-fruits; thus they are called "fruits" (*phala*). This refers to wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because it is clearly realized through the perfect cause, the subsequent text states: "Extending all the way to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the Buddha-realm is neither retribution nor non-retribution, yet it is termed such retribution.
This refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa; hence the subsequent text says: "One attains the fruit of immeasurable, untainted, and pure retribution.
Although the Buddha-realm is neither beginning nor end, it is spoken of in terms of beginning and end when appropriate.
To know that the root is the Buddha’s aspect (*ākāra*) and the branches are the Buddha’s retribution (*vipāka*) is the provisional [expedient] of self-cultivation.
To say that the Buddha-realm is neither equal nor unequal, yet is ultimately equal, points to the true reality (*dharmatā*); thus the chapter heading says "True Reality.
This is the reality of self-cultivation; because it is real while being provisional, it is called "root and branch"; because it is provisional while being real, it is called "becoming."
This is the Tathāgata’s own practice of the provisional and the real, which is most unsurpassed;

yet because its unsurpassed characteristics, up to its unsurpassed fruit and retribution, are vast horizontally and profound vertically such that nothing surpasses them, the heading of this chapter states:

"The True Reality of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharma-bhūtatathatā*). By analogy, one should also speak of the true nature, the true substance, and the true power of all dharmas, and even say simply "the Real."

The ultimate equality is merely illustrated here by citing each point individually to represent all Tathāgatas; their universal illumination pervades both horizontally and vertically, as if observing the fruit in the palm of one's hand.

However, for ordinary beings it is like two people blind from birth, for the followers of the Two Vehicles it is like those with impaired vision, and for Bodhisattvas it is like seeing in the dim light of night—obscure and incomprehensible, such that it cannot be described.
This is why [the Buddha] said, "Stop, stop," for the words and meanings cease right here. Thus it is.

Third, regarding the distinction between separation and union: if one considers that which is observed within the Buddha’s own mind—the ten realms and the ten suchnesses—all are supreme characteristics, even up to supreme retribution;
they are solely the single Buddha-dharmadhātu, like the ocean encompassing all rivers, or like a thousand chariots sharing a single track.
This constitutes the provisional and the real of his own practice (*svayam-ācāra*). However, when conforming to the intentions of others, there are the nine dharma-realms.

The ten suchnesses, the nature, and so forth constitute the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others. Although there is indeed a reality in the transformation of others, all are subsumed under the provisional;

although there is indeed a provisionality in one’s own practice, all are subsumed under the real. This means that while the provisional and real of one’s own practice and the transformation of others unfold when following others, they converge when following oneself.
Transversally and vertically pervasive, their unfolding and convergence are sovereign; though they unfold—
The immeasurable is immeasurable, yet it is one; though combined into one, it is immeasurable. Though immeasurable, it is one; yet it is neither one nor immeasurable.
Though neither one nor immeasurable, it is both one and immeasurable. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this;
ordinary beings slander it and do not believe, while those of the Two Vehicles are bewildered and do not accept it.
The Bodhisattva, however, has not yet clarified this meaning regarding the dust-like hindrances; therefore, he remains silent, ceasing all speech. Fourth, regarding the stages:
all sentient beings possess the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is inherently present from the beginning; this is precisely the manifestation of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Such a nature is the wisdom of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); such is its essence.
This is the principle of the Middle Way and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). It constitutes the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) which pervade the ten dharma-realms; these exist in every stage.
If one investigates these three virtues upon entering the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), it is called "such power" and "such action.
If one enters the forty-one stages (*ekacatvāriṃśad-bhūmi*), it is called "such cause" and "such condition. Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, it is called "such fruit."

If the fruit is thus the retribution, then the first three stages are called the "root" and the final three are called the "branch. Because the beginning and the end are identical in being the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), they are said to be ultimately equal.
In the initial stage, the Three Virtues pervade the evil and the good, the worthy and the sage, the Small and the Great, the beginning and the ultimate.
Although one may dwell in evil, one does not sink; although one dwells in good, one does not ascend; although one is among the worthy...
It does not descend into the sacred nor does it remain aloof; though present in the small, it is not narrow, and though present in the great, it is not expansive.
At its inception it is not new, and at its ultimate limit it is not old. Therefore, it is inconceivable and cannot be described; it is simply a cessation, a stopping, and the severance of speech.

Furthermore, regarding the ultimate equality of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), there are the distinctions of the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*) in terms of their characteristics and nature, their provisional and real aspects, and their opening and closing.
If one observes these various things with the great wisdom of equanimity as they truly are, they are ultimately all equal.

If one is deluded regarding this realm, there are the characteristics and natures of the six elements, which is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If one understands this realm, there are the characteristics and natures of the two vehicles, which is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Upon realizing that this is neither delusion nor understanding, there are the characteristics and natures of the fruit of Buddhahood for Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): if one regards it with this wisdom as equal to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then conventional truth is not delusion;

if one regards it as equal to ultimate truth, then ultimate truth is not awakening. Being neither awakening nor delusion, and being the negation of both delusion and awakening, it is simply termed "equality.

If one illuminates both simultaneously, then the provisional (*upāya*) is itself the real (*bhūta*), and the real is itself the provisional. Though they are two, they are non-dual; this is also termed [the Middle Way].
Furthermore, regarding the realm where the provisional and the real are non-dual, if the seven kinds of skillful means cannot [attain] this non-dual realm—
since only the Buddhas possess the wisdom of non-duality that is equal to the non-dual realm— it is called "ultimate equality."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Part Two: Verses in Praise. Section One: The first part of the verses restates the prose. Subsection One: The first part of the praise restates the words of commendation. Subsection Two:
The first part of the praise restates the two Buddhas and their two wisdoms. Section One: The first part of the verses restates the two wisdoms of all Buddhas.
"The World-Hero is immeasurable; among all classes of beings, including the devas and the people of the world, none are able to know the Buddha.

These two lines together praise the two Buddhas and their two wisdoms. Now, for the first line, "World-Hero" (*lokanātha*) praises the aforementioned "immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas," while "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) praises the aforementioned "profound and immeasurable"; this praises the true wisdom of the Buddhas.

Next, the three lines of verse praise the provisional wisdom of the various Buddhas. There are three differences here: first, above, both the persons and the dharmas were raised, hence it was said "the wisdom of the various Buddhas";
now, this verse praises only the persons, for one uses the person to glorify the dharma, hence it says "the Heroes of the World.
Second, the preceding text praised by opening [the categories] separately, whereas this praises by combining them; because the dharmas are distinct, it was necessary to open [the praise].

Because "humans" is a collective term, three categories must be combined. What was previously stated as "all those of the two vehicles do not know," is now expressed as "all classes of sentient beings do not know";
thus, these constitute three distinct points. △ Second, the verse explains the two kinds of wisdom of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, liberations, various samādhis, and all other Buddha-qualities cannot be measured by anyone.
Following the section on the Buddha’s powers, one verse praises the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni Buddha:

the first half of this verse praises his *jñāna* (real wisdom), such as the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, while the latter half praises his *upāya* (expedient wisdom) and other remaining qualities.
"Dharma" here refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming others, which is an auxiliary to true wisdom; it correctly summarizes the various causes and conditions mentioned above.
△ Second, the combined verse of the two Buddhas' praise and conclusion.
"From the time of countless Buddhas, I have fully practiced all paths—the profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma that is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of eons, I attained the fruit at the site of enlightenment; I have fully known and seen it all."

These two lines combine the verses of praise and the conclusion of the praise. [The phrase] "From countless Buddhas, he has fully practiced all paths" praises the aforementioned passage concerning the various Buddhas, specifically the text stating that the Buddha personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and exhausted the practice of their Dharma-paths.
"The profound and subtle Dharma" praises the aforementioned passage on the accomplishment of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which is profound and unprecedented.
There is a dharma that is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend; this verse concludes by praising the fact that the underlying intent of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is hard to understand.

"Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas" refers back to the preceding explanation of the text stating that Śākyamuni has fully perfected all *pāramitās* of knowledge and vision;
the first two lines of this verse cite the perfection of the causes, while the following line [cites the result].
Having already fully known and seen the perfection of the fruit, the preceding verse concludes the exposition on the vastness of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s twofold knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the verse praising that which transcends words in five parts; first, the verse on the inconceivable realm.
Such are the meanings of the various natures and characteristics of these great fruits of retribution.

These great fruits of retribution correspond to the verse on the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*); by citing only the beginning and the end, the intermediate sense may be understood by implication.
Furthermore, the word "meaning" (*artha*) therein also encompasses the verses on the ultimate [fruit] and so forth. △ Second, the subsequent verse points to the realm beyond words.
Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter.
Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter. To summarize the essential points in verse: the Buddhas have fully accomplished all things.
△ Third, the concluding verse praising that which transcends words.
This Dharma cannot be shown; its characteristics are quiescent and beyond verbal expression.
This Dharma cannot be shown; its characteristics are quiescent and beyond verbal expression. [The Buddha] followed this with a verse: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak.
The true reality has no location, therefore it cannot be shown; it is not the path of speech, therefore its characteristics are quiescent and beyond verbal expression. △
Fourth, the exclusion of those who do not understand. Part eight: first, the general exclusion of those who do not enter.

"None among the various other classes of sentient beings are able to attain understanding" refers to the initial general exclusion of those who do not enter, namely, the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). △ Second, the exclusion of those who are able to enter.

"Except for those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and solid"—this excludes those who are capable of entering [the teaching], as these refer to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
Thus, it is said that "those whose power of faith is firm and solid. In the prose section, the ultimate knowledge of the Buddha is clarified; in the verse, the initial [stage] is clarified.
