One should know with faith that these are merely mentioned in mutual reference. △ Third, distinguishing those of the Two Vehicles who do not know:

"The assembly of disciples of the Buddhas, who have made offerings to all Buddhas, whose outflows are entirely exhausted, and who abide in their final bodies—even such persons as these are unable to bear its power."
The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, even those whose power is insufficient to discern it, do not know it—this refers to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
△ Fourth, citing Śāriputra’s ignorance:
Even if the entire world were filled with beings like Śāriputra, and they exhausted their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
In these four lines and a half, the first line—beginning with "Suppose" (假使)—raises the case of Śāriputra being unable to fathom it through exhaustive thought and collective deliberation;
this refers to the exertion of all one's strength and the exhaustion of all one's wisdom. △ Fifth, raising the case that the great disciples were unable to know it.
Even if the ten directions were filled with beings like Śāriputra and the other disciples, and they were to fill all the lands of the ten directions,
even if they were to exhaust their thoughts and measure it together, they still could not know it.
△ Sixth, the raising of the branch: The Pratyekabuddhas do not know it.

Although Pratyekabuddhas possess sharp, untainted wisdom and are in their final bodies, and though they fill the ten directions in numbers like a grove of bamboo, even if such as these were to concentrate their minds for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they could not know even a small fraction of the Buddha’s true wisdom.
△ Seventh: It is raised that a bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind does not know this.
A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind has made offerings to countless buddhas, thoroughly understands all meanings and principles, and is moreover skilled in preaching the Dharma;
like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, they fill the lands of the ten directions, and with a single mind and sublime wisdom, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
All together contemplate [this], yet they cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom.

These three and a half lines have two meanings: the first two and a half lines present the Bodhisattva who has resolved on enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) as not yet having entered the discourse on the resolve;
alternatively, it may refer to the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) who, throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*).
The phrase "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*) may refer to the arousal of the mind for the practice of the six perfections as attained among humans and devas;
it may also be proposed as a distinct classification of the general and specific types of arousing the mind. △ Eighth: Raising the point that non-retrogressive bodhisattvas do not know [this].

Even if bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and sought to contemplate this with a single mind together, they would likewise be unable to know it.

The next line distinguishes that even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas do not know [this], because those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) who have retrogressed from the afflictions within the realm of desire cannot know it;

furthermore, regarding the distinct principle and the distinct teaching, even those prior to the stages possess the stage of realization-non-retrogression and practice-non-retrogression, yet [they still do not know].
Others likewise do not know it. △ Fifth, the verse on the fact that only the Buddha can know the realm of the true mark:
Furthermore, he addressed Śāriputra: "The untainted, inconceivable, profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma—I have now fully attained it;
only I know its marks, and so it is for the Buddhas of the ten directions."

This one and a half verses summarize the aforementioned difficult-to-understand Dharma: only a Buddha can know the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and inconceivable.
The following verse concludes the essentials by citing the realms where the provisional and the real abide: "The profound and subtle Dharma.
One line summarizes the aforementioned "Dharma that is most rare and difficult to understand": "I have now fully attained it," and so forth.
Regarding the three-line verse: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this," this clarifies that the Way of all Buddhas is identical, as they all reach the ultimate consummation;
therefore it says, "Only I know these marks, and so do the Buddhas of the ten directions. To explain the inconceivable:
it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which possesses not even a hair’s breadth of substantiality, yet can rain down all manner of treasures; such is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Birth can give rise to prajñā. △ Second, a brief exposition to resolve attachments and eliminate doubts. Part one: Explaining that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.
(Three sub-sections) First, explaining that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.
"Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas are not different.

This one line and a half clarifies that all Buddhas manifest the truth; "the words of all Buddhas are not different" means that this treatise explains that the Buddhas' methods of transformation are identical.
△ Second, exhorting them to give rise to faith.
One should give rise to great power of faith regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
△ Third, the actual revelation of the truth:
"After a long time, the World-Honored One must surely speak the truth."
Because this correctly reveals the reality, it is said: "The World-Honored One must, after a long time, speak of the truth. This is precisely what is meant by "revealing the true.

It is for this reason that past attachments are shaken and present doubts are produced; hence the passage below says: "Could it not be that a Māra has become a Buddha? This is precisely due to hearing these words.
Since the Buddha speaks according to reality, why would one fail to believe him? On the contrary, one should encourage faith.
Doubt is treated as a cause for prevention because slander arises from doubt; therefore, one must encourage faith. II. Explaining Śākyamuni’s Opening of the Three Vehicles. A.
First, the actual explanation of the opening of the three vehicles:
He addressed the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas: "I have caused you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa."
These two lines clarify Śākyamuni’s opening of the three vehicles into three sections. First, one line is the formal explanation of the opening of the three;
it indicates that the realization attained by the two vehicles in the past was neither [of the ultimate truth], hence it says, "they have attained nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the phrase "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvāṇa" refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle of the six perfections. How is this known? If...
By practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), one is freed from the bonds of the four miserable realms (*caturgati*), yet one has not yet entered *nirvāṇa*.

One should know that it is only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and a hundred *kalpas* that one attains *nirvāṇa*; the term "reaching" (*prāpti*) refers to the fact that it is reached only after a long duration. Furthermore, because the preceding practice of the six perfections is for the sake of delivering others, it is said, "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering";
because one subsequently realizes the untainted state (*anāsrava*), it is said, "one reaches and attains *nirvāṇa*. This is the distinction.

By inferring the meaning, one knows this refers to the vehicle of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā-yāna*). Furthermore, the subsequent line states: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifests the teaching of the three vehicles.
If this were not indicated, what would constitute the "three"? It is not appropriate to count the two vehicles twice over to make them three.
△ Second, the direct refutation of the three vehicles.
The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles;
these are all provisional and empty. △ Third, he establishes the three intentions:
to lead sentient beings who are attached to various places so that they may attain liberation.
The mind is a provisional means for leading one away from all sufferings; it is not the ultimate reality, but merely a gateway of skillful means.

△ Second, raising doubts to request instruction, in two parts: first, the narration of the doubts, in two parts: first, the narration by the sūtra compiler of the doubts of the twelve hundred [disciples]. First, the narration of the doubts of the twelve hundred.
At that time, within the great assembly were twelve hundred śrāvakas, including the Arhat Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others, whose outflows were exhausted.
△ Second, the narration of the doubts of the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had conceived the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

This is the introduction by the scribe. [The disciples] raised doubts and made their request because, having heard that three were false and one was true, their attachments were shaken and doubt arose.
However, while the previous section refuted all three vehicles as being merely expedient means, the present account of the doubts concerns only the two vehicles; this is because...
Because their attachments are heavy and their doubts are deep, [the text] cites them specifically. However, when we reach the section listing the doubts below, it says: "I seek from the Buddha;
the great number of bodhisattvas is eighty thousand, and they all have doubts. From this, we know that while the three vehicles all harbor doubts, the text again cites the two vehicles specifically.
△ Second, the actual doubts, in two parts: First, general doubt regarding the Buddha’s two types of wisdom; first, the general doubt.
The two wisdoms each form this thought: "Why does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise the skillful means?
Why does he so earnestly praise the skillful means? This constitutes a general doubt regarding both provisional and real wisdom. △ Second, the specific [analysis].
Regarding the two types of doubt concerning the two kinds of wisdom, first is the doubt regarding ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
One says, "The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand.
That "the Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand" is the doubt regarding ultimate wisdom. Second is the doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*).
The intended meaning of what he says is difficult to comprehend and is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the difficulty of comprehending the intended meaning of what he says, the following passage concerns doubt regarding his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Upon hearing the words of the Buddhas—which are without distinction—one must realize that they will surely speak the truth; yet from this, doubt arises: "How is it that the Buddha previously taught the wisdom of the three vehicles?"

We have realized the same truth without deviation; it is merely a matter of whether residual habits have been exhausted or not. Now, you suddenly praise the Tathāgata’s two kinds of wisdom as being beyond my reach;
for this reason, I doubt the Buddha’s two kinds of wisdom. △ Second, doubting what one has attained oneself.
"The Buddha has taught the meaning of the single liberation, and we too have attained this Dharma and reached nirvana;
yet we do not know where this meaning leads.
The śrāvakas then privately harbored doubts, thinking: "The noble path of the three vehicles is the true means of transcendence; I have cultivated this."
The principle also leads to nirvāṇa; yet now it is suddenly said that all are merely expedient means, and one does not know which is the ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is said that the destination of this meaning is unknown. This doubt arises from the preceding refutation of the three as being false.
△ Second, the request for a definitive decision. Part One: The Request. Section One: The Long Discourse. Subsection One: Stating the Doubt.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and by what condition do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
Since the distant past, I have never before heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Now, the entire fourfold assembly..."
There was doubt.
A second time they made their request:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise that which is profound and subtle?"
Regarding this Dharma that is difficult to understand:
within this formal request, there are three requests and two refusals. According to the preceding text, there are three refusals.

The masters Yao and Long state that the first refusal was because the principle is profound and difficult to understand; the first request was made by [the interlocutor] seeking a resolution for both himself and others; and the second refusal...

First, [the Buddha] acted so as to cause alarm, doubt, and disbelief; next, he requested [the teaching] so that those who had long planted roots would certainly attain understanding; finally, he ceased [speaking] so that those who would certainly slander and fall into evil realms would not do so;

and lastly, he requested [the teaching again] so that those of sharp faculties might obtain benefit. Tiantai says: "The Buddha knew in advance that the benefits obtained during the three weeks would not occur simultaneously;
therefore, he suppressed [his teaching] three times to await their three requests."
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses on the Six [Points]. First, the verse on doubting the true wisdom:
"The Sun of Wisdom, the Great Holy Honored One, Has finally proclaimed this Dharma after a long time."

This verse consists of eleven lines, with the text divided into six parts. First, the initial two lines praise the doubt regarding ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*). Second, [the following lines] praise the doubt regarding expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
It states that [the Buddha] himself has attained such inconceivable dharmas as the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), samādhis, dhyānas, and liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment, there is no one capable of posing questions; my own intention is difficult to fathom, and there is no one who can question me.
Without being asked, I shall speak of myself, praising the path I have practiced—the wisdom that is most subtle and profound, which has been attained by all Buddhas.
By the preceding verses stating that [the Buddha] has attained such [wisdom], the doubt regarding provisional wisdom is expressed. △ Third, the doubts of the three vehicles and the fourfold assembly:
"The various arhats free from outflows and those seeking nirvāṇa have now all fallen into a net of doubt; why does the Buddha speak thus?
Those who seek pratyekabuddhahood—monks, nuns, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—"
Gazing at one another with lingering hesitation, they look up to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings: "What is the meaning of this matter? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
The three lines following the term "anāsrava" (outflow-free) clarify the doubts held by the followers of the Three Vehicles and the fourfold assembly. The first line clarifies the Śrāvakas;
the second line mentions "those who seek Nirvāṇa," which clarifies the Bodhisattvas of the Six Pāramitās. How is this known? It is understood from what follows above.
Regarding the phrase "attaining nirvana": herein, the term "and" (及) signifies that this bodhisattva seeks nirvana for themselves and is also able to lead others to it;
thus, by distinguishing them from those of the two vehicles, one knows this to be a bodhisattva. The final two lines clarify the characteristics of the pratyekabuddha:
"viewing with hesitation" means being unable to reach a definitive conclusion regarding right and wrong, or advancing and retreating. The "Venerable One with Two Feet" (the Buddha).
This means that because he has fully perfected both types of adornment—merit and wisdom—he is the Honored One of the world.
△ Fourth, the clarification of Śāriputra’s doubt:
Among all the śrāvaka assembly, the Buddha declared me to be the foremost; yet now, regarding this wisdom myself, I am in doubt and cannot comprehend it.
"Is this the ultimate Dharma? Is this the path to be traversed?
△ Fifth, the doubts of the Buddha’s sons:
"O Son born from the Buddha’s own mouth, with palms joined we gaze up at you in expectation; we pray that you will utter a subtle and wondrous sound and speak according to reality."
△ Sixth, a general explanation of the request made out of shared doubt:
The various devas, nāgas, and spirits are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha number eighty thousand;
and furthermore, the wheel-turning sage-kings from ten trillion lands, having joined their palms with a reverent heart, desire to hear the complete Way.
"Numerous as the sands of the Ganges" means that they are as many as the sands of the Gaṅgā River. This river is also called the *Kauṇḍinī*;
translated into Chinese, it means "Coming from the Heavenly Hall. This river flows from the eastern side of the Elephant Mouth out of Lake Anavatapta and enters the great ocean.
Its sands are as fine as flour; if one scoops them up with the hand, the sand follows the water away. Because of this... [text ends]
And he provides an analogy for it. △ Second, the second "Cease.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were spoken, all the devas and humans in the world would become startled and doubtful."
△ Second, the second request, in two parts. First, the request:
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of it; we pray that you will speak of it. Why is this?
Because there are in this assembly countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have seen various Buddhas and whose faculties [are matured]."
Those with sharp and penetrating wisdom, having clearly heard what the Buddha has spoken, will be able to revere and believe it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, please speak; have no concern. Among the immeasurable multitude in this assembly, there are those capable of reverence and faith."
Śāriputra requested again. △ Second, the third instance of the Buddha’s refusal.
The Buddha again refused Śāriputra, saying: "If this matter were to be spoken, all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be struck with alarm and doubt;
those bhikṣus of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss. At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
He said: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive; if those with overweening pride were to hear it, they would certainly not show respect or faith.
This was the third request.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of it; we pray that you will speak of it.

Those in this assembly who are like us—hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions of beings who have already been transformed by the Buddha throughout successive lifetimes—will surely be able to revere and believe [this teaching], attaining peace and security for a long night and receiving great benefit. At that time, Śāriputra...
Wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, pray teach the foremost Dharma. I am the eldest son of the Buddha; please deign to explain it in detail for me.
The immeasurable multitude in this assembly is capable of reverently believing this Dharma. The Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed such as these."
With single-minded devotion and palms joined, we—these twelve hundred and others who seek Buddhahood—desire to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
We pray that you will, for the sake of this assembly, graciously distinguish and expound these teachings; upon hearing this Dharma, they shall give rise to great joy.

Regarding the request to "expound the supreme dharma," Master Rong states: Because the preceding passage refuted the three vehicles as being false, and because one has heard that after a long period all Buddhas must expound the true reality, yet among those on the level of the two vehicles it was not yet known whether the Lotus Sūtra was the truth;
therefore, based on the refutation that the three [vehicles] are not true, and given that there must necessarily be a further dharma beyond them, he says, "I pray you, expound the supreme dharma."

Furthermore, since the Dharma is profound and mysterious, its principles must be restrained; yet even when Śāriputra made his request with such earnest sincerity that he petitioned three times, the sublime sages, following the regulations for honoring the Dharma, still remained thus.
How much more so, then, should those of inferior station and common nature not treat it with negligence?
△ Second, the extensive exposition of the three to reveal the one. Part three: first, the explanation by way of Dharma; second, the explanation by way of analogy;

third, the explanation by way of causes and conditions. The first section [of the Dharma-exposition] further has five parts: first, the actual clarification of the Dharma-exposition; second, Śāriputra’s reception and understanding; third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation;

fourth, the bestowal of the prediction; fifth, the joy of the assembly. The first of these [five] further has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first of these [two] further has three parts.
First, the preliminary consent to speak, which is granted in accordance with the request.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak?
Second, the formal consent to speak.
Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it in detail for you. Listen attentively—this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
reflect well—this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); keep it in mind—this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This great sutra clarifies that the four wholesome dharmas are the causes for *nirvāṇa*. "The first is a virtuous friend," referring to the Tathāgata; the rest is easily understood. △ Three.

[The Buddha] selected and permitted [them]. While these words were being spoken, five thousand members of the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—immediately rose from their seats, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew. Why was this? Because the roots of the offenses of these people were deep and heavy.
Furthermore, there are those with overweening pride who claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized;
because such faults exist, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain them. At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves, but only the pure and solid core. Śāriputra, it is well indeed that such people of overweening pride should withdraw."
Listen well now; I shall speak for you.

There were five thousand people present in the assembly whom the Tathāgata had previously forbidden three times from hearing this teaching. Now, having granted permission to speak, he has secretly employed his majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) to dismiss them.

Therefore, they are called "the selected assembly. These individuals possessed deeply rooted and heavy afflictions (*kleśa*), were heavily obstructed by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), and were attached to the Lesser Vehicle, which is why their offenses were considered grave.
Those who obscure their great fame and whose roots are deep, yet have not attained what they claim to have attained, suffer from the fault of overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
Because they have not attained the three fruits nor realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they incur such faults as the three types of obstructive grasping and pride.

If one does not restrain these, then upon hearing the opening of the three [vehicles] to reveal the single [vehicle], the concise meaning will remain hidden; even if slander has not yet arisen, it is sufficient to become a cause for bondage.

The causes and conditions of the jewel are such that its departure brings benefit, whereas if one hears the extensive opening of the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, it may contradict one's disposition and give rise to slander;

thus, its remaining would cause harm. Therefore, it is not restrained. That this assembly has no further "branches and leaves" means that branches and leaves are minor and insignificant, unfit for use as vessels.
These [people] cling to the expedient of expedients; they are not vessels for the Great [Vehicle], just as large [vessels are not used for small things].
The *Śāstra* says: "To clutch at branches and leaves while abandoning the root—such a person is not wise. This is precisely that meaning. It would be better to withdraw;

for one who shields oneself with something small also obstructs the great light of others. Now, by withdrawing, there is no fault of slandering the Dharma, nor is there the transgression of hindering others;
therefore, it is said to be "better. Since the branches and leaves above have not yet been removed, it is as [described].

The three previous instances of cessation were now truly real; I wish to hear the reason. Śāriputra requested four times, and the Master and disciple discerned the capacity [of the audience], not merely out of stinginess or stubbornness.
[Śāriputra] asked the Buddha: "O Great Compassionate One, why do you not use your supernatural power to cause them to remain [in concentration] so they do not hear?

Why is it not like the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, where the deaf and mute are transformed? Why is it not like increasing the poison-drum for the sake of Nandika and Vijaya? [The Buddha] replied: "Each has their own [karmic] allotment."

One must understand that the final session of the *Avataṃsaka* has only now begun to open the gradual teachings, as it has not yet broken the attachments of the Hinayana; therefore, while seated here, we remain separated from the present.

In the distant future of all Buddhas' teachings, one must certainly preach the truth, for when the transformation through cessation is about to end, it is necessary to select and dispatch [the right people].
If both departing and staying lead to slander, one should speak forcefully like Nandika; if one departs now, there will be benefit.

"Why did he suddenly command him to stay? To stay would have caused harm; why did he not send him away? [The Buddha replied: "It was because of his joyful faculties that [the Buddha] spoke with compassion, and because of his pity that he sent him forth. [Question:
"If those five thousand in the assembly did not even receive benefit while remaining there, what benefit would there be in sending them away?

[Answer: "This was not because they were suitable vessels for the teaching, but because they were people with whom [the Buddha] established a karmic connection (*pratyaya*). This has already been explained above regarding the time of the Great Universal Buddha (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*)."

At that time, there were also immeasurable sentient beings whose minds gave rise to doubt, thinking: "Life after life we have been born together with our teacher, and now all have attained deliverance;
this person is just like us. When this Great Sūtra was being preached, fifteen thousand billion people did not give rise to faith in it.
These people shall also give rise to faith in the future; by this analogy, their benefit will come before long.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there were two kinds of people: first, those who deeply believed in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;

second, those who disparaged them and did not give rise to faith or joy. This is also an instance of the same principle. "Listen well now"—this is the formal granting of permission. △ Second, receiving the mandate.
Śāriputra said, "Yes, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.
To say "yes" (*wei ran*) refers to the act of receiving instructions and respectfully accepting one's mandate. As the *Quli* chapter of the *Liji* states:

"When a father summons [one], one does not say 'no' (*nuo*); when a teacher summons [one], one does not say 'no'; one says 'yes' (*wei*) and rises. Zheng Xuan’s commentary explains that this is the term used for responding.
I, your servant, can only respectfully assent. △ Third, the actual exposition, which has two parts: first, the general clarification of all Buddhas;
second, the chapter on Śākyamuni. The first section [the general clarification] is further divided into four parts.
First, the King praises the rarity of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals;
it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower.

This is both a praise of the Dharma and a simile for its rarity. As for the statement that it is preached 'only at rare intervals,' it is because all Buddhas appear together within the five turbidities."
The preceding section opened with three [vehicles], while the subsequent part reveals the one true reality.
Just as the World-Honored One has now revealed the truth after more than forty years—having waited for a long time and spoken only sparingly—it is said that he speaks only at the proper time.

That he did not speak for so long was because people were not yet capable, the time had not yet arrived, and the five thousand [monks] had not yet been dismissed. Now, however, people are capable and the time has arrived; thus, the five thousand have been dismissed.

Because it has already been explained that he definitively teaches the Mahāyāna, it is said that he speaks [this] only at the proper time. As for the *udumbara* flower, this refers to an auspicious omen;
it appears once every three thousand years, and its appearance coincides with the emergence of a Cakravartin King.

This symbolizes that only after those of the three vehicles have been matured does he preach the Sublime Dharma and bestow the prediction of Buddhahood upon them as Dharma Kings. △ Second, the teaching is not false.
Śāriputra, you and others should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
When it is said that you should believe, it is an exhortation to believe in that which is not false. This principle is most profound, for its principle differs from the former;
this teaching is most subtle, for its teaching contradicts the former; this practice is most universal, for its practice diverges from the former; this person is most... [supreme].
That which was previously inferior is now shown to be superior; the four kinds of coarse [practices] formerly referred to as "hired labor" are now all seen as sublime.
Fearing that sentient beings might give rise to slander, he encourages them to have faith. △ Third, the opening of the skillful means, in three parts: first, the opening.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, and their underlying intent is difficult to understand.
First, it is explained that because the Buddhas preach expedient means according to the three types of capacities, it is said they teach "according to what is appropriate";
yet because the Buddha’s intent lies in the ultimate reality and none can comprehend it, it is said that "the underlying intent is difficult to understand. △ Second, the explanation.
Why is this? It is because I have expounded all dharmas through countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression. Why is this?
That is to say, by revealing his underlying intention, he cites the present Buddha’s power of expedient means to explain that of all Buddhas.
Because the causes of skillful means and wisdom are identical, this is used to explain that "self.

Regarding the phrase "by innumerable skillful means," the Buddhas' opening of provisional teachings is also like my own. △ Third, the conclusion; fourth, the revelation of the reality. Fifth, first, the designation of the superior person and the Dharma.

This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it. Regarding the statement that "this Dharma is not [a matter of] deliberation," there are two meanings:
either it serves as a conclusion to the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*), or it directly reveals the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
If it is taken as a conclusion to the disclosure of the provisional, the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom; only a Buddha and a Buddha can understand and realize it.

Regarding "those who receive the teaching," it means that the three Buddhas know [reality] as being one and only. If this is taken as manifesting reality (*tattva*), it belongs to the subsequent section.
As for "designating the person and the dharma," it refers to the non-discriminative dharma which is known only by the Buddha;

that the Buddha, through non-discriminative wisdom, understands and knows the non-discriminative dharma is precisely what constitutes manifesting reality. △ Second, designating the intent of appearing in the world.
Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding "solely for the sake of one great matter," "solely" (*mātra*) means exclusively. One should know that there are two meanings to "one great matter":

first, a general explanation; second, an analysis of the individual characters. As for the general explanation: all Buddhas awaken to the aspect of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), and based upon this reality...
The Way appears in the world solely to enable sentient beings to attain this true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); it appears for this purpose alone and for no other.
Apart from the true mark of all phenomena, everything else is termed the work of Māra. Next, the analysis by characters:
"One" refers to the one true mark, which is neither five, nor three, nor seven, nor nine; therefore, it is called "one."
Furthermore, its nature is vast and expansive, encompassing the five, three, seven, and nine; therefore, it is called "Great.

It is the ritual for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world, and thus it is called "Phenomenon" (*dharma*). Because sentient beings possess the capacity to evoke the Buddha's response, it is called "Cause" (*hetu*).

Because the Buddha responds according to the capacity of sentient beings, it is called "Condition" (*pratyaya*). This constitutes the fundamental intent of appearing in the world. Now, this is opened...
Third, [the various teachings] act as introductory preludes to the One; just as when a person wishes to take something, they must first give it to them.
Although various paths are taught, their reality is the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna)—this is the meaning [of the passage].

The Record states that "it is not five, seven, or nine," because the three, five, and so forth are all skillful means (*upāya*); thus, "not" refers to the three vehicles of the Tripiṭaka, plus the five [vehicles] including humans and devas.
Adding the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching makes seven; adding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings makes nine. △ Third, the heading:
Śāriputra, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition?
Regarding the term "repeatedly highlighting": it means that, intending to provide a detailed analysis, one again raises the subject as the starting point for explanation.

Furthermore, this great matter is held in high esteem by the Buddha; as clarified in the *Śāstra*, when his father, the King, wished to hear the name of Prince Bahubuddhika, he spoke of it repeatedly without ever feeling satiated.
One should know that this Dharma is so extraordinary that the Tathāgata [expounded it] four times.
For more than ten years, this has been kept secret and not spoken; now that it is about to be revealed and extolled, how could one proceed with such casualness?

Thus, through repeated and earnest exhortations, the assembly is stirred to a state of deep reverence and longing, ensuring that their sincere hearts are filled with solemn veneration—this is precisely what is intended here.
△ Fourth, the actual explanation of the four [sections]; first, the principle; second, the initial explanation.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to bring it to purity;

they appear in the world because they desire to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings; they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
World. This explanation is logically unified and further comprises four points: first, regarding the four stages; second, regarding the four wisdoms; third, regarding the four gates;
and fourth, regarding the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the first, the four stages: the objects of the Four Truths are neither knowable nor visible. Regarding...

Only the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*) can know and see that which is to be known; the two types of knowledge and the four eyes cannot know or see it, whereas only the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom) and the Buddha-eye can know and see it.
As the Sūtra says: "If one wishes to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this does not refer to the Buddha’s own realization and vision of the fruit.
If one speaks exclusively of the Buddha’s fruit, one loses sight of sentient beings; if one speaks [only] of...

Sentient beings lack the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, they must not be grasped as partial. Furthermore, although practitioners of the three vehicles are sentient beings, because they do not yet possess the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, they are unable to know and see the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, those in the four stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) are also sentient beings;
yet, because they have partially attained the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, the meaning of "sentient being" is established through their wisdom and vision.

Since the principle is also established, these four stages are employed to explain the single reality, as in the auspicious signs where the rain of four flowers from heaven symbolizes that all myriad virtues converge in entering these four stages;
by using the flowers of the four stages to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, the principle is revealed through the stages.
"Opening" refers to the initial breaking of ignorance within the Ten Abidings, thereby opening the Tathāgata.

Regarding the principle of the true reality seen by the *garbha*: what is this principle of innate virtue that is stained and adhered to by both the general and specific delusions, such that it is difficult to comprehend?
Because the initial stage of the path can only achieve perfect faith and perfect subduing but cannot yet effect severance, it is not called "opening.
If, however, one internally applies contemplative practice and externally relies on the assistance of the rain of Dharma to shatter the general and specific delusions, the *garbha* [is revealed].

It manifests the true cultivation and the true nature; knowledge and vision are clearly developed, like the sun rising to dispel darkness so that the eyes become functional—therefore it is called "opening" (*kāya*).
Cultivating through conditions to destroy delusions is therefore termed "attaining purity. As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:

"The *prajñā* that enters into principle is called 'abiding' (*vihāra*)," which refers to abiding in the stage of the "Small White Flower" within the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*). "Demonstrating" (*darśana*) refers to [the removal of] delusions.

Once the hindrances have been removed, the essence of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) is revealed; as this essence is endowed with all virtues and the myriad qualities of the *dharmadhātu* are manifested with clarity, it is called "Manifestation" (*darśana*).
This is precisely the stage of the Great White Flower (*mahā-śvetapuṣpa*) within the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). For the awakened one, hindrances are removed and the essence is revealed;

the practices of the *dharmadhātu* become clear, and phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated such that no dualistic path remains. As the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* say: "In accordance with reality..."

Wisdom as suchness and wisdom as the measure are now non-dual in principle and measure; therefore, this is called "Awakening," which corresponds to the stage of the Small Red Flower within the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).

As for "entering," since phenomena and principle have already merged, one flows freely and without obstruction, spontaneously proceeding from the letter *A* to the letter *Ta*, entering the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
As the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* say: "In accordance with principle and in accordance with measure."
Thoroughly penetrating with mastery, knowing and seeing according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*) enables one to uphold all virtues;

knowing and seeing according to principle (*yathā-artha-jñāna-darśana*) enables one to obstruct all delusions—this is precisely the stage of the Great Crimson Flower (*mahā-rakta-puṣpa*) of the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*). However, within a single stage of the wondrous path of the Perfect [Vehicle], the merits of all forty-one stages are fully contained.
Merely by opening [the door], it encompasses and reveals the stages of Opening, Showing, Entering, and Realizing; it is not something separate.
The mind merely knows and perceives according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*) without the characteristics of distinction between shallow and deep;

it is only to manifest the knowledge and vision of things as they are (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna-darśana*) that the four stages are distinguished. Since it is said, "The initial resolve and the ultimate resolve are not two and are not different, yet of these two minds, the former is difficult," and since "difficult" and "easy" are mentioned, one knows that the initial mind and the ultimate mind must have differences in clarity and obscurity, as well as depth and shallowness.
The distinction between the "deep" [stages] is like the body of the moon, which is full both at its beginning and end; thus there is the difference between the new moon and the full moon.

One must know that the insight and knowledge of these four stages all clearly illuminate the true reality (*dharmatā*), yet they are spoken of with distinctions regarding their opening and entry. Next, concerning the four wisdoms (*jñāna*):
we now wish to correlate the four wisdoms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) with these four stages, rather than as they are treated in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) within the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The commentary explains that "one-path wisdom" refers to perceiving the true nature within the Path of Seeing; within this true nature, one attains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

"Path-seed wisdom" refers to knowing the distinct characteristics of delusion and awakening among the various paths of the ten dharma-realms, wherein each and every aspect is shown as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"All-encompassing wisdom" knows that all dharmas are of a single mark of quiescent extinction; this very extinction is awakening.

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision consists of the four kinds of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), by which he knows all phenomena as having a single mark—the mark of quiescent extinction—and recognizes all their various modes of activity, categories, and characteristics;

thus he enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Furthermore, the wisdom of the path that accords with principle is called "opening" the wisdom of the path, while that which accords with measure is called "showing" it.
When principle and measure are non-dual, this is termed "awakening" to the principle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

The measure [of the teaching] illuminates both [aspects] simultaneously as the entry; this also refers to the ultimate principle where there is neither shallowness nor depth, yet within that state, distinctions of shallow and deep are made.

Third, the four gates of the Perfect Teaching are explained horizontally regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): according to the gate of emptiness, "one is empty, all is empty," which is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
according to the gate of existence, "one exists, all exists," which is the revealing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is also...

Emptiness also has its gate: when all things are empty, there is the gate of "emptiness-and-existence," which is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; non-emptiness and non-existence also have their gate:
when all things are neither empty nor existent, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. That which enables penetration consists of four aspects, while that which is penetrated is one.
"Opening, showing, awakening, and entering" are the gates of penetration; what is known and what is seen are the principles of penetration.
Fourth, regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: contemplating the principle of the three truths within the nature of the mind is inconceivable.
This contemplation, being luminous and tranquil, is called "opening" (*kai*). Although it is inconceivable, one is still able to discern emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

their distinctness is perfectly clear without confusion, which is called "indicating" (*shi*). Emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are three yet one, and one yet three—this is called "naming" (*myō*).

To awaken to the fact that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are not themselves empty, provisional, or middle, yet to illuminate emptiness, the provisional, and the middle simultaneously—this is called "entry.
This constitutes the single mind’s threefold contemplation, wherein the distinctions between opening, showing, awakening, and entry are analytically revealed.

Therefore, regarding the fourfold interpretation, one should know that the realization of the principle arises from the stages, the stages are established by wisdom, wisdom is generated by the gates, and the gates are made pervasive by the gates.
Because one contemplates through contemplation, the gates become permeable; because the gates are permeable, wisdom is perfected; because wisdom is perfected, the stages are established;
because the stages are established, the principle is perceived; and because the principle is perceived, it is called "the unity of the principle. △ Second, the conclusion.
Śāriputra, it is for this sole purpose of one great matter that all Buddhas appear in the world.
This establishes the principle of the unity of the Dharma. (2) The Unity of the Two Persons.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas.

Although they may employ the skillful means of the past to teach and transform those of the three vehicles, in terms of ultimate reality, they teach and transform only bodhisattvas—just as that impoverished son considered himself a lowly laborer, yet was viewed by the elder in a different light."
In truth, they are his own children; this is the first identity. △ Third, the unity of practice:
whatever he does is always for one purpose—solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
All that is performed—the various practices of the three vehicles—is designated as "all" because they are intended to be perfected;
"all" is thus a single reality. To what does this practice lead? It leads solely toward the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is the single intent of practice. △ Fourth: One Teaching.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.

That which is called the "Single Buddha Vehicle" refers to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (yuan-dun-jiao), and is thus named the Single Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, the Introduction Chapter (Xùpǐn) states: [He] preached...

The Mahāyāna sūtras are themselves the teaching and its meaning. From the Separate Teaching (biejiao) onward, all are termed "teachings with remainder" (*śeṣa-artha*), meaning they are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and do not represent the Buddha’s single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
What is now spoken of as "exclusively by means of the single Buddha-vehicle" refers to the pure teaching of the Buddha-dharma, the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*).
"No other vehicles" means there are no teachings of the Separate Vehicle that involve expedient means (*upāya*) and remain incomplete.

The absence of "two" refers to the absence of the two [vehicles] within the *prajñāpāramitā*; the absence of "three" refers to the absence of the three [vehicles] that are contrasted therein in the Vaipulya.
If these two and three are both absent, how much more so the three within the Tripiṭaka? △ Fifth, the summary of the identity of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is also like this.
△ Chapter on the Buddhas of the Three Times, Part Three: First, the Buddhas of the Past; Second, first, the disclosure of the provisional.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression.
△ Second, revealing the reality:
Because these dharmas are all for the sake of the single Buddha-vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas,
will ultimately attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
These teachings are all revealed as reality for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna). Following the above, the "Single Buddha Vehicle" refers to the Unity of Teaching;
hearing the Dharma from the Buddhas refers to those who hear the Dharma, which is bestowed upon sentient beings—this is the Unity of Person;
ultimately, all attain the Knowledge of All Modes (Sarvākārajñatā), and that which is known by this knowledge is the Unity of Principle; that which knows it is the Unity of Wisdom.

This means that although the practice of the One is not sequential, the four Ones are simultaneously complete. △ Second, regarding the Buddhas of the future, there are two parts; first, the disclosure of the provisional:
"Śāriputra, all the Buddhas who shall appear in the world in the future will likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients..."
He expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions;
this may be understood according to the text. △ Second, revealing the reality:
Because these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain it.
"Omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) may be understood according to the text. △ Third, the Chapter on the Present, Part One: Indicating the Intent of Appearing in the World.
Śāriputra, among the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions...
It brings great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings.

For example, just as in the chapters on the Buddhas it is said that they appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter, so too does this [Buddha] appear in the world solely for the purpose of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings. △ Second, the Opening.
World-Honored One, these Buddhas likewise employ immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables,
and modes of expression to expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Third, revealing the reality in two parts; first, specifically clarifying the teaching of the present [time], in one section.

Because these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Second, a general explanation that the principle of the three periods of time is one.
Śāriputra, these Buddhas do nothing but teach and transform bodhisattvas, because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings,
because they wish to awaken sentient beings to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This is a passage that reveals the ultimate truth by opening up the provisional; it fully possesses the fourfold "one" (the Fourfold One), and its meaning is evident. The *Ji* (Commentary) states:
"The section on the Buddhas of the present begins from the very start as the revelation of the ultimate through the opening of the provisional.

From 'Śāriputra, these Buddhas... onwards corresponds to the general text. Therefore, in the previous analysis, it was stated that each of the sections on the Buddhas of the three periods clarifies both teaching and practice.
This generally clarifies the principles of human nature; according to this standard, one should first open the chapters by first distinguishing and then summarizing.

The reason they are not opened here first is that in the subsequent general text, there is no summary for the opening of the provisional (expedient means), but only the single phrase "revealing the real.

Therefore, because the provisional and the real are each associated with the three periods of time, the distinction between the general and the specific would be incongruous. Consequently, they are combined within the present section.
In the Chapter on the Buddha, because the text is fully formed and complete, it is said that "the text is complete. △ Second, the Chapter on Śākyamuni, Part Five:
First, Opening the Expedient Means.
"Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus: I know that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated inclinations..."
I preach the Dharma by employing the power of skillful means through various causes, conditions, parables, and terminology, in accordance with their respective natures.
I am none other than the present Śākyamuni Buddha; being first three and then one, I am no different from those four Buddhas.
The statement is likewise so: "knowing that sentient beings have various desires" refers to the faculties (*indriya*), inclinations (*ruci*), and dispositions (*gotra*) of the five vehicles.
That which was called "faculties" in the past is called "desires" in the present and "dispositions" in the future. That which is deeply attached to in the mind is the faculty;
skillful means (*upāya*) is the provisional teaching of the three vehicles according to what is appropriate. The Record states: "knowing..."
The various sentient beings depart according to their karmic responses; the various causes and conditions depart according to their corresponding manifestations. △ Second, revealing the four truths:
Śāriputra, all of this is for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes.

Such statements as these indicate that the provisional is the real; the Buddha Vehicle is the teaching, all-encompassingness is the practice, and the single kind of wisdom that knows is the principle.
△ Third, citing the five turbidities to explain skillful means.
Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, much less three.

Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of a degenerate age—namely, the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, and the turbidity of life.
Thus it is, Śāriputra: during the chaos of the turbid kalpa, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy; they are accomplished in stinginess, greed, and envy.
Because of the various unwholesome roots, the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
Even in the worlds of the ten directions there are no two vehicles, let alone three. This is intended to introduce the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) by first indicating its underlying purpose.

Although it was previously stated that the Buddhas open up the provisional to reveal the real, the manner in which they conceal the real to manifest the provisional has not yet been clarified; such is the nature of their teaching.
Pure and limpid as space, it is already devoid of the provisional vehicles of both the second (Prajñāpāramitā) and the third (Vaipulya);

how much less could there be the provisional vehicles of the single third (the Three Vehicles) or the single fifth (adding humans and devas)? It is solely because the obstacles of the five turbidities are so heavy that [the truth] cannot truly be proclaimed;
thus, one must employ the provisional vehicles of the single fifth and the single third, as well as those that encompass the second and the third. Therefore, it is said to be "one."

The Buddha’s vehicle is explained through distinctions as threefold. Regarding the "five turbidities" (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), there are four specific sections: first, the proclamation of their number; second, the enumeration of their names;

third, the explanation of their essential nature and characteristics; and fourth, the resolution of doubts. The proclamation of the number and the enumeration of the names can be understood according to the text.

The phrase "thus" (*evam*) clarifies the essential nature and characteristics of the five turbidities. Since the essence and characteristics of these turbidities cannot be fully described, they are briefly indicated by saying "thus."
The term "kalpa" is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "time-period" (*kāla-bhāga*). One should know that the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) has no separate substantial entity.
A kalpa is a long duration, whereas a *kṣaṇa* is a short duration; this conventional designation "turbidity of the kalpa" is established solely in reference to the four turbidities.

Furthermore, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) also has no separate substantial entity; it is a conventional designation established by taking the three turbidities—of views, pride, and karmic retribution—as its basis.

The defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) and the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) take the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-saṃyojana*) as their essence; the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) takes the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-saṃyojana*) as its essence;

and the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) takes the continuity of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) as its essence. Regarding the characteristics of these five defilements, one should know that the intensification of the four defilements is concentrated in this period:
namely, the intensification of malice (*vyāpāda*), the outbreak of weapons (*śastra*), and the increase of greed (*lobha*).
As famine intensifies, ignorance arises; as pestilence intensifies, the three calamities arise.

Consequently, afflictions flourish twofold, false views blaze ever more fiercely, and coarse, debased physical and mental states, along with evil reputations and foul names, prevail. The years diminish and the lifespan shortens as the various turbidities converge like waters rushing toward a dark abyss.
When wind and waves surge in fury and fish and dragons churn in turmoil, there is not a single thing to rely upon.
That which causes this to be so is like the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven at the beginning of a kalpa falling to earth, whereby the earth causes them to have desire;

it is also like the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven entering the Rough and Harsh Garden (*Kharasvaka-udyāna*), whereby the garden gives rise to a mind of contention. This is called the characteristic of the *kalpa-kāṣāya*. As for the *kleśa-kāṣāya*:
the ocean of greed receives all streams yet is never satiated; hatred is like a venomous serpent that inhales poison and agitates the world; and delusion is darkness.
Stubbornness and stupidity exceed the blackness of lacquer; arrogance leads to looking down upon others with no restraint;
entangled in webs of doubt and lacking sincerity, one cannot be told the truth. This is the characteristic of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
As for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), it consists of the sixteen types of knowledge and views, the sixty-two [wrong] views, and so forth—like a net, and also resembling a dense forest.

To be bound by fetters, to be bent and crooked, and to be unable to escape—this is the characteristic of the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). As for the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*):
grasping at form and mind, one establishes a single sovereign self. Like sticky glue to which nothing does not adhere, they drift through the six realms of existence, taking birth everywhere.
Whether called poor or short, rich or tall—this is the characteristic of the defilement of sentient beings. This is the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

That which is born in the morning and perishes by evening, appearing at dawn and setting by dusk, revolving like waves and circling like smoke, not remaining still for even an instant—this is the characteristic of the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
As for the sequential order: afflictions and views constitute the root; from these two turbidities, sentient beings are formed;
and from sentient beings, there arises the sustaining of life. When these four become slight, it is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
...and so forth. △ Fourth, Distinguishing the False and Encouraging Faith, in two parts: First, Distinguishing the True from the False; Second, Distinguishing those who are not true disciples.

Śāriputra, if my disciples claim for themselves to be Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, yet do not hear and do not know that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, teach and transform only Bodhisattvas—these are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they Arhats, nor...
The Pratyekabuddha.
This name serves to distinguish the false and to encourage faith. If a disciple of the Buddha can personally believe and understand [this], they are a true disciple;
if they do not believe and understand, they are neither a true disciple nor an Arhat. Therefore, the assembly is earnestly exhorted to believe, accept, and understand this. Within this...

There are two points of contention: first, those who have not heard and do not know [the Dharma] are not true disciples; second, those who have heard it but do not believe or accept it develop overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

For instance, if worldly disciples follow their teacher’s teachings and succeed in transmitting the lamp of the Dharma, yet if they have not heard and do not know it, there would be no Dharma to follow—how then could they be called disciples?
Furthermore, in the past, the Tathāgata spoke of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and opened up the three vehicles for you.
Having followed [the path] and attained nirvana, having heard and known [it], one is called a disciple.
Now that the five turbidities have been removed, I speak this single [truth] for you; why do you not hear it and not know it? "Not hearing" means not hearing the teaching;
"not knowing" means not knowing the practice. One who is not true is not in accordance with principle; one who is not a disciple is not [a disciple].
People are one and the same. △ Second, the failure of faith leads to the perfection of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves that they have already attained arhatship, that this is their final body, and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa;
consequently, they no longer aspire to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You should know that these individuals are all people of overweening pride. Why is this?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible.
Furthermore, from "Again, Śāriputra" onwards is the second section, which clarifies that those who lack faith develop overweening pride (*adhimāna*). This is intended to urge them toward faith:
"You claim for yourself that this is your final birth, yet even this body is still immeasurable; in truth, you are not in your final birth.

You claim for yourself that you have reached the ultimate goal, yet two hundred *yojanas* still remain; in truth, you have not reached the ultimate goal. To claim to have attained what one has not attained—is this not [overweening pride]?"
Those who possess overweening pride are not true Arhats. Those whose defilements have been eliminated and whose faculties are sharp know that [their attainment] is not ultimate;

they believe in the True Dharma as it truly is, yet do not consider themselves to be in their final body. They do not give rise to overweening pride, knowing that [their state] is not ultimate, and they believe in the ultimate.

This very belief is the realization of this principle. To be entirely free from overweening pride is to achieve the unity of practice; to have this single faith is to believe in the teaching—this is the unity of the teaching.
These disciples of the Buddha are one and the same as ordinary people. △ Second, resolving doubts by making exceptions has two parts.
First, making exceptions; first, removing [the restriction] regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha is not present before one.
Regarding the "Dispelling Doubts by Opening and Excluding," first, "opening and excluding" means that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one does not incur the fault of *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
If, while the Buddha was still in the world, one did not believe or accept this sutra when it was being correctly preached, yet claimed to be a true *arhat*, one would indeed incur *adhimāna*.

However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one has attained the state of an *arhat* but—due to partial attachment to provisional (*neyārtha*) sutras—does not believe in the perfect (*nītārtha*) Dharma, [the teaching] permits this as an exception.
Arrogance. △ Second, the difficulty of finding those with faith.
Why is this? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sutras as these are difficult to find.
Why is this? Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is difficult to find people of superior character, and profound sūtras are difficult to understand; yet one should not fall into conceit.
Although the Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, this sūtra still exists; if one fails to believe and accept it, that would indeed be conceit, which should be immediately dispelled.
Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, although this sūtra exists, those who can explain its words and meaning are rare.
Even if one encounters [this teaching] and causes an Arhat to lack faith or understanding, it is permitted that this is not due to overweening pride (adhimāna). △ Second, resolving doubts:
If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive resolution regarding this Dharma.
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can interpret the sutras are difficult to encounter—such that one who has attained arhatship enters parinirvāṇa forever—the commentary explains:
although such a person may conceive the thought of having entered extinction, after their life ends, they will be reborn in a remaining land beyond this realm;
there they will meet another Buddha, hear this sutra, and immediately attain definitive understanding.
The ninety-third chapter of the *Śāstra*, "Explanation of the Chapter on Certainty" (*Niya-ta-varga*), states:
"If an Arhat receives a body from a previous life, that body must necessarily perish; in what place does he abide while perfecting the Buddha-way? Answer:

"Since the causes and conditions of the outflows (*āsrava*) within the three realms have been exhausted for an Arhat, he is no longer reborn in the three realms. He exists outside the realms in a pure Buddha-land, free from affliction."
"Affliction" refers to this: having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* from the Buddha in this land, one fulfills the path to Buddhahood.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself states: "There may be arhats who, not having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, claim for themselves that they have attained nirvāṇa;
I shall explain these matters to them in other lands, and you shall all become Buddhas. Having already cited the sutra as proof, I shall now interpret the sutra's meaning by returning to it.

The *Lunjie* (Commentary on the Explanation) by Master Nanyue says: "Other Buddhas" refers to the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*). When an Arhat encounters them, he hears this sutra and attains definitive understanding.

Furthermore, when an Arhat practices the meditative concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions, they preach this sutra for him, whereby he immediately attains definitive understanding.

Moreover, when an ordinary practitioner (*pṛthagjana*) reaches the point of exhaustion through diligent practice and repents, he beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions; they preach it for him as well, and he likewise attains definitive understanding.
[End of section]. △ Fifth, No Falsehood, in three parts: First, exhorting faith in Śākyamuni.
"Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe, understand, accept, and uphold the Buddha’s words.
This clarifies that there is no falsehood, serving to stop the slanderous minds of sentient beings; this constitutes the first of the three [parts], the exhortation to have faith in Śākyamuni.
Because he speaks the truth, he says: "You all should with one mind believe, understand, and uphold the Buddha's words. △ Second, the exhortation to have faith in all Buddhas:
The words of all the Tathāgatas are without falsehood.

Next, in order to encourage faith in all Buddhas, it is said that the words of all Buddhas are not false; because the paths of all Buddhas are identical, one should further increase one's faith and acceptance.
△ Third, concluding that [the teaching] is not false.
There is no other vehicle; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle.
Because this is concluded at the end as being not in vain, it is said that "there is no other vehicle, only the single Buddha-vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

△ Second, the two verses in praise [of the response]. First, the verse praising the granting of the answer. First, the verse distinguishing what is granted. First, the verse on the five thousand who withdrew from their seats.
There were bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs harboring overweening pride (*adhimāna*), upāsakas with arrogance (*māna*), and upāsikās lacking faith.
Thus, among these four assemblies, there were five thousand who did not perceive their own faults; they had deficiencies in their precepts and cherished their blemishes.
These were those of small wisdom—the dregs and chaff who had already departed from the assembly.
It was by the majestic power of the Buddha that these people left, for they possessed little merit and were incapable of receiving this Dharma.
One must know that the fourfold assembly generally possesses both overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and self-conceit (*māna*), as well as a lack of faith;

however, among the two groups of renunciants who have practiced the path and attained meditative concentration, they mistakenly claim these to be the fruits of sainthood, giving rise specifically to overweening pride. If one is a layperson, being arrogant and self-important, one mostly gives rise to self-conceit.
As for women, their wisdom is shallow and they frequently produce deviant views; those who do not see their own faults suffer from the three losses that shroud the mind.

To conceal one's faults while flaunting one's virtues, yet being unable to reflect upon oneself, is to be a person without shame (*ahrīka*). If one recognizes one's own failings, one is a monk possessed of modesty (*hrī*).

Regarding those who have deficiencies in the precepts, their restraint (*saṃvara*) is impaired; this is termed a "deficiency" (*chidra*). When there is a failure regarding the meditative concentration associated with the Path, it is termed a "leak" (*srotas*), because the concentration of the Path and so forth are absent.
Thus, when evil thoughts arise within, it is like a jade containing a flaw; because there is no restraint, it is said to be "impaired."
Externally moving the body and speech like jade or dew, one covers over transgressions and thus naturally attains [merit]; this is called "protecting and cherishing.

Those who possess only small wisdom—neither the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) nor the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*)—but instead falsely claim that worldly, minor wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*), are the "smallest among the small," and are therefore called those of "small wisdom. As for "dregs and chaff," it refers to those who lack untainted dhyāna.
Because it is moistened by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is like dregs; because it is not nourished by wisdom (*prajñā*), it is like chaff.

These five thousand people possess worldly meditation, which is like dregs, and possess an understanding based on the literal text, which is like chaff. They cling to the words while losing the underlying meaning, like chaff that lacks the grain.
Furthermore, the analogy of dregs and chaff illustrates their lack of great spiritual capacity (*mahāyāna-śakti*). 2. Verse on the Assembly Having Become Pure.
This assembly has no branches or leaves, but consists only of the pure and solid.
"Branches and leaves" are a metaphor for those who are not fit vessels; since they are entirely unserviceable, they must be sent away. △ Second, the verse on the admonition and permission.
"Śāriputra, listen well.
This verse immediately follows the preceding exhortation, commanding him to listen attentively. △ Second, the verse on the actual response, which has two parts:

first, the verse on the four Buddhas; second, the verse on Śākyamuni. Regarding the first part, there are again four sections: first, a general verse on the chapter of all Buddhas; second... [and so forth].

Three verses on the chapter concerning past Buddhas; four verses on the chapter concerning future Buddhas; four verses on the chapter concerning present Buddhas. Regarding the first section, there are five parts;
the first is the verse on the employment of expedient means, which is further divided into two parts, the first of which is the verse on the actual employment of expedient means.
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through the power of immeasurable skillful means.

Having fully known the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings, the various paths they travel, their manifold desires and dispositions, and the good or evil karma of their past lives, the Buddhas—by means of various causes, parables, and verbal skillful means—cause all to rejoice; they may, for instance, preach the Sūtras.
The gāthās, itivṛttakas, jātaka, adbhutadharma, as well as the nidāna, avadāna, and further the geya and upadeśa sūtras—these verses of this chapter differ from the preceding prose in three ways:
first, that some are present in one but absent in the other; second, that they appear before or after [the prose].
In some versions, there are three instances where the opening and closing differ: in one, there is a verse praising the rarity of the Dharma but lacking mention of the five turbidities;

in another, there are the five turbidities but no praise for the Dharma; and in yet another, the praise for the Dharma comes first followed by the clarification that the provisional is opened to reveal the real.

Now, the provisional is first opened to reveal the real, followed by the clarification that it is not in vain. Previously, the exhortation to believe was explained in conjunction with "not being in vain," whereas now they are treated separately.
Regarding the encouragement of faith in the chapter on "Non-emptiness," Zhanran says: "The preceding [verse] uses Śākyamuni’s skillful means to explain the provisional aspects of all Buddhas;
the verse [here] uses Śākyamuni’s reality to explain the manifest aspect of all Buddhas, showing that 'one' is the four and the four are one.

As for "the Dharma attained by all Buddhas," this refers to attaining various provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the path, as well as immeasurable powers of skillful means—the latter being the content of the following verse.

The passage "With countless skillful means and various causes and conditions, he expounds all dharmas according to what sentient beings think in their minds" is a verse summarizing the aforementioned teaching of the Dharma according to suitability.
Within this verse, the characteristics of teaching according to suitability are extensively set forth;

that is, he teaches the seven expedient means by illuminating the capacities of the nine realms. Since it cannot be definitively determined whether there are nine or seven, it is said to be "various," according to their desires.

That which is appropriate to apply is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint); that which is appropriate to apply according to individual dispositions is the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (standpoint of human effort);

that which is appropriate to apply according to evil karma is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (standpoint of remedial counteraction). The manifestation of aspiration is called the "gate of mindfulness" (*smṛti-dvāra*);
