their differences are termed "various. That which was practiced in the past is called "nature" (*prakṛti*); present delight is called "desire" (*chanda*), or it may be termed "habitual desire" (*abhyāsa-chanda*).

The perfected nature gives rise to the habitual desires for wholesome and unwholesome karma; these seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are transmitted and mutually related as wholesome and unwholesome.

The Buddha perceives all of them with equal wisdom. Using his expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), he illuminates the dispositions and desires of those engaged in these various skillful means, and subsequently, through various causes, conditions, and parables, he preaches the ninefold and twelvefold divisions of the scriptures according to what is appropriate for each, as explained in the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning).
[The Buddha] spoke: "Second, the verse concludes the intent behind the provisional teaching of the Dharma:

'For those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are greedily attached to birth and death, who do not practice the profound and wondrous path under immeasurable Buddhas, and who are distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings—for their sake, I preach Nirvana.'"
These one and a half verses conclude the intent behind the provisional teaching;

it should be understood that because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the capacity in this life to hear the Great [Vehicle], it is said that they do not practice the profound and wondrous Way.

Because they were hindered by heavy attachments in previous lives and are now afflicted by manifold sufferings in this life, they can only hear the Small [Vehicle]; therefore, it is said that for their sake, Nirvana is taught. △ Second.
The verse reveals the fourfold reality; the first verse concerns the principle.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha’s wisdom, yet I have never said, "You shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not so said is that the time had not yet come; now is precisely that time, and I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna.
These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they take the entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, and for this reason I speak this sutra.
These three lines of verse share a single principle: they enable one to enter the Buddha’s wisdom, which is the "one great causal condition" mentioned above.
They definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna and provide a general summary that reveals, awakens, and leads to the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. These ninefold [teachings] of mine...
It is said that the Mahāyāna consists of twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*), whereas the Hīnayāna possesses only nine divisions.

This is because the Hīnayāna is a teaching of "ashes and annihilation" (*bhasma-uccheda-vāda*) and lacks the *cintāmaṇi-ratna* (wish-fulfilling jewel) body; therefore, it lacks the *vaipulya* division.

Furthermore, because it lacks the spontaneous sounding of the celestial drum, it lacks the *apraśnita-svayambhāṣita* (unasked self-proclamation) division. Although it contains *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), these are so few that they are not counted as a separate division.

Regarding the section on the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), this has been explained thus according to its specific classification; however, speaking in general terms, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*).
As for these twelve: first, *sūtra*, which is translated here as "Dharma-source" (*dharmamūla*); second, *geya*, which is translated as "repeated verse" (*punar-gāthā*);
third, *vyākaraṇa*, which is translated as "prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*); fourth, *gāthā*, which is translated as "un[adorned] verse" (*agāthā*)...
1. Geya (Verses): five udānas, here translated as "unasked self-explanations"; 2. Nidāna: here translated as "causes and conditions";
3. Avadāna: here translated as "parables"; 4. Itivṛttaka: here translated as "past events"; 5. Jātaka:
here translated as "birth stories"; 6. Vaipulya: here translated as "extensive teachings. 11.
*Abhūta-dharma* (阿浮達磨) is translated here as "the unprecedented" (*adbhuta*). *Upadeśa* (優波提舍) is translated as "discourse" (*upadeśa*).

What is called a "section" (*piṭaka*) refers to a distinct category or class; because there are twelve such distinct classes, the new translations—fearing confusion with the term for "volumes" (*piṭaka*)—refer to them as the "Twelvefold Teachings" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
The following verse establishes that entering the Mahāyāna is the fundamental basis: [Verse omitted per instructions]
This leads upward into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. II. Verses on the Person (1).
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, supple, and sharp; who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, have practiced the profound and wondrous Way.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra; I certify that such persons shall, in a future age, attain the path of Buddhahood.
Because they recollect the Buddha with a profound mind and cultivate the pure precepts, these individuals, upon hearing this, attain great joy that pervades their entire bodies.

Knowing their mental activities, the Buddha teaches them the Mahāyāna. Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, if they hear even a single verse of the Dharma I have taught, they will all undoubtedly become Buddhas.
These four and a half verses clarify that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas above teach and transform only bodhisattvas.
While the preceding section simply states "teaching and transforming bodhisattvas," these verses extensively set forth the various skillful means by which all people become true persons.
Those who possess the mind of a Buddha-son are those of the Distinct Teaching; for these sons, the Buddha preaches the Mahāyāna sūtras so that they may attain [realization].
When one’s mind is marked with joy, one becomes a person of truth according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas—if they are śrāvakas, they also include pratyekabuddhas; if they are bodhisattvas, they also include all bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) and those who practice the six perfections—all such as these will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
This is because the seven kinds of skillful means are none other than the sons of the Buddha.
△ Three verses teach this one point:
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
These exist merely as provisional names to guide sentient beings, spoken for the purpose of revealing the Buddha’s wisdom.

This single verse of three lines summarizes the above: that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna), with no other vehicles—neither two nor three.
That the Buddhas of the ten directions teach only this one Dharma is precisely the teaching of the "One" as a provisional designation;
it is the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*). There is no other vehicle, and within the non-dual teaching, there is no separate [vehicle], but rather the Perfect [Teaching].
This is the remainder following the entry into the distinct [teachings]. "There is no two" means there is no duality of the provisional and the full within the Shared Teaching;
"there is no three" means there is no triad within the Tripitaka Teaching.
Such dualities and triads are all merely provisional names used to guide sentient beings; the Dharma of today is solely the single, perfect vehicle of the Buddha. △ Four.
Verse on Practice, One:
The appearance of Buddhas in the world is for this one reality alone; the other two are not true.
They never deliver sentient beings by means of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but abide themselves in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), adorned with the power of the Dharma they have realized and wisdom.
By means of this, I deliver sentient beings and personally realize the unsurpassed path—the Dharma of equality of the Mahāyāna.
If I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is impossible for me.
These three lines of verse summarize all that has been discussed above: that all actions performed always serve a single purpose, which is to practice a single path.
This "purpose" is precisely the "practice," meaning that one never uses the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to deliver sentient beings;

this summarizes the meaning of the phrase "always performing a single task. The line "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna and thereby delivers sentient beings" summarizes the preceding [verse] "only... [i.e., only the Mahāyāna].
The subsequent line, "to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," explains the meaning of not delivering them by means of the Lesser Vehicle.
△ Third, the verse on exhorting faith has two parts: first, exhorting faith by citing the fruit; second, first, citing the internal mind.
If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata— who is neither deceptive nor possessed of greed or envy, and who has severed all evils among all phenomena—
then the Buddha alone is without fear throughout the ten directions.
These two and a half lines cite the fruit [of the teaching] to exhort faith; since the prose states, "Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken," this verse now reiterates it.

"If a person believes and takes refuge in the Buddha, for the Tathāgata does not deceive" clarifies that the Buddha’s mind is pure, that ignorance and stinginess have been severed, and that he speaks from within a pure mind where all evils have been eliminated.
Therefore, this is trustworthy. △ Second, citing external forms:
"I adorn my body with marks; its radiance illuminates the world; honored by immeasurable multitudes, I preach for them the Seal of the True Mark."

"Those who adorn their bodies with marks" (the first line) clarifies external form. Indeed, because the physical marks are brilliant and radiant, and the countenance is dignified and majestic, there is no darkness or delusion within and light shines forth without; thus, one’s speech is free from deception and one is honored by the multitude.
To preach the seal of the Mahāyāna is to be worthy of trust and acceptance. △ Second, citing the cause to encourage faith, in two parts: first, citing... [text breaks off]
Regarding my former vow:
Śāriputra, you should know that when I first established my vow, I desired to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
You should know that my former vow was not merely a personal pledge to attain bodhi, but a vow that all sentient beings should likewise enter [enlightenment] together with me.
The Buddha’s wisdom now fulfills his vow; therefore, this teaching may also be believed. △ Second, the fulfillment of the vow:
"As I vowed in the past, that vow is now fulfilled; I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way."

Now that enlightenment is fulfilled and sentient beings have likewise entered [the path], and since you yourself have personally realized the Buddha-wisdom, it is verified that my vow was not in vain.
This concludes the section on establishing the cause and exhorting faith. Question:

Since the original vow was universal, why do you say the vow is fulfilled when there are still so many sentient beings? Answer: The Buddha benefits beings throughout the three periods of time; here, we clarify the present.

And thus the fulfillment of the vow is discussed. △ Fourth, the verse on the five turbidities (pañcakaṣāya) has four parts; first, a general explanation that the five turbidities obstruct the Great [Vehicle]:
"If I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way, those without wisdom would become confused and deluded, and would not accept the teaching."

"If I encounter 'sentient beings' (sattva): According to the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 12, at the beginning of the kalpa, when beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to be born in this world, there were neither male nor female, nor distinctions of noble and base; all beings were born together. Therefore, they are called "sentient beings"—this refers to the very first instance.

If one gathers the various aggregates (skandhas) and applies a provisional name, it is called a "sentient being"—this refers to the period of receiving retribution for a single lifetime. If one says... [text continues]

Regarding the statement that "sentient beings" (*sattva*) are so named because they undergo birth in various places: this refers to the circulation through the five destinies (*gati*) by the power of karma.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that there are ten kinds of sentient beings, namely: long, short, square, round, triangular, blue, yellow, red, and purple.
As for how sentient beings undergo birth and death: while remaining long in the hells, their bodies experience inconceivable suffering.

With a mind of bitter suffering, one contemplates the immeasurable and boundless evils committed during the time as an animal, when bodies were alternately swallowed and devoured and minds were alternately oppressed and tormented;
during the time as a hungry ghost, when the body was like a burning mountain and the mind like a boiling cauldron, with fierce wrong views, head-butting insolence, and ignorant ferocity;
and during the time as a human, when body, speech, and mind constantly performed harmful deeds for oneself.
Toiling with body, speech, and mind, one constantly dwells on things that are not beneficial, thereby entangling oneself;

while in the heavens, one is addicted to the six sense-objects, indulging in wanton play, failing to hear the True Dharma, and blocking the source of merit—this is called the long duration of birth and death for sentient beings.
What is the short duration of birth and death for sentient beings? It is when, while in the hells, one is able to attain a single thought-moment of tranquility.

When in the state of an animal, one can still attain a moment of stillness of mind by taking refuge in the precepts; when in the state of a hungry ghost, one can still attain a moment of stillness of mind by relying on the Triple Gem;
when in the state of a human, one can cultivate the six perfections, filially support one’s parents, and show reverence to the Triple Gem.
Adorning one’s body, speech, and mind with these manifold virtues, when in the state of a deva, one can renounce heavenly life.

Delighting in the observance of precepts, delighting in meditation, teaching and reciting, practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and speaking little—these constitute the shortening of birth and death for sentient beings.
What is meant by the "direction" of birth and death for sentient beings? It is like that of Uttarakuru: regarding all things, they have no sense of "mine";
when they cast off their bodies, they necessarily ascend to heaven; from heaven they ascend further to heaven, always tending toward higher states of goodness.

The "square" of birth and death refers to the directions and corners. Why is it that the "round" of birth and death for sentient beings exists only within the three miserable realms and the four destinies, revolving in a circular manner like a whirling firebrand? What is the "triangular" birth and death?
It refers to wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and indeterminate karma, among others. Why is it that the "blue" birth and death of sentient beings constantly enters into darkness?
The dark hells where there is constant terror is this; what are the beings of the yellow birth-and-death? They are the hungry ghosts, emaciated by hunger and withered and pale.
What are the beings of the red birth-and-death? They are the animals who devour one another, their blood flowing brilliantly.
Purple refers simply to the asuras. What are the beings of the white birth-and-death? They are humans.

Regarding the white karma and the wholesome paths within the intermediate states (*antarābhava*), it is as when other devas say to a dying deva, "Go, you shall be born in the human realm," or when a wise friend says to a dying person, "Go, you shall proceed toward the heavenly realms. One should know that these two instances constitute white birth and death.
Furthermore, the fifth [treatise] states: "The mind paints hell black; the color of ghosts is that of crows, and that of animals is that of pigeons."
Question: Regarding the fact that those born as yellow people appear in a red heaven and white people in a blue one—what is the meaning of this?
Answer: The lower section explains the retributions of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*); here, we explain the karma created within the five destinies, and for this reason, they differ.

Furthermore, the karmic retributions of saṃsāra vary; as stated in the *Jiashishi Sanmei Jing* (Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra): "Those who come from hell have hoarse voices, sudden urgency, and tremble repeatedly."
They dream of great fires, boiling cauldrons, and the like. Those who come from the realm of animals are dark-witted, indolent, gluttonous, timid, and stammering;
their actions mostly resemble those of various insects and beasts. Those who come from the realm of hungry ghosts have yellow hair, are constantly hungry, and are stingy and greedy;
other destinies may be inferred by comparison. Thus, such beings as these are described extensively in the sutras.

Regarding the meeting with the Buddha: one should know that sentient beings scorch themselves with suffering and affliction, while the Buddhas rescue all things through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because compassion and suffering face one another, it is called a "meeting. Furthermore, the Buddha is suchness and sentient beings are suchness; they are a single suchness without duality.
Because their fundamental nature is interrelated, it is called a "meeting. One should know that great compassion constantly pities sentient beings.
If I were to instruct humans and devas according to worldly teachings, I would fall into darkness and delusion;

I would merely escape from the cycle of birth and death characterized by blue, yellow, red, white, purple, square, round, and angular forms, rather than teaching the Buddha-way. If I were to encounter sentient beings and cause them to practice the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed;
this is not permissible, as it would only lead to liberation from the twenty-five states of existence. If I encounter sentient beings, I must teach [the Mahayana].
If I were to cause them to cultivate only the specific [paths], I would fall into partiality and lose the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now, I cause all sentient beings to attain the wondrous wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), so that they may realize that everything is the Buddha-dharma and nothing is not the right path.
This is to teach them entirely by means of the Buddha-way, whereby the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted. I always speak thus, yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull.

The gravity of this offense cannot be expiated as he had wished. In a past life, there was a Buddha named Anihitasthita (Abiding in Non-abiding) who made a vow that the sentient beings of his own land would all attain Buddhahood on the same day and at the same time, and that they should enter parinirvāṇa on that very same day.

Furthermore, prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Samatā (Equanimity) who likewise vowed that the sentient beings of his own land and those of the ten directions should also attain Buddhahood on one and the same day. Thus it was.
"Today is the day of my parinirvāṇa; are there still Buddhas and sentient beings? The Buddha said, "Stop, stop!
Among all those who have obtained a human body, has anyone ever made a vow to cause those in the five realms of existence to attain Buddhahood on the same day?
[The interlocutor] said, "That is impossible; one cannot achieve the Unsurpassed Way with a body that is not a fit vessel. One must first transform the three lower realms..."
Only after attaining the natural state of a human being can one fulfill one's aspirations. Since the three [lower] realms are unwholesome paths, how could one achieve Buddhahood there?
It is like a person seeking a treasure trove; they do not seek it in the midst of empty space. △ Second, specifically explaining the hindrances of the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya).
Part One: The Turbidity of Sentient Beings (sattva-kaṣāya).
I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness; because they are stubbornly attached to the five desires and deluded by craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, they fall into the three evil realms and revolve through the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons and suffering.
These two lines clarify that the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers to the true mark of *tathatā*, the fundamental source of goodness.
Because one does not plant roots of goodness by relying upon this, one does not experience greatness. Those who are firmly attached to the five desires are the very root of all evils;
as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "From delusion and craving, my illness arises"—this is precisely what is meant. △ Second, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
The subtle form of conception constantly grows from lifetime to lifetime for those of meager virtue and little merit who are oppressed by manifold sufferings.

This single line specifically clarifies the contemplation of the mind regarding the impurity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). To explain: the moment a thought arises, it immediately constitutes karma for the future;
this karma is the "womb" (*garbha*), and the karma of the womb is inexhaustible, continuing without interruption from life to life. This non-interruption is precisely what constitutes "growth."
For a long time, one undergoes the subtle form of the womb; this form consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the aggregates are also termed "worldly life.

It is through the continuous maintenance of these that the aggregates enter the world. From the moment after the union of father and mother, [the embryo] is like thin curd at three weeks (*tri-saptāha*);
it is like thick curd at four weeks; it is like congealed butter at five weeks; it is like a membrane at six weeks; and it is like a lump of flesh at seven weeks.
Upon the mass of flesh, five blisters arise: one for the head, and eight or seven for the hands and feet; then another five blisters arise:
one for the head, two for the shoulders, and two for the wrists—nine or seven in total. Subsequently, twenty-four blisters arise: four blisters form the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue;
twenty blisters become the twenty fingers and toes. Seventeen times this manifestation of the abdominal form occurs, until gradually the skin and bones separate and dissolve.
Various distinct characteristics arise: seven hundred sinews and seven thousand vessels. According to the characteristics required, each is colored by a corresponding wind.
For the characteristic of whiteness, the white wind colors it; the same applies to the other winds. Because of the fragrant wind, one is secure, upright, and handsome;
because of the foul-smelling wind, one is insecure, then becomes ugly, deformed, and crooked. After emerging from the womb, one consumes the five [nutriments].
Grains produce eighty thousand species of worms. △ Third is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Entering the dense forest of false views—whether [things] exist or do not exist—one relies upon these various views, which fully comprise sixty-two types.
This one line of clear exposition reveals the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); one should know that the five views intermingle like a dense and luxuriant thicket.
Whether there is this view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) or that view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), from these two views arise the sixty-two views.

Some say that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon the self (*ātman*) according to four propositions: "form is the self," "the self is apart from form," "form is greater than the self," and "the self is smaller than form."
"I abide within form; I am great and form is small; form abides within me"—the same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandhas*). These constitute twenty [views].
When distributed across the three periods of time, they become sixty; together with the fundamental [five views], they total sixty-two. △ Four: Afflictions.
"Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, stubbornly clinging to them so that they cannot be relinquished; with self-conceit and arrogance, their minds are crooked and insincere.
This may be understood according to the text. △ Fifth, the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Those who for thousands of millions of *kalpas* have neither heard the name of a Buddha nor heard the True Dharma are difficult to save.

That there has been no Buddha-Dharma for such a long duration is what constitutes the *kalpa-kaṣāya*. Furthermore, because the aforementioned four turbidities (*kaṣāya*) converge within this period of time, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
"Turbidity" (*kaṣāya*) is like throwing a small amount of soil into clear water: the water loses its clarity, and the soil loses its distinctness.
Those such as these, being obstructed and hindered, are difficult to save because of the barriers of the five turbidities; since they do not believe in the One Vehicle, they cannot be saved.
△ Third, teaching the Lesser Vehicle for the sake of those in the five turbidities.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I have established skillful means to teach the path that exhausts all suffering and point toward it by means of *nirvāṇa*.
This may be understood according to the text. △ Fourth, explaining the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle for the sake of the Great Vehicle.
Although I speak of nirvana, it is not a true extinction; all dharmas have from the beginning been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence.
O Son of the Buddha, having practiced the Way, you shall in a future age attain Buddhahood.

This means that ultimately one must enter the Great [Vehicle] and exhaust the delusions of the three realms; by analyzing them until they are extinguished, one attains emptiness through the destruction of form, yet this is not true extinction.

If one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, this is true extinction. Although it is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, if one does not cultivate the Path, there is no way to realize this union.
Therefore it is said: "O Son of the Buddha, having practiced the Path, you shall become a Buddha in a future age. △ Five.
The verse does not deceive; first, it clarifies that Śākyamuni first opened the way for the three vehicles:
"I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the Dharma of the three vehicles.
Second, it clarifies that all Buddhas subsequently manifest the ultimate reality.
All the World-Honored Ones preach the One Vehicle path.

Śākyamuni opens up the three vehicles while the various Buddhas reveal the reality; these are merely manifestations of one another. △ Third, the correct clarification that [the teaching] is not false, which removes doubt.
Now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts and delusions; the words of all Buddhas do not differ, being solely and exclusively the One Vehicle.
What was previously expedient and what follows is the reality; these truthful words are not false—do not give rise to doubt. △ Second, the verse on the chapter of the past Buddhas, in two parts:
first, the verse on the opening of the three [vehicles].

Throughout incalculable kalpas in the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa—hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and billions in number, their count beyond measure.
Such World-Honored Ones have expounded the characteristics of all dharmas through various causes and conditions, parables, and countless powers of skillful means.
△ Second, the verses reveal the one and the two. First, a brief verse summarizes the preceding three [sections].
All these World-Honored Ones equally preach the One Vehicle Dharma to transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
"All preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle" refers to the uniformity of teaching (*shō-ichi*); "thereby transforming immeasurable sentient beings" refers to the uniformity of person (*nin-ichi*);

"causing them to enter the Buddha-way" refers to the uniformity of principle (*ri-ichi*), which also encompasses the uniformity of practice (*gyō-ichi*). II. Extensive Verses Elucidating the Two [Uniformities]:
First, a general exposition on the five vehicles to elucidate the one.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all beings among the devas and humans in the world,
employ various other skillful means to assist in revealing the primary meaning.
"Devas, humans, and all classes of living beings" refers to the unification of all vehicles to clarify the oneness of persons.

Furthermore, "by means of various other skillful means" refers to the unification of all practices to manifest the oneness of practice, while simultaneously attaining the oneness of the teaching. The primary meaning (*paramārtha*) is precisely the oneness of principle.

The true cause of Buddhahood (*tathāgatagarbha*) is the primary meaning and principle; if one clarifies the perfect and wondrous right contemplation, this is the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is precisely [the oneness of the principle].
It is not then called "different. If one employs the seven expedients (*saptopāya*) to observe and assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called "different expedients.
△ Second, specifically distinguishing the five vehicles to reveal the One and Three: first, opening up the Bodhisattva vehicle.
If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the Buddhas of the past, and whether they heard the Dharma, practiced giving, maintained the precepts,
practiced patience, exerted diligence, cultivated meditation, or wisdom— those who thus cultivated various forms of merit and wisdom— all such persons have already attained the Way of the Buddha.

These two lines open the way for the Bodhisattva Vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*). If explained according to the five vehicles, they refer solely to the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
If explained according to the seven skillful means (*upāya*), they encompass both the common and the distinct Bodhisattva Vehicles. Why?

Because although those of the three teachings of the Mahāyāna all practice the six perfections, their mental orientations differ. If one practices with a mind attached to marks (*nimitta*), [one remains within the common vehicle].
The six *pāramitās* constitute the Bodhisattva of the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*). If one practices them with a mind of non-characteristic (*animitta*), this is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

If one practices the six *pāramitās* through successive stages, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, this is the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). At present, we merely list the six *pāramitās* without yet definitively determining to which category they belong.
If one seeks the preceding text, it says: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means, it is not solely the six *pāramitās* [that lead to] Bodhi."
"Satsu" (薩) refers to the expedient means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattvas of the three teachings; it signifies that those who formerly heard the Dharma have all already perfected the "one teaching.
"Satsu" (昔) refers to the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); it signifies that they have all already perfected the "one practice.

Thus, these various people have all already perfected the "one person," have all already perfected the Buddha-way, and have all already perfected the "one principle. △ Second, opening the way for the two vehicles.
"After the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, if there are people with virtuous and gentle minds—such sentient beings have all already attained the Buddha-way.
This single line opens the way for both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to enter the One Vehicle. How is this known?

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* praises the Arhats for having minds that are disciplined, supple, and gentle; and as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Abiding in a disciplined mind is the mark of a noble sage."
By practicing in this way, one comes to know that the former virtuous and gentle minds have all been perfected in the present practice.
That "all people" refers to those who shall attain the Buddha-way; this is the principle. △ Third, opening the gates for the vehicles of humans and devas. Part One:
Initially, clarifying the vehicle of devas by means of the causal conditions. First, building stupas to clarify the vehicle of devas.
After the various Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics erect billions of kinds of stupas,
adorned and decorated with gold, silver, crystal, mother-of-pearl, agate, ruby, and lapis lazuli beads, all pure, vast, and magnificent;
or some erect stone temples made of sandalwood, aloeswood, *mukūla* wood, and other timbers, as well as bricks, tiles, clay, and earth.
If one piles up earth in the midst of a wilderness to construct a Buddhist temple, these three lines and a half clarify that the Deva-yāna (the Vehicle of the Gods) pertains to the time of the cause;

because at the time of the fruit—one’s spontaneous and natural enjoyment of bliss through the renunciation of wealth and jewels with a sincere mind—the result is attained effortlessly, it is therefore called the Deva-yāna. *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
The statement that even a Buddha-relic the size of a mustard seed, when placed within a small stūpa, brings about natural karmic fruition in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven refers precisely to this meaning.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that after the Buddha personally held up a relic and offered extensive praise, he commanded that a *stūpa* be erected at a crossroads.
The Buddha further declared that four types of persons should have stūpas built for them.
What are the four? They are the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata.
The wheel-turning monarch has no tiers; the arhat has four tiers; the pratyekabuddha has eleven tiers; and the Tathāgata has thirteen tiers. Ānanda asked the Buddha:

"The Tathāgata appears in the world out of compassion for sentient beings; after his parinirvāṇa, stupas are erected which yield great merit. As for the stupas of the other three [categories], how do they compare?"
"What benefit do sentient beings derive from this? The Buddha replied: "The Pratyekabuddha awakens to the causes and conditions of dharmas and enters into the profound nature of phenomena;
he is able to serve as a field of merit for humans and devas. The Arhat has exhausted the conditions for rebirth and is able to serve as a field of merit for the world.
The Wheel-Turning King transforms sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths of action. For these reasons, one should erect stupas and make offerings."
As for the Tathāgata stūpa, it is thirteen stories high; the Pratyekabuddha stūpa should be eleven stories; the Arhat stūpa is four stories;
and the Cakravartin stūpa has no tiers. Why is this? Because [the latter] has not yet escaped the various existences within the three realms.

Regarding the *mùjiǎn* (wooden nutmeg): there is a wood called *jiǎn* in Chang’an that may also be used to fashion images. Furthermore, the *Guǎngzhì* states that it originates from Jiāozhōu; this is its name.

The forests are said to consist of fragrant woods, and the jade is said to come from trees resembling the *huái* tree that emit fragrance. Gold, silver, crystal, tridacna shell, and agate have already been explained as above.
As for *méiguī*, it refers to the "fire-jewel" (*huǒzhū*). Furthermore, among stones, those of extraordinary beauty are called *méi*;

those that are round and pure are called *guī*. Guo Pu stated that these are "stone-beads" (*shízhū*), also known as *lánghān*, which originate from Mount Kūṇ-lún (Kunlun) and Mount Kāimíng (Kaoming).
Regarding *candana* and *agaru*: *candana* has already been explained as before. As for *agaru*, the *Yiwuzhi* states that it originates from the country of Jinnan (Dongnan).
Whenever one wishes to harvest it, one first cuts it down and leaves it on the ground for several years to allow the outer layers to rot away;
those parts within that remain firm and solid will sink when placed in water, and thus it receives its name. Those that do not sink are called *jixiang*.
△ Second, clarifying the karma of persons:
"Even those who, as children playing, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—all such people have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
The first line clarifies that playing with sand to make stūpas is the karmic cause of a person; at that time, it was merely a casual and leisurely activity.
However, when performing wholesome deeds, one applies the mind with diligent effort because of the desire to attain happiness; therefore, it is human karma.

Regarding the term "youth" (*dāraka*), Master Fa-shi says it is a general name for those from seven or eight years of age upwards until they have not yet married. As for the etymological explanation (*shiming*): at fifteen, one is called a youth;
thus, in the *Li*, there is the term "yang-youth" (*youyang tong*). A hornless ox or sheep is called a "youth" (*tong*); a mountain without grass is also called a "youth."
"Wood" refers to those who speak like children and have not yet donned the cap; they are like this. △ Third, the karma of the devas:

If a person, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images, carving and sculpting them into manifold forms, all such persons have already attained the path of Buddhahood—whether these images are made of the seven treasures, or of brass, red or white copper, pewter, lead, tin, iron, wood, or even clay.
Or those who have adorned and fashioned images of the Buddha using glue, lacquer, and cloth—all such people as these have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Those who paint images of the Buddha with its marks adorned by a hundred blessings, whether doing so themselves or employing others, have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.

Next, regarding the four lines concerning the merit of making images with a sincere mind, the text on the karma of the bright [deeds] states: "Those who carve, sculpt, paint, or draw images of the Buddha.
However, since there are various causes and conditions for the initial commencement of image-making, the *Ekottarika Āgama* says:

When the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he used his supernormal powers to restrain his disciples so that they would not know his location; the two kings, longing for the Buddha, thereby achieved great success.
The minister, concerned about this, said to the king, "One ought to create an image for veneration.
Thereupon, King Udayana carved a Buddha image out of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood, five feet in height; this was the beginning of such images.
At that time, when King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana had fashioned an image from incense, he then cast a Buddha image from purple-gold, also five feet in height.
This five-chi bronze statue was the beginning of such cast images. However, when the king first summoned artisans and offered them precious rewards, none were able to create it.
Viśvakarman manifested as a human being and came to work for the king; the sound of his axe striking the wood reached up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and those who heard it attained liberation.
The *Nèidiàn lù* (Record of Inner Scriptures) states that this occurred in the seventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han.
In the year [X], the envoy Qin Jing traveled to the kingdom of Yuezhi and obtained a statue of King Udayana; it subsequently arrived in Luoyang.
By imperial decree, the sacred features were depicted on the Westyang Gate for the public to gaze upon and take as a model.
This was the beginning of image-making in this land. According to the *Mingxiang ji*, there are a total of eighteen locations in this land where images were created.
Thus, the *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Land of the East* was compiled by the Śramaṇa Yancong of Hongfu Monastery in the Great Tang;

its text consists of three fascicles. In the middle fascicle, which lists over fifty entries concerning the occasions when sacred images manifested supernatural responses, the opening passage cites the *Records of Hidden Auspiciousness*, stating:
"In the first year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min of the Western Jin, [an image appeared] in Wujun..."
At the mouth of the Hudu Estuary in Songjiang, Wuxian County, a fisherman named Hua saw two figures suddenly appear floating upon the surface of the sea from afar.
Suspecting they were sea deities, the fisherman summoned shamans and priests to prepare sacrificial animals to welcome them;
however, the wind and waves grew even more violent. At that time, there was a lay follower of the Buddha named Zhu Ying, who heard of this and sighed, saying: "This will..."
"Is this not the descent of the Great Awakened One? Thus, they purified themselves through fasting and bowed their heads to welcome him.

In a brief moment, the surging waves suddenly subsided, and the two figures floated down the river; following the tide, they entered the estuary. As dawn began to break, they finally realized these were stone statues.
Inscribed on the backs of the statues were the names "Vipaśyin" and "Kāśyapa"; their era was unknown, yet the calligraphy remained distinct.

It was clearly stated that the statues were seven feet tall. There was a śramaṇa named Fākai who came from the Western Regions and proclaimed that the sutras state there are two stone images in the East;
those who offer worship or behold them shall eliminate the sins accumulated over kalpas.

Furthermore, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a man named Zhōu Xuānpèi, whose courtesy name was Shìzhì, who served as the Governor of Wǔxīng. His family had followed the Buddha for generations, and his daughter was especially [devoted].
A servant of the extremely diligent family was catching fish when he suddenly saw golden light overflowing the stream and reflecting upward along the current.
He immediately cast his net and caught a golden image about three feet high; its features were solemn and beautiful, and it floated upon the water, remaining still despite being pulled and pushed.
He hurried back to inform the master, who then sent his daughter in a boat to go and welcome it.
Seeing him from afar, she rejoiced and paid homage; drawing him toward her with her hand, she immediately boarded the ship and returned home to make offerings.
Later, one night, she suddenly dreamed that the Buddha called out in pain due to a sore on his left knee. Upon waking, she went to inspect it and found that there was indeed a hole.
She immediately mended it with a gold hairpin. Thus, the auspicious responses of this miraculous image were even more numerous; this is recorded in the *Mingxiang ji*.
This refers to the ten-fascicle work *Wen* (Records) by Wang Yan of Taiyuan during the Southern Qi dynasty, which states that lead is blue and tin is white;

while lead is soft, tin is hard, yet both are termed "blue metal" (*qingjin*). Furthermore, the *Wuli zhi* (Treatise on the Classification of Things) states that one may accumulate various grasses for several years, and as the days pass and months elapse, the sap of the grasses enters the earth and transforms into lead and tin. Alternatively, it says: [text fragment]...or [it is produced].
Regarding "glue, lacquer, and cloth," the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* prohibits the use of glue, stating that its use constitutes an offense of transgression (*āpatti*).
Yet, this [present] sūtra permits its use; regarding this, the ancient masters say that foreign lands use tree resin.

Guangzhai says that in some regions where tree resin is unavailable, one must be permitted to use ox-hide glue for the sake of the image. However, if other materials are available, one must not use it.
There are also those who say that soybean juice may serve as a substitute for glue; however, cowhide is ultimately an impure substance, and one will subsequently receive impure karmic retribution.
Furthermore, impure money is unfit for making images; it should be exchanged for pure money in accordance with the Dharma to create an image.
Moreover, the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichijing) does not permit the use of yellow arsenic or foul-smelling substances, as stated in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* translated by Amoghavajra.
The ritual manuals for recitation state that when painting an image, animal glue must not be used; instead, one should use fragrant glue.

Alternatively, it is auspicious to use rice-water from glutinous millet to mix with the pigments. Furthermore, the Vinaya prohibits the creation of half-length images, as doing so incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
This is because such images fail to manifest auspicious characteristics, causing one to fall into the cycle of birth and death without benefit to one's spiritual progress.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Merit of Casting Images* states that there are eleven merits: first, one’s eyes shall be clear and pure in every lifetime;
second, one shall be born in places free from evil; third, one shall always be born into noble families; fourth, one’s body shall be like the color of purple-polished gold;
fifth, one shall abound in rare treasures and playthings; sixth, one shall be born into families of the wise and virtuous; seventh, one shall be born to become a king.
Eighth, one becomes a Golden Wheel-Turning King; ninth, one is born in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa;
tenth, one does not fall into the evil realms; eleventh, in future births, one is able to again revere and honor the Triple Gem. It is further said:
if a person, at the time of death, speaks of creating an image—even one as small as a grain of barley—it can eliminate birth for eighty billion kalpas across the three periods of time.
The sin of death. △ Fourth, clarifying human karma:
"Even if a child plays, whether with grass, wood, a brush, or even with their fingernails, if they draw an image of the Buddha..."
This can be understood according to the text. △ Fifth, the conclusion that establishes the manifestation of reality:
"Such people as these, gradually accumulating merit and fulfilling the mind of great compassion, have all already attained the Buddha-way;
they merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes."
The next one and a half lines conclude by manifesting the reality: "Such persons as these constitute the 'person' [of the teaching];
gradually accumulating merit and being fully endowed with a heart of great compassion constitutes the 'practice'; attaining Buddhahood constitutes the 'principle';
having already attained Buddhahood, they are further able to transform others; transforming only Bodhisattvas constitutes the 'teaching'. △ Sixth, regarding the various...
The karma of making offerings to the bright deities:
if a person, with a heart of reverence, makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to stupas, temples, precious images, or painted images;
or if they cause others to perform music by beating drums, blowing horns, conchs, and ocarinas, or playing flutes, lutes, *kōng-hou*, *pipa*, and bronze cymbals.
Thus, those who offered all such various wondrous sounds as an offering, or who with a joyful heart sang hymns in praise of the Buddha’s virtues—
even those who produced but a single small sound— all have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
These three and a half lines concern the karma of making offerings to the Manifested Deities (*abhijñā-deva*) by means of various objects such as flowers, incense, banners (*patākā*), and canopies;

regarding "banners," the original text uses the character *fan* (旛), which is now also used interchangeably with *fan* (幡). As for those who make offerings with a reverent mind, the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states:
"When the Buddha was in the world, there was a person named Bhadrika who, in the past, once made a long banner at the stūpa of Vipaśyin Buddha."
From that time onward, for ninety-one kalpas, he was constantly sheltered by great banners in the heavens and among humans, receiving blissful merit and happiness.
Later, he left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship. It is further said:
"If a person hangs up a banner, with each turn of the wind, they shall receive the status of a Cakravartin King; this continues until the banner decays and turns to dust."
"One speck of dust is equivalent to one minor kingship. The *Baiyuan jing* (*Śatapañcāśatkathā*) states: "In the past, there was an elder named Ratnacchattra.

Because this elder once offered a precious jewel canopy over the stupa of the relics of Vipaśyin Buddha, from that time onward for ninety-one kalpas, he has always naturally possessed jewels among both devas and humans."
It is used as a canopy to cover one’s head; later, having encountered a Buddha and left the household life, one attains the fruit of sainthood.

As for "making music," the *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states that Ling Lun composed music during the time of the Yellow Emperor. As for "beating the drum," the *Shiben* states that Yi invented the drum;
it is called a "drum" because it is struck with a mallet (*bō*). "Blowing" refers to *guchui* (military music); the *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances) states: "He orders the musicians... [to perform].
Regarding the *zhèngxí* (the horn-blower), the *Tongdian* states that it is not recorded in the transmitted books of the scribes, though some claim it originated among the Qiang and Hu peoples;
Mā Róng says it originated between Wú and Yuè. The *bèi* (conch) is a large shell capable of holding several shēng;

both are blown to regulate the music and also originate from the Southern Barbarians. Regarding the *xiāo* (flute), the *Shìběn* states it was invented by Shùn; its shape is uneven, resembling [bamboo joints].
The phoenix-wing [flute] has ten tubes, each two feet long, and is also called a *lai*. In previous dynasties there was the *dongxiao*, which is also occasionally found in the present day.
Cai Yong said: "The *xiao* is made by binding together bamboo strips and providing a base. The large version has twenty-three tubes, while the small version has sixteen;
those that are longer produce deep tones, while those that are shorter produce clear tones. It is filled with dense wax..."

If the depth, length, or number of holes is adjusted appropriately, then its sound will harmonize with the flute. Regarding the *fengsu tong* (Treatise on Customs), it says that the *qiu* was created by Qiu Zhong and measures one chi four cun with seven holes.
Regarding the *qin*, the *Shiben* (Book of Origins) states it was created by Shen Nong.

Furthermore, the *Qincao* (Lute Manual) states that Fu Xi made the *qin* for the purpose of cultivating the self, regulating the nature, and returning to one's true essence. *Note: The character "耳" at the end of the passage serves as a concluding particle.*
The *Hutong* states: "The *qin* means 'to prohibit' (*jin*); it refers to that which prohibits licentiousness and depravity to rectify the human heart. The *Guangya* states:

"It is three feet and six inches long, symbolizing the three hundred and sixty days [of the year]. It has five strings, symbolizing the Five Elements. The largest string represents the Ruler—broad, harmonious, and warm;
the smallest string represents the Minister—pure, incorruptible, and orderly. [These were added by] King Wen and King Wu."
The King added two strings to harmonize the bond between sovereign and subject. The *Erya* states: "A large *qin* is called a *li*, and it has twenty-seven strings.
Although the instrument no longer exists today, the *Qinpu* (Qin Notation) says: "In the method of playing the *qin*, when rapid, it is like a multitude of stars without confusion;
when slow, it is like flowing water without interruption. The application within these movements is like a solitary cloud in the vast void."
Regarding the *konghou*: the *Baihu tong* states that Emperor Wu of Han commanded the musicians *Hou Tiao* to create it;
others say it was created by *Hou Hui*. Its sound was "kan-kan" as it responded to the rhythmic beats of the performance, and thus it was called *kan-hou*.
The name later underwent phonetic corruption to become *kong-hou*. The term *hou* (musician) was derived from the name of that particular musician. As for the *pipa*:
The Han dynasty dispatched the Princess of Wusun to marry the Kunmi (the King of the Yuezhi). Because she was mindful of his virtuous conduct, her longing for him was unceasing;

thus, she commissioned artisans to fashion the *zheng* and *zhu* zithers for music to be played on horseback. By pushing them back and forth with the hands to produce sound, they were named the *pipa*.
Regarding the *niao*, the *Tongdian* states: "The *niao* is like a set of chime bells (*bianzhong*), but it lacks tongues and has a handle."
It is shaken to stop the drum. Furthermore, among the *han-guchui* (Han military music) melodies there is the *nao-ge* (drum song).
The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "As for *nao*, it is so named because its sound is *nao-nao* (ringing). Regarding the copper cymbals (*tong-po*), the *Shu* (Commentary) says:

"The people of Chang'an call the dew-dish (*lu-pan*) 'copper cymbals'. As for *bai* (chanting), some say it is *bai-ni*; this is translated as "praise and hymn" (*zan-song*), and it originally originated in the Western Regions.
Regarding this land, according to the *Liang Xuanyan ji* (Records of Miraculous Experiences of the Liang Dynasty), Prince Caisi (Cao Zhi), styled Zijian, was the third son of Emperor Wu of Wei.
At the age of ten, he excelled in literature and the arts; he privately composed the *Zhuanqisheng* (The Seven Tones of Transformation).

Once, while traveling through the rocky valleys of Yushan, he heard the sound of sutra recitation echoing through the distant gorges with exquisite beauty. He then modeled his own work after it and composed [the *Zhuanqisheng*].

Regarding the seven tones of chanting, the *Fódàolúnhéng* states that Prince Chen Si (Cao Zhi) possessed the qualities of a jade vessel from his youth and was capable of composing literary works by the age of ten.

Whenever he read the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*), he would invariably pause, sighing in admiration and playfully appreciating them, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way (*zhìdào*).

Consequently, he composed the "Seven Tones for Chanting" (*zhuǎndú qīshēng*), producing sounds of ascending, descending, and melodic modulation; all those in the world who recite [the scriptures] now take these as their model.
Once, while he was traveling and fishing at Mount Yishan, he suddenly heard the sound of Brahmā-deities resonating from the air—clear, soaring, and plaintively beautiful.

Deeply moved in his heart, he listened alone for a long time; meanwhile, none of those following him could hear anything. Zhi was profoundly affected by this spiritual principle and gained an even deeper realization of the Dharma-sounds.
Consequently, out of admiration for that voice, he composed melodies to transcribe it as *fanbai* (Brahma-chants) and wrote down verses to form liturgical texts.
This was transmitted as a model for later generations; thus, the glorious manifestation of the Sanskrit voice began with this.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) states that when King Prasenajit was about to go on a military expedition, there was a bhikṣu within the Jetavana Monastery whose physical form was extremely short and ugly, yet his voice was extraordinarily beautiful, clear, and transcendent.
When he raised his voice in high chant, its resonance became increasingly harmonious and flowing.
The assembled troops listened with undivided attention, never tiring of it.
The King then asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions does this bhikṣu have such an ugly appearance, yet his voice is like this?

The Buddha told the Great King, "In the past, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa who, having finished delivering sentient beings, entered parinirvāṇa. The King collected his relics and erected a stūpa to make offerings to them."
The King commanded the supervisors and officials to each take charge of one side, yet because one supervisor was negligent, the work could not be completed.
The King then rebuked him; filled with fear, the man spoke these words: "This stupa is too high; when will it ever be finished?
After the King had departed, that stupa was subsequently completed and stood clearly visible. The man immediately repented of his former transgression and offered [an offering].
A golden bell was hung at the top of the stupa’s spire, and he made this vow: "May my voice be most exquisite in every lifetime;
may I behold the Buddha named Śākyamuni in the future and be delivered from the suffering of birth and death. Because of these causes and conditions, such is the fruit and retribution.
Because he resented the height of the stupa, his physical body became short; because he offered the bell, he has now received liberation.
Regarding the attainment of wondrous sounds, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus, 'I permit you to chant;
chanting is the expression of speech. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "This is so that the devas, upon hearing the chanting, may rejoice.
Alternatively, music, dancers, conchs, cymbals, flutes, and zithers may be employed to arouse a heart of joy through various kinds of offerings.
In the past, the clear resonance of Devadatta’s chanting reached the Pure Abodes, and the lute-song of Śākyamuni Buddha while in meditative absorption shook the stone chamber.
One should know that gardens, groves, pavilions, and towers are gateways to the Dharma-realm, and that sounds and speech are all the Dharma-words that accomplish the work of a Buddha.
△ Seventh: Dust-offerings by those with distracted minds clarify the karma of humans.
If a person, even with a distracted mind, offers so much as a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually come to see countless Buddhas.

The first line above clarifies that even using worldly objects (*rajas*) for offering while in a state of distraction constitutes a significant human karma. The *Mahā-cintī-brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:

"Even if one does not scatter flowers as an offering to the Buddha, though one may attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], the secondary environment (*upabhoga-pratyaya*) will not be complete. The *Śraddhā-prasāda-sūtra* (or *Xianyu jing*) states: "The house..."
In the kingdom of Wei, there was a wealthy and prominent elder who fathered a son of handsome and dignified countenance.

When it rained, a multitude of celestial flowers fell and filled his house; consequently, he was named Tianhua (Celestial Flower). Eventually, he left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "By what merit did Tianhua obtain such [a result]? The Buddha said, "In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin..."
In the village of Śi, there was a poor man who, upon seeing the Saṃgha, felt great joy.
He immediately gathered various wild flowers from a marshy meadow and scattered them over the assembly. The one who was that poor man at that time is now this Devapuṣpa.

Because he scattered these flowers, for ninety-one kalpas his body has been upright and handsome, and whatever he desired would arrive as soon as he thought of it. The *Hetuphala-sūtra* states: "If with even a single..."
Scattering flowers into the air as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions, their merit shall not be exhausted until the end of suffering.
△ Eighth, offerings through bodily action for devas and humans:
Suppose there is someone who prostrates, or perhaps merely joins their palms, or even raises a single hand, or perhaps slightly lowers their head.
To prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground while reciting a single phrase is the superior form of worship; this is the karma of the heavens (*deva-karma*).

To join the palms and bow the head is the middling form of worship; this is the karma of humans (*manuṣya-karma*). One should know that through worship, one humbles and subdues ignorance and deeply enters the ground of awakening (*bodhi-bhūmi*).
As for the ultimate expression of reverence, it should be like a tree falling or a mountain collapsing. Thus, the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* says:
In performing a single prostration to the Buddha—from the knees down to the soles of the feet—one attains the rank of a Cakravartin King for every particle of dust and gains ten kinds of merit:
first, one obtains a wondrous physical form; second, one’s words are trusted by others; third, one is fearless when among the multitude;

fourth, one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; fifth, one possesses great dignified deportment; sixth, all people draw near and attach themselves to one; seventh, all devas... [and so forth].
1. Loving respect; 2. Possessing the eight great qualities; 3. Having great merit; 4. Rebirth after the end of life; 5. Swiftly realizing nirvana.

The Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati said: "To prostrate with pure wisdom is truly because one has attained the Buddha’s realm, and because the mind of wisdom is sharp and clear, one thoroughly understands that the dharma-realm is fundamentally without obstruction.
Since beginningless time, due to following worldly conventions, we have taken what does not exist to be existent."

The perception of obstruction is itself the perception of non-obstruction; now, having realized that one’s own mind is empty, pervasive, and unimpeded, one performs prostrations according to the direct manifestation of the mind.
To prostrate to a single Buddha is to prostrate to all Buddhas; to prostrate to all Buddhas is to prostrate to a single Buddha. Why is this?
It is because the essence and function of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body are interfused and harmonious. Therefore, prostration to a single Buddha [is the prostration to all].
Prostrating, one universally penetrates the Dharma-realm, conceiving of all beings within the six realms and four modes of birth as Buddhas. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:

"Because the mind is neither born nor extinguished, one pays homage to that which is without an object of observation. When internal practice is equanimous and external conduct accords with reverence, the internal and external merge in mystery;
this is called the "Homage of Equanimity. Tiantai said: "At the time of prostration, although nothing is seen..."
The one who prostrates and the object of prostration both manifest as reflections within the Dharma-realm; before each and every Buddha, one perceives one’s own self performing the prostration.

Since the text concerning scattering flowers and prostrating has already appeared in the sūtras and śāstras as the sincere words from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], I shall hereupon cite and clarify them to assist in contemplation and cultivation, with the common aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood. All other matters should be understood accordingly.
△ Ninth, the formation of the nine knots reveals the reality:

through this offering to the image, one gradually beholds immeasurable Buddhas, personally attains the unsurpassed path, and extensively delivers countless multitudes before entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*,
like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted.

These one and a half lines conclude [the section] by showing that not only does he manifest the truth and personally attain the Buddha-way, but he is also able to reveal the provisional means (*upāya*) to transform others;
thus it says, "Extensively delivering countless beings, they enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
△ Tenth, the oral karma of making offerings clarifies the human karma.
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and recites "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the Way of the Buddhas.
Next, one line concerns the karma of speech; following the previous example, this should include the karma of devas and humans, but here only human karma is mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "reciting 'Namo Buddha' once," *namo* has many meanings; one should know that it simply signifies the sense of taking refuge. As for the word "once" (*yi*), it means...

"Save me" means "deliver us. That one who recites the Buddha’s name even once attains the Way of Buddhahood is a judgment made according to the intent of the revelation and clarification found in the present sutra;
thus, it pertains to the *Tongji* (General Record). The *Contemplation Sutra* also states:
"Reciting the Buddha’s name even once can eliminate the heavy offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says: "Recite with a loud voice..."
When the Buddha’s army has repelled the hosts of Māra, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are dull-witted and cannot understand through contemplation;
however, by merely maintaining the continuity of mindful recitation of the sound [of the name], they will naturally attain rebirth. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"For example, suppose there were a person who, as soon as he was born and fell to the ground, could travel a thousand li every day for a full thousand years, and during that time filled the space with the seven treasures to offer them [to the Buddhas]."
Giving is not equal to someone who, in the evil age of the future, utters the name of the Buddha even once; its merit surpasses that [of giving]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If a person, even with a distracted mind, recollects the Buddha until the end of suffering, their merit will never be exhausted. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The merit of providing the four types of offerings to all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa with a virtuous mind [is far greater]."
If one continuously recites the Buddha’s name for the duration of a single meal, its merit surpasses the aforementioned [practices] and is inconceivable and immeasurable.
The *Samādhirāja-ratna-sūtra* states: "One who bathes in the great ocean uses the waters of a hundred rivers;
likewise, one who recites the Buddha’s name will surely achieve samādhi. It is just as when a bright pearl is cast into turbid water—the turbid water cannot help but become clear."
Pure mindfulness of the Buddha gathers in the distracted mind; once the distracted mind has been brought to the Buddha, both mind and Buddha vanish together.
This simultaneous vanishing is concentration (*samādhi*); their simultaneous illumination is wisdom (*prajñā*).

When concentration and wisdom are balanced, what mind is not the Buddha, and what Buddha is not the mind? Since mind and Buddha are thus identical, the myriad objects and myriad conditions are none other than [the Buddha].

This is for those who have attained *samādhi*. As stated in the *Sūtra on the Differences in Karmic Retribution*: "There are ten kinds of merit for those who recite the Buddha’s name or chant the sūtras with a loud voice:
first, they can dispel drowsiness; second, celestial Māras are struck with fear; third, their voices pervade the ten directions; fourth, suffering ceases in the three miserable realms;
fifth, external sounds do not enter [the mind]; sixth, they cause the mind not to be distracted; seventh, they inspire courageous diligence..."
1. Advancing through the eight stages; 2. Rejoicing of all Buddhas; 3. The manifestation of samādhi before one; 4. Birth in a pure land. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"Whether for one day and night, or seven days and nights, if one performs no other activities, by small mindfulness one sees the small, and by great mindfulness one sees the great.
Furthermore, in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī asks the Buddha: "How can one swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? The Buddha [replies].

Answer: There is the Ekavyūha Samādhi. One who wishes to enter this samādhi must dwell in a secluded and quiet place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and refrain from grasping at external appearances.
Fixing the mind on a single Buddha, one should single-mindedly recite that Buddha’s name, facing the direction where that Buddha resides with the body upright and directed forward.
If one can maintain the continuous succession of mindfulness toward that single Buddha from moment to moment, this is precisely what is attained within such mindfulness.
One sees that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present constantly preach wisdom and eloquence day and night, never ceasing;
as the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: "In the third great assembly at the Hualin Garden, ninety-two billion people attained Buddhahood.
These are those who, within the current dispensation of Śākyamuni Buddha, have uttered even once the name "Namo Buddha."
By this, people come to know that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable and his profound penetration is rarely fathomed; it is like a magnet attracting iron or water flowing into a river.
Through the power of the roots of goodness born of compassion, such spontaneous efficacy occurs. For those who believe with a sincere heart, spiritual responses are manifest.
In this present age of defilement, this alone is the true, simple, and essential gateway—the sublime encounter and the path easy to practice.
Therefore, by extensively citing clear evidence, those virtuous ones who possess faith can surely follow this and receive profound benefit.
△ Second, revealing the reality by means of the "cause of understanding":
"Whether among the Buddhas of the past, those currently living, or those who have passed into extinction, all who have heard this Dharma have already attained the path of Buddhahood."
This single line clarifies that the examples of causal seeds all possess both the aspect of existence and the aspect of non-existence, as well as the aspects of neither existence nor non-existence.
Now, the seeds of the five vehicles—such as those of the concentrated mind and the distracted mind—are all opened up to enter into the One Reality (*eka-tattva*).

If one hears even a single phrase with a concentrated mind, it is the karma of a celestial being; if one hears even a single phrase with a distracted mind, it is the karma of a human being. Question: Why is this so?

The intent here is to extensively clarify the five vehicles from the perspective of past Buddhas in response to the fact that all Buddhas of the three periods of time possess the opening of the provisional.
However, because [the Buddhas of] the future have not yet arisen and those of the present have only recently begun their practice, the meaning of "realization" is weak.

Since the opening of the provisional by past Buddhas occurred long ago, all those who received transformation have already attained the fourfold unity; thus, throughout the ten directions, they have exercised the provisional to manifest the real, and the meaning of realization is established.

Since fabricated empty words are not as good as verifying them through reality, it is more convenient for the purpose of the meaning to explain the five vehicles extensively with reference to the Buddhas of the past.
△ Second, the verse on the chapter concerning the Buddhas of the future, in two parts: first, the verse opening the three [vehicles].
The future World-Honored Ones will be immeasurable in number; these Tathāgatas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means.
All Tathāgatas employ immeasurable skillful means.
The following one and a half verses distinguish the three [vehicles] as in the text, which can be understood accordingly. △ Second, the verses manifesting the one [vehicle]:
First, the verse on persons:
"To deliver all sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha’s untainted wisdom—if there are those who hear this Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha."
These five verses of praise manifest the first practice: liberating all sentient beings. (Verse 1) The second [section] consists of one verse on the practice:
"The fundamental vows of all Buddhas are such that the Buddha-way which I practice, I desire all sentient beings to likewise attain. (Verse 2)

Next, regarding the single verse on the fundamental vows of all Buddhas: practicing the path traversed by each Buddha and vowing to cause others to attain this same path—is this not the practice of "one"? △ Third, the verse on the "one teaching."
Although the Buddhas of future ages may preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality they are but the One Vehicle.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature and that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions; therefore, they speak of the One Vehicle.
Regarding the two verses of the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* concerning the future Buddhas: "One who knows that phenomena are eternally without nature (*svabhāva*)...

This means that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding and lacks intrinsic nature, even to the point of lacking the nature of being causeless; this absence of nature, and even the absence of that absence, is called "eternally without nature.

The commentary states: "Knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature, etc. refers to the non-existence of both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the single ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

The nature of nature is empty; thus, there are no four natures. Since it is said that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) lacks self-nature and so forth, we know this refers to the rational nature (*dharmatā*).

Because the nature is empty, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise known to be empty. Since there is no nature, there is also no characteristic; this is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Therefore, one knows that the single expression "absence of nature" found in the sūtras encompasses both types of absence of nature—that is, the absence of nature and the absence of characteristics.
Because their characteristics and nature are inherently present from the beginning, it is said that they are "always non-existent. "Knowing" refers to illumination.

This is fully explained in the fifth section of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, the "Inconceivable Realm," regarding the "three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-trisahasra-loka-dhātu*), which is neither self nor other and so forth. Since the four natures do not exist, the single thought-moment also does not exist;
this is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Since the single thought-moment does not exist, non-thought also does not exist; this is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

"Emptiness" and "the inconceivable" refer to these two kinds of emptiness. If one does not understand that our school establishes these two emptinesses by relying on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and other texts—following both their principles and their meanings based upon the nature of the mind—then such matters will be beyond the reach of those who lack any standard for comparison and who do not employ the categories of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, regarding the True Path, one must be proficient in the cultivation of the nature; if it were merely... [text ends]... the fundamental.
The two kinds of emptiness are themselves inherent virtues; if one investigates and enters into emptiness, this is what is attained through cultivation.

If investigation does not lead to realization, one must cultivate the myriad practices, combining the primary and auxiliary. When all practices are fully present within these deeds, they are then called the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Having heard this meaning, it is only then that [the text] speaks of "opening. One may inquire whether the causes and conditions of the mundane world can be categorized by way of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

Question: Since birth and non-birth are understood as being originally pure by nature and not dependent on causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), why is it necessary to investigate this through these four propositions?
Answer: The dharmas of worldly causal origination are likewise fundamentally without birth; it is only due to emotional conceptualization that they are said to have the principle of birth.

The nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is also like this: because one speaks of "self" and "other" and so forth, it is necessary to investigate them. If the two kinds of emptiness were not yet manifest, one would still need to proceed further.
If even this is so when considering the sequence of conditions, how much more so regarding the causes and conditions themselves?

That the Buddha-seed arises from conditions means that the Middle Way of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself the Buddha-seed. Those who are deluded regarding this principle give rise to sentient beings through the condition of ignorance;
those who understand this principle give rise to perfect enlightenment through the conditions of teaching and practice. To cause the Buddha-seed to arise, one must [rely on] the One.
The teaching of the vehicle is precisely the first [aspect] of the teaching in verse. Furthermore, "the absence of nature" refers to the Buddha-nature as the true cause (*dharmatā-buddhadhātu*).

"The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions" refers to the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the developmental (*pariniṣpanna*) [natures], by which the conditional aids the developmental so that the true seed may arise;
when it arises, all arise. These three natures are called the One Vehicle. △ Fourth, the verse on the unity of principle.

This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Teacher explains it through skillful means.
This fourth verse—“The Dharma abides in its fixed position”—is of one principle. Sentient beings and perfect enlightenment are of one suchness (*tathatā*) and not two;

none fail to emerge from suchness, for all are such as they are, and this constitutes their "position. Regarding "the characteristics of the world are eternally constant": this refers to that which transcends the world.
The Perfectly Awakened One takes suchness (*tathatā*) as his station and suchness as the characteristic of his dharmas; these characteristics abide eternally in the world.
Sentient beings likewise take suchness as their station and suchness as their characteristic—how could they not abide eternally in the world?
