Since the characteristics already abide eternally, is this not the oneness of principle? Furthermore, "the world" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*); "abiding eternally" means...

This is precisely the "True Cause" (*dharmatā-hetu*). Now, this True Cause is not identical to the six dharmas, yet the "Conditions" (*pratyaya*) and "Understanding" (*pariniṣpatti*) are not separate from the six dharmas;
because the True Cause is eternal, the Conditions and Understanding are also eternal. Thus it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

Having realized this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this passage cites the fruit to explain and establish the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real. At the site of enlightenment, all is luminous; this principle has long been pervasive among all things.

The third section on the application of skillful means for those with heavy emotional obstructions. △ Fourth, the verse on the Buddhas of the present, in three parts: first, the verse on the intent behind the manifestation of transformation.
The Buddhas of the ten directions currently present, who are honored by devas and humans, appear in the world in numbers as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, he likewise teaches this Dharma.
Regarding these four and a half verses, while the preceding section on the Buddhas of the present contains four [verses], here only three are versified;

the final concluding verse is not versified. Within this, the first one and a half verses versify the intention behind the transformative teaching, which is precisely for the sake of bringing peace and security.
Sentient beings. △ Second, revealing the reality:
Knowing the supreme quiescence, by the power of skillful means, although various paths are shown, their reality is the Buddha-vehicle.
The verse above reveals this reality—knowing the supreme quiescence—which corresponds to the "oneness of principle"; "their reality is the Buddha-vehicle" refers to the "oneness of teaching. Or...
Whether it be one verse of teaching or one verse of practice. △ Third, the disclosure of the provisional:

knowing the various practices of sentient beings, what their deep minds contemplate, the karma they have habitually practiced in the past, their inclinations, their vigor, and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, he speaks through various causes, conditions, parables, and also through words, employing skillful means as appropriate.

This verse clarifies the provisional [teachings] as per the text. △ Second, the verse on the chapter of Śākyamuni has two parts: first, a brief verse on the aforementioned provisional and real [teachings];
second, a verse on the manifestation of the real.
Now I am likewise; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim the Buddha-way through various dharma-gates.

These two lines of verse briefly summarize the preceding provisional and ultimate [teachings] to serve as the basis for the general analogy that follows. Regarding what is called the "basis of the analogy":
since those of superior capacity have already awakened to it while those of middling capacity have not yet understood, an analogy must be employed to illustrate the aforementioned dharmas once more.

Furthermore, because an analogy does not arise in isolation but is introduced with a specific purpose, it is termed the "basis of the analogy. Now, according to this summary verse, there are six [points].
The "mind" serves as the general metaphor for the six meanings. The root verse states: "Now I am also like this.
Here, "I" refers to Śākyamuni, the primary master of transformation. This serves as the basis for the subsequent metaphor of the great elder.
"Peaceful and secure" refers to the Great Nirvāṇa, the dwelling place of eternal bliss. Because this place is tranquil and free from the obstructions of the five turbidities, it is called "peaceful."

"Stable and secure" refers to that which is not stable or secure; namely, all the activities and transformations within the cycle of birth and death in the three realms, characterized by the five turbidities, are called "unstable. This serves as the basis for the parable of the burning house below.

"Sentient beings" refers to those among the five destinies who are to be transformed, serving as the basis for the parable of the five hundred people below. Furthermore, there is "stability and security."
That which is "peaceful" refers to the dharmas of security, which stand in contrast to the dharmas that are not secure; "not secure" refers to the dharmas of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This serves as the basis for the analogy of the fire starting below. Various dharma-gates serve as the basis for the analogy of being "not various.
Furthermore, the fact that there is "only one gate" serves as the basis for the following analogy. △ Second, the verse reveals the provisional (*upāya*).
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings and skillfully teach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy.
"Knowing the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings" refers to the root-natures of the five destinies, which have the distinctions of the three vehicles;
it serves as the basis for the analogy of the thirty children below, while looking upward it is a brief verse on the provisional and the real, and looking downward it is...
This serves as a general analogy for the mutual succession of the root and its branches, wherein the textual meaning is complete;

it shall be further cited below in the "Parable" chapter to corroborate what is recorded here. Regarding the phrase "the mutual succession of the root and its branches," etc., "root" refers to the discourse on the Dharma, while "branches" refers to the parables, and so forth.
II. Extensive Verses on the Six Meanings Above: 1. Verses on the Five Turbidities (divided into three parts). 2. Verses on Giving.

The three verses on skillful means reveal transformation; the four verses on reality manifest the truth; the five verses on the rarity of the Dharma express its marvelousness; the six verses on non-futility demonstrate its efficacy;
and the six verses on encouraging faith urge one toward conviction. Within the first section, there are further three parts, the first of which concerns the eye that perceives.

Śāriputra, you should know that when I observe with my Buddha-eye—referring to the first half-verse which establishes the single character "bright" (ming) as the basis for the elder's subsequent ability to see—I am observing with my Buddha-eye.
As for the phrase "I observe with my Buddha-eye," the subsequent text says: "The elder was standing outside the gate," which provides the lower-level evidence [for this].
The Buddha, knowing that he abides in the stage of the Dharmakāya and perceives all capacities with his eternally quiescent Buddha-eye,

preaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle through the form of Vairocana when roots are sharp, turbidity is light, and afflictions are slight; however, when roots are dull, turbidity is heavy, and afflictions are profound,
he discards his jeweled necklaces and appears in the guise of an aged bhikṣu to enter the burning house, employing skillful means to open the three stages of the bodhisattva path.

At that time, because he discerned the [disciples'] capacities, he said, "I see with the Buddha-eye. Question: If one observes material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), one should employ the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);

if one discriminates the faculties and capacities (*indriya-mūla*), one should employ the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). Why then do you say that he sees with the Buddha-eye? Answer: The Buddha-eye is all-pervasive and perfect;
by citing its excellence, it encompasses the inferior ones. Furthermore, when the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye, they are all collectively termed the Buddha-eye.
The Buddha-eye. △ Second, explaining what is seen: the five turbidities.
He sees the sentient beings of the six realms who are impoverished and devoid of merit and wisdom; they enter the perilous path of birth and death where suffering continues without interruption;
they are deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail; they shroud themselves with craving and attachment, blind and sightless, seeing nothing at all.
Seeking neither the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering, they plunge deeply into various false views, seeking to abandon suffering through further suffering.
Next, the two lines and three phrases of four characters below the section on sentient beings of the six realms clarify the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) as perceived:

the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), characterized by poverty, lack of merit, and lack of wisdom, is shown in the half-line verse; they enter the perilous path of birth and death, enduring continuous suffering.

The verse beginning with "Not abandoning" refers to the defilement of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). The single verse beginning with "Deeply attached to the five desires" refers to the defilement of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*).

The verse beginning with "Not seeking a Buddha of great power or the Dharma that cuts off suffering" refers to the defilement of the eon (*kalpakaṣāya*). The verse beginning with "Deeply entering into various false views, desiring to abandon suffering through suffering" refers to the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*).
Some say that by practicing the "five heats" (*pañcatapana*) to burn the body, one desires to abandon suffering, yet it results in the opposite.

One receives the retribution of suffering; some say that all views are themselves sensation (*vedanā*), and sensation is itself the practice of suffering. Since this cause of suffering is sought in the desire to abandon suffering, how could it ever be attained?
The *Puyao jing* says: "It clarifies the source of the five destinies: through the five precepts one becomes human, through the ten wholesome acts one is born in heaven;
through stinginess and greed one falls among the hungry ghosts, through obstinacy and aggression one falls among animals, and through the ten unwholesome acts one falls into hell."

The absence of the five destinies, the five aggregates, and the six sense-bases is *nirvāṇa*. Not abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and not dwelling in *nirvāṇa* is the reception of the prediction of *bodhi*.
"Hell" is a term from this region; in the language of the Hu it is called *niraya*, and in the language of Qin it means "non-existence.
Because there is no joy, no flavor, no delight, and no benefit, it is called "non-existence. As for "animals" (*tiryagyoni*), [it is as follows:]...
They are called "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*) because their forms and their movements are horizontal;

they are also called "those born sideways" (*tiryak-prasūta*) or "those existing everywhere" (*sarvatra-bhava*), for this realm exists pervasively throughout the five destinies, the four heavens, and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

However, the elephants, horses, and so forth ridden by those in the higher heavens are produced through the transformation of meritorious karma and do not belong to the category of sentient beings. Furthermore, as for animals...
This is called "blindness"; those who are blind possess much ignorance, and for this reason they are called animals (*tiryagyoni*). At the beginning of the kalpa, all understood the noble language;
later, due to differences in food and drink, their minds became deceitful and crooked, their speech underwent change, and they were consequently no longer able to speak.
"Ghost" (*preta*) is a foreign term; *śarīra* is the Qin (Chinese) term for "grandfather. Sentient beings were first born there.
The Way is called the "Grandfather" (Pitṛ); those born later are also called "Grandfathers.

Furthermore, because they fall into this realm due to stinginess and greed, and because this realm is characterized by much hunger and thirst, they are called *preta* (hungry ghosts). They are also driven into service by the various devas, and because they long for food and drink, they are called *preta*.
As for "human" (*manuṣya*), the foreign term is *mānuṣa*, which means "intention" (*manas*). Formerly, King Mūrdhaja first transformed [the world].
In all that one does, one should engage with proper reflection, careful deliberation, and mindful recollection;

thus, as the King has taught, because one first reflects upon and recollects everything undertaken, a person is called "mind" (*manas*). Furthermore, a person who can still the mind can cultivate the Path and attain the stages of realization.
It is also said that a person is defined by pride; among the five destinies, those with much pride are designated as belonging to the human realm.
As for the asuras, the term *asura* means "non-god" (*a-sura*). Because they are not gods, they are called asuras.

This refers to their constant fighting with the gods, and also because they lack the conduct of the gods. As for "gods" (*deva*), it means "natural," because they possess superior bliss, superior bodies, and superiority;
thus they are called gods. They are superior in all matters compared to other realms, and they constantly illuminate themselves with light.

The *Devatāsaṃyukta* states: "Sentient beings" is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), while the "elements" (*dhātu*) are dharmas. It means that the sentient beings of the five destinies are in conjunction with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
When sentient beings act with an unwholesome mind, they proceed together with the unwholesome element; when they act with a wholesome mind, they proceed together with the wholesome element;
when they act with a superior mind, they proceed together with the superior element; and when they act with a base mind, [they proceed together with the base element].

Because it is coextensive with the base realms, a bhikṣu should train himself thus: "One should skillfully understand the various realms. The preceding section explained the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*) by way of causes and conditions;
the subsequent section explains the six destinies by way of the contemplation of the mind. Now, these six destinies are called *saṃsāra* (the cycle of rebirth);
dying here and being born there, they have no beginning and no rest, like a water-wheel for drawing from a well, where ordinary beings and sages alternately rise and fall.
Mutually observing these six realms of existence is collectively termed "unwholesome," for one has not yet escaped the wheel of birth and death. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind.
One should know that the mind can create heaven and the mind can create hell; even the four noble stages are entirely derived from this one [mind].
Those with wisdom and mind should reflect deeply and constantly observe themselves, like a skilled herdsman who does not allow his cattle to run wild and trample the crops of others.
How much more so for one at the initial stage on this broad earth, where dullness and distraction race about; throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one must always exercise restraint.
When, after a long time, one’s nature is perfected, acting spontaneously in accord with the Way, one transcends the ordinary and joins the sages—is this not truly fortunate? O *gaurī* (wild ox)!
This beast resembles an ox with a long tail; the *Shuowen* states that among the Southern Barbarians there is the *mao-ox*, which loves its tail so much that it uses its body to protect it.
Because people love its tail, they kill its body. This is just like a person who, out of greed for the five desires, harms his own body—it is exactly like this.
△ Third, the manifestation of great compassion and the response to sentient beings.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Having given rise to this mind of great compassion—wherein the preceding section raised the subject of the one who sees and the subsequent section clarified the object seen—this section now clarifies that the mind is permeated by great compassion;
thus, he should enter the triple world (*tridhātu*) to establish skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and lead them toward the wisdom of the Buddha. II. Verses on Bestowing Skillful Means.
Regarding the first part of the transformation, the initial thought employs the Great Transformation, yet it does not attain the three [stages]. First, as for the intended suitability:
"When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the tree and also walking back and forth, during the thirty-seven days I contemplated such matters:
'The wisdom I have attained is subtle and profound, the most supreme.'"
This one line and a half clarifies the application of mindfulness through the Mahāyāna transformation;
if this is not attained, it is like having a hand with great strength that is not used, or like setting aside the Great [Vehicle] as an analogy for the original intent.

"Beginning to sit at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the fact that while the ultimate principle is timeless, one employs time to transform sentient beings—this constitutes the beginning of the transformation, hence the term "beginning. This concerns the matter.

The commentator explains that because he first cultivated and attained the Way at this location, it is called the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Because he attained *samyak-saṃbodhi* while sitting beneath this tree, it is called the "Tree of the Way" (*bodhidruma*).

Furthermore, out of gratitude for the tree's kindness and because he contemplated the virtue of the earth, when the path was completed and the ground became lush and fertile, he wished to employ the Great Dharma to suit the capacities of sentient beings. This is the interpretation from the perspective of contemplating the mind.
This tree is the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination; by deeply contemplating dependent origination, one spontaneously attains Bodhi.
Because one wishes to provide the shade of the forest of untainted dharmas for all sentient beings, it is called the *Cūdāmaṇi-sūtra*.

As for the practitioner, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the dharma for practicing the Path; by personally traversing all stages through these factors of the Path, one attains Buddhahood.
Question: Since the Way and the desire to transform and deliver sentient beings through this Dharma are without discrimination, is it necessary to requite their kindness?
Answer: The *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states: "It is precisely by means of universal transformation and the transmission of the Dharma that one is called 'requiting kindness.
The *Past Causes and Effects Sutra* (*Pūrvayoga-sūtra*) states: "In the first seven days after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he reflected upon himself..."
The Dharma is subtle and profound, and there was no one capable of receiving it. For two weeks, he contemplated the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings;
for the third week, he contemplated who should hear the Dharma first. He then went to Vārāṇasī to preach the Four Noble Truths to the five bhikṣus.
Cunda attained the pure Dharma-eye, as did Aśvajit, Bāṣpa, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, Mahānāman, and Kauṇḍinya.
When Śāriputra attained the Way, the Buddha again preached the Four Noble Truths, and four people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
When the Buddha again preached that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, five people attained Arhatship. The Buddha constitutes the Buddha-jewel;
the Four Noble Truths constitute the Dharma-jewel; and these five people together with the Buddha—these six Arhats—constitute the Sangha-jewel. Thus are the Three Jewels.

The undertaking begins from this point. Regarding the "thirty-seven days," former commentators say it refers to contemplating the principles of the teachings and so forth, while others say it refers to exhortations and admonitions.
Master Yao stated: "When matters are most profound and sacred, one still reflects before acting. During the first week, one contemplates the subtle and wondrous nature of the Buddha’s wisdom;
during the second week, one contemplates that the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ; and during the third week, one contemplates the myriad medicines of the Dharma."
This chapter immediately cites a verse to substantiate this: "The wisdom I have attained is subtle and supreme; yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull—how can they be delivered?
This clarifies that the Buddha, abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, is eternally quiescent yet constantly illuminating, forever surveying all things with the Buddha-eye without omission;
how could he have only just reached the site of enlightenment and remained there for twenty-one days contemplating before beginning his teaching?

Regarding this matter, the mention of "three weeks" clarifies that there is a symbolic significance: it indicates that the Buddha initially intended to preach the Dharma in three cycles. Thus, the term "three weeks" is used figuratively.

During the first week, he contemplated preaching through direct exposition (*dharmadeśanā*); during the second week, he contemplated preaching through parables (*avadāna*); and during the third week, he contemplated preaching through causes and conditions (*nidāna*).

Finding no receptive capacity [in his audience], he was unable to proceed; therefore, he ceased the Great Teaching and bestowed the Lesser. This explanation is specifically based on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

This is merely an explanation from the perspective of the Mahāyāna; however, if one explains it according to the general Mahāyāna framework: the first seven contemplations intend to explain the Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna);
the next seven contemplations intend to explain the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna); and the final seven contemplations intend to explain the Shared Teaching (Śrāvaka-yāna).
Since there was no spiritual capacity for the Mahāyāna in any case, he ceased the Mahāyāna discourse and taught the Tripiṭaka and the Three Vehicles as skillful means.
This is a transformation. △ Second, clarifying the lack of capacity, in three parts:
first, clarifying the heaviness of hindrances. "Sentient beings have dull faculties; attached to pleasure, they are blinded by ignorance.
These three lines clarify the lack of capacity and are further divided into three: first, half a line clarifies the heaviness of hindrances. △ Second, clarifying... [text continues]
They are unable to hear it.
How can such types as these be saved?
Next, the second half-line of this verse clarifies their inability to hear it. △ Third, the invitation by the Brahmās.
At that time, the various Brahma kings, Śakra the Lord of Devas, the four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, Maheśvara,
and the rest of the assembly of devas and their retinues— numbering hundreds of thousands of millions— respectfully joined their palms and paid homage, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma.

At that time, beneath the various Brahma Kings, there were two rows of luminous beings; although these Brahmās requested [the Buddha] to preach, the Great Buddha knew they lacked the necessary capacity (an-avakāśa) and therefore did not speak.
At that time, the "various Brahma Kings" mentioned separately refers specifically to the eighteen Brahmās;

however, if discussed in general terms, it should include all the Brahmās of the great trichiliocosm, as well as the gods of the desire realm and Śakra, Lord of Devas, who should likewise be included.
It is also said that there are eighteen Brahmā realms: the first dhyāna has three, namely the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā;
the second dhyāna has three, namely the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, and the Ābhāsvara; the third dhyāna has three, namely the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, and the Śubhakṛtsna;
and the fourth dhyāna has nine, namely the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Asaṃjñisattva, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, the Sudarśana, and the Akaniṣṭha.
Regarding the mention of the Heat (Ātapa), Good Appearance (Sudṛśa), Good Vision (Sudarśana), Akaniṣṭha, and the various Śakras of the Heavenly Kings:

this refers specifically to the heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). As for what are called "the various heavens," they are Mount Sumeru; that mountain has four corners, and at each corner there are eight heavens.
In the center is the Sudharmā Hall, where Śakra, the Heavenly King, resides and rules over the thirty-two [heavens]. This is the meaning of the present text.

This is why it is said that [the Buddha] presides over both the principal and the retinue. As mentioned above, the various hosts of devas all join their palms in reverence and earnestly entreat him to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Regarding the "Wheel of Dharma," whatever the Buddhas have taught is termed the Wheel of Dharma;
for "wheel" carries the meaning of revolving and crushing. That is to say, it refers to the turning of the True Wheel of Dharma and its crushing [of obstacles].

This is to forcibly restrain those who are outside [the teaching]. △ Third, regarding the thought that halting the great transformation would cause harm, there are two parts; first, the strong argument that it would be detrimental:
"I then reflected to myself: 'If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms.'"

These two verses clarify the cessation of the desire to teach through mindfulness; they further consist of two parts. First, one verse and a half clarify that teaching forcefully to those without the capacity for it causes harm upon hearing. Second, the cessation of the teaching:
"I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter into nirvana."

The latter half clearly elucidates the preparatory foundation for the skillful means of transforming through breath. △ Second, the contemplation of being equal to all Buddhas in employing the transformation of the Three Vehicles, which attains [the goal] in two parts:
first, the formal elucidation of attaining transformation; fourth, clarifying the suitability of the Three Vehicles. First, clarifying the suitability of the Three Vehicles.
Reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, [the Buddha thought: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught through the three vehicles.
This single line clarifies the suitability for the three vehicles. "Reflecting" means that although those [beings] lack the great capacity [for the One Vehicle], they must not be abandoned forever;

rather, they are to be guided and saved through skillful means. It does not mean that [the Buddha] is unaware of the opening of the three [vehicles], but rather that he intends to lead them [therein].

Because he is identical to all Buddhas, it is said that he "recalls and contemplates" them. △ Second, clarifying that there are those with the capacity [to receive the teaching], in two parts: first, clarifying the praise of all Buddhas, in five sections;
first, describing the manifestation of the Buddhas:
At the time he engaged in this contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and consoled him with Brahma-sounds.
The first three phrases are Śākyamuni’s own account of how all Buddhas manifest. As for "manifestation," it occurs through the power of the skillful means of mindfulness of the Buddha;
furthermore, manifestation occurs due to two meanings: the correspondence with the Dharma and the suitability for the assembly.
△ Second, the Buddhas formally praise Śākyamuni.
Excellent! Śākyamuni, the foremost guide, has attained this unsurpassed Dharma and employs the power of skillful means in accordance with all Buddhas.

This clarifies that while the Buddhas praise those who are superior and wish to greatly transform others, they do not praise those for whom there is no spiritual capacity (*anindriya*) in that regard. Now, [the Buddha] praises [this teaching].
If one wishes to explain the minor parables (*avadāna*) according to their roots and conditions, one will attain deliverance from beginning to end; this is why the Buddha praised them.
Because he can conceal the reality and establish skillful means (*upāya*), he said, "Excellent! By bestowing the One to lead the three, he introduces them into the Buddha-wisdom;
thus, those who obtain this unsurpassed Dharma obtain the subtle and supreme true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*). And...
Regarding "employing the power of skillful means," this refers to all Buddhas following [the needs of beings] by concealing their true reality and employing provisional expedients.
△ Third, it clarifies that the Buddhas likewise conceal their true reality and employ expedients:
"We have also all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma, yet for the sake of the various classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and teach the Three Vehicles."
△ Fourth, the explanation of the two meanings in four pairs.

Because those of little wisdom delight in inferior teachings and lack self-confidence regarding their attainment of Buddhahood, the Buddha employs skillful means to distinguish and teach various fruits.
This is because sentient beings of little wisdom are incapable of hearing the Great [Vehicle], and thus he conceals the reality while they simultaneously delight in the inferior.
The expedient application of power. △ Fifth, the double conclusion of the two meanings:
Although the three vehicles are taught, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas;
although the three are taught, they ultimately serve to reveal the reality. △ Second, Śākyamuni’s response in accordance with [the request], part one: the initial speech of response.
"Excellent!

Śāriputra, you should know that when I heard the holy lion’s profound, pure, and subtle voice proclaiming 'Namo to all Buddhas,' these two lines clarify how Śākyamuni responded to this 'Excellent. Having heard the praise and exhortation of the Buddhas, he replied: 'Namo, Namo.'"
There is no such thing as "respectfully following" [the Buddha] other than by conforming to the Buddhas' concealment of their true function and employment of expedient means.

△ Second, reflecting on the capacity of sentient beings: He further forms this thought: "I have appeared in this turbid and evil world; just as all Buddhas have taught, I too shall act in accordance with them."
△ Third, the transformation through the three knowledges (*trividyā*).

Having reflected upon this matter, he proceeded at once to Vārāṇasī; [realizing that] the mark of the cessation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śānta-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be proclaimed by words, he nevertheless preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus by means of skillful power (*upāya-bala*).
This one line and a half precisely clarifies that the various phenomena manifested through transformation are of a quiescent nature and cannot be expressed in words;
what follows below is the principle of the Buddha-seed as the Middle Way devoid of intrinsic nature mentioned previously.

It is precisely because this principle is neither numerical nor expressible that it is now taught through the expedient means of the Three Vehicles. Furthermore, it is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is described by means of...
Thus, he speaks of arising and ceasing; furthermore, the principle of partial truth is likewise ineffable, yet for the sake of skillful means, it is taught through the four gates.
First, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, he taught the gate of impermanence. △ Fourth, clarifying the practice and realization.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, which brings about the sound of *nirvāṇa* and the distinct designations of the *arhat*, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.

The next line clarifies the method of transformation for others through receiving, practicing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha-mind; causing others to enter that mind is called "turning the wheel of Dharma.

It is simply stated that as soon as one first attains the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), one immediately severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and partially realizes cessation (*nirodha*).
The Truths are also a portion [of the path] through which one attains *nirvāṇa* with remainder; the term "nirvāṇa" originates from this.
By virtue of this, one becomes an Arhat of the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and thus receives the name "Arhat. △ Second, resolving doubts.
"Since time immemorial, I have constantly taught and demonstrated the Dharma of Nirvana, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted.

This single line is an explanation of a doubt; for the Master [the opponent] might suspect that the Buddha was initially unable to discern the capacities of beings and only later, through reflection upon the Buddhas, came to know their root-natures.
To resolve this, he explains: "It is not that I did not know; rather, I employed skillful means specifically wishing to lead them along."
Therefore, one should reflect that the Buddhas did not begin to contemplate [the path] only now;

rather, it is known that from time immemorial, having perceived their inclination toward the Lesser Vehicle, they have praised and instructed them to bring an end to all suffering. Thus, upon hearing the Lesser Vehicle, they immediately attain liberation.

Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to how sentient beings could realize Arhatship after merely hearing [the teaching] for a brief moment in a single lifetime, it is explained that this has been so since time immemorial.

Because I have, throughout kalpas past, praised and instructed such-and-such individuals according to their original inclinations, they quickly attained the Way. △ Third, revealing the reality. Part four:
first, a verse on the person.
Śāriputra, you should know that I see those sons of the Buddha and others who are resolutely seeking the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis.
All, with hearts of reverence, have come to the presence of the Buddha; they have previously heard from various Buddhas the teachings on skillful means.
These six lines of verse above manifest the reality and fully contain the four [aspects]. First, "I see the sons of the Buddha" and the following two lines refer to persons;
those who practice the three vehicles are all sons of the Buddha. The preceding text also encompasses this meaning. Next, from... [text continues].

1. "I then had this thought" (one line of verse) explains the principle: the Buddha-wisdom is precisely the aforementioned *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect knowledge), which is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
2. 3. "Śāriputra, you should know" (two lines of verse) teaches that one should preach only the unsurpassed path;
this is the teaching itself. 4. From "When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma... onwards.
Regarding the first verse of the "Verses on Practice" (*Gāthā-pratipatti*), it states that "all shall likewise become Buddhas.
This verse is further analyzed according to four intentions. The first two lines clarify the arousal of the Mahāyāna faculty (*indriya*), also described as "seeking the fruit.
The next two lines and one phrase clarify the Buddha’s joy because sentient beings have obtained the benefit of the Mahāyāna. The final three phrases explicitly reveal the reality (*tattva*).

"Practicing and entering through illumination" means that illumination arises from the awakening of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*). Because the seeking of the fruit depends on the awakening of this capacity, it is so described.

This should be analyzed according to four propositions: there are cases where the obstacles have been removed but the capacity has not yet awakened, such as when various Arhats were in the period of the Tripiṭaka;
because they delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, although their turbid obstacles had been removed, [their capacity for the Great Vehicle had not yet arisen].

Because their faculties are dull and great, those whose wondrous capacities have not yet been awakened and whose obstacles remain unremoved—such as the various ordinary persons mentioned in this sutra—may still awaken their capacity despite not having severed the fetters, owing to their great and sharp faculties. There are also those for whom obstacles are removed simultaneously with the awakening of their capacity;
for example, when the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* was preached, those who had realized the fruits of the two vehicles [immediately attained the fruit of Buddhahood].

In this assembly, those with great capacity (mahā-indriya) immediately manifest it; those whose obstructions have not yet been removed and whose great capacity has not yet manifested are those such as the five thousand who withdrew.
Those who "sought the Buddha-way" were indeed seeking the Great [Vehicle] and not seeking the Small. Truly, there are three meanings to "seeking":
first, the sense of "eliciting a result" through great capacity—this "seeking" is discussed within the context of capacity; second, within the context of emotion...
To seek secretly whether one has attained it or not is precisely this meaning. To speak out three times and search with the mouth is the earnest triple request.
However, within the teachings of the past, there were already two types of seeking, though the words were not yet spoken; until today, these three searches are fully present.

Regarding the question of the former "seeking upon leaving the home," these three are the seeking of the sentient being's disposition (*jīngqíng*). As for the text stating "like... [it refers to the following].
Regarding the previous promise: "This is seeking three; what does it have to do with seeking one? The answer is that having gone outside and not seeing [the others], there must be a different path.
Taking the former promise of three as a means to seek a different intention, this is also equivalent to seeking one. It is said that all came to the Buddha’s dwelling with a heart of reverence;
one interpretation states that because they were ashamed of their small [capacity] and longed for the Great, their great spiritual resonance moved the Buddha, hence the statement.

"Arriving at the Buddha's dwelling" here clarifies that it is not merely that their spiritual capacity has reached the Buddha, but that they have actually arrived in person—just as in the *Anantārthaviniścaya-sūtra*, where the fourfold assembly surrounds him, joining their palms with a reverent heart, desiring to hear the complete Way.

"Those who have previously heard from various Buddhas the teachings spoken through skillful means" refers here to the first flavor: the subduing and practice of the Three Piṭakas and the six [perfections].

Because the three teachings—distinct, common, and so forth—are expedient means for deliverance, and through these [means] beings are brought to maturity, their obstructions are removed and their faculties are awakened, leading them to seek the Great [Vehicle].
△ Second, the verse on the Unity of Principle:
"I then had this thought: 'The reason the Tathāgata appeared was to preach the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely the time for it.'"
From the passage "As soon as I had this thought," there follow two lines and one phrase which clarify the removal of obstacles and the Buddha’s joy.
For the sake of the Buddha-wisdom, the Buddha appeared in the world; however, because past obstacles were heavy and they lacked the capacity, he could not immediately teach that Buddha-wisdom.

Although those obstacles were later removed, he still had not yet taught it. Now that their capacity has been awakened, this is precisely the time for the teaching. Furthermore, regarding the assembly of the past...
Because their faculties are dull and their wisdom small, there is fear that they might slander the Dharma and fall into evil states; therefore, this is not yet the time to teach them.

Now, because their faculties are sharp and their wisdom great, they will surely believe and understand upon hearing it. Thus, the Buddha joyfully said, "Fearless," meaning he is fearless because they do not fear clinging to the Small Vehicle, slandering the Great, and thereby committing sins that lead to falling into evil states—hence, he says "fearless. △ Third, the verse on the teaching (one verse).
Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and possessed by pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Now, joyful and fearless among all bodhisattvas, I directly abandon expedient means and preach only the unsurpassed path.
Among the verses concerning the bodhisattvas, the final three lines correctly reveal the reality. One should know that the five vehicles are crooked and not direct;
they are indirect, partial, and peripheral rather than central. Now, all such biased and crooked paths are abandoned, and only the single, upright path is taught.
△ Fourth, one verse on practice.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the Bodhisattva’s net of doubts has been entirely removed; the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.

Having heard this Dharma from the Bodhisattva, they have departed from their former practices, received and practiced the path of clear illumination, and attained entry into realization. One should know that the six perfections apply to both types of bodhisattvas.

Now, having first heard this brief exposition, their old attachments have been shaken and their new doubts resolved; it should be understood that these have now been entirely eliminated, not merely for one person alone.

The same applies to bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles; yet, regarding the statement that "all śrāvakas shall become buddhas," it was not taught in the former teachings that those of the two vehicles would become buddhas.
Now, through practice and the conferring of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), how could the prediction apply solely to the two vehicles? And in dispelling doubts, how could it apply solely to bodhisattvas?
It is because they exist in mutual relation that both are complete. Question: What are the doubts of the bodhisattvas? Answer: Within the Tripiṭaka, three [types of]... are taught.
In the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, it is said that when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not yet been severed, one enters the truth as soon as they are severed;

this is the teaching of the Shared Vehicle (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), which explains that Bodhisattvas sever the active afflictions (*kleśa*) while retaining the residual habits (*vāsanā*), and upon the exhaustion of these habits, they attain Buddhahood. Since the beginning of the present sutra, we have heard a brief exposition stating that all [past attainments] were merely skillful means (*upāya*).
Yet, where are those who attained "truth" and "Buddhahood" in the past? Furthermore, since the three vehicles study the same single path, for what reason do distinctions exist between them now?
Having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all doubts have been swept away, leaving not even a single grain of mustard seed behind. △ Fourth, praising the rarity of the Dharma has two parts.
First, a verse on this wondrous Dharma:
"Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time employ the ritual for preaching the Dharma, I now likewise preach this non-discriminative Dharma."

Regarding this single verse above, such is the wondrous Dharma; "wondrous Dharma" refers to the provisional and the real. "As in the three periods [of time]" means employing the provisional to lead others to be equal to all Buddhas.
The provisional is the ritual for leading sentient beings. By preaching the non-discriminative Dharma, one leads them to be equal to all Buddhas, thereby manifesting the real.
Since the real is where the path of language is severed, how could there exist any ritual? Furthermore, the provisional and the real are originally...
Those of dull faculties and small wisdom who discriminate between the provisional and the real through non-discrimination now return to realize that one and three are non-dual;
they thereby know that the Buddha’s teaching of three and one is itself non-discriminative. All Buddhas are thus; why should it be otherwise for me alone?
△ Second, regarding the second verse on the difficulty of the time, there are five parts. First, the difficulty of the person is raised:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote; it is difficult to encounter them.

These four and a half verses refer to the aforementioned "speaking at the [right] time. Regarding that "speaking," the *udumbara* flower was previously cited; now, within these verses, [the same point is made].
Furthermore, it is said: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world" refers to two lines [of verse]. When a long time has passed, a Buddha appears;
this raises the difficulty regarding persons (pudgala). △ Second, raising the difficulty regarding the Dharma.
Even were one to appear in the world and preach this Dharma, it would be difficult;

these two lines, "even were one to appear in the world," illustrate the difficulty of the Dharma, as it was only after more than forty years since the present Buddha appeared in the world that he revealed the truth.
△ Third, illustrating the difficulty of hearing the Dharma.
It is difficult to hear this Dharma even throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas.
The two phrases "immeasurable and incalculable kalpas" illustrate the difficulty of hearing the Dharma;

for instance, those like the five thousand [who left] had the Brahma-sound filling their ears as they rose from their seats and departed—was hearing the Dharma not difficult for them? △ Fourth, illustrating the difficulty of faith and acceptance.
Those who are able to hear this Dharma are likewise rare.

These two lines regarding those "able to hear" highlight that those who can believe and accept it are even rarer than the former. Among the assembly gathered above, only Śāriputra had previously attained realization;
although those of middling and lower capacities listened, they were still unable to fully comprehend it. △ Fifth, the verse on the parable.
The fourth difficulty:
For example, the udumbara flower is beloved by all; it is rare for gods and humans, appearing only once in a great while.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering a single word, is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is exceedingly rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
By using the udumbara flower as a metaphor for the four aforementioned difficulties, it is now shown that hearing [this teaching] is the most difficult; other examples may be understood accordingly.
△ Fifth, the verse on non-emptiness has two parts; first, the verse on not harboring doubt toward those worthy of trust.

"You all should not harbor doubts, thinking that I, as the King of All Dharmas, am universally addressing this great assembly merely to teach and transform bodhisattvas through the vehicle of the One Vehicle, and have no śrāvaka disciples."
These two and a half verses clarify that what has been stated above is not in vain. Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, one and a half lines stating that one should not harbor doubts regarding trustworthy persons; [this is because] "I am the Dharma King. As a human king, one’s word is non-dual;
how could a Buddha, who is the Dharma King, permit himself to speak falsely? △ Second, the verse on not harboring doubts regarding trustworthy teachings.
"Śāriputra, you śrāvakas and bodhisattvas should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
This skillful means may be provisional and expedient, yet it is ultimately true; how could it possibly be false? When hearing the Dharma King’s teaching of the Dharma, do not give rise to doubt.

△ Sixth: Verses on Distinguishing the Assembly and Encouraging Faith. Part Two: First, verses on distinguishing those who are not [worthy]. Part Three: First, verses on distinguishing the non-[worthy].
The disciples of the Buddha—beings such as these who, in this world of five turbidities, take pleasure only in attachment to various desires—will ultimately not seek the path of the Buddha.
These three lines of verse distinguish those within the five turbidities; the preceding line of verse distinguishes those who are not disciples of the Buddha. Why?
If one is attached to and delights in various sensual desires, this is the practice of Māra; therefore, it must be excluded.

In the preceding text, even attachment to *nirvāṇa* was said to disqualify one from being a disciple of the Buddha; here, attachment to *saṃsāra* is likewise addressed. These are mutual exclusions of what is not [the true path].
As for those who ultimately do not seek the Buddha-way, the verse above excludes those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who, having not attained the supreme Dharma, claim to have attained it.
Because of the aforementioned principle, such persons do not seek the Buddha-way. △ Second, a verse explaining that those who understand the meaning are difficult to find:
In future ages, evil persons, hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will be deluded and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into the evil realms.
In future ages, among evil people, those who can interpret the meaning of even a single verse after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa will be difficult to find.
△ Third, the verse on meeting other Buddhas:
For those who possess a sense of shame and modesty, whose pure resolve seeks the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
There is one verse on the purity of shame and remorse; if one encounters other Buddhas, one will immediately attain definitive understanding.
△ Second, the verse on encouraging faith, which has two parts: first, the verse encouraging faith in the provisional teachings.
Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: by means of ten billion skillful means, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
those who have not practiced it cannot understand this.
These three verses encourage faith; if one does not believe this Dharma, it is impossible [to attain enlightenment].
The first one and a half lines encourage faith in the provisional (upāya). △ Second, the verses encourage faith in the ultimate (paramārtha).
Since you have already understood that the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, employ various skillful means according to what is appropriate, you should no longer harbor any doubts or suspicions;
let your hearts give rise to great joy, knowing for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.
Next, one and a half lines express firm faith in the reality of the provisional and the real, being free from doubt and knowing for oneself that one will become a Buddha;
this concludes the text of the first fascicle.

△ Chapter Two: The Parable. *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Three: The Parable. First, the presentation of the chapter title.
"Parable" (*dṛṣṭānta*) means comparison; "analogy" (*upamā*) means instruction for enlightenment.

By relying on this to illustrate that, and entrusting the shallow to explain the profound, the preceding section extensively elucidated the five Buddhas' opening of the provisional for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom who attained awakening upon hearing it in its entirety. However, those of middling and inferior capacities still harbored delusion that had not yet been dispelled.
Thereupon, his great compassion remained inexhaustible and his skillful wisdom boundless; he once again stirred the wind of instruction to raise the banner of teaching.
The metaphor of the fan is used to cause awakening and understanding; thus it is called an "analogy" (*upamāna*). This interpretation applies to the general meaning. To explain it specifically:

worldly phenomena are compared to supramundane phenomena. Because one has previously heard what was never before heard, one leaps with joy and exultation, as the sutra uses the analogy of worldly father and son to illustrate the supramundane master and disciple, and further compares worldly birth-phenomena to the supramundane.
The Dharma that arises in the world causes those who hear the Buddha’s voice and teaching not to lose the Mahāyāna, as the sutra says:

"The father knows the former inclinations of his sons, each having their own preferred precious playthings. Furthermore, although worldly cessation is compared to supramundane cessation, even by attaining the outflow-free state, hearing [the Dharma] removes sorrow and affliction, as the sutra says: "I am their father; I should pull them from their suffering and hardship..."

To avoid the need for burning or cooking, one further compares the non-arising and non-ceasing of the mundane world with the non-arising and non-ceasing of the supramundane, causing them to abide securely within true wisdom.
[One thinks: "I shall certainly become a Buddha. As the sutra says: "Riding upon this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment.
One should know that the Buddha, using a single voice, speaks parables skillfully to enable those of middling and inferior capacities to attain the four *siddhāntas*.
It is called the "Parable Chapter" because it provides further benefit. This is an explanation based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*). Regarding the explanation based on the teaching (*śāsana*):

the Buddha’s original intention was to praise the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), but as sentient beings were unable to comprehend it, he followed the great compassion and skillful means (*upāya*) of former Buddhas by proceeding to the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*), where he praised the three vehicles.
For those of the two vehicles and below, who are capable of self-deliverance but whose grace does not extend to others, the Bodhisattvas act as their charioteers.
"The ox carries the others out of the house"—this is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka [Hīnayāna] teaching. Furthermore, the three types of persons all fear being burned or boiled:
the Śrāvaka flees straight ahead like a roe deer without looking back; the Pratyekabuddha is like that mother deer, galloping while repeatedly glancing back;

the Bodhisattva is like the body of a great elephant, which wards off the swords and arrows to lead the entire herd out—this is the meaning of the Shared (Pāryāya) Teaching. Furthermore, the two vehicles set forth..."

When the mind is close to its objects, the principle is shallow and wisdom is weak; it can only sever the common delusions (*sāmānyakleśa*) but cannot exhaust them to their limits or reach the ultimate ground.

This is not a *pāramitā*. If a Bodhisattva has long since resolved their mind, the principle is profound and wisdom is strong; they can sever the specific delusions (*viśeṣakleśa*), exhausting their source and reaching the limit of their nature.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The two vehicles are like fireflies; the Bodhisattva is like the light of the sun. This is the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

Furthermore, those who, upon first seeing my body and hearing what I have taught, immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—such people are easy to transform and deliver;
they do not cause the Tathāgata to experience weariness or distress. As in the *Avataṃsaka*, truth is realized through phenomena themselves without the need for metaphors;
yet for those who have not yet entered [this state], I have further employed [teachings] over more than forty years.
Through various skillful means, I now assist in manifesting the primary meaning;

today, in the city of Rājagṛha, I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna, universally causing all multitudes to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom, so that not a single person shall attain extinction alone.

As it is now, so it was at the beginning—without duality and without distinction. Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence who hear this will be able to understand it immediately, and I shall not allow... [anyone else to do so].

The Tathāgata’s birth amidst weariness and suffering does not require further illustration; it is solely because those of middling and inferior capacities give rise to doubt through their attachments and hesitate at the crossroads that he must now employ the parable of the great vehicle to bring them benefit—this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
The principles for contemplating the fundamental and the manifested, as well as the mind, may be understood by applying this analogy. △ Second, explaining the scriptural text, part one:

The explanation of the Dharma consists of two parts: the explanation by way of analogy. Regarding the first section, there are four parts: first, Śāriputra’s reception and understanding; second, the Tathāgata’s confirmation; third, the bestowing of the prediction; and fourth, the joy of the entire assembly. Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the prose narrative; second, the verse recitation. Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the narrator’s account; and second, the account of internal realization. Regarding the first of these: [Text follows] 1. At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and was filled with delight.
To "leap for joy and be filled with delight" means that understanding it within one's heart is called "delight," while this delight moving through the physical form is called "leaping.

Having heard the wondrous Dharma from the Wondrous Person and attained wondrous understanding, even encountering a single blessing would cause one to rejoice and exult; how much more so when there are three such blessings?
"How could one who possesses [this] not leap for joy? This describes the internal realization. △ Second, describing the external demeanor:
"Immediately rising and joining the palms to gaze up at the Honored Countenance.
"Immediately rising and joining the palms" means that the physical body attains realization; in the past, the provisional and the real were two, like palms that do not join.

Now, to explain that the provisional is identical to the real is like the joining of two palms. To say one faces the Buddha means that one knows that in the past, the provisional was not the cause of Buddhahood and the real was not the fruit of Buddhahood;
now, by realizing that the provisional is identical to the real, one perfects the Great Perfect Cause.

Since the cause must lead to the fruit, it is said that joining the palms and facing the Buddha to gaze upon the Honored Countenance expresses the realization of the Real, for the Real is itself the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the non-expedient methods: gazing upon the Honored Countenance without other thoughts expresses the intention of opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Understanding the Real (*satya*) also means understanding the Expedient (*upāya*), and experiencing the Expedient also means understanding the Real;
these are presented alternately from one side each to describe the external demeanor. △ Second, Śāriputra’s own array has three parts: first, the section marking the three joys.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy at what I have never before experienced.
The phrase "he addressed the Buddha" refers to the verbal comprehension [of the teaching]. That is to say, Śāriputra himself declares:

"Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One"—this indicates that he sees the Buddha's body through his own body, and thus experiences physical joy; hearing this Dharma-sound, he relies upon the Buddha’s own mouth [to express it].

Because he rejoiced upon hearing [the teaching], it is said that his mouth was joyful, having attained what he had never experienced before; because he understood the Buddha’s intent through his own mind, it is called the joy of the mind.
△ Second, the explanation of the three joys: first, citing the loss of his former body to manifest the understanding of his present body.

Why is this? In the past, I heard such a teaching from the Buddha, seeing that various bodhisattvas received the prediction of their future buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter;
I was deeply moved by the realization that we had lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
This clarifies that not having seen the Buddha in the past is a loss; that the former Buddhas bestowed predictions of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas, yet one did not participate in such matters;
and that seeing the Buddha is a profound significance. Since one has not seen the Buddha, there is no physical joy.

Those who hear such a Dharma as this—when the sun shines upon a high mountain—are secretly endowed with the meaning of hearing it, yet outwardly they appear as if deaf or mute, unable to hear the Way.

This Dharma is precisely that which was heard within the Vaipulya teachings; because the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna is no different from what is now [being taught], it is said that "he heard this Dharma.

As for receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it is also as in the Vaipulya sūtras, where predictions are granted to bodhisattvas while the followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*) are excluded from this matter, causing them profound personal grief.
In the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra*, they hear the praise of the Great Vehicle and the refutation of the Small Vehicle.
To be suspicious within and contemptuous without is called "sorrowful loss," which means losing all knowledge and vision—losing the vision of the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of the Buddha-wisdom.
△ Second, citing past verbal failures to manifest present verbal understanding: First, explaining the source of the transgression;
second, specifically identifying the transgression ("we..."); third, citing the transgression to take refuge in oneself ("this is I...").
“World-Honored One, whenever I dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly reflect:
‘Since we have all equally entered the Dharma-nature, why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna teachings?
This is our own fault, not the World-Honored One’s.’”
This clarifies that the failure to hear the Dharma in the past was due to one’s physical dwelling in mountain forests while the mind clung to inferior paths;
thus, because one did not hear the Dharma, there was no joy in speech regarding the thought, "I always dwell alone.

This place of reflection on one's faults is where those who have entered the same *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) correctly emerge from the error of clinging to the inferior. Having already grasped the single principle into which they enter, they may then harbor doubts regarding the three teachings.

The gateway through which one enters is one, and since the principle is identical, it is I who have lost my understanding and vision. Since the three teachings differ, the Bodhisattva receives his prediction (vyākaraṇa);

yet because the Tathāgata’s bestowal of this prediction appears partial, it results in error. Now, in describing this fault, I say that my repentance for these transgressions is due to our own faults:
"It is because I was deluded regarding the provisional [teachings]—what concern does this have with the principle or the teaching? It is because I was confused regarding the real."
How does this relate to the Buddha specifically recounting past errors? It is an expression of gratitude to the Tathāgata for leading one’s own faults to light and taking refuge [in him].
△ Third, raising the past failure of intention to reveal the present understanding of that intention.
Why is this? If we had waited for the explanation of the causes by which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna.
However, we did not understand the skillful means used in accordance with what was appropriate;
upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, we immediately accepted it with faith, contemplated it, and took it as our realization. World-Honored One, from the past until now...
Throughout the day and throughout the night, he constantly reproached himself.

This clarifies that his mind lacked the faultlessness of true understanding; for since he did not wait for an explanation of the underlying causes, he lacked real understanding, and since he did not recognize skillful means, he lacked provisional understanding.
Because these forms of understanding were absent, he lacked mental joy. Since his past errors had already...

"Manifesting what is now attained" means that self-evident realization does not depend on verbal explanation. "The cause" refers to two meanings: first, it does not depend on the former [the two truths]; second, it does not wait for the latter [the ultimate truth]. Just as the sun first illuminates the high mountains, the wisdom that clarifies the three truths is what is attained. "Not understanding the reality" is a self-reproach for failing to understand the real; "not understanding the skillful means" is a self-reproach for failing to understand the provisional.

Thus, the meaning of the cause is twofold. First, it does not depend on the former two; second, it does not wait for the latter. As the sun first shines upon the high mountains, so too is the wisdom that clarifies the three truths attained.
The Buddha, for this reason, waited for me; yet because I did not accept [the teaching], I missed it previously.

Since the teachings of all Buddhas must ultimately speak the truth after a long time, and I did not wait for it later, I have hurriedly grasped the minor [teachings] between these two poles without understanding the true and the provisional.
This can be understood according to the text. △ Third, the conclusion forming the three joys.
Second, the initial conclusion:

"Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never before heard, all our doubts and regrets have been severed; our bodies and minds are serene, and we have attained a sense of swift peace and security."
This clarifies the formation of the three joys: first, the formation [of the body] from the Buddha constitutes the joy of the body; second, hearing the Dharma constitutes the joy of the mouth;
and third, severing all doubts and regrets constitutes the joy of the mind. △ Second, the accomplishment.
Today I have come to know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma.
Today I have come to know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, drawing near to the fulfillment of the Buddha’s meaning. Born from the Buddha’s mouth, my bonds are severed.
"Being born through transformation from the Dharma" refers to birth by mental formation (*manomaya*).
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses in Praise (Three parts): First, verses praising the three types of joy.
Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before; my heart harbors great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed.
This single verse marks the three joys; since it mentions "I have heard," it simultaneously implies that I have attained [the vision of] the Buddha.
II. Verse Explanation of the Three Joys: A. First, the verse on the joy of seeing the Buddha.
From of old I have been graced by the Buddha's teaching and have not lost the Mahāyāna; the Buddha’s voice is most rare, for it can remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
Having already attained the exhaustion of outflows, hearing it now further removes my grief and distress.

The prose section clarifies the loss of knowledge and vision; now, within this verse, it clarifies that the Mahāyāna is not lost. The preceding treatise discusses the loss from a remote perspective, whereas this verse discusses the loss from a proximate perspective;
the texts merely manifest these points reciprocally. △ Second, the verse on not hearing the Dharma, part one:
first, the verse on not hearing because of physical distance.
Whether dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter, sighing with deep self-reproach:
"How can we deceive ourselves? We too are sons of the Buddha, having equally entered the dharma of outflowlessness;
yet we are unable to proclaim the Unsurpassed Way in the future—the golden body, the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations."
While dwelling together within the same Dharma, I have failed to attain these qualities—the eighty minor marks, the eighteen unique dharmas, and other such merits;
I have lost them all. As I was walking alone, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly, his fame filling the ten directions and bringing vast benefit to sentient beings.
Reflecting on this, I thought to myself: "I have lost this benefit; I have deceived and betrayed myself."
Day and night, I have constantly contemplated this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I have erred or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the bodhisattvas; therefore, throughout the day and night, I have deliberated upon this very matter.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate—this outflow-free, inconceivable teaching that leads all beings to the site of enlightenment.
When I constantly speak of "day and night," you should know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is the night and nirvāṇa is the day.
Is it that nirvāṇa exists within birth-and-death, or that nirvāṇa exists outside of birth-and-death? When awakening is attained, both doubts are simultaneously dispelled.
Furthermore, the doubt that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equally the night is removed; this is called "day," just as when the sun rises.
At that time, both doubts were simultaneously dispelled. 2. Verse on Not Hearing [the Teaching] Due to Entering the Dharma-nature:
"Originally I was attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodoxy and preached Nirvana.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization within the Dharma of emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself that I had reached extinction."
To be attached to false views is the attachment of ordinary people; to be attached to entering the dharma-nature is the attachment of the two vehicles. Both of these fail to hear the Dharma.
△ Third, a verse on the joy of attaining wondrous understanding through the aforementioned mind.
Now, for the first time, I have realized that this was not true extinction.

When I attain Buddhahood and am endowed with the thirty-two marks, revered by devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits—only then can it be said that [defilements] are forever exhausted and extinguished without remainder.
When the Buddha spoke among the great assembly, "I shall become a Buddha," upon hearing such a sound of the Dharma, my doubts and regrets were entirely removed.
When I first heard what the Buddha taught, my heart was greatly startled and filled with doubt: "Could it be that a Māra has become a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?
Then the Buddha, through various causes, analogies, and skillful words, explained it to me; my mind became as calm as the ocean, and having heard this, the net of my doubts was severed.
The Buddha further told me that in the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have attained parinirvāṇa and dwelt in skillful means all likewise preached this Dharma.

The Buddhas of the present and the future are infinite in number, and they likewise expound such a Dharma through various skillful means, just as the World-Honored One now has—from his birth, his renunciation, his attainment of the Way, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma—also taught through skillful means.
The World-Honored One speaks of the true Path; Pāpīyān could not have done this. Therefore, I know with certainty that this is not a Māra who has become a Buddha.
Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra.
These nine and a half verses clarify that the mind previously attained a wondrous understanding and rejoiced in the superior clarity without depending on external causes;

they did not explain the skillful means. In these verses, it is now clarified that one has attained the causes and also understands the skillful means. Why is this so? One must know that this refers to what is heard.
To become a Buddha is the cause; hearing that the Way of the five Buddhas is identical is the understanding that Māra is not Māra—this is the understanding of skillful means.
This is intended to mutually clarify one aspect of the meaning. That "Chapter on the Five Buddhas" is precisely the text of the summary-understanding (*anujñāna*);
as for calling him Pāpīyas, it is also named Pāpīyan, which here is translated as "Evil One," meaning he constantly harbors evil and brings it to fulfillment.
Regarding those who practice unwholesome dharmas, "Māra"—in Sanskrit *māra*, which here means "the killer"—refers to that which severs the life-force of wisdom in sentient beings;

this is what is meant by the deeds of Māra. It should be understood that although this section contains both prose and verse, it belongs entirely to the text of Śāriputra’s own confession and realization. This is because in the past, at the Deer Park, Śāriputra’s resolve...

The Tathāgata who delights in minor dharmas employs skillful means to guide those who are capable according to their capacity, preaching the Four Noble Truths so that they may realize the One True Reality.
What they have realized is no different from that of the Buddha, and the Buddha likewise confirms it as being no distinct from his own.

Since the present sutra has appeared, he has briefly revealed and clarified this, yet [some] disparage it as a mere skillful means; thus they are struck with alarm and doubt, claiming that a Māra has falsely assumed the form of a Buddha. This is indeed the case.

The Tathāgata, out of his compassionate and subtle skill in teaching, extensively cited the five Buddhas as having first employed expedient means and subsequently revealed the Perfect Vehicle (pariniṣpanna-yāna) to serve as a basis for faith and understanding. Since this was so in the past, how could it not be so now? Thereupon, Śāriputra attained the removal of doubt;
his mind became as tranquil as the ocean. Having heard extensively at this great assembly, he attained wondrous awakening to the eternal and true, penetrating the abyss of the Dharma-nature.

Since its source is identical to the knowledge and vision of the Buddha-eye, it is precisely here that my present realization, my expression of gratitude for the absolution of my transgressions, and my self-proclamation of my virtuous state reside.
△ Third, the conclusion in verse:
Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound and exceedingly subtle, as he expounds the pure Dharma, my heart is filled with great joy.

Doubt and regret are forever exhausted; abiding securely within true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha, honored by devas and humans, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to transform and guide all bodhisattvas.
These two and a half verses conclude the preceding section as written. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment [of the teaching], in three parts:
First, the past instruction on the Great [Vehicle].
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now, among this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas..."
In the middle [section] it says: "I formerly, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, constantly taught and transformed you in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas;
you also followed me through the long night to receive instruction. Because I guided you by means of skillful expedients, you were born into my Dharma."
Regarding the "explanation and confirmation": in the preceding passage, Śāriputra himself recounted his realization; here, the Tathāgata confirms that this understanding is not false.

This section has three parts: first, [the Buddha] had previously taught the Great [Vehicle]; second, [Śāriputra] temporarily forgot it and took up the Small [Vehicle]; third, [the Buddha] again teaches him the Great [Vehicle].
The reason for citing the previous teaching of the Great Vehicle is to describe the conditions for his seeing the Buddha; as for the temporary forgetting and taking up of the Small, it describes...
Regarding the regret over one's failure to hear the Dharma, the text explains that the very conditions for hearing it lead back to the teaching of the Great [Vehicle];

by describing how his realization and understanding were not in vain, it fulfills the three preceding points. As for the "Unsurpassed Way," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The unsurpassed body refers to the primary and secondary marks;
the unsurpassed reception and maintenance refers to the fulfillment of self-benefit and benefit for others; and the unsurpassed life, view, and precepts refer to the perfection of these qualities."
Unsurpassed wisdom refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); unsurpassed inconceivability refers to the six perfections (*pāramitā*);
unsurpassed liberation refers to the ability to destroy the two obstacles; unsurpassed practice refers to the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*) and the Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*).
Furthermore, unsurpassed body is named the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*); unsurpassed upholding is named great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); and unsurpassed fulfillment is named reaching [the goal].
The supreme wisdom of the other shore is called "all-encompassing knowledge" (sarvajñā); the inconceivable supreme is called "Arhat"; the supreme liberation is called "Great Nirvana";
and the supreme practice is called "Samyaksaṃbuddha. The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, fascicle thirteen, states:
"The Path should be pure; that which is defiled and turbid is not the Path. The Path requires single-mindedness; manifold thoughts are not the Path."
The path that is not the Path requires contentment; the path that is not the Path requires the elimination of excessive desire; the path that is not the Path requires reverence rather than arrogance;
the path that is not the Path requires restraint of the mind rather than heedlessness; the path that is not the Path requires illumination rather than self-concealment;

the path that is not the Path requires continuity rather than lack of practice; the path that is not the Path requires awakening from folly and delusion; the path that is not the Path requires the instruction and transformation of those who are stingy.
"Every path leads to the proximity of good friends, while practicing evil constitutes a non-path," and so forth—these various teachings clarify the Unsurpassed Path.
