Now, this sutra takes perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) as the Unsurpassed Path; whether partial or sequential, these are all discussed in other sutras.
You, too, have followed me for a long night as a student; although my great transformation has been vast, you have not yet shattered the darkness of ignorance and delusion within your mind."

Having followed the Buddha to receive his teachings, even though the cause of realization was distant, it did not yet perish; how much more so now that there is true awakening—how could this be false?
Thus, by citing the former instruction, he describes the non-delusion of his vision of the Buddha. The phrase "I used skillful means to bring them into my Dharma" implies a dual connection:
if they were transformed by the Great Transformation in the past, they now possess great understanding in this life; this pertains to the first [category].

As for the second intention: if one were to avoid the evil realms through expedient means, this constitutes the second intention. Within the second [section], there is the forgetting and grasping of the small.
Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way; you have now forgotten it all, yet you claim for yourself—
"You have attained extinction (nirvāṇa).
You have now completely forgotten [the Great Vehicle]; having abandoned the Great midway and practiced the Small, you are called 'one who forgot midway.
If you now claim for yourself that you have already attained extinction, this is because you have now completely forgotten [the truth]. It is due to your forgetting the Great [Vehicle]."
"I vow that you shall immediately practice the Lesser Vehicle so as not to incur regret, and that you may hear the Dharma without it being in vain. △ Third, returning to preach the Great Vehicle:
"I now wish to cause you to remember your original vows and the path you have practiced; therefore, for the sake of the śrāvakas, I speak this."
The Mahāyāna Sūtra is titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, which teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas' mindful recollection.
I now wish to cause you to remember your original vow; this is to recount that your attainment of understanding was not in vain.
Having first bestowed provisional teachings to establish intermediate minor virtues, I subsequently revealed the ultimate reality to fulfill your original vow and great aspiration.
△ Third, the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa), in two parts. First, the prose section, in ten parts. First, the time:
"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed..."
△ Second, the cause of practice:
making offerings to several tens of billions of buddhas, upholding the true Dharma, and fulfilling the path practiced by bodhisattvas.
△ Third, the attainment of the fruit.
You shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Flower Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct,
Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
△ Fourth, the four lands.
The name of the land is Vimalā; its terrain is level, upright, pure, adorned, secure, and prosperous with abundant joy. Gods and humans are numerous and flourishing.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with eight intersecting roads demarcated on their sides by golden cords. Beside each [road], there are...
The rows of trees made of the seven treasures were always in bloom and bore fruit.
△ Fifth, regarding the preaching of the Dharma:
Śāriputra, although that Tathāgata Flower-Light also taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the Three Vehicles when he appeared in the world...
It is not in an evil age that he preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles by virtue of his original vow.
△ Sixth, the name of the kalpa:
That kalpa is named Mahāratnavyūha. Why is it called Mahāratnavyūha? Because within that land, through the [Bodhi-]...
Because the Bodhisattvas are a great treasure.
△ Seventh, the number of the assembly:
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
There is none who cannot know this through the power of the Buddha's wisdom. When they wish to walk, precious flowers receive their feet. These bodhisattvas have not newly resolved their minds;
they have long planted the roots of virtue, having purified and cultivated the Brahma-faring under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas, always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, possess great supernormal powers, and are well-versed in [the teachings].
The gateways of all dharmas are straightforward and without falsehood, and their resolve and mindfulness are firm;
such bodhisattvas fill that land. △ Eighth, the Lifespan.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣparāja is twelve minor kalpas—excluding the period when he was a prince and had not yet attained Buddhahood;
the people of that land have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
△ Ninth: The Stage of the Successor (Upapadya).
After twelve intermediate kalpas had passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati shall next become a Buddha, named Padmapratiṣṭhitagati, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha. Such shall be his buddha-field."
It is also thus. △ Ten:
The Abiding of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Flower-Light, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
The Semblance Dharma will also remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.

Regarding the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): Śāriputra came forward and personally declared his own realization, whereupon the Buddha confirmed it as true; thus, he granted him the prediction.

If one attains great understanding and knows for oneself that one shall become a Buddha, what need is there to wait for a prediction? There are four intentions behind the granting of a prediction: first, for those who previously had not [attained it].

The prediction for the two vehicles is now made; specifically, the prediction for the two [vehicles] as being of middle and lower capacity is because they have not yet attained realization, and it serves to encourage them.

Third, it is to establish a karmic connection for those who hear it; fourth, it is to fulfill their original vows—therefore, the prediction is given. Regarding the title "Tathāgata Arhat Flower-Light" and so forth, these are the specific designations among the ten epithets. Now, as for the explanation of these ten epithets: [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the standard exegesis on the *daśanāma* (ten epithets) based on the context. First, "Tathāgata" (*tathā-āgata*) means "thus come," signifying that he has realized the truth exactly as it is. Second, "Arhat" (*arhan*) means "worthy one," signifying that he is worthy of offerings from gods and humans. Third, "Samyak-saṃbuddha" means "perfectly awakened one," signifying his complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena. Fourth, "Vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna" means "perfected in knowledge and conduct," signifying his mastery of both wisdom and practice. Fifth, "Sugata" means "well-gone," signifying that he has reached the ultimate destination. Sixth, "Lokavid" means "knower of the world," signifying his thorough understanding of the various realms of existence. Seventh, "Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi" means "unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed," signifying his skill in guiding sentient beings according to their capacities. Eighth, "Śāstā-deva-manuṣyāṇām" means "teacher of gods and humans," signifying his role as the guide for the celestial and terrestrial worlds. Ninth, "Buddha" means "awakened one," signifying his awakening to the nature of reality. Tenth, "Bhagavat" means "possessor of glory," signifying his endowment with the six excellences of virtue. Thus, the ten epithets are distinguished and recorded here. However, regarding the detailed explanation of these ten epithets... [text continues].
The meanings are very numerous; for now, I shall record and explain one type. That which is called "without falsehood" is named Tathāgata;
being able to act as a field of merit for sentient beings, it is named Arhat; knowing the dharmas of the ten realms, it is named Samyaksaṃbuddha;

being fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge, it is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; not returning again, it is named Sugata; and knowing the lands of sentient beings, it is named... (Lokavid).
He who understands the world is peerless; he is named the Unsurpassed One (*Anuttara*). He who tames the minds of others is named the Tamer of Men (*Puruṣadamyasārathi*).

He who serves as the eye for sentient beings is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). He who knows the three groups of beings is a Buddha. He who destroys Pāpīyas is named Bhagavān—that is, the World-Honored One (*Bhagavat*).

Furthermore, there are the lands, the preaching of the Dharma, the names of kalpas, the enumeration of assemblies, the measure of lifespans, the stage of the successor (*Kṣetrasaṃkhyā-dharmadeśanā-kalpanāma-gaṇanā-āyuḥpramāṇa-parivartadharma*), and so forth.
The duration of their dwelling, whether long or short, may be understood according to the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Part Two: Verses in Praise (Gāthā) Section One: Verses in Praise of the Long Prose Exposition Subsection One: Verses in Praise of the Third [Attainment], the Attainment of the Fruit.
"Śāriputra will become a Buddha in a future age; his universal wisdom shall be honored by the title 'Flower Radiance' (Puṣyarāja), and he shall deliver immeasurable multitudes.

This verse consists of eleven and a half lines, divided into two parts. The first ten lines summarize the nine preceding points, omitting the verses on the successor’s long-term offerings to the *śarīras*.
The final one and a half lines conclude with a eulogy. The first line of this section is an anticipatory summary (*atideśa*).
1. Attaining the fruit; 2. The subsequent offering (one line); 3. Tracing back the causes (three lines); 4. The immeasurable [eons] (the latter half-line);
5. The names of the eons (four lines); 6. The names of the worlds (one and a half lines); 7. The purity of the land (one and a half lines); 8.
The number of the bodhisattva assembly in that land (one and a half lines); 9. The preaching of the Dharma (the latter half-line). These correspond to the seven points.

The Buddha speaks two lines of verse for the King concerning the lifespan of the eight Buddhas and their parinirvāṇa; following this, one and a half lines concern the duration of the Dharma’s abiding;
nine lines concern the extensive distribution of the śarīra relics; and a further half-line describes the offerings made to these relics.
From the subsequent section on the Flower-Light Buddha (Puṣyarasmi), one and a half lines conclude with a summary of praise. △ Second, the verses on the causes of the second [period].
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas and fulfilled the bodhisattva practices, one realizes the unsurpassed path through the merits of the ten powers and so forth.
Regarding the fulfillment of the bodhisattva practices and the merits of the ten powers and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "The Buddha possesses the ten powers;
does the bodhisattva possess them as well? The answer is: "He also possesses them. This refers, first of all, to the firmness of the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
1. The power of not abandoning sentient beings; 2. The power of great loving-kindness; 3. The power of being fully endowed with great compassion; 4.
The power of diligence in believing in all Buddha-dharmas; 5. The power of wisdom, conduct, and meditative concentration; 6. The power of wisdom that eliminates the two extremes;
7. The power of bringing sentient beings to maturity; 8. The power of contemplating the true mark of phenomena; 9. The power of entering the three gates of liberation; 10. [The power of...]
The power of knowledge regarding non-obstruction. △ Third, the verse on the name of the sixth kalpa:
After immeasurable kalpas have passed, the kalpa is named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment).
△ Fourth, the verse on the fourth buddha-field.

The world is named Vimalaviśuddhānupakleśa (Stainless, Pure, and Without Defilement); its ground is made of lapis lazuli, its paths are demarcated by golden cords, and its trees, adorned with various colors of the seven treasures, are always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
△ The seventh section on the number of the assembly in five verses:

The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness; they have fully perfected the perfection of supernormal powers and have skillfully trained in the bodhisattva path under countless buddhas.
△ The sixth verse explains the fifth [topic], the teaching of the Dharma:
such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower Radiance (Puṣyarasmi).
△ The seventh verse explains the eighth [topic], the lifespan.
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The World-Honored One Flower-Light Buddha dwelt in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas, and the people of that land had a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
△ The tenth section on the duration of the Dharma’s abiding consists of eight verses.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
Once the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall remain for thirty-two [minor kalpas].
△ Ninth verse: Offering to the relics.
The relics are widely disseminated, and gods and humans everywhere make offerings to them.
△ Second: Concluding praise.

All the deeds performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha were exactly like this; that most supreme and peerless Honored One among two-legged beings was none other than your own self—you should truly rejoice at this.
"One should rejoice" is the explanation for entering the first stage of the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
At the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one can act as a Buddha within a hundred Buddha-worlds; on the subsequent stages of practice, this increases manifold.
**IV. The Joy of the Multitudes.** 1. The Prose Exposition (*gadya*). 1. The Narrator’s Account of the Multitudes’ Joyful Offerings. 1. The Account of the Multitudes’ Joy.
At that time, the great assembly— the fourfold community of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others—
seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before the Buddha, felt great joy in their hearts.
They were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
This concludes the section on understanding and rejoicing. △ Second, the presentation of offerings:
Each person removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it to the Buddha, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-deva-rāja, and the others.
Together with countless sons of gods, they also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *mandārava* flowers, and great *mahāmandārava* flowers,
scattering these celestial robes while remaining suspended in mid-air and revolving on their own.
Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music played simultaneously in the sky, and a rain of various celestial flowers fell.
△ Second, the formal acknowledgment and understanding.
He spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he has again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."

Thereupon he spoke these words; what follows is the formal summary and understanding. First, "initially summarizing the opening of the provisional" refers to the previous section; now, "only then turning back again" summarizes the revelation of the ultimate reality.
At that time, the various devaputras, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
△ Second, the two verses: first, the verse on revealing the Real by opening the Provisional.
Formerly at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths, analytically teaching the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of all phenomena;
now you again turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma—this Dharma is extremely profound and subtle, and few are those capable of believing it.
△ Second, the verses on self-statement of attaining understanding, sympathetic joy, and dedication:
"From of old we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One preach such profound, wondrous, and supreme Dharma as we have never heard before.
World-Honored One, regarding this Dharma you have preached, we all rejoice. The Greatly Wise Śāriputra has now received the Tathāgata’s prediction."
We, too, shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and unsurpassed among all worlds. The Buddha-way is inconceivable;

he teaches with skillful means according to what is appropriate. Whatever merit we have acquired in this life or past lives, as well as the merit from seeing the Buddha—all of it we dedicate entirely to the Buddha-way.
"We are also like this" means that it is as Śāriputra understood, as Śāriputra was confirmed, and as Śāriputra received his prediction.
Question: "Kāśyapa and Subhūti and the other great śrāvakas have not yet attained understanding;
among these four assemblies now, who has attained awakening first? Answer: "The four assemblies, including devas and humans, also possess three grades."

Those of superior faculties are the same as Śāriputra; those of middling and inferior faculties may be known by this analogy. Furthermore, it is explained that both Śāriputra and Kāśyapa were practitioners of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

This was truly because those of middling and inferior faculties had not yet attained awakening; thus Kāśyapa Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra manifested as if he did not understand. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"As long as the illnesses of sentient beings are not cured, the Bodhisattva’s illness is likewise not cured. This is what is meant. This is the unsurpassed Great Dharma.
Regarding the "wheel," as stated in the fifty-ninth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, turns the great wheel of Dharma through ten matters:
first, being fully endowed with the four pure fearlessnesses; second, giving rise to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) that accord with the sound of speech;
third, skillfully understanding and elucidating [the teachings]; fourth, acceding to the unimpeded understanding (*anāvaraṇapratibhāna*) of all Buddhas."
Fifth, they are able to cause the minds of all sentient beings to be filled with pure faith; sixth, all their speech is never in vain;
seventh, they are sustained by the empowerment of the power of great compassion and vows; eighth, the sounds they produce pervade the ten directions;
ninth, they preach the Dharma without interruption for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; tenth, in accordance with what they have preached...
All dharmas—such as the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), and samādhis—are produced;

these dharmas are profoundly deep and mysterious because their merit is supreme, their transformative virtue crowns the five periods, and they extend horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three time-pasts without exception.
This is why it is said: "The Buddha-way is inconceivable. "Inconceivable" (*parikalpya*) means "not possible" (*na śakya*); it simply means that it cannot be grasped.
This is what is meant by "conceivable. △ Second, providing a metaphorical explanation for those of middle capacity, which has four parts:
first, the metaphor that opens [the teaching] to reveal the three; second, clarifying how those of middle capacity attain understanding;

third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation; fourth, bestowing the prediction. Regarding the first section, there are again three parts. First, the request. Within this, first, he states his own lack of doubt.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret;
I have personally received from the Buddha’s own presence the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

From the passage where Śāriputra addressed the Buddha at that time, the second major section follows, consisting of the "Explanatory Discourse by Simile for Those of Middle Capacity," which comprises four chapters.

This first chapter is precisely the simile that reveals the One Vehicle by opening up the Three Vehicles; it clarifies the faith and understanding through which those of middle capacity attain liberation.
It describes the medicinal herbs, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and bestowal of the prophecy, and the definitive assurance—these four parts are all explained by means of similes.
The following four sections all explain, by means of causes and conditions, how Cūḍapanthaka understood the parable of the tied pearl;

they further cite the case of King Śūnyarāja receiving a prophecy, and provide an analogy for the Dharma-exposition, which should have included the joy of the fourfold assembly of middle-capacity followers, yet is absent here. This is due to two reasons: first, the scribe has omitted details for the sake of brevity;
second, the preceding and succeeding examples allow this to be known. The subsequent text is found in the "Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta" (Chapter on the Dharma Master), where a request is made.
The middle section is as described and can be understood from the text itself. △ Second, describing that others possess afflictions:

These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds formerly dwelt on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), and the Buddha constantly taught them, saying, "My Dharma can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
These individuals, both those still in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), each likewise [considered themselves] liberated.

Those who held views such as the view of a self, or views of existence and non-existence, thinking they had attained nirvana, now hear before the World-Honored One what they have never heard before and fall into doubt and confusion.

As for the others, because they were fellow practitioners who cherished old ties, it was necessary to request the fourfold assembly; this is the sphere of transformation, where a new movement is now set in motion.
Great Compassion universally entreats the Buddhas to constantly transform those who cling to the "three" of the past teachings;

yet now, before the World-Honored One, they cling to the "one" principle of the past. Because the former teaching of the "three" as ultimate and the current teaching of the "one" as true are contradictory, they fall into confusion;

thus it is said that all have fallen into doubt. Some say that Śāriputra [is new]... (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* regarding the transition from the three vehicles to the one vehicle. The final phrase "Shenzi xin" [Śāriputra is new] likely refers to a specific doctrinal point concerning the realization of the Great Vehicle by a disciple.)

Previously, there were two doubts concerning the twelve hundred [disciples], which were resolved; now there is only the "present doubt. To claim that those of superior capacity have few doubts while those of middling and inferior capacity have many is a mistaken interpretation.
△ Third, the universal request on behalf of the fourfold assembly.
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.

Excellent, World-Honored One! [The passage] "for the sake of the fourfold assembly below" is a general invitation; the "causes and conditions" therein refer to the causes and conditions of the three preceding and the one following.
△ Second, the response, which has two parts: first, the initiation; second, the initial suppression.

At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma through various causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means of speech, all for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
All that has been taught is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas."
Regarding "restraining and encouraging": restraining causes them to become indignant and courageous; encouraging causes them to advance swiftly.

When I previously did not speak of "the lower pointing to the upper" and "opening through provisional means," it was because all [provisional means] are for the sake of Bodhi; when I spoke of "pointing to the upper" and "revealing the real," it was because all [real teachings] are for the sake of transforming Bodhisattvas.
One should know that whether provisional or real, they all enter the Buddha-way of non-abiding Nirvana. This has already been clarified above.
To say, "How is it that you now cling to the teaching with such delusion and ignorance, failing to understand? and thus rebuke him—this is called "suppressing.
△ Second, the Citation:
"However, Śāriputra, I shall now further clarify this meaning by means of a parable; for those who possess wisdom, [it is understood] through a parable..."
This is an analogy for attaining understanding.

Now, Śāriputra, you should immediately accept this as a means of guidance and consolation; for since my previous censure was so severe, I feared that he might feel contemptuous resentment and sink into despair.
Thinking that I now permit him to clarify this meaning through an analogy, if he is able to understand it here—
This may be called wisdom. △ Second, the parable, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections:

first, opening the parable; second, applying the parable. The first section [opening the parable] also has two parts: first, a general parable of six elements; second, the specific parables. Regarding the first [the general parable], there are three points concerning the analogy of the elder:
first, his name and conduct.

Śāriputra, regarding the cities, towns, and villages, as for what is called the "opening analogy" and the "concluding analogy": the opening analogies differ from one another as already explained above. Now, there are two intentions:
first, the general; second, the specific. The general analogy refers to the two lines of verse in the chapter on Śākyamuni: "Now I am also thus."

The brief verse opens up the provisional to reveal the real. The specific analogy corresponds to the chapter on Śākyamuni, wherein the forty-one lines and a half of verse beginning with "With my Buddha-eye I behold" extensively expound upon opening the provisional to reveal the real. Within the six general analogies, there are six specific meanings:
first, the analogy of the elder represents "I," and this "I" refers to Śākyamuni, the master of one transformation [of the Buddha's life]. Second... [text continues].
1. The burning house is a metaphor for the aforementioned state of insecurity within the three realms (*tridhātu*), as opposed to the security of that higher abode.

2. The single gate is a metaphor for the aforementioned teaching of the Buddha-way. 3. The five hundred people are a metaphor for sentient beings. 4. The outbreak of fire is a metaphor for the aforementioned factors of insecurity:
the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) and the eight sufferings (*aṣṭau duḥkhāni*). 5. The thirty children are a metaphor for the aforementioned [sentient beings].
Regarding the knowledge of the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings—those who practice according to the three vehicles—there are three further meanings within the analogy of the elder:
namely, name, practice, and station; designation, virtue, and function. One should know that "name" is like a guest and "practice" is like a host.

Since practices have degrees of intimacy and names have degrees of distance, the location is cited to manifest the names and practices. Furthermore, when territories are demarcated to form a state, it is said:
The most distant domain of governance is the town; the central settlement is the neighborhood; and the closest is the immediate vicinity.
Because of his reputation as an elder, his conduct pervades these three areas: he does not see their petty flaws from nearby, yet from afar he admires only their lofty character.
His speech is free of censure, his actions are free of censure, and his mind is free of censure regarding the Dharma; thus his name and conduct correspond, making him a truly great man.

Within humans, this corresponds to the Tathāgata’s three karmas acting in accordance with wisdom; manifesting transformation according to the capacities of beings, his fame is universally heard and his virtue pervades the Dharma-realm.
Traditionally, the places where the compassion of the void of the ten directions reaches are called "kingdoms" (*rāṣṭra*);
a trichiliocosm is a "village" (*grāma*), a single four-continent world is a "hamlet" (*kheṭaka*), and a great trichiliocosm is a "kingdom."

The intermediate chiliocosm is the "village" (*grāma*) and the small chiliocosm is the "hamlet" (*sanniveśa*), but these designations are no longer used here. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 60, states: "The patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) is the hamlet;
the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the village; and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the city. This is a metaphor for cause and effect taken together.
In the present sutra, however, the metaphor is applied directly to the fruition-virtue; thus, the Land of Real Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*) is taken as the "kingdom."

There are other lands that serve as cities, while this land serves as a village; thus, from the fundamental [principle] one manifests traces, and by gathering these traces one returns to the fundamental—this is called the correspondence of practice and appearance, where there is no distinction between guest and host. It is brilliantly radiant and overflowing, pervading the three lands.
Furthermore, regarding "village" (*grāma*): Wei Zhao’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that a small district is called a "village," which is where people reside. (From the *Zuozhuan*)

The *Chuán* (Tradition) says it means "to gather"; the *Guǎngyá* (Extended Lexicon) says it means "a place of residence. Because it is where many people dwell together, it is called a "village" (*zhùluò*).

The *Nánshān* (Southern Mountain) school, citing the *Shísòng lǜ* (Ten Recitation Vinaya) and the *Duōlùn* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra), states that a gathering of many people constitutes a village. △ Second: The Designations of the Two [Categories].
There are three types of great elders:
first, the worldly elder; second, the supramundane elder; and third, the elder who contemplates the mind.
Regarding the worldly elder, he is endowed with ten virtues: first, a noble lineage; second, high status; third, great wealth; fourth... [and so forth].

Majestic and fierce, he possessed the five wisdoms; deeply venerating his elders for six years, he purified himself through the seven practices and was complete in the nine rites. Above, he received honor; below, he attracted devotion.
By lineage, he was a descendant of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors, belonging to a family where left and right were adorned with *diao* feathers.

In rank, he served as a counselor, a prime minister, a "salt-and-vinegar" statesman, or an "Ar-heng" regent. In wealth, he owned copper hills and golden valleys, abounding in luxury and splendor. In authority, he was formidable.

His dignity was so profound that he achieved gravity without formal severity; his wisdom was such that his breast was like a military arsenal, containing weapons of extraordinary and transcendent power.
In age, he was hoary and imposing, a figure whose appearance was described by all things. In conduct, he was as flawless as a white jade tablet, acting exactly as he spoke.
In ritual, his measured decorum provided a model for the world to gaze upon; above, he was revered by the Sovereign, and below, he was honored throughout the four seas.
One who possesses the ten virtues to which all return is called a Great Elder (*mahā-śreṣṭhin*). If this Great Elder is one who has transcended the world, he is the Buddha.

Born from the *tathatā* (suchness) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) throughout the three periods of time, his merit is perfected and his Way is manifest. He possesses the ten titles (*daśa-nāmadheya*) and the infinite [qualities];

the ten powers (*daśabala*), the myriad virtues, and the wealth of the Dharma are all fully complete. With the fierce prowess of the ten powers, he subdues Māra and restrains externalists; thus, through the single mind, the three wisdoms are realized.

Not having attained thorough penetration, it has been as long since his realization of perfect enlightenment; his three karmas move in accordance with wisdom without fail, and he possesses the majestic deportment of a Buddha.
His mind is as vast as the ocean, and he is praised by all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions. Those of the seven stages of expedient means come to rely upon him;
this is called the World-Transcending Buddha, the Great Elder. This is the long duration of the contemplation of the mind.
The wisdom that contemplates the mind arises from the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and is born into the lineage of the Buddha-family; its nature is truly authentic, and the three delusions do not arise.
Although one has not yet manifested the truth, this is precisely to be clothed in the Tathāgata’s robe and to be called the patience of quiescence (śānti-kṣānti).
The three truths contain all merits; the wisdom of correct contemplation subdues craving and views, while the Middle Way simultaneously illuminates both the provisional and the real.

It further clarifies that those who have long accumulated roots of goodness are able to cultivate this contemplation. Yet, this contemplation transcends the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).

If this contemplation observes the nature of the mind, it is called the "Supreme Samādhi" (*uttama-samādhi*); thus, the three karmas are free from transgression, and one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) remains unerring throughout all encounters with conditions and objects.
To be able to contemplate in this manner is termed the characteristic of profound faith and understanding; all Buddhas [attest to this].
Because those who uphold the Dharma are joyfully praised and venerated by the fourfold assembly of devas and nāgas, the subsequent text states:
"The Son of the Buddha abiding in this stage is himself a Buddha, [enjoying] walking, reciting, and sitting.
Since such a person is already called a Buddha, could they not also be named the Elder Who Contemplates the Mind? △ Third, the Merit of Action.
In his advanced years, his wealth was immeasurable, and he possessed many fields, houses, and servants. His virtues were twofold:

internal and external; internally, he possessed wisdom and strategy, while externally, he possessed material resources. One should know that being advanced in age means being broadly versed in both the present and the past, which is like the Buddha’s virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
Being advanced in years also means that one's faculties and resolve have reached full maturity, which is like the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Wealth is used as a general metaphor for immeasurable external virtues, while fields and houses serve as specific metaphors for the myriad virtues.

Fields can nourish one’s life; this metaphor represents meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) which relies upon wisdom (*prajñā*). Houses provide a place for the body to dwell; this metaphor represents the true realm (*bhūta-artha*) which serves as the locus for true wisdom.
Briefly stated, these are the eighteen gates of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*); extensively stated, they are the infinite gates of emptiness. If we discuss them...

If one discusses merit, there is no practice that is not cultivated; if one discusses wisdom, there is no object that is not illuminated. Therefore, it is said that he possesses many fields and houses.

As for "servants," these are those who provide attendance and carry out errands. This is a metaphor for the fact that his skillful means (*upāya*) and knowledge-and-vision (*jñāna-darśana*) are already fully perfected;
he blends his light with the six realms and adapts flexibly to myriad capacities—these are the servants of true wisdom. △ Two.
The analogy of the house: its house is vast.
That "its house is vast" is an analogy for the aforementioned security, which stands in contrast to insecurity; "insecurity" serves as the point of comparison.

The three realms are the nesting places of sentient beings; all beings dwell within these three realms. Because the Tathāgata, through his responsive transformations, presides over and makes them his home, they are said to be "vast and great.
△ This is the third: the analogy of the single gate.
There is only one gate.
"Only one gate" is a metaphor for the various Dharma-gates mentioned above that proclaim the Buddha-way; it refers to taking principle as the teaching and what is elucidated by it as the gate.
As the Sūtra says: "By means of the Buddha’s Dharma-gate, one exits the suffering of the triple world and attains [liberation]."
The realization of *nirvāṇa* is precisely what this refers to. Furthermore, there are two types of gates: first, the gate of the house; second, the gate of the vehicle.

"House" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); "gate" refers to the essential path for departure [from it]. This is the explanatory meaning of the provisional teachings. "Vehicle" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma;
"gate" refers to the explanatory meaning of the Perfect Teaching. △ Fourth, the analogy of the five hundred people.
A great multitude of people—hundreds, two hundred, or even five hundred—reside therein.
These five hundred people are likened to the superior sentient beings, namely the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). △ Fifth, the Parable of the Arising of Fire.
The halls and pavilions are dilapidated and old, the walls have collapsed, the bases of the pillars are rotten, and the beams and rafters are leaning and precarious;
all around, a fire suddenly breaks out at once, burning down the house and its dwellings.
The analogy of the halls and pavilions below refers to the state of security above, while the "unsecure dharmas" correspond to the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*). First, that which emerges...
The burning of the house is used as a metaphor for the retributive fruits of the six realms; next, the fire that burns it is clarified as a metaphor for the eight sufferings and the five turbidities.

The hall represents the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the upper stories represent the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), the walls represent the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), their crumbling represents decline and loss, and their tilting and peril represent shifting transformations.
The foundations of the pillars represent life-force (*jīvitendriya*), and the beams and rafters represent consciousness (*vijñāna*) decaying.
Defeat is like being in peril; it will not last long. To make this easier to understand, I shall provide another explanation through visualization:

the hall represents the lower part of the body, the pavilion represents the upper part such as the head, the walls represent the skin and flesh, their crumbling represents senility, the bases of the pillars represent the two feet, their rot represents impermanence, the beams and rafters represent the spinal vertebrae, and their tilting and collapse represent the arrival of the great end.
The "obstructive and tortuous" refers to the small and large intestines; it is also said to refer to the mind, and so forth. The passage below on "surrounding" clarifies the fire that burns:
because these eight sufferings pervade the four great elements and the four modes of birth, they are said to be "surrounding.

Because all are equally impermanent, they are said to arise "simultaneously and suddenly," which serves as a metaphor for that which was originally non-existent now coming into being. This is precisely because this suffering was originally absent, yet arises due to...
Existence [arises] because of ignorance. △ Sixth, the Parable of the Thirty Sons:
Suppose a householder has ten, twenty, or even thirty sons within this house.
This parable of the "householder's sons" from below illustrates the aforementioned passage concerning the knowledge of the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings.
If one studies the Buddha-dharma with a natural affinity, the principle of being a "son" is established; however, their dispositions and desires differ.
For instance, ten may be sons of Bodhisattvas, while twenty or thirty may be sons of the Two Vehicles.
Because these capacities all succeed in leaving the house, they are called "sons. Those who lack such capacity are the five hundred people. The term "perhaps" (or "some") refers to...
The appearance and disappearance of these Pratyekabuddhas differ; some are subsumed under the Hīnayāna and others under the Madhyayāna.

All are said to possess "ten" because they all inherently possess the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). It is as if it were said that while the internal nature of wisdom exists, there is merely a lack of the nature of "knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
△ Second, the specific analogies for the four [stages]; first, the analogy of seeing fire; first, clarifying the capacity to see.
The elder sees it.
Just as the elder sees this sign emerging, which serves as an analogy for my seeing with the Buddha-eye above.
△ Second, clarifying what is seen.
This great fire breaks out from all four sides.
This illustration clarifies what was seen above: the sentient beings within the six realms of existence. △ Third, the manifestation of alarm and fear:
they are struck with great terror and think to themselves, "Although I am able to reach safety through this gate that is being consumed by flames..."
"Emerging" and being "greatly startled and terrified" is a metaphor for the aforementioned arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of these sentient beings.

One is startled by the thought of their retreating from the Great Good, and terrified by the concern that they will give rise to grave evil; this is precisely the counterpart to loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
That which is without joy or fear corresponds to compassion (*karuṇā*) and sorrow (*śoka*).
As for the statement, "Although I am able to emerge safely from this gate that is being consumed by fire," this establishes the meaning of the alarm and compassion.

The phrase "although I am" (*yady api*) is a term indicating that [the capacity] is not yet fully exhausted; this clarifies that the Buddha, through the power of wisdom, is able to seek out the authentic teaching and perceive what is to be seen.

Because the realization of the Truths is not endangered by the five turbidities or the eight sufferings, it is called "peaceful. Because it cannot be moved by the violent winds of the four inversions, it is called "hidden.
Because it is serene and beyond all burdens, it is called "attaining liberation. Sentient beings are not like this; they are burned by the fire [of afflictions].
Because the Tathāgata’s compassion is likewise burned by the fire of sorrow, it is said that [the Buddha] is also [subject to it]. As the Sūtra says: "That which..."

One who burns away the "gate" (mukha) should know that the gate consists of both the provisional (prajñapti) and the empty (śūnya). Without the provisional, there would be no means to mark the gate; without the empty, there would be no means to penetrate through it.
The provisional may be reduced to ashes, but the empty cannot be burned. In the teaching, there is the distinction between the expressive (vācaka) and the expressed (vācya):
if there were no expression and discernment, there could be no teaching; if there were nothing expressed, how could one emerge [from bondage]?
Thus we know that while the means of expression (the *vyañjana*) may be impermanent, that which is expressed (the *artha*) is not impermanent;
it is because one attains that which is expressed through the teaching that one is called "securely emerged.

Because the means of expression is subject to decay, it is said that "the doors of burning" do not emerge from the "doors of burning"—how else could one be securely emerged? This, then, relies upon the verbal teaching to accord with [reality].
Regarding the referent (*abhidheya*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is permanent. This is precisely its meaning; one should understand it thus.
If it is the teaching of impermanence of the Hīnayāna, this emerges from the perspective of that which is burned.

If it is the teaching of eternal abiding of the Mahāyāna, the very words are liberation; this teaching is the principle-body (*dharmatā-kāya*), wherein one realizes that there is neither burning nor non-burning.
Thus, one emerges safely; if one proceeds according to the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it is as if emerging from the door of what is being burned;
if one proceeds according to the essence of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), one emerges safely from within that which is being burned.

Therefore, the meaning is this: one first uses a cloth basket or a small table to bring [the child] out, rather than later attempting to bring him out by means of impermanence. △ Fourth, expanding upon what was previously seen.
Yet those sons, within the burning house, were so attached to their play and merriment that they were neither aware nor cognizant of it;

they were neither startled nor terrified as the fire approached and assailed their bodies, and though the pain was cutting to the quick, their hearts felt no aversion or distress, nor did they have any intention to seek escape.
The phrase "the sons within the burning house" refers extensively to the second type of fire previously observed;
this further explains the meaning of being terrified. One should know that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena constitute the four sides of the house;
from these four sides arise the fires of the four inversions—such as regarding the impure as pure—and the eight types of suffering, whereby all sufferings [arise].
If one realizes that the body is impure, suffering, and impermanent, then the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*) will be extinguished. Those who delight in play and sport:
attachment to views is called "play" (*hī*), while attachment to craving is called "sport" (*khi*). Furthermore, being addicted to the four views is "play," and to squander one's merit is "sport.
Attachment to craving is likewise so named. Furthermore, being addicted to the five sense objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) is "play," while being empty-handed and gaining nothing is "sport."
It is like children playing with fire who, though they die, feel no sense of weary detachment; being neither aware nor cognizant, they do not say at all that there is fire.
To say one is "unaware" means one does not understand that fire is a phenomenon of heat;

to say one "does not know" means that because one does not know fire is hot, one does not fear injury to the body, does not startle at the prospect of losing life, and thus has no dread. You should know this.

Sentient beings are entirely unaware of the five aggregates and the eight sufferings; they do not know the four inversions or the three poisons. Since they do not recognize delusion, how could they have anxiety?
One must know that delusion invades the *dharmakāya* and harms the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).

Thus, they are unaware of suffering (*duḥkha*) and ignorant of its origin (*samudaya*); they are not startled by the injury to the Path (*mārga*), nor do they fear the loss of cessation (*nirodha*). This is because they have not heard the Four [Noble Truths].
Regarding the teaching on the truths (*satya*), one lacks the name "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) because one does not awaken to them and does not attain them;

furthermore, one lacks the name "wisdom derived from reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) because one does not know them, and lacks the name "understanding through vision" because one does not awaken to them and does not attain understanding through reflection.

One awakens with shock upon seeing the truths, and feels weary and terrified upon reflecting on them. Moreover, because one does not awaken to present suffering and does not know future suffering, the subsequent passage states:

This refers precisely to the meaning that one currently undergoes manifold sufferings and subsequently undergoes the sufferings of the hells and so forth. "Fire coming to press upon the body" refers to the five consciousnesses;
"the mind" refers to the mental consciousness, the sovereign of the mind (*citta-rāja*). Thus, while the body is pressed by the eight kinds of suffering, the mind does not feel weary or distressed.

Here, the burning house is fundamentally a metaphor for the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); "playing" is a metaphor for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and "sporting" is a metaphor for the [turbidity of] afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The afflictions of delusion and turbidity—being without awareness, without knowledge, and without alarm or fear—are like the *sattva-kaṣāya* (affliction of sentient beings).

The fire coming to press upon the body, with its pain cutting to the very core, is like the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (affliction of lifespan). The mind feeling no weariness or distress and lacking the intent to seek liberation is like the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (affliction of the eon).
II. The Analogy of Abandoning the Bench to Use the Cart. Part One: The Analogy of Abandoning the Bench. Sub-part One: The Door of Exhortation. Section One: The Appropriate Application.
Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: "My own hands and body possess strength;
I shall carry him out from the house using my lap or a small table.

To say that he set aside the table and used a carriage is a metaphor for the superior [practice] being large and the inferior being small; one should know that the preceding six lines and a half clarify this.
The first eleven lines clarify that the "great provisional application" (da-yi) does not succeed, while the latter eleven lines clarify that the "small provisional application" (xiao-yi) succeeds.

Regarding the former failure, there are three points: first, the great provisional application is applied; second, there is no receptive capacity (ji); third, the transformation is ceased. Now, the analogy is divided into two parts:

first, the provisional application using the gate of exhortation (quan-men); second, the provisional application using the gate of admonition (jie-men). Within each of these two gates—exhortation and admonition—there are three points, the first of which is the provisional application itself.
It is appropriate to [accept] two and not to accept three; thus, one relinquishes the first. Regarding the three gates of exhortation:

first, following the Elder, one reflects that "the hands and body possess strength" (from below, this illustrates the above reflection on employing great transformation). During the twenty-one days, one reflects upon such matters as the hands and body.
This refers to citing the passage from below to harmonize with the illustration, stating: "But by means of spiritual power and wisdom..."

The power serves to explain this analogy: the body represents supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), while the shoulders represent wisdom (*prajñā*). The lifting and supporting represent the extraction [of beings from suffering].

Based on the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are supernormal powers; based on the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna*) through wisdom, there is the preaching of the Dharma.

By the power of wisdom and abandonment, one is able to accomplish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This wisdom and abandonment, in turn, enter through the two gates of exhortation and admonition. One should...

Knowing that "exhortation" (*kuan*) constitutes the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals) and "admonition" (*jiei*) constitutes the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment), these two *siddhāntas* serve as skillful means (*upāya*) for the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth). Why is this so?

Because when the Tathāgata first intended to employ the gate of exhortation to adapt to sentient beings, he caused them to practice all manner of good deeds, thereby bringing to fulfillment the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Because sentient beings could not endure it, he next intended to use the gate of admonition to suit their capacities, demonstrating Great Nirvana through the principle that "all evils should not be committed.
Since sentient beings could not endure this either, there was no spiritual affinity (*avakāśa*) and his transformative activity ceased.

Thus we know that the application of mindfulness in the Mahayana consists merely of the two *siddhāntas* of exhortation and admonition, which are nothing other than supernatural powers, wisdom, and the abandonment [of afflictions]. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom."
To deliver sentient beings by means of this is precisely its meaning. The previous praise of the elder for being advanced in years is a metaphor for wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*);

wisdom and severance are themselves the strength of his body and hands. Regarding the "cloth basket" (*yīkè*) and the "small table," the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that the cloth basket is a foreign vessel used for holding flowers, employed to store them when presenting offerings to persons of high rank. This has been the usage since ancient times.
The "cloud-garment" (yīdì) is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna cause, and the "desk" (jìyuàn) is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna fruit;

this means that initially, when one attempts to present the Mahāyāna cause and fruit, there is no receptive capacity [in the listeners]. An old commentary further states that these objects are metaphors for the Mahāyāna precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Now, let us explain them by correlating them with the text of the parable itself. As it says: "If I were to merely use the power of my supernatural abilities and the power of my wisdom to praise the Tathāgata..."

Regarding the power of knowledge and vision and the fearlessnesses: one should know that when sentient beings cannot be liberated by these [powers], the supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) is the body and the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*) is the hand;
the meaning is as previously explained. Knowledge and vision are likened to a garment or a basket, fearlessness is likened to a staff, and the ten powers are likened to the handle.
It is because the Tathāgata employs these three dharmas through his supernormal powers (*abhijñā-bala*) and wisdom.

The Wisdom [of the Buddha] proclaims that these three dharmas lack the capacity [for ordinary beings], and thus cease their transformative activity; terms such as "robe-satchel" (*kaṭhina*) or "table" are used merely to distinguish between the three modes of exposition—concise, intermediate, and extensive.
The concise exposition is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision: "knowledge" refers to the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience), and "vision" refers to the Buddha-eye.
The names are concise while the meanings are profound, like a robe-satchel which, though having only one opening, contains much within; this is the intermediate exposition.
These are named the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). In their essence, they correspond to the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), like a small table;

thus, they are somewhat broad regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and provide a modest degree of security for sentient beings. Alternatively, when explained extensively, they are called the ten powers (*daśabala*).

These encompass all things both horizontally and vertically, like a desk with many legs that cannot be overturned; thus, they are even more extensive regarding phenomena and provide great security for sentient beings during the three weeks [following enlightenment].

At midday, he contemplated that he wished to compose such extensive and abbreviated teachings on the Buddha-dharma, but because sentient beings were unable to bear them, he spoke of the "sleeve-bag" and the "writing desk. △ Second, the refusal to accept.
He further reflected that this house had only a single door, which was moreover narrow and small, while the children were young and lacked discernment,
being attached to their playthings. Second,

he further reflected on the lower part [of the parable] to clarify that the children did not accept [the offer], which serves as an analogy for the aforementioned lack of spiritual capacity (*anvaya*), as it is said of sentient beings:

How can those with dull faculties be delivered? There is but a single gate, and moreover, it is narrow. The meaning of the "gate" is as explained above; now I shall further clarify its general and specific aspects.
Regarding the specific: "one" refers to the one principle and the one path; "pure gate" refers to the correct teaching; "general" refers to that which is universally applicable;

and "small" means it does not admit of the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, nor does it encompass the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*) and so forth. This should be understood.

The doctrine and principle are vast and extensive, not narrow; yet because sentient beings are unable to communicate with them through these principles and teachings, they are said to be "narrow" on account of their lack of capacity.
Furthermore, "penetrating" refers to the purity of the principle without admixture, hence it is called "one";
because this principle can penetrate all things, it is called a "gate"; and because it is subtle and difficult to know, it is called "narrow. Moreover, as for the "teachings," there are ten...
When one seeks with true discernment, there is no other vehicle; because there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, it is called "One. Because this teaching can lead one through, it is called a "Gate.

This teaching is subtle and wondrous, such that ordinary people do not know its point of departure—this is their ignorance of the provisional—and they do not know its point of entry—this is their ignorance of the real.
Those of the Two Vehicles, having heard [the teaching], gain a slight knowledge of the essential means of departure, yet they never know how to enter into Bodhi.

Although Śāriputra knew he was emerging [from the Lesser Vehicle], he did not know how to enter it; nor did those who had attained the seven stages of expedient means (saptavidha-upāya) know how to enter or emerge from it.
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "If I were to praise the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to understand it through their own instruction.

This speaks of the lack of capacity [for the Great Vehicle], hence describing it as "narrow and small. Furthermore, the practitioner’s perfect cause consists of practicing the Great [Vehicle] directly for oneself.
Because the Way is free from obstacles, it is called "One"; because the Bodhisattva’s path of good conduct leads straight to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), it is called a "Gate.
Because its wondrous practices, difficult deeds, and skillful means are beyond the reach of those without capacity, they are said to be "narrow and small.
You sons, who are young and immature and have not yet attained any realization, should know that you were taught the Unsurpassed Way by twenty thousand Buddhas through the Mahāyāna.
Weakness of the roots of goodness is called "infancy"; if, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, one is able to give rise to slander and disparagement, this is called "not yet having any discernment.
The former [passage] clarifies that goodness is weak, while this clarifies that evil is strong;

this means that at the time of the cause, there is deep attachment to views and craving, and at the time of the fruit, there is deep attachment to the primary and secondary [elements]. Thus, those in the Desire Realm are attached to the six sense objects, while those in the Form Realm are attached to...
The "flavor of dhyāna" refers to being attached to formless concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*). As stated in the preceding text: "The faculties of sentient beings are dull;
blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, they are incapable of hearing the Mahāyāna. △ Third, relinquishment.
Or they may fall and be consumed by fire.
From "Or they may fall and be consumed by fire" onwards is the analogy for relinquishing skillful guidance;
it refers to the cessation of transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity, as expressed in the passage: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana. Or.
Regarding those who fall, there are two meanings to their falling: first, because the immature remember their former playgrounds, they fall;
furthermore, because they lack all discernment and their grasp of things is not firm, they fall—this is like being attached to the five desires and falling into the three miserable realms.
Second, because their goodness is weak and they lack discernment, they slander the Mahāyāna and fall into the three miserable realms. △
Second, the section on the admonition, which has three parts.
First, the preliminary intention: "I shall now speak of matters that cause fear; this house is already burning, you must quickly depart at once so that you are not consumed by the fire.
Having formed this thought, he informs his sons in accordance with what he has considered: "All of you, come out quickly!"
This gate of admonition is also called the gate of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), and it likewise possesses three meanings: namely, "preparing for suitability" and so forth.

First, preparing for suitability as a counteractive measure means admonishing through fear to bring about the characteristics of its counteraction. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it says:

"The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the Mahāyāna because they are ungraspable (*anupalabdha*); thus they differ from the Hīnayāna. Since [the practitioner] has already become attached...
Because it is a place of play, he speaks of terrifying matters so that one may escape being burned by the fires of the five turbidities within the house of the five aggregates;

one ought to abandon and depart from it, for if one dwells and clings to it for long, one will surely sever one's roots of goodness. Thus it is said: "Do not let yourself be burned and harmed by the fire."
2. They did not accept it.
Although their father, out of compassion, enticed them with kind words and gentle persuasion, the sons were so attached to their play that they refused to believe or accept his words;
they felt neither alarm nor fear, had no intention of escaping, and furthermore, they did not know what fire was or what the house was.
What constitutes a failure?

Although the father feels compassion, the son does not accept his admonitions; he is neither startled nor afraid—meaning he does not give rise to hearing or reflection as previously described—and thus fails to recognize the eight sufferings and the five turbidities that can burn away the roots of goodness, just like one who lacks knowledge.
Fire does not recognize the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, which are the vessels of all suffering;
it is like failing to recognize one's house and thus not knowing the cause of the loss of the Dharma-body, as if not knowing what it is that has been lost. △ Third, relinquishment.
"Only running back and forth in play while looking at his father"—these two phrases refer to the words "abandoning suffering.

One should know that turning one's back on light and heading toward darkness is like the rapid coming and going of birth and death, which is as swift as galloping. Among these, [the former] refers to this.

The arising of views and attachments is like a play; although one may employ great [means] to counteract them, because they do not follow the Great Teaching, it is said that one merely regards them as a father.
△ Second, the analogy of the chariots, in four parts: first, the analogy of the three chariots appropriate for the occasion.
At that time, the elder had this thought: "This house has already been consumed by a great fire;
if I and my sons do not exit immediately, we will surely be burned to death. I must now devise a skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity."
This uses the parable of the chariots to illustrate the aforementioned eleven verses on "recalling the past Buddhas' power of skillful means.

There are four sections in the preceding text, and now there are likewise four parables: first, the parable of preparing the three chariots, which illustrates that the past Buddhas also performed transformations through the three vehicles;
one must understand that the merit of the Mahāyāna transformation constitutes the father’s life-force.
Sentient beings take great goodness as their child's life; if that great goodness is exhausted, the child's life is severed.

When the child's life is severed, the merit of transformation is also nullified, which is equivalent to the father's own life being severed. As stated previously, even when suffering is acute and cuts to the very core, one has not yet died;

yet now it is said that one will certainly be consumed by fire, which carries the meaning of death. One may ask: in the preceding passage, it was said that one finds peace and security within the gate of what is burned.
It is said: "If one does not emerge at the proper time, one will surely be consumed by fire. What is the meaning of this? Answer:

The "emerging" mentioned previously refers to the emergence of the *dharmakāya*. The present statement, "if one does not emerge at the proper time," refers merely to the *nirmāṇakāya* manifesting in accordance with illness.
One should know that when sentient beings possess goodness, the *nirmāṇakāya* emerges at the proper time; if sentient beings lack goodness... [the Buddha does not appear].
If one were to sever [the connection] so that it does not emerge at the proper time for the *nirmāṇakāya*, then both would be consumed by fire.
Now, wishing to manifest the *nirmāṇakāya* in a manner appropriate to the occasion, I shall employ skillful means; from here below, he intends to explain the provisional [teachings].
△ Second, the parable of knowing the sons' former thoughts.
The father knows that each of his sons has their own particular inclinations for various rare treasures and extraordinary objects to which they are surely attached.
Second, the father, knowing their prior inclinations and preferences, reflects upon them in this way while the Buddhas of the ten directions [are present].

"All appear" clarifies that there exists the capacity for beings to attain deliverance. That they once practiced the Small Vehicle in the past shows that their prior mental dispositions and sexual natures differ;

this shows that each has their own preferences. Furthermore, it is known that sentient beings once practiced the Great Vehicle, yet their practice of the Great was not yet deep—this constitutes being "weak in the Great. Because they weary of old age, sickness, and death, they are approached through the Small; this is [the reason].
The "small strong one" refers to the sixth mind among the six minds in which Śāriputra regressed from the Great [Vehicle]. The "six minds" refer to the sixth mind within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It is because he had previously practiced the name "Great" that he recognized the weariness with old age and death within his former mind; thus, each has their own preference.
△ Third, the praise of the rarity of the three vehicles, illustrated by a parable, has three parts; first, the exhortation to turn [the wheel].
And he addressed them, saying: "These toys for which you have such delight are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later.
Third, he praised the rarity of the three vehicles as a parable, comparing it to the aforementioned actual bestowal of the three vehicles. Having reflected upon this matter, [he spoke].
This refers to proceeding to Vārāṇasī, which has three intended meanings: namely, exhortation, demonstration, and realization. From the passage "From rare and precious playthings...
onwards is the exhortation to turn [the wheel]. △ Second, the demonstration of the turning [of the wheel].
"Such various kinds of goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate for you to play with.
This is the turning of the teaching through demonstration (deśanā-vivarta).
△ Third, the turning of the realization (sākṣātkriyā-vivarta): "You should all quickly come out from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."
This is the realization of the transformation. △ Fourth, the parable of satisfying the sons' wishes:
At that time, the sons, hearing their father speak of rare and precious playthings that suited their desires, each felt their hearts bristle with vigor;
they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to be the first to flee from the burning house.

The fourth is that which accords with the wishes of the sons [of the Buddha], illustrated by the analogy of receiving, practicing, and awakening to the supreme [teaching]; this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma.
The previous verse was brief, while the present illustration is extensive; it extensively clarifies the cultivation of causes leading to the fruit based on an explanation of six phrases.

Regarding "accords with wishes," this refers to the compatibility between the capacity [of the disciple] and the teaching, which is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Regarding "courageous and sharp," this refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

"Stirring the mind" (*donglü*) refers to the skillful means of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Mutually pushing and displacing" (*xiāng hù tuī pái*) means to investigate the four noble truths and to suppress and subdue the afflictions of wrong views;

because right and wrong have not yet been definitively resolved, this is termed "mutual. This stage belongs to the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and pertains to the levels of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit).
"Competing" (*jìng*) means competing to grasp the superior principle; this refers to the initial contemplation of the thirty-two aspects of the Truths during the stage of *kṣānti* (Patience).
"Competing for the true path" refers to the subsequent stage of observing the dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Commonality" means that at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one observes the same single truth, and thus there is no difference from the fourfold observation of the dharma-patience regarding suffering.

"Rushing forward" refers to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and swiftly perceiving the principle within fifteen moments of mind; this is analogous to the sound of Nirvana being heard immediately above [the stage of Supreme Mundane Dharmas] within the Path of Seeing.

"Attaining Nirvana" refers to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which strives for deliverance. "Striving to exit the Triple World" means achieving the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) and exhausting the delusions of thought;
only then does one emerge from the burning house. This corresponds to the aforementioned verse and the distinct designations of the Dharma and Sangha of the Arhat.
Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: it is the Middle Way’s correct contemplation that directly perceives the true reality (*tathatā*) of the mind-dharmas.

"Corresponding" means that because the objects of one's aspirations are boundless, the contemplation is likewise boundless; this is called "courageous. To investigate the objects with a sharp mind is called "keen";

the mutual investigation of the characteristics of objects is called "mutual pushing and shoving. The rapidity with which the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) engage their objects is called "racing together";
traversing all aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) such that none are not the true nature (*dharmatā*) is called "pervasive."

This is for the purpose of exiting the burning house. △ Third, the analogy of the bestowal of the great carts, in four parts: First, the analogy of the elder’s joy upon seeing his children escape the calamity.
At that time, the elder saw that all his children had safely emerged and were gathered together in an open space at the crossroads.
Sitting there, he was free from all obstacles; his mind was serene, and he leaped for joy with great delight.
This section of the parable—the analogy of the father bestowing great chariots upon his sons—illustrates the aforementioned true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
This passage consists of four parts: first, the analogy of the father’s joy at seeing his sons escape danger, which corresponds to the aforementioned thought: "I then had this thought."
Therefore, from the time I appeared in the world until now, I have delighted in taking two lines and one phrase of a verse as the basis [for my teaching].
Second, the parable of the sons seeking carts illustrates the arousal of the potential for the Great Vehicle;
those whom I see as my children, who aspire to seek the Buddha-way, all come to the Buddha’s presence with a heart of reverence, taking these two lines of verse as their basis. Third...

The analogy of bestowing great chariots upon the sons illustrates the passage above concerning how, among all bodhisattvas, [the Buddha] directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path;

this is based on the three-line verse. The analogy of the sons receiving the chariots and rejoicing illustrates the passage above where bodhisattvas, hearing this Dharma, have all cleared away the net of doubt;
this is based on "one practice. Furthermore, this refers to the section on the teaching of the Dharma within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
First, the arousal of the capacity (*indriya*) is clarified; next, the removal of obstacles and the Buddha’s joy and fearlessness are explained.
Now, within the analogy, first the avoidance of calamity is clarified, followed by the seeking of the vehicle. If discussed exhaustively, there should be four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1.

There are those for whom obstacles are removed first and the capacity is aroused later, such as the four great *śrāvakas* who were in the *Tripiṭaka* [period] when their obstacles were removed at the end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Dharma.

The "flower" refers to the initial arousal of the great capacity; the fact that the two obstacles have not yet been removed while the Mahāyāna capacity has been aroused is as seen in the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where various ordinary beings attain entry into the Buddha-wisdom. The remaining two phrases are as explained above.

If the great capacity is first activated and the obstacles are subsequently removed, it is as described in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*). If the obstacles are first removed and the capacity follows, [it is as follows...]
The "expedient movement" (*upāya-kauśalya*) is as previously explained; through the mutual manifestation of the removal of obstacles and the expedient movement, they together form a single intent.
Furthermore, while the "Chapter on Expedients" clarifies the Buddha’s joy and fearlessness, this section clarifies the joy of the sons; because the sons rejoice, the father also rejoices.
This, too, is a mutual manifestation that together forms a single intent. Within the context of escaping danger, both [joy and fearlessness] are fully present.
The meaning is as follows: "Delighting in being free from calamity" refers to a father’s anxiety when his son has not yet escaped danger;

once he is freed from the fire, the father’s mind becomes serene. Thus, delighting in being free from calamity serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s joy, because when the son rejoices, the father likewise rejoices.
Regarding the phrase "at the crossroads," this thoroughfare is the direct path.

For example, the Four Noble Truths are like a crossroads because they are viewed differently through their four aspects; yet the Four Truths converge as one when the truths are realized, just like the junction of roads.
If the delusions of view have been eliminated but the delusions of cultivation still remain, it is not called "the open ground.

Only when the delusions of cultivation within the three realms are exhausted is it called "dwelling on the open ground. Because one abides in the fruit and does not advance further, it is said that one "sits" there. It is not for the sake of [further] action.

Because they were constrained by [the delusions of] views and thoughts, it is said they were "at ease"; because they gave rise to the perception of extinction and the perception of peace, it is said they were "joyful.
△ Second, the parable of the sons requesting the vehicles:
At that time, each of the sons addressed their father, saying, "Father, regarding the playthings you previously promised us—the goat-drawn carts and the deer-drawn carts—"
"Please grant us the ox-carts.
Regarding the expression "seeking the carts," the text says, "We pray that you grant us the three kinds of precious carts.

Although the word "seek" (*suo*) does not appear in the text, its meaning is evident from this phrasing of the request; it is based on this that some say the followers of the two vehicles seek the carts.

The Bodhisattvas do not seek [the fruit]; this is the first of the ten difficulties. It says that while the followers of the Two Vehicles go outside the triple world to the place where the chariots are promised and there seek the chariots of the fruit, why does the Bodhisattva suddenly seek the chariot before even reaching that promised place? ... And so it continues until the tenth difficulty, which says:
