Do not preach it to worldlings of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires, for they would be unable to comprehend it upon hearing it. Do not preach it to them either.
These thirty-six lines and a half clarify that if one employs the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one must not speak of it to evil persons;
for if one first draws in the wicked, they will inevitably give rise to malicious slander and incur evil retributions. Therefore, great compassion should not be explained to them.

Within this, there are two intentions: first, to clarify that by slandering the sutra, one falls into the evil realms; second, from the words "In such a manner... onwards, to clarify [the consequences].
Because they fall into the evil realms, they do not encounter a Buddha. Since this section of the sūtra is lengthy, the commentaries have been brief;
although the divisions (*kośa*) therein exist, they are not fully detailed. I shall now cite the preceding sūtra text and divide it segment by segment.
By doing so, the underlying intent will become clear, and subsequent passages may be understood accordingly. First, from "Furthermore, having abandoned... [and so forth].
Ānanda, having incurred such offenses as these, the initial intention is clarified within this passage through four points.
First, for two lines, it clarifies that one should not insist on preaching because of great compassion. Second, it clarifies that if one slanders [the teaching], one will fall into hell.
If a person does not believe in this sutra and slanders it, they sever the seeds of the Buddha for all the world;

or if they frown and harbor doubts, you should hear of the retribution for such a person's sins. Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, if there are those who slander such a sutra as this, or who look with contempt, hatred, and jealousy upon those who read, recite, copy, or uphold it—[their retribution shall be as follows].
Yet harboring resentment toward this person, you shall now hear of their karmic retribution: at the end of their life, they enter the Avīci Hell for a full kalpa;
when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas.

Next, regarding those who do not believe in the cessation [of afflictions] up until the point of innumerable kalpas, the *Sūtra on Falling into Hell* states that those who sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world do so because Vimalakīrti regards afflictions as the seeds of the Tathāgata; this refers to the nature of the objective realm (*ālambana*).

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is taught that one studies the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) through prajñā; this refers to the nature of the causal condition (*nimitta-hetu*) for the seeds of the Buddha.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the principle of the mind-nature (*cittaprakṛti*) is taken as the uninterrupted true cause for Buddhahood;

here, in this sutra, even minor good deeds are clarified as leading to Buddhahood, taking the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) as the seed of Buddhahood. To disbelieve that minor good deeds lead to Buddhahood is to sever all worldly seeds of Buddhahood.
Regarding what is called "nature" (*prakṛti*), there are five types, the first being the true cause nature (*tathatā-hetu-prakṛti*).
Second is the nature of the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), and third is the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Upon these three, two further types are added:

some say the nature of the objective field (*viṣaya-hetu*) and the nature of the fruit (*phala-hetu*); others say the nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-the-fruit (*phalānuphala-hetu*);

still others say the nature of the cause (*hetu-hetu*) and the nature of the cause-of-the-cause (*hetuhetu-hetu*). To explain their meaning: the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) is called the nature of the revealing cause; it is immeasurable.
Merit is termed the nature of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Within all phenomena, the presence of the nature of peace and bliss is termed the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*).

Good and evil deeds, being distinct, are termed the nature of the objective field (*viṣaya-hetu*). When discussed solely in terms of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), it is termed the nature of the fruit (*phala-hetu*); when discussed concurrently with the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and *nirvāṇa*, it is termed the nature of the fruit of fruits (*phalaphala-hetu*). When discussed solely in terms of the objective realm of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), it is termed the nature of the cause (*hetu-hetu*); [when discussed concurrently with its cessation, it is termed the nature of the fruit].
Regarding the wisdom that contemplates by way of causes and conditions, it is termed the "nature of the cause of causes. Although there are various explanations, the number reaches five.
If one treats it as the nature of the object (*ālambana-svabhāva*), then the "nature of the fruit of fruits" (*phala-phala-svabhāva*) is subsumed within the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*).

If one opens up the nature of the fruit of fruits, then the nature of the object is subsumed within the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*); and the nature of the cause (*hetu-svabhāva*) and the nature of the cause of causes are likewise subsumed. As for those...
The nature of cause is subsumed under the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the nature of causal condition is subsumed under the contributing cause (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is because the text clarifies that the Buddha’s various manifestations are themselves his very nature. If this meaning is further applied, it may also be explained in five sections.
Regarding "frowning": it means the eyebrows do not spread. △ Third, falling into the animal realm.
Upon emerging from hell, one shall fall among the animals—such as dogs or jackals—with a body that is emaciated, dark, and covered in scabies and sores;

it will be tormented by the touch of others and held in contempt and disdain by people. Constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, with flesh and bones withered away, one undergoes agonizing suffering while alive and is pelted with tiles and stones at death.
Because one has severed the lineage of the Buddha, one receives this retribution for one's sins; or, one may become a camel.
Or they may be born among donkeys, their bodies constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to the lash of whips; they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.

Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these: they become jackals that enter villages, their bodies covered in scabies and sores, and being blind in one eye, they are beaten and pelted by children, enduring various pains and sometimes meeting death.
Having died there, they will further receive the body of a python, its form vast and great, five hundred yojanas in length;

deaf, dull-witted, and footless, it crawls on its belly and is devoured by small insects; day and night it undergoes suffering without respite, for having slandered this sutra, such is the retribution incurred.
Third, having emerged from hell, they stop and receive such retribution as this: it is clearly explained that they fall among the animals.

"Emaciated" means their physical forms are withered and their hair and fur are thin and sparse. "Tawny and dark" means their facial features are blackened. "Dying under tiles and stones" means being covered and buried;
since they lack coffins or outer shrouds to conceal their bodies, all that remains to cover them are tiles and stones. [They become] camels.
Regarding this, Guo Pu said: "The sun travels three hundred li per day and can carry a thousand *qian*.
The 'veins of all waters' refers to water gushing forth when the ground is trampled by feet. As for the *mang* (python), the *Erya* calls it the 'King Snake';

it is essentially the leader of the various snakes. 'Deaf and stupid' means dull-witted and foolish. 'Winding and turning'—*wan* here means to unfold or stretch out. 'Sucking, eating, boring, and biting'. △ Four.
They fall among the lowly.
Even if they obtain human birth, their faculties will be dull and dark; they will be short, ugly, hunchbacked, lame, blind, or deaf.
Whatever they say, people will not believe or accept; their breath will always be foul-smelling; they will be possessed by malevolent spirits; and they will be poor, lowly, and servile to others.
Afflicted by many ailments and emaciated, they have no one to rely upon; though they seek the company of others, no one pays them any heed.
Whatever they may acquire, they soon lose again. If they practice medicine and treat illnesses according to the prescriptions, it only increases the patient's malady or even causes death.
If they themselves fall ill, there is no one to provide relief; even if they take excellent medicines, their condition only worsens. If others commit acts of rebellion...
4. If one is born as a human, one merely avoids meeting with such untimely calamities;
it is clarified that one falls among the lowly and base—those who are stunted, deformed, hunchbacked, or lame. "Stunted" (*kūṇa*) refers to a body that is short and small;

"lame" (*paṅgu*) refers to hands and feet that do not extend fully; "hunchbacked" (*kubja*) refers to a curved spine, like that of one carrying a load while walking. "Consumptive" (*kṣaya*)... [text fragment].
"Emaciated" refers to the disease of thirst; furthermore, "xiāo" (emaciation) is synonymous with "xiāo" (wasting away), meaning the flesh has diminished until only the bones remain.

"Robbed and plundered" means to seize and take by force. "To suffer calamity crosswise" means to encounter painful suffering through unrighteous means. △ Second, it clarifies that because they fall into the evil realms, they do not encounter a Buddha.
Such a person of sin shall never see the Buddha, the King of Sages, preaching the Dharma to transform and instruct beings.
Such a person of sin will always be born in difficult circumstances—mad, deaf, and mentally deranged—and shall never hear the Dharma for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From birth to birth they shall be deaf and mute, with their sensory faculties incomplete, and shall constantly dwell in hell as if it were a pleasure garden, while remaining in other evil realms.
Just as one’s own home has camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs as its inhabitants, so too does one who slanders this sutra incur such offenses.
If they should obtain a human birth, they will be adorned with deafness, blindness, muteness, poverty, and all manner of misfortunes;
they will have dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and the like as their clothing, and their bodies will be perpetually foul-smelling, filthy, and impure.
Deeply attached to the view of self, they increase their anger and lust, which blaze so fiercely that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts;
because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
Next, from such offenders who do not even distinguish between humans and beasts, it is clarified that they shall incur such offenses and forever dwell in the eight difficult conditions.
Not seeing the Buddha refers to the difficulty of being before or after a Buddha; the "difficult places" refer to the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
Never hearing the Dharma refers to the difficulty of possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence while lacking faith in cause and effect.
Being born deaf and mute refers to the difficulty of being blind and mute from birth, which occurs naturally and is not caused by injury or grief. Constantly...
Those dwelling in hell are those who face the hardship of hell; those who are camels, donkeys, pigs, or dogs are those who face the hardship of the animal realm;
and those in other evil destinies should include those in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) and the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (Asaṃjñisattva-deva).
Regarding "using [the scripture] as clothing": ordinary people use clothing as a means to sustain the body to ward off cold and heat; now, those who slander the scripture...
They take the suffering of illness as their very clothing. △ Second, the conclusion:
I tell you, Śāriputra, that if one were to speak of the sins of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For this reason, I say to you: do not preach this sutra among people who lack wisdom.
△ Second, explaining the gate of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), it should be taught in two parts. First, five pairs clarify that such good persons are suitable for teaching.
First, the pair of the past and present:
if there are those with sharp faculties, clear wisdom, extensive learning, and strong memory who seek the Buddha-way—such persons [are suitable].
One may then preach it to such a person who has previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and possesses a deep and firm resolve;
to such a person one may preach this.
These seventeen lines explain the application of great compassion when propagating the sutra; there are virtuous people to whom it should be proclaimed.
It is said that one must ensure the Dharma is not lost; the essential point in propagating the Sūtras lies in harmonizing these two gates so that each finds its proper place.
If they find their proper place, the transmission will be excellent; if they do not, it will be a false proclamation. There are five pairs of categories:
first, the characteristics of virtuous persons for whom the teaching may be proclaimed. Furthermore, the past and present constitute one pair; "sharp faculties" refers to the present.
Planting roots of goodness is the past; furthermore, having a powerful memory is the present; seeing hundreds of thousands is the past.
△ Second, the pair of "above and below":
If a person is diligent and constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, not begrudging even their own body or life, then one may preach [the Dharma] to them. If a person is respectful...
To those who have no divergent thoughts, who are free from all ordinary and foolish people, and who dwell alone in mountains and marshes—only for such persons may this be taught.
Second, the pair of "above" and "below": practicing loving-kindness toward those below is compassion; showing reverence toward those above is respect.
Third, the pair of "internal" and "external."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends,
such a person may be taught this. If you see a son of the Buddha who maintains pure precepts like a polished bright pearl and seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras, such a person may be taught this.
Third, the pair of "outer" and "inner": abandoning evil and befriending the good is the outer seeking; guarding the precepts like a precious jewel is the inner protection.
Fourth, the pair of "self" and "others":
if a person is free from anger, upright, gentle, and flexible, always compassionate toward all beings, and respectful toward all Buddhas—such a person [is one who has perfected these qualities].

One may then explain it to those sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, preach the Dharma with a pure mind through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions without impediment; to such persons as these, one may indeed explain it.
Fourth, the pair of practicing for oneself and transforming others: being upright and revering the Buddha is practicing for oneself;
using analogies to preach the Dharma is transforming others. Fifth, the pair of the beginning and the end.

If there is a bhikṣu who seeks the Dharma in all four directions for the sake of omniscience, receiving it with palms joined at his crown, and who delights only in upholding Mahāyāna sūtras—even to the point of not accepting a single verse from any other scripture—only to such a person may you preach this.
It is like a person who, with a sincere heart, seeks the relics of the Buddha; having sought the sūtra thus and received it upon their crown, that person no longer [seeks anything else].
Those who aspire to seek other sutras and have never even thought of the texts of external paths—only for such persons may this be preached.
First, the beginning and end constitute a pair: seeking the Dharma in the four directions is the beginning of requesting instruction;
receiving it upon the crown of the head and practicing it with single-minded devotion is the end of taking refuge. △ Second, the summary.
"Śāriputra, I tell you that those who seek the Buddha-way in such a manner could not be fully described even at the end of an eon;
such persons as these are able to believe and understand—therefore, you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them."

This is the summary. Regarding the "characteristics," there are many auspicious signs; here, ten characteristics are briefly cited to demonstrate the method for circulation and to clarify the essential points concerning what may or may not be transmitted through the two gates of compassion and wisdom.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Three;
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Shou-lun of Qiyun, Jinxi, Keshan, Song Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Faji of Púttí Ān in Yùxī, Ming Dynasty;
proofread and carved for publication by the Layman Mín Mèngdé of Bīngchéng in Wúxīng. △ Third:
Explanation of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta). Part Two: First, explaining the title of the chapter.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Four: The Parable of the Faith and Understanding.
This chapter clarifies that those of middling capacity attain understanding. For such individuals, faculties may be sharp or dull, and afflictions may be thick or thin;

thus, the teachings may employ both direct exposition and parables, and awakening may occur earlier or later. As for the analogy used before the Lotus Sutra assembly—likened to a pea—it is recorded as being like a raw pea.
The beans were so hard that the awl could not pierce them. The text says: "Since the Tathāgata had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated there with my body weary and exhausted;
I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and regarding the Bodhisattva teachings, I lacked even a single thought of joy or interest.
When I first heard the brief exposition, my attachments were shaken and doubt arose; when I heard extensively the revelations of the five Buddhas, I remained dimly aware and unclear."
Now, having heard these parables at dawn, one rejoices with leaping joy; faith arises and understanding is born, while doubt departs and principle becomes clear.

Furthermore, "rejoicing" refers to the world (*loka-dhātu*); "the arising of faith" refers to persons (*pudgala*); "doubt departing" refers to the counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*); and "principle becoming clear" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For these reasons, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. Furthermore, having received the teachings of both the Small and Great Vehicles, one undergoes an initial transformation.
In general, the attainment of sainthood each has its own sequence of stages. However, for those of the Hīnayāna who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), understanding arises from hearing.

When the clear realization of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) dawns, if one follows by faith, it is called "following by faith" (*śraddhā-carita*); if one follows the Dharma, it is called "observing the phenomena" (*dharmacarita*). When the clear realization of the Dharma dawns, it is called "following the Dharma.

If a person following by faith turns toward the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are renamed "one resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*). If a person following the Dharma turns toward [the path of cultivation], [they are renamed "one attained through vision"].

The transformation of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) into what is termed "attainment through vision" (darśanaprāpta) follows the same principle when comparing the Small Vehicle to the Great Vehicle; therefore, it should be understood in this way.

Consequently, those of middling faculties, upon hearing the teaching of the parable, first shatter their doubts and enter the path of vision (darśanamārga) of the Mahāyāna—hence it is called "entering by faith" (śraddhā-praveśa)—and subsequently enter the path of cultivation of the Mahāyāna—hence it is called "understanding" (adhimukti).
As the text says: "The unsurpassed treasury of jewels is obtained spontaneously without being sought. We [are these people].

Today, it is truly the case that the śrāvakas cause all to hear by means of the sound of the Buddha-way; because they hear the Perfect Teaching and enter the Perfect Stage, this is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.

Regarding its provisional and ultimate aspects (*honjaku*): the four great disciples have long entered the Mahāyāna and achieved the Buddha-dharma, yet they provisionally manifest the stage of initial faith and understanding for those of medium capacity; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. II. Explanation.
The text has two parts. First, the narrator describes their state of joy. Second, there are two sub-sections;

first, the description of their inner thoughts: At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching, as the World-Honored One had conferred upon Śāriputra the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Upon receiving the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind, leaping for joy with exultation.
As for the Venerable Subhūti, among all those who possessed wisdom in the past, his wisdom was foremost;

the Buddha commanded him to turn and teach the Prajñāpāramitā. Because he was commissioned by the one of supreme wisdom, he is called "Wisdom-Life" (Hui-ming); the other three [disciples] are not so designated.
Regarding the disciple’s generation of a mind of rare wonder as previously explained, this is the cause for attaining joy.
From afar he heard the five sections of the Dharma discourse on skillful means; the narrator merely recounts two types: hearing the rare Dharma and receiving the prophecy.
Alternatively, it may be that "hearing the rare Dharma" refers to the first four sections, while "receiving the prophecy" constitutes the fifth section. Thus he heard.
Seeing what has never been seen before is the cause of joy; "giving rise to a mind of rare wonder" refers to the fourfold exposition of recent hearsay and parables.
Because this rare wonder arises from the arousal of the mind, it is termed "faith. Through faith, one enters [the path];
entering the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is precisely the meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhābhūmi*). △ Second, the description of external veneration.

He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with a single-minded focus, joined his palms, bowed in reverence, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
Rising from his seat describes his external respect; following the precedent of Śāriputra above, his understanding through realization should likewise involve the three types of action (trikarma).

The preceding section is understandable. △ Second, the self-announcement to the Buddha in two parts: first, the formal presentation of having attained understanding; second, praising the depth of the Buddha’s grace.

The first part [of the second section] is further divided into two: first, the prose; second, the verse. The prose is further divided into two: first, the brief explanation by way of the Dharma; second, the extensive explanation by way of analogy.

The first of these [the brief explanation by way of the Dharma] is further divided into two: first, the formal Dharma-exposition; second, the brief citation of a simile. The first of these [the formal Dharma-exposition] is further...
Second, first clarifying that they previously received [the teachings] from the Three [Buddhas], there are two parts; first, the heading of the three.
First, because they occupy the head of the Saṃgha, they address the Buddha, saying: "We occupy the head of the Saṃgha."

Regarding the first point, concerning those who dwell at the head of the monastic community: since my years of ordination (*dharma-lakṣa*) are already advanced, those of late learning take me as their model.

Yet, they suddenly alter their path and change their course, abandoning the minor for the major, thereby incurring the resentment of later generations. To firmly protect them, I therefore do not seek to be recorded;
this describes the three things not sought, beginning with dwelling at the head of the monastic community, which describe past failings. First, the initial failing:

If one clings to the small number of years [of ordination], then the Great Dharma will be entirely lacking; yet not abandoning the small is due to not yet understanding the opening of the Three Vehicles.
To remain self-enclosed is to cling to the small without shifting, and to protect that state is to be deluded regarding the Great Path. △ Second, because of the advanced age of their secular years.
Both of us are advanced in years.
Since our worldly ages have already declined—if we were Bodhisattvas, we ought to single-mindedly undertake the Great Way to extensively deliver sentient beings;
but now that we are aged and decrepit, we are incapable of such tasks. For this reason, we do not seek the prediction [of future Buddhahood]. This is the first of the second set of faults.

Because they have severed birth and realized [the truth], they despise themselves for being of advanced age; yet, as the "败种" (ruined seed) has not been removed, their view of incapacity still persists.
△ Third, because they have already attained realization, they claim to have already attained *nirvāṇa* and, deeming themselves incapable of further effort, no longer seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"O World-Honored One of Tripiṭaka Awakening, since the Buddha first began preaching the Dharma long ago, I have been present in the assembly;

my body has become weary and exhausted, and I have only contemplated emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. My mind finds no joy in the Bodhisattva teachings, nor in the playful exercise of supernormal powers, the purification of Buddha-lands, or the maturing of sentient beings."
Third, having already attained the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state of true reality (samyaktva-niyāma), one is unable to give rise to the Great Mind;
this is likened to a lotus not growing on high ground or dry land. Once the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) is fully established, there is nothing further upon which to rely or seek.

As for the record stating that the third failure arises from the past delusion regarding the essential meaning, where one merely calculates the merit of the state of true reality, it is because of this very [attainment] that [the Great Mind is obstructed].
The emotion is great, yet the mind is difficult to arouse. △ Second, the explanation has two parts; first, the explanation of realization and attainment.
Why is this so? Because the World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana.
Why is this? To explain the three things not sought: first, the text explains the non-seeking of attaining *nirvāṇa*, though it does not follow the sequential order.
△ Second, the explanation of advanced age:
"Furthermore, we are now already decrepit in years; regarding the Buddha’s transformation of us into *bodhisattvas* for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
He did not give rise to even a single thought of longing for the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).

Next, regarding the explanation of his advanced age and lack of desire [for leadership], this simultaneously refers to his position as the head of the Saṃgha; or it may indicate that because he had long been preaching the Dharma, his mind no longer found joy in it.

This explains his residence at the head of the Saṃgha and his lack of desire. Since it is said he was "already seated" and yet further described as being "advanced in years," we know this refers to Śāriputra.
The Head of the Sangha. △ Second, explaining that one naturally attains [realization] because the present assembly is one:
"We who have now heard before the Buddha the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas feel profound joy;
we have attained what we have never had before, for we did not expect to suddenly hear such a rare Dharma at this time."
I rejoice deeply at having obtained this great and wholesome benefit.
This account of how I attained understanding proceeds from what was heard from afar through five chapters that briefly expand upon the three [vehicles] to reveal the One;
thus, "rejoicing deeply at having obtained this great and wholesome benefit" specifically describes the attainment of understanding, which refers to what was heard nearby through the four similes.
This rare and marvelous Dharma has been attained through awakening; such awakening is itself a sublime benefit. △ Second, a brief illustration by means of analogy:
immeasurable treasures are obtained spontaneously without seeking.
This is a brief citation of parables to illustrate how that which was not sought in the past is now spontaneously attained—the rare Dharma-treasure.
In the past, when the *Prajñāpāramitā* was received and taught, it was considered the Dharma for Bodhisattvas alone; who would have imagined that today we would receive its full and equal bestowal?

△ Second, the detailed explanation through parables, in two parts: first, opening the parable; second, applying the parable. The first part [opening the parable] is further divided into two: first, the inquiry and inspiration.
“World-Honored One, we now wish to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.

Regarding the term ‘to consult and initiate’: ‘consult’ (zī) means earnestly; it also refers to presenting a petition or making a formal announcement. It should be understood according to worldly etiquette:

when one wishes to resolve a matter, one must first consult and initiate the discussion. 2. Elucidating the Parable (in four parts): First, the Parable of the Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other.
Second, the analogy of father and son meeting; third, the analogy of pursuit and enticement; fourth, the analogy of receiving and entrustment. In the first section, there are again four parts:
first, the son leaves his father; second, the initial departure from the father.
It is like a man who, being young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another country for ten, twenty, or even fifty years.

This illustrates the analogy of the father and son losing sight of each other; viewed closely, it summarizes the parable of the burning house, and viewed from afar, it encompasses the entire [parable of] the directions.
To briefly summarize this passage, there are four points within it. These four refer to: first, the son’s departure from his father;
and so on, up to the fourth, the father’s anxious concern. Each of these four sections contains two points.
Regarding the first point—his departure from his father—the phrase "it is as if there were a person" refers to the twenty sons, while the second point refers to the father himself.

The conduct of those who ride upon the stage of a Bodhisattva is difficult to know; let us for now consider only those who have already been led [to the path]. As for those who are still young and immature:
because they are heavily shrouded and obstructed by ignorance (*avidyā*), their mind of understanding lacks power, and thus they are called "young and immature.

To "abandon their father and flee" means to retreat from the Great Vehicle, which is the abandonment of the father; to be "shrouded by one's own ignorance" is called "fleeing," and to "head toward birth and death" is called...

Śāriputra asked: "If it is after the Buddha has relinquished his response to sentient beings that they give rise to delusions, is this because the father has abandoned the son, or is it because the son has abandoned the father?
The answer is: It is because sentient beings lack the conditions for resonance that the Buddha then departs from the world; thus, it constitutes the meaning of the son abandoning the father.

As for "dwelling long in another country," the Dharma-realm of Nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s own country, while birth-and-death and the five desires are the "other country. This is the fundamental principle.
Because they seek liberation yet fall back and do not return, it is said they "dwell for a long time.

Alternatively, ten refers to the heavenly realm, twenty to the human realm, and fifty to the five destinies; since these are all encompassed within a single person as they cycle through the various paths, it is said to be "ten, etc.
△ Second, returning toward the source.
As he grew older and became increasingly impoverished, he traveled in all directions in search of food and clothing. Wandering on by degrees, he eventually encountered his native land.
Subsequently, having grown up and departed from that country, he returned; yet, as a youth, he possessed two characteristics: first, he was foolish and small-minded.

Therefore, because these two have not yet encountered suffering, they do not know how to turn back; this is illustrated by the analogy of those who, after forming a karmic connection [with the Buddha], have not yet reached a deep realization and thus do not return due to their delusion.
Furthermore, while they still possess residual merit, they remain immersed in confusion and do not return. Now, when their habitual karma is subtly perfumed, they gain a faint awareness of the Path;

yet, upon encountering suffering and losing their pleasures, they contemplate seeking the essential means of liberation. These two types of beings serve as the catalysts that strike the Buddha, which is termed "gradual" [awakening].

Regarding the "Return to the Father’s Kingdom," the preceding text states: "If a person encounters suffering, one preaches *nirvāṇa* to them; if they possess the two virtues of humans and devas, these do not constitute conditions for perceiving the Buddha.
Once their years have grown long, their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have been permeated and nurtured, and they gradually desire to attain renown;
this is called 'growing up. Furthermore, those who are impoverished and destitute within the three realms do not see the Buddha-Father; is this not poverty?"

Furthermore, because they have not attained the method for reaching the essential [liberation] and are scorched by the exhaustion of the eight sufferings, they wander in distress through the four directions in search of food and clothing.
As it was traditionally said, the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of humans and devas each possess their own cause and effect;

these are treated as the "four directions" used for one's own sustenance. Moreover, within the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), they engage in livelihoods to seek food and clothing. Therefore, the following passage states:
It is said that only after one hundred and thirty kalpas has he now obtained this single vision;

yet, throughout those kalpas, it was not that there were no human or celestial beings with causes and effects, for they were unable to evoke the Buddha. Thus we know that these roots of goodness were not yet the karmic capacity to see the Buddha.
Before the Buddha had appeared in the world, ordinary persons gave rise to the four inverted views regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, seeking the True Path therein.
Just as one seeks food, seeks assistance on the path, or seeks clothing, so too does one seek the principle out of weariness with suffering; this constitutes the conditions for being converted.
This is the meaning of the fact that when the Buddha first appeared in the world, those of the various non-Buddhist paths were all the first to attain deliverance.

As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "Carefully observing the four directions is a metaphor for the Four Noble Truths"; by this standard, it can be understood that he gradually traveled about until he encountered [the conditions].

Regarding those who are heading toward their own country: this clarifies that although they seek nirvana through mistaken means—out of weariness with suffering and a desire for liberation—this is not their original intention;

nevertheless, because they have encountered the Buddha, it is said they "encounter" [the path]. Their "own country" is as explained above. As for the city and house mentioned in the text below, how should one distinguish them?
One should know that all Buddha-dharmas constitute the "country"; this meaning is broad, whereas the term "city" is narrow and esoteric.
Thus, he takes the cessation of afflictions (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and *nirvāṇa* as his fortress and dwelling to ward off transgressions and resist evil;

furthermore, because they are kin, he takes the great compassion of the same essence (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*) as his dwelling. △ Second, seeking the child and stopping midway, in two parts: first, the father seeks the child but does not find him.
His father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him.

This passage also contains two meanings: first, from the perspective of withdrawing from the Great Vehicle, the Buddha constantly seeks an opportunity (the *tīkṣṇendriya* capacity), yet because no such opportunity arises, he is said to "not have found" him. Second, [he] stops at a certain city.

In one city he had a family of great wealth and immeasurable treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like—such that all his granaries and treasuries were overflowing.
He possessed numerous servants, ministers, officials, and subjects, as well as countless elephants, horses, carriages, cattle, and sheep.
His income and interest extended throughout other lands, and he was engaged in trade with merchants and traders.
They were also extremely numerous.
Among them, those who resided in one particular city did not abandon their family affairs for the sake of a single son;

likewise, the Buddha did not cease his transformative teachings in other regions simply because there was no spiritual affinity in one place. (The old tradition states that this period was after twenty thousand Buddhas and before Śākyamuni Buddha.)

The space between the two central pillars constitutes the "place of cessation" (*zhongzhi*). While it is acceptable to speak of this in terms of the meaning of "center," the terms "state" (*guo*) and "household" (*jia*) are both unsuitable for its application.

Now, taking what is convenient, there is surplus land that constitutes the state; within the shared dwelling of the *sambhogakāya* (real recompense), the space between the two [pillars] constitutes the center.
*Nirvāṇa with remainder* constitutes the city; abiding in this *nirvāṇa* is called the place of cessation, and this is the household from which one sets out.
There are two types of responsive manifestations, the superior and the inferior. The inferior response accords with the śrāvakas, while the superior response accords with the bodhisattvas.

Those five classes of people who have severed the pervasive afflictions are born together upon that [Pure Land], all serving as bodhisattvas; the Buddha responds to them with his superior manifestation and instructs them exclusively in the family business of the Mahāyāna to practice and study.
He halts his activity here to await the opportunity of those "co-resident children," seeking not merely those who are of middling capacity.

When the meaning is attained through synthesis, the kingdom, city, and household affairs are all clearly manifest. That family which is greatly wealthy takes the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*) as its household goods;
being endowed with ten thousand virtues, it is called "wealth" (the five perfections); merit and virtue are called "treasure";
and Prajñā-wisdom is called "jewel. Because this Prajñā guides everything, it is entirely Mahāyāna, and is thus called "immeasurable gold, silver, and pearls."
These are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) of the Mahāyāna; this summarizes the meaning of the elder’s great wealth mentioned above.

"The granaries and treasuries are overflowing" means they are full within and overflowing without: "granary" (*kūṭāgāra*) refers to the abundance of rice, while "treasury" (*kośa*) refers to the storage of goods.

The granary is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which can give rise to the one hundred and eight samādhis; the treasury is a metaphor for the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which can bring them forth.

By means of the wisdom of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, one fills oneself and overflows for the sake of transforming others; this summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned possession of many fields and houses.
"Servants" refers to the complete perfection of the *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *prajñā-pāramitā* (perfection of wisdom);

their adaptability according to capacity, and their conformity to circumstances and principles, summarize the aforementioned possession of many attendants. If established according to their positions:
In terms of speech, those of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching up to the thirty minds of the Separate Teaching are all like servants;

the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of both the Separate and Complete Teachings are like ministers, the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) are like assistants, the ten practices (*caryā*) are like officials, and the ten abidings (*vihāra*) are like commoners.

Although they have all entered the realm of the Buddha—the entire territory where no one is not a subject of the King—they are still compared to officials and assistants when measured against the status of a true subject.
These [stages] are still somewhat remote; the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*) involve the distinct cultivation of various dharmas with much exertion, like officials on tour.

The ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) involve principles and matters that are slightly deeper, and their offices are closer to the King, like assistants. The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) assist the Buddha in his transformative activities, subduing demons and overcoming adversaries;
therefore, they are like ministers. As for the "innumerable elephants, horses, chariots, oxen, and sheep," one should know that—

The single-mind threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trisamādhi*) is like an elephant drawing the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*); the sequential threefold contemplation is like a horse drawing the Great Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (*pratibheda-yāna*).
Contemplating emptiness through analysis (*vibhajya-śūnyatā-darśana*) is like an ox drawing the Great Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), etc.

Contemplating the analysis of phenomena (*dharma-vibhāga-darśana*) for one’s own practice is like deer or sheep drawing the teachings of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). As for the innumerable [teachings], all provisional and real dharmas are...

The names of the vehicles are the provisional, while the wisdom of contemplation is the real; the names of the elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep refer to the teachings, which are exceedingly numerous, yet the wisdom of contemplation is likewise infinite.
To emerge from duality and enter non-duality is "entry"; to be in non-duality and yet manifest as duality is "emergence.
Furthermore, to be in non-duality and yet manifest as duality is "entry"; to be in duality and yet be non-dual is "emergence. Moreover, the immeasurable returns to the one.
Entering the one from within the immeasurable is "entry" (入); emerging again for the sake of transforming others is "exit" (出).

To employ this for the benefit of others is "exit," while returning the merit of transformation to oneself is "entry. To provide benefit through the Dharma is "exit," while bringing the fruits of transformation back to oneself is "entry.
As for "pervading other lands," it means pervading the three lands; practicing where there are no paths and attaining mastery over the Buddha-way—this is its meaning. Only...
Regarding the statement that "the merchants and traders of one's own country are also exceedingly numerous," it refers to the bodhisattvas who are these merchants.
Furthermore, because they enter all three lands (*tri-bhūmi*) to seek the benefits of the Dharma, they are said to be "numerous.

Bodhisattvas of this land travel to other directions to hear the Dharma, while great beings (*mahāsattva*) from other directions come here to hear the sutras; thus, they come and go to gather profit. Moreover, it should be understood as follows:...
The two transformation bodies are like merchants who take this true Dharma and enter the three lands to benefit sentient beings through transformation before returning to the Dharma-body;
thus they are said to be "very many," just as people in the world cause others to seize wealth and engage in business while also engaging in business themselves.
△ Third, the child encounters his parents; first, he seeks food and clothing.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities.
Because he lacked the merit and the wealth of the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, he was called a "poor son. Having fallen away from the Mahāyāna, he subsequently encountered all manner of sufferings;
he gave rise to a profound sense of weariness and sought liberation, yet because his grasp of the principle was incorrect, he fell into heterodoxy.
Deviant causes arise from perverse wisdom; as they pass through the mind, it is easy to enter the correct path. Seeking transcendence is the reason for perceiving the Buddha.

To contemplate the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as a village, the twelve bases (*āyatanas*) as a town, and the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) as a kingdom, and to seek the principle through these, is called "seeking food and clothing. △ Second, he eventually arrives at his father’s city.
He then arrived at the city where his father resided.
"Arriving at the city where his father resided" means that taking the realm of suffering as the catalyst for awakening, he invokes the Great Compassion of the Buddha;
this is called "arriving at the city. The city is *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is universal.
Because half and all sentient beings possess the practice and understanding that allows for the attainment of nirvana, it is said that they have "reached the city.
△ Fourth, the father’s anxious concern, in two parts: first, the suffering of grieving over the loss of his son.
The father constantly thought of his son with whom he had been separated for over fifty years, yet he never spoke of such a matter to anyone;

he merely pondered it within himself, harboring regret and remorse. He thought to himself: "I am old and decrepit, yet I possess abundant wealth, gold, silver, and rare treasures, filling my storehouses to overflowing.
Since I have no offspring, once I pass away, my property will be dispersed and lost, with no one to whom it may be entrusted."
For this reason, he constantly and earnestly remembers his son.
This passage also contains two meanings: first, the thought that losing his son is suffering; second, the thought that regaining his son is joy.
Regarding the first meaning, from the past until now, the Tathāgata has always contemplated his son’s great capacity for awakening; therefore, it says, "he constantly remembers. Fifth.
"The ten or more years" refers to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). "The remainder" refers to the opening of the way for ghosts and the emergence of asuras;

thus it is said that "the remainder has not yet been taught," meaning that the karmic conditions for having such a son have not yet been explained to the ministers, officials, and commoners within the *upāya-śeṣa* (land of skillful means with remainder).
Furthermore, since his appearance in the world, from the time of the ancient *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, [he has remained].
I have never before spoken to these great beings of how these śrāvakas were originally sons of the Mahāyāna;

yet, being neither sons of the Buddha nor understanding the Dharma, they are like those who are deaf or mute, or like flowers that adhere to their seats, or they cast aside their bowls and stand bewildered—failing in every way and meeting with reprimands.
Their hearts harbor regret, lamenting that in the past they did not diligently follow instructions.
He caused [the son] to flee without instruction, regretting that the son did not contemplate his kindness and righteousness, and that he alienated his own kin to embrace others within.
Internally, he felt as if the Tathāgata had failed to urge him earnestly to enter the inner [path]. Thus, he allowed the ordinary person to eventually fall away and lose their original understanding.

He lamented that [the son] lacked the resolve for diligent practice and a firm will, fleeing and not returning; hence, it is called "regret and resentment. As for "reflecting on his own old age": [it refers to the father’s realization of his own decline.]
"The period of my transformation is nearing its end, yet there is no one to whom I may transmit the Great Dharma; I am like an old man who has no son.
He asked, "Since all the bodhisattvas transformed by the Dharmakāya are capable of succeeding you in the position of Regent, why do you suddenly harbor such anxiety?

He replied, "That which is transformed by the Dharmakāya is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; who would speak of 'old age'? This is not what we are discussing here. Now, I shall clarify the retinue of the Nirmāṇakāya."
There are two types: first, those who are Dharma-body bodhisattvas whose traces appear as disciples though they may originally have been teachers;
these do not consider themselves "old and decrepit" based on this status.

Second, those ordinary beings living together with us who, having first developed the aspiration for the Way under a transformation Buddha, are called "sons"; as sons, they succeed to their father’s legacy so that the lineage shall continue.

If Śāriputra had received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood as the Buddha Puṣpārāma, then the lineage of Buddhas in one direction would have continued without interruption, and the family estate of the Mahāyāna would have been transmitted from one to another.
If there were no sentient beings in Śāriputra’s capacity to be transformed, then the Dharma-wealth of the Mahāyāna would currently have no one to whom it could be entrusted;
where, then, would the seeds of Buddhahood for future sentient beings be placed? It is precisely for this reason that I, in my old age, am moved to such deep lamentation.
This refers to that. △ Second, the thought of obtaining the joy of having a son:
He further thinks, "If I were to obtain a son to whom I could entrust my wealth and possessions, I would be at ease and joyful, free from any further anxiety."
He further reflects thus: "If I were to obtain a son"—this is the second thought, wherein obtaining a son is considered a joy.

There is a capacity for deliverance which is termed "obtaining a son"; bestowing upon him the Buddha’s prediction is termed "entrusting the Dharma-treasure," and this accords with his original intention, hence he speaks of it as "happiness.
△ Second, the analogy of the father and son meeting. Part two: the son seeing the father. Section four: the first sight [of the father].
As for the father’s approach:
at that time, World-Honored One, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of work, happened upon his father’s house.
This clarifies the analogy of the father and son meeting: it refers proximately to seeing the fire within the Burning House, and distantly to the Chapter on Expedient Means.

Regarding the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), for the sake of convenience in the textual arrangement, we shall treat this as two sections: first, the son seeing his father; second, the father seeing his son.
Within each of these two sections, there are further four parts. First, regarding the son seeing his father, the four are as follows:

(1) the cause for seeing his father, which arises from wearying of suffering and rejoicing in bliss, whereby he seeks the flavor of principle and gradually accumulates practice until he finally establishes supramundane roots of goodness (*lokottara-kuśalamūla*).
Therefore, it is said that by means of this root of goodness, obtained through successive labor for hire, one is able to strike upon the Buddha’s compassion;
hence it is said that one "encounters the father's house. The father is a metaphor for the Dharma after the Path, and the house is a metaphor for unconditional compassion.

Because both the Great and Small vehicles can simultaneously strike this house, and because there is a "Great capacity" within this house, it is said that one "sees the father from afar"; yet because there is a "Small capacity," it is so stated.
If he were abiding by the side of the gate and possessed only the small [body] without the large, he would not be able to see the body of the Honored One’s special marks;

nor would the father be able to say, "I now have something to entrust to my son regarding my wealth and storehouses. If he possessed only the large [body] without the small, he would not be abiding by the side of the gate;
nor would the son be able to say, "This is not a place where I obtained goods through hired labor. △ Second, the Vision.
At the place where his father was,
he stood by the side of the gate and saw his father from afar;
the very place where he saw his father was by the side of the gate, and by means of the two observations, the two sides of the gate were made perfectly round.

The capacity of those of intermediate [faculties] corresponds to the "gate" (dvāra), as their correct vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) pertains to the partial truth of the Two Vehicles; thus it is said they are at the side of the gate.

They possess only the samādhi of emptiness and the partial truth of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which peers sideways at the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and gazes afar at their father. Regarding this correct vision, there are two kinds:
first, near vision; second, distant vision. Here, it is said that because the great capacity has only just begun to arise and the matter of the summons is remote, it is called "gazing afar."
Furthermore, since the faculties [of those beings] were so subtle that he was unable to respond to them directly, this is termed "remote. △ Third, the vision of his father’s appearance:
He sat upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet;

all the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders respectfully surrounded him, their bodies adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million coins, while officials, commoners, and servants held [offerings] in their hands.

White fly-whisks stood at his left and right, and he was sheltered by a jeweled canopy from which various flower banners hung down. Fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground, and a multitude of famous flowers were scattered about.
Precious objects were arranged in rows, being brought out and taken in; with such various adornments as these, his majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime.

Regarding "sitting upon the lion throne": it means that the Dharma-body of perfect retribution dwells securely within the principle of emptiness, free from the fears of the two types of delusion—both pervasive and specific—as well as the eight māras;

thus, it is said that one sits upon the lion throne. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains that the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) constitute the throne.
As for the jeweled footstool supporting the feet: meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are the feet, and the ultimate truth (*satya*) is the footstool. This is precisely...
The concentration and wisdom of non-arising rely upon the realm of *tathatā* (suchness).

The Brahmin refers to a pure practitioner of noble lineage and high integrity, namely a Bodhisattva on the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is equivalent to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The Kṣatriya refers to the royal caste, from the first ground upward through the ninth ground.
The Householder (*gṛhapati*) is wealthy but not of noble birth, referring to those in the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśac-cittotpāda*). As for the pearl necklace:
The "four necklaces" are the dhāraṇīs of precept, concentration, and wisdom, along with samādhi.

That which is "worth ten million" refers to the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*) used to adorn the Dharma-body. Regarding the "officials, commoners, servants, and attendants": these represent the distinct categories of clear meaning;

specifically, those who receive the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and Shared teachings and sever the delusions of the shared realm are called "commoners," while those who receive the Distinct teaching and sever the delusions of the shared realm [are called "officials"].
This is called an "official" (*li*). If one who clarifies the meaning is of the same school, this is still the *upāya-pāramitā* (skillful means).

Internally, it is identical to true wisdom; externally, it is identical to the conditions of sentient beings. It is likened to an official: an official has the duty of serving internally and performing labor externally.

The white fly-whisk represents the function of provisional wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*); "left and right" refers to this, where "right" signifies the function of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which sweeps away [delusions].
The dust of the four abidings enters from the left; this is the wisdom of entering the provisional, used to sweep away the dust of ignorance.
These two constitute the skillful means of the Middle Way; thus it is said they stand in attendance. "Covered with precious canopies" refers to true compassion. "Hanging various flower banners":

the flowers are the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the banners are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). "Sprinkling the ground with fragrant water" refers to the raining down of the water of Dharma.
Sprinkling the ground of the bodhisattvas' minds to drench the dust of delusion is likewise the water of meditative concentration sprinkled upon the scattered ground of the mind.

As for scattering various named flowers, it means spreading the flowers of the seven purities—namely, the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the purity of concentration (*samādhi*), the purity of wisdom (*prajñā*), the purity of overcoming doubt (*vicikitsā-prahāṇa*), the purity of knowing the path and the non-path (*mārgāmārga-jñāna-darśana*), the purity of knowledge and vision of what has been abandoned (*prahīṇa-jñāna-darśana*)—and so forth. Regarding "ethical discipline," it refers to the three types of discipline, such as the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and so on. Regarding "concentration"...
"Samādhi" refers to the Śūraṅgama and others; "wisdom" refers to true wisdom; "severing doubt" means having already transcended doubts regarding the two truths;
"purity of the path and non-path" means practicing upon what is not the path while attaining penetration into the Buddha-way;

"purity of knowledge and vision" means the perfection of the virtue of wisdom and clearly seeing the Buddha-nature; and "severance and knowledge" refers to the accomplishment of the virtue of severance.
Ignorance is forever exhausted. "Arranging precious objects" refers to the arrangement of the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The explanation of "taking out and putting in" is as previously interpreted. His majestic virtue is uniquely honored;

his radiance is boundless, his forms are boundless, and his ocean of marks is boundless—lofty, dignified, and sublime. This meaning must refer to the Buddha Vairocana; how could it refer to anyone else?
[The Buddha] said, "Yes. △ Fourth, the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance:
Upon seeing that his father possessed great power and authority, the impoverished son immediately felt terror and regretted having come here.
He thought to himself in secret, "This man might be a king or perhaps a royal official; this is not a place where I can obtain wealth through hired labor. It would be better to go elsewhere..."
"In this poor neighborhood, there is ample ground for exertion; food and clothing are easily obtained. If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced into labor.
Having formed this thought, he fled away in haste.
This clarifies that seeing his father, [the son] feared and avoided one of great power;

"great wisdom" (*jñāna*), "great strength" (*bala*), "great supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi*), and "great majesty" (*mahānubhāva*) signify that his physical hands and arms possess power, as described above. "Terror" refers to those of inferior capacity who are weak and timid, fearing the Great Way.
"Regretting having come here" means that the Buddha originally intended to present the Great Dharma to him, yet it was not in accord with his disposition.
Because the capacity [of the listener] merely possesses the intention to regress from the Great Vehicle, it is said that "regret has come.

Regarding the thought "I have secretly conceived this," such a thing exists latently and secretly within the capacity; it is not a case of manifestly encountering the Superior Response Body (the Nirmāṇakāya).

As for the phrase "or perhaps kings and their like," Pāpīyas is the king, and his followers constitute the "like"; they are those of inferior capacity for whom the path of words is extinguished like ashes.
Transcending all forms and images, he manifested a supreme transformation body that was beyond the reach of gods or humans.

The characteristics of the Dharma he preached were utterly distinct from those of the two vehicles. Those of meager virtue, who had never before seen or heard such things, immediately claimed it was Māra or the teaching of Māra.
Śāriputra, briefly opening his understanding yet manifesting doubt, wondered: "Could this not be Māra acting as a Buddha to disturb my mind?"
If one initially uses the great to address the small, it is suspected that the Buddha has become a demon; such was the fault of today’s [opponents].
Furthermore, the "Victorious One" (Jina) is illustrated by the analogy of the elder (*gṛhapati*); the elder represents the Sambhogakāya Buddha.

Therefore, the Dharma-body Buddhas, such as the King, are the Teachers of the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The Teacher is like the King; many sūtras bear the title "King of Sūtras," for wisdom accords with the Dharma, and this is precisely wisdom.

Because he is equal to the Dharma, he is called the *Sambhogakāya* (Reward Buddha). This is the reward of the Mahāyāna Dharma and not a place where one gains benefit through the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Alternatively, it is like a king or a nobleman, and not a place where one obtains goods by hiring out one's labor;
those of small capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation (*mahā-vinaya*). It is not like going to a poor neighborhood where even food and clothing are easily obtained.
Regarding "attainment," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states that one can deliver those of inferior capacity through the Dharma they delight in—poverty.

This refers to the principle of mere emptiness (*śūnyatā*) which does not contain the myriad virtues; because it is not the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is called a "poor neighborhood. It is termed "partial emptiness" because it accords with the wisdom of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the phrase "a place to exert effort" and "one who exerts effort": "exerting" (*si*) means to extend or unfold; it refers to the act of stretching out or unfolding [the mind].
The "storing of goods" refers to those who hire out their labor for wages; for such people, clothing and food are easily obtained, and they may even have a surplus.
Nirvāṇa is without outflows (anāsrava), and its "clothing and food" are simply practice: the practice of conduct is the clothing, and the practice of wisdom is the food.
If one dwells here for a long time, one might encounter pressure and be forced to perform tasks; because the path of the Mahāyāna passes through immeasurable kalpas, it is said to be "long."

"I dwell in my original state, weary of and terrified of birth and death; yet if I were to cultivate the Mahāyāna, I would inevitably enter into birth and death to extensively study the myriad practices.
Therefore, it is said that [the father] "oppresses" him. "I originally delighted in the Small Vehicle, yet now he compels me to give rise to the great bodhicitta;

Seeing his son’s location,

△ Second, recognizing the child upon seeing him.
"Recognizing the child upon seeing him" means knowing that he is a sentient being with whom one formed a karmic connection in the past. △ Third, rejoicing upon seeing the child.
Joy! The mind is greatly rejoiced. As for this great rejoicing of the mind:
it is because the Buddha alone constantly observes his son’s capacity, and now that capacity has arrived, it accords with his compassion; therefore [he rejoices].
"Rejoicing" refers to giving rise to great compassion upon hearing the teaching of the supreme Dharma;

He then thought to himself: "My wealth and storehouses now have one to whom they may be entrusted. I have constantly longed for this son, yet had no means to see him;

He then had this thought: "The treasury now has one to whom it may be entrusted. This is the vision of his son, fulfilling his long-held wish.

Previously, he saw sentient beings falling away from the Great Vehicle and taking up the Lesser Vehicle, seeking food and sustenance in impoverished quarters where their livelihoods were difficult; he constantly desired to give them wealth, but finding no opportunity, he was unable to do so.

My constant remembrance signifies not merely that he was poor and lacked great wealth, but rather that he was tormented by the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra and pained by my great compassion; thus it is said, "I constantly remember him.

There are three intentions for illuminating the sections [of the text], which may be seen therein; for now, we shall clarify the first intention. Regarding "sending away the bystanders":

this refers to the initial stage of exhortation, which is the "provisional suitability" (*niyi*). Here, wisdom is that which sends away, and the teaching is that which is sent away. The meaning of principle (*liyi*) is primary, while the meaning of the teaching (*jiaoyi*) is secondary.
This [teaching] emerged from the Buddha as the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna, following a provisional suitability; however, sentient beings lacked the necessary capacity (*mēngji*).
Because he does not accept it as being like milk, it is said that "he dispatches an attendant. Furthermore, "attendant" refers to ministers and assistants;
this means dispatching the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas to preach the Mahāyāna, such as when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has four Bodhisattvas explain the forty stages (*bhūmi*).
This is what is meant by "dispatching an attendant. "Quickly running to seize him" refers to the Mahāyāna.
The meaning of this is that it is manifest, upright, and used to respond to capacities so as to hasten toward Bodhi; therefore, it is said in the *Mahāyāna* [Sūtra]:

"Its swiftness is like the wind. If one considers the Bodhisattva to be a bystander, the Bodhisattva possesses their own supernatural powers and is further empowered by the Buddha, such that they too can cause others to swiftly enter Bodhi. △ Second, those without capacity.
The impoverished son was startled and cried out in grievance, shouting, "I have done you no wrong; why are you seizing me?

Startled and alarmed, he immediately urged [the gatekeeper] to let him pass, for since the lack of affinity had manifested, even though he had previously resolved upon the Great Mind in the distant past, he had long since forgotten it.
Suddenly hearing this Great Teaching, it conflicted with his mind; thus he was startled by its unfamiliarity and alarmed by his failure to recognize it. He cried out in grievance and lamentation.
The "one who calls out" refers to those of the Hīnayāna who regard afflictions as enemies and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as suffering.

If one were to urge them that "afflictions are themselves bodhi," it would be like crying out in great distress while accusing others of injustice; if one were to hear that "birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa," it would be like crying out in great distress while lamenting one's own pain.
For this reason, they lack the capacity [for awakening] and do not accept the gate of exhortation. "I do not offend them" means that I—

"What is the intent of this earnest entreaty? It is to transform me through this great teaching. Regarding these two points of the "Gate of Exhortation," the former has not yet been understood, so the transformation remains incomplete.
△ Second, understanding the "Gate of Admonition" regarding the suitability of the capacity [of the recipient]. Part one: Suitability.
The messenger seizes him with increasing urgency and forcibly drags him back.
"Seizing him with increasing urgency" refers to the gatekeeper who should issue a warning;
the previous encouragement toward goodness was still done with leniency, whereas now, when I shall explain matters of fear, it is like being urgently and forcibly dragged back—this is the warning.
By using harsh words to cause him to distance himself from evil, although he lacks internal capacity for it, he is externally coerced by the Great Transformation;
this is what is meant by forcibly leading him back. △ Second, Lacking Capacity.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself: "Though I am innocent, I have been imprisoned and seized; this must mean certain death. He became even more terrified.
Fainting and falling to the ground, he thought to himself:
"Those who are without fault do not receive this gate of instruction; those with faults possess compassion.

Because sentient beings have faults, they enter the prison of birth and death; if Bodhisattvas likewise entered the prison because of their faults, then those of the Two Vehicles would not possess the Great [Vehicle].
Compassion is called "sinless," yet entering into birth and death is to be imprisoned therein.
To enter birth and death without great skillful means is to inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; therefore, it is said that one will surely die.
Reflecting on such matters, one speaks of becoming even more terrified. This is because if one is forcibly constrained by the Great Teaching, those of small wisdom will not understand it.
To say that one faints and immediately gives rise to slander will inevitably lead to falling into the three miserable realms;

thus, to say one "collapses to the ground" also refers to being deluded and drowning in the mire of ignorance. △ Third, summarizing the exhortation to cease the Mahāyāna transformation, part four: first, contemplating the cessation of the transformation;
second, first, knowing that the great resolve is weak.
The father saw him from afar and said to his attendants, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come.

This clarifies the exhortation to relinquish [the Lesser Vehicle] and rest within the transformation of the Mahāyāna. This section consists of four parts; the first contains two points. Regarding "the father saw him from afar":
because the Small Vehicle is far removed from the Great Vehicle, it is called "afar"; because he is a child with whom [the father] has established a karmic connection, it says "saw him."

Regarding the statement that the teaching is the messenger: since the teaching is spoken based on the wisdom of the messenger, once that wisdom knows there are no [suitable] capacities, then by means of that wisdom, the teaching ceases and the messenger also ceases. If, however, the person is taken as the messenger, it is said to various bodhisattvas:

"There is no need to manifest your sublime and wondrous body so that those of the two vehicles may see it. Therefore, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, you were told to withdraw your bodily fragrance.

The meaning is that he causes those sentient beings to give rise to delusion and attachment; when Samantabhadra enters this Sahā world, he contracts his body to make it small—all of this is for that purpose.
"Do not force them to come" means that since they lack the great capacity (mahā-avakāśa), one fears it might damage their roots of goodness;
therefore, it says "do not force. Zhanran [Zhang’an] said: "There is no need for these people" refers to the gate of contemplation and cessation, intended as a prohibition against [forcing them].
Regarding those who come with forceful intent, one should contemplate the gate of restraint and reflection; this is what is meant by "knowing their great ambition is weak.
△ Second, regarding those whose small ambition is strong:
sprinkle cold water on their face to bring them to their senses, and do not speak with them further.

Sprinkling cold water on the face is the second [method]; it signifies that one has small aspirations and should sever the flow of worldly affairs with ash to eliminate the heat of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

"Face" refers to turning away from birth and death and facing toward *nirvāṇa*. One who attains awakening hears the "small" teaching suited to their capacity, enabling them to leave behind vexation and realize the Four Noble Truths.
Do not [further... *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Lotus Sūtra (likely the *Fahua wenju* by Zhiyi). The final phrase "莫復" (do not further... is incomplete.*
One who engages in such discourse must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna. △ Second, the explanation of the intent behind ceasing the transformation [of beings].
Why is this so? It is because the father knows his son’s disposition to be inferior; he knows himself to be noble and wealthy, which the son finds difficult to accept;
yet, knowing clearly that he is indeed his son, he employs skillful means and does not speak to others, saying, "This is my son."
Why is this? The following section explains the intent behind the cessation of his transformative ministry:

because he was correctly weary of suffering and delighted in emptiness, yet remained intimate with inferior states and lacked a heart of compassion, he feared the Great Dharma as difficult and relied instead upon petty wisdom; thus, he suppressed the Buddha’s original intention and ceased his ministry.
However, it is clearly known that at the sites of twenty-two billion Buddhas, he had previously resolved upon the Great Mind, and it was not the case that he entirely lacked it.
The great capacity [of the disciples] has for now ceased, yet the Great Transformation Buddha’s intention is not yet finished; he awaits a later period.

He does not speak of this to others because, within the former teachings of the Small Vehicle, he spoke according to the intentions of others through skillful means, concealing [his true intent] and being designated as a "gate-keeper of sound" (śrāvaka);
he did not speak according to his own intention, and thus was not called a Bodhisattva. △ Third, the formal clarification of the cessation of transformation.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you wish.
By saying "I now release you," he knew that the person's great capacity was weak;
by saying "go wherever you wish," he knew that the person's minor goodness was strong. For these two reasons, he ceased his great transformation. △ Four.
The transformation was appropriately concluded.
The impoverished son, filled with joy at having experienced something unprecedented, rose from the ground and went to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.

"The impoverished son was filled with joy" (the fourth section below) signifies that the transformation was brought to rest in accordance with his capacity, such that he was no longer constrained by the Great Teaching.
Therefore, because they rejoice and are free from the great sin of slandering the Mahāyāna, they escape the three miserable realms; thus it is said that "from the ground, small goodness arises.
Furthermore, it is said that they "arise" because previously, when they were intended for the Great Dharma, they were bewildered and unable to understand, lying upon the ground of ignorance;
now, by being accommodated with the Small [Vehicle], they are able to awaken, and thus it is said that "from the ground they arise" regarding the Four Noble Truths.

Because he seeks the Dharma of the Way, it is said that he goes to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing; or, because he seeks the Way among the four views, it is said he goes to a poor neighborhood.
Furthermore, as for "neighborhood" (*li*), according to the *Rituals of Zhou* (*Zhouli*), five households constitute a "neighbor" (*lin*) and five neighbors constitute a "neighborhood.
II. Sending two people to entice the two [sons]. Part One: The Equal Teaching Leads to Four. Sub-part One: Leading the Superior [Sons] According to Their Suitability.
The Three Carts.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised an expedient means and secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
"You should go to where that impoverished son is and speak gently to him, saying: 'There is work to be done here; we shall pay you double wages.'"
"You are indeed a poor man's son; if you consent to come, I will employ you. If you ask what you are to do, you may simply say:
'I will hire you to remove the refuse; we two shall work together with you.'"
This refers to the guidance provided by the *Śaikṣa* (Trainee) teachings. In the near term, it guides [beings] with the three vehicles to save their children;

in the distant term, it guides them toward the turning of the wheel at Vārāṇasī through the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*). Now, first, we shall explain the guidance provided by the *Śaikṣa* teachings. The text of the "Parable" chapter consists of four parts: first, employing skillful means to provide a provisional fit;
second, knowing their prior inclinations; third, praising the three vehicles; and fourth, fulfilling their respective wishes. The "Expedient Means" chapter likewise has four parts; now...
The "Leader" (the Buddha) also has four [aspects] from the point where he intends to entice [the son] downward; this is the "Leader on High" regarding the timing of what is appropriate.

At that time, two messengers immediately seek out the impoverished son; having already found him, the Leader on High recognizes the son’s prior disposition and provides the necessary means to present the matter above.
