The Leader on High praises the rarity of the three vehicles; the impoverished son first takes the price, and the Leader on High fulfills his wish through competition.
Regarding the departure from the burning house: initially, when intending to entice and lead them forth, once the great transformation has ceased, one cannot allow them to be abandoned in isolation.

Desiring to establish skillful means, it is said that "he intends to secretly dispatch two people. This refers to the four great disciples, who, being of equal standing [with the Buddha], each take charge of their own portion and do not involve themselves with the bodhisattvas;

hence they are called "two people. If this is discussed in terms of the Dharma, it concerns the causes and conditions and the Four Noble Truths; if discussed in terms of principle, it concerns the ultimate truth.
This is the "active" (saṃskṛta) distinction between the ultimate and the conventional as applied to persons: it refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who initially aspire to the Mahāyāna.
It is said that by dispatching an attendant, one expresses the single ultimate truth; this is the teaching of the One Mahāyāna for the person of a bodhisattva.

Now, it is clarified that the provisional conceals the ultimate, which is designated as "esoteric"; the partial truth is designated as "expedient. Regarding the teachings, the concealment of the *mañjuśrī* (full) syllables is designated as "esoteric," while the pointing toward the *ardha-mātrā* (half) syllables constitutes the expedient.

Regarding the term "expelling" (*chāyana*): it is called "secret" because one internally conceals the practice of a bodhisattva; it is called "expelling" because one externally manifests as a śrāvaka.

As for "having a haggard appearance": within the teachings of the two vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), but instead preaches suffering, impermanence, and impurity—this is what constitutes a haggard appearance. Regarding the person: it refers to those bodhisattvas who conceal their original [nature].

The form displayed by color is a provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) and not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); because it lacks the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), it is said to be "without majestic power.
When it says, "You may go to him," this means that the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*) is adapted to those of lesser capacity;

whereas the Great Teaching (*mahāyāna*) clarifies principles that are direct and substantial, thus it says, "run swiftly to seize him. Because the principles clarified by the Lesser Teaching are circuitous and obscure, it says, "speak slowly."

Regarding this "place of practice," the two paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are the places where afflictions are severed; I shall give you double the price for these.

As for the five precepts and ten wholesome actions, they merely enable one to escape the three miserable realms (*durgati*); however, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can enable one to transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*), which constitutes the first multiple.
Furthermore, while the six practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) can only suppress the afflictions, practicing the Four Noble Truths can [actually eradicate them].
To sever delusions and attain nirvana constitutes the second doubling. If the impoverished son consents, one should know that he possesses the capacity;
this consent means that the teaching is established. If he does not consent, it is because he lacks the capacity, and thus the teaching is not established.

What does he wish to accomplish? Those of the Two Vehicles desire only to eliminate delusions and realize the fruit of verification; they do not concern themselves with purifying Buddha-lands or bringing sentient beings to maturity.

The reason for saying, "We hire you to remove the dung; we two shall also work together with you," is that those of the Two Vehicles possess dull faculties and must rely on the teachings to practice before they can cultivate their tasks. In terms of principle, this refers to wisdom and the Truth mutually supporting one another;
in terms of persons, it refers to the provisional person practicing together with the real person. △ Second, acknowledging and knowing the prior inclinations of the sons.
At that time, the two messengers sought the impoverished son;

having found him, the text says "the two messengers sought the impoverished son" because they had secondly ascertained that he possessed the capacity [for the teaching], thus "having already found him" refers to their prior understanding of the son's underlying disposition. △ Third, the acceptance and praise of the three vehicles.
He related the aforementioned matters in full.
[The phrase] "relating the aforementioned matters" marks the third section: the narration of hiring laborers and receiving praise for the three carts. △ Fourth:
Receiving the wishes of the eldest son.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth; when his father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at him.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth—this concludes the fourth section.

Immediately thereafter, [the Buddha] acted as a leader, so that they might justly emerge from the burning house; this refers to how those of the Two Vehicles, aspiring to the fruit, practice the cause, and thus first inquire.
Because it has value, it is said that he first takes [the price]; taking the path to extinguish it means removing the filth of suffering and its origin.

His father saw his son and felt pity and wonder for him: he pitied him for attaining the fruit of Arhatship and wondered why he did not seek the Buddha-way, for what was lost was great while what was gained was meager;
thus he is said to have "wondered. △ Second, the summary of the intent in four parts.
At first, he employed provisional wisdom to determine the appropriate means;
furthermore, on another day, he saw his son’s body from afar through a window.
This refers to the underlying intent: the spiritual wisdom has long shone forth, having previously established provisional strategies; thus, the arduous pursuit was not merely following after him.
Regarding the beginning of the path of cessation under the tree, the causes and conditions have already been explained above. However, this section of the text contains four intended meanings:
first, the phrase "on another day" implies that he had previously, through provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), long desired to provide an appropriate teaching;

second, seeing his son’s emaciated state indicates that he had long known the skillful means (*upāya*) suited to his preferences; third, it refers to the detachment from the sublime and the attachment to the coarse; fourth, [it concerns] the transformation of the mind.
"Those who have long known" refers to those who understand that they must praise the three vehicles;

"the four intimate teachers instructing their sons" refers to those who have long known that their wishes are now fulfilled and who accept and practice [the teaching]. Now, regarding the first instance: the word "also" (yuè) is used for emphasis.

It intends to lead one to grasp the ground of the Dharma-body, where the capacities of the great and small vehicles have long been known, and where the teachings of the One and Three are bestowed as transformations. Thus, it reiterates the Buddha’s intent and therefore sets forth [this title].
The chapter title uses the terms "also" (yù) and "another day" (tārì). When the two vehicles refer to themselves as "themselves," they mean their own skillful means;
when they refer to others, they mean that which is not the two vehicles—this refers to the Dharma-body. "Day" signifies time, and it also signifies wisdom.

Because one relies on the temporal function of the Dharma-body to employ wisdom to illuminate the capacities of beings, it is called "another day. According to this principle, when true wisdom illuminates reality, it is "self"; when expedient means [illuminates] [reality], it is "other."

When wisdom-illumination employs skillful means to provide uniform instruction for others, it takes up the activities of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as "for others," while the activities of the *nirmāṇakāya* that are not for others are taken as "for oneself.
Alternatively, if one considers the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s own practice regarding the provisional and the real, all are termed "for oneself";

if one considers the Tathāgata’s illumination of the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others, all are termed "for others. This is the method of investigating and encompassing the Dharma.

The temporal application of the body is the expedient wisdom that transforms others; it illuminates the opportune conditions of expediency as being either existent or non-existent, and it illuminates the functions of expediency as being either appropriate or inappropriate.

Since all these are illuminated by expedient wisdom, it is said that on another day, if one understands through this principle, one comprehends the expedient matters of transforming others according to the teachings.
Thus, when the followers of the Two Vehicles comprehend by investigating their own affairs, they achieve such comprehension.

The provisional means for oneself and others: this provisional means is not the matter of the Two Vehicles, and is thus called "other. Although there are two meanings, both are accomplished on another day.
Now, based on what is received by the Two Vehicles and following the text regarding that "other day," we investigate what is received:
it is the reception of the illumination of sentient beings within the Dharmakāya. As for the "window and door": partial views are small; this symbolizes how provisional wisdom illuminates them.

The "partial" (*piānjī*) refers to the remote; because it departs from the great by a small distance, it is called "remote. As for "seeing the son," this refers to having previously planted [the seeds of] the Great [Vehicle], which is termed "son";
because the Great is used as a standard of comparison, it is called "seeing. Because the window and door are partial and narrow, they are not yet suitable for the Great Transformation;
therefore, the Great is suspended and the Small is bestowed. △ Second, leading them to first know that there is the Small.
Emaciated and haggard, defiled by excrement, soil, and dust, and impure;

next, from "emaciated" downwards, the second [term] refers to the leading knowledge that there are minor worldly pleasures—having little power of wisdom from cultivating causes constitutes being "emaciated," having little power of merit from cultivating causes constitutes being "haggard," internal fear of impermanence constitutes being "haggard," and external encounters with... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The eight sufferings are the withering weeds; the four abodes are the soil and dust; ignorance is the grime and filth. △ Third, acknowledging that he has known this for a long time, he must now praise the three vehicles.
He immediately removes his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments, and puts on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes.
With dust covering his body, he holds a refuse-removing vessel in his right hand and appears as if filled with fear.
Third, "immediately casting off his necklaces" refers to the third stage, where the leader first perceives the rarity of the three vehicles;
"casting off his exquisite garments" is a metaphor for concealing the immeasurable merit of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) and the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the forty-two stages.
The *dhāraṇīs* and other such ornaments represent the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*), which is like fine, soft, and superior clothing.
The various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are the implements for adornment. If these garments and ornaments were displayed in full, sons [of the Buddha] would be startled and terrified;

because those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are not fit to behold these marks and signs, he removes them and puts on coarse, tattered clothing, manifesting a body sixteen feet tall—this is the dharma of coarse birth.
The two types of patience refer to those whose bodies are covered in the dust and filth of afflictions—the manifest defilements, conditioned phenomena, and outflows (*āsrava*).
"Holding a broom" refers exclusively to the treatment of the outflowing dharmas of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions), and does not concern the pure wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The left hand is a metaphor for actual wisdom (*prajñā*), while the right hand is a metaphor for expedient wisdom (*upāya*); through the ease of expedient application, one uses this dharma for oneself.

Having severed the fetters and attained Buddhahood, he further uses this to transform others; by manifesting as one who appears to have things to fear, he shows himself to be the same as those who dread birth and death.

Furthermore, there were retributions such as the cold wind and the horse-barley. △ Fourth, receiving and knowing that one’s wishes are fulfilled and practicing accordingly, in seven parts: first, the analogy for the four foundations of mindfulness.
He spoke to the laborers:
"This fourth analogy of instructing a son to work is precisely the seven categories of the *dharmapada* (sections of the path) used to manifest the manner of removing filth.

First, the analogy of speaking to the laborers represents the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), which correspond to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). Second, he caused...
"Exert yourself and do not be indolent" illustrates the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
"O man, do not go elsewhere" illustrates the four bases of power (*ṛddhi-pāda*). "From 'Be well-composed in mind' downward is called 'consolation'" illustrates the five faculties (*indriya*).
"From 'For what reason? downward is called 'the absence of the five faults'" illustrates the five powers (*bala*). The first four [of these]...
The phrase "the second stage of the inner ordinary person" refers to the six [limbs]. The phrase "at that time the elder named him 'son'" is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path.

The phrase "seventh, although he rejoiced at this encounter," and so forth, is called the teaching that constantly orders the removal of filth; it is a metaphor for the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
These two phrases constitute the third stage, the stage of the noble ones. As for the words "all the laborers," this refers to those who are spoken of [in the sutra].

The Tripiṭaka Master explains that the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are a vessel for removing filth and a realm for severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*); thus, the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If one constantly relies on the foundations of mindfulness to practice the Path, one can destroy the four inversions. This refers to the zeal and vigor appropriate to the burning house, which constitutes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
△ Second, the analogy for the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
"You all must exert yourselves and not allow for even a moment of indolence; by means of such skillful methods, you shall draw near to that son.
The instruction "do not allow for even a moment of indolence" is intended to cause them to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

If one gives rise to indolence, one will be unable to extinguish the two evils and give birth to the two virtues; however, through these two forms of diligence, one is able to ignite the fire of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*)."

Pushing one another out of the burning house, they enter the stage of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Because of skillful means (*upāya*), they are able to draw near to their child.
Although the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have not yet attained the principle, the fire’s warmth has already heated the mind; yet it is still remote and cannot be approached.
By means of having first attained the skillful means of warmth, one can then approach it. △ Third, the analogy for the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Later, he spoke again, saying: "Ho, man! You shall always work here; do not go elsewhere. I shall increase your wages.

Whatever you require—such as basins, vessels, rice, flour, salt, or vinegar—do not hesitate or find it difficult to ask for. I also have old and worn-out servants who shall provide whatever you need."
Regarding the third point, "O man": "O" (*dū*) is a word used for startling or awakening, and it is also a term of reproach. A text states that "O" is a shout of rebuke.
Within right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), agitation is itself the factor of wisdom (*prajñā-dharma*). Wisdom is like a man, being of a masculine nature;

the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are factors of concentration (*samādhi-dharma*), like a woman, being of a feminine nature. This is because one cannot be spurred into action by right effort alone.
Because it accords with reality, one is startled awake and reproached so as to cause the mind to abandon distraction and enter stillness; thus it says: "O man!
You must always act in this way and never go elsewhere. One should know that if mindfulness and right effort are not focused and unified, they are not called "constant.
Within the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration does not differ from its object; when one contemplates, there is concentration, and through contemplation, there is concentration.

Because it definitively severs [afflictions] with single-minded focus and remains constantly undisturbed, it says, "Do not go elsewhere again. This still occurs within the process of mutual exclusion;
it is precisely the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) dharma. Regarding the phrase "the price shall be added to you":

because one cannot yet give rise to the true *yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā* (contemplation of reality as it is) through right effort alone, but can give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [wisdom] through contemplation, it is said that "the price is added. All [of this refers to the aforementioned].

Whatever one requires—whether outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), wholesome, auxiliary to the path, or the direct path—all is sought through the contemplation of "as one wishes" (*yathābhiprāya*);

as soon as one desires it, it is obtained. The essence of the four *dhyānas* contains a forest of factors (*aṅga-vana*), like a basin or vessel. The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is coarse like rice, while the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is subtle like flour;
this is the direct path. Within the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths, the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*) is like salt and bitter.

Just as vinegar assists [the flavor], so too does this assist the Path. Just as rice and flour are difficult to eat and must be mixed with salt and vinegar, so too is the True Path difficult to manifest and requires the support of the auxiliary practices (*upāya*).
Do not harbor doubts or difficulties yourself; this concludes the preceding discussion on the True and Auxiliary practices.

Since they are definitively present within the *Yirui guan* (Contemplation of Wishing for Fulfillment), do not doubt them. Because one should regard them as one's own property, it is said: "do not find them difficult," and likewise, "do not harbor doubts."

There are those who are like aged and decrepit servants; if one wishes to directly employ supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to replace their hands and feet, as if employing such servants for labor, this power is also found within the sphere of mental mastery (*kāmacchanda-vaśitā*), yet it is inferior and weak.

Although they are not robust, they are still capable of being employed for tasks. Furthermore, when seeking the principle through the Right Path, because the power of that Right Path is weak, it has not yet been able [to achieve this].

To give rise to true desire, one requires the aids to the Path, such as the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the ten notions (*daśasaṃjñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). These aids to the Path cause the practitioner to engage in contemplation according to their will;

within this very method of contemplation, these dharmas are also present. If one attains these aids, they assist the primary [path], and one thus becomes a person of "liberation through both" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
△ Fourth, an analogy for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
"Be at peace with yourself; I am like your father, so do not worry further.

Regarding 'be at peace with yourself' as the fourth point: it means that you have attained the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) which are stable and difficult to destroy. Regarding 'I am like your father':

because [this stage] is adjacent to True Suchness through patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) and understanding, yet is still a semblance rather than the reality itself, it is said to be 'like a father'; it is also 'like a son.'"
"Do not worry any further" means to allow the mind to find peace by destroying both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). △ Fifth, the analogy of the five powers. Why is this so?
"I am old and aged, while you are young and vigorous; when you work, you never have deceit, indolence, anger, resentment, or complaints;
I do not see these various evils in you at all, as I do in other laborers. From this day forward—"

"Just like a son born [to me], the fifth [point]— 'I am old and you are young'— means that because the Buddha has reached the end of the path and is fully endowed with wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), he is called 'old,' while you,
being at the beginning of the path and not yet possessing wisdom and abandonment, are called 'young and vigorous. This refers to the stage of the *kṣānti* (receptivity) dharma."

Regarding the five faults: by attaining the five powers, one leaves behind the five unwholesome dharmas. Because one attains the power of faith, one does not deceive. Because one attains the power of diligence, one does not become indolent.
Because one attains the power of mindfulness, one does not become angry. Because one attains the power of concentration, one does not harbor resentment.
Because one attains the power of wisdom, one does not bear grudges. As for other practitioners, they are those who, at a distance, seek the various views of external paths.

The principle is called "the work of another"; this refers proximately to the four stages beginning with *uṣmagata*, which still fail to avoid the five faults and are thus also called "the work of another.
This text [describes] that which is free from the five faults, which are precisely the five powers (*pañcabala*). From now on, regarding the phrase "like the child born":
the duration of the sixteen moments of the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) is still long; although the middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) contracts its contemplation, it is not yet [complete].

In a single moment, if one attains the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), this is the final momentary mind of the mundane stage that is adjacent to the ultimate truth and presses upon the noble state;
therefore, this position is called "the son born according to the Dharma," which is the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*). △ Six: An analogy for the Eightfold Noble Path.
Immediately, the elder further gave him a name, calling him "Son. Regarding the phrase "the sixth, the elder further gave him a name, calling him 'Son'":
because one attains the Eightfold Noble Path and enters the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), racing forward together [toward liberation], it is said that he is named "Son.
This refers to the Worldly Supreme Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) and the Truth (satya).

Because it is not long [after the previous], it is said "immediately. The Āgamas speak of five kinds of sons of the Buddha: namely, the four fruits and the pratyekabuddha, who are called the true sons of the Buddha;
as for the bodhisattva, they are sons whose fetters have not yet been severed and whose purpose is not yet accomplished. △ Seventh: The Seven Similes for the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;
for this reason, for twenty years he was constantly made to clear away dung.
The seventh analogy is that of being constantly employed as a laborer: although he considers himself a son, his delusions are not yet exhausted;
because he still dwells in the stage of training (śaikṣa) and has not attained freedom from difficulty, he is made to clear away dung for twenty years.

Furthermore, he knows for himself that he is incapable of inheriting the great [lineage] and must simply rely on the teachings to practice and exhaust suffering. Therefore, it is said: "He still calls himself a lowly hired laborer."

If one attains the first fruit [of the path] and, weary of the small [vehicle], aspires to the great, and if the capacity for the Great Vehicle has been awakened, one should immediately bestow the Mahāyāna;

there would be no further need to progress by severing the remaining residual fetters. It is precisely because they do not abandon their small [vehicle] aspirations that the capacity for the Great Vehicle does not awaken;
therefore, for the time being, they are made to exhaust their outflows in accordance with the teaching. For this reason, it is said that for twenty years he constantly...

Regarding the statement that one was made to remove excrement for twenty years: it is because one attains one unimpeded path and one liberation through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and nine unimpeded paths and nine liberations through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that it is said to be twenty years.
Furthermore, it is said that severing the fetters within the two paths of seeing and cultivation constitutes the twenty years.
Again, it is said that the five lower-tier and five upper-tier fetters constitute the twenty years. Moreover, it is as if...
In the teachings of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), because the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are severed, it is called "twenty years.

Furthermore, it is said that based on the two types of persons (*pudgala*), they together sever the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*); thus it is called "twenty years. Because the capacity for the Two Vehicles has arisen and moved toward the perception of the Buddha, it is said:
"Since I saw my son, twenty years have already passed. If one abides in the stage of the Two Vehicles and is turned toward the Mahāyāna teaching, it is called [the turning of the wheel].

For twenty years he managed the household affairs; these twenty phrases each have their own significance, and this single phrase specifically indicates the stage of struggling to escape from the burning house of the triple world. △ Fourth, the parable of the entrustment, which has two parts:
first, the entrustment of the family estate; second, the initial mind of mutual trust and understanding. First, explaining the mutual trust and understanding.
After this period has passed, their minds come to trust one another, and they enter and exit [the house] without difficulty.
This is the analogy for receiving the family estate: it refers, in the near sense, to receiving the great vehicle as a gift from the burning house and so forth;

and in the remote sense, to receiving the unsurpassed path within the "Teaching of the Dharma" (dharmaparyāya). This is divided into two parts: first, the reception, and second, the entrustment. Each of these is further divided into two, namely, the joint reception and...
The four intentions regarding the granting of the carts within the "Burning House" parable are likewise the four intentions for revealing the Truth (*tattva*) in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Regarding the first section, there are two points: first, the mind’s nature of trust, which corresponds to the aforementioned attainment of escape from calamity;

second, entrusting them with the family business so that they gradually attain prosperity and fulfill their great aspirations, which corresponds to the subsequent section on seeking the carts. Regarding the second section, there are two points: first, the entrustment of the family business.
He immediately took charge of the great carriage bestowed upon him; he was filled with joy at being entrusted with it, for he experienced great delight upon receiving the superior vehicle.

Because his mind was characterized by trust and sincerity, he was granted the family estate; having become thoroughly familiar with and fully cognizant of the affairs of the household, he accomplished his great resolve.
Because his will was harmonious and untroubled, he was entrusted with the family estate, and thus he obtained the estate.

Therefore, this joy arises from degrees of distance; if one had not first instructed them in labor and provided a day’s wage, how could there have been mutual trust, the entrusting of tasks, and the handing over of wealth?

Internally, it corresponds to the three collections of the Tripiṭaka for severing the fetters, being capable of hearing the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, receiving the refutations of Vimalakīrti, and turning to the teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* before the wealth was entrusted. One should know that this is like taking wages for labor.
The "price" refers to the remote cause, which consists of faith; the "entrusting of the task" refers to the proximate cause.
Furthermore, in the previous allegory of the inducement, there was a simultaneous reception beginning from the Bodhi tree and ending with the departure from the house;

there was also a sequential reception beginning from the Dharma-body and ending with the exhaustion of thought. Now, this reception is likewise twofold: the sequential reception begins with the compassionate four flavors that mature [the beings], and ends...
Regarding the ultimate single flavor of the received teachings, the five flavors are discussed in terms of their distance and proximity, as well as their beginning and end.
What is this? It refers to the person standing beside [the Buddha]; what that person says is likened to the *Avataṃsaka*, for this teaching is the very first.

The person standing beside [the Buddha] is likened to the cow, and what they say is likened to milk. Together, these emerge from the Buddha as the twelve divisions of the scriptures; this is the first flavor.
The Tathāgata used this analogy because the people of the two vehicles lacked the capacity and would not accept it;
thus they became bewildered and fell to the ground, for their entire life was like milk. Next, it clarifies the secret dispatching of two men to preach the method of removing filth;

this is a metaphor for the period after the cessation of the Great [Vehicle], when the Three [Vehicles] were bestowed at the Deer Park. Regarding the Small [Vehicle], faith immediately transforms the ordinary person into a sage, just as milk is transformed [into curds].
Regarding the curd within [the milk], it emerges from the twelve divisions of the canon as the ninefold *sūtras*;

this is the second flavor. Next, the characteristics of the mind are clarified: its essence is faith, and its entry and exit are without difficulty. This is illustrated by the period following the Tripitaka, when the *Vaipulya* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* were taught;

these exalt the Great Vehicle and subdue the Small Vehicle. Those who hear the Great Vehicle do not slander it, and those who have been subdued by the Small Vehicle do not regress. This is truly because of the Tripitaka.
Because they receive their daily wages, they are permitted to indulge in praise or censure;

yet, as long as they have not severed their fetters, they are incapable of hearing the exaltation of others, just as previously mentioned regarding the "Gate of Not Accepting Encouragement," nor are they capable of hearing the disparagement of others, just as previously mentioned regarding the "Gate of Not Accepting Admonition.
That they do not now slander or regress is because they trust one another based on their mutual characteristics. Since the relatives have personally realized the Lesser Vehicle, they believe [in it].
Because he has not obtained the price of nirvāṇa in vain, his substance is broken yet he does not become angry;
although it is not his own affair, he does not doubt or slander it. This mind is matured like the production of ghee from curds;

internally, it corresponds to the emergence of the Vaipulya Sūtras from the Sūtra [Piṭaka], which is the third flavor. Next, it clarifies that the elder knows for himself that he will soon die, and so forth.

For example, one whose mind is vast and equal, who possesses the substance of faith, and who enters and exits [the teachings] without difficulty, may subsequently be entrusted with the family business and made to lead the instruction.

When the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is expounded for such a great bodhisattva, having received and understood the various matters and mastered the comprehensive system of the Dharma-gates, their realization of form and mind becomes harmonized, their mental clarity and verbal eloquence increase ever further, and they take even greater delight in it; yet they only regret dwelling in the Lesser Vehicle, which is not the ultimate truth.
"To further permit liberation within one's own portion—how joyful this is! Thus, the mind gradually becomes clear and expansive, and one accomplishes the Great Resolve.
It is like refined butter being produced from clarified butter; it emerges from the Vaipulya [Sūtras] as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, which is the fourth flavor.
Next, when he was about to pass away, he summoned his son; this is a metaphor for the Prajñā[pāramitā].

Later, he judged that their natures were fixed as father and son; they met, and the three vehicles were unified into one. He entrusted them with his wealth and bestowed upon them the records, preaching the teachings of the Lotus Sūtra.
He opened up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and revealed the true aspect. The doubts of the bodhisattvas were removed, and the śrāvakas became Buddhas;
all were brought to nirvāṇa by means of the Tathāgata’s own nirvāṇa—just as clarified butter is extracted from matured cream, so it is from this [sūtra].
The *Prajñāpāramitā* (the *Hē*) brings forth the Great *Nirvāṇa*, which is the fifth flavor.
The four great disciples deeply grasped the Buddha’s intention and explored the sequence of the teachings on the five flavors throughout the beginning and end of his transformation of beings;
the text from which this emerges speaks of "mutual trust in the nature of the mind," meaning that father and son trusted one another. This refers to attaining *nirvāṇa* within the Tripiṭaka.
Since this [teaching] of Purna is not false, the present preaching of this Mahāyāna for the sake of the Bodhisattvas is likewise not false;

this is the son believing his father. The Buddha knows that such individuals have already severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), so that upon hearing they will certainly not slander it;

their untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are sharp, so that upon hearing they will certainly give rise to faith; this is the father believing his son. Because of this, they see the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of sublime marks) and hear...
In the Mahāyāna teachings, this is called "entering," yet it is still subject to censure; seeing only the six-foot [Buddha] preaching the Hīnayāna dharma, this is called "exiting.
Thus, there is no doubt or difficulty regarding the entering and exiting of the Great and Small Vehicles. △ Second, remaining in one's original position.
Yet their place of abiding remains as it was before.

"Their place of abiding remains as it was before" means that although they enter and exit [the world] without difficulty and hear of the Mahāyāna, they consider it the business of bodhisattvas and not within the scope of their own wisdom;
thus, unwilling to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they remain as they were.
The fact that the Han [emperor] did not say he would attain Buddhahood in the future is a summary of the teachings from the *Mahāsannipāta*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Sarpis* (Ghee) [scriptures].
△ Second, the mandate to oversee affairs has two parts; first, the mandate to know the household affairs has four parts, the first of which clarifies the timing.
World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill and knew for himself that he would not live much longer.
He entrusted his household affairs to this Great Vehicle [disciple], who was commanded by the Buddha to propagate and teach the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

"Will not live much longer" means that when the conditions for transformation are present, one responds as being born; when the conditions for transformation are exhausted, one passes away as being dead. Now, as the conditions for transformation were nearing their end, [he entrusted the teachings].
He should apologize for not having done so sooner. △ Second, the actual explanation of receiving the family estate:
He says to the impoverished son, "I now possess much gold, silver, and precious treasures; my storehouses are overflowing with them.
You should know fully how much is to be taken and how much is to be given to you."
He says to the impoverished son: "I now possess much gold and silver. [This constitutes the second part of the command to know the household affairs.
Here, "gold" refers to the principle of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), and "silver" refers to the principle of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

The True Truth (*satya*) elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* does not exceed these two; yet, it is said that he "possesses much. This is because, although the principle is not manifold, it may be described as "much" by way of its various gateways (*mukha*). This is the analogy.
Just as space is not eighteen [in itself], yet by refuting the eighteen dharmas it is called the "eighteen emptinesses";

so too, the Chapter on Encouraging Study clarifies that all dharma-gates are treasuries of jewels. The gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the storehouse of the one hundred and eight samādhis;

the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the realm of the eighteen emptinesses. Within these treasuries of concentration and wisdom, according to both the universal and particular teachings, are contained and concealed all things.
Because meditative concentration and wisdom are without deficiency, overflowing from within and surging outward, it is said that they "overflow within.
As for the degree of this abundance, it arises from the teaching of Prajñā, which has two gates: the extensive and the concise.

A Bodhisattva practicing Prajñā should understand the characteristics of these two—the concise is "few," while the extensive is "many. Practice for oneself is called "appropriating," whereas transforming others is called "teaching."
Because it was said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "You should preach this for the sake of the bodhisattvas," it is here stated, "You all know this.
△ Third, the admonition to embody my mind:
"My mind is thus; you should embody this meaning. Why is this? Because now I and you are no different.

"My mind is thus" marks the third section, the admonition regarding the essence of my mind. "My mind" refers to the Buddha’s taking Prajñā as his mind; you who now transmit the lamp should speak in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.
Furthermore, regarding the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), their fundamental understanding is the emptiness of dharmas through analytical disintegration;

you should take this meaning as your life. This means that when transmitting the teaching, you must admonish others to accord with me and realize the emptiness of dharmas. Moreover, [the text continues: "My mind is thus... [and so forth].
In the past, you were commanded to transmit the Lamp to others; now you know that the Buddha has caused me to recognize the gateway to the essence.
Therefore, it is said: "One should realize this meaning; now I and you are indeed not different. There are three ways to explain this:

first, being empowered to speak so as to be no different from the Buddha; second, from the perspective of principle (*li*), because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); and third, [the realization] attained through this.
One should know that they are not different; Subhūti, because the Tathāgata’s suchness is one suchness, and there is no second suchness, they are therefore said to be not different.

Third, regarding the present time, it is only now that he realizes the father-son relationship is by nature originally non-different, whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles merely claimed themselves to have been granted a different [status]. Fourth, the command not to let it be lost.
"You should apply yourself with diligence so as not to let it be lost.
Regarding "you should apply yourself with diligence," this is the fourth instruction. As for "so as not to let it be lost," there are two meanings:
first, that you, as a bodhisattva, must preach the teachings of Prajñāpāramitā without letting them be lost; second, from the perspective of ultimate principle, this is your own dharma.
Since these will be used at a later time, do not let them be lost or wasted. △ Second, receiving the mandate and taking charge, in four parts:
First, the formal reception and taking charge.
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of all the goods, gold, silver, rare treasures, and various storehouses.
The correct reception of the command and its understanding may be explained according to the text. △ Second, the mind is free from seeking or grasping;
that is, there is not even the slightest intention to seek or grasp a single morsel of food.
Yet he harbored no desire to take even a single morsel of food; although Subhūti preached the Prajñāpāramitā, he considered it the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, saying, "I have no share in this.
△ Third, remaining in his original place.
However, because they remain in their original state, they have not yet abandoned their inferior mind.

Furthermore, those who have not yet abandoned their inferior mind while still dwelling in their original state—though they may aspire to the Great [Vehicle] while abiding in the stage of an Arhat—have not yet definitively declared their intent to become Bodhisattvas;
nor have those who have not yet abandoned their inferior mind, though they may feel shame for the Small [Vehicle].
The preceding statement regarding "renunciation" refers to the realization of the Lesser Vehicle. △ Fourth, the Father knows the Son’s Intent:
After a short time had passed, the father perceived that the son’s mind was gradually becoming open and at ease; he had achieved his great ambition and came to despise his former thoughts.
Furthermore, after a short time had passed, the father understood the son’s intention; this refers to the parable of receiving the carriage from above.
Since he had already disparaged his former mind and desired to seek the Great Way, the great capacity (*mahā-śakti*) had already been awakened.

When it is asked what "a short time" refers to, one answer states: it is after the *Prajñāpāramitā* has been preached, when [the Buddha] travels and observes elsewhere, seeking out and contemplating that which was previously received.

When one reflects on such matters as whether it is a loss or no loss to give rise to a mind that delights in the gateways of the vehicle of practice (*yāna*), this is precisely the time when the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened.
Because at this time one is not far from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that "in a short time.

Furthermore, why do we know that the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened at the time when the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī* (The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) was being taught? It is because within the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī*, the seven [stages] are clarified.
The various skillful means, immeasurable and whether gradual or sudden, all arise from a single Dharma. Upon hearing this teaching, one immediately reflects:
"The three Piṭakas and the three vehicles of the past all arise from this single Dharma; likewise, these three vehicles should also enter into the One.
When reflecting in this way, one gradually becomes clear and expansive, and the great mind is immediately awakened; therefore, it is said that one accomplishes the great resolve.

...and so forth. △ Second, the formal entrustment of the family inheritance, in two parts. First, the entrustment of the family inheritance, in four parts. First, the time of the entrustment of the family inheritance:
"When about to pass away. "About to pass away" clarifies the timing; it refers to when the Tathāgata’s work of transformation was nearing its end after eight years at Vulture Peak.
This was also the time when he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and announced his entry into *nirvāṇa*. The *Fajie lun* by Bodhiruci states:

"The Buddha began preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* forty-two years after his attainment of enlightenment. This refers to the passage stating that for over forty years he kept it secret and did not speak of it.
△ Second, the command to assemble the multitude as witnesses.
He then summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders; when they had all gathered, he summoned his son.

[The phrase] "the second assembly of the multitude" refers to those disciples transformed by twenty trillion Buddhas, who were called "sons" because their great faculties had matured and they had gathered from the ten directions like clouds; they were surrounded by the fourfold assembly mentioned above.

This is it. Furthermore, regarding the gathering of kinsmen: the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body throughout the ten directions act as his kinsmen, for these hosts of manifestations were all fellow-practitioners of Śākyamuni in the past;
they were all together with the Tathāgata at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas where they jointly engaged in transformation and edification.
Since they all stand in the relationship of uncles and cousins, this [gathering] is used for that purpose.
Regarding those who are kings among kinsmen, there is no scripture—whether gradual or sudden—that does not extol this as the king of sūtras in its definitive exposition;

it benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, its arising and ceasing occur at specific times, and each section is distinct, thus it is called a "kingdom," with all declaring it the foremost, which is precisely what constitutes a king.
Furthermore, since this sūtra synthesizes and harmonizes all teachings, is it not a gathering of kingdoms?

Because it is the King [of Sutras], it was already compiled therein from the outset within the *Anantārthasūtra*. As that text states: "First, the Four Noble Truths and the twelvefold dependent origination were taught;
next, the Vaipulya sūtras in twelve divisions were taught; and finally, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the ocean-like emptiness were taught.
This is the reason it is named "The Universal Collection," for it integrates all sutras and brings together the gradual and sudden teachings into a single harmony.
The assembled kings, as well as Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas, are all Equal-Enlightened Ones (Samyaksambuddhas) and are thus called "Ministers.
Those from the first to the ninth stages are of the Kṣatriya lineage of Dharma Kings; those who have cultivated the thirty minds are "Householders.
All of these were transformed by Śākyamuni. △ Third, the conclusion: the reunion of father and son.
He then made this public declaration: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, begotten by me.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, he fled and wandered in hardship for more than fifty years. His original name was so-and-so, and my own name is so-and-so.
Formerly, while in that city, I searched for him with deep anxiety; now, unexpectedly meeting him here, I have found him. This is truly my son."
I am truly his father.
This third assembly for the reunion of father and son means that he has indeed received instruction from me;
he is truly my son, having attained understanding through me and being born of me. I have indeed constantly taught the Great Dharma to him in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas.

Therefore, you should know that I am truly the father in such-and-such a city. It should be understood that while this sutra abounds in texts in the Western lands (India), it is very scarce here in this land (China).
One might perhaps speak of the names of former kingdoms and lands, as in the case of the causes and conditions of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;
however, here we have omitted the names for brevity and simply state "a certain person. These sentient beings turn their backs on this Mahāyāna.

Because ignorance has fled into the darkness of birth and death, it is said that he abandoned me and ran away; because he has undergone the trials of the six realms of existence, it is said that more than fifty years have passed.

Since he was originally in his native city, harboring anxiety and searching for [me], he has constantly used the two wisdoms (*dvividha-jñāna*) from within the ground of the primordial *dharmakāya* to observe and seek those with the capacity for transformation. It is only today that the resonance between cause and effect has been realized; therefore, it is so stated.
Suddenly, while in this place, he encountered and saw him. △ Fourth, the formal entrustment of the family estate:
"All the wealth and property I now possess are yours, my son; all that has previously been disbursed or received is known to you."
Now, that which I possess—the fourth and final entrustment of my family estate—should be understood as all the myriad practices and myriad virtues of the Mahāyāna;

thus it is called "all that I possess. That which was previously brought forth and entrusted to this son refers back to what was formerly assigned to him in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Daipin*):
the extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā*, both common and uncommon dharmas.

Because that which you know belongs to you, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, rather than extensively explaining all other modes of practice. △ Second, the explanation of joy.

At that time, World-Honored One, the impoverished son, upon hearing these words from his father, was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before, and he thought to himself:
"Originally, I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now, this treasure store has come to me spontaneously."

This refers to those who, having previously received great vehicles upon which they were seated, experienced something unprecedented; yet, looking back at themselves, they had no aspiration for the Buddha-way.
Now, suddenly hearing that they have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, it is said that "what was not sought has been spontaneously attained.

One should know that in the past, their original intent in the Tripiṭaka did not seek the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna), and because they felt shame regarding the Lesser Vehicle, their hopes were severed; thus, they did not seek it within the Prajñāpāramitā either.
Although he has obtained it, because it was not his own portion, he did not seek it; though he did not seek it, he has now obtained it of itself, and for this reason he rejoices.
△ Second, combining the analogies, part one: combining the analogy of the father and son who lost each other.
The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata; we are all like his sons.

Regarding the analogy of the wealthy elder and the son who has lost each other, there are four parts to the preceding analogies; here, however, the father and son are combined as a whole to encompass the remaining meaning.
The Tathāgata corresponds to the father, and "like" (or "resembling") corresponds to the son. It should be understood that this "likeness" carries two meanings.

First, taking those of great capacity as his children: because they had not yet escaped [the mundane] since ancient times and, not being in the true stage, still resided among the external ordinary beings (bālapṛthagjana), it is said they are "similar" (*sadṛśa*).
Second, taking those of small capacity as his children: because those of small capacity resemble the root-nature (*indriya*) of the Mahāyāna;

however, since these children have turned their backs on their father, they are disparagingly called "similar. Regarding the first interpretation, the commentary on the chapter title states: "They have already attained entry into the truth (*satya*)."
This word "seemingly" (*sadr̥śa*) is a response to the following: when this son fled from his father, it was therefore said to be "seemingly.
At the beginning of this chapter, it was explained that when the son attained enlightenment, your question was incorrect. △ Second, the analogy of the father and son meeting.
The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons.
[In the analogy of] "The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons," this corresponds to the father and son meeting;

within this, it specifically corresponds to the elder seeing his son and immediately recognizing him. △ Third, the correspondence to the analogy of the pursuit and enticement, in two parts: first, the correspondence to the dispatching of attendants.
People pursue the two [extremes], yet the union of the two gates lacks the opportune moment.
World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we undergo all manner of feverish afflictions within birth and death, remaining deluded and ignorant.

This section combines the "pursuing from above" (*shang-zhui*) and the "pursuing from the side" (*bang-zhui*). While there were two types of inducement (*you*) in the former [section], here they are likewise two.

In the preceding text, first a bystander was sent to pursue him, then he pursued him again, and finally he let him go. Here, the two gates are combined: having no affinity (*wu-ji*), why was he caught?

He thought to himself that he was without fault; this corresponds to the absence of a great affinity (*wu-da-ji*). △ Second, combining the cessation of transformation for those with strong minor aspirations.

They take pleasure in and are attached to inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*). Those who take pleasure in and are attached to inferior teachings are here joined with those of "inferior resolve" (*hīnāśaya*), yet this does not accord with [the principle of] relinquishment.
△ Second, combining the dispatching of two people to entice the two: First, combining the simultaneous instruction to lead them; first, combining the full recounting of the aforementioned matters.
"Today the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
Second, it accords with the wishes of the worthy sons:
'Within this, we shall apply ourselves with diligent vigor to attain the price of a single day’s wage—Nirvana—and having obtained this, [we shall rejoice].'"

With great joy in their hearts, they considered themselves sufficient and said to one another: "Because we have applied ourselves with diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma, what we have obtained is vast and abundant.
Among us, those who apply themselves with diligent effort shall, by following the superior path, attain Nirvana; those who follow the inferior path shall remove filth."

This corresponds to the previous section on "first taking the price. △ Second, the correspondence regarding the inquiry and reception. First, the correspondence regarding the initial intention to provide a suitable teaching.
Now, the World-Honored One already knew us;
this corresponds to the previous "inquiry and reception" analogy which had four parts, but here we only correspond three parts and do not correspond to the actual teaching itself.

This also refers to the aforementioned diligent application of removing filth; once this is accomplished, it is already inclusive [of the latter], and thus need not be combined again. Above it was said that he saw from afar;
now it is said that he knows beforehand. △ Second, combining [the points] shows that there is a small amount of prior knowledge.
The mind is attached to base desires and delights in inferior teachings.
Previously it was said they were emaciated and haggard; now it is said their minds are attached to base desires. △ Third, combining the previous knowledge with the praise of the three vehicles.
He then sees that they are left free and not subjected to discrimination, [thinking], "You shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

Previously it was said that he immediately removed his necklaces and put on coarse, tattered clothes; now it is said that he sees them being left free and not subjected to discrimination regarding their share of the treasure-store.
△ Fourth, the analogy of the entrustment is combined with the teaching, in two parts: first, combining the entrustment of the family estate; second, first...
Combining the aspects of mind, body, and faith, there are two parts. First, combining the body and faith:
The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, has preached the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

This combines the analogy of entrusting the family estate mentioned above; since there is both the reason for the entrustment and the act of entrustment, the present combination likewise consists of two parts. First: [The reason for the entrustment].
I believe that the two commissions and the two tasks now merge into one. Furthermore, I believe there are two aspects:

first, those who, by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), speak of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—what was formerly called the cause of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—is now held to be the fruit of the Two Vehicles.

Now it is clarified that because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna is taught while carrying along the skillful means of the Three Vehicles, it is said: "by the power of skillful means. At this point...
We previously stated that the Mahāyāna Dharma is also characterized by the ease of both entering and emerging through the power of skillful means;

it emerges by distinguishing the Two Vehicles and enters through the Buddha’s wisdom-power to clarify the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If you do not embody this faith, how could you clarify the Buddha’s wisdom before us?
△ Second, "merging while still remaining in their original place."
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day’s wages for nirvāṇa, considering this a great gain; thus we have no aspiration or seeking for this Mahāyāna.
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day’s wages for nirvāṇa, and having descended from here, we remain as we were in our original place.
△ Second, the combined section on receiving the mandate and inheriting the family enterprise. First, the combined section on receiving the mandate and inheriting the enterprise:
"Furthermore, we rely upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom to reveal and expound it for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
Regarding this, one who is fit to inherit the family estate possesses both the mandate and the acceptance; now, however, there is only the fitness for acceptance. There are four types of acceptance:

first, accepting the mandate and inheriting the estate; second, having no desire for acquisition; third, not abandoning what is inferior; and fourth, the mind gradually becoming expansive and at ease.
Now, there is only the fitness for two of these: first, accepting the mandate and inheriting the estate. △ Second, the fitness for having no desire for acquisition. Part one: the actual application.
Yet, regarding this, I myself have no aspiration.
Thus, by not aspiring to this and by relinquishing it, one simultaneously attains all else.
"Having no aspiration" means that I clarify that it is through the Buddha’s bestowed power that [the teaching] is spoken in accordance with the Buddha’s mind; therefore, I do not aspire to it.
Aspiration. △ Second, the explanation of the underlying intent:
"Why is this? Because the Buddha, knowing that our minds delight in inferior teachings, has spoken to us according to our capacities through the power of skillful means;
yet we did not realize that we were truly the sons of the Buddha."

Why is this? The following passage explains the intention of having no desire for gain: by means of skillful power (*upāya-bala*), [the Buddha] speaks according to the minds of those of the Hīnayāna, saying that there is no portion [of the Dharma].
Because of this, they do not know that they are truly sons of the Buddha; thus, they do not accept the Buddha.
One should know that when [the Buddha] speaks according to us through skillful power, the Buddha employs skillful power to share the Dharma of true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) with these two [groups].
Based on what has been taught, we did not recognize the meaning of "not shared" (asādhāraṇa), and thus we did not know that we were truly sons of the Buddha.

△ Second, the entrustment of the family business in its entirety, in two parts: first, the entrustment of the business itself; second, first, clarifying that the Buddha is without stinginess regarding the Great Dharma.
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One is without stinginess regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
Regarding this entrustment of the family business, there are two aspects: the act of entrusting and the joy [thereof]; likewise, the present case also possesses these two.

Furthermore, while the aforementioned entrustment of the business had four parts, here they are combined as one; within this, the initial entrustment has two parts, the first of which clarifies the Buddha.
This is based on the great absence of parsimony. △ Second, the explanation of "absence of parsimony.
Why is this so? We have been true sons of the Buddha since ancient times, yet we have delighted only in the Lesser Dharma.
Had we possessed a mind that delights in the Great, the Buddha would have taught us the Mahāyāna Dharma. Within this sutra, it is taught that there is only one [vehicle].

In the past, while riding [in the assembly], he disparaged before the Bodhisattvas those Śrāvakas who delight in the Lesser Dharma; yet in reality, the Buddha teaches and transforms beings through the Mahāyāna.

The two explanations for his lack of parsimony are precisely because they delighted in the Lesser and did not receive the Great early on; in this sutra, the latter part cites the present to provide proof.
Since the principle has been one and the same from the past until now, we know that the three [vehicles] of the past were not real; they were merely taught because [beings] were as yet incapable.
Thus, prior to the Great Vehicle, the small vehicle was disparaged in order to cause them to abandon the false and grasp the true. This was certainly not out of stinginess;
rather, it was said so because the Buddha truly sought to teach and transform them through the Mahāyāna. △ Second, the combined joy.
Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind with any aspiration, yet now this great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously;
all that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been obtained.
This harmonious joy is also the meaning of the aforementioned "three things not sought.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

△ Second, the two verses in praise [of the Buddha’s grace]. First, the verse summarizing the preceding dharma and analogy; second, praising the profundity of the Buddha’s grace. The first section further has two parts: first, the verse summarizing the dharma-exposition.
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s voice and teaching; with joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before. The Buddha spoke to the śrāvakas:
"When one attains Buddhahood, the unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking.
These two lines of verse constitute the explanation through the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). Within this, there is no verse on "not seeking," but only on "obtaining spontaneously.

△ Second, the explanation by analogy (*upamānadeśanā*), which has two parts: first, the verse on the opening of the analogy; second, the verse on the application of the analogy. Regarding the first part, there are four sections, the first of which is the verse on the father.
Regarding the first verse of the "Son's Loss": the son turns his back on his father and departs.

For example, it is like a young boy, immature and lacking understanding, who abandons his father and flees, wandering far away to other lands and traveling through various countries for more than fifty years.
These one and a half lines merely praise the son’s departure from his father and omit the return to his native land; however,
in the preceding "Parable of the Burning House," it was explained that the kingdom, cities, towns, and villages ruled by the elder were broad in scope,
whereas here it is explained that the impoverished son’s transmigration through the three realms is termed "various kingdoms" and his passage through the six destinies is termed "fifty-odd years."

"Flowing through various lands" refers to those śrāvakas who wander and transmigrate throughout the five realms of existence, entering birth and death like drifting duckweed or broken twigs, reaching every possible destination. II.
Verses on the Father Seeking His Son and Stopping Midway. Part One: Verses on Not Finding the Son.
His father, filled with anxiety and concern, searched for him in all directions.
These seven lines are a verse summarizing the preceding prose on the father’s failure to find his son; there were two sections in the prose, and this verse likewise has two.
The first half-line summarizes the failure to find the son, while the subsequent six and a half lines summarize the exhaustion from searching for him.
The preceding verse concerns not abandoning one's household affairs because of the loss of a single child. As for "searching in all four directions," this differs from what preceded;

whereas the former "four directions" referred to inferring the truth according to the Four Noble Truths, the present "four directions" refers to seeking among the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) for a sentient being who may be saved. △ Second, the verse on ceasing [the search].
Having grown weary from his search, he settled in a single city where he built a residence and amused himself with the five desires.

His family was immensely wealthy, possessing vast quantities of gold, silver, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearls, and lapis lazuli; they owned elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, palanquins, carriages, and vehicles, as well as extensive lands and numerous servants and dependents.
Their income and profits were so great that they extended throughout other countries, and they engaged in trade and commerce as merchants and traders.
There was no place where he was not surrounded by thousands of millions of followers who paid him homage;

he was constantly cherished by kings, and all the ministers and noble clans revered him together. Because of these various circumstances, those who came and went were numerous; he was thus wealthy and possessed such great power and influence.
"Building a dwelling" refers to the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) within other lands;

it means establishing the house of compassion and relying upon the abode of the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*). "The multitude coming and going" refers to the bodhisattvas from various lands coming and going to listen to the Dharma.
The Record states that "stopping suddenly at one city": "suddenly" (*don*) refers to being exhausted or weary, which signifies the manner of manifesting traces.
To "stop" while being in want is likewise not to act; it is simply to seek the opportunity for the child within this very state.
Now, it may also be said that "sudden" means to settle, and "stopping" means to abide—to dwell securely therein while awaiting the opportunity for the child.
One should know that the construction of a house and dwelling refers to lands with remainder, wherein the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) naturally manifests its excellence.

The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), yet it exists fundamentally; because it further exercises compassion based upon emptiness therein, it is said to be "constructed.
△ Third, the verse transcends [the previous] and his anxious concern deepens.
As his years grow old, he becomes increasingly anxious for his son, thinking day and night that the time of death is approaching and that his foolish son has abandoned him.
"What shall become of the various goods in the storehouses over these fifty-odd years?

These two lines express a profound intensification of anxiety through the use of *atiśaya* (superlative) verse. "Increasing anxiety" (*yì yōu*) signifies that the concern becomes ever more intense and severe.
However, while the preceding passage contained two meanings, here the verse merely commemorates the suffering of having previously lost one's son, with no other recourse.

The reason for my anxiety is recorded in the *Ear-Marks*: it merely praises how the son turned his back on his father and departed, which represents the sorrow of losing a son and the absence of the joy of gaining one.
Both the loss of sorrow and the attainment of joy reside within the father’s breast;

therefore, at the time of the loss, he already harbors joy because he knows for certain that the son will return later. Looking afar at the conditions and capacities [of beings], they do not yet equal those of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "contemplating day and night," some say that acting for oneself is "night" and benefiting others is "day. This is not correct.
One should know that "day" (sù) refers to early morning—that is, rising at dawn—and "night" (yè) refers to evening—that is, the hour of dusk.
Thus, "day" represents the beginning of the great transformation, while "night" represents its end. The beginning and end of this great transformation may be understood by analogy with these times.

If one knows that even a sixteen-foot Buddha constantly preaches impermanence as a transformation for those with desires, and at the time of his end, he proclaims extinction limb by limb—if one were to say that his own practice constitutes "night," how could he be practicing while also saying, "the time of my death is approaching"?
△ Fourth, the verse following the prose on the son encountering his father has two parts; first, the verse on seeking food and clothing.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from kingdom to kingdom;
sometimes he obtained something and sometimes he obtained nothing, until he became emaciated by hunger and malnutrition, with sores and scabs breaking out upon his body.
These two and a half verses correspond to the third section above, "Gradually Returning to the Father. The prose above contained two parts; now these verses also contain two.
The first two lines of verse describe the cause for approaching the father, which arises from seeking food and clothing.

The phrase "from village to village" refers to the mutual interaction of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and objects (*viṣaya*), just as villages constitute a kingdom. Cultivating tainted wholesome deeds (*sāsrava-kuśala*) is like having something [to sustain one].

One attains the cultivation of untainted goodness; yet, as if having nothing to obtain, one does not receive the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna, becoming hungry and lacking the power of function, thus emaciated by a lack of great merit.
When views and afflictions arise from within this state of having or lacking goodness, it is like a festering sore.
△ Second, the verse on reaching the native city.
Gradually proceeding, he arrives at the city where his father dwells.
Next, gradually proceeding through the latter half of the verse, he draws near to his father’s city. △ Second, the verse on the analogy of the meeting between father and son, in two parts:
first, the verse on the son seeing his father, in three parts; first, the verse on the cause for seeing his father.
Through successive rounds of hired labor, he eventually arrived at his father’s house.
Regarding these six lines and a half of verse, the preceding section on the son seeing his father consisted of four [lines], whereas this current verse has only three;
the first half-line describes the cause by which he saw his father—namely, that it was through hired labor that he ultimately reached his father’s house. △ Second, the verse on seeing [his father].
The marks of a father:
At that time, the elder sat upon a lion throne within his gate under a great jeweled canopy, surrounded by his kinsmen and attended by various people;
some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, while others recorded the income and expenditure of his property in written ledgers.
Next, from "At that time, the elder... downward, there are two and a half verses following the third section on the signs of seeing his father.

While the preceding section clarifies the location where he sees his father—that being the side of the gate—here, by stating that the elder is "within the gate," the specific location is also included.
The description of the great jeweled canopy and so forth constitutes the actual signs of seeing his father.
"Everywhere there are lion thrones" means that the King’s Dharma-body is both the Teacher and the Sovereign. "The retribution is the elder;

the notes and vouchers are the bestowal of prediction" means that these clearly illustrate the practice of cultivation. Zhiyi (Zhang’an) said: "Using the extensive to manifest the concise constitutes the commentary (*zhù*);
the conferral of the decision constitutes the prediction (*jì*); the four great vows constitute the voucher (*quàn*); and the practice of cultivation constitutes the voucher-statement (*shū*).”
The *Súwén* states: "To record things is called a *zhù* (annotation). The *Wénxīn diáolóng* says: "A *quàn* (bond) means to bind together;

it refers to clear and explicit stipulations made to guard against sincerity and deceit. Thus, its character form consists of 'half' (*bàn*) and 'divide' (*fēn*). Therefore, in the Zhou dynasty it was called a *pànshū* (divided document), and a *quàn* is also a *qì* (seal/contract).
In antiquity there were iron bonds (*tiěquàn*) to solidify oaths and pledges. It is further said that small bonds or short writings are termed [small *quàn*].
This is the commentary. △ Third, the verse on the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance:
When the impoverished son sees his father’s great wealth, nobility, and majestic dignity, he thinks him to be a king or someone like a king;
struck with alarm and wondering at himself why he has come here, he reflects within himself: "If I remain for long, I may be coerced or forcibly compelled to labor."
Having reflected thus, he hurried away, inquiring after a poor neighborhood where he might go to seek employment as a hired laborer.
From the third line of the passage "The impoverished son saw his father," there are three lines and a half which constitute the verse on the fourth point: the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.
△ Second, the verse on the father seeing the son, divided into two parts: first, the verse on the place where he saw the son.
At that time, the elder was on the lion throne.
Regarding this single verse, the father’s perception of his son involves four aspects: first, seeing the location; second, recognizing him upon seeing him;
third, rejoicing upon seeing him; and fourth, having his wishes fulfilled. Now, this verse summarizes only two of these; one should know that the first half-verse summarizes the aspect of seeing.
The place where the son was. △ Second, the verse on recognizing the son upon seeing him:
"From afar he saw his son and silently recognized him.
The second half-line from "From afar" [onward] versifies the meaning of "seeing the son and immediately recognizing him" mentioned above. △ Third, the verse on pursuing [the son].
Regarding the two parts of the analogy for enticement, first, the verse dispels the bystanders;
second, the verse urges the gatekeeper that there is no receptive capacity [in the son], whereupon he commands the messenger to pursue and seize him. The impoverished son is startled and cries out.
△ Second, the verse on the gate of admonishing those without the capacity;
they fall to the ground in confusion and distress.
△ Third, the verse on the cessation of the transformative activity.
This man thought to himself, "I shall certainly be killed; what use have I for food and clothing that would lead me to this place?
The elder knew his son was foolish and narrow-minded, and thus did not believe his words, nor did he believe him to be his father.
△ Second, the two verses on sending two people to entice the two [sons]. First, the verse on hiring the men according to the instructions.
First, the verse on the appropriate expedient means:
"By means of this expedient, you should further dispatch other men who are one-eyed, short-statured, ugly, and lacking in majesty; you may speak to them thus:"
"I shall hire you to remove all manner of filth and excrement, and I will pay you double the wage.

These three verses illustrate the analogy of hiring labor; the preceding prose section contains four points: first, the provision of skillful means; second, obtaining [the labor] immediately upon seeking it;
third, the description of the hiring; and fourth, receiving the wage for removing the filth. Here, however, only two points are versified, namely the first two.

This verse refers to the first [section] concerning the employment of skillful means. "One-eyed and short-statured" (miaomu cuolou): "one-eyed" is a metaphor for the partial wisdom of emptiness belonging to the Two Vehicles;

the *Shuowen* dictionary states that "miao" means one eye is small. "Short-statured" (cuo) refers to being vertically deficient, meaning they do not exhaust the source of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
"Ugly" (lou) refers to being horizontally narrow, meaning they lack the adornment of the manifold virtues of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "lacking majesty and virtue": it is not that he lacks majesty because he does not possess the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); rather, it means he lacks virtue because he does not possess the [four] extraordinary qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
△ Second, the verse on fulfilling his wishes:
Upon hearing this, the impoverished son rejoiced and followed along, clearing away filth and purifying the various rooms.
