The impoverished son hears this and utters the following verse, which is the fourth: "Taking the Price.
"To clean the rooms" refers to the rooms of the six sense faculties, meaning the dwelling of the five aggregates. II. The verse on the instruction to act as a search and acquisition has four parts;
first, the verse on the initial intention to provide what is appropriate.
The elder constantly sees his son through the window.
These four and a half verses correspond to the four sections of the preceding prose instruction;
the first half-verse corresponds to the section on "at the window. △ Second, the verse praises the prior knowledge that [the son] was small.
"Reflecting on how my son is foolish and inferior, delighting in base matters.
This reflects the second half-verse of the preceding section, which describes seeing his son emaciated and weak. △ Third, the verse on abandoning the sublime and clinging to the coarse.
Thereupon, the elder put on worn-out, soiled garments, took up a dung-removal tool, and went to where his son was.
In this, the elder donned the lowest of the three types of clothing—this verse line indicates that he cast off the fine and put on the coarse. △ Fourth, the verse on instructing the son to work.

Using skillful means, he spoke to him nearby, urging him to work diligently, saying: "This will increase your wages; furthermore, you shall have oil for anointing your feet, food and drink in abundance, and thick, warm bedding.
Thus he spoke these harsh words to urge him to work diligently, yet he also used gentle words, saying: "You are like my own son."

In the fourth verse, regarding the seven categories of Dharma teachings for correctly instructing the sons [of the Buddha]: the "four foundations of mindfulness" (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) are for making them diligent;
the "four right efforts" (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni) follow next. From the line "Since I have increased your value," one verse refers to the "four bases of psychic power" (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ).
Alternatively, it is said that the analogy of oil applied to the feet enabling one to walk through deep water represents the supernormal powers (abhijñā); furthermore, oil can...
The removal of wind is analogous to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Having sufficient food and drink" refers back to the aforementioned rice and flour.

"Thick and warm mats and bedding" refers to the four types of meditative cultivation: *dhyāna*, *bhāvanā*, *vāsanā*, and *abhyāsa*. Because one cultivates these concentrations, one is able to eliminate discursive movement.
Such bitter words as "you should diligently practice" constitute a summary verse for the fourth stage, "Peaceful Abiding."

The fifth consolation is that there are no five faults; once the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are perfected, one is then able to endure harsh speech. Furthermore, with gentle speech, half of the practice is complete.

The general verse above [concerns] the sixth, the letter *kṛ* (作), which refers to the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). The seventh, "causing constant practice," refers to the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
These thirty-seven factors of the path (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*) are commonly discussed as the seven factors of enlightenment in the context of the stage of the child (*putrabhūmi*).
Because the eightfold path is presented here in its sequential order prior to the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path precedes the seven factors of enlightenment.

△ Fourth, the verse on the entrustment through analogy has two parts: first, the verse on receiving the family business; second, the verse on the mind’s manifestation of trust. First, the verse on the mind’s manifestation of trust.
The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually causes [the heir] to enter and exit.
Within these three and a half verses concerning the management of the household affairs, there are two intended meanings.

First, regarding "the elder possesses wisdom," the latter half-verse summarizes the mental state of mutual trust, which constitutes the entering and exiting. Second, the verses on entrusting the management of the affairs [of the family]. 3.
The first verse describes his receiving the command and taking charge;
for twenty years he managed the household affairs, showing him the gold, silver, pearls, and crystal, and ensuring he understood all their income and expenditure.
Following the "twenty years" section, the second part consists of three lines which are a verse summarizing the preceding detailed account of inheriting the family estate.

In the prose above, the inheritance of the estate involved both the life-span (*āyus*) and the experience (*vedanā*); here, however, only the experience is versified. Furthermore, the preceding section on inheriting the life-span had four aspects, but here only three are versified.

The first one and a half lines summarize the "inheriting the life-span for twenty years without being able to ascend," which refers to the aforementioned removal of the *kleśas* of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya*).
"Twenty years" refers to the period during which he clearly mastered the affairs of the household;

some say it refers to the time he turned the Mahāyāna teachings to instruct the bodhisattvas, severing the specific delusions of the Mahāyāna—namely, the afflictions of view and thought—which is called "twenty years.

Others say that when he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the duration was twenty years; the *Ratnaketu-Parājitā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for twenty-eight years. △ Second.
The verse remains in its original position.
Still standing outside the gate, dwelling in a thatched hut, he reflects on his poverty, thinking, "I have no such thing.
He still remains at the threshold; this is the second line of the verse, wherein he has not yet abandoned his inferior state of mind.
△ The three verses [describe] the father’s knowledge of his son’s intent.
The father knows that his son’s mind has gradually become vast and expansive.
"The father knows" (the third half-line of the verse) refers to the movement of the great vehicle (Mahāyāna) faculty—the superior state of tranquility and the great aspiration. △
The second verse concerns the entrustment of the family estate, which has two parts. First, the initial verse correctly entrusts the estate: first, it commands the son to assemble the multitude.
Desiring to bestow his wealth and goods, he immediately gathers his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
These four and a half verses correctly entrust the family estate; whereas the preceding text contained four sections, here only three are versified, as the section on the "time" is omitted.

First, the initial desire to bestow [the estate] corresponds to one line of verse, which versifies the second preceding section on "assembling the kinsmen. Second, the acceptance and formalization of the father-son relationship corresponds to the following.
To this great assembly he said: "This is my son, who abandoned me and traveled elsewhere for fifty years.
It has now been twenty years since I saw him come here. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; having wandered about in search of him, I have finally arrived at this place."
In the following section, there are two and a half verses which establish the third point: the natural relationship between father and son.
△ Third, the verses on the formal entrustment of the family estate:
"Whatever houses and people I possess, I entrust them all to you; use them as you please."
"Whatever I possess"—the third line of the first verse; the fourth line of the second verse [above] is the formal entrustment of the family estate.
△ Second, the verse on joy:
"The son reflects that formerly he was poor and his aspirations were base, yet now from his father he has obtained great treasures as well as a house."
All his wealth and possessions brought him immense joy, such as he had never experienced before.

These two lines of verse correspond to the joy obtained upon meeting [the father]. △ Second, the verses that combine the parables, in four parts: first, the verse combining the parting of the father and son.
The Buddha is also like this.
The Buddha is also like this in uniting the first part concerning the loss of father and son. △ Second, the verse on uniting the meeting of father and son.
"Knowing that I delight in the small"—this single phrase combines the analogy of father and son meeting. The *Ji* (Commentary) states:

"If one were to combine the meaning of 'the Father and Son meeting' using only the phrase 'The Buddha is also like this,' the intent would still not be fully revealed. Next is "knowing that I delight in... [the Great Vehicle].

The meaning of the first phrase, which concerns the meeting of father and son, is likewise not yet fully revealed. Why is this? The preceding phrase relies on the following phrase to establish that one knows [the Buddha] delights in the Lesser Vehicle;

thus, in terms of meaning, they ought to be at odds. Next, the following phrase relies on the preceding phrase to show that the Buddha knows [the son] delights in the Lesser Vehicle; thus, they are able to meet.
One delights in the Lesser Vehicle because one has regressed from the Great Vehicle, and one regresses from the Great Vehicle because one delights in the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore, they are at odds.
Therefore, we meet one another. △ Third, the verse on the combined analogy of pursuing and enticing. Part One: The verse on the combined pursuit by bystanders.
"I have never said to you, 'You shall become Buddhas.

This one and a half lines combines the analogy of pursuing and enticing; the first two lines combine the preceding analogy of calling out from behind. This concludes the first verse of the repetition.

The preceding verses describe how they could not be summoned; this verse now summarizes the meaning of their ultimate abandonment. Second, the verse describes how the two individuals were enticed, saying:
"We have attained all that is out-flow-free and have become disciples of the Small Vehicle, the śrāvakas."
The single verse spoken here regarding "us" below corresponds above to the two chapters on the "Secret Dispatching of Two Persons to Entice" and the "Simultaneous Teaching" and "Probing Teaching.
Now, this single verse merely summarizes their general meaning in verse. △ Fourth, the verse on the correspondence between the entrustment and the acceptance, in two parts:
first, the verse on the correspondence between the entrustment of the family estate; second, the long verse on the command to accept and know.
The Buddha commanded us to expound the supreme path, stating that those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood.
This single line is an extended verse intended to inform the superior recipients of what was not previously stated:
the supreme path is precisely the emptiness of Prajñāpāramitā, and there is nothing superior to it. 2. The actual verse on receiving the command without seeking gain:
Second, first combining this with the formal reception of the mandate:
"I, following the Buddha's teaching, act as a great bodhisattva to expound the unsurpassed path through various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and manifold expressions.
These sons of the Buddhas, having heard the Dharma from me, contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent application."
At that time, the Buddhas immediately bestowed upon him this prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Yet, while all Buddhas expound the actual reality of the secret treasury of the Dharma solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas, they did not explain these essential truths to me.
These five verses correctly receive the mandate. That the sons of the Buddha, upon hearing the Dharma, attain realization and record it, clarifies that they turn the teaching to benefit others.
At that time, it is said that turning the teaching to transform and edify bodhisattvas does not mean acting for one's own sake.
II. Verses on the Convergence of Non-seeking and Non-grasping. Part One: Repeating the Simile and Applying it to the Meaning.
Just as that impoverished son, having come near his father, though he knows of the various goods, does not wish to take them;

this reiterates the previous parable. "Reiterating" (dié) carries the sense of piling up or repeating; by bringing forward the previous parable again, it serves to reinforce the metaphor in the present text.
△ Second, the actual application regarding the absence of desire to take; Part One: The direct verse on the absence of desire.
The meaning of "taking" is as follows:
although we speak of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, it is likewise the case that we ourselves have no aspiration for it.
This single line is a direct verse expressing the absence of any desire to take. △ Second, clarifying that because one possesses wisdom and eradication, there is no aspiration.
Taking the first of the three headings, it indicates the second heading, which concerns the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
We [the Śrāvakas] consider our internal cessation to be sufficient; we understand only this matter and believe there is nothing further.
These two lines are designated as the second intention: the first line indicates that because the perfection of abandonment is complete, there is no desire for further attainment.

The commentary states: "The first line indicates the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). This is because the text says "internal extinction" (*antardhāna*), where "internal" refers to the essence of the afflictions;

since the afflictions of the three realms have been exhausted, it is called "internal extinction," which belongs to the virtue of abandonment. △ Second, the indication of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we would have no joy or delight whatsoever.
Next, if we were to hear of the second [category], which marks the perfection of wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*), there is no longing to receive the prediction [of enlightenment].
Regarding the phrase "next, marking the perfection of wisdom-virtue": since the text states, "If we were to hear," one should know that this refers to hearing.
Because the teaching belongs to wisdom, it is called the "virtue of wisdom. Since they possess only that limited wisdom, they do not aspire toward great wisdom.
△ Second, the explanation:
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent, without arising and without ceasing, and without being great or small.
With such untainted and unconditioned reflections, they do not give rise to joy or delight, thinking:

"For a long night we have been without craving, without attachment, and without further aspiration for the Buddha’s wisdom; yet we ourselves have regarded our own [attainment] regarding the Dharma as final.

For a long night we have practiced the dharma of emptiness, attained liberation from the afflictions and sufferings of the triple world, and dwell in the *nirvāṇa* with remainder within our final bodies."
If that which the Buddha has taught and transformed leads to the attainment of the Way without fail, then one has already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
These six lines provide a dual explanation for the two chapters on Wisdom and Abandonment (*prajñā* and *prahāṇa*). First, as for why this is so:
"Ceasing [to give rise to] joy and pleasure" explains the chapter on Abandonment. Next, from "We have long been... up to "is called the ultimate," explains...

"Intelligence" (*jñāna*)—the three lines beginning with "We have for a long night remained in *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*)—are a re-explanation of the abandonment [of the four truths].
The single line following "The Buddha’s teaching" is a re-explanation of intelligence. Thus, we know that the first two lines clarify abiding in one's own small abandonment;
the next one and a half lines clarify the loss of great intelligence; and the subsequent one and a half lines re-explain the small [abandonment].

The final line, which explains the statement regarding the loss of great wisdom—“all phenomena are empty and quiescent,” etc.—refers to the fact that the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty, eternally abiding, equal, pure, and unconditioned. “The final body” refers to the Arhat.

“Nirvāṇa with remainder” means that while the fetters of the afflictions (*kleśabandhana*) have been exhausted, the fetters of the fruits [of existence] (*phalabandhana*) still remain. “That which is taught by the Buddha,” etc., refers to...
This reveals the fault by means of the attainment. Because one lacks great wisdom, there is no aspiration or joy; if one possessed great wisdom, one would give rise to aspiration and joy.
To cultivate this and attain the Way is to repay the Buddha’s kindness. △ Third, the conclusion.
"Although we have preached the Bodhisattva Dharma to the sons of the Buddhas and others in order to seek the Buddha-way, we have forever lacked any aspiration for or delight in this Dharma.
These one and a half lines conclude the explanation of their own lack of desire to take [the Dharma]. △ Third, clarifying that the Buddhas see their abandonment and accord with it.
There is no expectation of gain.
Because the Teacher perceives my mind and sees that I have been abandoned by him, he did not initially urge me forward or speak of any real benefit.
This single line clarifies that the Buddha’s seeing me as abandoned accords with having no expectation of gain. △ Second, the verse on the entrustment of the family estate. 2.
The first verse combines the main teaching with its entrustment in two parts; first, it reiterates the analogy and applies it to the teaching:
just as a wealthy elder, knowing his son’s inferior disposition, uses the power of skillful means to soften and subdue his mind, and only thereafter entrusts him with all his wealth.

These three lines are a direct verse on entrusting the family business; however, while the preceding text combined [the metaphor and the application] to formally entrust it, these lines now provide a general summary.
Only the first one and a half lines repeat the metaphor and apply it [to the meaning]. △ Second, the direct verse on entrusting the task.

The Buddha is likewise; manifesting rare and marvelous events, he perceives those who delight in the small [vehicle] and, through the power of skillful means, tames their minds before teaching them the great wisdom.
Perceiving those who delight in the small [vehicle] and taming their minds through the power of skillful means clarifies the teaching of the five periods.

The teachings of the Three Vehicles criticize the partial and disparage the small, while praising the Great and extolling the Perfect, so as to cause those of the Small Vehicle to admire the Great and turn them toward the teaching for the sake of harmonizing their capacities.
Once their faculties have become mature, they are then fit for the revelation [of the ultimate truth]. Thereupon, the four great Śrāvakas, understanding the intent behind their former subduing, said:
[This concludes] Section Two: Verses on Mutual Joy.
Today we have attained what we have never before experienced; that which we did not previously hope for, we now receive for ourselves, just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasures.
World-Honored One, we have now attained the Way and its fruits, and within the untainted Dharma, we have attained the pure eye.
For a long night we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and it is only today that we finally obtain their fruition within the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
"Having long cultivated the pure conduct, we have now attained the untainted, unsurpassed, and great fruit.
We are now truly śrāvakas who, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause all to hear. We are now true arhats;
among all the worlds—whether devas, humans, māras, or brahmās—we are worthy of receiving offerings."

Regarding these seven lines of verse: the second line, "attaining the joy of entrustment," means that those who have attained the Way have attained the Way of the True Mark (lakṣaṇa), and those who have attained the Fruit have partially attained the fruit of practice of the Mahāyāna. These two phrases clarify the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge;
"attaining the pure eye regarding untainted phenomena" (anāsrava-dharma) clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s vision to perceive the principle of the True Mark.
In the past, seeing the outflow-free state did not cause one to fall among ordinary beings; today, seeing the outflow-free state does not cause one to fall among those of the Two Vehicles.
In the past, the eye of wisdom saw emptiness; now, with the pure eye, one sees the Middle Way. Regarding the retribution for upholding the precepts:

in the past, the practice of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) was shared with the manifestation of the outflow-free state, wherein the body was reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished, such that no one received this fruit of retribution. Today, [the practice of] pure conduct...

Being able to attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) is the meaning of the "revealing cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) that grasps the fruit; maintaining the precepts is the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (*ālambana-hetu*);
attaining the pure eye and perceiving the principle is the meaning of the "causal cause" (*hetu-hetu*). To say "we are truly śrāvakas" refers to the true stage of the Mahāyāna.
One who has attained the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) can, with a single voice, pervade the trichiliocosm; this resembles the Path but is not yet the true entry into the [ten] abodes.
Abiding is itself the Real. The true Arhat has three meanings; here, only the single meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) is cited.
If one does not give rise to the killing of the transformative death or the general and specific delusions, this is the meaning of "killing the thief.
Being capable of serving as a field of merit for the ten realms is the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings. △ Second, praising the profound kindness of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, with great kindness, has out of compassion taught and benefited us through such rare events; who could ever repay this over immeasurable billions of kalpas?
Even by providing for us with hands and feet, prostrating with our heads at your feet, and offering every form of service, none of these can repay it.
Even if one were to carry you upon the crown of one's head or on both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, honoring you with all one’s heart and offering delicious food—
Even if one were to use immeasurable precious robes, various bedding and furnishings, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood,

and all manner of rare jewels to construct stupas and temples, and even spread precious robes upon the ground— performing such acts of offering for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—
it would still be impossible to repay the Buddhas' rare, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable great supernormal powers.
The King of all dharmas—both untainted and unconditioned—is able to endure such matters for those of inferior capacity.
For ordinary people who grasp at signs, he teaches according to what is appropriate. The Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over all dharmas;

knowing the various desires, inclinations, and capacities of sentient beings, they teach the Dharma through immeasurable analogies according to what each can bear, in accordance with the needs of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, knowing which roots of goodness from past lives have matured and which have not, and having discerned them through various forms of deliberation and analysis, he teaches the One Vehicle path as three according to what is appropriate.
These thirteen practices praise the Buddha’s profound kindness that is difficult to repay. Regarding the phrase "the Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One," Zhanran says: "First."

First, when the Tathāgata first established his compassion, he extracted beings from the suffering of the six realms and granted them the bliss of the four noble ones, universally encompassing the ten dharma realms within the Four Great Vows;
this is the grace of the Tathāgata’s dwelling. Second, while the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he instructed, taught, benefited, and gladdened others;
although he may have temporarily forgotten the Mahāyāna teachings he once imparted, his wisdom and vows were never lost, just as...
Third, entering the chamber of the Tathāgata is the grace of great compassion that bestows peace and joy; it is like a father who, seeing his children encounter suffering, regards them as his own.
The Buddha observes their needs and follows them like a calf following its mother, fully practicing the six perfections to benefit sentient beings.
This "chamber of the Tathāgata" wards off the cold and obstructs the heat, which is the grace of great pity that uproots suffering. Fourth—
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, he could have enjoyed the bliss of unconditioned nirvana and concealed his divine virtues;
yet he employed the Dharma favored by the poor—the five precepts and ten wholesome actions—and sprinkled cold water upon their faces to bring them to awakening.
This is because the Buddha’s robe is precisely the grace that wards off the heat of greed and desire. Fifth, he manifested the appearance of an aged bhikṣu as a skillful means to draw near to them.
Sixth, after this period has passed, they accord with one another in heart and trust, using censure and disparagement to feel shame for the small and to aspire to the great;
this is the robe of the Buddha, which is the grace that conceals their ugliness. Seventh, they are entrusted with the family estate, including gold, silver, and treasuries.
That all the hidden treasures were made known was surely the grace of the Buddha’s robe, which bestowed upon me the adornment of being.

Eighth, that the kinsmen were assembled, the father-son relationship was confirmed, and the family estate—the unsurpassed treasury of jewels—was entrusted to me so that it was obtained without seeking, was surely the grace of the Tathāgata’s seat.
Furthermore, as for the ninth and tenth [points], once I had sat upon that seat, my body and mind...
Being composed and swiftly attaining peace and security, one causes the sound of the Buddha-way to be heard by all;
that all devas and humans universally receive offerings therein is the seat of the Tathāgata.

That it enables me to fulfill the grace of both self-cultivation and transforming others is such that even bearing the Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One upon my two shoulders cannot repay it. This is what is meant.
Regarding this *gośīrṣa-candana* (ox-head sandalwood), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that it originates from Mount Vimala; if used to anoint the body, fire cannot burn it.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that in the northern continent there is a mountain named Mahāgiri;
on the peaks of Mahāgiri there is much *gośīrṣa-candana*, because the shape of these mountain peaks resembles the head of an ox. This is why it is called [ox-head sandalwood].
From this point on, the name "Dāna" (Giving) is established. The above concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.
This marks the end of the second fascicle of the annotated *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
[End of Fascicle Four] Annotated *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle Five.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Shou-lun of Qiyun Monastery in Kexian, Jinxī, Song;
revised and edited by the Śramaṇa Fa-ji of Puti Hermitage in Yuxi, Ming;
and collated for publication by the Layman Min Mengde of Pingcheng, Wuxing.
△ Chapter Four: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs (2). First, the presentation of the chapter title:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Five, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

This chapter elucidates the Tathāgata’s confirmation [of the Bodhisattvas’ realization]. Within the text, there are parables such as those of the mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain, which stand alone.

Why are they designated by the names of medicinal herbs? One should know that the land is that which can produce, the clouds and rain are that which can moisten, and the grasses and trees are that which are produced and moistened.
While all that is produced and moistened has utility in general, the utility of medicinal herbs is particularly potent;

it is for this reason that they are so designated. Furthermore, all conditioned wholesome dharmas are capable of eliminating evil, yet [medicinal herbs] are without... [the remainder of the passage is incomplete].
Among those free from outflows (*anāsrava*), the four great disciples used parables to lead others to understand the Buddha’s profound parables that accord with the Sage’s mind;

thus, the Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent! This is most rare. To describe their attainment of understanding by likening it to specific individuals, he titled this the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (*Bhaiṣajyavarga-parivarta*).
Now, medicinal herbs grow in thickets for a long time, yet once they receive the rain from the clouds, they are sustained and flourish.
The vegetables are lush and the sprouts and stems are abundant and verdant; externally they are nourished by external forces, while internally they are moistened by their own essence.

This is like one dwelling in the final body within the state of outflow-free nirvana with remainder, who no longer aspires for the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, yet now, upon hearing this sutra, attains the Buddha-vehicle of his own school and simultaneously carries others across. As the text says: "We of today are truly śrāvakas."

By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, it causes all to hear; because it possesses superior power and function for both the internal and external, as well as for oneself and others, it should be understood that this is titled the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
One should know that medicinal herbs can eliminate the four great elements of wind and cold, nourish the five viscera, restore youth, and arrest the aging of the complexion.
Now, having encountered the clouds and rain, they suddenly become the "King of Medicines" (Bhaiṣajyarāja); when ingested, they universally treat all ailments and transform the body.

The "Immortal" (Sage) is a metaphor for those who are free from outflows (*anāsrava*); having heard the sutra, they have shattered the delusions of ignorance and opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The text says: "Today we are truly the sons of the Buddha; this unsurpassed treasury of jewels was obtained without seeking.

Whatever a son of the Buddha ought to obtain, we have all already obtained; we have received our prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) before the Buddha's very face. Thus, the excellence is manifest and the praise is subtle.

This refers to the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter. One should know that the first section conveys the meaning of the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint) through the dialogue between teacher and disciple;
the second section, which generates wholesome roots, is for the purpose of benefiting others (*puruṣakāra-artha*);

and the third section conveys the meanings of both the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial standpoint) and the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint). This is called the "Exegesis of Causes and Conditions. If explained according to secular treatises:

Regarding medicinal herbs, the *Shennong Jing* states: "Superior medicines nourish life, referring to the five minerals (*pañca-dhātu*) that refine the physical form and the six fungi (*ṣaḍ-cīnā*) that prolong the years;
middling medicines nourish nature, referring to the *he-huan* which dispels anger and the *yan-cao* which forgets sorrow;

inferior medicines cure disease, referring to the *da-huang* which eliminates constipation and the *dang-gui* which relieves pain. As for the term "herbs" (*cao*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as the collective name for all plants (*śata-vanaspati*).

Explaining the name: "Cao" (grass) means "early. It refers to that which withers before autumn; generally, anything whose substance or trunk is not firm and lacks the utility of a cultivated plant is called "grass.
II. Explaining the Sūtra Text: The Tathāgata’s Confirmation and Fulfillment. This has two parts:
first, the brief confirmation and fulfillment. First, the dual exclamation of "Excellent."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits; it is exactly as you have said."

"Excellent, excellent!"—the meaning of this double exclamation is as follows: one "excellent" describes how both [Kāśyapa and Ānanda] have realized the reality (satya), and one "excellent" describes how both have realized the skillful means (upāya).
When it is said that Kāśyapa has "well spoken" of the Tathāgata’s true merits, it is because his expression is refined and skillful;
thus, he is said to have "well spoken," and since all these are the Buddha-dharma, they are called "true. It is "true" in the sense of being real.
To describe their actual merit is to describe their provisional [teachings]; that which is "as stated" is the purport of definitive establishment.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* is intended to lead one toward the real; the Tripiṭaka is intended to guide one through the provisional.

The essence of the Vaipulya and the instruction of the *Prajñāpāramitā* both lead to both the provisional and the real. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, however, exclusively discusses the entrustment of the treasure.
It is indeed so. △ Second, acknowledging what is beyond one's reach:
"The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits; you would not be able to exhaustively describe them even in immeasurable billions of kalpas."

He describes that which the mind cannot grasp: whether it be retreating or advancing, horizontal or vertical, both horizontal and vertical, or neither horizontal nor vertical—all these are beyond its reach.
Why is this so? One should know that the great cloud covers all universally, bearing a refreshing coolness;
the great rain falls everywhere, moistening all without exception, causing the entire world to perceive and realize what has never been known before.

Furthermore, when the Dharma suddenly ceases its instruction, those who lead the two vehicles and those who have attained benefits—whether humans, devas, or "small weeds"—are what is meant by "regression," as they fall short of [the ultimate].

Moreover, Bodhisattvas are called "superior weeds" or "small trees"; yet even though these "great trees" flourish and grow luxuriantly, benefiting both themselves and others, they still do not lead [others to the ultimate], which is what is meant by "progression," as they too fall short. Furthermore, regarding the ten dharma-realms:

Since all equally accomplish the Dharma-realm, why suddenly stop at acknowledging only the two vehicles? That the remaining eight Dharma-realms are not mentioned at all is what is meant by "incomprehensibility in the horizontal dimension.

Furthermore, since the seven stages of expedient means proceed from shallow to deep and all enter into reality, that the other five expedient means are not included in the discourse is what is meant by "incomprehensibility in the vertical dimension. Moreover, the benefits bestowed throughout the three periods of time have never...
To temporarily set this aside: it is that which neither horizontal nor vertical [conceptions] can reach. Mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys are collectively termed "the earth.

This earth is capable of producing all things without ever making distinctions between what it excludes and what it accepts. Yet, the seeds of grasses and trees all rely upon this earth as their support, having no other basis.
When a single cloud gathers, its density is uniform everywhere; when it rains, the flavor of the rain is of one taste.
Without distinction between the withered and the flourishing, the universal moisture is equally shared; all alike attain growth. The Tathāgata’s impartiality is inconceivable:
it is truly not that he is sudden at first and gradual later, nor that he is the same at the beginning, middle, and end.

Just as when a dragon rises and auspicious clouds rain everywhere upon all bodies and minds—where the rain does not fall, heat is removed and coolness is attained—this constitutes the five vehicles and seven expedient means.
The ten directions and the three periods of time are equal, vast, profound, extensive, and far-reaching, inconceivable and without differentiation;
this is what is neither horizontal nor vertical, beyond the reach of the neck [of comprehension]. Yet, the meaning of being "beyond reach" does not mean it is entirely and suddenly negated;
rather, it is said to be "inexhaustible" because the initial mind, when compared to the subsequent mind, has not yet reached the ultimate ground. Furthermore, regarding the initial awakening:

The initial letter *a* also possesses the merits of the final letter *ḍa*; however, this merely aligns with the scope of the teaching, as there has not yet been leisure to advance toward a comprehensive mastery that encompasses both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva practicing through skillful means should act in this manner. △ Second, the detailed exposition, which consists of two parts:

first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] further consists of two sections: first, the exposition establishing the opening of three and the manifestation of one; second, the concluding praise.
The first section also has two parts. First, the teaching by way of Dharma; second, first, citing the fact that the Dharma King does not speak falsely to encourage faith:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the king of all dharmas; whatever he says is never false."

This cites the Dharma King’s exhortation to inspire faith: whereas worldly kings have nothing to fear externally and their words are not inconsistent internally, the supramundane Dharma King possesses the integration and clarity of myriad virtues and has exhausted all evils; thus, his speech is truthful and sincere.

Therefore it is said that "whatever he speaks is never false. The old commentary states: "This describes how [the teaching] is not false for those of middling faculties, while encouraging those of inferior faculties."
Believe and accept these present words: although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real; beyond the provisional and the real, there is no other dharma.
Yet, because the claim that there are "immeasurable" teachings is difficult to believe, the King of Dharma is cited here to encourage faith.

Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the subsequent analogy of the great cloud. △ Second, the formal exposition of the opening of the three and the revealing of the one. First, clarifying this according to the teachings.
Regarding the two aspects of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real," first is the exposition of opening up the provisional according to the teachings.
"To expound all dharmas through the skillful means of wisdom"—"all dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (the *saptavidha-upāya*).
Taken horizontally, they correspond to the one true reality (*eka-tattva*); taken vertically, if one were to say it is not so...

For what reason did those who first resolved their minds toward Great Awakening under twenty trillion Buddhas subsequently take the Lesser Vehicle, again transmigrate through the five destinies, and even cycle within the ten realms of existence?
If this is true for a single person, how much more so for those at the seven stages of the *upāya* (expedient means)?

Although these phenomena are numerous, when illuminated by the *pāramitā* of *upāya*, they are exhaustively revealed without exception; it is according to the various classes of beings that they are taught through their respective sounds.
Not lingering in provisional interpretations, [the teaching] explains the precepts for humans and devas; it explains the Truths for the Two Vehicles; it explains phenomena for the Tripiṭaka;
it explains the Paramitas for the Shared Teaching; it explains non-arising for the Distinct Teaching;

and it sequentially reveals the Tathāgatagarbha—this is called describing the reception and opening of the provisional according to the teachings. △ Second, describing the manifestation of the real according to the teachings.
The Dharma he expounds all reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
This is an exposition according to the teaching that reveals the ultimate reality; it all reaches the stage of omniscience. "Stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because it is ultimately non-dual, it is called "one" (*eka*); because its nature is vast and expansive, it is called "all" (*sarva*); it is quiescent yet eternally...
Because it illuminates, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); because it establishes all phenomena upon its foundation of non-abiding, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
This is an explanation according to the definitive teaching of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Whatever is taught therein causes all sentient beings to reach this ground of wisdom.
For example, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* extensively traverses all phenomena, they are all the Mahāyāna; "yāna" (vehicle) is the Great Vehicle, and the vehicle is the true mark (*tathatā*).
The "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) are precisely the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). The preceding text states, "Only this one fact is real," which refers to this very ground;

"the other two are not true" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*). This passage describes the revelation of the provisional and the manifestation of the real according to both the sudden and gradual teachings.
△ Second, describing the revelation of the provisional and the manifestation of the real by way of wisdom. Part one: Describing the revelation by way of wisdom.
Mastery:
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena, and he understands the profound mental activities of all sentient beings with unimpeded penetration.
To observe the destination to which all phenomena return is the illumination of the provisional; to exhaustively and clearly understand them is the illumination of the real.
Because these two types of wisdom unimpededly penetrate both the partial and the perfect objects of illumination, they are able to expound the two teachings of the provisional and the real;
this passage explains the teachings by means of wisdom. To know the destination to which they return is the consciousness of the medicine within the profound mind.

Practicing these is knowing the illness; both the illness and the medicine are provisional dharmas (*upāya-dharma*). Each provisional dharma has its own specific destination: precepts, wholesome deeds, and the like lead proximately to the realms of humans and devas;
if they serve as distant conditions, even the simple acts of bowing the head or raising the hands lead distantly to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and so forth lead proximately to *nirvāṇa*; if they serve to adorn merit, then what you all practice is the path of a bodhisattva.

The path is long and leads to the place where the treasure resides; furthermore, the various paths—such as the six perfections (pāramitās), both general and specific—differ in their immediate and distant destinations.

Moreover, the precepts and wholesome deeds are the medicine for those seeking the realms of humans and devas, while the truths, conditions, and perfections are the medicine for those of the three vehicles.

Even the general and specific [perfections] may be understood in this way. Regarding the practices of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), there are two kinds: first, that which is characterized by deep attachment to...

Regarding the two aspects of the environment and the inhabitants: attachment to the phenomena of the environment and inhabitants gives rise to the profound and heavy ten non-virtues, which obstruct the vehicle of humans and devas;

attachment to the phenomena of the environment and inhabitants gives rise to the four inversions, the three paths, the six obscurations, the four abodes, the five abodes, and so forth, which obstruct the four vehicles of the noble ones.
One should know that these manifestations of deep-seated mental illness differ; through the illumination of expedient wisdom, they are all thoroughly penetrated and transcended.
This section, concerning wisdom, describes the disclosure of the provisional. △ Second, concerning wisdom, it describes the manifestation of the real:
"Furthermore, having thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, he reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom."

This describes the manifestation of true reality through wisdom; it is that which is illuminated by true wisdom. Because all provisional dharmas enter into reality, it is said to be "thoroughly exhaustive.
Because it is what is seen by the Buddha-eye, it is said to be "clear. Because it is what is known by true wisdom, it is said to be "comprehended.
If this wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, it does not illuminate that medicine and that illness; furthermore, if that wisdom illuminates that, it does not [illuminate] this.

That which can illuminate the distinctions and differences among these types is the illumination of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). If a single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses, that is the illumination of ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
Because it can demonstrate to sentient beings such a realm and wisdom that are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), it is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarva-jñāna*).
Furthermore, "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*) refers to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*); these ten realms—
Each individual has different desires, and their respective karmic fruits and destinies are likewise distinct. One who knows that all phenomena are exhausted is said to know the disease;
one who knows everything to which the deep mind is attached is said to know the medicine—only because the medicines vary in depth and shallowness.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One knows the mind of greed, the mind of anger, and the mind of delusion as they truly are, through the wisdom that knows reality."

It is called "knowing the profound mind" because it penetrates things according to reality without obstruction. If one employs all medicinal dharmas—such as the precepts, the truths, the objects of cognition, and the perfections—with the wisdom that knows things as they truly are, this is called "penetrating without obstruction.

Furthermore, in the previous section on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), the phrase "penetrating without obstruction" was discussed in terms of the provisional to illustrate the real; now, regarding this real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) as well:
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas" refers to the mutual manifestation of the provisional and the real through discourse based on both the ultimate and the conventional:

this clarifies that the real is the provisional-real and the provisional is the real-provisional. One should know that, ultimately, they are neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated.
Through the skillful means of wisdom, the provisional possesses differentiation; yet upon reaching the ground of wisdom, there is no differentiation, just as with the earth.
The various grasses and trees differ from one another; some are many, some are not many, and some are neither many nor not many.

Furthermore, when discussing the Dharma in relation to the mind, and the mind in relation to the Dharma, the mind possesses numerical categories while the Dharma does not. The mind is not separate from the Dharma, and the Dharma is not separate from the mind.
Though it is without number, it is numbered; though it is numbered, it is without number. The provisional and the ultimate are likewise so. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy.

The second part consists of two sections: first, the illustrative parable; second, the reaffirmation of the thesis with praise. The first section further divides into two parts: first, the introduction of the parable;
second, the six distinct similes. First is the simile of the land:
"Kāśyapa, it is as if, for example, there were the lands of mountains, rivers, valleys, and ravines within a trichiliocosm."
The trichiliocosm is a metaphor for the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*). The mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands are metaphors for the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*).

There is no separate dharma apart from the world that constitutes the mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands; likewise, there is no separate dharma apart from sentient beings that constitutes the five aggregates.
Since land serves as a general metaphor for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it also metaphorically represents the mountains and rivers.

The ravines and valleys are likened to the four aggregates (*skandhas*). Although grasses and trees depend upon the earth and other elements, the earth and such are not identical to the grasses and trees.
The substance and trunk of the grasses and trees are merely designated as "grasses and trees. As for the seeds of grasses and trees, they have no name other than that;

one merely takes the functional capacity to produce [the plant] and calls it a "seed," while the substance and trunk produced from them are called "grasses and trees. All are planted with their roots in—

The stages (bhūmi) are the root; internally they correspond to the causes and fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu* and *vāsanā-phala*). Although these depend upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregates themselves are not identical to the cause and fruit.
It is by depending upon the aggregates that there is the growth and fulfillment of the cause of habituation, which is termed the "fruit of habituation.
Since cause and fruit arise in dependence upon the aggregates, it is like mountains, rivers, and soil serving as the basis for the growth of plants from seeds once they have received moisture.
This is an exhaustive illustration. Furthermore, to clarify the distinct metaphors: although a mountain is high and steep, it possesses five characteristics such as depressions and elevations;

likewise, even though land is level, it possesses five characteristics such as mounds and ponds. These correspond to the five vehicles and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). The mountain represents the five aggregates of a Bodhisattva;
the stream represents that of a Pratyekabuddha; the valley represents that of a Śrāvaka; and the land represents [the aggregates of] ordinary beings.

The analogy of the celestial valleys represents the heavens, while the lower valleys represent humans; each of the five aggregates possesses both the causal conditions and the resultant fruits of habituation (*vāsanā*).
Their basis is like mountains, rivers, and valleys, for the land serves as the foundation for seeds, the physical trunk, and so forth.

Furthermore, the trichiliocosm is used as an analogy for the principle of the true cause (*samyak-hetu*), which universally serves as the basis for all things, just as mountains and rivers serve as the foundation.
The land of the valleys and gorges is a metaphor for the form and mind that constitute the retribution of sentient beings' aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).

The grasses, trees, thickets, and forests are metaphors for the habitual causes of sentient beings. These three factors are inseparable; the habits depend upon the aggregates and sense-bases, and the aggregates and sense-bases do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Just as grasses and trees depend on mountains and rivers, and mountains and rivers depend on the world, so it is according to the worldly scriptures.
Regarding the explanation of mountains, rivers, valleys, and land: the *Guangya* states that "mountain" (*shan*) means "to produce," signifying its ability to produce the myriad things.
Furthermore, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "mountain" (*shan*) means "to spread," signifying that it spreads forth vital energy (*qi*) to generate the myriad things.

Regarding "river" (*chuan*), Cai Yong’s *Yueling Zhangju* says that the confluence of many streams flowing into the sea is called a river. The *Shiming* states that "river" (*chuan*) means "to pierce."
This refers to water flowing through excavated ground. Regarding "khi" (溪), the *Erya* states: "Water that pours into a stream is called a khi.

Regarding "gu" (谷), the *Shiming* states: "It means 'to cover' (*fu*); it refers to the hidden and deep recesses of mountain crags. Regarding "tu" (土), the *Shiming* states: "It means 'to emit' (*tu*);
it refers to the emitting and giving birth of the myriad things. Regarding "di" (地), the *Shuowen* states: "The primordial qi first divided; the light and clear became Yang and formed Heaven."
The heavy and turbid aggregates constitute the earth. △ Second, the analogy of plants and trees:
the various species of herbs, trees, groves, and medicinal plants that grow therein differ in their names and forms.
Regarding "the herbs and trees that grow": "herbs" (*tṛṇa*) is the general name for grasses, and "trees" (*vṛkṣa*) is the collective designation for forest trees.
When many grasses form a clump and many trees form a grove, those possessing superior power to cure diseases are called "medicines" (*oṣadhi*).

Just as within the wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), all are capable of curing evil, so too the untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*) excels in the sense of curing afflictions (*kleśa*) over the inferior herbs and trees among the groves of forest trees.
Because the branches and trunk provide extensive shade and the vessels and utensils are vast, they serve as metaphors for the various types of the two bodhisattvas.
"Various" (*nānā*) refers to the fact that the seeds of the five vehicles and seven wholesome causes and effects are not uniform.

These various types each have their own designations, which are "name" (*nāman*); each has its own substance and characteristics, which are "form" (*rūpa*). Therefore, it is said that name and form are distinct.
Furthermore, regarding "various kinds" (*jātīya*): "kind" (*jāti*) refers to seed; "type" (*prakāra*) refers to a class or category.
"Various" (*nānā*) means "like this" (*nānā*), where *nānā* signifies number. △ Third, the analogy of dense clouds.
Dense clouds spread far and wide, covering the trichiliocosm.

Regarding "dense clouds spreading far and wide": the clouds possess form and color; their "covering and shading" refers to what follows in the text. The thunderous sound echoing in the distance represents the Buddha’s compassionate response to the world;
the form and color represent the Buddha appearing in the world; and the thunderous sound represents the Buddha’s verbal teachings. Thus, the dense clouds symbolize the Buddha.

This refers to the three mysteries (*triguhyāni*): compassion is the mystery of mind (*manomahāguhya*), form and color are the mystery of body (*kāyamahāguhya*), and the sound of thunder is the mystery of speech (*vāṅmahāguhya*).

"Pervasive" (*mibù*) means all-encompassing; because it is both secret and pervasive, it is called "pervasive. Since one permeates the responsive bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) with compassion and preaches the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it is called "pervasive.
The *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) states that there are five kinds of clouds.
When the color is blue, wind is predominant; when red, fire; when yellow-white, earth; and when black, water. There are four masters of lightning:
Śarīrasvāmin in the east, Śatapati in the south, Ajagara in the west, and Aśvalāyana in the north. Because these four masters of lightning contend with one another, there is thunder.
Furthermore, because earth, water, fire, and wind contend, there is thunder. When these five elements are out of harmony, there is no rain. Wind is the first [cause].
1. Two fires arise and blow forth; 2. Three fires arise and burn; 3. The hands of the Asuras receive them and cast them into the sea;

4. The Rain-Master becomes licentious; 5. The king does not attend to governance. Because the Rain-Master is enraged, it does not rain. Regarding the "dense clouds," the *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes), in the *Xiuxu* hexagram, states:
"Dense clouds do not rain, from my western outskirts. The *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) commentary says: "The upward movement of Yang [qi]..."
When the two energies are stored and mutually clash, rain is produced. △ Fourth, the analogy of pouring rain:
"Pouring down equally at one time.
This means that the eightfold voice and four analytical eloquences of the Buddha’s mouth pour down the rain of the Dharma equally at one time, benefiting and nourishing all beings.
The eight qualities of the voice are: first, extremely beautiful; second, soft and gentle; third, harmonious and appropriate; fourth, noble and wise;

fifth, not feminine; sixth, unerring; seventh, deep and far-reaching; eighth, inexhaustible. The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: first, unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);

second, unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); third, unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); fourth, unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). △ Fifth, the analogy of receiving nourishment.
Its moisture universally permeates the trees and forests, as well as all medicinal herbs—those with small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves;
those with medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, and medium leaves; and those with large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves.
This rain of Dharma universally moistens the ground of the hearts of the seven kinds of sentient beings;
the seeds of their habitual causes immediately sprout as the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is called "universally soaking the roots, stems, branches, and leaves.

This is because faith serves as the root, precepts as the stem, meditative concentration as the branches, and wisdom as the leaves—each supporting the next in succession—and thus these four are used as a metaphor. The small roots, stems, and so forth refer to...

The faith, precepts, and so forth of humans and devas constitute the minor roots, stalks, and so on; the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the two vehicles constitute the major roots, stalks, and so on;
and the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of bodhisattvas [constitute the great roots, stalks, and so on]. △ Sixth, the analogy of growth.

Among the various trees, large and small, each receives nourishment according to its superior, middling, or inferior nature; though rained upon by a single cloud, they grow and flourish according to their respective species, producing flowers, fruits, and seeds.

This is further briefly restated to clarify that grasses and trees receive moisture according to their respective capacities due to two causes: past habituation and karmic retribution. Since wholesome dharmas...

"Receiving the rain of the Dharma, both the fruits of practice (*śikṣā*) and retribution (*vipāka*) each attain growth, corresponding to their respective natures (*gotra*)," clarifies the employment of skillful means (*upāya*) according to capacities:
for those of lesser capacity, they do not exceed their limit; for those of greater capacity, they do not fall short. This refers precisely to the seven kinds of causes of practice and retribution.
"The flowers and fruits unfold and bear fruit" refers to the two fruits of practice and retribution. Furthermore, it is said that "growth" carries three meanings.
To accord with their respective spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) is the cause for their growth; teaching according to the capacity of the recipient is what is meant by this.
That each attains growth is the explicit clarification of growth. The flourishing of flowers and fruit is the characteristic mark of growth. △ Second, the analogy of non-differentiation.
Although they are produced from the same ground and moistened by the same rain, each of the grasses and trees has its own distinctions.
This analogy of non-distinction illustrates the single reality; this [reality] is threefold:

first, that which is produced from the same ground refers to what is produced from the stage of the mind-ground prior to the Path as the ultimate cause, and the stage of wisdom subsequent to the Path; second, that which is rained down by the same cloud; and third, the single voice.
The Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle that is proclaimed develops five kinds of roots of goodness within the path; ultimately, it is a teaching of equality through a single voice.

Just as the three types of grass and two types of trees receive benefit without being aware of it themselves, so too do those with the five kinds of roots of goodness, having received the rain of the Buddha-dharma, increase according to their respective capacities without themselves knowing it; these five causes all rely upon the One [Vehicle].
The Buddha-nature likewise does not know for itself that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna, nor does it know for itself that they all ultimately converge in the Buddha-wisdom;
only the Tathāgata is able to know this. △ Second, the integration of the parables, in two parts:
first, the integration of the parable of differentiation, in six sections. First, the integration of the third [parable], the dense clouds.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata likewise appears in the world like the rising of a great cloud;
with a great voice, he pervades the world of devas, humans, and asuras, just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm.

Regarding the sequence of the analogies: it clarifies that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he preaches the Dharma with his eightfold voice; in preaching the Dharma, there are sentient beings who undergo transformation.
When these sentient beings hear the Dharma, each receives the nourishment of the Path. While their receiving this nourishment is identical, there is no lack of distinction in its growth.
First, the analogy of the dense clouds is joined [to the preceding]; first the Buddha’s body is raised as being like the form of dense clouds, and subsequently...

The Buddha’s secret mouth is like the union of clouds that produces sound; the Tathāgata is likewise so when appearing in the world—this is precisely the union of the appearance of the Saṃbhogakāya (Response Body) in the world. Just as a great cloud arises, this provides the analogy for clarification:
it shows that the Tathāgata, through his great compassion, manifests a body to cover and nourish all beings. "With a great voice" refers specifically to the Buddha’s secret mouth.
"The gathering clouds have sound" refers to the fact that devas, humans, and asuras—specifically citing the three wholesome realms—receive the benefit of the secret of speech.
This means that those with the capacities of the three vehicles, the thirty sons, individually receive the benefit of the sound.
"Like that great cloud" provides the analogy; "the gathering clouds have sound, covering the great trichiliocosm" universally cites all beings.

All these are the sons of the Buddha who equally receive the benefit of the Buddha’s secret oral teachings. Sometimes, only the five similes are combined to correspond with the "entire world" (*prabhūta-loka*);
the phrase "downward including the lands of the world" further corresponds to the "land" (*bhūmi*).

The "world" is the world of the realm of nations (*deśa-loka*), while "humans, devas, and asuras" are the world of the provisional names of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*). Thus, the provisional names of the five aggregates correspond to the aforementioned "five aggregates" of the world.
This includes the mountains, rivers, and valleys. △ Second, combining the fourth analogy of pouring rain, in two parts: First, the heading of the section.
In the midst of the great assembly, he proclaims these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."

The Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—he causes those who have not crossed over to cross;
he causes those who have not been liberated to be liberated; he causes those who have not found peace to find peace; he causes those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*.
He knows this world and the world beyond as they truly are; I am the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One, and I know.
"The Way" refers to the one who opens the Way and speaks of the Way.
This corresponds to the fourth section on the analogy of rain above; therein, first the topical headings are set forth, followed by the exhortation to listen and receive.
The topical headings consist of six parts: first, the ten titles, namely Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth; second, the four great vows, namely causing those not yet crossed over... [to cross over].

1. The three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) regarding the present life, future lives, and so forth; 2. The four types of one-pointed mind and threefold wisdom (*ekacittatrayajñāna*), namely:
"I am the all-knower"; 3. The five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), namely: "I am the all-seeing one"; 4. The three types of action (*trikarma*) practiced together with wisdom:
the path of knowing through the mind being unguarded, the path of opening through the body being unguarded, and the path of speaking through the mouth being unguarded.
The Protector is also called the Guide, meaning one who knows the path and so forth. △ Second, the exhortation to receive [the teaching]:
"You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
"You, gods and humans, should descend to exhort sentient beings to listen and receive the six kinds of Dharma-gates expounded by the Buddha’s eightfold voice;

speaking from the perspective of the majority, you should exhort those in the three wholesome realms that they ought to go and listen to the Dharma. △ Third, combining this with the first analogy of the land.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that "sentient beings exist by grasping at karmic retribution, just as worlds exist by depending on mountains and rivers," this refers to the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms.
Here, we are specifically speaking of the differences among the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
The separate assignment as described above, or [the statement] "from you, O devas and humans," both accord with the analogy of the mountains and rivers.
△ Fourth, combining this with the second analogy of the grasses and trees:
at that time, the Tathāgata observed the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of these sentient beings, as well as their diligence or indolence.
Regarding "at that time" (*tatkāla*): if one discusses the gradual beginning, it refers to the time of the first preaching of the Three Vehicles at the Deer Park;

if one considers the intermediate period, "at that time" may be discussed in various contexts. Regarding "the sharp and the dull": in general, those in the three miserable realms, whose causes are evil and whose fruits are suffering, and who are unable to receive the Path, are termed "dull.
Those of the seven kinds of expedient means who gain benefit upon hearing the teaching are termed "sharp. These are the distinctions.

To judge those among humans and devas who merely accept karmic retribution and are unwilling to accept the Way is called dullness; those of the three vehicles' faculties who sever delusions and transcend the realm are called sharp.
Furthermore, śrāvakas who contemplate arising and ceasing are called dull, while bodhisattvas who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing are called sharp.
One may discern the distinctions between sharp and dull by alternatingly discussing them across the three teachings—Shared, Distinct, and Complete—as well as in terms of diligence and indolence.
Those in the three miserable realms who are heedless are called "lazy"; those in the human and heavenly realms who observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths are called "diligent.

Not being weary of suffering is laziness in humans and devas; fearing impermanence is diligence in humans and devas. Greedily seeking only personal realization without aspiring for Buddhahood is laziness in the two vehicles;
the bodhisattva’s resolve to seek the Buddha-way is diligence. △ Fifth, combining with the fifth [section on] receiving.
The analogy of moisture:
according to what each can bear, he preaches the Dharma in various and immeasurable ways, causing all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"According to what each can bear" means that it accords with their individual capacities without the fault of excess or deficiency; thus they rejoice and swiftly obtain [benefit].
"Excellence and benefit" refers to each receiving the nourishment of the Dharma and attaining its advantages. △ Section Six: The Sixth, "Increase.
These sentient beings, having heard this Dharma, attain peace and security in the present life and are reborn in good realms in future lives, experiencing happiness through the Path.
Having also attained the opportunity to hear the Dharma, and once they have heard it, they become free from all hindrances, acting according to their capacity within all phenomena.
Gradually attaining entry into the Way,

being at peace and secure in the present life and reborn in a good realm in the future, is the result of the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), which corresponds to the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*) like a flower blooming and growing. Furthermore,
being able to hear the Dharma and even enter the Way is the result of the causal condition of practice (*abhyāsa-hetu*), which draws forth the fruit of practice (*abhyāsa-phala*).
The superior fruits increase; having heard this Dharma, one attains the causes for increase through the peace and security of the present life, which is the mark of increase.

Furthermore, being reborn in a favorable realm is the mark of increase. The Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all three realms of suffering, providing nourishment and growth; as it is said, this is like the clear ground of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, it is said in various sutras that dragons, birds, ghosts, spirits, and others also hear the Dharma and attain the Way.
If the fire is extinguished and the boiling water cools, this is peace and security in the present life; if one is reborn among devas or humans, this is a favorable state in a future life.
To cultivate the Way among devas and humans is to experience bliss through the Way. If humans or devas hear [the Dharma]...
When one upholds the Dharma and observes the precepts, the merit supports the body such that ghosts and dragons cannot harm it; this is peace and security in the present life.
Alternatively, devas may be reborn as humans, or humans may be reborn as devas, or devas and humans may be reborn interchangeably; this is birth in a good realm in future lives.

Furthermore, being able to understand and awaken is to receive happiness through the Way. When those of the Two Vehicles hear the Dharma, they attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is [the third category].
"Peace and security in the present life" is as stated in the following passage: "This person conceives the thought of parinirvāṇa regarding the merit they have attained;
I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name, and this person shall hear this sutra in that land.
This refers to the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*); it is a favorable place, and because one hears the sutra there, one receives [the fruit] through the Path.

If a Bodhisattva of the stage of birth-body hears the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), they will find peace and security in the present life and be reborn in a pure and perfect realm as a member of the retinue of the Dharma-body. This is the "excellent place.
To receive bliss through the Path and be free from all obstacles is what constitutes peace and security in the present life; one shall gradually attain it according to one's capacity.
Entering the Way is precisely receiving joy through the Way in future lives. △ Second, the application of the analogy:

Just as that great cloud rains upon all the herbs, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal plants, each receives its full nourishment according to its own nature and attains growth accordingly.
This analogy of the rain-cloud has six intended meanings: 1. The rain-cloud provides both form and sound as benefits; 2. It rains upon all things; 3.
This is the second chapter of the sixth section on the Dharma-gate; 4. Regarding the various plants, trees, and forests, it corresponds to the fourth point:

the sentient beings who receive transformation—whether of dull or sharp faculties, indolent or diligent, and whether their causes for practice are shallow or deep—each receives nourishment in accordance with their own nature (*gotra*).

The fifth section combines [the points] on receiving moisture and attaining the benefit of the Dharma, whereby each attains growth; the sixth section combines [the points] on being secure and flourishing in the present life.
△ Second, combining the analogy of non-differentiation: first, the combination of non-differentiation.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has but a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—which ultimately culminates in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

As for the "single characteristic," it means that the minds of sentient beings are identical to the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*); this is the One Ground (*ekabhūmi*). As for the "single flavor," it means...

The Dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) explains the same single principle; this is the "one rain. In the past, through skillful means (*upāya*), the one true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) was opened up into seven aspects.
Within the teachings of the One Vehicle, they are distinguished as seven schools. The Buddha knows that in the end, all ultimately return to a single aspect and a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
This refers to the following [verse] which explains the single aspect and single flavor: the nature of the minds of sentient beings is...

These three characteristics—the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the tranquility of detachment (*viveka-śānti*)—are taught by the Tathāgata in a single voice as these three dharmas, which are themselves the three samādhis.
These three characteristics constitute the practice of the Middle Way arising from conditions as the objective realm;
ultimately, they result in the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, it is said that one reaches the ultimate state of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore...
Next, "non-differentiation" refers to the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), the single flavor (*ekarasa*), and the convergence upon the single stage (*ekabhūmi*).

The "characteristic of liberation" means there is no characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); the "characteristic of detachment" means there is no characteristic of nirvāṇa; the "characteristic of cessation" means there is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic, but only the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is called the "single characteristic. This single characteristic is the root of non-abiding, from which all things are established.
The Dharma is non-abiding and signless, which is precisely its lack of differentiation. The establishment of all dharmas involves differentiation;

this differentiation is like that of various plants and trees, while the lack of differentiation is like the single earth. Although the earth has no differentiation, it can produce the various differences of peach, plum, and other plants and trees.
Although the peach, plum, and other plants and trees differ from one another, they are equally of the same single, solid nature.
If one knows that the earth possesses peaches and plums, one recognizes that within the reality (the real) there is the provisional (the expedient);
this lack of distinction is itself distinction. If one knows the solid nature of the peaches and plums, one recognizes that within the provisional there is the reality;
this distinction is itself non-distinction. For this reason, the single characteristic is joined with the preceding analogy of the earth; "one flavor" is precisely this.

The True Teaching is pure and without admixture; by taking one characteristic as an example, it can be understood. Regarding the characteristic of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*), it is the absence of the karmic bonds of the two extremes—namely, the *paricchinna* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative) births.
Regarding the characteristic of detachment (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*), it is the attainment of Middle Way wisdom; this wisdom is able to remain far removed from the two extremes and is without attachment.
Regarding the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is the attainment of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* through the cessation of the causes of the two extremes. The two extremes are...
This is because, through the cessation of the fruit, one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder; it is the ultimate arrival at all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If one attains the characteristic of the cessation of both extremes, then the two types of delusion—the pervasive and the specific—are exhausted, and one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
When one practices *prajñā* within the mind of all-knowledge, the initial aspiration and the ultimate state are not distinct; this is precisely the Buddha-wisdom.
[End of section]. △ Second, the five distinctions combined: First, sentient beings' lack of awareness.
There are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma of the Tathāgata, uphold, read, recite, and practice it as taught, yet do not themselves realize or know the merit they thereby obtain.
