Regarding those who are called "sentient beings," it refers to people who do not understand the Dharma of humans and dharmas—namely, those who hear the teaching of a single sound and yet maintain and expound it.
This correctly clarifies that their maintenance and exposition are not the same; their practices differ, and they hold distinct interpretations:

those among humans and devas interpret it as the precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles interpret it as the Truths, the Conditions, and the Means of Deliverance (*pāramitās*). Since these interpretations are already different, this constitutes the differentiation of what is attained.

Regarding "those who do not self-awaken to their own merit," this clarifies that although these five types of people each receive the teaching, they do not know that the Buddha’s teaching is of a single flavor without differentiation.
Furthermore, they do not know that the seven kinds of expedient means each produce distinct interpretations, yet each clings to their own interpretation as being the reality.
This constitutes ignorance of the provisional (upāya) and failure to recognize the real; it is precisely what is meant by "differentiation."
They do not realize or know it themselves. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s ability to know, in four parts. First, knowing by means of the four dharmas.
Why is this? Only the Tathāgata knows the species, characteristics, essence, and nature of these sentient beings.
Regarding the four dharmas, they are: seed, characteristic, essence, and nature. As for "seed," it refers to the three paths as the seeds of the three virtues.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The entire host of afflictions constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata. This clarifies that through the path of affliction, there is *prajñā*. It further states:
"The five deeds of immediate retribution all give rise to the aspect of liberation. This arises from the unwholesome.
The wholesome dharmas that liberate all sentient beings are the very mark of nirvāṇa and cannot be extinguished; this [very state] is birth-and-death as the Dharmakāya.
This is discussed in terms of relative categories. If one discusses them in terms of their essential nature, every lowering of the head and raising of the hand is the seed of liberation;
all worldly wisdom and the minds of the three vehicles that seek liberation are Prajñā.
All those who possess the seed of the aspiration for enlightenment shall become Buddhas; this is the seed of the Dharmakāya.

The Tathāgata fully knows all the various distinctions among these seeds. All seeds are, in fact, a single seed—this is non-differentiation—and the Tathāgata is likewise able to know that differentiation is itself non-differentiation, and that non-differentiation is itself differentiation; the Tathāgata is able to know this as well.

Regarding the three aspects of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*svabhāva*), and nature (*dharmatā*), they are explained within the context of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
If one discusses their differentiation, these are the characteristics of the ten realms; if one discusses their non-differentiation, these are the characteristics of the single Buddha-realm.

Regarding differentiation and non-differentiation, the Tathāgata is able to know that differentiation is precisely non-differentiation and non-differentiation is precisely differentiation; the Tathāgata is likewise able to know their essence and nature.
This can be understood by way of example. △ Second, knowing the three through the three dharmas: first, the objects of the three types of wisdom. What does mindfulness contemplate?
What does reflection ponder? What does cultivation practice?
These three dharmas are precisely the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. "What does mindfulness contemplate? refers to clarifying these three wisdoms.
To employ mindfulness to grasp the object of thought is precisely the sphere of the three types of wisdom. △ Second, the essence of the three types of wisdom:
what is mindfulness, what is reflection, and what is cultivation?
What is mindfulness? Mindfulness is the recording of the teachings one has heard; it is the very essence of mindful wisdom.
△ Third, the causes and conditions of the three types of wisdom:
by what dharma does one practice mindfulness, by what dharma does one contemplate, and by what dharma does one cultivate?

By means of which dharma does one contemplate the lower [realms]? This is precisely the three types of wisdom (trividya) apprehending their objects; hearing the Dharma is its causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, because the objects, the wisdom, and the causal conditions of these three wisdoms converge, they constitute the "three dharmas," which are also termed causal conditions.

Thus, regarding the three vehicles and the three wisdoms, it was previously held that the objects, the essence, and the causal conditions differ, which constitutes their distinction. However, upon entering the perfect and subtle [state], [these distinctions vanish].
The three types of wisdom are without distinction; this [distinction] and non-distinction the Tathāgata is able to know.
Furthermore, that which is distinct is without distinction, and that which is without distinction is distinct—the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this. △ Third, knowing by means of two dharmas.
By what dharma does one obtain what dharma?
These two dharmas refer to the pair of cause and effect. By what dharma—that is, by the cause—one obtains what dharma—that is, the fruit.
The causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits; this is the differentiation of sentient beings, just as with the Buddhas.
The suchness of one is the suchness of non-two; there is only one cause and one fruit, which is non-differentiation.
Differentiation and non-differentiation—the Tathāgata can know that difference is non-difference, and non-difference is difference. The Tathāgata can also know this.
△ Fourth, knowing by means of a single dharma.
Sentient beings dwell in various stages, which only the Tathāgata perceives as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.
Because the seven stages of expedient means consist of seven distinct positions, they are called "various stages. This constitutes their differentiation;
yet when the Tathāgata perceives them with his Buddha-eye of reality, they are like the many rivers flowing into the ocean, where they lose their original flavors and become indistinguishable.
When one speaks by conforming to the intentions of others through the skillful means of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know their distinctions;
yet when the Dharma he teaches reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), the Tathāgata is able to know it as being without distinction.
△ Third, the analogy is raised and applied.

Just as those flowers, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures—this analogy is cited to correspond to sentient beings who do not know [their own capacities].

This refers to the people of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), each of whom does not know for themselves whether they possess superior or inferior [faculties]. Because they do not know this, it is revealed that only the Tathāgata is capable [of discerning it]. △ Four.
To summarize the preceding points regarding that which can be known:
the Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor— namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation,
the characteristic of ultimate nirvāṇa, the characteristic of eternal quiescence, and that it ultimately reverts to emptiness.
The single characteristic and single flavor are explained as before. Liberation, detachment, cessation, and so forth, serve as conditions for discernment;
this is the infinite within the one, the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Ultimately returning to emptiness is the one within the infinite.
This is a reiterated explanation of non-differentiation based on what preceded. Why? Because the single characteristic and single flavor... [are] liberation.
To be liberated from cessation—if this were the essence of the Dharma-body of the Two Vehicles, it would still be a statement of differentiation.
Now, establishing the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the Mahāyāna, which ultimately returns to emptiness, it universally reaches the undifferentiated ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This concludes the preceding phrases: none of these belong to the *sopadhiśeṣa* or *nirupadhiśeṣa* of the Two Vehicles; rather, they are the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, eternally quiescent.
Regarding the "characteristic of cessation," the preceding phrases refer not to the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather to the eternally abiding quiescence.
As stated in the previous text, "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are by nature eternally in the state of quiescence"—this is precisely that meaning.

Regarding "ultimately returning to emptiness," this is not the emptiness of annihilation (the voidness of ashes), but rather the emptiness of the primary truth of the Middle Way. This is indeed [the teaching of] Zheng.
This is merely a reiteration of the palm-strike to distinguish the Real from the Provisional. △ Fifth, resolving doubts:
Having known this, the Buddha observes the inclinations of sentient beings' minds and protects them; for this reason, he does not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
To sever the doubts of those who object: "If the Buddha already knew from beginning to end that all is one, why did he not immediately preach the Truth at the Deer Park?
The explanation states: He observed the inclinations of sentient beings' minds and, in accordance with the three *siddhāntas*, sought to protect them;

fearing they might slander [the Dharma], he did not immediately preach the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom). II. Conclusion and Praise: 2. Returning to the Main Thesis and Addressing the Title.
Regarding the first part of the praise, it states:
"O Kāśyapa, you are truly rare and extraordinary, for you are able to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and you are able to believe and accept it.
First, the reason for praising their rarity is that while ordinary worldlings may occasionally benefit from hearing the Dharma, Bodhisattvas have already accomplished this.
The interpretation is not particularly novel: that those of the Two Vehicles can now renounce and enter the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) is truly rare;
that they can know how to rejoice in and preach the Dharma describes their capacity for reception and opens up three points of discourse.
To say they "can believe and accept" describes their reception and reveals the first point. △ Second, the explanation of the praise.
Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.

Why is this so? This passage explains the underlying intention, clarifying that while the Buddha speaks of three [vehicles] within the One Way—a profound and mysterious teaching that is difficult to comprehend—you are nevertheless able to believe it.
Zhiyi asked: "The preceding text states that the Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable merits."
Your explanations cannot exhaust [the full meaning], as the subsequent text states: "You are truly rare and marvelous!

Yet the Buddha’s grace is universally bestowed, like clouds and rain, reaching everywhere without exception; the Buddha’s grace universally sustains all, like the great earth, bringing everything to life and growth.
How could it be intended for only a single individual or a single region? Therefore, it is said that your explanations cannot exhaust it. Thus it is concluded.
Although the Buddha’s grace is universal, sentient beings do not realize it in their daily lives;

they are like the three types of grass and two types of trees that take root in the earth and receive nourishment from the rain, yet remain unaware of it. That you are able to recognize these tenfold graces from beginning to end is truly rare.
"To deliver those not yet delivered" and so forth describe the grace of the Buddha’s Four Great Vows. May there be peace in this present life.
That after his passing he is born in auspicious realms and experiences happiness through the Path describes the kindness of Great Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in bestowing joy.
Having heard the Dharma, one is freed from all obstacles and gradually enters the Path according to one's capacity; this describes the kindness of Great Compassion (*karuṇā*) in uprooting suffering.
That the Wheel-turning Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā are like minor medicinal herbs describes the kindness of encouraging virtue and removing the feverish afflictions of the mind.
It is also known that the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) can attain *nirvāṇa* and the realization of a *pratyekabuddha*;

this refers to the medicinal herbs, which describe the kindness of eliminating all burning fevers of views and craving. The superior grasses and small trees describe the kindness of putting shame upon the small and aspiring toward the great.
The large trees describe the kindness of their majestic adornment. The most fundamental reality is the single ground.
The "One Rain" describes the kindness of bestowing knowledge, entrusting wealth, providing seats, and granting mastery over body, mind, and the wealth of the Dharma, resulting in peace and happiness.
This concludes the text of the praise for the ten kinds of kindness, which praises their distinctions.
If one were to praise them without distinction, it would simply be the one great kindness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
△ Second, the verses in praise; first, the praise of the Dharma-exposition; second, first, praising the initial citation of the Dharma-King to encourage faith.
The Dharma King who destroys existence has appeared in the world.
Now, the first two lines of the verse encourage faith that the Dharma King’s teachings are not in vain. As for the meaning of "destroying existence":

when the Tathāgata appears in the five turbidities, he manifests sudden and gradual transformations according to the capacities of beings, both great and small, with the intent to cause sentient beings to break and destroy the two [extremes].
Fifteenth, there are the karmas of birth and death; he also destroys the causes of transformation and the moistening of rebirth, causing [beings] to realize the supreme path.

Furthermore, because cause and effect do not perish, there is the Tathāgata; since he has already destroyed this king among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), he is called the "King who Destroys Existence. △ Second, the verse on opening the three to reveal the one. First, the verse:
Regarding the two aspects of the provisional teaching’s revelation of the truth, first is the verse on the provisional teaching’s opening of the expedient means.

"According to the desires of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways"—this one and a half verses concerns the provisional teaching’s preaching of the Dharma in various ways according to the desires of sentient beings; that is to say, the seven [vehicles].

The expedient means (upāya) involve the Tathāgata’s power of skillful wisdom (kauśalyajñāna), which, according to the differing dispositions and desires of each individual, provides teachings as appropriate to their capacities;
this verse reveals the provisional (ābhisamdhika). △ Second, the verse reveals the ultimate (paramārtha) by way of the teaching.
"The Tathāgata honors wisdom that is profound and far-reaching; he has long remained silent on this essential point and does not strive to speak of it hastily.
Regarding "the Tathāgata honors wisdom that is profound and far-reaching," this verse reveals the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Regarding "he has long remained silent on this essential point," this refers to his keeping it secret and not speaking of it for more than forty years. Regarding "he does not strive to speak of it hastily," this is because sentient beings' capacities (*indriya*) were as yet unable to bear it.
One should not reveal it to them so hastily. △ Second, the verse on revealing through wisdom has two parts: first, the verse on revealing the provisional through wisdom.
"Those with wisdom, if they hear it, will be able to believe and understand; those without wisdom will doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss."

These two verses clarify [the teaching] by means of wisdom. The first verse is a commentary on expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna). Second, the following verse clarifies the ultimate reality (paramārtha) by means of wisdom.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, [the Buddha] teaches according to their capacities, employing various conditions to enable them to attain right view.
The next line is a verse explaining that true wisdom, according to various conditions, expounds various teachings so that all may attain the correct view of the Mahāyāna;
everything prior to this is termed false view. This verse expresses the Tathāgata’s four *siddhānta* intentions: the intention of refutation (*pratikṣepa-siddhānta*) is to destroy [wrong views];

the intention of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*) is to face [the afflictions]; the intention of worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti-siddhānta*) is to follow the desires of sentient beings; and the intention of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*) is wisdom.
To lose forever the hearing, faith, understanding, and freedom from doubt and regret—this is the human mind. To cause them to attain right view is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The first three *siddhāntas* are as stated above: by means of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), one expounds for them so that they may attain right view;
this is a verse summarizing the attainment of the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). △ Second, the verses on the parables, in two parts: first, the verse on opening [the parable].
The analogy of the two verses is divided into two parts, the first of which contains six distinct analogies. The first verse concerns the third analogy, the dense cloud:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud arising in the world, pervading everything; the cloud of wisdom contains moisture."
Flashes of lightning dazzle and the sound of thunder reverberates afar, bringing joy to the multitude; the sunlight is eclipsed and the earth becomes cool.
Massing clouds hang low as if they could be grasped.
These nine and a half verses distinguish the metaphor of the "wisdom-cloud containing moisture": the cloud is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). The *nirmāṇakāya*...
Because it accords with the movement of wisdom, it is called a "Cloud of Wisdom. Because it is able to fully possess the twelve divisions of the Dharma, it is said to "contain moisture.
If the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) does not preach the Dharma—such as in the cases of Vimalakīrti or Prabhūtaratna—then this cloud does not contain moisture.

Its body emits great radiance like the flash of lightning, and its mouth resounds with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) like the sound of thunder, causing the ninety-five kinds of heterodoxies...
Because its light does not manifest, it is said to "obscure"; it removes the ninety-eight kinds of afflictive heat, like the coolness upon the earth that can be grasped.

The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) descends into the world appearing as if identical to the three realms of existence; though one might go toward it with a mind to grasp it, it is truly impossible to grasp.
"Grasping" (承攬) is the appearance of seizing. △ Second, the verse on the fourth [topic], the pouring down of rain.
That rain falls equally upon the four directions, streaming down in immeasurable torrents to saturate the entire land.
Because the Dharma-rain is proclaimed and poured forth through the eight tones and four analytical knowledges, it is heard by all at once; therefore, it is said that the four directions are equal.

Furthermore, these "four equalities" are none other than the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—which constitute the four directions for all who possess a mind.
Because all have received profit and benefit, it is said that "the whole land is filled and saturated. This constitutes both the fulfillment of the preceding and the fulfillment of the following;
the analogy of the mountains and rivers is thus established. Furthermore, regarding "the whole land" (*shuìtǔ*), the *Shī* says: "Under the vast heavens, there is nothing that is not the King’s land;

along the borders of the whole land, there is no one who is not the King’s subject. The commentary states: "Vast" (*pǔ*) means great; "rate" (*shuài*) means to follow; "bǐn" means the edge or shore. This refers to the King’s—
The land is vast; now the Dharma King rules over the great trichiliocosm, which is likewise vast. △ Third, a verse on the first topic:
the lands, mountains, and rivers.
The mountains, rivers, and perilous valleys.

The mountains, rivers, steep valleys, and the aforementioned first category of land refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings in the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
Now they receive the rain of the Dharma, so that their body and speech become supple and soft, just as the earth receives moisture. △ Fourth, the verse on the second category:
plants and trees.

The herbs, trees, and medicinal plants that grow in the deep recesses—those "growing in the deep recesses" refers to the second analogy in the preceding verse concerning the differences in the habitual causes of sentient beings.

Because the habitual causes planted by sentient beings over a long period are hidden within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), they are said to be in "deep recesses. Now, they receive the rain of the Dharma.
Because they all attain full development, it is said that they are "produced. △ Fifth, the verse on the fifth [stage], receiving nourishment:
The various trees, both large and small, the hundred grains, seedlings, sugarcane, and grapes—all are made abundant and sufficient by the rain;

even parched ground is universally moistened, and medicinal herbs and trees flourish together. The water of a single flavor issued from those clouds causes the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests [to thrive].
Each receives nourishment according to its capacity.
"The hundred grains" is a general term; here it refers specifically to the five grains, which serve as a metaphor for the five vehicles capable of producing the hundred virtues.

Sugarcane and melons represent meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā). "The parched land being universally moistened" represents causing those who have not yet had faith to gain faith. As for "the sprouts and crops of the hundred grains":
Yang Quan’s *Wuli Lun* states: "If grain-qi (*guqi*) overcomes primordial qi (*yuanqi*), the person will be fat but not long-lived.
The art of nourishing life is to always keep grain-qi minimal so that illness does not arise. The five grains are millet, broomcorn millet, hemp, rice, and wheat;

they are called "grains" because they are the fruits [of the plants]. These five are completed in their fruit, hence the name. Furthermore, "liang" (rice) is a general term for millet and broomcorn millet.
"Rice" (*tiáo*) is the general name for both non-glutinous and glutinous varieties; "beans" (*shū*) is the general name for various types of legumes.
Each of these three categories contains twenty varieties, totaling sixty. The fruits of vegetables and trees that assist the grains each also have twenty varieties, totaling forty.
Adding these to the previous sixty makes one hundred. Regarding "grain crops" (*míào zhà*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Grass growing in a field. *Cāng*.
The *Xie pian* states that "jia" refers to grain before it has sprouted; furthermore, sowing is called "jia" and harvesting is called "se.
Regarding sugarcane and grapes, the *Ji* says that the substance of sugarcane represents "determination" (*ding*), while the many forms of the grape correspond to "wisdom" (*hui*).
The *Bowu zhi* states that when Zhang Qian returned from his mission to the Western Regions, he obtained grapes, walnuts, and other such items—as in the aforementioned examples.
This can be understood. △ Sixth, the verse on the sixth [topic], "Increase":
Among all the trees—superior, middling, and inferior—they each grow according to their respective sizes;
roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as their luster and color, all become fresh and radiant wherever the single rain reaches.
△ Second, the verse on non-differentiation:
Just as their substance, characteristics, nature, and portions—whether large or small—are all moistened by one [water] and each flourishes accordingly.
This single line of verse concerns non-differentiation; whereas the preceding section had three [points], they are here omitted, as the single ground is not separately versified.
That which is produced encompasses both [the rain and the trees], according to their physical characteristics and the magnitude of their respective natures;
this verse describes that which is produced and that which moistens. That the moisture is one is described by this verse as the "moistener," which signifies non-differentiation.
That each flourishes luxuriantly is described by this verse as "differentiation" while remaining unaware of itself. △ Second, the verse on the combined analogy, part one.
The two verses on the analogy of the distinction between the combined and the undifferentiated; the first section further contains six parts.
First, the verse combining the dense clouds. First, the verse combining the dense clouds:
"The Buddha likewise appears in the world."
This single verse combines the analogy of dense clouds with the two preceding lines, identifying the body with the clouds. △ Second, the verse presents the analogy and applies it to the subject:
"Just as a great cloud universally covers all."
The final two lines cite a simile and apply it to the subject at hand. △ Second, the verse on the application of the two similes of rain. Part one:
the verse on the application of the headings. First, the verse on the Ten Epithets:
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings, the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, analyzes and expounds the reality of all dharmas.
Amidst the entire assembly of devas and humans, he proclaims these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Honored One among two-legged beings;
having appeared in the world, I am like a great cloud.

These eight and a half verses combine the analogy of raining down with the preceding headings; first the chapters are established, followed by the exhortation to listen and receive. The first three lines [establish the initial section].
The brief verse on the Ten Epithets is concise in wording yet comprehensive in meaning. "One who has transcended the world" refers to the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*) and the Buddha (*buddha*).

"He who discriminately expounds for the sake of all sentient beings" refers to the Perfectly All-Knowing One (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) and the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*).
"World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) is the tenth epithet. "Among gods and humans" refers to the Tamer of Men (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) and the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).

"Tathāgata" is the primary title; "well-come and well-gone" (sugata) encompasses both aspects, while "one who has emerged from the world" refers to the "Knower of the World. △ Second, the verse on the Four Great Vows.
It moistens and nourishes all withered sentient beings, causing them all to be free from suffering and to attain the peace and happiness of the world,
as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Following the phrase "moistening and nourishing all," there is one line and a half which is a verse on the four great vows for moistening and nourishing all.
"Those who are withered and parched sentient beings" refers to the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
"Causing them all to leave suffering behind" means causing them all to leave behind the suffering of cause and effect; this is the vow to sever innumerable afflictions.
"Attaining peaceful and secure happiness—the happiness of the world"—as well as [the happiness of] Nirvana, refers to the vow to study immeasurable Dharma gates.
"Delighting in the wheel" refers to the vow to achieve the unsurpassed path of the Buddha;
it means causing all those of the five vehicles to attain the supreme bliss that exists within worldly pleasures. △ Second, the verse on the collective exhortation to listen and receive.
All you hosts of devas and humans, listen with single-minded devotion; you should all come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.

I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal, appearing in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. For the great assembly, I shall preach the pure Dharma of ambrosia.
This Dharma is of a single flavor—liberation and nirvana—and with one wondrous voice, I shall expound this meaning, always for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, as a causal condition, he next exhorts [the audience] to listen and receive [the teaching]. Within this exhortation, there are two intentions: first, the initial two lines praise the Buddha;

second, the phrase "for the sake of the great assembly" reveals that because the speaker is venerable, the Dharma he teaches is sublime. All seven excellences (saptasauṣṭhava) inevitably converge here.

Because there is but the One Vehicle, he exhorts [them] to listen and receive [the teaching]. This passage cites non-differentiation to explain away distinctions. △ Third, the verse on the combination of lands, earth, mountains, and rivers:
"I contemplate that all things are universally equal; there is no mind of attachment or aversion toward self or other, and I am free from greedy clinging."
Furthermore, being without obstruction, they constantly preach the Dharma equally to all; as they do for one person, so it is for many.

They always expound the Dharma without ever engaging in other matters, and whether going, coming, sitting, or standing, they never grow weary. They satisfy the world like rain that universally moistens all things.

These four lines, taken together with the preceding analogy of mountains and rivers, mean the following: "Mountains and rivers" refers to sentient beings comprised of the seven kinds of five aggregates.

"Rain falling equally" means that the Buddha’s teaching is impartial, bestowing it upon all without discriminating between valleys and peaks. Thus, there is no distinction of "this" or "that": whether one has the capacity [to understand] or lacks it;

whether one plants roots of goodness or commits acts of love, or conversely, commits acts of rebellion or hatred; whether it is a Buddha-activity or a Mara-activity, for oneself or for others. All are treated with equal impartiality.
To respond to those who come first is "coming," and to respond to those who follow later is "going. To enter into reality is "sitting," and to emerge through expedient means is "standing.
When the Buddha observes sentient beings in this manner, it is precisely the intent of raining [the Dharma] equally upon mountains and rivers.
This verse praises the countless billions of kinds of sentient beings who came to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma. △ Fourth, the verse on the convergence of grasses and trees.
Whether rebuking or praising, whether addressing those of high or low status, those who maintain the precepts or violate them, those whose dignified deportment is complete or incomplete,
those with right view or wrong view, and those of sharp or dull faculties— he rains down the rain of Dharma upon them all without weariness.
These two verses above correspond to the fourth [section], where the Tathāgata at that time observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of these sentient beings;

this corresponds to the second [section] regarding the growth of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests. "Noble and base, high and low" refers to those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), serving as a successive analogy.
"Noble and base, high and low" refers to their respective positions; it concerns those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them.

This is according to practice; it is according to habituation whether one possesses sharp or dull faculties. One must also fully traverse the five vehicles and seven goodnesses to explain this in successive stages.
△ Fifth, the verse on the convergence of receiving moisture has three parts: first, a general explanation of receiving moisture.
"All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide in various stages.
This single line generally clarifies the reception of nourishment, summarizing the meaning of the previous verse regarding how all the various and immeasurable [beings] are made to rejoice.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of receiving nourishment, in five parts; first, the small herb.
Those who dwell among humans, devas, universal monarchs (cakravartin), Śakra, and the various Brahmā kings are the small medicinal herbs.
These seven lines specifically clarify the reception of moisture. The first line clarifies that humans and devas alike have not yet severed their afflictions;
together they constitute the "small herbs. △ The second [set] constitutes the "medium herbs."
Those who know the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are able to attain *nirvāṇa*, give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), obtain the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*),
dwell alone in mountain forests constantly practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and realize the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*— these are the medicinal herbs.

Next, knowing the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) that transcend existence consists of two types of practice; clarifying that both vehicles possess both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) constitutes the middle and small medicinal herbs.
△ Third, the superior medicinal herb:
seeking the place of the World-Honored One with the thought, "I shall become a Buddha," and practicing the samādhi of vigor—this is the superior medicinal herb.
Third, the "Seeking the World-Honored One" section: there is one verse on the clear understanding of the six perfections;
Bodhisattvas who aspire to Buddhahood and transform others are superior to the two vehicles, being like the highest grass. △ Fourth, the "Small Trees."

Furthermore, those sons of the Buddha who single-mindedly focus on the Buddha-way, constantly practice compassion, and know for themselves that they will become Buddhas with absolute certainty—these are called "small trees.

Fourth, there are those sons who, having departed, possess one and a half lines [of teaching] to clarify the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) and have already severed the delusions common to it; they vow to support the remaining [afflictions].
Because they have practiced and engaged [in the path] with the aspiration to transform others, yet are inferior to those above and superior to those below, they are called "small trees.
△ Fifth, the Great Trees:
Bodhisattvas who abide securely in supernatural powers, turn the non-retrogressive wheel, and deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
It is called the "Great Tree.

Regarding the five abidings, the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the departure, and the one and a half lines of the distinct teaching (*vyatireka-śāsana*) concerning self-cultivation and the transformation of others—because it is supreme in its height and breadth, it is named the "Great Tree.
This is based on the three types of bodhisattvas, each acting as three trees; the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are correlated with the three assemblies (*saṃgha*).
The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) refers to the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages; the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) refers to the thirty minds [of the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences].
△ Third, the conclusion regarding the moistened and the moisture-giver: first, an analogy is presented to explain the moistened.

The Buddha’s impartial teaching is like a rain of a single flavor; yet according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, just as the nourishment received by various plants and trees varies.
These three lines conclude the section on that which is moistened and the agent of moistening. The first one and a half lines present a simile and provide an exegesis of that which is moistened.
However, although the moisture received clarifies these seven kinds of skillful means, the seven are but a small portion, like a single drop in the ocean.
△ Second, clarifying that which moistens:
By means of this analogy, the Buddha uses skillful means to reveal various words and phrases to expound upon a single Dharma within his Buddha-wisdom.
It is like a single drop in the ocean.
Next, the Buddha uses this analogy to clarify that the capacity to moisten the Buddha’s wisdom is as vast as the ocean—this concludes one and a half lines.
△ Sixth, the verse on the combined increase has two parts: first, the general summary of the increase; second, the specific explanation of the increase. First, the general summary of the increase.
I rain down the Dharma-rain to fill the world with the single-flavored Dharma, which beings practice according to their capacity.
These two lines are a general summary; the first line is a summary of the increase. △ Second, the illustration is cited and explained.
Just as those forests, medicinal herbs, and various trees gradually increase in size and become lush and beautiful according to their respective dimensions;
the next line is the citation of the analogy followed by its explanation. △ Second, the specific explanation of growth, in four parts: first, explaining the growth of humans and devas.
The Dharma of all Buddhas always employs a single flavor to cause all in the world to universally attain fulfillment; through gradual cultivation, they all attain the fruits of the Path.
These six lines and a half specifically clarify "increase. Of these, the first line and a half clarifies the increase of humans and devas.
"May all long attain fulfillment" refers to peace and security in the present life; "gradually practicing cultivation" refers to receiving joy through the Path in future lives.
△ Second, clarifying the growth of the two vehicles.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who dwell in mountain forests in their final bodies, hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruit, are called medicinal herbs that each attain growth.
Next, regarding the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there is one line and a half [of verse] which describes the growth of the two vehicles. They dwell in the ultimate... [text fragment].
Regarding the "last body," ancient sources state that those of the Two Vehicles attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and dwell in their final existence;

having been ripened by the Buddha through the five flavors, they enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and upon hearing the Mahāyāna, they attain liberation—this is precisely what is meant by "increase. △ Third, the increase of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*).
If bodhisattvas possess firm wisdom, thoroughly comprehend the three realms, and seek the Supreme Vehicle, this is called a small tree attaining growth. Third,
if bodhisattvas possess firm wisdom and depart from one and a half lines [of practice], this is the growth of the Shared Teaching.
Firmness is the wisdom that realizes the nature of dharmas; thorough comprehension of the three realms is the exhaustion of delusions.
△ Fourth, the increase of the Separate Teaching:

Furthermore, there is one who dwells in dhyāna and attains the power of supernatural faculties; hearing that all dharmas are empty, his heart is greatly rejoiced, and he emits countless rays of light.
Saving all sentient beings is called the "great tree" that attains growth.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and depart from existence; these two practices constitute the growth of the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*). Question:

What is the difference between the "single cloud and single rain" and the "single sound"? Answer: At the lower stages, the single sound causes others to hear a single dharma; the Buddha, with his single [sound], [causes them to hear all dharmas].
Sentient beings each understand according to their own kind; now, this single cloud and single rain are precisely that "one sound" which accords with their respective types.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that one sound responds to all voices, while the *Vibhāṣā* states: "The Buddha speaks the Four Truths with a single sound;
humans hear it as human speech, the eighty thousand devas hear it as celestial speech, and those in the hells and yakṣas each hear it in a way that accords with their own."
The speech that proclaims [the Dharma] as far as the Brahma-heaven is called the "Brahma-voice" (*brahmasvara*);

it is also the pure sound obtained as a karmic reward of the Buddha, most wondrous, which is designated as the Brahma-voice. If it were merely a Brahma-voice obtained as a karmic reward, people would not hear it, and even if they did, they would not understand it.
△ Second, the verse on the non-differentiation of the harmonious [teachings], in two parts: first, the verse on the differentiation within non-differentiation.
Thus, the Dharma taught by Kāśyapa Buddha is like a great cloud that moistens human flowers with rain of a single flavor, causing each to attain its fruit.
These five lines of verse correspond to the preceding analogy of non-differentiation; together with the previous one and a half lines of verse, they constitute the [analogy of] non-differentiation.
The three and a half verses following the section on distinctions explain the non-distinction within distinctions.
For example, "like a great cloud with rain of a single flavor" corresponds to the aforementioned non-distinction of the single-flavor rain;
"moistening human beings and flowers so that each attains its fruit" corresponds to the aforementioned distinctions. △ Second, the verse on the non-distinction within distinctions.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the various causes, conditions, and diverse parables used to reveal the Buddha-way are my skillful means;
all Buddhas act likewise. Now, for your sake, I shall speak of the most ultimate reality: none of you śrāvakas have attained final nirvāṇa.
The path you have practiced is the bodhisattva-way; by gradually training and studying it, you shall all become Buddhas.

Kāśyapa, you should know that all such causes and conditions are precisely the manifestation of skillful means (*upāya*); "skillful means" refers to differentiation, which corresponds to what arises from the union [of the two truths].

Now, for your sake, I speak of the most ultimate reality, which is the manifestation of reality (*tattva*); "reality" refers to non-differentiation, which corresponds to the single stage (*ekabhūmi*) mentioned above.
That "none have attained parinirvāṇa" means they have not yet transcended the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). [This] is spoken solely to the two [vehicles].
The vehicle is so called because its assurance is firm; neither humans nor devas regard the fruit as *nirvāṇa*, for the Bodhisattva does not take realization midway.
You who practice what is the Bodhisattva path must also sever the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*) while practicing that path;

that you have already severed them completely is precisely the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that this refers to the regression of one who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment].
Regarding the statement that "the previously cultivated roots of goodness, having been restored, are not extinguished and are identical to those attained later as the fruit;

this wisdom and abandonment of the two vehicles constitutes the path of the bodhisattva": because the two vehicles cling to their own fruits, [this teaching] refutes them by declaring, "This is the path of the bodhisattva," wherein "path" refers to the cause.

Question: Does the bodhisattva also possess a fruit? Answer: It is said that they attain both the path and the fruit. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin): "They attain the path and they attain the fruit."
It is said that "existence" (dharma) is the bodhisattva path and "non-existence" (adharma) is the bodhisattva fruit. To answer this point, it should also be understood as follows:
what is called either the path or the fruit is all the cause of Buddhahood; the cause itself is the path.
△ Fifth, the commentary on the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies," Part Two. First, the presentation of the chapter title:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Six, "The Bestowal of Prophecies.
This chapter clarifies the bestowal of prophecies upon the four great disciples. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *vyākaraṇa*; this is translated here as "bestowal of prophecy" (*shouji*).

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "One receives the prediction from the arising of suchness; one receives the prediction from the cessation of suchness. Since suchness has neither arising nor cessation, one knows there is no prediction. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-sūtra* states:

"To wish not to hear the name of the prediction is called 'great'. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The bestowal of a prediction is a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). How, then, does the present sutra clarify the bestowal of a prediction? Answer:
If one perceives a prediction or a person who receives a prediction, this perception must be shattered by the Bodhisattva.

This vow of prediction must be granted according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it is not granted according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for there are no four *siddhi*s (modes of success) at such times, as will be explained below.
If it is a general prediction, it is like that at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter; if it is a specific prediction, it is like those given after the three assemblies;

if it is a prediction based on the direct cause (*hetu*), it is like that of Sadāparibhūta; if it is a prediction based on the contributing cause (*pratyaya*), it is like that in the tenth section of the "Dharma Master" chapter.
Regarding the various types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) based on offerings: if it is a prediction based on the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause), it is like bestowing the three roots upon a person;

if it is a prediction based on the *dhātu-hetu* (causal essence), it is extensive; if it is a prediction based on the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) or the *vijñapti-hetu*, it is narrow. Furthermore, there may be predictions that are delayed or predictions that are immediate.

There are predictions made by the Buddha as in this text, or predictions made by Bodhisattvas, such as that of Maitreya (Ajita), who, although lacking a fixed designation of eon or land, nevertheless received such a prediction and even gave a further prophetic declaration.
Those described in the "Chapter on the Phantom City" are the future disciples. Other sutras record only bodhisattvas and not the two vehicles;
they record only the good and not the evil; they record only men and not women; and they record only humans and devas and not animals. This present sutra records all of them.
If the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* has four kinds of records, this present sutra possesses them all; they have not yet been revealed.

The "Mind and Prediction" (Cittavyākaraṇa) refers to the three cycles of prediction regarding the arising of the mind and non-arising (*anutpāda*) as found in the "Never-Disparaging" chapter (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*).

In the ninth fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (or *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*), there are eight kinds of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): namely, [the Buddha] knows while others do not; everyone knows while he does not; he and the assembly both know;

the assembly knows while he does not; he and the assembly both do not know; near awakening while far from realization; far awakening while near to realization; and [far awakening while] far from realization.

When one is near [to awakening] yet does not perceive it, while others both perceive and do not perceive it, and one knows for oneself that others do not know— this is the initial resolve made by a vow;
because it has not yet extensively reached others and one has not yet attained the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) or skillful means (*upāya*),
it is when all people know [the truth] while one does not, that one makes a vast resolve and attains fearlessness and skillful means, thereby reaching the stage where all know.

Those who do not know [this] because they have attained the contemplation of emptiness through the skillful means (*upāya*) and fearlessness of the seventh stage are those who have not yet entered the seventh stage and have not yet attained the practice of non-attachment (*asaṅga*). Those who do not perceive it from afar are Maitreya and others;

those who do not perceive it from nearby are those who, though their faculties are fully developed, have not yet abandoned the Tathāgata’s practice of non-attachment, and thus are unable to expound upon the noble ones (*ārya*).

One whose conduct is such that both the near and the far are awakened is the Bodhisattva of the Lion’s Chest (*siṃhahanu*), who possesses all faculties and does not abandon nor cling to the practice of non-attachment.

One whose conduct is such that both the near and the far are unawakened is the Bodhisattva who has not yet attained skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and is unable to fully know the Tathāgatagarbha and other such practices. Another sutra further states: "The near is known..."
Those who receive a prediction from a present Buddha, such as Maitreya and others, are "those who know from afar.

Those who do not receive a prediction from the present Buddha but will receive one from a future Buddha, as when the Buddha spoke to the evil Māra saying "Maitreya shall give you your prediction," are "those who know both near and far.

Those who receive predictions from both the present and future Buddhas are "those who know both near and far. Those who receive neither from the present nor the future Buddha are "those who know neither near nor far."

This is the prediction [of enlightenment]. Originally, all Buddhas appeared in the world for the sake of the great causal event, desiring to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now that the great event has been revealed, the Buddha’s teaching is complete, and sentient beings have entered [the path], fulfilling the Buddha’s original intention;
the wishes of sentient beings are satisfied, and according to the Dharma, they should be granted this prediction. Is it not like a father meeting his son whom he does not bestow upon?

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner’s immeasurable practice of vows over countless lifetimes, the present Buddha states that because their fundamental vow was such, they have obtained this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

These two conditions constitute the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint); thus, the prediction is granted. Moreover, when the followers of the Two Vehicles hear the sutra, they transform from the Small Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle;
since the causes for perfection are already sufficient, the cause must necessarily bring about its fruit. Therefore, at the time the Buddha grants the prediction, the assembly...

All know that they should make vows, either vowing to become internal and external retinues for the *nirmāṇakāya* and *dharmakāya*, or vowing simply to be born in those lands to benefit sentient beings.
These two are the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the definitive teaching for persons) and the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the bestowal of predictions upon those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), this is intended to break the desire of bodhisattvas who would otherwise regress and enter the Lesser Vehicle. Why? Because if there were definitively such a thing as regressing from the two vehicles, [it would not be necessary].

If one has already abandoned the Lesser Vehicle, there are no longer two vehicles; what, then, could be regressed from? Furthermore, as for those who have destroyed their desire to give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, they will naturally abandon it upon realization—why then would I take it up?

Moreover, as for those who have not yet changed their inclination toward the Lesser, they will change it once they realize the Lesser; as for those who are about to realize the Lesser, I do not allow them to realize it.
These four types of *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial tenets) are given as predictions, and the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) manifests before them.

It is because one must necessarily attain true understanding to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision without error, and clearly realize the Buddha-nature, that the prediction (vyākaraṇa) is bestowed.
Although those of the Hīnayāna enter into reality and are certain to become Buddhas, why is no such prediction granted to all sentient beings?

It is because sentient beings merely possess the correct [nature] but lack the conditions; now, having heard this sutra, their faith and understanding provide the complete sufficiency of both conditions and correctness.
To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (buddhajñānadarśana) means to know the Buddha-nature, see the Buddha-dharma, and see the Buddha-nature.

These two [aspects] constitute the ultimate *siddhānta* and the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, these four types of prediction encompass all the aforementioned instances of receiving prediction. "Bestowal" (*śāsana*) is also called "receiving prediction," "receiving the decision" (*vyākaraṇa*), or "receiving the prophecy" (*vyākarana*).

"Bestowal" (*śāsana*) has the sense of giving; "receiving" (*śāsana*) has the sense of attaining; and "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) has the sense of recording the matter. "Decision" (*vyākaraṇa*) is... [text fragment].
The "Definitive Prediction" (*niyata-vyākaraṇa*) refers to the explanation of the name "planting and transplanting.

For those of medium capacity who, upon hearing the Dharma through the two weeks of the Parable and the Analogy, fully comprehend the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one, the Tathāgata provides a formal confirmation (*anumodana*).

Although they know for themselves that they will become Buddhas, the specific time and circumstances remain uncertain; however, if they receive the Buddha’s sincere words conferring their future fruition regarding the kalpa and the land, [the prediction is definitive].
Having definitively understood the near and far [distances] through the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), he is now greatly rejoiced;

because he has received this name from the Buddha, it is called the "Chapter on the Prophecy" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*). This text is an allegorical exposition. Of the four sections above, the first three were all explained by means of parables;
here, the prophecy likewise employs an allegory. Question: For what reason is there no fifth section concerning the fourfold assembly?
Regarding the joyful response of Yaśoda, there are two interpretations: first, it is said that [the text] refers both to what precedes and what follows, omitting them for brevity;

second, it is said that within the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," it is clarified that all who receive moisture attain growth, and it is known with certainty that the fourfold assembly has all obtained benefit, though the scribe of the sutra omitted this for brevity.
△ Second, the exegesis of the scriptural text, which has two parts: first, the actual bestowal...
The prophecy for those of medium capacity consists of two parts; the first permits [the teaching] as a narrative of past lives for those of inferior capacity. The initial section also has two parts:
first, the prophecy for Kāśyapa; second, the prose section, which has six parts, the first being the causes of their practice.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words:
"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold three hundred myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones;
he shall make offerings to them, revere them, respect them, and praise them, and shall widely proclaim the immeasurable Great Dharma of those Buddhas."
This passage contains six points: 1. At that time, the World-Honored One "stayed" in immeasurable great Dharma;
this clarifies the cause of his practice and realization (vidyā-caraṇa). 2. Attaining the fruit:
in his final body, he attained Buddhahood and was named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vairocana (the Radiant One).

The One Perfected in Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—finally, in his last body, this World-Honored One attains the fruit. △ Third: The Kalpas and Lands.
The name of the land is Radiant Virtue, and the name of the eon is Great Adornment.
Regarding the phrase "the three lands named Cessation of Great Adornment," this refers to the adornment of the names of both the eon and the lands. △ Fourth, the lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twelve small kalpas.
Regarding the four Buddhas whose lifespans are twelve small kalpas, this refers to their life spans. △ Fifth, the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma remains in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for twenty small kalpas.
"5. The True Dharma remains in the world for twenty minor kalpas" clarifies the duration for which the teachings of the True and Semblance Eras abide in the world.
△ 6. Purity of the Land: The boundaries of the land are magnificently adorned, free from all filth, evil, rubble, thorns, excrement, and impurities; its terrain is level and even.

There are no elevations, depressions, pits, ravines, mounds, or hills; the ground is made of lapis lazuli, with rows of jewel trees and golden cords demarcating the sides of the roads, strewn everywhere with various precious flowers, making the entire land pure and serene.

There are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas in that land, and the assembly of śrāvakas is likewise incalculable. No demonic activities exist there; even though Māras and their followers are present, they all provide protection.
The Buddha-dharma.
The adornments throughout the boundaries of the six kingdoms all serve to protect the Buddha-dharma and exhaustively manifest the purity of the civilized lands;
yet, as the sections and divisions of this scripture’s text are brilliantly clear, I fear that beginners may not yet fully comprehend them, and have therefore divided it below.
"Third, 'being free from all impurities and evils' means being without the impurities of the four *gatis* and the evils of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*);
the rest is to be understood accordingly. Regarding 'tiles and pebbles,' the *Shuowen Jiezi* states they are small stones.

Regarding 'thorns and brambles,' Prince Zhanghuai’s commentary on the *Hou Han Shu* says they are *zhen* and *bian* thickets; alternatively, it is said that those without thorns are called *jing*, while those with thorns are called *ji*."
As for "Ji-keng" (Thorny Pit), the *Erya* says it means "ruins"; Guo Pu explains it as a "ditch" or "trench.
As for "kan" (Trench), the *Shiming* says it means "dangerous" or "a pitfall. Its shape resembles a jar. As for "dui" (Mound), it means "heaped earth.
As for "fu" (Hill), the *Shiming* says it means "thick," and the *Guangya* says a mountain without stones is called a "fu. The rows of jeweled trees are demarcated by cords of gold.
"Beside the paths" means that the quarters and corners are demarcated by cords made of gold; "boundary" (jie) likewise implies division.
Thus, when it is said that rows of jewel trees have golden cords delimiting the paths, this is merely citing the excellence of the adornments of the Pure Land.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses on the Six Initial Causes.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "With my Buddha-eye, I see that this Kāśyapa, in a future age beyond incalculable kalpas..."
When you attain Buddhahood, you shall in a future age make offerings to and behold three hundred million buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; for the sake of the wisdom of a Buddha,
you shall purify your brahma-conduct, and having made offerings to these supreme among two-legged beings, you shall cultivate all unsurpassed wisdom.

This verse consists of twelve and a half lines. The first four lines, which address the bhikṣus and speak of "stopping" for the sake of unsurpassed wisdom, describe the causal practice. △ Second, the verses on attaining the fruit.
In his final existence, he attains Buddhahood.
The two lines of verse concerning "next, in his final existence, attaining Buddhahood" describe the attainment of the fruit. △ Third, the verse on the purity of the land.
That land is pure, with ground made of lapis lazuli; many jewel trees stand in rows along the sides of the roads, which are demarcated by golden cords, bringing joy to all who behold them.
It constantly emits exquisite fragrances and is strewn with various famous flowers, adorned with all manner of wonders.
The ground is level and even, without mounds or pits, and the assembly of bodhisattvas there is beyond measure, their minds being harmonious and supple.
There were those who had attained great supernormal powers and upheld the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas;
these śrāvakas, who were sons of the Dharma King in their final bodies free from outflows, were likewise incalculable, such that even with the divine eye one could not count or know them.
Third, regarding the purity of its cessation which cannot be fully calculated: these six lines of verse describe the purity of the land.
Fourth, the verse on the lifespan:
that Buddha’s life span shall be twelve minor kalpas.
"Fourth, 'That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas'—these two lines praise his longevity. Fifth, praising the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma shall abide in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise abide for twenty minor kalpas."
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas; this single verse concerns the duration of the True and Semblance Dharmas.
△ Sixth, the summary:
Such were the events concerning the World-Honored One Prabhāsa.
"The matter of the World-Honored One Prabhāsa was thus"—these two phrases serve as the concluding summary.
△ Second, the bestowing of predictions upon three persons: 1. First, the request for a prediction; 2. First, the narration by the scribe.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others were all struck with awe;
with single-minded devotion they joined their palms, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting their eyes for a moment, and then spoke these verses in unison:

This concludes the section where the Venerable Ānanda, as the compiler of the teachings, recounts the manner in which the three great disciples, with solemn deportment and reverent practice, addressed the Buddha and requested the Dharma;
"tong-li" (悚慄) refers to being startled, terrified, and trembling with awe. II. Requesting by means of verses, in four parts:
first, the formal request.
The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, the Dharma King of all Śākyas, out of compassion for us, has bestowed this Buddha-voice.

These seven lines of verse possess four meanings. First, from "The Great Hero, the World-Honored One" to "bestowed this Buddha-voice," these one line constitutes the formal request. Second, the opening of the analogy.
If one knows that my deep intention is to grant them the prediction of enlightenment, it is like being sprinkled with ambrosia to remove heat and attain coolness; yet,
like someone coming from a land of famine who suddenly encounters the meal of a great king, their mind remains filled with doubt and fear, and they do not dare to eat immediately,
but only after receiving the king’s command do they then dare to eat.
Next, if one knows that my profound intention is to cease [eating] and only then dares to eat, these two and a half lines constitute the opening of the analogy.
△ Third, the application of the analogy: "We are also like this;
we constantly contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna, not knowing how we shall ever attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom."
Although we hear the Buddha’s voice saying, "You shall become Buddhas," our hearts still harbor anxiety and fear;
it is as if we do not yet dare to eat, for only when we receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment will we find true peace and joy.
"Third, 'We also abide thus, and only then are we truly at ease and happy'—these two and a half lines constitute the *saṃgraha-upamā* (the synthesis of the analogy).
What is called the *udghāṭana-upamā* (the unfolding of the analogy) refers to the expansion and detailed exposition of the parable;
what is called the *saṃgraha-upamā* refers to bringing forth that parable to synthesize it with this Dharma. This is because the parable must necessarily illustrate the Dharma."
Because the subject and object are equal, like two halves of a tally, they are called "conjoined. The preceding and succeeding passages may be understood according to this principle.
△ Fourth, the conclusion of the intent:
"The Great Hero, the World-Honored One, constantly desires to bring peace to the world; we pray that You grant us a prediction, just as one who is hungry requires instruction on food."
The final line immediately concludes the intent. △ Second, bestowing the prediction (vyākaraṇa), which has three parts: first, Subhūti; second, Kātyāyana; third, Maudgalyāyana.
The first section [Subhūti] further has two parts: first, the prose section, which has seven parts; first, the narration by the scribe.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the minds of his great disciples.
This passage contains seven points; first, "at that time, the World-Honored One [knew] what was in their minds" is the narration by the scribe of the sutra.
△ Second, the cultivation of causes.

He addressed the bhikṣus: "This Subhūti shall, in a future age, behold three hundred trillion nayutas of buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them, while constantly practicing the pure conduct and fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva."
Next, he addressed the bhikṣus: "Ceasing the bodhisattva path" refers to the cause of clear conduct (*vidyā-caraṇa*). △ Third, attaining the fruit:

in his final body, he attained the state of Buddhahood and was named Mingxiang (Nāmarūpa) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Third, regarding "finally ceasing," the World-Honored Buddha clarifies the attainment of the fruit. △ Fourth, the eon and the land:
the eon is named Youbao (Possessing Jewels) and the land is named Baosheng (Jewel-Born).
"The fourth eon is named Zhibao-sheng" (Ceasing Jewel-Born) refers to the names of both the eon and the land. △ Fifth, the purity of the land.
That land is level and even, with crystal for its ground, adorned with jewel-trees and free from hills, pits, gravel, thorns, or the impurities of excrement and urine.
Precious flowers cover the earth everywhere in pure abundance. The people of that land all dwell in precious terraces and exquisite pavilions;
the śrāvaka disciples therein are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
The assembly of bodhisattvas consists of countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.
That five *nayutas* of that land remain is precisely what constitutes the purity of the land. △ Sixth, the lifespan.
The Buddha’s lifespan is twelve small kalpas.
That "the six Buddhas have a lifespan of twelve small kalpas" refers to their life spans. △ Seventh, the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
The True Dharma remains in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for twenty small kalpas; that Buddha constantly dwells [therein].
The void preaches the Dharma for the multitude, delivering immeasurable bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
The seven correct dharmas cease, and the assembly of śrāvakas is exhausted; this clarifies the duration for which the True, Semblance, and Final Teachings abide in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
**II. Verses in Praise (Six Sections)** **First, the Exhortation to Listen:** "O assembly of bhikṣus, I now address you all: you must all listen with a single mind to what I shall say."
These twelve lines of verse contain six intended meanings. First, the initial line exhorts the assembly to compose their minds and listen attentively.
Second, the verse praises the causal basis for practice:
"My great disciple Subhūti shall attain Buddhahood; his name shall be Saṃjñādruma, and he shall make offerings to countless [Buddhas]."
"Ten billion Buddhas, following the practice of the Buddha, gradually perfected the Great Way.
Next, my great disciple [Śāriputra] also gradually perfected the Great Way. These two lines of verse concern the causes of practice.
△ Third, the verses on attaining the fruit.
In his final existence, he attains the thirty-two marks, being upright, beautiful, and exquisite like a mountain of jewels.
This single line of verse—“In his final existence, he attains tranquility like a mountain of jewels”—describes the attainment of the fruit.
△ Fourth, the verse on the purity of the land.
That Buddha-land is foremost in its majestic purity; among those who see it, there are none who do not feel love and joy.
Within it, the Buddha delivers immeasurable multitudes of beings. In his Dharma, there are many bodhisattvas, all of whom possess sharp faculties and turn the wheel of non-retrogression.
That land is constantly adorned by bodhisattvas, while the assembly of śrāvakas is beyond counting, and all have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Possessing the six supernormal powers and dwelling in the eight liberations, he possessed great majestic virtue; when that Buddha preached the Dharma,

he manifested immeasurable supernormal transformations and inconceivable miracles, and all the devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, joined their palms together to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.
Fourth, regarding his Buddha-land, there are six and a half verses concerning those who merely listen to and receive the Buddha’s words; this refers to the purity of the land.
As for "dwelling in the eight liberations" (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), these are the eight renunciations (*aṣṭa-pratipakṣa*). Now, the meaning of "renunciation" (*pratipakṣa*) is as follows:

"renouncing" (*prati*) means to purify the five desires, and "abandoning" (*pakṣa*) means to cast off attachment to them. Only when one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and severs the fetters of the three realms can it be called "liberation."

Regarding the eight liberations mentioned: first, possessing the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; second, lacking the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms;

third, the liberation of the beautiful, which is personally realized through the body; fourth, the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness;

seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; eighth, the cessation of sensation and perception. If one wishes to examine these eight meanings in detail, [one should proceed as follows].

The explanation of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) has already been provided in the preceding text, as stated in the *Fajie Cidi* (Stages of the Dharma Realm).
△ Fifth, the verse on the lifespan: That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve minor kalpas.
5. Regarding the statement that "the lifespan of this Buddha shall be twelve small kalpas," this half-line verse concerns his life span. △ 6. The verse on the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:
The True Dharma shall abide in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise abide for twenty small kalpas.

The sixfold True Dharma shall remain in the world for twenty minor kalpas; this single verse omits the intermediate kalpas and the names of the lands within the periods of the True and Semblance Dharmas.
△ Second, the prediction concerning Kātyāyana, in two parts: first, the prose section, in five parts; first, the causes of his practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus: "I now tell you, O bhikṣus:
this Mahākātyāyana shall, in a future age, honor, serve, revere, and respect eight thousand billion buddhas with all manner of offerings.
After those buddhas have passed into extinction, he shall erect for each of them a stupa-temple one thousand yojanas in height, and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."
Having made offerings to the stupas and temples with flowers and necklaces composed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl,
agate, pearl, and rose-gem— as well as with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers,
he shall thereafter likewise make offerings to twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas; having made offerings to these Buddhas, he will fully perfect the path of a bodhisattva.
This passage contains five points. First, "at that time" refers to those who have perfected the bodhisattva path, clarifying the cause of practice.
"Scented ointment" (vilepana) is fragrance for anointing the body. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the land of India, it is hot and the body has an odor;
therefore, one anoints the body with fragrance to make offerings to the Buddhas and the Saṃgha. △ Second, the attainment of the fruit.
He shall attain Buddhahood and be named Jambunadaketu-prabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Next, one shall attain the state of a Buddha, a World-Honored One who has realized the fruit. Regarding "Jambūnada-gold":
*Jambū* is also called *Cāmpeya*; it is the name of a tree. It stands on the northern shore of Lake Anavatapta in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa).
Beside this tree there is a river, beneath whose waters purple-burnished gold (*cāmpeya-suvarṇa*) is produced; the radiance of this gold outshines all others.
The sun and moon trees are twenty *yojanas* high; because this gold emerges from beneath those trees at the bottom of the river, it is named accordingly.
*Nadi* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "river. It is likely that the name of the present Buddha was derived from this. △ Third, the purity of the land.

That land is level and even, with crystal for its ground and adorned with precious trees. Golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads, and exquisite flowers cover the earth, which is everywhere pure;
those who see it rejoice. There are no four evil paths—the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras.
It abounds with devas and humans, and with immeasurable assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Ten billion adornments embellish that land.
Regarding the phrase "three times the adornment of its soil," this refers to the purity of the land. △ Fourth, the lifespan:
the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve small kalpas.
The lifespan of the four Buddhas being twelve small kalpas refers to their life span. △ Fifth, the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma:
the True Dharma remains in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remains for twenty small kalpas.
The five periods of the True Dharma lasting for twenty minor kalpas clarify the duration of the True and Semblance Ages.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Part Two: The Verses in Praise (consisting of four sections). First, the exhortation to listen.
All you bhikṣus, listen with a single mind to what I shall say, which is true and without deviation.
Of these seven lines, the first line is an exhortation to listen. The [next] two lines concern the cause.
This Kātyāyana shall, with various kinds of exquisite offerings, make offerings to the Buddhas;
after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, he shall erect stupas made of the seven precious substances and likewise honor their relics with flowers and incense.
Next is Kātyāyana, who dwells in making offerings to the śarīra; these two verses concern the practice of the cause.
△ Third, the attainment of the fruit: in his final body, he attains the wisdom of a Buddha and achieves equal and perfect enlightenment.
Third, regarding the attainment of the fruit, these three lines of verse concern those who, in their final body, attain equal enlightenment:

"The purity of the land; the land being pure, they deliver immeasurable billions of sentient beings, all of whom are venerated by the ten directions. △ Fourth, the purity of the land. The land is pure, delivering immeasurable trillions of sentient beings, all of whom are venerated by the ten directions.
The Buddha’s radiance is unsurpassed; that Buddha is named Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Jambu Golden Light).
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas have severed all existence, and his land is adorned with immeasurable and innumerable ornaments.
Regarding the fourth [section], "The Purity of the Four Lands," there are three practices and one verse that adorn the land;

within this purity of the land, the Buddha’s lifespan, the True and Semblance Dharma periods, and so forth, are omitted. △ Third, the record concerning Maudgalyāyana, in two parts: first, the prose section, in six parts;
first, the causes of his practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly: "I now tell you, Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
you shall provide various kinds of offerings to eight thousand buddhas, honoring and respecting them;

after each of those buddhas has entered parinirvāṇa, you shall erect stūpas for each, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and musaragalva."
With agate, pearls, roses, and necklaces made of the seven treasures, as well as various flowers, powdered incense, ground incense, burning incense,
