As for the third class of people, they have never heard the Mahāyāna and have thus been wandering in saṃsāra; these individuals take their first hearing of it during this minor period as the initial formation of a karmic connection.
Furthermore, having practiced only the minor [teachings] in the interim, they now encounter the Prince and first hear of the "small person" seeing Śākyamuni.
In one portion of the provisional teachings, those śrāvakas who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment are judged to be forever extinguished and incapable of generating the aspiration;
this is because they do not understand the Tathāgata’s long-term transformation. △ Third, clarifying that today he again preaches the Lotus Sutra, in two parts:
first, reconciling the past and present; second, specifically reconciling the teacher’s past and present. First, reconciling the teacher’s past and present.
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they currently reside in buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.
Of those two śrāmaṇeras, one has become a Buddha in the eastern direction."
The first is named Akṣobhya in the Land of Joy; the second is named Sumerukūṭa. In the southeast, there are two Buddhas:
the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa and the second is named Siṃhadarśana. In the south, there are two Buddhas: the first is named Gaganastha and the second is named Nityapraśānta.
In the southwest, there are two Buddhas: the first is named Indradhvaja and the second is named Brahmaketu. In the west, there are two Buddhas: the first is named A... [text truncated]
The two names of Amitābha are: [1] Savior from All Suffering and Affliction of the World; [2] [Amitābha]. The two Buddhas of the northwest are:
[1] Divine Power of Tamālapatra-Candana Fragrance; [2] Summit Appearance. The two Buddhas of the north are:
[1] Cloud Sovereign; [2] Cloud Sovereign King. The Buddha of the northeast is named Destroyer of All Fear in the World.
16. It should be known that I, Śākyamuni Buddha, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system;
these sixteen śrāmaṇeras were Buddhas of the eight directions in the past, and they are the present ones. △ Second, the assembly of disciples.
In the two initial assemblies of the past and present, there were those in the fourth stage of non-retrogression.
"O Bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, we each taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who heard the Dharma from us and [set their minds] on Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, those who have regressed and dwell as śrāvakas:
"Among these beings, there are those who currently dwell on the stage of the śrāvaka;
I constantly teach them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for these individuals should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma."
△ Third, the explanation of the intention behind retreating and remaining.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
△ Fourth, the formal conclusion connecting the ancient and the present.
Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time are you, all you bhikṣus.
Second, the assembly for the future has two parts: first, the formal assembly;
this refers to my śrāvaka disciples in the future world after my parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, resolving doubts:
After my parinirvāṇa, there may be disciples who have not heard this sutra and thus do not know or perceive the conduct of bodhisattvas;
they will give rise to the notion of parinirvāṇa regarding the merits they have attained and think they shall enter nirvana. I shall become a Buddha in other lands [to guide them].
Furthermore, there is another name for this: although these people conceive the thought that they have attained extinction and enter into *nirvāṇa*,
they actually seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land and hear this sutra, attaining extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle and no other vehicle,
except for the various skillful means (*upāya*) by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma.
The doubt is raised: if they exist in the present, they will hear the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the path of the single reality;

thus they would belong to the class of those with whom [the Buddha] has formed a karmic connection. If they exist in the future, they will not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before entering parinirvāṇa;

how then could they abandon the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle? The commentary explains: although they have entered parinirvāṇa, they will ultimately still be able to hear me preaching it elsewhere.
In this land, those who have become Buddhas hear this sutra; as for "other lands," these are lands where the teachings common to the three vehicles prevail.
The phrase "except for the skillful means taught by the Tathāgatas" serves to eliminate doubts; these three are taught through skillful means, yet in reality there are not three.
△ Second, clarifying the return to preaching the Lotus Sutra, first: the purity of the assembly at that time.
O monks, when the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and when the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm,
they have thoroughly mastered the dharma of emptiness, and have entered deeply into meditative concentration—
at such a time, when the time for parinirvāṇa has come, that is, when the period of the Buddhas' appearance in the world and the completion of their teaching are near, he then speaks this sūtra.

Just as Kāśyapa Buddha, Candrasūryapradīpa, and others, having finished preaching this sutra, immediately entered *nirvāṇa*, so too Śākyamuni, having finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, proclaimed that he would soon pass away.
Furthermore, "purity" refers to the perfection of cessation (*prahāṇa-sampad*);

"firmness of faith and understanding" means that "faith" refers to the four kinds of indestructible faith (*aveccappasāda*), while "understanding" refers to the four kinds of untainted right comprehension (*anāsrava-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) through which one penetrates and realizes [the truth].

The True Dharma is fully endowed with all meditative concentrations; this is established through wisdom and severance. At that time, one is capable of being taught the Great Way and will certainly believe and understand it upon hearing it.
Furthermore, "the assembly is also pure" means that they have obtained the benefit of the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and are thus spared from calamity.

Those whose faith and understanding are firm possess a heart that embodies mutual trust regarding the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) teachings. Having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, upon hearing it...
The teaching of Prajñā states that when one attains realization within the dharma of emptiness, that is the intent of the transformative teaching.
△ Second, the formal exposition of the Lotus Sūtra:
He immediately gathers the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas to preach this sūtra, [declaring] that in the world there are no two vehicles.
They attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle; this is what is meant by "attaining extinction.
He then gathers all the bodhisattvas, which is like assembling one's kinsmen and so forth; it is for this reason that he preaches this sutra.
Therefore, when the previous passage explained "kinsmen" as referring to the assembly of Dharma-body bodhisattvas who are their reflections, this text serves as the verification for that meaning.
"Manifesting" refers to the gathering of the various bodhisattvas in this assembly; "relatives" refers to the assembly of śrāvakas; and "summoning his son" refers to the Buddha himself.
△ Third, explaining the three meanings previously opened:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, deeply penetrates the nature of sentient beings and knows their inclinations toward the Lesser Dharma."
Because they are deeply attached to the five desires, for their sake he speaks of *nirvāṇa*, and when these people hear it, they immediately believe and accept it.
If there were no followers of the two vehicles who attain extinction (*parinirvāṇa*) in the world, why did the Tathāgata previously speak of provisional teachings? Therefore, he explains:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means deeply understand that sentient beings have small aspirations and natures, and are attached to..."

Because the five objects of sensory desire (*pañca-viṣaya*) obstruct the [five] turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), he first speaks of three [vehicles] to cause them to break through these obstructions and escape their calamities;
only then does he speak of the One. △ Second, the illustrative explanation of establishing karmic conditions has two parts: first, the opening of the analogy; second, the application of the analogy.
The first section further has two parts: first, the analogy of the guide; within this, first is the analogy of the five hundred *yojana*s.
For example, "five hundred yojanas.
A *yojana*—also translated as *yuzhenana*—is a measure of distance in the Western Regions (India) corresponding roughly to a stage of travel (*ji*) here in this land.
However, the figures given in the sūtras and śāstras differ; some calculate it at eighty *li*, while others...
Regarding the numbers sixty, forty, or sixteen—where forty *li* is generally taken as the standard—the mention of "five hundred" is now judged according to this sutra as follows:
the places of retribution within the three realms constitute three hundred; the places of provisional lands constitute four hundred;
and the places of the land of true recompense constitute five hundred. Therefore, the subsequent passage that synthesizes the parable says: "He knows..."

The various cycles of birth and death—that is, the very locus of birth and death—are now clarified. However, because the Buddha’s intent is difficult to comprehend, it must be further explained extensively.

Furthermore, taking the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) as one hundred and five, the lower [delusions] constitute two hundred and five, the upper [delusions] three hundred, the *rajas* and *sikatā* (dust and sand-like delusions) four hundred, and ignorance (*avidyā*) five hundred; therefore, the subsequent passage provides an analogy, stating: "the afflictions."

The meaning of "perilous paths and evil realms" is that they support one another. Furthermore, entering the contemplation of emptiness can overcome three hundred [stages], entering the contemplation of the provisional can overcome four hundred, and the contemplation of the Middle Way can overcome five hundred; therefore, the subsequent passage provides a combined analogy, stating:

"skillfully knowing the characteristics of the obstructions and openings of perilous paths" means simultaneously knowing the two kinds of five hundred [stages] regarding cause and effect. This is its meaning.
They support one another. △ Second, the analogy of the perilous and evil paths:
"The perilous and evil paths are vast and desolate, a place of fear where no people dwell.

The "perilous and evil paths" are an analogy for the causes and effects of birth and death, as well as the *pariṇāmanika* (transformation) and *aupapattika* (segmented) realms; these results are seen as perilous and difficult.
Contemplating the sands of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of ignorance, this cause is perilous and difficult. Because of these causes and conditions, it is called the "evil path.
There are two types of paths: first, that which has something upon which one can rely; second, that which has nothing upon which one can rely.

"Having" refers to the presence of *nirvāṇa* within *saṃsāra* and *bodhi* within afflictions (*kleśa*); this generally refers to the three teachings of the Mahāyāna. "Not having" refers to *saṃsāra* and afflictions...
If there were no nirvana or bodhi for those who cause affliction, this would be a desolate void where no one could rely upon;

this primarily refers to the three baskets and the two vehicles, and according to principle, it also applies generally to the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). △ Third, the analogy of the great multitude.
If there is a great multitude—
if there is a great multitude, this is an analogy for the multitude of those being transformed by the prince who have not yet been delivered. △ Fourth,
the analogy of desiring to reach the place of treasure.
Desiring to pass beyond this path to reach the place of rare treasures;
desiring to pass beyond this perilous road before reaching the stage of "Discernment of the Elements" (vibhaṅga), it is said that one has reached the place of rare treasures.
△ Fifth, the analogy of the single guide.

There was a guide who was wise, intelligent, and profoundly discerning, well-acquainted with the characteristics of the dangers of the path and the signs of its passability or impassability. This "guide" is none other than the sixteenth prince;

"wise and profoundly discerning" means his eyes and ears were pure—this is called "wisdom," and his mind was pure—this is called "discernment. In sum, this refers to the purity of the six sense faculties.
"Intelligence" (*jñāna*) refers to the threefold wisdom of the one mind; "clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to the full possession of the five eyes and the three insights (*trividyā*);
and "pervasion" (*prabhāvanā*) refers to the attainment of the ten powers (*daśabala*). △ Second, the analogy of leading and guiding, in three parts: first, the analogy of the people being led.
He intends to lead the multitude across this perilous difficulty.
△ Second, the parable of those who grow weary and retreat midway. Part one: The retreat at the great mountain. First, the retreat midway:
the multitude he leads grows weary and retreats midway.
Regarding the phrase "the multitude of people being led," this refers generally to the assembly gathered through past karmic connections;
however, if discussed specifically, it refers to those who have already received great benefit in the past but have not yet attained great benefit—these are precisely the ones being led.

If one calculates based on the five hundred people, they are those among the thirty sons who have not yet attained awakening. This is not the "midway" of a journey, but rather what is termed the "middle path."

Because one begins with the initial arousal of the mind and ends with the attainment of Buddhahood, the interval between these two pillars is called the "middle path" when one gives rise to thoughts of retreat. △ Second, addressing the Guide:
They addressed the Guide, saying: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear. Regarding their address to the Guide:
there is the Guide by virtue of the universal path of compassion, as the text says, "There was a guide who led a great multitude.
There is also the Guide by virtue of having established a karmic connection, as the text says... [the rest of the passage].

The act of addressing the Teacher on behalf of the multitude is this very thing; it represents the Teacher’s own skillful means (upāya-jñāna), as the text says, "the Teacher possesses many expedient means.
It also represents the Teacher’s own true wisdom (jñāna), as the text says, "the Teacher knows these people.
What is now called "addressing the Teacher" is precisely the formal request for the establishment of a karmic connection (kṣaṇa-bandha).
He is the Guide; because he withdraws from the Great [Vehicle], the Great is extinguished, and because he receives the Small [Vehicle], the Small arises.
This arising and extinguishing is perceived by the Dharmakāya, which calls this "white. Furthermore, the Prince knows that withdrawing from the Great is precisely what is heard as its "whiteness.
Because his roots of goodness are feeble and he is obscured by ignorance, it is said that he is exhausted and weary of birth and death.
Suffering is called fear. △ Third, being unable to advance further: "Unable to advance further;
the path ahead is still long, and now one wishes to retreat. "Unable to advance further;
the path ahead is still long" means that the afflictions of views and thoughts, the dust-like and sand-like [afflictions], and ignorance are difficult to sever abruptly.
Likewise, there is also the meaning of progress in using the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to guide them, rather than allowing them to return immediately to their original state.
△ Second, the demonstration of guidance, in four parts: first, the analogy of many skillful means.
"The Teacher possesses many skillful means.

This clarifies that he approaches them by means of the Small [Vehicle] to lead them out of the burning house; his skillful means in opening the Dharma of the Three Vehicles all contain four underlying intentions, and this present case is likewise so.
First, "possessing many skillful means" is a metaphor for the appropriate application, specifically employing the Small [Vehicle] as a provisional fit.
[This is] a transition. △ Second, lamenting the loss of the treasure, he forms this thought:
"These [beings] are to be pitied; how can they abandon such great treasures and wish to turn back?"

Next, the passage beginning with "Then he had this thought" constitutes the second section, which uses the parable of grieving over the loss of the treasure to illustrate that one recognizes the possession of the small while lacking the great.
△ Third, the parable of the conjured city has two parts; first, the creation of the conjuration.
Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), he creates a city within the perilous path at a distance of three hundred *yojanas*.
This is the actual application of skillful means; the text contains two meanings, the first of which begins from "having formed this thought."
This is precisely the analogy of the conjured city. Regarding the analogy of mounting the carriage, it says: "I have created these carriages for you.
Since the city now exists, it must first be constructed. △ Second, the teaching of the conjuration.
He addressed the multitude, saying: "Do not fear, and do not turn back. You may stay within this great city and do as you please;
if you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security, and if you can proceed further, you may also reach the place of jewels."

Next, he addresses the multitude, saying: "Go! This is the correct explanation of the parable of the conjured city, which corresponds to the preceding passage on exhortation, demonstration, and realization.
Why is this? The text says, "Do not be afraid; do not turn back," which is the exhortation to proceed further into the city.
Now, the passage from "this great city" up to "as you wish" is the demonstration of that [city].
"The city is habitable; if one enters this city, one will swiftly attain peace and security"—this is the proof of the turning [of the wheel], meaning it praises the security of the city.
"If one can proceed forward to the place of treasure, one may also go there"—however, within the Tripiṭaka teaching, the forward progress is not yet discussed;
this statement is made based on the subsequent revelation of the present royal city. This is the correct interpretation.
This describes the intention of employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) from the past. △ Fourth, the Parable of Entering the City:

At that time, the exhausted multitude felt great joy and marveled at what they had never before experienced, thinking, "We have now escaped this evil path and have swiftly attained peace and security.
Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, giving rise to the thought that they had already reached their destination and feeling a sense of rest.
This secret visualization illustrates the entry into awakening through the Three Vehicles. "The mind is filled with great joy" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

"Exclaiming that it is unprecedented" refers to the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*). "Being freed from the evil realms" refers to the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). "Swiftly attaining peace and security" refers to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).
The "stage of patience" (*kṣānti*) corresponds to this; those who previously entered the city correspond to the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*);

and those who have already conceived the thought that they have attained deliverance correspond to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). This is analogous to the sons in the burning house who, having fulfilled their wishes, emerged from the house with vigorous haste.

Furthermore, the thought that one has already attained deliverance is like attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the thought of peace and security is like attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Moreover—
Having fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), he has already crossed over and realized the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), remaining in peace and security.
△ Third, the parable of extinguishing the illusory city and leading them to the place of jewels, in two parts:
first, knowing they have rested. At that time, the guide knew that these people had already found rest and were no longer weary.

This passage contains two meanings: first, "having attained rest and no longer experiencing fatigue" is a metaphor for the arrival of the time of *nirvāṇa*, when the assembly is further purified, escapes from calamity, and the great capacity [for awakening] is aroused. Second, it refers to being led to the place of jewels.
He immediately extinguishes the conjured city and says to the multitude: "Come, you all; the place of treasure is near.
That great city we headed toward was merely a conjured resting place.

Next, he extinguishes the conjured city and leads them toward the actual site of the treasure. This is a metaphor for the aforementioned correct preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, which reveals the ultimate truth.
It is likewise so with the "Treasure Store" (ratnagotra), which possesses two meanings. If one takes the ultimate perspective, the fruit of perfection is the Treasure Store;
thus the preceding text states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

If one divides it according to entry [into the stages], then the first stage of the Bodhisattva path, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*), is the Treasure Store; thus the preceding text states: "The unsurpassed mass of jewels is not sought [elsewhere]."
Furthermore, it is said that one has personally attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma; whatever a son of the Buddha ought to attain has already been attained.
This precisely refers to the fact that the "place of treasure" is near at hand. The aforementioned "great city" was manifested by me as a provisional means;

this is simply an illustration using a metaphor of abandoning the provisional to reveal the real. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "The wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand."
"All you people should enter the Buddha’s wisdom gradually by means of this Dharma. This refers to the statement within the *Upāya-kauśalya* [chapter]:

"I cause you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvāṇa," which indicates that the Buddha, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-vaśena*), has manifested the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*tri-yāna*).
Furthermore, regarding "you who go and come": "go" (*gacchatha*) means to proceed; "come" (*āgacchatha*) is an auxiliary particle used for emphasis, as in the expression "you who proceed."
"The place of treasure is near; this is what that refers to. △ Second, the combined analogy, in two parts: first, the formal application;
second, the initial application of the analogy of the guide, in five parts. First, the application of the guide.
"O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is also like this.
This passage consists of five points, though they are not presented in their original order. First, "the Tathāgata is also like this" corresponds to the fifth point, the Guide.
Second, it corresponds to the multitude of people.
"Now I act as your great guide.
"Now for you all" combines with the third [section], "the vast multitude of people. △ Third, combining the perilous and evil paths.
One knows that all births and deaths, afflictions, and evil realms are perilous and difficult.
Knowing these births, deaths, and afflictions corresponds to the second peril. (The four [perils] together amount to five hundred yojanas.)
"Far off. These two characters, "far off," together constitute the first [stage] of five hundred yojanas. △ Fifth, reaching the place of the precious treasure.
One should go; one should cross over.
Those who should go and be delivered are combined with the fourth [section], reaching the place of the precious treasure. △ Second, combining the analogy of leading and guiding;
third, first, combining the people and multitudes being led:
"If there are sentient beings..."

"If there are sentient beings" refers to the group of people previously mentioned in the first section. △ Second, combining those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle] with those who are received into the Small [Vehicle].
First, combining those who have regressed midway due to indolence. First, combining those who have regressed midway due to indolence.

"Those who hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle" corresponds to the second [category] of those who regress from the Great and are led to the Small; this is the second analogy for those originally destined for the Great who regress and are led to the Small.
Now, combining these cases, there are three types of regression from above: "those who hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle" corresponds to the regression due to weariness midway.
This is the meaning of "insentient. △ Second, the combined statement addressed to the Guide:
"I do not wish to see the Buddha; I do not wish to draw near to him.
This combined statement addressed to the Guide—“I do not wish to see the Buddha; I do not wish to draw near to him”—signifies that one does not accept his admonitions and exhortations.
△ 2. The two [feet] join together so that he cannot advance further.
He then thinks: "The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished.
He then thinks: "My lower [foot] joins with my upper [foot], and I cannot advance further"—this is the intent of ceasing his transformative activity. △ 2. The two join.
In the initial stage of connecting the minor [teachings], many skillful means are combined.
The Buddha knows this intention:
that these combinations connect by means of minor analogies; whereas originally there were four, now they are combined into three. The Buddha knows this intention of their combination.

The "Supreme Guide" possesses many skillful means (*upāya*); this refers to his intention of adapting [the teaching] to the capacity [of beings]. △ Second, "combining these who are pitiable": those who are timid, weak, and inferior.
By the power of skillful means, he addresses those who are timid, weak, and inferior;
this combines with the preceding "these who are pitiable," indicating that they possess small faculties (*hīna-indriya*). △ Third, combining.
Manifesting as a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) for the sake of providing rest along the way, two types of *nirvāṇa* are taught.
Because it serves as a place of rest midway, [the sūtra] subsequently correlates this with the third simile: manifesting as a conjured city so that the multitude may enter.

The city serves as a metaphor; herein, two types of *nirvāṇa* are taught within the middle way. When the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms—viewing and conceptualization—are exhausted, yet the "dust-like" ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been shattered, one distinguishes between *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder) at this midpoint between the two pillars.

This is also the dual *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, wherein the *pariccheda-śarīra* (fragmentary existence) is already ended, but the *pariṇāmi-śarīra* (transformative existence) has not yet been eliminated.

Because death is distinguished as being with remainder or without remainder, it is called the "Middle Way. △ Third, combining the extinguishing of the conjured city to lead [beings] to the treasure place;
first, combining the knowledge that [suffering] has ceased.

If sentient beings abide in the second stage, it corresponds to the third [stage], where the transformation toward reaching the treasure-place is about to occur; this is the analogy. In the preceding text there were two [parts], and now these are combined into two as well.
"If sentient beings abide in the second stage" corresponds to the knowledge that they have already come to rest. △ Second, the combination of the leading [analogy].
Toward the place of jewels, the Tathāgata then immediately spoke for their sake: "What you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you dwell is near to the Buddha-wisdom.
You should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality; it is merely [a provisional state] of the Tathāgata."
By the power of his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately preached for them, which is like leading them toward the place of treasure. △ Second, citing the parable and applying it to the teaching, in two parts:
first, reiterating the analogy of the retreat and applying it to the bestowal of the three vehicles.
Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great city;
this passage from "that guide" downward constitutes the second layer of the analogy, which links the preceding metaphor of the retreat to the subsequent application of the three [vehicles].
△ Second, the layer of the analogy for the extinction of the conjuration, which links back to reveal the One.
Once they have known that their breath has ceased, he tells them: "The place of treasure is near; this city is not real; it was merely my transformation.
"Once they have known that their breath has ceased" is a repeated illustration of cessation and transformation, brought together to manifest the One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses in Praise (Gāthā) A. Two parts: First, verses praising the causes for establishing the connection; second, the specific content. 1. First, verses praising the distant cause. a.
First, verses praising the events prior to the attainment of Great Penetrating Enlightenment.
For ten kalpas, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Throughout this time, the devas, nāga kings, asura hosts, and others constantly rained down celestial flowers as an offering to that Buddha;
the devas beat celestial drums and performed various kinds of music, while fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers and rained down fresh and beautiful ones in their stead.
Regarding these six lines of verse: whereas the preceding prose on the Great Attainment of the Way contained five sections, the current verses contain only three.

Here, the first three lines of verse correspond to the second section of the preceding prose, which concerns the events prior to his imminent attainment of the Way. △ Second, the verses on the actual attainment of the Way.
After ten minor kalpas had passed, he finally attained the Way of the Buddha; all the devas and the people of the world felt great exultation in their hearts.
Next, after another ten minor kalpas had passed, the second section concludes with one verse. Third, the correct attainment of the Way.
△ Third, the verses requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, each surrounded by a retinue of thousands of millions of billions, all went together to the place where the Buddha was.
They bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and entreated him to turn the wheel of Dharma, so that the holy lion’s rain of Dharma might fill them and all beings.
Third, regarding the sixteen sons of that Buddha, the third section consists of two lines of verse.

This includes the request for the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the fifty-sixth prince, as well as verses on the fourth point—the offering made by the retinue after the attainment of enlightenment;

the first point, the long duration of the Buddha’s lifespan, is omitted from the verses. △ Second, the verses on the requests of the Brahmās of the ten directions, divided into two parts: first, the verses on the movement caused by his majestic radiance.
Radiant! It is extremely difficult to encounter a World-Honored One; appearing but once in the course of a vast eon, he awakens all sentient beings and causes all things to tremble.
△ Second, the verse on the Brahmās of the ten directions seeking the light and coming [to him]. Part one: A specific verse on the eastern direction.
In the worlds of the eastern direction, across five hundred trillion lands, the Brahma palaces were filled with a radiance such as had never been seen before.

When the various Brahmas perceived this sign, they each came to where the Buddha was, scattering flowers as an offering and presenting their palaces while requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
They praised the Buddha with verses; however, knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted their request by remaining silent and seated.
△ Second, a general verse on the nine directions:
The three cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, as well as above and below, are likewise thus. They scatter flowers, offer palaces, and entreat the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma:

"The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; we pray that by means of your original compassion, you will widely open the gate of the nectar of immortality and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."

△ Second, the verses on the immediate [cause] consist of two parts. First, the initial verse requests the turning of the wheel of the *ardhākṣara* (half-syllable) Dharma. Part one: the verse on accepting the request.
"O Bhagavat of immeasurable wisdom, you have accepted the request of those multitudes."
△ Second, the verses on the actual turning [of the wheel].
To proclaim the various dharmas— the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination— from ignorance through old age and death,
all of which arise from birth as their condition and involve such manifold afflictions, you should know them thus.
△ Three verses on attaining the Way through hearing the Dharma:
While this Dharma was being proclaimed, six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* beings reached the end of all suffering and all became Arhats.
During the second discourse on the Dharma, an assembly as vast as ten million *Gaṅgā* rivers attained Arhatship by not grasping at any dharmas.
From this point onward, those who attain the Way are immeasurable in number; even through calculations spanning ten trillion *kalpas*, one cannot reach their limit.
Regarding the term "sixty trillion *hai*": as for *hai*, some versions write it as *gai*. The *Fengsu Tong* states:
ten thousand is a "wan," ten wan is a "bi," ten billion is a "zhao," and ten zhao is a "jing. From *jing* comes *zi*; from *zi* comes *gai*; and from *gai* comes *rang*.

From *ruǎng* (moist soil) comes *gōu* (ditch); from *gōu* comes *jiàn* (streamlet); from *jiàn* comes *zhèng* (channel); and from *zhèng* comes *zài* (burden). "Burden" (*zài*) refers to that which the earth cannot contain or support.
Thus, ten billion is a *zhào*, one hundred billion is a *jīng*, one thousand billion is a *zǐ*, and ten thousand billion is a *hái*;
these are simply the *nayuta* found in the *Dīrgha-āgama* and are also among the fifty-two numerical units in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
This is the tenth number among them. It says: one is the beginning of numbers; ten ones make ten; ten tens make a hundred;
ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand; ten ten-thousands make a lakṣa; ten lakṣas make a prayuta;
ten prayutas make a koṭi; ten koṭis make a madhya; ten madhyas make an ayuta.
*Yutuo yutuo* (庾多阿庾多) is equivalent to *nayuta*; this is likely due to differences between the older and newer translations.
△ Second, the verse on requesting the full syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*), part five: first, the verse on the prince’s renunciation.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras.
II. Verses on the Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma:
"We all together request that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma; we and our retinues shall all attain the path of Buddhahood."
May I obtain a wisdom-eye like that of the World-Honored One, the foremost in purity.
△ Third, the verse on the Vaipulya Prajñā:
The Buddha, knowing the mind of the youth and his practices in past lives, [taught] through immeasurable causes and conditions and various parables.
He expounded the six pāramitās and the matters of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), distinguishing the true Dharma and the path practiced by bodhisattvas.
△ Fourth, he spoke in verse on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
reciting verses of this *Lotus Sutra* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
△ The five verses describe having entered meditative absorption.
After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he entered dhyāna-concentration in a quiet chamber and sat with a single-minded focus on one object for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
The seventh verse describes having entered absorption; the third [verse], concerning the eighty seekers brought by the father king, is omitted from the verse.
The section on those who have left the household life and the fifth group—the assembly that hears the sutra—includes both those who understand and those who do not, as well as the sixth point:

the long duration of the time when the sutra is preached. II. Verse Summary of the Formal Conclusion of the Karmic Connection (Zheng jieyuan). A. First, the verse summary of the Dharma-exposition (Fashuo). 1.
First, the verse summary of the past shared karmic connection. a. First, the verse summary of knowing the Buddha had entered meditative concentration.
These śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had not yet emerged from his meditative concentration.
△ Second, the verse on the princes' re-exposition:
For immeasurable billions of beings, they expounded the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom; each sat upon a Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, he propagated and assisted in the transformation of beings through the Dharma.
△ Third, the verse on the benefits obtained by the assembly:
among the various sentient beings saved by each of the śrāmaṇeras and others, there were as many as six hundred million *koṭis* of Ganges-sands.
The fourth [point]—the Buddha arising from samādhi and uttering praise—is omitted and not versified. △ Second, the verse on their subsequent mutual encounters:
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these who heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in various Buddha-lands wherever they may be.
△ Three verses now return to the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra. Part One: Connecting the Past with the Present.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras have fully practiced the Buddha-way; they are currently in the ten directions, each having attained perfect enlightenment.
Those who heard the Dharma at that time are now each in the presence of various Buddhas. Among them, those who remained as śrāvakas were gradually taught the Buddha-way.
"In the past, during the sixteen-count [eons], I also spoke for you; therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I have led you toward the Buddha-wisdom.

These three lines of verse conclude and harmonize the past and present. However, while the preceding text contains two meanings—present and future—the first three lines here only conclude and harmonize the present relationship between teacher and disciple. △ Second, the verses on returning to preach the Dharma.
In the first verse of the second chapter, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," the purity of the assembly at that time is established;
for this reason, this second single-line verse returns to explain the preceding passage of the Lotus Sūtra, which contains three intended meanings. Now, the first line:

This verse praises how the assembly of the first period was purified through their past causes and conditions, such that today this assembly has escaped calamity and the karmic potential has been activated.
△ Second, the verse on returning to preach the Lotus Sutra.
Now, by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I cause you to enter the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm.
Next, from "Now, preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*" below, the second three lines of verse [comment on] the second [section], which is the preaching of this sūtra;

the third [section], which explains the intent of opening up the provisional, is omitted from the verse. △ Second, the verses on the parable, divided into two parts: first, the verses on the introductory analogy; second...
The first verse provides five analogies for the Teacher; the first verse describes the perilous and evil path:
it is like a treacherous and wicked road that is remote and isolated, abounding in venomous beasts, and furthermore lacking water and grass—a place feared by all people.
△ Second verse: A great multitude of people.
Countless thousands of myriads of beings wish to pass through this perilous path.
△ Third verse: Five hundred yojanas.
The road was extremely vast and distant, spanning five hundred *yojanas*.
△ Fourth, the verse on "There is a Teacher":
At that time, there was a teacher.
△ Five verses describe one who is wise, discerning, and sagacious;
possessing a powerful memory and wisdom, with a clear mind and firm resolve, he rescues the multitude from perils.
△ Two verses provide a simile for the leader; first, one verse describes the multitude being led.
The Multitude.
△ Second, the verse on weariness and retreat along the way. First, the verse on retreating from the Great Vehicle:
"All of us are exhausted," they said in verse to the Guide, "and we now wish to turn back from here."
△ Second, the verses on the regression; first, the verse lamenting the loss of the Great [Vehicle]:
The Teacher thought thus: "These people are truly to be pitied; how can they wish to turn back and lose the great treasure?"
△ Second, two verses on forming the thought:
immediately upon this, he contemplates the means, intending to employ supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*).
△ Third, three verses on performing emanations (*nirmāṇa*); the first verse describes the performance of the emanation.
He manifested a great city with magnificent houses, surrounded by gardens, streams, and bathing pools,
featuring double gates and lofty towers, all filled with men and women.
These one and a half verses contain two intended meanings. The first line and a half provides the primary analogy for the act of transformation:
"various houses" refers to the objects of the various meditations on emptiness; "gardens and groves" refers to the groves of untainted dharmas and the dhāraṇīs of the two vehicles;
"canals" refers to the nine successive attainments; "bathing pools" refers to the eight liberations; and "double gates" refers to the three gates of emptiness.
Furthermore, the profound emptiness samādhi and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising constitute the lofty pavilion.

Men and women represent the mind that understands through concentration and wisdom; their wisdom-essence is all-encompassing like a city wall, and their perfect fulfillment of wholesome dharmas is like the surrounding moat.
Taking ultimate emptiness as one’s dwelling, true goodness can accomplish one's own practice, just as a man is capable [of leadership].
Managing household affairs through compassionate external transformation is like a woman who has married out of her family. △ Second, the verse on transformation:
Having performed this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying: "Do not fear; you may enter this city, each according to your own inclination."
Next, from "Immediately after having performed this transformation" onwards, the second section consists of one verse which summarizes the aforementioned transformation.
△ Fourth, the verse on entering the city:
Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were all filled with great joy; they all conceived the thought of security and each considered themselves to have already attained deliverance.
△ Section Three: Extinction of the Transformation and Guidance to the Treasure Place (2 parts). First, one verse on knowing that [the beings] have rested.
The Guide, having known they have rested...
Second, two verses on leading them toward the treasure place.
He assembled the multitude and addressed them, saying: "You should proceed forward; this is merely a conjured city.

Seeing that you were exhausted and wished to turn back midway, I employed the power of skillful means to temporarily manifest this city. You should now exert yourselves with diligence, and together we shall reach the place of treasure."
△ Second, the two verses that synthesize the analogy. Part one: the first verse synthesizes the main point. Part two: the first verse synthesizes the five hundred *yojanas*.
"I am likewise thus, acting as the guide for all."
△ Second, combining the analogy of the guide. Part one: A verse combining the exhaustion and retreat midway. First, combining the retreat from the Great [Vehicle]:
Seeing those who seek the Way exhausting themselves and falling away midway, unable to cross over the perilous paths of birth-and-death and afflictions.
△ Second, the combined verse on the cessation of the retreat.

Thus, by the power of skillful means, for the sake of providing rest, he speaks the words of *nirvāṇa*, saying: "O you, your suffering is extinguished; that which was to be done has all been accomplished.
△ Second, the verses combining the cessation of the transformation and leading toward the place of treasure. Part one: the verse combining the knowledge that they have already rested.
Having known that they had all reached nirvana and attained arhatship.
△ Second, the verse on collectively leading them toward the treasure place:
Thereupon, he assembled the great assembly and expounded the true Dharma; by the skillful power of the Buddhas, he distinguished and taught the three vehicles.
There is only the single Buddha-vehicle as the place of rest; therefore, two [vehicles] were taught. Now I shall speak the truth for you: that which you have attained is not extinction.

To become a Buddha with all-encompassing wisdom, you must exert great diligence. When you realize all-encompassing wisdom, the ten powers, and other Buddha-dharmas, and are endowed with the thirty-two marks, that is true extinction.
In this passage, there is the meaning of the secret treasury of the three virtues. Why is this so? Your realization of all-knowledge is the virtue of *prajñā*;
your possession of the thirty-two marks is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; and your true cessation is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
These three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; this is precisely what it means to see the Buddha-nature. △ Second, the verse provides an analogy to illustrate and apply [the meaning].
The Teacher of all Buddhas, for the sake of bringing rest, speaks of nirvāṇa; once they have known this rest, he leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.
This single verse concludes the summary of the text from the third fascicle above.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Five;
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Shoulun of Qiyun, Jinxi, Keshan, Song Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Faji of the Puti Hermitage at Yuxi;
edited and carved for publication by the Layman Min Mengde of Pingcheng, Wuxing.
△ Seven: The Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples Receiving Predictions, Part Two: First, the Presentation of the Chapter Title.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.

This chapter constitutes the second section within the discourse on causes and conditions. Why is it that while the chapter records the prophecies for twelve hundred disciples, the title specifies "five hundred"?
One should know that these five hundred received prophecies under the same name, and furthermore, they were five hundred in number.

Because Chen (Cundī) has attained understanding, she is used to title this chapter. △ Second, the explanation of the scriptural text, which has two parts: first, the bestowing of the prediction upon Pūrṇa;
second, the bestowing of the predictions upon the twelve hundred disciples. The first section [of the first part] also has two parts: first, the narrative of silent acceptance and understanding;

second, the Tathāgata’s recounting of the prediction. The first of these [two parts] also has two parts: first, the narrative of the joy of attaining understanding; second, the initial narrative of the causes for attaining that understanding. First...
The preaching of the Dharma through the two cycles of revelation and manifestation has been heard.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means, expounded according to what was appropriate for each occasion.
Hearing this wisdom from the Buddha refers to the manifestation of the ultimate truth (*bhūtatathatā*) in two locations within the "burning house" of skillful means (*upāya*).

That "skillful means accord with what is appropriate" refers to the revelation of provisional teachings (*prajñapti*) in those same two locations. △ Second, hearing the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon the five great disciples.
Furthermore, he heard that the various great disciples were granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Hearing that the various great disciples [were so designated] refers to the revelation of the provisional means (*upāya*);
being granted the prediction of *bodhi* refers to the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*tattva*). △ Third, hearing of past events.
Furthermore, they hear of the matters concerning causes and conditions from past lives.
To hear of the causes and conditions from past lives is to comprehend and manifest the ultimate reality. △ Fourth, hearing of the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, one hears that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).

To hear that all Buddhas possess such great sovereign spiritual power means that by means of the Tathāgata’s threefold unhindered penetration (*trividyā*), he perceives the distant past as if it were today;
this is precisely the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties, which distinguishes [the Buddha] from the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

"Ceasing and aligning [the faculties] at eighty thousand [moments]" refers to the opening of the provisional means (*upāya*). △ Second, the narration of the joy of attaining understanding, in two parts:
first, clarifying internal joy.
"Attaining what was never before attained," the mind becomes pure and leaps with exultation.
This passage describes the joy of attaining understanding; it first clarifies the internal joy of realization.

Because they have now heard what was previously unheard—the revelation of the provisional to reveal the ultimate—they say, "I have attained what I never had before. Because they have removed attachment to *nirvāṇa* and severed specific delusions, their minds are purified.
Because they have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they leap for joy. △ Second, the external expression of reverence.

He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without for a moment averting his eyes.
Next, it clarifies that external physical reverence leads to liberation because it arises from the Buddha. △ Second, the description of silent contemplation.
Section Two: Comprehension. First, the formal explanation of comprehension through silent contemplation.
They formed this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; his deeds are rare and marvelous.

According to the various dispositions of those in the world, whether gradual or sudden, he employs skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma for them, thereby uprooting the sentient beings' attachments to their respective places. We..."
The Buddha’s merits cannot be fully expressed in words.

This passage clarifies that silent contemplation constitutes understanding, and it contains two intended meanings: although in the previous two cycles of teaching those who attained awakening all spoke aloud to express their understanding, why is it that here they contemplate in silence?
One should know that in the former instances, because those of inferior capacity had not yet awakened, it was necessary for matters to be made manifest through speech.
I have already exhorted those of inferior capacity today; since they have realized that there is nothing further to be exhorted, I remain silent and do not speak.
Furthermore, while previously I only accepted their understanding without seeking to reveal my own status, speaking then would not have been an object of reproach;

now, however, I both understand and reveal. Because I understand, I am mindful of avoiding public censure; therefore, it is most appropriate to remain silent and reflect. Thus, I silently accept their understanding.
This great realization through understanding is like the silence of Vimalakīrti; it is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

Furthermore, the provisional and the ultimate are inconceivable—beyond both speech and thought. Yet, by speaking where there is no speech and thinking where there is no thought, one speaks where there is no speech.
Therefore, while the foregoing was a realization expressed through oral discourse, this present moment is a realization through silent contemplation. What was the intention behind the former?
He did not seek to reveal his true identity because those of inferior capacity had not yet attained awakening; therefore, he did not seek to reveal his identity.

Now that those of inferior capacity have understood, the purpose of his provisional transformation is fulfilled. If he were to reveal his identity to those of inferior capacity, they would realize that even the middle and superior capacities are provisional.

This is because, from the perspective of the superior and middle capacities, such a revelation would be inappropriate for those of inferior capacity. The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; what he does is rare and marvelous.

To comprehend ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) while preaching the Dharma in accordance with the various dispositions of worldly beings is precisely to comprehend provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*;

*prajñā-śūnyatā*); this is indeed the fundamental nature of the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). This is the intent of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṭala*) in revealing the ultimate by opening up the provisional.
To "extricate sentient beings from their attachments everywhere" is to comprehend the Burning House (*Gṛha-dāha*).

This reveals the provisional to manifest the real. When we say, "We cannot proclaim the Buddha’s merits," this refers back to the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, where it was stated that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merits beyond your reach.
Since it says they "cannot be proclaimed," it also implies they are beyond the reach of thought. △ Second, clarifying how [the disciples] silently seek and reveal their origins.
"Please grant us this record.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our profound inner resolve and original vows;

only the Buddha can know [this]"—the phrase "only the Buddha can know" below refers to silently praying for the revelation of their true origins and requesting a record. The term "we" refers generally to all.

One should know that the manifestation of various human traces through the invocation of mindfulness is based upon the profound mind; this present manifestation of traces is the original vow, which is the vow of great compassion.
II. The Tathāgata’s Narrative Record (in two parts): A. Prose Exposition; B. Verse Recitation. The first part [the prose exposition] is further divided into three sections:

A. Describing the Original and the Traces; B. Bestowing the Prophecy; C. [The third section]. The first section [describing the original and the traces] is further divided into three parts. First, regarding...
Regarding Śākyamuni’s worldly conduct as the cause for manifesting his origin, first, he introduces the person:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Do you see this Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra?"
"Do you see them?"—this question contains two meanings: first, seeing their manifested traces as being small; second, seeing their fundamental merit.
The multitude sees only the traces and regards them as śrāvakas, unable to know that they are fundamentally bodhisattvas; therefore, it asks, "Do you see them?
△ Second, the general introduction to the chapter on the fundamental and the manifested has two parts: first, the manifested.
I have always praised him as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
This indicates his outward manifestation; he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma in terms of his manifested traces.

If it were not for the wondrous, fundamental Dharmakāya, there would be no way to bestow such a supreme trace of excellence. Hitherto, people have spoken only of preaching the Dharma within the realm of manifested traces.
First, it is not so now; having long ago attained the foremost rank in the unsurpassed Dharma, this [passage] cites the traces to reveal the fundamental source.
△ Second, the essence: he also constantly extols its various merits.
Furthermore, he constantly extols these [teachings] to manifest his original ground, for they are the dharma-gates of the myriad practices of merit and wisdom; thus it is said they are "various.
Since there are already various dharma-gates in the original ground, why would he manifest only for the sake of the two vehicles in his traces?
This cites the original to clarify the trace. △ Third, the separate explanation of the original and the trace, in two parts: first, the separate explanation of the aids within the trace.
They shall proclaim the Dharma of the Half and the Full [Vehicles],
diligently protecting and upholding it to assist in the propagation of my teaching; they shall instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly,
fully expounding the Buddha’s true Dharma to bring great benefit to their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.

This is a detailed explanation. Those who assist in proclaiming my Dharma are those who, within the provisional manifestations (*nirmāṇakāya*), assist in proclaiming the "half-leakage" (*ardha-āsrava*) Dharma at the Deer Park;
as such, these provisional manifestations serve as the basis for those of inferior faculties, the *śrāvakas*, and thus they assist in proclaiming the "curd" (*dadhi*) Dharma.

This continues until, within the provisional manifestation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they attain awakening, whereby they protect and assist in proclaiming the "ghee" (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) Dharma. The aforementioned general summary states: "I..."
The constant praise of his various merits refers precisely to this meaning:

that he is fundamentally endowed with the merits of both the provisional and the real, yet manifests traces within the five flavors of the Dharma to assist the Buddha in bringing beings of true practice to maturity.

Is this not the intent of diligent assistance in proclaiming the teaching? Regarding the separate explanation of the merits of the fundamental and the manifested: "being able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly" constitutes one part.
"Distinct from the teaching of half-syllables" means that the "complete explanation" assists in proclaiming the teaching of full-syllable Prajñā.
"Greatly benefiting" means assisting the Buddha in benefiting sentient beings of both the half- and full-syllable teachings.

"Fellow practitioners of Brahma-conduct" refers to the disciples of both the half- and full-syllable teachings who were transformed within the traces [of his manifestation]. △ Second, a specific description of the merits of the original ground.
Except for the Tathāgata himself, none is able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
Except for those equal to him—that is, from those below the Buddha down to the practitioners of the seven stages of expedient means—none can know the eloquence of his fundamental ground.
△ Second, manifesting his original practice by reference to the world of past Buddhas.
"You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming my Dharma;

he has also, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas in the past, protected and assisted in proclaiming the true Dharma of those Buddhas, and among those who preached the Dharma, he was also the foremost.
Furthermore, regarding the teaching of emptiness spoken by those Buddhas, he clearly and thoroughly understood it, attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
He was always able to preach the Dharma with careful discernment and purity, free from all doubt, and was fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva.
Throughout his entire lifespan, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). To those Buddhas and the people of that world, he was universally regarded as being truly a śrāvaka.
Yet, through these skillful means, Pūrṇa benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and further transformed countless others.

He causes incalculable numbers of people to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of purifying his buddha-field, constantly performing the work of a Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings.
This refers to his original practices manifested during the era of past Buddhas; it means that he did not merely assist in proclaiming the teachings within my own [dispensation].
The teachings of the Half and the Full were long ago proclaimed by the Buddha, and [the present text] likewise assists in proclaiming these teachings of the Half and the Full.

Taking the assistance in proclamation today as the "manifestation of the trace" (*jūki*), and taking the assistance in proclamation in the past as the "revelation of the origin" (*kenpon*), one should know that there are two ways of revealing the origin:
first, the distant origin; second, the proximate origin. Because the distant origin is profound and remote, it is difficult for people to believe; therefore, it is omitted and not described here.

However, because he possesses the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) regarding the recent past, and because he can know the distant through the recent, he cites the recent to testify to the distant;
thus, by means of the ninety billion texts, he clearly elucidates and assists in proclaiming the teachings of the five flavors (*pañca-rasa*) to mature sentient beings.
To protect, assist, and proclaim these is precisely to assist in proclaiming the "half-letters" (*ardha-kṣara*), which is the curd-flavor (*dadhi-rasa*) of the Buddha’s true teaching.
The Dharma that corresponds to the flavor of the "fresh butter" (*pīyūṣa*) of the Vaipulya teachings is the clear understanding of the dharma of emptiness;

furthermore, that which corresponds to assisting in the proclamation of the flavor of the "matured butter" (*ghṛta*) is likewise as when the present Buddha turns the wheel of teaching and expounds the *Prajñāpāramitā*, clarifying how the six *pāramitās* mutually encompass one another and revolve without obstruction. At the abodes of nine billion Buddhas, he also assisted in its proclamation, just as he does now.
There was no difference from that Buddha; all people of the world at that time considered him truly to be a śrāvaka.

Since his true identity had not yet been revealed, he was merely said to have been empowered by the Buddha’s command to turn the *Prajñāpāramitā*. It was not said that he was a great bodhisattva who transforms immeasurable sentient beings and establishes them in *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers precisely to assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma of the *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter), which is understandable from the text.
△ Third, regarding the causes cultivated by the Buddhas of the three periods of time:
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa was foremost among those who expounded the Dharma under the seven Buddhas, and he is likewise foremost among those who expound the Dharma under me;
he shall also be foremost among those who expound the Dharma for all future Buddhas within this Bhadrakalpa.
Among humans, they are likewise foremost, protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma; furthermore, in the future,
they shall protect and assist in the proclamation of the immeasurable and boundless teachings of all Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings,
establishing them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and constantly exerting themselves with diligence in teaching for the sake of purifying their buddha-fields.
"Sentient beings.
This refers to the causes cultivated by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as explained in the text;

this also follows the previous examples regarding the assistance in proclaiming the Dharma of the Half and Full Teachings in their five flavors, benefiting those of both Great and Small capacities. △ Second, the bestowing of predictions, in seven parts: first, clarifying the perfection of the cause.
Gradually, he will fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.
△ Second, clarifying the perfection of the fruit:
after immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this land.
He was titled the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
△ Third, the Pure Land of the Country of Threefold Clarity (Tri-vidyā). First is the Great Adorned Purity of the Country of Clarity.
Its Buddha takes as many trichiliocosms as there are sands in the Ganges River as a single buddha-field.

The ground is composed of the seven treasures and is as level as the palm of a hand; it is devoid of mountains, hills, ravines, gullies, or chasms, and is filled with towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures.
The palaces of the various devas therein are situated close to the void, where humans and devas meet and are able to see one another.
Regarding the statement that "the ground is as level as a palm," the sutra simply says "like a palm" and does not specify "palm of the hand. This is because the palm of the hand is not level;
therefore, one should know that what is being cited refers to a stone at the bottom of the ocean called "Palm" (Tala), a stone upon which not even a single speck of dust exists.

The allowance for inequality is likely comparable to the palm of the ocean; furthermore, the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* explicitly clarifies that it refers to the palm of a Buddha’s hand, not citing the palm of a human hand.
△ Second, explaining that it consists exclusively of wholesome paths.
There are no evil realms, nor are there women; all sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from sexual desire.
△ Third, it clarifies that humans and devas are fully endowed with merit and wisdom.
Having attained great supernormal powers, their bodies emit radiance, they fly with ease, and their resolve and mindfulness are firm;
through diligence and wisdom, they are entirely golden in color, adorned by the thirty-two marks of a great man. The sentient beings in that land always subsist on two kinds of food:
first, the food of Dharma-joy; second, the food of dhyāna-bliss.
Regarding "those who feed on the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna," the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, chapter nine, states: "The food of the Dharma, the food of joy, and the food of dhyāna.
While the scriptural text speaks of them collectively as the "joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna," when divided specifically, there should be three distinct varieties.
△ Fourth, it clarifies that the number of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas is vast.
There were immeasurable, incalculable, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who had attained great supernormal powers and the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom,
and were well able to teach and transform sentient beings; their assembly of śrāvakas was beyond the reach of calculation or reckoning,
and all had fully attained the six supernatural faculties, the three types of clear knowledge, and the eight liberations.
△ Fifth, the summary:
That Buddha-land is thus adorned and perfected with such immeasurable merits.
As stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Candragarbha-sūtra*: "By refraining from killing, one attains ten kinds of merit: first, toward all sentient beings..."
Attaining fearlessness, up to the tenth: at the end of life, one is reborn in a good realm and subsequently becomes a Buddha-land;
being free from harm and possessing the necessary implements, the people of that land have long lives and do not steal—these are the ten meritorious fruits.
The first fruit is the perfection of all affairs, being decisive and free from difficulty or obstruction, up to the tenth: dying and being reborn in a good realm, subsequently becoming a Buddha-land.

The ten merits of being filled with the adornment of precious flowers and being free from lust: first, the restraint of the sense faculties as one's primary practice leads to a decisive resolution, such that even at the time of death one is reborn in a good realm;
later, when one becomes a Buddha, there are no women in that land. The ten merits of not speaking falsely:
first, sentient beings believe his words, such that even at the time of death they are reborn in a good realm; later, when one becomes a Buddha, there are no [falsehoods] in that land.

Foul odors are constantly absent; precious flowers abound; one refrains from double-tongued speech—these are ten merits. First, the body cannot be destroyed; second, one is reborn in a good realm until death;
third, after death one is born in a Buddha-land; fourth, Māras cannot destroy one; fifth, one’s retinue does not engage in harsh speech—these are ten merits.
First, one speaks with gentle words; second, [one is reborn in a good realm] until death; third, after death one is born in a Buddha-land; fourth, the sound of the Dharma fills [the land].

The ten merits of refraining from frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*): first, being loved and respected by devas and humans, up to being reborn in the good realms after death and subsequently becoming a Buddha in a buddha-field where sentient beings possess strong memory and do not forget. The ten merits of non-greed (*alobha*):

first, having no deficiency in one's physical faculties, up to being reborn in the good realms after death and subsequently becoming a Buddha in a buddha-field free of Māras and non-Buddhist paths. The ten merits of non-anger (*adveṣa*): first... [and so forth].

Free from all anger, they will even after death be reborn in the good realms; later, when they become Buddhas, the people of their lands will attain samādhi and be free from wrong views—these are the ten merits.
With a single-minded nature that is gentle and virtuous, they will even after death be reborn in the good realms;
later, when they become Buddhas, the people of their lands will possess right faith. This is what is meant by being adorned with immeasurable merit. △ Fourth, the eon, the land, and the name.

that Buddha’s life span lasted for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

First, the inconceivable Dharma is introduced:
"O Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Because the Son of the Buddha has well studied the skillful means of his path, it cannot be conceived.
Second, the reason for manifesting traces is explained.
Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

by means of countless skillful means, they transform various classes of sentient beings, while themselves declaring, "We Śrāvakas are very far from the Buddha-way."
He delivers immeasurable multitudes so that they all achieve fulfillment; though some have small desires or are indolent, he will gradually cause them to become Buddhas.
"Small desires" indicates those who seek the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and "indolence" indicates those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Through skillful means, he guides those of true practice to transform all sentient beings, gradually causing them to become Buddhas. △ Fourth, clarifying that he inwardly harbors the Great Way.
Internally they keep secret their bodhisattva practices, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas with few desires who are weary of birth and death;

though they are in truth purifying buddha-fields, they show the multitude that they possess the three poisons and further manifest the appearance of false views. My disciples employ such skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
It is not only that he manifests as a śrāvaka; he also manifests as a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) and as an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) under the influence of the three poisons.
Śāriputra manifesting anger, Nanda manifesting greed, and Devadatta manifesting delusion are all examples of this category. △ This fifth finger briefly suppresses the extensive [explanation].
If I were to fully describe the various manifestations of my supernatural powers, sentient beings who heard them would harbor doubts and confusion.
△ Second, the specific manifestation of the traces of fulfilling vows, which has two parts: first, a verse revealing the original state in the past.
Now this Pūrṇa, having diligently cultivated the path under a thousand billion Buddhas in the past, has proclaimed and protected the teachings of those Buddhas;
seeking unsurpassed wisdom, he has manifested as a chief disciple among those Buddhas, possessing great learning and wisdom,
speaking with fearlessness and being able to gladden the assembly without ever experiencing weariness, thereby assisting in the Buddha’s work.

Having already attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, he knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all beings and constantly preaches the pure Dharma,
expounding such meanings to instruct thousands of billions of assemblies, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma while he himself purifies his own Buddha-field.

One who possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) is one who possesses: first, the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid); second, the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid);
third, the unimpeded knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid); and fourth, the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid). The Patriarch said:

"If one wishes to propagate the Great Way, one must possess unimpeded eloquence. These four are collectively termed "unimpeded knowledges" because the Bodhisattva, regarding these four dharmas, [attains mastery].
This is because their wisdom is swift, discerning, clear, penetrating, and unimpeded. △ Second, the verse on the causes for practice throughout the three periods of time:
"In the future as well, they will make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, protect and assist in proclaiming the True Dharma, and will also purify their own Buddha-lands."
Constantly employing various skillful means, he preaches the Dharma with fearlessness, delivering incalculable multitudes and accomplishing all-knowledge.
△ Second, the verse on the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) has four parts; first, the verse on the perfection of causes.
"Making offerings to all Tathāgatas and upholding the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.

These seven and a half verses constitute the prediction (vyākaraṇa) for the preceding section; of these seven, four are now versified here, while the remaining three—concerning his lifespan, the duration of the Dharma's abiding, and the construction of stupas after his parinirvāṇa—are omitted. △ Second, the verses on the fulfillment of the fruits.
Thereafter, he attained Buddhahood, and his name was called Dharmaprabhāsa.

The assembly of bodhisattvas is exceedingly numerous, their count being immeasurable billions; they have all attained great supernormal powers and are fully endowed with majestic virtue and strength, filling that land.
The śrāvakas are likewise innumerable, having attained the three vidyās, the eight liberations, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
With such as these as their Saṃgha, all the sentient beings in that land will have completely severed lustful desire;

they will be born solely through transformation, possessing bodies adorned with the marks of excellence, nourished by the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, having no further thought of food, and being without women or any of the evil realms.
Bhikṣu Pūrṇa, when his merits are fully perfected, he shall attain such a pure land.
The assembly of noble sages is so vast that such immeasurable matters can now only be briefly explained by me.
△ Second, the bestowal of predictions upon the twelve hundred [Arhats]. 3. First, the initial thought and request.
At that time, the twelve hundred Arhats who had attained mastery over their minds thought to themselves: "We have attained this with great joy."
"It would be most wonderful if the World-Honored One would likewise grant a prediction of enlightenment to each of us, just as he has done for the other great disciples.
△ Second, the granting of predictions, in two parts: first, the prose section, in three parts; first, the general prediction for the twelve hundred.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"These twelve hundred arhats, I shall now personally bestow upon them, in due order, the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, the individual bestowal upon Kauṇḍinya:
"Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas;

The One Perfected in Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Although five hundred names are identical, they must each receive their individual prediction; the question concerns seeing these five hundred receive their predictions, yet not seeing the twelve hundred.

The "seven hundred" is actually one thousand two hundred. Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* states:
