The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Buddha's Past Deeds) states that his mother was the daughter of an elder who followed her husband to another country.
After a long time she became pregnant, and as her delivery drew near, she longed to return home. While traveling halfway there, she gave birth to her son; this occurred twice in total.
The two sons were distinguished by their relative sizes: the elder was Cūḍapanthaka (translated as "Born by the Side of the Small Road"), and the younger was Svāgata (translated as "Welcome").
Furthermore, Cūḍapanthaka is also called Cūḍapanthaka or Cūḍapanthaka;
he is also translated as "Snake-Slave" (*Ahidāsa*), as his nature was characterized by much [confusion].
In a former life, this dull-witted man was a Dharma Master who was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras and had five hundred disciples;
however, out of secret stinginess regarding the Buddha-dharma, he refused to teach others. Consequently, in this present life, he experienced the karmic retribution of being dull and ignorant.
Some say that Zhouli (Cūḍapanthaka) is the same as Zhoutuobantuoqie (Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa), also known as Shajiata (Sagata).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses in Praise (of the Two) First, the prediction for Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the five hundred [monks]:
The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable Buddhas; after an incalculable number of kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he will then achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Constantly emitting great radiance and fully endowed with all supernormal powers, his fame pervades the ten directions and he is revered by all;
because he constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path, he is named Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance). His land is pure, and its bodhisattvas are all valiant;
they all ascend exquisite pavilions to travel through the lands of the ten directions, offering unsurpassed articles of worship to all Buddhas.
Having made this offering, his heart was filled with great joy, and in an instant he returned to his own country.

Possessing such supernatural power, the Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas; the True Dharma remained for twice that duration, and the Semblance Dharma for twice that again. When the Dharma was extinguished, gods and humans were filled with grief.
Those five hundred bhikṣus will successively become Buddhas, all sharing the same name, Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance), as they receive their predictions in succession.
"After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha; the world he transforms shall be as majestic and pure as my own land today,
and his supernormal powers, his assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the duration of his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma,
and the length of his lifespan in kalpas shall all be exactly as described above."
△ Second, the general bestowal of predictions upon all śrāvakas:
"Kāśyapa, you already know that these five hundred masters [will attain enlightenment]; the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise do so.

they immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and prostrated themselves, touching their heads to his feet.

This is the repentance and self-reproach.

“World-Honored One, we have always harbored this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
We now repent and reproach ourselves for our former delusions—being content with the small and failing to seek the Great. △ Second, reproaching the dull faculties for their difficulty in awakening.
Now I have come to know this.
This is to blame my dull faculties for not awakening early; having known it now, I realize that what was previously considered minor is not ultimate, while the Great is the true reality.
△ Second, the illustrative explanation, which has two parts: first, the brief illustration; second, the initial brief presentation of the analogy.
They are like those who lack wisdom.
△ Second, explaining the meaning of "lack of wisdom":
Why is this? We ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, yet we instead consider our own meager wisdom to be sufficient.
△ Second, the actual presentation of the parable, in two parts. First, the opening of the parable, in three parts. First, the parable of the poor man and the intoxicated friend.
First, the parable of the kinsman fastening the jewel.
World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend and lay down, intoxicated with wine. At that time, the friend had official business...
He should then take an invaluable jewel, tie it inside the person's garment, give it to them, and depart.

This analogy of the drunken man illustrates the teaching of the Dharma; the self-reproach for being content with a small attainment while failing to seek the Great [Vehicle] illustrates the preceding analogy of the Dharma.
It refers to the intention of employing skillful means (*upāya*) in past lives, which itself contains three points: first, [The remainder of the text follows this structure.]
The parable of the tied jewel illustrates the intention behind the Prince’s forming of karmic connections. "There was a person" refers to those of the Two Vehicles.
"A close friend" refers to the Sixteenth Prince of former times. "The house" refers to the Mahāyāna teaching as one's home.
"Falling asleep while intoxicated with wine" means that at that time, his great capacity for awakening temporarily arose and his ignorance was temporarily suppressed.
Having heard the sutra, there was a slight internal understanding; yet, because ignorance was heavy, he once again fell into confusion and lost it.

"Intoxication" has two meanings: first, heavy intoxication, where one is entirely unaware; second, light intoxication, where one perceives slightly but immediately forgets—this is also called non-awakening.
Although there are these two meanings, in the end it is like the parable of the tied jewel; it is merely like the sound of a poison-drum when one is about to carry out an official duty.

Because the Prince perceives opportunities for spiritual activity arising elsewhere and proceeds to respond to those conditions, it is said that he "shall go forth" to propagate the Dharma and transform others.

Since this is not a private undertaking, it is called "official business. The "priceless jewel" refers to the wisdom-treasure of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the One Vehicle’s ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
"Tying it within his garment" means that shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and patience (*kṣānti*) can obstruct anger and prevent external evils; that is to say—
This outer garment represents the heart of faith and joy, while the inner wrapping of roots of goodness constitutes the inner garment.

At that time, hearing the Dharma and giving rise to subtle faith, joy, and desire is the seed of the wisdom of the "cause of realization" (*vyañjana-hetu*). △ Second, the analogy of being intoxicated and lying down without awareness.
That person lies drunk and does not perceive anything at all.
Second, the analogy of lying drunk and being unaware illustrates how the mind of ignorance is heavy;

subsequently, one no longer remembers this realization, which represents the failure to receive the Great Dharma due to indolence and regression in the interim. △ Third, the analogy of rising and wandering about.

Having arisen, he wanders to another country; for the sake of food and clothing, he seeks them with diligent effort amidst great hardship, and if he obtains even a small amount, he considers it sufficient.
Third, "having arisen, he travels abroad" is a metaphor for receiving the transformation of the three vehicles through the intermediate stage mentioned above.
Because his roots of goodness are about to emerge, he feels weary of suffering and seeks happiness; thus it is said that "having arisen, he travels abroad.

Because he is shrouded by ignorance and does not know how to return to the source to seek the clothing and food of the Mahāyāna, it is said that "he goes to another country to seek the clothing of the Hīnayāna."

Regarding food, if one compares the Buddha and Māra, the realm of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and the realm of Māra are both foreign lands for the Buddha-dharma; whether great or small, they are all foreign lands.
If one compares the small and the great, those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) have not yet escaped the death-and-rebirth of transformation (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa) and thus remain in a foreign land;

only those of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), who have forever escaped birth-and-death, may be said to be in their own land. This clarifies that turning one's back on the Great Vehicle is ultimately a departure from the source.
In former times, when people lived in the lands of the Hinayana, they did not know how to obtain their livelihood from the pearl;

instead, they supported themselves through manual labor, feeling satisfied with whatever small wage they earned in a single day. △ Second, the analogy of awakening through a kinsman, in three parts: first, the reprimand.
Later, a close friend encountered him and said, "Alas, O man! Why have you come to such a state for the sake of food and clothing?
This friend, having awakened [him] through this parable, now bestows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other teachings based on these original causes and conditions.
The "great vehicle" refers to the intention [of the teaching]. That which first constitutes the reprimand is what the sutra calls: "Alas, O man!
Why do you act for the sake of food and clothing to such an extent? This is an analogy for the initial movement of attachment and the arising of doubt. △ Second, showing the jewel.

In the past, wishing to enable you to obtain peace and happiness and to enjoy the five desires at will, on a certain day and month of a certain year, I tied a priceless jewel within the lining of your garment;
it remains there even now, yet you do not know of it. To toil, suffer, and grieve in order to sustain yourself is truly foolish.

Second, "In the past, I wished to enable you to attain peace and happiness," etc., refers to the showing of the jewel; this is an analogy for the aforementioned causes and conditions from previous lives.
"A certain year, month, and day" points to the time at the presence of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. △ Third, the exhortation to trade.
"You may now trade these jewels for whatever you require; thus you shall always have your wishes fulfilled and never lack anything.
Third, "You may now trade these jewels for [other goods]"—this is the exhortation to trade, which is analogous to the three cycles of receiving the prediction of Buddhahood.

All three cycles contain these three intentions. Within the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), the statement "I cause you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering" is the expression of censure (*paribhāṣa*).
The revelation within the chapter on the five Buddhas is the "showing the jewel"; Śāriputra receiving his prediction is the "encouragement to trade.
In the parable, my previous statement that all shall attain bodhi is the "reproach"; the three carts becoming one cart is the "showing the jewel.
Those of middle capacity receiving their prediction is the "encouragement to trade. As for those of inferior capacity, you should [reflect upon] the causes and conditions from your past lives.
"Listening well" corresponds to the censure of the secret exposition; "returning to form karmic connections" corresponds to the preaching of the Great [Vehicle];

"showing the jewel" corresponds to the manifestation of the jewel; and "inferior roots receiving a prediction" corresponds to the encouragement to trade. As for the three meanings within the "Tying the Jewel" parable when viewed in relation to the three cycles [of teaching]:
being at the Bodhi tree corresponds to the "tying of the jewel" by means of the Great [Vehicle]; and the cessation of transformation due to a lack of capacity corresponds to "falling asleep drunk."
Seeking the means of giving is the analogy for initiating practice; the presence of twenty *nayuta* of Buddhas is the analogy for tying on the jewel;

being sent by an attendant to pursue [the Buddha] while fainting and refusing to accept is the analogy for lying drunk; being led out by the three vehicles is the analogy for the causes and conditions of initiating practice;
and reaching the place of the Greatly Penetrating Wisdom-Supreme Buddha is the analogy for tying on the jewel midway and then becoming weary and retreating.
That is to say, when one is lying drunk, one receives [the jewel] while in that small state, and immediately upon rising and walking, these are all termed "receiving the provisional authority.
△ Second, the combined analogy, in two parts. First, combining with the analogy of being intoxicated by wine; third, first, combining with the analogy of tying the jewel.
The Buddha was likewise so when he was a bodhisattva, teaching and transforming us so that we might give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).

This is the "correspondence" (*saṃgati*). Generally speaking, what is called a "correspondence" refers to using present phenomena to correspond with the preceding metaphors, so that the meanings of both sides accord and the various capacities of sentient beings may easily understand; this is why it is said thus. All you wise ones—
Is it not by means of this analogy that one attains understanding? The various preceding and succeeding passages may be understood according to this principle.
△ Second, combining [the previous points] with being intoxicated and lying down without awareness:
subsequently, one becomes negligent and forgetful, neither knowing nor perceiving.
△ 3. Having arisen from the state of meditative union, he wanders about.
Having attained the path of Arhatship, he considers himself liberated; yet his livelihood is difficult, and he is content with what little he receives.
△ 2. The analogy of being awakened by a friend has three parts; first, the rebuke.
The vow for omniscience remains intact and has not been lost; now the World-Honored One awakens us by speaking these words:
"O bhikṣus, that which you have attained is not ultimate cessation."
△ Second, joining the hands to show the jewel:

"For a long time I have caused you all to plant the roots of merit for Buddhahood; it was by means of skillful expedients that I manifested the appearance of nirvana, yet you believed that you had truly attained extinction."
△ Third, the exhortation to trade together.
"World-Honored One, it is only now that I truly know that this is indeed a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I am filled with great joy and have attained what I never had before. At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya—
In order to restate this meaning, they spoke these verses.
The two verses consist of two parts: first, the verse on the internal attainment of understanding; second, the verse on joy. [The verse on joy:
"Having heard the voice of the unsurpassed, peaceful prophecy, we experienced a joy never before known; we pay homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom."
△ Second, the verses on repentance and reproach:
Now, before the World-Honored One, he personally repents for all his transgressions.
△ Second, the verses on personally declaring his realization and understanding, in two parts: first, the verses on the Dharma-exposition.
Regarding the immeasurable Buddha-treasures, they obtain but a small portion of *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the verses on the parable, which have two parts: first, the verses briefly presenting the parable; second, the verses briefly citing the analogy.
"Like an ignorant and foolish person."
△ Second, two verses explain the meaning of lacking wisdom;
they consider themselves sufficient.
△ Second, two verses present the actual analogy. First, one verse opens the analogy. First, one verse describes the failure to recognize the jewel after abandoning it.
For example, suppose a poor man goes to the house of a kinsman. That household is very wealthy and has prepared various delicacies;
[the kinsman] secretly ties a priceless jewel inside the man's inner garment and departs. At that time, the man is asleep and does not perceive it.
Once he has risen and is traveling to another country, he seeks food and clothing to sustain his livelihood, finding it extremely difficult.
Having obtained a little, he considers it sufficient and no longer aspires to anything better; he does not realize that within his inner garment there is a priceless jewel.
△ Second, the verse on the awakening by the kinsman:
The kinsman who gave him the jewel later sees this poor man and sternly rebukes him, then reveals to him the jewel he had tied [within].
When the poor man saw this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy; he became possessed of all manner of wealth and enjoyed himself at will with the five desires.
△ Second, the verse that synthesizes the parable:
"We are also like this, O World-Honored One; throughout the long night, you have always taken pity on us, taught and transformed us, and caused us to plant the unsurpassed vow."
"Because we lacked wisdom, we were neither awakened nor did we know that we had attained only a small portion of nirvana and considered ourselves sufficient, seeking nothing further.
Now the Buddha has awakened us, saying: 'What you call final extinction is not true; only when one attains the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha is that true extinction.
Having now heard from the Buddha this account of the adornment of our predictions and the succession of our receiving of the prophecy, our bodies and minds are filled with universal joy."
△ Eighth: An Explanation of the Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
Part Two: First, the Presentation of the Chapter Title. *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nine: "Bestowing Prophecies upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.

To investigate the truth and sever delusions is called "training" (*śaikṣa*); to exhaust delusions by reaching the ultimate limit of truth is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). This refers to investigating and cultivating the true principle... [recruit].
Seeking superior vision is called the stage of training (*śaikṣa*); this stage consists of the three fruits and four paths, which are truly untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
The fruit of Arhatship is so named because one has thoroughly investigated the principles and reached the pinnacle of superior vision, such that there is nothing further to learn;
thus, it is called the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Now, these two thousand people are either those in training or those beyond training, yet they all belong to the same stream.
Because they received their predictions at one time and share the same name and title, this is treated as a separate chapter; it constitutes the second section within the "Bestowal of Predictions.
II. Explanation of the Scriptural Text, in two parts: A. Initial Request for Prediction, in two parts: 1. The Two Individuals Request [Prediction], in two parts:
a. Receiving the Prediction through Silent Contemplation.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought: "If we were to receive a prediction [of our future enlightenment], would it not be most delightful?
Thinking thus in silence, they harbored their desire within their hearts, not daring to speak it aloud, but keeping it hidden and secret.
Regarding the term "attainment" (*prāpti*), it is perhaps tentative; I do not yet dare to employ definitive or bold language. △ Second, the verbal request for a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Part one: Citing an example.
Immediately rising from their seats, they went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha together, saying: "World-Honored One, we..."
In this regard, there should also be a share [of the merit] for us, as we are those who take refuge in the Tathāgata alone.
This passage contains two meanings: first, the citation of an analogy, which is: "In this matter, we too should have a share.
Second, the citation of an aspiration.
Furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras;
Ānanda has always served as the attendant and upheld the treasury of the Dharma, and Rāhula is the son of the Buddha.
If the Buddha would grant us the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, our own aspirations would be fulfilled and the hopes of the multitude would be satisfied.
Furthermore, we were known as objects of esteem by all the devas and humans of the world; this refers to our being held in high regard.
For when these two individuals were most intimate, they were the ones upon whom the assembly relied:

Rāhula was the Buddha’s son, most dear and honored among the laity, while Ānanda held the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma, most excellent and esteemed among those on the Path. Yet these two did not receive special [treatment].

Question: If [the Buddha] were to bestow predictions upon the entire assembly, it would not satisfy their expectations; yet if he were to grant them predictions as "heavy" or "superior," they should have been ranked among those who attain the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).

For what reason are they here? Furthermore, if—as in the listing of the assembly—these two individuals were already included among those above, why is it that they now receive their predictions while remaining below?
Answer: He bestowed the predictions upon the twelve hundred in general. Since these two had already attained the status of Upstreamers, they are now merely seeking individual predictions. Moreover...
Ānanda is a practitioner (*śaikṣa*), and Rāhula is at the stage of a disciple; therefore, they are included only in the chapters on those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
△ Second, the request of two thousand [monks]:
At that time, two thousand śrāvaka disciples, both those in training and those beyond training, all rose from their seats and bared their right shoulders.
Arriving before the Buddha, they single-mindedly joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One; then, like Ānanda and Rāhula, they stood to one side with the same aspiration.

These two thousand śrāvakas requested a prediction [of their future enlightenment], yet they did so only through silent reflection, for the two intentions of citing these examples were identical to those of the two individuals.
Therefore, it is said that for those such as Ānanda, their ears do not produce speech; there is no matter of "repetition" or "superiority," and so forth.

△ Second, the bestowal of predictions, which has two parts: first, the prediction for two individuals; second, the prediction for two thousand people. The first section [of the first part] further has two sections;
first, the prediction for Ānanda, which has five parts. First, the prose exposition.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-vaśitā-abhijñā-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
You shall make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas and protect them."
Having upheld the treasury of the Dharma, he then attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and transformed twenty koṭi-nayuta Ganges-sands of bodhisattvas, causing them to achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The name of that land was Constantly Erected Supreme Banner; its soil was pure, made of lapis lazuli, and the kalpa was named Pervasive Wondrous Sound.
The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable, spanning countless thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one could not know it.

The True Dharma shall remain in the world twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall remain twice as long as the True Dharma. Ānanda, this is the Mountain Ocean Wisdom Sovereign Supernatural Power King.
The Buddha was praised and his merits extolled by immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, throughout the ten directions.
Ānanda, the people of Rājagṛha were of the Kṣatriya caste; his father was King Śuklodana, who was the younger brother of the Buddha.

In the Sanskrit language, Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi) and is also called "Rejoicing" (Huanxi). He was born on the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, and thus he was named accordingly.
His fame was widespread and his understanding profound; his wisdom was unimpeded. The World-Honored One constantly praised him as foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.

Furthermore, because of the great merit accumulated in past lives, he received and upheld the treasury of the Dharma like water being passed from one vessel to another. It was for these reasons that [the Buddha] commanded him.
After serving as his attendant, King Ajātaśatru said to him: "Virtuous One, both the Tathāgata and the venerable Kāśyapa—these two supreme masters—have already entered parinirvāṇa;
due to my many transgressions, I was unable to behold them. When you, Virtuous One, enter parinirvāṇa, I pray that you will grant me leave.
Ānanda consented. Thereafter, he thought to himself: "My body is frail and brittle, like a cluster of foam."
"Bubbles, how much more so for one who is aged and infirm; how could such a person endure for long?
Furthermore, recollecting that King Ajātaśatru had made an agreement with him, he went to the royal palace and said, "I wish to enter parinirvāṇa; I have come to bid you farewell.
The gatekeeper said, "The King is asleep; you may not announce this. Ānanda said, "Wait until the King has awakened, and I shall speak to him on your behalf. At that time, King Ajātaśatru...
In a dream, he saw a precious parasol adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions who gazed up at it in reverence.
Suddenly, a violent wind and rain arose, blowing its handle apart and causing the precious necklaces and ornaments to fall all over the ground;
his heart was filled with great wonder and alarm. Upon waking, the gatekeeper related these events in detail. Having heard the account, the king broke into a loud wail of grief and lamentation.
Moved by emotion, he arrived at the city of Vaiśālī and saw Ānanda sitting cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River.
The king prostrated himself and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms, who has come here leaving me behind.
For the sake of relying upon the power of your compassionate vow, do not enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank.
He further spoke in verse: "Venerable One, why do you return so swiftly to the field of nirvana?
Pray remain for a moment and accept my offerings. At that time, Ānanda, seeing that both kings had come together to entreat him, spoke this verse:
"O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve with sorrowful longing. Nirvana is tranquil and without [suffering]."
"Ānanda, because of these reasons, I further consider that it would be impossible for me to enter parinirvāṇa while favoring one country over others, leading to disputes among the various nations;
rather, I should deliver all sentient beings with impartiality. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River, intending to enter nirvāṇa.
At that moment, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways, and within the Snowy Mountains...
Five hundred rishis, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air and arrived; they prostrated at Ānanda’s feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and said:
"O Elder, you shall bear witness to our attainment of the Buddha-dharma. We pray that you will bestow upon us your great compassion and deliver us.
Ānanda silently accepted their request, immediately transforming the Ganges River entirely into golden ground, and there he preached the Dharma for the sake of the rishis.
Ānanda silently thought to himself that his former disciples should now assemble;
in an instant, five hundred arhats descended from the sky and conferred the full precepts upon the sages.
Among the assembly of sages were two arhats, one named Śāṇakavāsin and the other named Madhyāntika. Ānanda knew them to be vessels of the Dharma.
He addressed him, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa; Kāśyapa entered into meditative absorption and transmitted it to me.
Now that I am about to pass away, I transmit it to you. Having received my teaching, you should listen to this verse:
'The Dharma originally entrusted exists; Once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves; Having awakened, [it is realized as such].'"

Having finished transmitting the Dharma to Ananda, Wumufa leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations. He entered the *Vāyu-vega-samādhi* (Wind-Swiftness Samādhi) and divided his body into four parts:

one part he offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one part to the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King, one part to King Viśālī, and one part to King Ajātaśatru, so that they might make offerings to them. Immediately—
The twelfth year of King Li was the year of Gui-si.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses.
△ Second, the verse recitation.

I now declare within this Saṃgha that Ānanda, the upholder of the Dharma, shall make offerings to all Buddhas and subsequently attain Perfect Enlightenment, receiving the name Sāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-vaśavarti-rāja Buddha.
His land shall be pure and named Constantly Erected Exalted Banner;
he shall teach and transform bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and his great majestic virtue and renown shall fill the ten directions.
His lifespan shall be immeasurable out of compassion for sentient beings; the True Dharma shall last twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma twice as long again.
Within this Buddha-dharma, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River shall plant the causes and conditions for the path to Buddhahood.
Regarding "I now speak within the Saṃgha": *saṃghāya* in Sanskrit is translated here as "assembly," which means preaching the Dharma in the presence of a vast multitude of people.
As for the name "Constantly Erecting the Victorious Banner," Master Kumārajīva said that in foreign lands, when one defeats an enemy and achieves victory, one raises a banner of victory;
likewise, the subduing of Māra at the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*) also manifests this sign of victory. △ Three.
Eight thousand bodhisattvas gave rise to doubt.
At that time, eight thousand newly resolved bodhisattvas in the assembly all thought to themselves:
"We have not yet heard even the great bodhisattvas receive such a prediction; by what cause and condition do these śrāvakas receive such [a prediction]?"
Resolution:

Those bodhisattvas who harbored doubts regarding the śrāvakas— doubting that those who have only today resolved their minds could receive such a prediction from the Buddha concerning the purity of their lands—
[now see] that in the past Vaipulya sūtras, it was recorded that various bodhisattvas only after accumulating practices through diligent toil for immeasurable kalpas [attained such results].
What is the reason for their receiving this prediction? △ Fourth, the Tathāgata resolves their doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family, I and Ānanda and the others simultaneously resolved our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha King of Space."
"Ānanda, because you have always delighted in much learning and I have always been diligent and energetic, I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, Ānanda, you shall protect and uphold my Dharma, as well as the Dharma-treasuries of all future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to maturity the assembly of Bodhisattvas; because your original vow was such, you have obtained this."
Record: The Tathāgata reveals his origins and resolves doubts, saying: "That Ānanda, in former days, together with me, gave rise to the Great Mind;
thus we were fellow students. Because I was diligent, I surpassed him and attained Buddhahood first; because he relied on much learning, he has remained as he is."
Since the original ground of Dhṛtipada, who served as his attendant, was such as this, what cause is there for doubt regarding his present marvelous prediction?
△ Fifth, Ānanda reveals his own origin and expresses his praise:
Ānanda personally heard before the Buddha’s presence the bestowal of his prediction, the adornment of his land, and the fulfillment of his vows. His mind...

Filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before, he immediately recollected the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas of the past;
he attained unimpeded penetration as if hearing them now, and also recognized his own original vows. At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous! He has caused me to recollect the teachings of the Buddhas of the past in immeasurable numbers, just as I have heard them today.
I now have no further doubt; I shall abide securely in the Buddha-way, acting as an attendant through skillful means to protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas."
△ Second, the prediction for Rāhula. Part one: the prose section.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Tāḍita-saptaratna-puṣpa (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flower) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi..."
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, shall make offerings to as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten worlds,
constantly acting as their eldest son just as he does now. His Buddha-land’s adornments, his lifespan, the number of kalpas,
and the disciples he transforms, as well as his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma, shall be like the ocean and the mountains.
The Tathāgata Prajñāvibhutvavikrāmin was no different; he also served as the eldest son of this Buddha, and after this period, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
II. Verses in Praise:
When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha, he has received the Dharma as my Dharma-son.
In future ages, he shall see immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son, single-mindedly seeking the path to Buddhahood.

Rāhula’s secret practices are known only to me; appearing now as my eldest son to demonstrate this to all sentient beings, he abides securely in the Buddha-dharma, possessing immeasurable billions of koṭis of incalculable merits, as he seeks the unsurpassed path.
"Their merits are incalculable" means they cannot be measured or calculated. △ Second, the prediction for two thousand people.
Part one: the prose section.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the minds of these two thousand persons—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—were supple, tranquil, and pure.
The Buddha, observing their minds, said to Ānanda: "Do you see these two thousand people, both those in training and those beyond training?
"I see them, World-Honored One," Ānanda replied. "These people shall make offerings to Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in fifty worlds;
they shall reverently honor and respect them, and protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Finally, they shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood in various lands throughout the ten directions."

All these Buddhas share the same title: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Ratnākara. Their lifespan is one kalpa;
the adornments of their lands, as well as their śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, are all exactly equal.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses of Recitation:
"These two thousand śrāvakas now standing before me— I bestow upon them all the prediction that in the future they shall attain Buddhahood."
The number of Buddhas they shall serve, as described above, will be as numerous as atoms; they shall protect and uphold their Dharma-treasuries and subsequently attain perfect enlightenment.
In lands throughout the ten directions, they shall all share the same name and simultaneously sit at the site of enlightenment to realize unsurpassed wisdom.
They shall all be named Ratnalakṣaṇa (Jewel-Mark), and their lands, disciples, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma shall all be equal and without any difference.
All [of them] shall deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions by means of their various supernatural powers; their fame shall spread everywhere as they gradually enter into nirvana.
3. Joy at Receiving the Prediction.

At that time, the two thousand disciples—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—heard the Buddha bestow these predictions and, leaping for joy, spoke these verses:
"O World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom! Having heard the sound of this prophecy, my heart is filled with joy, as if I were being drenched by the sight of nectar.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher.
In this chapter, the Tathāgata himself speaks of the merit of propagating the sutra and commands its circulation. There are five ways of being a dharma-preacher:
first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining and expounding; and fifth, copying and transcribing. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra clarifies these six [ways].

By virtue of the power of faith, the Dharma-preacher accepts [the teachings]; by virtue of the power of mindfulness, he maintains them. To examine the text is "reading"; to hold it without forgetting is "reciting"; to proclaim it is "explaining," and to expound it is "preaching.
However, because the scriptures of the Sages are difficult to understand, they require interpretation. Thus, the six types of Dharma-preachers are now consolidated:
accepting and maintaining [the teachings] is combined into one; explaining and preaching are combined into one; reading and reciting are opened up as two; and writing is added as the third.
The five distinct treatises are written as follows: four persons represent those who practice for themselves, while one person represents those who transform others.

Furthermore, "Dharma" (dharma) refers to the rules and norms, and "Master" (ācārya) refers to a teacher or craftsman. Although the Dharma provides the standard, its essence does not propagate itself; it depends upon people.
Therefore, those who thoroughly understand the sutras in these five ways may all be called "Masters. By upholding the Dharma, they perfect their own practice, all by means of the wondrous Dharma.

Because one serves as a teacher by personally accomplishing the wondrous Dharma, one is called a "Dharma Teacher" (*dharmabhāṇaka*). Furthermore, because five types of persons are able to instruct and mold others with the wondrous Dharma, the term "Dharma" is used to designate the "Teacher. The first part consists of five praises of those who can uphold the Dharma; the second part consists of praises of the Dharma upheld, showing the method for its circulation.
The initial section further has two parts: first, the disciples who received the Way, whose merit is profound and their blessings heavy;

At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see these immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and [upāsikās] within this great assembly?"

Vaiśyas who seek the voice-hearer path, those who seek the pratyekabuddha path, and those who seek the Buddha-way—those now being selected for distinction may belong to the eight classes of beings, or to the four assemblies and the three vehicles.

Regarding the "basis" (yin) mentioned in the context of the Lotus Sūtra assembly, where it refers to the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas] due to the instruction of Bhaiṣajyarāja: "basis" (yin) means to rely upon or entrust oneself to. It is intended that...
The Sublime Dharma is entrusted to Bhaiṣajyarāja so that he may receive these instructions and cause them all to circulate throughout the eighty thousand [worlds].
"You see these great assemblies" refers to those who uphold this sutra and attain merit. △ Second, distinguishing the conditions for receiving the prediction.
All such persons as these— who, in the presence of the Buddha, hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
or who rejoice for even a single moment— I shall all bestow upon them the prediction that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"All before the Buddha" clarifies that the time was when the Buddha was seated. "A single phrase or a single verse" indicates that the hearing of the Dharma was extremely minimal.
"Even down to a single thought of sympathetic joy" clarifies that the duration of the time was most brief.
"All are given the prediction that they shall attain Bodhi" clarifies that even those who heard the Dharma for the shortest time and during the briefest interval [shall attain it].

If even those who merely rejoice in this merit can ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood, how much more so for those who fully hear it, receive and uphold it throughout their lives, propagate it in five ways, and make offerings through the three karmas?
△ Second, the disciples after the extinction [of the Buddha], part two: first, the classification of the disciples.

The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja: "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there is anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment."
The precedent for those who excel their peers can be understood from the above. △ Second, he also bestows a prediction:
"I also bestow upon you the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
I, too, shall grant them a prediction [of enlightenment] as explained previously regarding the retribution for their merit.

Thus, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, should there be anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of this sutra, or even conceives a single thought of sympathetic joy, they shall all receive a prediction of Buddhahood through the universally vast compassion of the Buddha.
How could there be any doubt about their attaining Buddhahood? It may be said that every person possesses this share. △

Second, the section on the Preceptor who Bestows the Path, whose merit is profound and whose blessings are heavy. This has two parts: first, the prose (long-form) exposition; second, the verse (gāthā) praise. The first part [the prose] further has two sections:
first, the specific [explanation]; within this, first, the present life; within this, first, the inferior-grade preceptor; within this, first, the clarification of the preceptor’s characteristics.
Furthermore, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
and who regard this scripture with the same reverence as they would a Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense,
silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and musical performances, and even joining their palms in reverent salutation.
To clarify what constitutes a "Dharma Master": it refers to the five kinds of Dharma Masters and the ten kinds of offerings.
Regarding the ten kinds: first, flowers; second, incense; third, necklaces; fourth, powdered incense; fifth, unguents; sixth, burning incense; seventh, banners and canopies;
eighth, robes; ninth, music and performance; tenth, joining the palms. △ Second, clarifying the karmic rewards.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas;
having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have out of compassion for sentient beings been born into this human world.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone should ask, "What kind of sentient beings will attain buddhahood in future ages? you should point to these people as those who will attain buddhahood in future ages.

They will certainly attain Buddhahood. Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or copies even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and makes various offerings to the scripture—such as flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music—and with palms joined in reverence, such a person...
One should regard such a person as worthy of the veneration of all the world, and should honor them with the same offerings one would offer to a Tathāgata.
You should know that this person is a great bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and out of compassion for sentient beings,
has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The passage "It clarifies that those who previously made offerings have deep causal roots" indicates that their past causes were profound.
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, they are born into this human realm" clarifies that their merit in the present life is great.
If someone asks why, the subsequent section explains the nature of the heavy retribution in the future. "Out of pity for sentient beings, they vow to be born in this world" [is the reason].
As stated in the *Myōgen* (The Wondrous Profundity) regarding "affiliates": the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings and all Buddhas is non-dual; they are spontaneously father and son.

Regarding the "rational-nature affiliates" who are taught and transformed through the preaching of the Dharma: those with whom one has previously established a karmic connection but have not yet attained liberation are drawn into the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*).
Having encountered a Buddha and received deliverance, they become "karmic-born affiliates. Although they had established a connection in past lives, their suffering was not yet severed; however—

Because they vow to be born [in this world], they hear the Dharma and attain liberation. Those who vowed to be born among their retinue encountered a Buddha in a previous life and gave rise to true insight into the Truths;
whether they were in the upper realms or in other directions, they now come to be born in the lower realm through supernatural power to assist the Buddha and propagate his transformation.

As for those born through supernatural powers within the retinue: having shattered ignorance and attained the fundamental Dharma-body, they are able to manifest responsive appearances and enter [the world].

Regarding birth within the cycle of birth and death, there are those who manifest as kinsmen; those born through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) still possess a retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) at their original place of receiving retribution, yet they come here by dividing their forms through the power of their physical supernormal faculties.
As for those who are born through the power of aspiration, they have no body at their place of retribution, having descended to be born below through the force of their vow-power.
△ Second, clarifying the teacher of the superior grade. This has two parts: first, illustrating the characteristics of the teacher of the superior grade by way of comparison.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive and uphold [this teaching] and provide various offerings.
This comparison brings forth the characteristics of a superior-grade teacher. 2. Explaining the karmic rewards of the superior grade:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person, having personally relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, out of compassion for sentient beings after my parinirvāṇa..."

Therefore, one who extensively expounds this sutra while born in an evil age—O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person has personally relinquished the retribution of pure karma; this clarifies the superior grade of merit and retribution.
△ Second, clarifying [the results] in future lives. Part one: Clarifying the inferior teacher. Sub-part one: Clarifying the characteristics of the teacher.
"If there be good sons or good daughters who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to secretly preach even a single phrase of the Lotus Sūtra for a single person..."
One who is able to secretly explain [the Dharma] to a single person possesses wisdom but lacks extensive learning;
such a person is only capable of private instruction and is unfit to stand before a multitude, and is thus considered a teacher of the lowest grade.

Although one may attain an understanding of a single phrase by secretly explaining it to one person, because they have not heard widely nor studied many different meanings, they cannot explain all manner of difficult questions within a great assembly.
If there is something that is not fully understood, it will cause the correct principle to fail to be proclaimed and propagated;
as the *Śāstra* clarifies, having wisdom without learning is like light rain without thunder. If one wishes to expound this single phrase of correct speech, one should do so in private for now.
△ Second, explaining the merit and retribution.
One should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, sent by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata.
One should know that this person is indeed an emissary of the Tathāgata; this clarifies the merit and reward.

It must be understood that this sutra is spoken by the Wisdom of Suchness (Tathatā-jñāna) and teaches the principle of Suchness (Tathatā). Today, the practitioner who upholds these teachings according to Suchness proclaims the principle of Suchness.

These are the tasks assigned by the Tathāgata; those who perform the work of the Tathāgata take the illumination of suchness through such-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) and the realization of suchness-principle (*tathatātattva*) as their task.
Today’s practitioners act in accordance with the teachings of suchness, and thus realizing suchness-principle is precisely performing the work of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, taking the transformation of sentient beings through such-wisdom and suchness-principle as their task, today’s practitioners are able to possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) by means of this.
In the sutras, explaining the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain benefit is also called "performing the deeds of a Tathāgata.
That which is dispatched by the Tathāgata is the wisdom of contemplation arising from *tathatā*.
To perform the deeds of a Tathāgata means to pass through all phenomena such that there is nothing that is not *tathatā*; *tathatā* itself is the Buddha-deed. △ Second, clarifying the superior grade.
Master, how much more so for one who extensively explains this to others amidst the great assembly!
This clarifies that the merit and retribution of the superior grade— which was previously omitted from the inferior grade when comparing the former to the latter— is now established.

The meaning can be understood; however, these four categories are designated as distinct precisely because human discourse distinguishes between superior and inferior levels, and because there are temporal differences between the present and the future.
Thus it is said. △ Second, the general [classification] has two parts. First, explaining that those who act in opposition incur transgression.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him,
his transgression would still be light; however, if a person were to disparage with a single evil word those— whether lay or ordained— who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra,
their transgression would be exceedingly grave.
This passage generally clarifies that those who oppose these five kinds of Dharma-preachers incur transgressions, while those who follow them obtain merit;

however, herein the gravity of the transgression or merit is not determined by the richness or poverty of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), but rather by the weight of the initial and subsequent intentions.
Thus, if a practitioner with an initial resolve already possesses afflictions (*kleśa*) or encounters obstacles, their practice will be abandoned, and consequently they will incur [transgression].

If one has many offenses, the Buddha remains impartial; since evil cannot afflict or constrain him, how could it create an obstacle? Thus it is said that the offense is light. The same applies to making offerings:
if this person is in need and receives an offering, the practice they have cultivated will succeed, and thus the merit of such giving is superior.
The Buddha, however, has no needs, as all matters are already fulfilled; therefore, although one may present offerings to the Buddha, there is no further benefit for him. Thus it is said.
The gravity of retribution is illustrated by this analogy: suppose a prince is in a state of distress;

the merit of providing him with what he requires for his sustenance is very great, yet if one brings dishonor upon the royal lineage, the offense incurred is no small matter—thus, both the transgression and the merit are grave.

Conversely, if one offers food and clothing to a great king as a mere minor service, you might attempt to insult or harm him, yet you can cause him no injury; thus, both the transgression and the merit are slight. △ Second, explaining those who act in accordance [with the Dharma].
One shall obtain merit.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that anyone who reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha;
they are borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata. Toward whatever direction such a person goes, one should turn and pay homage with single-minded devotion.

With palms joined in reverence, one should honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to them with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, delicacies, and various musical performances—offering these supreme human gifts.
One should also hold celestial jewels and scatter them, and present the precious hoards of the heavens. Why is this so?
Because this person joyfully preaches the Dharma and hears it for even a brief moment, they immediately attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for "adorned by the Buddha," this means that by following [the Buddha's teaching], one obtains merit; the Buddha adorns this person with concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

This is because one is able to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom. That which is borne on the back by the Tathāgata is called a "load" (hē), while that which is borne on the shoulders is called a "burden" (dàn).
Cultivating the dharma-body, which is neither provisional nor ultimate, is what constitutes being "borne by the Tathāgata.

The function of the two wisdoms—skillful means and the ultimate—is what constitutes being "borne as a burden by the Tathāgata. One should pay homage according to whichever direction one is facing as one proceeds.
The former passage clarified taking the Dharma as one's teacher; this passage now clarifies those who are capable of being teachers for others.
Whatever these individuals aspire toward is entirely in accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*). All such persons are worthy of reverence and compliance.

"Compliance" refers to following [the path], while "reverence" refers to paying homage and offering service. Those who thus comply and offer such support will together experience superior merit and wondrous rewards. However—

This section is titled "General" because it does not distinguish between the high and low among people or the present and future of time, but universally clarifies that for those who act contrary [to the Dharma],
retribution arises as sin, while for those who act in accordance [with the Dharma],
there is the reward of merit. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the verses in praise (consisting of three parts): First, exhorting the practice of self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), one should always diligently make offerings to and uphold those who receive and maintain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Those who wish to quickly attain the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) should receive and uphold this sutra and also make offerings to those who uphold it."
These two lines do not summarize the prose section but rather encourage the merit and retribution resulting from one's own practice and the transformation of others.

△ Second, the verses on the teacher’s lineage, divided into the specific and the general; first, the verses on the specific; first, the verses on the present life; first, the verses on the teacher of inferior grade;
first, clarifying the characteristics of the teacher.
If there are those who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
one should know that they are sent by the Buddha to take pity upon all sentient beings. (2) This clarifies the merit and reward.
△ Second, the two verses on the superior teacher. Part one: clarifying the characteristics of the teacher.
"All those who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Part two: clarifying the merit and retribution.
Having relinquished the pure lands, they are born here out of compassion for sentient beings;

you should know that such persons can be born wherever they wish by their own sovereign power and extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this degenerate age. One should honor these teachers of the Dharma with celestial flowers and incense, celestial precious garments, and heaps of exquisite celestial jewels.
△ Second, the verses on future lives, in two parts: first, the verse that transcends [the present] to illustrate the superior teacher; second, the initial verse on the characteristics of the teacher:
"In the evil world after my parinirvāṇa, those who can uphold this sutra..."
△ Second, the verse on the merit and reward:
One should join the palms in reverent prostration, as if making offerings to the World-Honored One with the finest delicacies, various sweets, and diverse garments;
such a son of the Buddha hopes to hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
In the prose section, the retribution for merit was originally omitted, whereas it is now present in these verses. △ Second, the subsequent verses on the teacher of the lower grade, in two parts:
first, the verses introducing the person.
"If one is able to receive and uphold this sutra in future ages..."
△ Second, clarifying the merit and retribution:
"I dispatch them to act as Tathāgatas among those who dwell in the human realm.
△ Second, the verses summarizing the two [sections]; first, the verse on those who oppose [the teaching] incurring sin:
If one were to constantly harbor an unwholesome mind, assume a wrathful expression, and revile the Buddha throughout an entire kalpa, they would incur immeasurable heavy offenses;
yet if someone who reads, recites, and upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* should be subjected to malicious speech for even a brief moment, their offense would exceed that of the former.
△ Second, the verse on those who follow [the teaching] attaining merit:
Suppose there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for the duration of an eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses;
because of this praise of the Buddha, they would attain immeasurable merit. Yet the merit of one who extols and praises a holder of this sutra exceeds even that.

If, for eight thousand billion kalpas, one were to offer the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures to those who uphold this sutra—and having made such offerings—were then to hear it for even a moment, one should rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I have now attained a great benefit."
These four verses clarify that among the merits obtained by following [the teaching], there are two points of significance:

the first two verses clarify that although the merit of praising the Buddha’s benefits over many kalpas is vast, it does not equal the supreme excellence of the meritorious retribution for upholding this sutra;

the latter two verses clarify that even one who merely briefly hears the sutra gains greater merit than those who offer the most sincere worship to its upholders, let alone those who actually obtain the opportunity to hear it.
Is this not the foremost teaching of the Buddha Vehicle? △ Third, verses praising the supreme excellence of the sutra:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, the Lotus Sūtra is the most supreme."
△ Second, praising the Dharma that is upheld and showing the method for penetrating the sutra, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses.
The first [part] has two sections; the first is praising the sutra-dharma, in five parts. First, praising by way of the dharma.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras I have spoken—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—among them, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sūtra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others."

This sutra has been protected by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and though it has never been openly proclaimed since ancient times, even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?

This, according to the Dharma, is also called "comparative evaluation" (kalāpaka) or "praise. That which has already been discussed refers to the various gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* upward.
That which is now being discussed refers to the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing), spoken at the same seat.
That which is yet to come refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others represent the gradual and sudden [teachings].

All previous teachings were presented with skillful means so that they might be easily accepted; the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* taught that from one arises the immeasurable, yet the immeasurable does not return to the one, which was likewise easy to believe.
Now, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, regarding the Dharma, all distinctions are integrated and unified into one;

regarding the persons, both teacher and disciples, as well as their original and manifested forms, have long been remote, such that both the person and the Dharma are entirely different from those of the past.

Therefore, that which is difficult to believe and understand, and difficult to encounter when facing such matters, has already been taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it can then be believed when the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* follows.
That which is called the "Secret Essential Treasury" (*guhyaka-kośa*) is "secret" because it was hidden and not spoken; it is "essential" because it encompasses all dharmas;

and it is a "treasury" because it contains within it True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). That which cannot be distributed is because the Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe, and can only be transmitted to those of profound wisdom.
Because those who lack wisdom and harbor disbelief incur sin through slander, one must not speak recklessly.

Regarding the phrase "from of old," it is stated that within the Tripitaka, it is not taught that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor is the fundamental and manifested reality (*honjaku*) of master and disciple clarified.

Although the Vaipulya and Prajñā sutras teach the treasury of the true aspect (*shōsō*), they have not yet taught that those of the Five Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor have they yet revealed [this truth].
Since the various sūtras that reveal the traces do not yet harmonize with the fundamental [truth]—whether sudden or gradual—they are termed "secret.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* fully expounds the Dharma previously kept secret; it is thus the opening of the secret treasury and is itself the secret treasury.
This secret treasury was guarded from of old, and is now finally revealed. There are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy—forty [such individuals].

In other years they could not be taught; though he now wishes to teach them, five thousand have already withdrawn. If it was thus even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, how much more so in the future?
It is a matter of principle that they are difficult to transform. △ Second, praising by way of the persons.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, whoever is able to write, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and explain it to others, the Tathāgata will cover them with his robe, and they will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently dwelling in other directions.
Such a person possesses great power of faith, power of aspiration, and power of all roots of goodness; you should know that this person is equal to...
If one dwells together with the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata’s own hand shall stroke one’s head.
This Dharma, when present in a person, makes that person as venerable as the Tathāgata. That which is covered by the Tathāgata’s robe is the cultivation and study of great patience;
this is what constitutes the "robe. As stated in the preceding passage, this is the "Tathāgata’s adornment. That which is protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The Buddha’s true wisdom is the son; by honoring the true mark (*dharmatā*), one gives rise to true wisdom, which is then protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "this person possesses great power of faith," the four kinds of faith constitute the power of faith, the four great vows constitute the power of aspiration, and great wisdom constitutes the power of roots of goodness.
As for "faith," it is faith in the principle; this principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Aspiration" refers to the establishment [of the vows].
Every practice is itself liberation; when the roots of goodness are firm and difficult to shake, this is precisely Prajñā.
One should know that these three powers are the secret treasury of the three virtues. When the beginner dwells within this, they are no different from a Buddha;

therefore, it is called "dwelling together with the Tathāgata. As for the hand rubbing the head: this person, through the power of their vows and the power of their goodness, practices expedient means.

I truly regard this as the resonance of the spiritual stimulus; "stimulus" refers to the head. The Tathāgata, by means of his two wisdoms—expedient and real—for the sake of transforming others, uses these as "hands" to open and develop the heads of those before him, which embody their own practice of the expedient and real. Because the resonance between the stimulus and the response is thus established, it is said that he "touches the head.
To touch the head is precisely to bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Third, praising according to the location.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this [sūtra] is taught, read, recited, written, or where its scrolls are kept, one should erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, making it exceedingly high, wide, and magnificently adorned. It is unnecessary to enshrine relics therein. Why is this?
Because within this very place resides the entire body of the Tathāgata. This stūpa should be honored with all kinds of flowers, incense, and garlands.
Adorned with jeweled nets, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and accompanied by music, songs, and hymns, they were offered as worship, veneration, respect, and praise.
If anyone should see this stupa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, you should know that such persons are all drawing near to Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Wherever this sutra is located, that place is noble—whether it be the site of the Buddha’s birth, his attainment of the Way, his turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or his entry into Nirvana;
indeed, wherever the Dharma King has traveled, one should erect a stupa there.

Yet this sutra is the very place where the Dharma-body was born, the field for attaining the Way, the true essence of the Wheel of Dharma, and the cave of Great Nirvana; wherever this sutra resides, [it must be honored].

Regarding the fact that it is unnecessary to place physical relics (śarīra) within a stūpa for the purpose of making offerings, as stated in the *Śāstra* (Shèlùn): "Fragmented bones are the relics of the birth-body (jāti-kāya);
sūtra scrolls are the relics of the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya). Since this sūtra is itself a relic of the Dharma-body, there is no need to further enshrine relics of the birth-body.
Furthermore, the two bodies—the birth-body and the Dharma-body—each have both complete and fragmented forms. A record states: "The birth-body is complete."
The "shattering" refers to the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna; the two teachings of various skillful means are the shattering of the Dharma-body.

This present sutra, with its single jewel-mark, is the complete Dharma-body. Since the four teachings and five periods can be clearly distinguished in detail, we know that while other sutras consist of a mixture of the whole and the shattered, only this *Lotus Sutra* is the entire body of the Dharma-body, with no other dharma remaining.
Because they all enter into reality. △ Fourth, praising by way of the cause:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both lay and ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path;

yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path."
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to practice the bodhisattva path well.

Those who have not yet practiced the bodhisattva path well are said to have received the three preceding teachings; these are the fragmentary *śarīra* relics of the Dharma-body, which cannot skillfully deliver beings.
If one enters the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is the complete *śarīra* relic, and only then can one skillfully deliver beings.
This is what is first called "good conduct. △ Fifth, praising [the merit] in terms of the fruit, in five parts: first, clarifying the proximate fruit.

"If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way and either see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it—know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
To "attain proximity to *sambodhi*" is equivalent to what is termed the "proximate stage" (*upaniṣad*) within the *Anurakṣaṇā-pratipad* (Practice of Peaceful Abiding).

This fruit of *bodhi* takes as its essence the sphere of knowledge and vision of the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom; it is of two kinds: first, the *bodhi* of the initial mind, and second, the *bodhi* of the final mind.

What is here called "proximity" refers specifically to being near the *bodhi* of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), and when viewed in relation to the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*), it is likewise proximate.
To cultivate the perfect cause and attain a semblance of understanding is called "drawing near"; this is a praise based on the cause.
If one cultivates the common and specific causes, this is merely being unskilled in practice, meaning one is far from the perfect fruit.
If one cultivates the perfect cause, this is skillful practice, and one is near to the perfect fruit. Now, taking the perfect, suchness-as-it-is wisdom as the cause, one further employs it as...
The *tathatā* prior to the path of fruition is the direct cause (*zhengyin*); the *tathatā* within the path is the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*), also termed the "revealing cause" (*liaoyin*);
and the *tathatā* after the path is the perfect fruit (*yuan-guo*). Thus, the *Puxian Guan Jing* states: "That which is the Mahāyāna cause is the true reality (*shixiang*);
that which is the Mahāyāna fruit is likewise the true reality. The *Shi lun* (Commentary) states: "First, one contemplates the true reality."

The explanation of the names based on the cause is concluded. Regarding the fruit of the names, if discussed according to the principle, True Suchness and the ultimate reality have no corresponding cause and effect, nor do they possess sequence.
However, if considered in terms of the practice of sentient beings, there is indeed sequence as well as cause and effect. △ Second, the opening of analogies.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau;
seeing only dry earth, they know the water is still far off. Yet, not ceasing their labor, they see moist earth and gradually reach mud;
their mind becomes certain that the water must be near.
The minds of sentient beings are possessed of all manner of afflictions, which are likened to a high plateau;

the cultivation of contemplative wisdom is like digging and boring through it to realize the flavor of the principle, just as one obtains clear water. If one relies on the Middle Way of perfect contemplation—which is neither empty nor provisional yet illuminates both emptiness and the provisional—it is like reaching moist mud;
upon entering the first dwelling (bhūmi) and giving rise to the true understanding of the Middle Way, one immediately shatters ignorance.

Just as when mud is clarified, the middle way can be seen, like seeing clear water; thus the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states, "The water of the dharma-nature should be known to follow a sequence," which refers precisely to this.
If explained according to the gates of the teachings (*śāsana-mukha*), the earth is a metaphor for the scriptural teachings and the water is a metaphor for the Middle Way;
the teaching clarifies the Middle Way just as the earth contains water. In the Tripiṭaka teaching gate, the Middle Way has not yet been clarified.
The Way is like dry soil; when the Prajñāpāramitā teachings incorporate skillful means, they explain the meaning of the Middle Way, which is like seeing moist soil.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teaches with direct and manifest clarity, explaining the Unsurpassed Way, which is like seeing mud.

Because of this teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one gives rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation, thereby awakening to the Middle Way and truly perceiving the Buddha-nature; the true wisdom thus awakened shall never again [revert].
Based on the text, it is as if one has obtained clear water and no longer perceives the appearance of soil;

thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the wisdom-body of a Bodhisattva in the Ten Abodes is realized without depending on others—this is precisely what that refers to. △ Third, the synthesis of the analogy.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they have not yet heard, understood, or practiced this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If, however, they hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it, you must know that they are close to attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

To obtain hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the perfect contemplation of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*), which alone can bring one close to the fruit;
this is not the case for the hearing, reflection, and cultivation found within the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, or Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the phrase "corresponding to the parable," it should be understood that the three meanings mentioned above—piercing through, etc.—correspond precisely to the current three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; thus, their meanings are perfectly aligned. Therefore, it is said:
This is the synthesis. △ Fourth, the explanation of the "near" [approach].
Why is this so? Because all the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs to this sutra;
this sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the mark of reality. This treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is profound, firm, and far-reaching.
No one can reach it today except for those who have been transformed and perfected through the Buddha’s teaching and to whom he reveals it.
"All Bodhisattvas" here clarifies the various provisional causes; "Samyak-saṃbodhi" clarifies all provisional fruits.
These provisional causes and provisional fruits are all subsumed within this sutra, just as dry and moist things are both contained within the category of wood.

Since all lands equally depend upon water, they are said to be "subsumed" [under it]. Question: Is the skillful means itself the gate, or is it a gate because it leads to the true reality (*dharmatā*)?
Answer: It possesses both meanings. As for its being a gate to the true reality, this is easy to understand. Regarding its being the gate in its own right:
as in the *Avataṃsaka*, by seeking out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one attains various dharma-gates—such as counting sands or contemplating the ocean.
Regarding these two dharma-gates, each has its opening and closing: previously it was not said that "three" is the skillful means, so this gate was closed;
now it is said that "three" is the skillful means, so this gate is opened. Previously it was not said that "one" is the ultimate reality, so the gate of reality was closed;
now it is said that "one" is the ultimate reality, so the gate of reality is opened. Furthermore, regarding these skillful means...
Because it penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*), the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Three Vehicles serve as the gateway to the One Vehicle. This true reality also has two senses:

first, because it is inherently empty and pervasive, it is called a "gateway," such as the "Gate of Non-duality" in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* or the "Dharma-realm Gateway" in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
