Second, it can act as a gateway by enabling the penetration of the provisional means. Furthermore, it may be explained through the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). All [teachings] belong to this sūtra.

This is precisely the perfect *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing). This sutra’s opening of the provisional means is precisely the perfect *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection).

Its demonstration of the true aspect is precisely the perfect *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation). These three are profound and remote; that the Buddha now reveals them allows one to behold the truth. △ Fifth, the exclusion of what is not [the true].
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sūtra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified,

you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. If there are śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sūtra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those of overweening pride.
If a bodhisattva hears this teaching and becomes startled or doubtful, or if śrāvakas harbor overweening pride—these are all like dry soil;
they are not even moist soil, let alone having seen water. △ Second, showing the method and procedure, in two parts: first, showing the method, in three parts;
first, the heading of the chapter.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to expound this Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly, how should they expound it?
Those sons or daughters of good family must enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
only then should they extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly.
Regarding the "signs" (biaozhang): this refers to the three—robes, seat, and chamber—which serve as the standard method for wide dissemination. Question:

For what reason must one clarify [the procedure] by means of these three factors? Answer: If we discuss the matter from a general perspective, whenever the Dharma is preached, one must first ascend the hall, adjust and arrange one's robes, and then take one’s seat to expound and elevate the teaching; this is indeed the constant protocol.
△ Second, the explanation:
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
the Tathāgata’s robe is gentleness and patience; the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena.
△ Third, the exhortation to practice:
Abiding therein, one should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of all bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
The five kinds of Dharma-preachers employ these three methods as their own internal discipline; thus it is said they "abide therein. They employ them to transform others;
thus it is said, "thereafter, with a mind free from indolence," and so forth—this is the exhortation to practice. Cultivating the "Tathāgata’s chamber" refers to great compassion.
If considered in terms of the identical essence (*samatā-kāya*), it is the *dharmakāya*; if it covers sentient beings, it is liberation.
Liberation can also cause sentient beings to realize their identity with the same essence; this is the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s robe of Prajñā.
If one considers that which is covered, it is the Dharmakāya; if one considers that which covers and adorns the body, it is the patience of *śānti* (nirvāṇa), which is Prajñā;
if one considers the harmonizing with light to benefit others, it is Liberation. Regarding the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s seat, if one considers that which is able to...
Sitting is itself *prajñā* (wisdom). That which one sits upon is the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body). The harmonious correspondence between the body and the seat is *vimukti* (liberation).

Furthermore, great compassion and peaceful bliss constitute the track of "provisioning and fulfillment" (*sambhāra-mārga*). Gentleness and subduing anger to sever delusions constitute the track of "contemplative observation" (*vipaśyanā-mārga*).
Sitting upon the seat is the track of the "true nature of the *dharmakāya*" (*dharmatā-mārga*). △ Second, clarifying the benefits, in five parts:
First, regarding the dispatching of transformation beings:
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I dispatch transformation beings to assemble a congregation for them to hear the Dharma.
If their initial resolve is not yet pure, one may only dispatch transformation beings; one must not yet dispatch the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of supernatural beings.
Because seeing devas and nāgas leaning against this [tree] would cause them to become conceited and obstruct their path, they must not be allowed to see it; how much less so the Buddha.
△ Second, he dispatched transformed manifestations of the fourfold assembly.
He also dispatched manifested bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to his preaching of the Dharma. These...
The manifested beings hear the Dharma, believe and accept it, and follow it without opposition.
△ Third, the dispatching of the eight classes:
If the Dharma-preacher is in a secluded place, I shall at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth.
The asuras and others listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
△ Fourth, seeing the Buddha’s body:
"Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause the preacher of the Dharma to see my body."

If the mind is free from attachment, one is capable of seeing the Buddha; how much more so for devas and nāgas, and how much more so for attaining dhāraṇī and realizing self-benefit? △ Fifth, bestowing dhāraṇī:
If you forget or lose any phrases or clauses of this sutra, I shall explain them for you again so that they may be complete.
Regarding "losing the phrases and stops" (*wàngshī jùdòu*), the original text uses the character *dú* (read), which is a phonetic transcription for *dòu*. *Dòu* means "to stop.
The phrase "the three armies lingered and did not advance" refers precisely to this matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the verses in praise, which have three parts; first, the general exhortation:
"Those who wish to abandon all forms of indolence should listen to this sutra; this sutra is difficult to encounter, and those who can hear it and accept it with faith are likewise rare."
This single line is a general exhortation; it does not repeat the exhortation found in the prose.

It universally addresses the fourfold assembly, urging them to receive and uphold [this sutra] with diligence, for within kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges it is rarely encountered and propagated, and its name is difficult to hear throughout immeasurable lands.

Therefore, one should listen to and study this sutra with all one's strength and utmost sincerity. △ Second, the verse section corresponding to the prose, in two parts: first, the verse praising the Dharma of the sutra.
The middle section praises the two [aspects] by way of the fruit; the first verse provides the analogy:
"Just as a person thirsty for water digs in a high plateau and sees only dry earth, knowing that water is still far off;
but when he gradually sees moist soil and mud, he knows with certainty that water is near."
△ Second, the verse that combines the analogy:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these, who have not heard the Lotus Sūtra, are very far from the Buddha’s wisdom.
If they hear this profound sūtra—which definitively clarifies the Dharma of the Śrāvakas and is the king of all sūtras—and having heard it, reflect upon it with deep attention..."
One should know that these persons are near to the Buddha’s wisdom.

The verse combines the analogy and omits the remaining three points concerning the results of proximity; it explains "proximity" by distinguishing it from what it is not. △ Second, the verse shows the method and procedure, which has two parts:
first, the verse presents the heading of the method and procedure; second, the verse elaborates on the method and procedure. First, the verse presents the heading.
If a person speaks this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
amidst the assembly, being fearless, they should explain it in detail for the sake of others.
△ Second, the explanation in verse:
Great compassion is the chamber; gentleness and patience are the robe; the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat—this is where he preaches the Dharma.
△ Third, the exhortation to practice in verse.
When preaching this sutra, if someone should revile one with foul language or strike with knives, staves, tiles, or stones, one should endure it for the sake of mindfulness of the Buddha.

These three and a half verses provide the method and rules; in the Dharma-ending age, when propagating and expounding [the teaching], one should take these three—the robes, the seat, and the dwelling—as the great instruction.
This applies whether one encounters evil Māras, adverse conditions, verbal abuse, or humiliation.
One should reflect upon the Buddha’s admonitions regarding the use of swords, staves, tiles, stones, and the like, and thus practice patience even more diligently.
△ Second, the verses on the benefits, in six parts; first, the general explanation of the five benefits.
"In thousands of millions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.

This verse generally clarifies the Tathāgata’s intention to benefit others through five matters; it is precisely because the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) pervades the ten directions that it can provide protection for practitioners through these five matters. △ Second, the verse dispatching the fourfold assembly.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be those who can preach this sutra, I shall dispatch emanated members of the fourfold assembly—
monks, nuns, and laymen and laywomen— to provide offerings to that Dharma-preacher.
△ Three verses on dispatching emanated beings:
To guide all sentient beings and assemble them to hear the Dharma, if anyone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles,
or stones, he then dispatches emanated beings to act as their protectors.
△ Four Verses on the Dhāraṇī:

If there is a person preaching this Dharma who dwells alone in a secluded and quiet place where no human voice is heard, and recites this sutra, I shall at that time manifest for them a body of pure radiance;
if they forget any passages or verses, I shall explain them so that they may master them.
△ Five verses on seeing the Buddha’s body:
If a person possesses these virtues, or explains emptiness to the fourfold assembly, or reads and recites the sutras in a secluded place, they shall all be able to see my body.
△ Six verses on dispatching the eight classes of beings.

If there is a person in a secluded place whom I have dispatched—such as devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, and spirits—to serve as an audience for their Dharma teaching, that person will delight in preaching the Dharma and will be able to analyze it without obstruction;
because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, they can cause the great assembly to rejoice.
△ Sixth, the exhortation to practice:

If one draws near to the Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path; by following and learning from this teacher, one attains the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Second, the explanation of "Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa," in two parts: first, presenting the title of the chapter.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *stūpa* or *thūpa*, which is translated here as "square mound" (*fangfen*) or "sacred shrine" (*lingmiao*).
A *caitya* refers to a site where there is no physical body; since this stūpa contains the entire body without dispersal, it is not termed a *caitya*. This is clarified in the Āgamas.

The four sites of commemoration (*catur-stūpa*) refer to the places where [the Buddha] was born, attained the Way, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa; stupas were erected at these four locations.
This precious stupa is a site of commemoration for the entry into parinirvāṇa of a previous Buddha; therefore, the sutra says:
"The three bodies of the Buddhas are born from this sutra; all Buddhas sit upon the site of enlightenment here, and all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma here."
The Buddhas of the past have entered parinirvāṇa within this very place; this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself is the fourfold limb of verification for all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the past already resided here, the Buddhas of the present sit together here, and the Buddhas of the future shall do likewise.
This stūpa emerged from the earth to manifest and reveal this matter, which was witnessed by the fourfold assembly; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa. △ Second.
The explanation of the scriptural text has two parts: first, the prose (long passage), and second, the verse (stanzas). The first part [of the prose] further has three sections:

first, the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna; second, the distant gathering of the emanated bodies; and third, Śākyamuni’s call for volunteers. The first of these [three] further has six sub-sections; first, the appearance of the stupa.

At that time, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels—five hundred yojanas in height and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth—emerged from the earth before the Buddha and remained suspended in mid-air.
It was adorned with various kinds of precious objects, featuring five thousand railings and tens of millions of countless chambers.
It was further embellished with innumerable banners and streamers, and hung with jeweled necklaces and ten thousand precious bells.
A hundred million [parasols] were suspended above it, and from all four sides issued the fragrance of *tāmālapatra* sandalwood, pervading the entire world;
these various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—
and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.

That the stupa is made of the seven treasures clarifies that it is the ground of the Dharma-body; it is through one's nature that one obtains the seven factors of enlightenment and the treasures of the seven sages.
The "stupa" is the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*), the locus upon which the Dharma-body relies.

Its height of five hundred *yojanas*—equivalent to twenty thousand *li*—vertically clarifies the ten thousand practices within the cause and the ten thousand virtues within the fruit. Its breadth of two hundred...
Fifty *yojanas* is equivalent to ten thousand *li*; this represents being adorned crosswise with the ten thousand virtues. "Ground" refers to the ground of the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is by means of that which has nothing to shatter that one shatters ignorance, and by means of that which has no abiding place that one dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"Various precious objects" refers to the manifold adornments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Railing" refers to the dhāraṇīs.
The thousands of millions of niches and chambers are the chambers of immeasurable compassion and are also the dwellings of immeasurable emptiness.
The banners and streamers are the supreme signs of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The hanging jeweled necklaces represent the application of the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*) to adorn the Dharma-body above and to cover sentient beings below. The billions of jeweled bells refer to the eight [liberations].

The four sounds represent the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The fragrance emanating from the four directions represents the wind of the Path of the Four Noble Truths blowing the fragrance of the four virtues.

Its height reaching as far as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings represents the thorough investigation of the principles of the Four Noble Truths. The present text explains this by correlating it with the Dharma-gates through their symbolic correspondence;
for a thorough investigation of all phenomenal characteristics, the preceding section provides the details. △ Second, the offerings of the various devas.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods rained down celestial *mandārava* flowers as an offering to the jeweled stūpa; likewise did all the other devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Tens of millions of billions of beings made offerings to the jeweled stupa with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies,
and music, honoring, respecting,
and praising it with reverence. The Heaven of the Thirty-three, collectively known as Trāyastriṃśa— the second heaven of the desire realm— resides upon Mount Sumeru.
The Summit (Kūṭāgāra) rests upon the earth and is also called a "Earth-Abiding Deva" (Bhūmiśvara).

Regarding the characteristics of Mount Sumeru’s height and breadth, as well as the four-colored celestial flowers, the eight classes of dragons and spirits (nāga-aṣṭakula), and so forth, these have all been explained above. To explain according to the principle (tattva):

the thirty stages of mind (triṃśaccitta) constitute thirty; the ten stages (daśabhūmi) constitute one; Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) constitutes one; and Sublime Enlightenment (Pratibhānaprāpta) constitutes one. Combined, these total thirty.
The three share the same reliance upon the realm of true reality (*dharmatā*). Regarding the raining down of *mandārava* flowers:

the initial mind also possesses the merits of the forty-two stages, and the final mind is likewise so; all these take the causal flowers of the forty stages as offerings directed toward the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
As for the other devas and nāgas mentioned below, they include those of the inner and outer stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who also rely upon true reality.
This refers to practicing the causes directed toward the fruit. △ Third, the praise by Prabhūtaratna:
At that time, a great voice issued from within the jeweled stupa, exclaiming: "Excellent, excellent!

Śākyamuni World-Honored One, you are able to take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—which is taught through the great wisdom of equality for the sake of instructing bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas—"
The great assembly declared: "It is so, it is so! All that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni has spoken is true.
This praise by Prabhūtaratna confirms that the preceding revelation of the provisional to manifest the real was indeed not in vain.
"Being equal to the Great Wisdom (Mahāmati)" means that it is the wisdom of all Buddhas, just as walking forward with even steps is the principle of correctness.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of equality: first, the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), which refers to the Middle Way principle contemplated by Great Wisdom;
second, the equality of sentient beings (*sattva-samatā*), meaning that all sentient beings equally employ the principle of causes to reach the fruit and thus collectively attain Buddhahood.
If the principle observed by wisdom were different from that of sentient beings, it would not be called "Great Wisdom. "Great" carries the meaning of being lofty and vast, as explained previously.
If we speak in terms of the contemplation of the mind: the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is equal vertically; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) is equal horizontally;

and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*) is equal in both horizontal and vertical dimensions. To simultaneously illuminate these two equalities is precisely the Great Equal Wisdom (*samatā-mahā-prajñā*). "Thus, thus" means...
First, "in accordance with the characteristics of reality" means praising the Buddha’s teaching as being in accord with the truth;
second, "in accordance with the nature of the faculties" means praising the Buddha for teaching the *Lotus Sūtra* only upon reaching the fifth period, so as not to miss the capacity of the listeners.
Both are called "true" because they are taught in accordance with the characteristics of reality. △ Fourth, the assembly’s astonishment and doubt: first, they attain the joy of the Dharma.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air and heard the sounds issuing from within it;
they all attained the joy of the Dharma.
They were filled with delight because hearing the Dharma accorded with their minds. △ Second, the assembly’s doubt and wonder.
Filled with unprecedented wonder, he rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Because he was struck by such unprecedented wonder, he was moved by both awe and doubt; furthermore, it was to manifest the infinitely remote origin that the high and vast stūpa was displayed.
Once the hearts and eyes of the fourfold assembly were thus stirred, the two Honored Ones had a basis upon which to unfold their transformative teachings. △
The Fivefold Inquiry of Mahāpratibhāna: First, the inquiry as to why this stūpa exists.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna who, knowing the doubts in the minds of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions does this jewel [stūpa] exist?"
Stūpa. △ Second, the question: Why does the stūpa emerge from the earth?
Why does it surge forth from the earth?
△ Third, the question: For what reason is this sound emitted?
Furthermore, why is this sound emitted within that [assembly]?
△ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s response to the three [questions]: First, the response to the second question.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna: "Within this precious stūpa is the entire body of a Tathāgata.
In the past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddha.
In it was a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna. When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a great vow: 'If I should attain..."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, wherever the Lotus Sūtra is being preached in the lands of the ten directions, my stūpas will manifest before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as witnesses and praising it, saying: "Excellent!"
Previously, the second question was answered as to why [the Buddhas] emerge from the earth;
now it is answered that these Buddhas emerge from the earth solely because they have made a vow to bear witness to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. △ Second, the retrospective answer to the first question.
After that Buddha had attained enlightenment and was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the great assembly of devas and humans:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stūpa."

In response to the first question above—asking by what causes and conditions this precious stūpa exists—the present answer states that it was because, when that Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he issued a command to construct this stūpa. △ Third, the answer to the third question.
By the supernatural power of his vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be those who preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that precious stupa will emerge before them;
the entire body of the Tathāgata remains within the stupa, praising them, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāpratibhāna!
Now, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is being preached, the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has emerged from the earth."
A voice surged forth, praising: "Excellent, excellent!
The [text] above asks why this sound was produced; the Buddha now answers that it was produced because that Buddha acted as a witness.
The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna did not preach the Dharma but entered parinirvāṇa.
The Master explains that it is not so; that Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Regarding the transformed persons who receive the teaching, what is meant by 'not speaking'?
It means that while they too may open the three [vehicles], they do not reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to manifest the reality.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: 'They are simply unable to preach the Dharma. For this reason, although they have entered parinirvāṇa, wherever they may be..."
There are those who, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* being preached, rejoice and realize it for themselves;

it is because Prabhūtaratna provides such testimony through his vows made during the causal stage and his supernormal powers realized in the resultant stage that he utters this sound. △ Second, the distant gathering of the divided bodies, in seven parts:
First, the request from Delight-in-Speech to see Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāsāhasrapramardana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, we wish to behold this body of the Buddha.

By means of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, he intended to open the stūpa; however, it was necessary to assemble the primary bodies and the emanated bodies, and once they had assembled, [he proceeded].

One should entrust [the teaching] because it must be entrusted; thus, one must summon those from the lower regions. Once those from the lower regions have emerged, one should immediately reveal the near to manifest the far.
This is the reason for this great matter; is it not the Buddha’s spiritual power that causes this inquiry? △ Second, the gathering of the manifested bodies.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāratnakūṭa: "The Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a profound and solemn vow:

'If my jeweled stupa emerges before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and there is anyone who wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly, then all those emanations of that Buddha who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions shall return.'"

Only after they have gathered in one place will my body appear. Mahāsukha-pratibhāna, you should now cause all the emanations of mine—the Buddhas who are preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions—to assemble here.
△ Third, the request for the assembly by Mahāpratibhāna.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we also wish to see the Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, in order to pay them homage and make offerings."
△ Fourth, the distant summons by emitting light:
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair, and immediately the lands of five million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of Buddhas in the eastern direction were seen;
in all those lands, the ground was made of crystal, and there were precious trees and jewels.
They use robes as their adornment, and it is filled with countless thousands of millions of *bodhisattvas*. Precious canopies and jeweled nets are spread everywhere above;
the Buddhas of that land preach all dharmas with great and wondrous voices.

Furthermore, one sees immeasurable thousands of millions of *bodhisattvas* filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes in the south, north, west, the four intermediate directions, and above.
The places illuminated by the light from the lower part of the ūrṇā-kośa mark are likewise so.
The reason the light from the ūrṇā-kośa illuminates the eastern direction first is that the east is the foremost of the directions; therefore, it is illuminated first.

Subsequently, it illuminates all ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—and wherever the light reaches, both the primary and secondary environments are magnificently adorned.
They are equal and without distinction. △ Fifth, all Buddhas come together.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Good sons, we should now go to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world, as well as to make offerings to the precious stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna."
Since the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed the bodhisattvas, saying, "I shall now go to the Sahā world," the significance of their coming together is clear.
△ Sixth, Adorning and Purifying the Realm of the Land (in three parts): First, Transforming the Sahā World.
At that time, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity, with lapis lazuli as its ground and adorned with precious trees.
Golden cords demarcated the eightfold paths, and there were no villages, hamlets, camps, cities, oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, or marshes.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground, which was covered by a canopy of precious nets and curtains.
Above, various jeweled bells were suspended, leaving only those present at this assembly, while all other devas and humans were moved to other lands.
At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great Bodhisattva as an attendant and arrived at the Sahā world, each reaching beneath a jeweled tree;
every one of these jeweled trees was five hundred yojanas high, adorned in succession with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Beneath each precious tree was a lion throne five *yojanas* high, likewise adorned with great jewels.
At that time, the various Buddhas each sat cross-legged upon their respective thrones; thus, spreading out in succession, they filled the trichiliocosm.
Yet, as for the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha in a single direction, they still remained as before.
Not yet finished.
First, regarding the transformation of the Sahā world: "Sahā" is a Sanskrit term newly transliterated as "Suohuo," which refers to the domain ruled by Śākyamuni.
Within it, there are ten billion suns and moons that illuminate it; this is called a Great Trichiliocosm (Mahāsāhasralokadhātu). △ Second, the transformation.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate the various Buddhas who had manifested as his emanations, further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions,
making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Furthermore, he moved the asuras and other devas to another land, a transformed realm where the ground was made of lapis lazuli and adorned with precious trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arrayed in successive tiers of splendor.
Beneath each tree stood a precious lion throne five yojanas high, adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda,
the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, or Sumeru and other such kings of mountains; rather, it was a single Buddha-field with a ground of jewels,
level and even, entirely covered by jeweled latticed canopies, from which banners and parasols were suspended and great precious incense was burned.
Celestial jewel flowers were spread everywhere across that ground.
Next, two hundred *nayutas* were transformed—wherein a *naya*, *naśu*, or *nayuta* refers to one hundred *lakṣas* as a *koṭi*, and two *koṭis* as one *ayuta*; and two *ayutas* as...

A *nayuta* is equivalent to ten thousand billion (*koṭi*). Now, when it says "two hundred million billion *nayutas*," this indicates an expansion so vast and profound that it is almost beyond the capacity of ordinary minds to calculate. The realm of the Buddhas is as profoundly deep as this.
*Mucilinda* means "stone mountain"; *mahā* means "great"; and *rāja* means "king. This is like...
In the *Avataṃsaka*, there are the ten mountain kings, such as the Snowy Mountains and the Fragrant Mountains.
"Jeweled latticed canopies" refers to curtains made by interlacing various jewels; because they are suspended in space without any covering above, they are called "exposed.
△ Third, the further transformation.
For the sake of the Buddhas who were to come and sit therein, Śākyamuni Buddha further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions,
making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras;
he also moved the devas and humans to other lands, and the lands thus transformed were likewise made of lapis lazuli.
It was adorned with precious trees; the trees were five hundred yojanas high, beautifully arrayed in succession with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, or the Iron Mountains.
The surrounding mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*Mahācakravāḍa*), Mount Sumeru, and all other kings of mountains collectively constitute a single Buddha-field.
Its ground is made of jewels, level and even, and is completely covered by jeweled latticed canopies.

Banners and parasols are suspended above, great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn everywhere across the earth. At that time, there were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha from the eastern direction.

From as many lands as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers, the Buddhas each came from their respective places to preach the Dharma and assemble here;
in this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions all arrived and sat in the eight directions.
At that time, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the four million billion nayuta lands in each direction, completely filled [the space].

Among these, regarding these three transformations that purify the land: because light is emitted to summon the emanated bodies from afar to assemble, it is necessary to transform the defiled into the pure, as those emanated bodies originally reside in pure lands.
The Commentary states: "Emitting light to summon [them] from afar, [there are] three..."

Regarding the purification of the land: this is precisely due to the three samādhis and two samāpattis. First, the transformation of the Sahā world is the *parivartana-vimokṣa* (liberation of turning away), which can transform the defiled into the pure.
Next, the transformation of two hundred nayutas [of worlds] is the *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery), wherein one possesses mastery over transformation.

Finally, the transformation of another two hundred nayutas is the *kṛtsnāyatana* (sphere of totality), wherein there is no obstruction regarding the object. Furthermore, this refers first to the initial [stage].

The first transformation and purification represents the purification and removal of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). The next transformation and purification represents the purification and removal of the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*).

The final transformation and purification represents the purification and removal of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, examining this text in detail, we verify that the first refers to transforming the defilement of the *sahā-loka* (the realm of shared residence) into purity;
the second transforms the *sahā-loka* into the *upāya-bhūmi* (the stage of skillful means); and the third transforms the *upāya-bhūmi* into [the ultimate stage].

There is truly no doubt regarding the stage of True Reward (sambhoga-kāya). Why is this? For within the text, it is stated that "the impure is transformed into the pure," which clearly indicates the Stage of Common Residence (sahā-loka).
Next, it says "the skillful means of the superior realm," which clearly indicates the Stage of Skillful Means (upāya).

Following that, it says "unimpeded with respect to objects," which clearly indicates the Stage of True Reward. Thus, by correlating the three delusions with these three transformations, the meaning becomes even more evident. Therefore...

It is because when conditions converge, the capacities of cause and response coincide, the Buddha’s power adds its invisible support, and the primary and secondary realms mutually encompass one another such that cause and effect are harmoniously integrated;
it is for this reason that it is so. The subsequent text states: "The eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ) are:

first, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms... up to the cessation of sensation and perception; these are called the eight liberations. First, having the perception of internal forms, externally...
Contemplating forms as few, whether beautiful or ugly, up to the white *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery)—these are called the eight *abhibhvāyatanas*.
Blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—these are called the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (spheres of totality).
Since all phenomena existing in the world are fully subsumed within these ten types, they are called "totalities" (*kṛtsna*), meaning universal and pervasive.

Furthermore, what is there that the term "all" does not encompass? Now, the reason why the three transformations of the land are explained here is precisely because one wishes to clarify the majestic spiritual power of the Great Sage and the realm of all Buddhas, wherein physical transformations are sovereign and the small contains the large, such that the environment and its inhabitants mutually include one another;
thus, within a single hair-tip, he manifests jeweled royal lands, and within a minute speck of dust, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
The Great Dharma-Wheel can cast the great trichiliocosm into other directions without the characteristics of coming or going;
it can condense one kalpa into seven days and extend seven days into one kalpa; it can pour the great ocean into a single pore without disturbing the turtles or fish.
When one traces the source of such spiritual transformations, they reach the level of a Mahāsattva of the Dharmakāya.

When those who have attained the fruit of wondrous enlightenment cultivate the causes, there are none who do not achieve it by practicing contemplation, training, and perfuming through the gates of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the various dhyānas, progressing from the shallow to the deep. What is clarified here is precisely this:
because the causes encompass the ocean of the fruit and the fruit reaches the source of the cause, the environment and its inhabitants are mutually fused, and cause and effect are interpenetrating.

Now, because one wishes to manifest the Tathāgata’s lifespan, which is as vast as the dust motes of kalpas, it is necessary first to display the deeds of transformative supernatural powers (*nirmāṇa-ṛddhi*);
that these do not arise in isolation but emerge through conditions is precisely what is meant by this. △ Seven: Granting Consent to Open the Stūpa (5):
First, the Buddhas inquire after one another’s welfare and preach the Dharma.
At that time, each of the Buddhas was seated upon a lion throne beneath a precious tree;
they all dispatched their attendants to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha, each carrying a handful of precious flowers and addressing them thus:
"Noble son, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides, and speak these words on my behalf: 'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you vigorous and strong?'"
The Blessed One, the Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas were all at ease and secure. Scattering these precious flowers as an offering to the Buddha, they spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha has granted his consent for this precious stūpa to be opened; other Buddhas have likewise sent their messengers."
Regarding the various Buddhas granting their consent (*chanda*) to open the stupa together, this is like the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) within the Saṃgha for granting consent.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies that numerous Buddhas grant their consent; the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* also speaks of numerous Buddhas of the ten directions reciting the *Avataṃsaka* together;

and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* likewise states that a thousand Buddhas recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* together. None of these, however, state that they are emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni.

If one compares this with the present sutra, it should be understood that because those [other] emanations were associated with skillful means (*upāya*), they did not explicitly reveal themselves during that time.
The present sutra, however, not only lists them in great numbers, but also directly states that these emanations have all come to offer their consent (*chanda*).
As for the meaning of "offering consent": "to offer" (*yu*) means to join together; "consent" (*yù*) means aspiration and delight. Therefore, consent is characterized by longing.

"It must be for the sake of the Dharma that these emanated bodies have all assembled; they have no other intention than to wish that the stupa be opened so they may see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. 2. Śākyamuni Opens the Stupa:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha saw that the emanated Buddhas had all arrived and were each seated in their respective places.
Upon the lion thrones, all heard the various Buddhas grant their consent for the joint opening of the precious stupa. Immediately, they rose from their seats and stayed suspended in mid-air.
All fourfold assemblies stood up, joined their palms, and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, producing a great sound like that of removing the bolt and unlocking a massive city gate.

The phrase "opening the gate" (kai-mon) signifies the opening of the provisional (kwan); "revealing the Buddha" (hyō kenbutsu) signifies the manifestation of the real (jitsu). This also serves as a confirmation of what preceded and a preparation for what follows.

The expression "removing the bolt and key" (kyaku kan-yaku): "removing" (kyaku) means to eliminate; the "bolt" (kan) is the horizontal wooden bar that holds the gate closed, while the "key" (yaku) is... [the lock].
The "lock" signifies that the obstacles of clinging to traces have been removed and the capacity to manifest the fundamental has been activated.
△ At that moment, the entire assembly saw and heard alike; all those present in the gathering beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna sitting upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa.
His entire body remained unmoving as if he had entered a state of meditative concentration, and he was heard to say: "Excellent, excellent!
Śākyamuni Buddha, you have skillfully preached this Lotus Sūtra. It is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha who had passed into extinction immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago speaking such words, marveled at it.
There was once an occasion when a multitude of *divyapuṣpa* (celestial jewels) were scattered over the Buddhas Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni;

the fourfold assembly all witnessed and heard this together, seeing the entire body of Prabhūtaratna and hearing that Buddha praise Śākyamuni for skillfully preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. △ Fourth, the two Buddhas share a seat and sit.
At that time, within the precious stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words:
"Śākyamuni Buddha, you may take this seat. Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stupa, sat upon that half-seat, and assumed the full lotus posture.
△ 54. The Assembly Requests an Addition.
At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas seated cross-legged upon lion thrones within the seven-jeweled stupa.
Each thought to themselves: "The Buddhas are seated so high and far away; we pray that the Tathāgatas, by means of their supernatural powers, will cause us [to see them]."
As they all stood together in the void, Śākyamuni Buddha immediately employed his supernormal powers to receive the great assembly, so that they all remained in the sky.
The fourfold assembly, being of one mind, requested the Buddha’s majestic empowerment; the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, granted their request and received the great [assembly] into the void.
The assembly together dwelt in the void. △ Third, Śākyamuni’s Proclamation of a Recruitment. Part One: The Loud Proclamation of a Recruitment.
With a great voice, he universally announced to the fourfold assembly: "Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this Sahā world-system?
Now is precisely the time."
The Tathāgata seeks those who will propagate [this teaching]. △ Second, it clarifies that the time for the entrustment has arrived:
before long, the Tathāgata shall enter nirvana.

When the great task is nearing completion, the fuel of the capacity [for teaching] is exhausted, and thus the fire of the response should also cease. △ Third, it clarifies that there is an entrustment.
As for "having a recipient": the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to one who serves as such a recipient.
One who serves as a recipient is like the Buddha when he was in the world, benefiting sentient beings according to their capacities by preaching the True Dharma himself, without depending on others.
Now that the Buddha’s conditions for transformation have come to an end, he wishes to ensure that this Dharma brings benefit without limit; therefore, it must be entrusted for circulation.

Regarding those to whom it is entrusted, there are two intentions: first, to ensure its presence in the near term by entrusting it to the eighty thousand and twenty thousand bodhisattvas who have long resided here to propagate and proclaim it in this land; second, to ensure its presence in the distant future by entrusting it to his original disciples.
He causes Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds below, to cause this to circulate wherever it is touched, and he also initiates their lifespan.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the verses in three parts; first, the verse on the parinirvāṇa of Prabhūtaratna:
"The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though long since passed into extinction, still remains within the jeweled stupa for the sake of the Dharma.

How can people not be diligent for the sake of the Dharma? This Buddha entered parinirvāṇa countless kalpas ago, yet he has traveled everywhere to hear the Dharma because it is so difficult to encounter."
Regarding that Buddha’s original vow—"After my parinirvāṇa, wherever [this sutra] may be, I shall always go there to hear the Dharma"—there are two intentions.
The first two and a half lines are likely intended to use the exalted to instruct the humble;
they urge and exhort the capacities of those in the present and future, implying: "If even Prabhūtaratna acts thus, how much more so others? The final line is the actual [vow].

This clarifies that Prabhūtaratna has come because of his vow to assist and support the transformation [of beings] through correction and praise. II. Verse on the Gathering of the Emanated Buddhas from Afar:
Furthermore, my immeasurable emanated buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have come desiring to hear the Dharma and to see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa;
each has abandoned their own wondrous lands, as well as their assemblies of disciples, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, and all matters of worship.
In order to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, they have come here to sit; by the supernatural power of the Buddhas, immeasurable multitudes have been moved so that the lands are purified.
Each Buddha proceeds to the foot of a jewel tree, which is adorned with lotuses like a cool pond.
Beneath those jewel trees are lion thrones upon which the Buddhas sit, their radiance and adornments appearing as if in the midst of a dark night.

Yet, emitting great torches of fire from their bodies that produce wondrous fragrances pervading the lands of the ten directions, sentient beings who are perfumed by them experience a joy beyond measure, like small tree branches swayed by a great wind;
through such skillful means, they cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.

Regarding these eight and a half verses on the gathering of the emanated Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*), the preceding section contained seven [verses], whereas the present text is very concise and lacks sequential order.

The first three lines of verse summarize the meaning of the second [section] concerning the assembly, which includes Mahāpratibhāna’s desire to see [the Buddha] and his request for the gathering, as well as the Buddhas taking their seats.
One line of verse praises the adornment and purification of the buddha-fields. The remainder generally summarizes all [other matters].

The Buddhas came together and each relinquished their wondrous lands, retinues, disciples, and the five exquisite sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), desiring to circulate [the Dharma] so that it might widely reach the final age and serve as eyes for the future; therefore, it is said that "they cause the Dharma to abide long.

Furthermore, it is said that the light of the Buddhas' bodies and their fragrances pervade the lands of the ten directions, and because sentient beings with the capacity for awakening are perfumed by them and find fulfillment and comfort, they "cannot contain their joy. △
The three verses on Śākyamuni’s entrustment are divided into two parts. First, citing the three Buddhas to encourage the circulation [of the sutra]. Part one: seeking out the qualified person.
[The Buddha] addresses the great assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa, who among you will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha..."
He speaks his own vow. To speak one's own vow means that one restrains one's own mind; this is what is called a "vow.
If Bodhisattvas feel compassion for sentient beings and desire to circulate this sutra to provide great aid to the distant future age, they must adorn themselves with a great vow.
To strictly restrain the mind so as not to regress is precisely why the Tathāgata has caused them to personally make this vow.
△ Second, citing three Buddhas to encourage the circulation [of this teaching].
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, by virtue of his great vow he utters this lion’s roar:

"The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and my own person, as well as all the emanated Buddhas gathered here, should understand this intention: 'O sons of the Buddha, who among you is able to protect the Dharma?
You should make a great vow so that it may endure for a long time.'"
△ Third, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation:
Whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra thereby makes offerings to me and to Prabhūtaratna;

for this Buddha Prabhūtaratna constantly travels throughout the ten directions within his jeweled stupa for the sake of this sutra, and they likewise make offerings to all the manifested Buddhas who have come.
Those who adorn and embellish all worlds—if they preach this sutra, it is as if they have seen me, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and all the manifested Buddhas.

△ Second, citing the dharma that is difficult to uphold to encourage its circulation, in two parts: first, the actual citation and exhortation; third, the initial admonition. First, the actual citation and exhortation. Third, the initial admonition.
Exhortation to Formulate Vows:
"O sons of good family, each of you should carefully contemplate this difficult undertaking and resolve to make great vows.
"Each of you should carefully contemplate" is an injunction; "resolve to make great vows" is the exhortation to formulate vows. "Carefully" (di) means to examine with thorough scrutiny.

One should deliberate upon what is appropriate, meaning that one ought to mobilize a profound mind and exert both mental and physical effort to widely proclaim and disseminate [the teaching], ensuring it is never interrupted.
△ Second, specifically citing what is difficult to uphold as an exhortation for its circulation.
Although other sutras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges may speak of these things, it would not yet be considered difficult;

even to take Mount Sumeru and hurl it to countless Buddha-fields in other directions would not yet be considered difficult; nor would it be considered difficult to move the great trichiliocosm with a toe and cast it far away to another land;
nor would it be considered difficult to stand at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and expound immeasurable other sutras for the sake of the assembly.
It would not yet be difficult if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one were able to preach this sutra in an evil age; that would indeed be difficult.

Even if someone were to grasp empty space with their hands and travel about, it would not yet be difficult; but if, after my parinirvāṇa, one were to write it down oneself or cause others to write it, that would indeed be difficult.
It would be even more difficult than placing the entire great earth upon the tip of one's toenail.
To ascend to the Brahma Heaven is not yet difficult; but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to read this sutra even briefly amidst the evil age—this is truly difficult.
Even if one were to carry dry grass upon one's shoulders and enter the conflagration at the end of the kalpa without being burned, that would not yet be difficult.
But after my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for the sake of a single person, that is indeed difficult. If one upholds the eighty thousand [dharmaskandhas]...

To expound for others the four great treasuries of Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, enabling all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers—even though one can do this, it is not yet difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sutra and inquire into its meaning and intent—that indeed is difficult.
If a person preaches the Dharma so that immeasurable, countless, and infinite beings, as numerous as the sands of ten million billion Ganges Rivers...
To attain arhatship and be endowed with the six supernormal powers, though such benefits exist, is not yet difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, if one can receive, uphold, and recite a sūtra such as this, that indeed will be difficult.
All the parables cited here concern matters that are utterly beyond human capability in this world, used as metaphors for the supramundane, unsurpassed, and most venerable Dharma.
Their intent is to cause those with various capacities to be struck with awe and alarm upon hearing them, so that they conceive the thought that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter.

Furthermore, those whom he exhorts do not go beyond the five types of Dharma-preachers—those who receive and uphold, read and recite, explain, copy, and preach—and these constitute the six [categories].

Regarding supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there is a distinction between those obtained as a karmic retribution and those obtained through cultivation. Those obtained as a retribution refer to the attainment of supernormal powers only after one has already acquired the capacity for transformation.
Those obtained through cultivation refer to first practicing transformations and subsequently attaining supernormal powers. The *Yingluo jing* states:

"The term 'spirit' (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind, and 'penetration' (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom. Because this innate wisdom illuminates all things without obstruction, it is called supernormal power."

One who cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣurabhijñā) attains, within deep meditative concentration, the pure derived matter (upādāyarūpa) of the four great elements of the form realm which abides within the eye-faculty;

by means of this, one is able to see the death and rebirth of beings in the six realms, as well as all the various forms and colors of the world—this is called the supernormal power of the divine eye. As for the supernormal power of the divine ear (divyaśrotrābhijñā), one is able to hear...

The supernormal power of knowing others' minds refers to the development of the knowledge of others' minds, by which one can know the minds of sentient beings in the six realms of existence, as well as their various mental objects, thoughts, and reflections.
The supernormal power of recollecting past lives refers to the development of the knowledge of past lives, by which one can know [the events of] the past... one [life].
One is also able to know the deeds performed in past lives throughout two lifetimes, up to hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, and even across eighty thousand great kalpas;
one likewise knows the past lives and the deeds performed by sentient beings within the six realms of existence.

Regarding the "body according to will" (kāya-vaśitā), this refers to the attainment of the power of bodily movement (kāya-vibhutva), which is of two kinds: first, traveling swiftly by flight over mountains and rivers without...
Regarding the power to obstruct others: it is the ability to transform one's own body, the bodies of others, and all things in the world according to one's will.
As for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*): it refers to the attainment of true wisdom through which the three outflows are forever exhausted.
The three outflows are the outflows of the three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Each of these six supernormal powers follows the same principle as the first.

Regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is taught that it all arises from the illumination attained through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). △ Third, the explanation of the meaning of "upholding with difficulty":
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras;
among them, this sutra is the foremost. If there is anyone able to uphold it, they are upholding the body of the Buddha.
Regarding the meaning of "releasing the difficult-to-maintain mind": if one is able to maintain it, one maintains the Buddha-body.
The phrase "this mind is not easy for me" refers distantly to the time when the Tathāgata first attained the Way at his original ground.
From that beginning until the present, throughout immeasurable lands across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, although he has extensively expounded all [dharmas]...
Among all sutras, this sutra is the most supreme. △ Second, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation, in three parts: First, the renewed recruitment of those who uphold the sutra.
"O sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, who among you is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, speak your own vow."

A second recruitment was issued for those who would uphold this sutra. Thus the sutra says: "Even if one were to carry [the sutra] upon the crown of one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, or offer one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm, yet if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, in the end there can be no way to repay its grace.
△ Second, it clarifies that the Buddhas rejoice and praise those who can uphold what is difficult to uphold.
This sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and all Buddhas likewise do so.
Such a person is praised by all Buddhas.

To clarify that those who can uphold what is difficult to uphold are joyfully praised by the Buddhas, it is said: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world occurs only after a vast interval of time."
To encounter a Buddha appearing in the world is difficult; to hear this Dharma being preached is even more difficult; and those who are able to listen to this Dharma are likewise rare.
It is like the Udumbara flower, which all love and cherish, yet is rarely seen by gods and humans, appearing only once in a great while.
This sutra, however, is the fundamental root of all living beings and the very eye of all Buddhas.
The King of all Sutras, the Secret Treasury: whoever holds it even for a moment, Śākyamuni Buddha rejoices and all Buddhas praise them.
It is just as when an heir is able to inherit the family business; how could the father not rejoice? As it is said:
"If I obtain a son to whom I may entrust my wealth and possessions, I shall be at ease and happy, no longer having any anxieties. This is precisely that matter. All [the Buddhas].
The reason the Buddha offers such praise is that his unconditioned great compassion and his original vows from the past are of one and the same intent.
△ Third, it clarifies that being able to uphold what is difficult to uphold constitutes the supreme practice.
This is indeed valor; this is indeed diligence. One who maintains the precepts and practices the dhūtas will swiftly attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
Those who are able to read and uphold this sutra in future ages are true sons of the Buddha, dwelling in the ground of pure goodness.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will be able to explain its meaning; they are the eyes of gods, humans, and the world in an age of fear.
One who can expound this for even a brief moment should be honored by all devas and humans.

Being able to maintain what is difficult to maintain, one perfects their supreme practice; possessing both faith and the intent to teach, they follow this path, benefiting themselves and others—such merit is truly preeminent.
Within these words, the meaning of the six perfections is also implicitly contained; this, then, is "courage."
The "Fierce One" (Mong-ja) is *dāna*; the "Vigorous One" (Pi-ri) is *vīrya*; the "One Who Maintains Precepts" (Si) is *śīla*; the "One Who Practices Dhūta" is *dhyāna*;

the "One Who Abides in Pure Goodness" (Jun-seon) is *kṣānti*; and the "One Who Can Understand Their Meaning" is *prajñā*. These are the true children of the Buddha, that is, beings of great resolve (*mahācitta*).
As the Sūtra says: "For those who seek to become Bodhisattvas, one should preach the six *pāramitās*"; this refers precisely to them.
That which can be accomplished in a future age may yet be achieved in the present time; for the era of the Buddha is considered the "present age.

Thus, if one can propagate this sutra during the current degenerate age (*tṛtīya-yuga*), one will naturally accomplish the supreme practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). As the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* says:
"If there are sentient beings who, throughout the six periods of day and night, pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, recite Mahayana sutras, and contemplate..."

In a single snap of the fingers, one removes the offenses of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas through this profound Dharma of emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). One who practices this is a true son of the Buddha, born from all Buddhas;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions serve as his preceptors. This is called being fully endowed with the bodhisattva precepts; there is no need for [further ordination].
The *karmas* are spontaneously accomplished, and one should receive the offerings of all humans and devas in this world of fear. Why is this?
In India it is called *saṃvarta*; furthermore, the sūtras and śāstras correctly call it *bhadraka*, which is simply another name for the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Eon).

One who can explain even a brief moment—according to the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, one *kṣaṇa* constitutes one thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), and there are one hundred and two [moments] in a single [unit].
Ten *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; this is called one instant (*muhūrta*). Sixty instants constitute one breath (*śvāsa*).
One breath is called one *lava*. Thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta* (translated as "a brief moment").
Thirty such moments constitute one day and night. Within one day and night, there are calculated to be six hundred and thirty...
The Buddha stated that one hundred and eighty thousand *kṣaṇas* constitute one *kalpa*, while a *kṣaṇa* is a short duration.
Its brevity is likened to the time it takes for two strong men to sever a single hair; thus it receives its name. Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya* states:
twenty *nimeṣas* (thought-moments) make one *tatkṣaṇa*; twenty *tatkṣaṇas* make one finger-snap (*acchaṭā*); and twenty finger-snaps [make one *lava*].
Twenty *lāyu* make one *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night.
This concludes the text of the fourth fascicle above.
*Kezhu Miaofa Lianhua Jing*, Fascicle Six.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.

revised and edited by the Śramaṇa Faji of Puti Hermitage, Yuxi, Ming Dynasty.
