△ Three: The Chapter on Śakra Devendra, Part Two. First: Presenting the Title of the Chapter.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Devadatta.

The commentary cites Baochang’s *Catalogue of Scriptures* (*Jingmu*), which states that during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty, Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated this scripture in twenty-eight chapters at Caotang Monastery and commissioned Sengrui to lecture upon it. Sengrui divided it into nine sections (*jié*).
At that time, the twenty-eight chapters were requested by palace women in Chang’an and remained detained within the inner quarters; consequently, only the [first] nine chapters reached Jiangdong.

The tradition was that only twenty-seven chapters were extant; during the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Man lectured on the sutra one hundred times in Chang’an and offered his own body as an act of devotion, subsequently placing this chapter before the "An-chi" (Ananda) chapter—this was his personal arrangement and was not heard of elsewhere.
During the Chen dynasty, Master Nanyue placed this chapter after the "Bao-ta" (Jeweled Stupa) chapter and continued [the text] from there.
When compared with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it fits like a seal and its impression; thus we know that these two masters have profoundly grasped the intent of the scripture.

As for Devadatta, he is also called Dādu; this is translated as "Heavenly Fever" (*tiānrè*), because he caused a schism in the Saṃgha, drew blood from the Buddha’s body, incited King Ajātaśatru to release a drunken elephant to trample the Buddha, killed the nun Utpalavarṇā, and inflicted injury by placing poison on his ten fingernails.
Because he committed acts of hostility toward the Buddha, at the time of his birth, the hearts of humans and devas burned with heat; it is from this that he derives his name.

This is the meaning according to his manifested traces (*traces*); if one considers it according to his fundamental essence, it is because sentient beings suffer from afflictions (*kleśa*) that the Bodhisattva also suffers from heat, practicing in accordance with their illness to deliver them.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Because sentient beings are ill, I too am ill"—this is what is meant.
Furthermore, this chapter cites the deeds of ancient Buddhas who propagated the sutra to prove that the benefits derived from such teaching and transformation are not empty;
by citing the past to exhort the present, it ensures its circulation. △ Second, the explanation of the sutra text has two parts:

first, explaining how Dharmodgata attained mastery of the sutra in the past and Śākyamuni achieved Buddhahood; second, explaining how Mañjuśrī attains mastery of the sutra today and the dragon girl achieves Buddhahood.
The first section also has three parts: first, clarifying the manner in which the teacher and disciple upheld this sutra in the past; second, correlating the ancient and the present;
third, exhorting faith. The first of these [three] also has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first of these [two] also has four parts:
first, clarifying the time when the Dharma was sought.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence.
△ Second, the actual explanation of seeking the Dharma, in two parts: first, the explanation of making the vow.
Throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king and made vows to seek unexcelled bodhicitta, never allowing it to regress.
△ Second, clarifying his practice, which has two parts: first, clarifying that in order to fulfill *dāna*, he diligently practiced giving.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, he diligently practiced giving with a heart free from stinginess, not begrudging elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives,
children, male and female slaves, attendants, or even his own head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, body, hands, and feet, nor sparing his life.

For those who wish to fulfill the six pāramitās: since the path of a bodhisattva consists of the mutual support of aspiration and practice, once the great vow has been made, one must necessarily engage in cultivation. These so-called six pāramitās are the very foundation of a bodhisattva’s correct conduct;
therefore, the preceding passage states: "For those who seek to become bodhisattvas, I shall teach the application of the six pāramitās and exhort them to diligent practice."

Dāna is what is translated as "giving" (bùshī). When there is internal faith, external fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and the presence of material wealth—when these three converge and one exercises the mind of relinquishment—one is able to destroy stinginess and greed;

this is called *dāna*. Furthermore, there are two kinds of giving: first, material giving (*āmiṣadāna*); second, the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Material giving refers to food, drink, clothing, fields, and so forth.

One's house, livestock, slaves, servants, precious treasures, all personal belongings for one’s livelihood, as well as one’s wife and children, even unto one’s own life—all these belong to the gift of wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
Therefore, it is said that even the relinquishing of one’s body belongs to the gift of wealth;
whatever is required by others, being able to give it all away, is called *dāna*. As for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), if one [receives it] from the Buddhas or...

When a spiritual friend hears the teachings on mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas, and through the power of their own contemplative practice is able to understand them clearly from the sūtras and śāstras, and then expounds them for others with a pure mind—this is all called the gift of Dharma (dharma-dāna).
If a bodhisattva, with a straightforward mind, practices these two types [of giving], they are both called dāna-pāramitā. "Pāramitā" is a Sanskrit term.

Regarding the term *pāramitā*, the translations found in various sutras and śāstras differ; here, I shall briefly summarize them according to three types: first, the "consummation of the task" (*kṛtyaparisamāpti*);
second, "reaching the other shore" (*pāra-uttaraṇa*); and third, "transcending the infinite" (*ananta-pāra*).

This means that when a bodhisattva cultivates these six dharmas, they are able to ultimately accomplish all matters pertaining to both the general and specific causes and effects, as well as all practices for self-cultivation and the transformation of others; thus it is so called.

The task is thus completed. Because one can, by means of these six dharmas, travel from this shore of the two kinds of birth-and-death to that shore of the two kinds of nirvāṇa, they are called "Pāramitās" (Reaching the Other Shore).

Furthermore, because one can, by means of these six dharmas, cross over the vast and distant expanse of all phenomena—both general and particular, both phenomenal and principled—they are termed "Dù wújí" (Infinite Crossing). Regarding the Bodhisattva’s practice within *dāna* (giving):
When one is able to fully cultivate five kinds of mental states, then giving is called a *pāramitā*.

What are these five? First, knowing the true nature of giving; second, giving rise to a mind of compassion; third, making a vow; fourth, dedicating the merit; and fifth, being endowed with skillful means.
"Knowing the true nature of giving" means that one understands that the three factors—the giver, the recipient, and the object of giving—are all [empty of inherent existence].
One who gives rise to great compassion while [realizing] emptiness must understand that the three factors of giving are all empty; this is called "giving of the true mark" (*lakṣaṇa-dāna*).
While constantly exercising a mind of compassion, one desires to use this giving to extract all suffering and bestow all happiness upon others.
As for making vows, one hopes that through this giving one may attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, without seeking the two vehicles of humans or devas.
Regarding "dedication of the fruit": at the time of giving, one dedicates this merit toward the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) so that it reaches all living beings.

Regarding "being endowed with skillful means": one is able to take the single dharma of giving and transform it so as to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas and universally cultivate all practices. If a bodhisattva can employ these five...

When the mind follows all that exists, it is spoken of as the cause within the context of giving; this is also called the perfection of the task (*kṛtyapariṇiṣpatti-pāramitā*), which is the *pāramitā* of crossing over to the other shore.
△ Second, explaining the seeking of the wondrous Dharma in order to fulfill Prajñā.
At that time, the people of the world had immeasurable lifespans; for the sake of the Dharma, he renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince.
He beat a drum to proclaim a decree to the four quarters, seeking the Dharma: "Whoever can explain the Mahāyāna to me, I shall serve them as their messenger for the rest of my life."

In Sanskrit it is called *prajñā*, which here is translated as "wisdom" (*hui-zhi*). This refers to the illumination that realizes all phenomena are ungraspable, thereby enabling one to penetrate all things without obstruction.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: first, that of the *śrāvaka*; second, that of the *pratyekabuddha*; and third, that of the *tathāgata*.
Within the category of *śrāvaka*, there are themselves three types: namely, those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). [The latter] is not...
Regarding the statement that "learning is not non-learning," and so forth, up to the comparison of the wisdom of a Pratyekabuddha with the wisdom of a Tathāgata:

from the moment a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, they practice the six pāramitās, destroy the hosts of Māra and all afflictions, and attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to accomplish the Buddha-way.
This continues until they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, in accordance with the power of their original vows.
All the wisdom contained within this interval, including both general and specific characteristics, knowing them all completely is called Buddha-wisdom.
If a bodhisattva cultivates these three kinds of wisdom with a sincere and pure mind, it is called Prajñāpāramitā;
furthermore, within that, they possess five kinds of minds: first, realizing the reality of wisdom.
The marks are neither objects nor wisdom; the mind has nothing to apprehend, yet it is able to universally study the wisdom of the three vehicles as well as all mundane knowledge and views.
The remainder is to be understood according to the preceding notes on *dāna*. △ Third, seeking to find a Dharma Master.
At that time, there was a seer who came and said to the king: "I possess a Mahāyāna sūtra called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you.
△ 4. Receiving the Dharma and Practicing It.
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king rejoiced and leaped for joy;

he immediately followed the seer, providing all that was required—gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food—even using his own body as a bed and seat without weariness of body or mind.
Thus he served him for a thousand years, diligently attending to him for the sake of the Dharma so that he lacked for nothing.
The preceding text has already stated that the lifespan of the people of that age was immeasurable;
this refers to when the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path during his past causal stages, passed through immeasurable numbers of *rajas* kalpas.

Therein, he cast himself as food for tigers, cut his own flesh to save a hawk, became a bridge, and provided his flesh as grain for fish—there was no instance of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) or acting in common with others that he did not employ.
For the sake of the Snow Mountain youth, he cast away his entire body for the sake of a half-verse; seeking the wondrous Dharma as a sovereign of the world, he endured toil for a thousand years.

Disregarding life and valuing the Dharma, he repaid virtue and requited kindness by relinquishing the glory of supreme nobility to assume the most humble and lowly office of a minor official. This was not merely because he leveled high and low or unified the holy and the common.
The wise and the foolish are merged, and distinctions between self and other vanish; who could possibly reach such a state?

Thus, now that the Way is perfected and enlightenment is fulfilled after traversing the dust of kalpas, he again reveals his initial causes and practices those deeds difficult to perform, providing a model to guide future generations. Beholding these extraordinary traces, those who see the worthy will think of emulating them;
how could there not be those who admire and seek to follow his example?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verse Recitation (Five Parts). First, the verse on the period for seeking the Dharma:
"I recall a past kalpa, when for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma,"
△ Second, the verse correctly clarifies the quest for the Dharma:
"Though I were a king of the world, I would not crave the pleasures of the five desires. Ringing the bell to announce to the four quarters:
'Who possesses the Great Dharma? If you can explain it to me, I shall become your servant.'"

Although he acts as a king of the world, because he does not crave the pleasures of the five desires, he is not ensnared by the objects of the five sensory realms—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. △ Third, the verse on attaining the state of a Dharma-preacher.
At that time, the Rishi Asita came and addressed the Great King, saying: "I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world;
if you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you."
△ Four verses on receiving the Dharma and practicing it accordingly.
At that time, upon hearing the words of the seer, the king’s heart was filled with great joy;

he immediately followed the seer and provided whatever was required, gathering firewood and fruits and offering them with due respect at all times. Because his mind was set upon the sublime Dharma, his body and mind were free from weariness or fatigue.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently seeks the Great Dharma.
Regarding the terms "fruit" (*guǒ*) and "gourd" (*luò*): that which grows on trees and has a seed is called a fruit; that which grows on vines or herbs and lacks a seed is called a gourd.
△ Fifth, the verse concludes the proof and exhorts belief.
Nor was it for the sake of my own person or for the pleasures of the five desires that I diligently sought and obtained this Dharma as a great king;
rather, I have now attained Buddhahood, and therefore I speak it for you.
△ Second, the correlation of the past and present, in two parts. First, the formal correlation of the past and present:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "The king at that time was none other than myself; the rishi at that time was the present Devadatta."
As in the text. △ Second, explaining that the merits of both teacher and disciple are fully perfected. Part one: explaining that the disciple’s causal retribution is already fulfilled.
Sub-part one: explaining the fulfillment of causes.
It is because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I have brought the six pāramitās, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, to full completion.
Renunciation.
There are three kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): first, the external protector; second, the fellow practitioner; and third, the teacher of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the external protector: one does not discriminate between the "black" and the "white," but simply provides whatever is required for sustenance, like a mother nourishing her child or a tigress carrying her cub.
First, one who provides proper care and treatment is called an external protector (*bāhya-rakṣaka*) spiritual friend.

Second, a fellow practitioner who mutually encourages and exhorts one another so that they do not become dull or distracted, but rather renew themselves daily through mutual refinement and polishing, sharing the same heart and unified resolve as if riding a single boat, and respecting one another as they would the World-Honored One—this is called a fellow-practitioner (*sahāya*) spiritual friend. Third, the teaching...
The instructor is one who can thoroughly discern all internal and external skillful means, as well as obstructions and hindrances;
who skillfully preaches the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden others, thereby transforming and breaking through the minds of people—this is called a spiritual friend who provides instruction.

One who is fully endowed with the six *pāramitās* has many meanings for "crossing over," as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Giving away one's basis of existence and its enjoyments is named *dāna*; it prevents the seven [afflictions].

The name "precept" (*śīla*) refers to refraining from striking or reviling others; "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the absence of such names [of anger]; "diligence" (*vīrya*) refers to the beginning and end of an undertaking;

"meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to the four dhyanas and eight concentrations; and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the cessation of disputes. This explains the meaning of the six perfections according to the Tripiṭaka.

Furthermore, citing the *Candragarbha-sūtra*, the six perfections are elucidated in their perfect clarity according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It states briefly: whether walking or sitting...
Abandoning thoughts of objective referents is *dāna*; not ceasing the pursuit of objective referents is *śīla*;
not allowing afflictions to arise toward objects is *kṣānti*; not abandoning detachment is *vīrya*; the mind being non-negligent regarding activities is *dhyāna*;
and the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is *prajñā*. This merely cites the general outline by mentioning the beginning and the end. Furthermore:
From the *Dharmadhātu-krama*, I have briefly cited the remaining four perfections here to present them so that readers may understand their general outline.
Second is *śīla-pāramitā*, which is translated as "good conduct" (*haoshan*). This refers to one who delights in practicing the path of goodness and does not indulge in self-indulgence.
Whether one practices good by receiving the precepts or practices good without receiving the precepts, both are termed *śīla*.
Briefly stated, there are two types: first, that of the laity; second, that of those who have left the household life.

The śīla of the laity refers to the three refuges, the five precepts, and the eight precepts. The śīla of those who have left the household life refers to the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, the six rules for śikṣamāṇās, and the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, up to the three [garudhammas].
The thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand rules of conduct pertain to the ordained;
as for the Bodhisattva’s ten grave precepts and forty-eight light precepts, these apply to both the laity and the ordained and are termed "common precepts.

If a Bodhisattva, with a sincere and pure mind, abides within these two kinds of *śīla* (ethical discipline) and simultaneously cultivates them while possessing the five kinds of mind, this ethical discipline...

The fifth of the names for the *pāramitās* is first: knowing the true nature (*dharmatā*) of ethical discipline (*śīla*), wherein although offenses are unattainable, one delights in practicing the path of goodness and does not abandon oneself to negligence. Third is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, translated here as "patience" (*ren-ru*).
This is so named because the internal mind is able to endure external objects that must be endured. There are two kinds of patience: first, patience in birth (*janma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the two types of patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*), within the context of patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*), there are further two kinds:

first, being able to endure respectful offerings and worship such that the mind does not give rise to attachment or arrogance; second, not giving rise to resentment, malice, or vexation when faced with anger, abuse, or injury.
For these reasons, they are collectively termed "patience toward beings. Patience toward phenomena is also of two kinds: the first is non-mental...
"Phenomena" refers to the twin torments of cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, and thirst, as well as old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
"The second" refers to the phenomena of anger, grief, doubt, regret, sensual desire, pride, and various false views.
That a Bodhisattva remains serene and unmoved amidst these two types of phenomena is called the patience of phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Fourth is *vīrya*, here translated as diligence, which means:
It is so named because of diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas without self-indulgence; furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the body, and second, the mind.

Regarding the body, it refers to diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas by practicing the Path, performing prostrations and recitations, preaching and explaining, exhorting others, enlightening the ignorant, and reforming the stubborn—this is called physical diligence (*kāya-vīrya*).
Regarding the mind, it refers to diligently directing wholesome thoughts so that they follow one after another in succession without interruption—this is called mental diligence (*citta-vīrya*).
Mental diligence (*citta-vīrya*): Furthermore, diligently practicing the wholesome dharmas of generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) is called bodily diligence;

diligently practicing patience (*kṣānti*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) is called mental diligence. Fifth is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, here translated as "cultivation through contemplation" (*manasikāra-bhāvanā*).
This refers to all practices of collecting the mind, binding the mindfulness, and training in various *samādhis*, which are all termed cultivation through contemplation. It also has two aspects.

There are two kinds of meditation: first, mundane; second, supramundane. First, mundane meditation refers to the fundamental four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and so forth; this is the meditation practiced by ordinary worldlings.
Second, supramundane meditation also has two types: first, supramundane meditation; second, the most excellent supramundane meditation. Supramundane [meditation] refers to the six subtle wonders.

The sixteen special victories (*ṣoḍaśaviśeṣa*), the universal clarity (*sāmānyapratibhāsa*), the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti*), the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*),

the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), the refinement of dhyāna (*dhyānaparikarman*), the fourteen transformations (*caturdaśavikurvaṇa*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the summit dhyāna (*mūrdhadhyāna*),

the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*), the king of samādhis (*samādhirāja*), the lion’s bound-fury samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhitasamādhi*), the transcendent samādhi (*vyutkrāntakasamādhi*), and even the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)— such as these.
These types are all called "world-transcending dhyāna" and are also called "dhyāna shared by the two vehicles.

As for "superior-to-the-world dhyāna," this refers to the nine kinds of great dhyānas such as the *svabhāva-dhyāna*, the one hundred and eight samādhis such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and the one hundred and twenty-three samādhis such as the "immovable" samādhi of all Buddhas; these are all called "superior-to-the-world dhyāna" and are also called "unshared [dhyāna]."

Dhyāna (meditative concentration) refers to that which is not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles. Compassion (*maitrī*), loving-kindness (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are called the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*).
They derive their names from their objects, because since the sentient beings who are the focal objects are immeasurable, the cognizing minds that take them as objects likewise become immeasurable;
thus, they all receive the name "immeasurable mind. First, the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness is that which can bestow happiness upon others.

The mind that is free from anger, hatred, resentment, and vexation, which is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions, is called the "immeasurable mind of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-apramāṇa-citta*).

Second, regarding the "immeasurable mind of compassion" (*karuṇā-apramāṇa-citta*): the mind capable of uprooting the suffering of others is called the "mind of compassion," which is free from anger, hatred, resentment, and vexation, and is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions; this is called compassion.
Regarding the third immeasurable mind, *muditā* (sympathetic joy): when one rejoices at others attaining happiness and gives rise to a heart of gladness, it is called the mind of sympathetic joy.
When this is free from malice, resentment, and vexation, and is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions, it is called the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā-apramāṇa-citta*).
Regarding the fourth immeasurable mind, *upekṣā* (equanimity): if one directs the mind toward others with a state of mind that is neither hateful nor loving, it is called...
This state of equanimity—free from anger, resentment, and vexation, vast, immeasurable, and pervading the ten directions—is called the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa-citta*).
These four are also termed the four immeasurable concentrations (*catvāri apramāṇa-samādhayaḥ*). △ Second, clarifying the fulfillment of the fruit.
Possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a purple-golden complexion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,
the four means of integration, the eighteen unique qualities, and the power of the divine path, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment and extensively delivered all sentient beings.
Regarding the thirty-two marks: the Tathāgata’s body of transformation manifests these various marks to symbolize that the Dharma-body is perfectly consummate and endowed with all virtues.
This causes those who see it to feel love and reverence, knowing there are supreme qualities to be honored;
thus he is the Honored One among gods and humans, the King of all sages. First, the soles of his feet are level and even, like the bottom of a cosmetic box. Second...
1. The soles of his feet are marked with the thousand-spoked wheel; 2. the three parts of his hands and feet are long and superior to those of other men;
3. his hands and feet are soft and supple, surpassing other parts of his body; 4. his fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane, surpassing that of other men;
5. his heels are full and beautiful; 6. his ankles are high and beautiful, in proportion to his heels; 7. his calves are like those of the eneya deer, slender and beautiful; 8. when standing...
10. At that time, his hands reach his knees; 11. his male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse-king;
12. his body is perfectly symmetrical in length and breadth; 13. each and every pore is blue and soft; 14. the hair on his body points upward, is blue in color, and curls to the right;
15. his golden radiance is subtle and exquisite; 16. the light from his body extends one zhang in every direction; 17. his skin is [smooth].
17. His skin is fine and smooth, such that it does not retain dust or dirt, nor do mosquitoes or gadflies alight upon it.
18. Both his armpits are full. 19. His body is like that of a lion. 20. His body is upright and straight. 21. His shoulders are well-rounded and handsome.
22. He possesses a full set of forty teeth. 23. His teeth are... [even/white/spaced] (as per standard list).
24. His teeth are white, even, and closely set; 25. His four canine teeth are the whitest and largest;
26. His jaw is like that of the lion king; 27. The moisture in his throat perceives the most excellent of flavors; 28.
His tongue is large and thin, covering his face up to the hairline; 29. His Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like [the sound of] a *bherī* drum.
29. His voice possesses the quality of the *gaṅgā* river; 30. his eyes are like refined gold; 31.
his eyelashes are like those of a bull king; 32. the tuft of hair between his eyebrows is like *tūla* cotton.

These thirty-two marks, along with the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) interspersed among them—all of which are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*)—together adorn the Buddha’s body, manifesting its wondrous splendor.
The primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are general, whereas the secondary refinements (*anuvyañjana*) are specific; for if the marks were devoid of these refinements, they would not be complete.

Thus, even wheel-turning kings, Śakras, and Brahmās possess them, yet because they lack these refinements, their marks are not subtle or wondrous. The Great Sage cultivated his body through compassion and thereby manifested these pure and marvelous marks and refinements:
first, the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa-śiraskatā*); second, the mark of the high nose with unobstructed nostrils (*tuṅga-nāsa*).
1. His three eyebrows do not appear [separately], being like the crescent moon and the color of dark lapis lazuli; 2. The four ear-lobes are formed with the characteristics of spokes and hubs;
3. His body is as solid and firm as Nārāyaṇa; 4. The joints of his bones are like hooked chains; 5. When he turns his body, it does so all at once like an elephant king; 6.
When walking, his feet leave the ground four inches while the marks of the wheels appear; 7. His nails are like red copper.
10. The skin is thin, fine, and lustrous; 11. The ten knee-joints are prominent, round, and beautiful; 12. The body is clean and pure; 13. The body is soft and supple; 14.
The body is straight and not crooked; 15. The fingers are slender and rounded; 16. The finger-veins are concealed; 17. The veins do not protrude;
18. The ankles do not protrude; 19. The body is well-proportioned and symmetrical; 20. The body is naturally dignified and self-sustained.
Twenty-one: His body is not crooked; twenty-two: He is fully endowed with all dignified deportments; twenty-three:
His physical appearance is perfect and complete; twenty-four: He dwells in peace and security, such that no one can disturb him;
twenty-five: His majesty overawes all beings; twenty-six: All beings delight in beholding him; twenty-seven: His face is neither overly large nor small.
28. His facial features are upright and his expression is never distorted; 29. His face is perfectly round and full; 30. His lips are like the *bimba* fruit;
31. His voice is deep and far-reaching; 32. His navel is deep, round, and beautiful; 33.
The hair on his body curls to the right; 34. His hands and feet are full; 35. His hands and feet are as he desires; 36. His hands...
36. His lines are straight; 37. his lines are long; 38. his lines are unbroken; 39.
all beings with malicious minds become harmonious and joyful upon seeing him; 40. his face is broad and beautiful; 41.
his face is like the pure full moon; 42. he speaks with harmony and joy according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
43. Fragrance issues from the pores of his body; 44. His mouth emits unsurpassed fragrance; 45.
His physical appearance is like that of a lion; 46. His gait and movements are like those of an elephant king;
47. His deportment is like that of a swan king; 48. His head is like the *mānada* fruit; 49. He is fully endowed with all components of vocal resonance.
94. The teeth are white and sharp (50). 51. The tongue is red. 52. The tongue is thin. 53. The color of the tongue is crimson. 54.
The body hair is soft, supple, and pure. 55. The eyes are wide and long. 56. The orifices are complete and well-formed. 57.
The hands and feet are reddish-white, like the color of a lotus. 58. The navel is not... [incomplete].
58. His abdomen is prominent; 59. his abdomen is not protruding; 60. his abdomen is slender;
61. his body does not sway; 62. his body is dignified; 63. his body is large; 64. his body is tall; 65.
his hands and feet are soft, pure, and smooth; 66. his bodily radiance extends one zhang in each of the four directions.
67. Six rays of light illuminate his body as he walks; 68. He regards all sentient beings with impartiality; 69. He does not treat sentient beings with contempt; 70.
He adapts to the voices of sentient beings without increasing or decreasing [his own]; 71. He teaches the Dharma without attachment; 72.
He teaches the Dharma according to the languages of sentient beings; 73. His utterance of sound responds to the various sounds of the multitude.
Seventy-three: He teaches the Dharma with sequential causes and conditions. Seventy-four: No sentient being can fully perceive his physical marks.
Seventy-five: Those who behold him never tire of doing so. Seventy-six: His hair is long and beautiful. Seventy-seven: His hair is not disheveled.
Seventy-eight: His hair curls beautifully. Seventy-nine: His hair is like blue pearls. Eighty: [The mark of] his hair is well-arranged.

The hands and feet possess the marks of virtue. Furthermore, the *Zuochan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) states that there is the character "De" (德) upon the chest and the character "Ji" (吉) upon the hands and feet.
Another sūtra states that there is the *svastika* character upon the chest.

Inferring from these marks and excellences, they all fundamentally arise from practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad deeds as their basis. "Purple-polished gold" (*zi-mo*) refers to the finest quality of gold. As for the "ten powers" (*daśa-bala*):
First is the power of the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*):

the Buddha knows the fixed nature of the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of all sentient beings, just as flowers inevitably yield fruit without fail. Thus it is said that "goodness does not fail to bring its reward" and "evil naturally invites calamity"—this refers precisely to this matter.
Second is the power of the knowledge of karma (*karma-jñānabala*): the Buddha knows the causal karma created by all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
1. The power of concentration: the Buddha knows all the characteristics of the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and their distinctions regarding defilement and purity.
2. The power of the faculties: the Buddha knows the sharpness or dullness, and the superior, middling, or inferior degrees, of the faculties of sentient beings.
3. The power of aspirations: the Buddha knows the various different inclinations and desires of sentient beings. 4. The power of dispositions: the Buddha knows the various dispositions of the world.
The power of knowing the seven ways of rebirth as they truly are: the Buddha knows the destination of all paths. The power of recollecting past lives:

the Buddha knows various past existences, including their common characteristics and causal conditions—whether one life, two lives, or even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas—knowing that "I was there, with such a name, such food and drink, such suffering and pleasure, such rise and fall, and such a long or short lifespan."
10. The Power of the Divine Eye: The Buddha’s divine eye is completely pure and surpasses that of human eyes;
he perceives all sentient beings as they are born and die, whether in high or low states, beautiful or ugly, and whether reborn in good or evil realms—he knows them all.

These are the ten [powers]. 11. The Power of the Exhaustion of Outflows: Because all outflows have been exhausted, the Buddha knows for himself that birth has ended and that there will be no further existence. These are the ten.
Because the Buddha knows all things universally, and because he cannot be destroyed or surpassed, these are called "powers" (*bala*). Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*):
since the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the ten powers fills him internally with certainty and clarity, he is from the outset entirely free of fear regarding external conditions.
These four are collectively termed "fearlessnesses" because, amidst the eightfold assembly, he extensively proclaims his own and others' wisdom.
Because he has definitively severed [all doubts] without error, there is not even the slightest sign of fear.
First, regarding the fearlessness of omniscience, the Buddha himself truthfully declared: "I am one who possesses perfect knowledge.
If any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else were to say according to reality that I do not know or do not see such a dharma..."
This refers to the presence of even a slight sign of fear; for this reason, I have attained peace and security. Because I roar like a bull king and am like a lion king, I am called "Fearless.
Second is the Fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*): the Buddha himself truthfully declares, "All my outflows are exhausted.
Third is the Fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*): the Buddha himself truthfully declares, "I [have taught] all things that obstruct the path..."

The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are: (1) proclaiming the obstructive dharmas that can hinder the fruit of the Path; (2) proclaiming the path for the exhaustion of suffering; (3) the Buddha’s own sincere declaration:
"I have proclaimed the Noble Path which enables transcendence from the world; if one relies upon and practices it, one can exhaust all sufferings";

and (4) proclaiming these four meanings as entirely definitive and unsurpassable. Because there is nothing that can contradict them, they are called "fearlessnesses. Regarding the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they are great... [text fragment ends].
The skillful arts for guiding others are essential techniques that follow the inclinations and preferences of various dispositions to entice them toward aspiration, just as water flows downward.
Once beings have become attached, one then transforms them—just as clouds first draw them in with desire-hooks and subsequently lead them into the Buddha-way.
First is the means of attraction through generosity (*dāna-saṃgraha*), which consists of giving material wealth and the Dharma.
Second, through the gathering of giving, the Bodhisattva bestows whatever they are capable of receiving; once they have received this grace, they develop a sense of intimacy and attachment.
Third, through the gathering of kind speech, the Bodhisattva employs virtuous words to guide, console, and enlighten them, causing those sentient beings to give rise to love and joy in their hearts.
Fourth, through the gathering of beneficial conduct, the Bodhisattva engages in physical, verbal, and mental actions as appropriate, enabling all beings to individually receive its benefits.

The four benefits are gathered through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); observing their faculties, one establishes transformation according to their inclinations and desires. One divides forms and disperses reflections, harmonizing light with the dust of the world to participate in their activities.
First acting in common with them and later becoming distinct, one transforms the causes of their karma so that they may advance toward the fruits of the Path.
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), these are the dharmas of the ultimate stage of all Buddhas, not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
These are named as such because they are shared by all great Bodhisattvas. First, there is no failure of the body:

because the Tathāgata has, throughout immeasurable kalpas, cultivated his body through the perfuming of precepts, concentration, wisdom, compassion, and loving-kindness, his merit is fully perfected and his afflictions are forever exhausted;
thus, all his bodily actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, and therefore he is without failure. Second, there is no failure of speech; the meaning is as follows: [text continues]

His body is identical [to that of a Buddha]; he possesses the three mindfulnesses without fail; he has long and skillfully cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness and various profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) such that his mind is never distracted;
he is free from the four types of partiality, viewing all sentient beings with equanimity as if they were his only child, like rain falling evenly upon all or the sun shining universally;
fifth, his mind is never unsettled, being like a cloud or a *nāga* who always remains in meditative absorption.

In the six indefinite times, there is nothing that the Buddha does not know before he relinquishes them; regarding all phenomena, he illuminates and knows them exhaustively, only then relinquishing them after having thoroughly investigated their principles and exhausted their natures.

Seventh, his desires do not diminish: because the Buddha knows the debt of gratitude for wholesome dharmas, even though he is fully endowed with all virtues, his aspiration for the Dharma does not cease.
Thus it is said: "The Tathāgata does not discard even the merit of threading a needle. This is an analogy.
Although that wheel-turning king’s precious horse traverses the four continents in a single day, his mind remains unsatisfied;

yet for the Buddha, his eightfold vigor never diminishes, as both his physical and mental vigor are already fully perfected. Furthermore, his resolve to deliver sentient beings and gather in those who can be trained never ceases.
Ninth, there is no diminution of mindfulness: regarding the Buddha’s wisdom and its characteristics across the three periods of time, [he is ever-present].

It is because [the Buddha] is thus: (10) Wisdom is undiminished, for the Buddha has attained all-encompassing wisdom, having perfected and brought to ultimate completion the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four types of unimpeded knowledge; (11) Liberation is undiminished, which is of two kinds:
first, conditioned liberation, meaning liberation associated with untainted wisdom; second, unconditioned liberation, meaning [freedom from] all afflictions.
12. He has eternally exhausted [all defilements] without remainder; his knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) never diminishes.
Regarding all liberations—namely, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the inconceivable, the unimpeded, and so forth—he possesses a clear and distinct knowledge and vision.
He distinguishes and firmly establishes all paths of liberation, such that there is nothing he does not know. 13. All his bodily actions follow wisdom.
14. Because the Buddha first realizes through the practice of wisdom and subsequently initiates all activities, he manifests his body in every place without fail to benefit sentient beings;

15. All verbal karma follows the movement of wisdom; 16. All mental karma follows the movement of wisdom—these two are explained according to the same principle as bodily karma; 17. Wisdom knows the past without obstruction.
17. The Buddha’s wisdom illuminates and knows all that exists throughout the limits of the past, whether sentient or insentient, penetratingly understanding them all. 18.
With unimpeded wisdom, he knows the future world, illuminating the limits of the future regarding both sentient and insentient beings without any obstruction.
19. His wisdom knows the present world without obstruction; thus, these three [knowledges] are unimpeded.
Regarding the twelve marks, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth, they are now cited and elaborated upon because the intention is to enlighten those of initial capacity.
△ Third, the conclusion on the benefits derived from the master’s thorough study of the sutras.
All is due to Devadatta as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
△ Second, explaining that the wondrous fruit of the Dharma Master shall be attained. Part three: First, the formal explanation of the attainment of the fruit.
He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be called..."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Devarāja; his world is called Devamārga.
The *Puṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Devadatta will become a buddha named T'i-ho-lo-ye (Dīpaṃkara); 'T'i-ho' in the Han language means 'Heavenly King,' and the name of his land is T'i-ho-yueh (Dīpavatsa);
'T'i-ho' in the Han language means 'Heavenly Path. △ Second, explaining the transformation and deliverance.
At that time, the Buddha Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the aspiration for Pratyekabuddhahood;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gave rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way, attained the patience of non-arising, and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
△ Third, the benefits after the parinirvāṇa.
After the Tathāgata Devendra-Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remains in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.

A stūpa made of the seven precious jewels is erected over his entire bodily relics (śarīra), sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth, [to which] all devas and human beings [pay homage].
With various flower powders, incense, burning perfumes, unguents, robes, necklaces, banners, streamers, precious parasols, and musical performances and hymns,
they paid homage and made offerings to the wondrous stupa of the seven jewels; thereby, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship,
immeasurable sentient beings realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the Bodhi-mind and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
△ Third, the exhortation to believe.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, develop a pure heart of faith and reverence and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into hell."
Those born as hungry ghosts or animals will always hear this sutra wherever they are reborn before the Buddhas of the ten directions;
if they are reborn among humans or devas, they will enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss, and if they are before a Buddha, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower.

Regarding those born by transformation from a lotus, the *Tāisheng jīng* (Sūtra on Birth) states: "Those born from a lotus are not among the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, or transformation;

though called 'transformation,' they are in reality not the same as the 'transformation' found within the four modes of birth. The *Guānshìyīn púsà jīng* (Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) says they are "born by transformation from a lotus" because they lack parents.
The *Wúliàngshòu jīng* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life) refers to those who dwell for a long time upon the lotus pedestal as being "born from a womb."
In truth, this is not birth from a womb; it is analogous to birth from a lotus, which is described as being born from moisture or an egg, yet is neither moisture nor an egg.
This lotus-birth is a transformational birth (*upapāduka*), for while the pure karma has been perfected, consciousness still relies upon the power of vows to take refuge within the womb of the lotus.
Since this is neither caused by the deluded karma of ignorance nor by the greedy love of parents, it is not birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation in the conventional sense.

Due to these conditions, one is entrusted to a lotus-womb and thus possesses this physical form; its meaning is that of "transformational birth" (*upapāduka*), which differs from the "transformative being" among the four modes of birth.
This is because, although that transformative being does not pass through a womb or egg, it nonetheless arises from the mutual resonance of deluded karma;
taking one's own karma as the cause and the five elements of the world as the condition, it manifests with a physical form from within the midst of emptiness and non-existence.
Since this is a transformation produced by the power of karma, its principle is distant from that of "lotus-birth" (padma-upapāduka).

Those who are "womb-born" (jarāyu-ja) within the calyx of the flower—compared to the superior grade which immediately attains the vision of the Buddha without any delay—are now, having passed a long duration, analogous to womb-birth;
yet because they lack the suffering of a worldly womb-prison, it is said that they are not [the same]. This is the analogy.
As for the statement that Padmasambhava is also called "Moisture-Egg" (śītoṇḍa) yet is not equal [to those born from moisture or eggs]:
this is because the lotus depends upon water, which is like "moisture," and the flower remains contained within it for an eon without blooming, which is like an "egg.

Furthermore, regarding the excellence of the celestial palaces within those flowers, their superiority and inferiority differ by factors of ten million times an eon; how could they possibly be the same? Moreover, in the *Mahāratnakūṭa*...
It is said that if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower in the presence of all Buddhas:
first, not speaking of the faults of others even at the cost of one's life; second, transforming people so that they take refuge in the Triple Gem;
third, establishing all beings in the bodhicitta; fourth, remaining untainted by the brahma-conduct; and fifth, crafting images of the Buddha and placing flowers upon them.
Sixth, while seated, he is able to remove the grief and afflictions of sentient beings; seventh, toward those who are arrogant and haughty, he is always humble and self-effacing;
eighth, he does not vex others. △ Second, clarifying how Mañjuśrī today mastered the sutra and the dragon girl attained Buddhahood.
Part one: first, clarifying that Mañjuśrī requested to withdraw. Initial section: first, clarifying that Jñānākara requested to withdraw.
At that time, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa), who had come from the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna in the region below, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying,
"I shall now return to my own land.
The *Píngtáluójīng* (Puṇḍarīka Sūtra) states that the bodhisattva who came from the Buddha in the region below was named Bānrèjùluó (Prajñākūṭa), which in the vernacular means...
Jñānakośa, Jñānakośa—so named because he had emerged to bear witness to the sutra and to exhort the circulation of its teachings—having completed these tasks, requested to return.
△ Second, Śākyamuni Buddha restrained him.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakośa, "Good son, wait but a moment;
there is a bodhisattva here named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet and discuss the sublime Dharma, after which you may return to your own land."
The commentary explains that the World-Honored One stopped [the assembly] to command them to wait for the proof of the benefits of the transmission of the sutra.
Regarding the reason the World-Honored One stopped them: although the matters of the Trace Gate (Jikimon) were concluded, the Essential Gate (Honmon) had not yet been revealed;
