"These bhikṣus, out of greed for gain and offerings, preach the discourses of non-Buddhists and have composed these sūtras themselves to delude the people of the world;
seeking fame and reputation, they have made such distinctions regarding this sūtra."
Constantly amidst the great assembly, because they wish to disparage us, they slander us before kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of bhikṣus,
speaking ill of us by saying we are people of false views who preach the discourses of external paths.
The seven lines above clarify the arrogance of those who falsely claim sainthood. The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle six, states that *āraṇya* is translated as "without affairs" (*wushi*).
*Dhūta* is translated as "shaking off" (*douso*). The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* refers to it as the "place of the *āraṇyaka*.
The *Ji* (Record) states that *ā* means "no," while *araṇya* is named for "contention" (*zheng*). The text here says "affairs" because there are affairs; the *Sūtra* says "dwelling."

An araṇya is a place where one does not contend with the world; it is neither too near nor too far, convenient for begging food, possessing tree shade, abundant flowers and fruits, and sufficient pure water;
it is free from difficulties, without rugged obstacles, and easy to ascend. Being alone without a companion, one recites what has been heard.
When kings, ministers, elders, or others come to visit him, he should say: "Welcome, welcome."
When someone comes to your dwelling, you should invite them to sit; if they do not sit, do not sit alone.

If they will not accept a humble seat, you should comfort them in various ways and preach the Dharma for them. If they do not delight in a detailed exposition, you should provide a brief one and so forth.
To act otherwise is not the practice of an araṇyaka. One dwells in the forest retreat (araṇya) in order to subdue the afflictions (kleśa).
Or, to exalt oneself while disparaging others is not the practice of non-contention. △ Third, a general indication of the purpose for wearing robes:
"Out of reverence for the Buddha, we shall endure all these evils;
when others treat us with contempt, saying, 'You are all Buddhas,' you must all accept such insults and slights. In this turbid age and evil world, there are many terrors."

Evil spirits shall enter their bodies to revile and insult us; yet we, who revere and have faith in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience for the sake of expounding this sutra and endure these various hardships.
We do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only pity the Unsurpassed Way.
In future ages, we shall protect and uphold that which the World-Honored One has entrusted to us; may the World-Honored One himself know that there will be evil bhikṣus in the turbid world.

Not understanding that the Buddha teaches the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate, they speak with harsh words, frown, and are repeatedly expelled and kept away from the stupas and monasteries;
yet for all such evils, they should endure these matters out of mindfulness of the Buddha’s admonitions.

These seven lines clarify the intention behind wearing the robe; it is precisely this meaning that is expressed in the "Dharma Master" chapter, where the three modes of propagating the sutra take gentleness and patience as one's garment. △ Second, entering the room to propagate the sutra.
"In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to each of their places and preach the teachings entrusted to me by the Buddha.

These three lines each convey a single meaning; the first clarifies "entering the chamber," which refers to taking compassion as one's chamber and responding to conditions as they arise—hence the phrase "I shall go to each of their places. △ Third, sitting upon the seat to propagate the sutra.
"I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; dwelling among the assembly, I am fearless. I shall skillfully preach the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace.
Next, it says that "dwelling among the assembly without fear" is the seat of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnya*). △ Fourth, the conclusion and request for understanding.
Before the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this vow, saying: "The Buddhas themselves know my heart.
This constitutes the three requests.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anle-xing-pin) has two parts: first, by way of the chapter title.
The Fourteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "On Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-bon*).

This chapter is explained in three parts: first, the practice based on physical matters; second, the attachment to the text; and third, the dharma-gate. Regarding the practice based on matters: because the body is free from danger, the mind is at peace;
because the mind is free from anxiety and affliction, there is joy. Since the body is thus at peace and the mind is joyful, one is able to advance in practice.
Furthermore, regarding those who attach the text: "To don the Tathāgata’s robe" means the Dharma-body is at peace; "to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber" means the mind of liberation finds joy;
"to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat" means that Prajñā guides one's practice as one advances. This is the commentary on the text of the Superior Chapter.
Because one dwells on the ground of patience, the body is at peace and not violent or impetuous; because the mind observes the reality of all phenomena with joy, it is serene.
This is the commentary on the text of the "Chapter on Attachment" regarding the practice of advancing based on signs. As for the "Dharma-gate":

"Peace" is named Immovability (*acala*), "Bliss" is named Non-appropriation (*anupādāna*), and "Practice" is named Non-action (*apracāra*). "Immovable" means that which cannot be moved by the six realms of birth-and-death or the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles;
since it does not take the two extremes as its object, the body is without agitation. As the preceding text says: "The body and..."
The hands and feet are tranquil and remain unmoving; the mind is constantly serene and never distracted.
Thus, one dwells securely and immovably, like the summit of Mount Sumeru, abiding in the Dharma-gate of eternal immovability.

As for "pleasure," it refers to the vast function of the Samādhi of Non-acceptance (*anupādāna*), which does not accept the five sensations (*pañca-vedanā*) of ordinary beings, nor even the five sensations within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Even the views of birth are all not accepted; where there is acceptance, there is suffering, and where there is no acceptance, there is no suffering.

Where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, this is called "Great Bliss. For one who practices nothing, if there is anything accepted, then there is something practiced; if there is no acceptance, then there is nothing practiced.
Because one does not practice the conduct of ordinary beings and does not practice the conduct of noble ones, it is said that one "practices by practicing nothing."
Because the Middle Way is thus, practicing it extensively is itself a Dharma-gate. △ Second, explaining the scriptural text in two parts: first, the question;
second, first, praising the Bodhisattvas of profound practice in the preceding chapter for being able to propagate the sutra in this manner.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
it is truly rare for these bodhisattvas to have such reverence and compliance toward the Buddha that they have made a great vow to protect, uphold, read,
and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the future evil age."
△ Second, the question regarding how a bodhisattva of shallow practice can proclaim this sutra in an evil age:
"World-Honored One, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva be able to preach this sutra in the evil age to come?"
△ Second, the response, which has three parts: first, the presentation of the fourfold topical outline; second, the explanation of the methods of practice;
third, a general clarification of the signs of successful practice.
Now, for the first part: The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the future evil age, wishes to preach this sutra..."
One should abide in four dharmas.
△ Second, the explanation of the method of practice has four parts: first, the peaceful practice of body; second, the peaceful practice of speech;
third, the peaceful practice of mind; fourth, the peaceful practice of vow. Regarding the first text, there are again two parts: first, the long prose; second, [the verse].
First, the brief indication of practicing through proximity.
First, by abiding in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of association (*sevā-vihāra*), one is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
Second, the detailed explanation of practicing through proximity. Part one: explaining the sphere of practice.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the "sphere of practice" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the ground of patience, being gentle, compliant, and harmonious, neither impetuous nor startled in mind;
furthermore, if they do not engage in any activity regarding phenomena, yet contemplate all phenomena as they truly are, and neither practice nor discriminate—this is called a bodhisattva.
This is the sphere of activity of the Mahāsattva.
Now, regarding the sphere of activity as clarified by way of three dharmas: first, there is the single object-condition, which is the single Truth (satya).

This single Truth is that to which all things return and upon which all things are based; it is pervasive and non-conceptual. That which is the "returning place" for all is the stage of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi).
"Earth" (*ti*) is precisely the Middle Way; because all dharmas return to it, it is called "earth. Because all practices come to rest within it, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

This is the practice of non-practice. That which serves as the foundation for all things is like how the myriad phenomena grow by obtaining earth, while the various practices are accomplished by obtaining the Principle (*li*). If one obtains the root of the Principle, then even amidst the firm and strong, one remains capable.
In those who are weak, one can bring about compliance; in those who are violent, one can bring about governance; in those who are startled, one can bring about peace.
From this ground of the Middle Way, immeasurable merit arises. Though merit arises, it is non-arising. When merit is pervasive and free from discrimination, one does not discriminate.
Because there is no distinction between non-action and action, it is said: "Furthermore, one neither acts nor discriminates," and so forth.
That is to say, regarding the two dharmas of "neither practicing nor not practicing," there are the two types of patience regarding arising and dharmas;
regarding the three dharmas, there are the three inconceivable truths (*triratna*). As for "dwelling on the ground of forbearance" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), this refers generally to the three truths:
if one has a ground upon which to rely, one can then practice forbearance, gentleness, and compliance; "compliance" refers specifically to the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because one is able to endure false views, craving, cold, heat, and so forth, it is said that one is "well-accommodating.

Because the mind is not impetuous and does not become startled, one is "at ease" within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because one endures the conditions of the various faculties and accords with their specific capacities, it is said that one is "not impetuous.
Because one can embody the endurance of both the adverse and the favorable, the mind does not become startled. Regarding the phrase "there is no practice of any phenomena," this means that—

Because one can truly endure the two extremes while abiding in peace, it is said that there is "no place of practice. Because one correctly dwells in the Middle Way, it is said that one "contemplates the true mark" (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, because even the Middle or the reality cannot be apprehended, it is said that one "does not discriminate. This is based on the ground of the Three Truths;

it is called "patience in abiding" (*sthiti-kṣānti*) and "practice in action" (*caryā-caryā*). It is also divided into three: namely, the practice of cessation (*śamatha-caryā*), which is itself the practice.
Not practicing contemplative cultivation is neither practicing nor not practicing; practicing compassion is likewise neither practicing nor not practicing.

To practice in accordance with one's robes, seat, chamber, and so forth—this is the method for elucidating the locus of practice by means of these three dharmas, thereby clarifying the procedure for propagating the sutra.
△ Second, the explanation of the proximate bases (upaniṣad). Part three: first, discussing the proximate by means of the remote. First, being remote from those of high status and power.
What is called the proximate base of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials.
The following section explains the "near abodes" (*upasthāna*) by clarifying that the ten afflictions (*daśa-kṣobha*) are distant; thus, it discusses the near based on what is distant.

This is also an adjunct to the gateway of the precepts (*śīla-dvāra*) that aids meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Whereas the preceding [section] directly took the principle as its object and dwelt in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), the present gateway of the precepts extensively sets forth the various conditions for humiliation that one should practice distancing oneself from.
This is not like ordinary people who merely defend themselves with blades and clubs, nor is it the same as the two [preceding stages].

One abandons and does not dwell upon them, but distances oneself from them through right wisdom; this is what is meant by "proximity" (*upaniṣad*), as it refers to being far from [evil] while being near [virtue].
First, regarding distancing oneself from power and influence: one does not associate with kings and the like.

The Record states that this is because people might rely on such connections and thereby lose the Right Path; thus, while there may seem to be a slight benefit at first, there will be great harm in the long run. △
Second is the practice of distancing oneself from those of heterodox views: not associating with various non-Buddhist brahmins, Jainas, and others, nor composing worldly writings,
nor praising external scriptures, nor following the Lokāyatikas or the Prati-Lokāyatikas.
Next, the second [category], the distant dharma of those with deviant persons, refers to those who are stained by deviant teachings and deluded regarding correct principles;

although their right contemplation has not yet been perfected, they must urgently prevent and sever [such errors]. Because they do not receive the internal teaching, they are called *bāhiraka* (outsiders) or *brahmacārī* (Brahmins);
this is translated as "Pure Conduct. Those among them who remain householders and serve Brahmā are named *brahmacārī*.
If they are non-Buddhist renunciants, they are collectively termed Nirgrantha; "Nirgrantha" here means "one who has severed ties. Regarding the terms "wen" (文) and "bi" (筆):
"wen" refers to works such as songs and poetry, while "bi" refers to genres such as inscriptions and rhapsodies. As for "praise" (*praśasti*) and "eulogy" (*geya*):

praising virtue is called "praise," while expressing one's sentiments is called "eulogy. *Lokāyata* is translated here as "evil discourse" (*kudṛṣṭi*) or "destructive discourse"; it is also called "contrary discourse."

This is the discourse on subverting one's sovereign and father; furthermore, *Lokāyata* is called a "good discourse" and also "the teacher defeating the disciple," whereas subverting *Lokāyata* is called an "evil discourse" and also "the disciple defeating the teacher. △ Third, avoiding violent and dangerous games.
Furthermore, one should not associate with those who engage in various violent games, such as boxing, wrestling, or the various performances of the *nara* (clown-actors).
Thirdly, one should distance oneself from violent games; for boxing and wrestling are indeed violent games, and the *nara*—this...
"Cloud-strength" (*baladeva*) refers to wrestling contests and also to displays of physical prowess. Furthermore, the *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"Nārāyaṇa refers to superior acrobatic performances; it is also said that one paints his body to create various transformative appearances, such as climbing poles, tumbling, and the like.
The *Ji* (Record/Notes) states: "Regarding those who engage in violent games, fearing they may become dissipated or negligent, one 'chā' (pronounced *chūjiè*) them—that is, one strikes them."
*Pū* (pronounced *báo*, or alternatively *pǔbǔ*) means to strike; it refers to a light blow. △ Fourth, regarding the distant Caṇḍālas:
furthermore, one should not associate with Caṇḍālas, nor with those who keep pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, fishermen, and those who follow other evil disciplines.
If such persons should occasionally come, one should preach the Dharma for them without harboring any expectations.
Next, the fourth distant *caṇḍāla*—*caṇḍāla* is translated here as "butcher" (*tuzhe*) and also as "fierce and blazing" (*yan chi*).
This refers to one who adorns themselves with fiercely burning evil karma. To associate with such a person causes others to lose their compassion;
they raise pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs, and engage in hunting, fishing, and trapping—all of which involve killing.
The mind is called "non-restraint" (*akuśala-saṃvara*). When such a person comes, one should skillfully preach the Dharma for them to turn their heart toward killing;
one must not harbor any expectation of gain. A hunter is so named because they clear away pests from the fields;
"hunting" (*tían*) is thus a term for swift action. The *Báihùtōng* states: "Hunting conducted during the four seasons is collectively termed 'hunting' (*liè*); 'tían' is a general term."
Regarding "hunting," the *Yì* says: "To hunt and to fish. The commentary states: "Taking wild animals is called *tián*; taking fish is called *yú*.
△ Fifth, [avoiding] those of the Two Vehicles:
Furthermore, one should not associate with or seek out *śrāvaka* bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, nor should one...
When inquiring after their well-being— whether in a room, on a walking path, or in a lecture hall— if they do not dwell together but occasionally come to visit,
one should preach the Dharma to them as appropriate, without harboring any expectations.

Next, the fifth point regarding distancing oneself from those of the Two Vehicles: because those of the Two Vehicles focus exclusively on self-benefit and are rarely able to benefit others, and because they do not aspire to the superior practice of Bodhi, one must distance oneself from them. △ Sixth, distancing oneself from thoughts of desire.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not preach the Dharma while perceiving signs in a woman’s body that could give rise to thoughts of desire,
nor should he take pleasure in seeing her. If he enters another's home, he should not converse with young girls,
virgins, widows, or the like.
Next, regarding the sixth [point], distancing oneself from thoughts of desire:

because thoughts of desire can destroy the bodhicitta, "virgins" refers to unmarried women living at home, while "widows" refers to those who have no husbands. △ Seventh, distancing oneself from impotent persons.
Furthermore, one should not associate closely with the five types of impotent persons as intimate friends.
Next, regarding the seventh [precept], one should keep those who are impotent at a distance; the record states that the impotent person disrupts the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The five types of impotent persons are: those born so, those afflicted by disease, those envious, those transformed, and those who are half-born; from birth, these individuals lack the male organ.
The *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuch) has his virility removed by means of a blade; the *paṇḍaka* (impotent) develops a mind of envy and lust only upon seeing another engage in sexual intercourse.
Regarding those who change, in this life they become [hermaphrodites], being able to act as males for half a month and unable to act as males for the other half.

Furthermore, there are five types of non-females, namely: the conch-like (*śaṅkuka*), the tendon-like (*snāyuka*), the drum-like (*muruka*), the horn-like (*vaṃśaka*), and the vein-like (*dhamanika*). Moreover, those who are not males are called *pandaka*.
"Ṭa" translates as "eunuch" (pandaka). A eunuch possesses both male and female physical characteristics but is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse with either gender.
△ Eighth, regarding the danger of being far from home:
not only when entering another's house, but even if there is a necessary reason to enter alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
Next, the eighth is "keeping far from harm," which the commentary states means one should not enter places of danger or difficulty. Ninth is "keeping far from ridicule and reproach":
if one preaches the Dharma to women, one must not smile showing one's teeth nor expose one’s chest; this applies even when doing so for the sake of the Dharma.

If one should not even maintain close intimacy with those who are distant and subject to reproach, let alone engage in other matters; and if one should avoid exposing one's teeth when smiling or revealing one's chest while preaching the Dharma to women for fear of increasing their unwholesome thoughts—
then it is not even fitting to maintain close intimacy with such persons, much less engage in other affairs.
...Indeed. △ Tenth, distancing oneself from keeping [disciples]:
one does not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or small children, nor does one delight in sharing a teacher with them.

Regarding the sequence of distancing oneself from keeping [disciples]: it is because keeping small children hinders the cultivation of the right practice; therefore, one must distance oneself [from them].
From the beginning, distancing oneself from the powerful and influential, up to this point of distancing oneself from these ten kinds of afflictions and disturbances, constitutes two extremes:
nine pertain to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and one pertains to *nirvāṇa*. To distance oneself from both is merely another name for quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
These ten dharmas are consistent across all teachings; they differ slightly from other teachings only in that they do not draw near to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
This is because those who practice the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) now propagate the uniquely wondrous sutras of the Mahayana;
therefore, they must distance themselves from those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles of the Hinayana. △ Second, discussing the near in terms of the near.
Always delighting in sitting meditation in secluded places to cultivate and collect the mind—Mañjuśrī, this is called the first stage of close approach.
Being able to distance oneself from the ten kinds of faults mentioned above is the strategy for advancing on the Path; one should therefore remain in seclusion.

Regarding "dwelling in a secluded place to cultivate concentration": once one dwells in a quiet location, far removed from all clamor and distraction, since the dust [of afflictions] has neither taken root nor found a mate, it is precisely possible to pasture the mind within and illuminate it; therefore, it is said that one "cultivates and collects the mind.
△ Third, the section on "neither near nor near" discussing proximity, which has three parts: first, a general indication of the object and wisdom.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that all dharmas are empty.
"Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way; "all dharmas" refers to the objects of the ten dharma-realms.

If one were to discuss wisdom alone, there would be no object for that wisdom to contemplate; therefore, by citing "all dharmas," it is revealed that they are all empty. △ Second, the specific [analysis].
Explaining the object and wisdom:
as it truly is, the mark of reality (lakṣaṇa) is non-erroneous, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing; like space, it is of a nature of non-existence;
all paths of language are cut off; it is unarisen, unemerged, and unoriginated; it is nameless and signless; in truth, it is utterly non-existent and without self-nature.
The measure is boundless, unimpeded, and without obstruction.

That which is called the "true aspect" (yathābhūtalakṣaṇa) refers to the two extremes and the three truths being neither one nor different; it is not named according to the seven stages of expedient means, but is truly named according to reality.
Because it takes reality as its characteristic, it is called the true aspect. To be non-erroneous means to be free from the eight inversions. Not...
"Moving" means not being moved by the two types of death. "Non-retrogressive" means that mind after mind is quiescent and extinguished, flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
"Non-turning" means not turning through birth and death like ordinary beings, nor turning between the ordinary and the holy like the followers of the Two Vehicles.
"Like empty space" means there is only a name, yet this name cannot be apprehended; this is the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Wisdom, too, exists only as a name; even when sought, it cannot be found. Its nature of non-existence means it lacks the nature of self, other, both, or causelessness.
That which is cut off from all paths of linguistic expression is inconceivable. That which is unarisen means that neither delusion nor wisdom, nor their underlying principle, arises.
That which does not emerge means that what was to be remedied by the Tathāgata has ultimately ceased to exist.
Furthermore, that which does not arise again is the quiescence of all skillful means. That which is nameless cannot be named; that which is signless cannot be characterized by signs;
that which is non-existent is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence; that which is immeasurable is not a quantifiable phenomenon;
that which is boundless has no spatial location; and that which is unimpeded and unobstructed pervades all as one.
"Everywhere" refers to all locations. Furthermore, "contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena as their true reality" indicates the essence of the contemplation.

From "not being inverted" to the ninth phrase, the characteristics of the contemplation are explained: not being moved by the two extremes or the eight inversions is called "non-inverted and non-moving";
not falling into the stages of the two vehicles or ordinary beings is called "non-retrogressive and non-reversing. This...

The second phrase clarifies that the application of wisdom through principle does not arise because it is not of the future, does not emerge because it is not of the past, and does not originate because it is not of the present.
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), fascicle 51, states: "Just as space has no entering, no emerging, and no abiding, etc., so too is the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
there is no place of entry in the future, no place of emergence in the past, and no [place of abiding]."
The forty-third current dwelling states: "Because it does not arise from conditions, it is called 'not emerging';
because it does not arise from boundaries, it is called 'unborn'. This is the proof. △ Third, the conclusion.
Because that which exists arises from causes and conditions and from inversion, one should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena;
this is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The preceding section clarified the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way; here we clarify the simultaneous illumination of both extremes.

The principle of nature is ultimately pure, as previously stated: it is neither liberation nor delusion, yet from the conditions of delusion, birth and death arise, and from the conditions of liberation, nirvana arises.
Furthermore, that which exists through causes and conditions exists within nirvana. That which arises from inversion...
"Born within birth-and-death" here reveals the meaning of the twofold illumination; "constantly contemplating such dharmic characteristics" refers to the dharmas of the three truths in equality.
Furthermore, the phrase "merely existing through causes and conditions, arising from inversion" concludes the inconceivable realm of the three truths.
Therefore, "speaking" refers to the inconceivable teaching, and "constantly contemplating" concludes [the practice].
This is the inconceivable threefold contemplation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
Part Two: Verses in Praise; Section Three: First, the verses praising the headings.

If there is a bodhisattva who, in the future evil age, desires to preach this sutra with a mind free from fear—referring to the aforementioned desire to preach this sutra, one should abide in four dharmas;

because by abiding in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), the mind is not startled or terrified, it is said to be "a mind free from fear. Now, the following verses provide a detailed explanation of the prose passage.
The combination of verses and their expansion appear alternately. △ Second, the verses on the practice of cultivation, part one: verses on the distance and proximity of objects.

One should enter the spheres of practice and those of association, while always remaining far from kings, princes, ministers, high officials, those who engage in violent games, caṇḍālas, non-Buddhists, and brahmins; nor should one associate with those of overweening pride.

One must not associate with those who are greedily attached to the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna, bhikṣus who have broken the precepts yet bear the name of "Arhats," bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter,
upāsikās who are deeply attached to the five desires and seek parinirvāṇa in this present life— none of these should be approached.
If such persons should come to the Bodhisattva with a sincere heart for the sake of hearing the Buddha-way, the Bodhisattva then...
With a mind free from fear and without harboring expectations, one should preach the Dharma.
One must not associate with or form intimate bonds with widows, virgins, or those of indeterminate gender;
nor should one associate with butchers, executioners, hunters, fishermen, or those who kill for profit, sell meat for a living, or traffic in women. One must not associate with any such persons.
Do not associate with those who engage in the violent sport of sumo wrestling, nor with various kinds of entertainers or prostitutes.
Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place; if you must preach the Dharma, do so without jesting or laughter. When entering a village to beg for alms, take a companion bhikṣu;

if there is no companion, remain single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha. These two—[the aforementioned] sphere of activity and the sphere of proximity—are what is meant by "the sphere of activity and the sphere of proximity."
This can be explained with ease.
Regarding these fourteen verses, the matters of the "far" and "near," and the "superior" and "long" found in the prose [commentary], consist of ten types of abandonments;

these are now omitted in this verse for brevity, as they can be seen in the text. Furthermore, these verses capture the essential meaning of the practices for purifying the person (pudgala-śuddhi) and are intended to supplement the preceding verses.
Because there are three reasons regarding proximity, the verse says: "This is called the sphere of activity; one who is close by must always distance himself from kings. Therefore, the Buddha said:

1. Poisonous ministers contend with one another; 2. Seven and two kingdoms wage war against each other; 3. The king is stingy and does not bestow gifts upon the people;

To slander a bhikṣu in this way is to slander the Dharma and to slander the Buddha. Therefore, the Buddha [forbade it].
He did not allow non-Buddhist brahmins who had attained the *māṇḍalika*—the first person was named Brahmā, who created one *veda*;

The verses, when compiled together, total one million two hundred and eighty thousand verses in seventeen hundred fascicles.
Next came Puṣya, who had twenty-five disciples; each was able to extensively analyze one of the Vedas, resulting in twenty-five Vedas.

In this manner, they were further transformed into one thousand two hundred and six Vedas. This Veda-śāstra is here called the *Jñāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Knowledge).
It was composed by Vyāsa and consists of four types: first, the *Śruti-bala-veda*, which clarifies the ritual worship of fire and the extinction of sin; second, the *Yajur-veda*... [text truncated].
The *Veda* (Vidyā) is the knowledge for making offerings to Brahmins and attaining merit; the *Sāmaveda* (Trisāmaveda) is the knowledge for harmonizing two kingdoms;
the *Atharvaveda* (Ātharvaṇaveda) is the knowledge for waging war. One who studies these four treatises claims to be omniscient (*sarvajña*).
The *Vyākaraṇa* (Vyākara) is called the "Treatise on Grammar" (*śabdavidyā*); Pāṇini composed it, as well as various scriptures and other works.

The *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Grammar), composed by Uruka; translated here as "Most Victorious" (*parama-jaya*). Eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he elucidated the six principles (*ṣaṭ-tattva*).
Kāpila is translated here as "Yellow-Headed" (*pīta-śiras*) and is also known as "Turtle-Lineage" (*kūrma-gotra*).
He composed a treatise named *Sāṃkhya*. *Sāṃkhya* means "without a summit" (*anuttama*); because the treatise is named after its founder, it is called Kāpila, who taught the twenty-five [principles].
Those who cling to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and study the Tripiṭaka [should know that]:

and when the Buddha was at the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, he first taught the Abhidharma Piṭaka to the son of the Vṛji.
In the Abhidharma-piṭaka, five hundred Arhats assembled during the first watch of the night to compile the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* and the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*;

this constitutes the study of the Three Piṭakas. Those who are deeply attached to the five desires and perceive the characteristics of desire—including the inhabitants of the four continents, the Nāgas, the Cakravartins, and the Four Heavenly Kings—all have their faculties reach as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they take the wind as their activity; [this extends further to] the Yāma Heaven.

In the Tuṣita Heaven, they engage in affairs by drawing near one another; in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, they engage in affairs by holding hands; in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, they engage in affairs by looking at one another;
and in the higher heavens, they engage in affairs through mental intention alone. As for those who have abandoned desire—widows, spinsters, and virgins—Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, how should one regard women? The Buddha said: "Do not look upon them. Even if you should see them," [do not speak with them].
Do not converse with them; if you must converse, do so with single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha. Regarding those who enter villages to beg for alms, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
"There was once a sheep that went to a dung heap, ate its fill, and returned to the flock with pride, saying, 'I have obtained excellent food.
Monks are just like this: having received the four requisites, they give rise to thoughts of attachment and desire, and do not know the way of escape. If they do not... [the text continues].

One who constantly harbors conceited thoughts, and upon receiving alms from the bhikṣus, treats others with arrogance and contempt, thinking, "I have attained this while they have not," is a sheep-like bhikṣu.
A lion king, when encountering a large beast, devours it without savoring its taste or becoming attached;
when encountering a small beast, it devours it without disdain or disparagement. The bhikṣu is also like this regarding the attainment of the four [dhyānas].
Regarding material offerings, he does not give rise to defiled attachment nor harbor thoughts of desire; he knows for himself the path to liberation.

Even if he does not obtain gain or support, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts, maintaining a mind free from increase or decrease. This is the practice of the Lion King Bhikṣu regarding alms-gathering.

Regarding the four matters—alms-gathering, walking, labor, and illness—there are eight periods before and after each. These clarify the eight types of diligence and the eight types of indolence concerning alms-gathering.

Previously, one forms this thought: "In order to cultivate the Path and mend the wounds of hunger, I shall beg for food. Although one has not yet obtained it, one does not cease the mindful practice of begging;

once it has been obtained, one maintains the thought of repaying its kindness and does not interrupt the cultivation of the Path. During both the preceding and succeeding periods, one redoubles one's diligence;
the same applies to the other three matters before and after. To act contrary to this is called the eight kinds of indolence. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* clarifies the practice of begging for food.
One-fourth [of the food] is offered to fellow practitioners of the holy life; one-fourth is given to beggars; one-fourth is bestowed upon spirits and deities;
and one-fourth is consumed by oneself. △ Second, the verse on being neither far nor near.
Furthermore, not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, nor conditioned or unconditioned, real or unreal dharmas;
not discriminating between male and female; not attaining any dharmas, and neither knowing nor seeing them—this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
That all dharmas are empty and non-existent, that there is no permanence, and that there is neither arising nor ceasing—this is called the wise one.
Regarding the places one frequents, one should discern through inversion that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal, neither arising nor non-arising.
Abiding in a secluded place, one cultivates the gathering of the mind, remaining as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
One contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, like empty space, lacking solidity, neither arising nor emerging, neither moving nor receding.
"Abiding eternally in a single characteristic is called the 'place of proximity'.

"There is no timidity.

This one line and a half marks the completion of the practice; when the practice is accomplished, the external demeanor does not fail, and when the principle is accomplished, the internal mind has no obstructions;
therefore, it is said that "there is no timidity. △ Second, the explanation.
At times, the bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber and, with right mindfulness, contemplates the Dharma according to its meaning.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he teaches and expounds this sutra for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others;
his mind is peaceful and secure, free from any timidity or weakness.

These three lines explain the cause of peace and happiness (*sukha*). By practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one ceases transgressions and evils, thereby attaining the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
externally, one does not suffer harm. By practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one is free from all attachments, thereby attaining the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*);
internally, there is no inversion. Thus, the mind is not timid or weak; therefore, it is called "peaceful and happy. △ Third, the conclusion.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the first dharma in which a bodhisattva dwells securely so that they are able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future ages.
This single line and two phrases of verse summarize the preceding prose. △ Second, the peace and happiness of speech, in two parts: first, the prose;

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the period of the Final Dharma, those who wish to preach this sutra should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Abiding.

Whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of persons or of the scriptures.

From the outset, one who does not take pleasure in speaking of a person's good or evil qualities or the faults of the scriptures will find that when others listen, there may be evil [consequences]. What fault is there in the scriptures?

One must know that the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are the Buddha’s words spoken according to the intentions of others; they are called "provisional meaning" (*neyārtha*). If one were to criticize them...
The method [of such practice] would distress that person; it is not a state of peaceful and blissful conduct. △ Second, not being arrogant:
one also does not look down upon other Dharma masters.
"Not being arrogant" means not relying on the Perfect [teachings] to despise the Partial, nor valuing the Real while disparaging the Provisional. △ Third, not...
He neither praises nor disparages others; he does not speak of the good or evil, the long or the short regarding other śrāvakas, nor does he mention their names to speak of their faults or evils,
nor does he mention their names to praise their virtues.
One who does not speak of the long and short of others never speaks of people in general, nor does he single out individuals;

specifically regarding śrāvakas, since all people loathe hearing of their faults, one does not discuss their shortcomings. Because praising someone to their face implies disparaging them behind their back, one does not extol their virtues either.
Furthermore, one does not discuss the length of Zhang or Zhao, fearing that Zhao might think one is using another's length to mock one's own shortness, or that one is merely using it as a pretext.
He recites this [verse] as well, yet he does not speak of Zhang’s excellence or Zhao’s shortcomings, fearing that others might say of him:
"Since you have already slandered them behind their backs, you will surely slander me as well. For this reason, neither good nor evil should be discussed;

furthermore, one who does not speak of long or short is foremost in the *Rizang* (Treasury of the Sun), for it says: "In the first, middle, and last watches of the night, diminish sleep and apply yourself with diligence."
Advancing in seated meditation, reciting the sutras, and cultivating the Way, they turn their backs on birth and death and head toward the path of Nirvana;
they do not speak of the shortcomings of others nor the virtues of themselves, remaining humble and modest without self-conceit or arrogance;

content with whatever food and clothing they receive, they practice the dhūta austerities with diligence and heedfulness, maintaining mindfulness and reflection so that the mind does not wander, and they give rise [to compassion] toward all sentient beings.

The mind of compassion is further as described in the sūtras: one should personally recite and teach others to recite the *Kārikās*, not disparage others, not speak of their faults, and not boast of one's own virtues.

Regarding śrāvakas whose faculties are indeterminate, if one praises the two vehicles, it may cause them to regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small; if one disparages the two vehicles, it may cause them to fall into the Small.
"Great loss" refers to the absence of both [subject and object] that can be grasped. △ Fourth, being free from resentment and aversion:

This means that what is called "base and inferior" is precisely the mind of aversion; as soon as the mental faculty stirs, verbal expression arises, which is the source of obstructing the path and transgressing the precepts.
Therefore, one should not give rise to resentment or aversion. △ Second, the contemplation of practice.
Because they have well cultivated such a mind of peace and happiness, all who listen do not oppose their intentions;

To cultivate well such [practices] as these is the gate of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). It consists of contemplating that all phenomena are empty and that there is nothing to be grasped or attached to;
not holding fast with a parsimonious mind, not opposing the intentions of others, and not contravening the characteristics of dharmas.

To answer not with the teachings of the Hīnayāna but only with those of the Mahāyāna—should one perceive a lack of great capacity [in a listener] and yet speak of the Lesser Vehicle, one thereby gains the benefit of skillful means. If...

Simply focus the mind with single-mindedness on the causes and conditions for expounding the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and causing all beings to do likewise;

the mind is free from envy, anger, and various afflictive obstructions, nor is there sorrow, abuse, or fear.

The wise person who thus skillfully cultivates the mind can abide in peace and happiness as I have explained above.

First, freedom from envy and flattery: One should not harbor a mind of jealousy, flattery, or deception.
Now, while those of the Two Vehicles seek to quickly emerge from birth and death by first eliminating desire, Bodhisattvas eliminate only anger, views, and envy.
This defilement of anger is a stain upon deceit; this defilement of views is jealousy. To violate the mind of compassion is not the method for transforming others;
to be deceitful and fraudulent is to deviate from the path of wisdom and is not the method for one's own practice. Since wisdom will be obstructed, how can one seek the higher?
Since compassion will be hindered, how can one transform those below? A Bodhisattva practicing the Course of Ease and Bliss must resolutely abandon these.
△ Second, do not treat others with contempt or revile them.

one should not use the practices of the Perfect Teaching (En) to revile those of the Distinct Teaching (Betsu), as their capacities are knowable. If they are ignorant, one should simply refrain from reproaching them.

"You are very far from the Way and will ultimately never attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this?
Because you are a person of negligence and are indolent regarding the Way.

If a bhikṣu is of inferior capacity, one should not reprimand him with the Perfect Teaching; for although he lacks the fundamental great potential, one should not forcibly apply the Perfect Teaching to him.

The path becomes circuitous and is said to be extremely remote. This affliction specifically affects those who practice the Individual Vehicle (Pratyekabuddha-yāna), who sink into emptiness and grasp at realization, termed "not attaining this.

This clarifies the two objects of compassion and loving-kindness (*maitrī-karuṇā*). First, regarding the object of the vow of loving-kindness:

it universally includes those who have previously aroused the mind of skillful means but have not yet transcended the triple world, termed "lay," as well as those who have exhausted all pervasive delusions, termed "renunciant.

This encompasses both the Two Vehicles of the two teachings and the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings; since these groups all possess ignorance (*avidyā*), they should also be the objects of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because those who have previously aroused the universal small mind must accord with the vow of compassion and grant them the bliss of the perfect path and perfect fruit, it is said that they give rise to the mind of great compassion. △ Second, the object of the vow of compassion.
One gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward those who are not bodhisattvas.
Regarding the objects of this compassion: "those who are not bodhisattvas" refers generally to those who have not yet generated the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*).

This includes all such individuals, let alone those who have never turned toward skillful means at all, much less those who possess it truly. This object of compassion encompasses all three types of beings.

Regarding those within the realm [of sentient beings], these too must be granted happiness; however, because their cyclic existence is boundless, it is precisely in accordance with the vow of compassion that one should uproot the causes and effects of their suffering—this is why it is said that "the mind of great compassion arises.
△ Second, the reasons for making the vow, which has two parts. First, the reasons for giving rise to the vow of loving-kindness.
One should reflect thus: "Such a person has suffered a great loss regarding the Tathāgata’s skillful means of preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
From this reflection, one should cease [criticizing] the preaching according to what is appropriate; this is the basis for giving rise to a compassionate vow.
Because they delight in the Lesser Vehicle, they cling to the Buddha’s skillful means as being ultimate reality and fail to realize the Perfect Path; therefore, it is said that their loss is great.
This is the reason for losing the vow of compassion. △ Second, the reason for giving rise to the vow of pity (*karuṇā*).
"Not hearing, not knowing, not perceiving, not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding.

Following this, "not hearing, not knowing" and so forth are the reasons for losing the vow of pity; because the mind of the partial or the perfect has not yet been aroused, one does not hear [the Dharma].
Because there are two paths—the partial and the perfect—those who do not hear the partial path lack the wisdom of hearing;
those who do not know it lack the wisdom of reflection; and those who do not awaken to it lack the wisdom of cultivation. Furthermore, they lack the three wisdoms of the perfect path. Why?

Because they do not inquire, they do not hear, they do not believe, they do not know, they do not understand, and they do not cultivate. Thus, both the provisional and the real aspects of the three wisdoms of the partial and perfect paths are entirely absent; this is truly lamentable.
It is precisely here that the cause for giving rise to compassion through pity lies. △ Third, the formal establishment of the vow:

"Even if such persons do not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, wherever they may be, I shall lead them by means of my supernatural powers and the power of wisdom, causing them to abide in this [sutra]."
Within the Dharma, this correctly clarifies the vow: although they do not inquire or believe in the two paths of the partial and the perfect, the Bodhisattva does not make a vow based on the partial;
rather, because he desires to bestow upon them the three types of wisdom of the perfect path, it is said that "although they do not inquire or believe."

After I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall lead them to enter [this path]. Furthermore, the vows, *bodhi*-wisdom, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are all obtained through the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-caryā*).
Why is this? Because by deeply contemplating the Tathāgata’s seat, one obtains the power of wisdom;

adorned with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one is able to extract [beings] by means of wisdom. This is because of deeply contemplating the Tathāgata’s dwelling and the Tathāgata’s robe.

Therefore, having attained the power of great quiescence, he manifests various majestic demeanors, supernatural powers, and the adornments of merit while remaining in the meditative concentration of non-arising and non-extinction;
he first moves by means of samādhi. △ Third, the conclusion in three parts: first, a general summary that there is no fault.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this fourth dharma after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
there will be no fault when they preach this dharma.
This concludes the summary of being free from fault. Since there are no faults, how is the practice of conduct accomplished?

It is accomplished by virtue of having established the great vow; the practice of entering the Tathāgata’s chamber is accomplished by virtue of knowing the deficiencies of the fourfold assembly regarding the perfect path;
and the Tathāgata’s robe is accomplished by virtue of vowing to restrain the mind so that it does not become indolent.

Because the three practices are accomplished and fully established, it is said that the accomplishment of practice is free from fault. Because compassion is accomplished, there is no fault of the stain of anger;
because the Tathāgata’s robe is accomplished, there is no fault of indolence; because the Tathāgata’s seat is accomplished, there is no fault of flattery and crookedness.
△ Second, the specific conclusion regarding the accomplishment of the practice of compassion.

He is constantly honored, revered, respected, and praised by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others; even the devas of the void always attend upon him as his followers in order to hear the Dharma.
Whether he is in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, if there are people who come to him...
Those who wish to pose difficult questions are constantly guarded day and night by the devas for the sake of the Dharma, enabling all listeners to attain joy.

This concludes the distinct section on the accomplishment of the practice of loving-kindness and compassion; because it is accomplished through loving-kindness and compassion, one gains the offerings of the fourfold assembly, humans, and devas.
Because the vow to cultivate and listen to the Dharma has been fulfilled, the Buddha’s supernormal powers are manifested and the devas provide protection;
because the Tathāgata’s seat has been established, those who listen are filled with joy. △ Third, the explanation of the fulfillment of the practice of vows.
Why is this so? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
This explains that since even the Buddhas of the three periods of time protect it when their vows and practices are fulfilled, how much more so the devas? △
Second, praising the difficulty of hearing the sutra. Part one: the explanation by way of Dharma. First, because it was not previously revealed, it could not be obtained in the past.
Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* could not be heard.
This sutra is truly the great principle for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and the secret essence of all Buddhas;

thus, for more than forty years, it was kept secret and not spoken of, like a lotus flower closed and yet unopened, so that throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust and grains of sand, its name could not be heard. △ Second, "Today, at last, it is obtained."
How much more so for those who have actually seen it, received, upheld, read, and recited it?
Now that it has been revealed and made manifest, having obtained the opportunity to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, would one not surely regard this as a rare encounter?

△ Second, the illustrative explanation has two parts: first, the analogy of not giving the jewel, which illustrates how it was not previously revealed; second, the initial opening of the analogy, which has six parts. First:
He subdues all nations.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King who desires to bring all nations under his authority through his majestic power.
The text contains six points, which can be seen by examining the sections; first, the Wheel-Turning King is likened to the Tathāgata transforming the world and subduing all [beings].
The kingdom is a metaphor for the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), bases (āyatanas), and all objective spheres.

Second, "the petty kings do not obey": the various petty kings who do not comply with his commands represent the afflictions (kleśas) and so forth that have not yet attained the discipline of outflow-free wisdom (anāsrava); thus they are said to "not obey his commands."
Third, he raises an army and goes forth to wage war.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various kinds of troops and proceeds to subdue the enemy.
The raising of these various troops is analogous to the methods of the Seven Sages serving as the vanguard; among them, the *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* constitute the foremost ranks.
The method is as follows: the middle army, which consists of the Arhats, is that which breaks the rear army;

those who are able to destroy the eighty-four thousand thieves of affliction (*kleśa*), such as the three poisons, are the officers and soldiers of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates. △ Fourth, rejoicing in merit.
When the king sees that his troops have performed meritorious service in battle, he immediately feels great joy.
From the four attendants down to the common soldiers, they likewise feel joy upon seeing the merit achieved. △ Fifth, the bestowing of rewards according to merit.
According to their merit, they were rewarded with fields, houses, villages, and cities; or with clothing and articles for adorning the body;
or with various kinds of rare treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, chariots, and male and female slaves.
The five types of rewards bestowed according to merit are as follows: the fields are *samādhi*; the residences are the accumulation of wisdom; the villages are the first and second fruits (*phala*);
the towns are the third fruit; and the city is *nirvāṇa*. The clothing consists of the wholesome dharmas of shame and patience, which are the ornaments for adorning the body;
the auxiliary dharmas of the path are the various kinds of seven treasures, such as the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), elephants, horses, and chariots.
The two vehicles—the wisdom of exhaustion and the wisdom of non-arising—are like the servants; the supernormal powers are like the common people;
and the wholesome dharmas with outflows are like the subjects.
△ Sixth, [the father] does not give him the jewel. Why? Because the single bright pearl in the topknot is kept for himself alone.
If one were to give this jewel to the king and his retinue, they would surely be greatly astonished and amazed.

The sixth [case]—where the jewel is kept only in the topknot—is like not giving the jewel at all; this is a metaphor for those whose capacity has emerged from the realm of分段 (paryāya-bheda) and achieved minor merit, and those whose capacity has emerged from the realm of 變易 (pariṇāma-vikāra) and achieved great merit. As for "astonishment and amazement," it refers to having no great merit yet suddenly [receiving such a reward].

When the topknot jewel was bestowed, all the ministers were filled with doubt and wonder; this is like sentient beings whose great capacity has not yet been stirred suddenly hearing this sutra, causing those of the Two Vehicles to be perplexed and the Bodhisattvas to be struck with amazement.
△ Second, the combined analogy in six parts: first, combining the subduing of the various kingdoms through majestic power.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is likewise; by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the Dharma-realm and reigns as king over the three realms.
Each of these six analogies corresponds exactly to the text. △ Second, the analogy of the minor kings who do not submit.
Yet the various Māra kings were unwilling to submit.
△ Third, they mobilized their armies to go forth and wage war;
the Tathāgata’s worthy and holy generals fought against them.
4. Rejoicing together in merit;
those who possess merit also rejoice in their hearts.
5. Bestowing rewards in accordance with merit.
Within the fourfold assembly, he preached various sutras to gladden their hearts, bestowing upon them the wealth of the dharmas of dhyāna,
liberation, the untainted faculties and powers, and further granting them the city of nirvāṇa, saying they had attained extinction;
thus he guided their minds, causing them all to rejoice.
△ Although he traveled through the six directions, he did not give him the jewel;
nor did he preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him.
△ Second, the analogy of giving the jewel illustrates what is heard today. Part one: Opening the analogy. Part two: Having great merit.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have achieved great merit, feels profound joy.
This passage has two meanings: first, from "Mañjuśrī" downwards, it indicates that [the bodhisattvas] have immediately achieved great merit; second, it concerns the bestowing of the jewel.
Because this pearl, so difficult to believe in, had long resided within the topknot and was not recklessly given to others, it is now bestowed upon you.
Regarding "difficult to believe" below: the pearl being in the crown signifies that which is venerated as the ultimate fruit;

its being within the topknot signifies that it was truly concealed by the provisional. Untying the topknot is the opening of the provisional; bestowing the pearl is the revelation of the real. △ Second.
The first of the three applications of the analogy concerns having great merit.
The Tathāgata is likewise so: within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King who teaches and transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma;
seeing the army of the noble ones engaged in battle with the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, he achieves great merit.
When his merits extinguish the three poisons, he emerges from the triple world and shatters the net of Māra; at that time, the Tathāgata also rejoices greatly.
△ Second, the bestowing of the jewel:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), yet it is met with many enmities and is difficult for the world to believe.
That which was not previously spoken, I shall now speak: Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas;

among all teachings, it is the most profound. It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king, having long guarded a precious jewel, finally grants it to another. Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* belongs to all Buddhas.
The secret treasury of the Tathāgata stands supreme among all sutras;
having been guarded throughout the long night and not recklessly proclaimed, it is only today that I shall expound it for you.
To enable sentient beings to reach the wisdom of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) is the fruit; this is called the "one-ness of practice.
This teaching is the "one secret treasury," which is the "one-ness of principle" and simultaneously encompasses the "one-ness of attainment."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
△ Second, the verses in praise [of the two]; first, the verses on the methods of practice; first, skipping ahead to praise the accomplishment of practice.
Only by constantly practicing patience and showing compassion for all beings can one expound the sūtras praised by the Buddha.
This single line of verse summarizes the accomplishment of practice; whereas the preceding section explained the accomplishment of practice in general, this verse now specifically reveals it.

"Constantly practicing patience" refers to the accomplishment of the practice of donning the robes; "showing compassion for all beings" refers to the accomplishment of the practice of entering the chamber. Now...
