△ 2. The reason for the vow:
It would be a great loss if these people were not to hear or believe this sutra.
△ 3. The formal establishment of the vow.
When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall employ various skillful means to preach this Dharma for them, so that they may abide within it.

△ Second, the verse praising the sutra has two parts: first, the verse illustrating the analogy; second, the verse on the analogy of not giving the jewel. First, the verse on the analogy of not giving the jewel.
For example, when a powerful wheel-turning monarch has achieved merit in battle, he joyfully bestows various rewards:

elephants, horses, chariots, ornaments for the body, as well as fields, houses, villages, and cities; or he grants clothing, various kinds of rare jewels, male and female slaves, and wealth and goods.
△ Second, the verse on the analogy of the jewel.
It is like a king who, being brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, unties the bright pearl from his topknot and bestows it upon him.
△ Second, the verse combining the analogy. First, the verse combining the analogy of not giving the jewel.
The Tathāgata is likewise the King of all Dharmas; possessing the great power of patience and the treasure-store of wisdom, he transforms the world according to the Dharma through great compassion.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and desiring liberation, he engages in battle with the Māras and, for the sake of these sentient beings, preaches various teachings.
By means of great skillful expedients, he expounds these sūtras.
△ Second, the verse combines this with the analogy of the jewel.

Having known that sentient beings have already obtained its power, he finally preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra for them—just as a king unties the bright jewel from his topknot to give it away.
This sutra is the most honored, the highest among all sutras; I constantly guard it and do not reveal it recklessly.
Now is the very time for me to speak this for you all.
△ Third, a summary of the signs of accomplishment resulting from practice, exhorting one to cultivate the path. This has three parts: first, the summary and exhortation; second, the four practices.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way and wish to attain tranquility while expounding this sutra should personally cultivate these four dharmas. △ Second,
citing the three retributions to provide exhortation— also called the purification of the three obstacles— first, the transformation of the obstacle of retribution.
Regarding present retribution:
those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, as well as free from illness; their complexion will be bright and pure.

As the three obstructions are purified and transformed, and evil karma from both the present life and future lives is exhausted, they shall immediately obtain superior retribution in both the present and future lives.
For those who first read this sutra, this single practice extinguishes the afflictions of the present life, thereby eliminating the retribution of painful sensations;

this is the transformation of the mind of present retribution. The absence of illness and pain is the transformation of the physical form of present retribution. △ Second, the transformation of karmic obstructions, which transforms the retribution of future births.
One will not be born into poverty, low status, or ugliness.

Second, regarding the phrase "not being born into poverty" and the subsequent line concerning the transformation of evil karma: while an evil karmic cause should normally result in an evil fruit, through the power of the sutra, that evil cause is transformed so as to yield a good fruit;
this refers to the transformation of the retribution to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*). As for the term "not being born": it means...

By not performing unwholesome deeds in the present life while upholding this sutra, one does not create the karma for poverty, and thus will not be born into a lowly or inferior state in future lives.

△ Third, the transformation of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the subsequent retribution, in two parts: first, the specific explanation of the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances;
third, the specific explanation of the transformation of the hindrance of greed.
Sentient beings delight in seeing [him], longing for him as they do for noble sages; the various celestial youths serve as his attendants.

These three lines specifically clarify the transformation of the three obstacles. First, "sentient beings delight in seeing" and so forth—this one line specifically clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of greed (*rāga*).
Those with excessive desire are then treated with contempt by others; furthermore, because the obstacle of desire prevents birth in the Brahma-heavens, this obstacle is transformed. Therefore...
One will delight in having celestial youths as attendants. △ Second, specifically clarifying the transformation of the obstacle of anger:
Weapons and staves cannot be applied, and poisons cannot cause harm; if someone reviles one with evil words, the mouth [of the reviler] shall be closed;
one wanders without fear, like a lion king.
Next, one line and a half beginning with "swords and staves are not applied" separately clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of anger;

by transforming and abandoning anger, one removes the internal sword-arrows, so that when entering battle, external blades do not wound. △ Third, the separate clarification of the transformation of the obstacle of ignorance.
The radiance of wisdom shines like the sun.
Regarding the second half of the third section on the radiance of wisdom, it specifically clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of ignorance.
△ Second, a general clarification of the transformation of all afflictive obstacles: first, entering the ten stages of faith in a dream.
If, within a dream, one sees only auspicious things— seeing all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones, surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus as they preach the Dharma;
and seeing nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, respectfully joining their palms,
while one sees oneself preaching the Dharma to them.
This generally clarifies that the transformation of all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is likewise a transformation of future retribution (*paścād-vipāka*).
However, one should know that the present manifestations resulting from upholding this sutra are signs that have long been accomplished in the past, merely being triggered now by present conditions.
Furthermore, since the characteristics of the causes and effects of attaining Buddhahood and so forth are all future retributions, one perceives within dreams the signs of these future retributions.

The events of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are contained within a single thought-moment; this dream-like manifestation serves to illustrate the inconceivable nature of the wondrous Dharma.
Within the one there is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable there is the one; these signs appear before us, and the future fruition shall surely be realized.

Thus, beginning with the arousal of confident faith and culminating in wondrous enlightenment, the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight marks is entirely the adornment of the Tathāgata, which is itself self-adornment.
This is the retribution for patience. Furthermore, regarding the current three lines on dreaming of entering the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), they are divided into two meanings:

the first two and a half lines concern the retribution for compassion (*maitrī*) and kindness (*karuṇā*); the subsequent half line clarifies the retribution for right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and freedom from delusion (*amoha*). △ Second, dreaming of entering the ten abodes (*vihāra*).
Furthermore, he saw the bodies of all Buddhas, golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminated everything, as they expounded all dharmas with Brahma-sounds.
These Buddhas were teaching the unsurpassed Dharma to the fourfold assembly; seeing himself standing amidst them, he joined his palms in praise of the Buddhas.
Hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and made offerings to them, attaining *dhāraṇī* and realizing non-retrogressive wisdom. The Buddhas knew his mind.

"Having deeply entered the Buddha-way, you shall receive the prediction of attaining supreme perfect enlightenment. O son of good family, in a future age you shall attain the Great Way of the Buddha Immeasurable Wisdom;
your buddha-field will be adorned and pure, vast and beyond compare, and there shall also be the fourfold assembly with palms joined, listening to the Dharma."

Since it is said that realizing non-retrogressive wisdom constitutes being granted a prediction [of enlightenment], one should know that this refers to attaining the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), where one receives the prediction through the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
△ Third, dreaming of practicing the ten practices (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Furthermore, one sees oneself practicing wholesome dharmas within mountain forests;
furthermore, one sees oneself within mountain forests knowing these ten practices and cultivating wholesome dharmas. △ Fourth, the dream-awakening of the Ten Dedications.
To realize all true marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

To realize all true marks is to know that this is the stage of the Middle Way within the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). △ Fifth, dreaming of entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Entering deeply into meditative concentration, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Entering deeply into meditative concentration refers to the stainless samādhi within the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), wherein one enters the adamantine concentration (*vajra-samādhi*) and all Buddhas appear to confer empowerment by touching the crown of the head. △ Sixth: Dreaming of Entering Wondrous Enlightenment.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color and adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings; hearing the Dharma and preaching it for others, one constantly has such auspicious dreams.

Furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king, abandoning the palace, the retinue, and the most exquisite five desires, proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), sitting upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, seeking the Way for more than seven days, and attaining the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained the unsurpassed path, he shall arise and turn the wheel of Dharma, preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas;
he shall preach the subtle Dharma free from outflows to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, and thereafter he shall enter nirvāṇa, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended.
Dreaming of the Buddha in his eight aspects signifies that one knows the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

herein, this may refer to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*) where one is capable of attaining Buddhahood through the eight aspects, which is merely a provisional discourse on the ultimate fruit based upon the preceding stages.

Furthermore, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is to attain firm and unshakable faith within the Three Jewels such that nothing can destroy it; the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) is to attain the four right efforts (*catvāri samyak-prahāṇāni*).

Furthermore, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is the diligent cultivation of the skillful means of the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) to subdue craving and attachment.

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is the attainment of the four dhyānas. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the understanding of the principle of the Four Noble Truths and knowing them as they truly are.
Moreover, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is the pure faith attained by generating the bodhicitta in the presence of the Tathāgata. As for the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), it is—
The diligence initiated by the resolve of the Tathāgata; the faculty of mindfulness is the mindfulness initiated by the Tathāgata’s resolve;
the faculty of concentration is the samādhi initiated by the Tathāgata; and the faculty of wisdom is the wisdom initiated by the Tathāgata.
The Eightfold Right Path is the way of the śramaṇa and it is also the dharma of the śramaṇa. Up to...
If one achieves the exhaustion of all afflictions such as greed and hatred, this is the meaning of being a śramaṇa; the four fruits are the fruits of the śramaṇa.

As for dreams, everyone from the srotāpanna up to the pratyekabuddha has dreams, but only the Buddha does not dream, because he is free from doubt and possesses no residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā). One has dreams due to five causes, as the verse says: "Because of doubt..."
The mind discriminates based on five factors: learning, causes, present events, non-humans coming to speak with one, and dreams;
furthermore, there are things previously experienced through hearing or seeing, as well as various afflictions—due to these seven factors, dreams occur. Question:
Since the present mental consciousness does not yet perceive forms, how can the mental stage (manobhūmi) perceive forms within a dream? Answer: These are all things previously seen or heard.

Therefore, it is merely a mental construction, and it is simply a sign of good or bad fortune. Since there is no supernormal power (*abhijñā*) or knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) within a dream, how can one see the affairs of future lives?
Answer: This is not the domain of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*); rather, it is known through inference (*anumāna*).
Because people have previously had such dreams and experienced such results, one now infers [the future] based upon this. Question: Who [infers this]?

Question: Are there states of sleep (*middha*) in all five realms of existence as well as in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? Even those in the womb whose sense faculties are complete possess sleep; even the Buddha possesses sleep. Question:
Sleep is both delusion (*moha*) and an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*); how is this to be reconciled? Answer:

Even when the Buddha sleeps, it is because he wishes to adjust his body in the present moment. Thus, this sleep is neither an obscuration nor a delusion. △ Third, the summary of the completion of practice.
If, in the evil world of the future, one speaks of this supreme Dharma, that person will obtain great benefit and the various merits mentioned above.
In the evil world of the future, now is precisely the time; this sutra alone is honored as the Supreme Dharma, and those who propagate it shall receive benefits as fully elucidated previously.
△ Second, regarding the Root Chapter, there are three parts: first, the opening of the near to reveal the far; second, the introductory section; third, the main body of the teaching;
fourth, the dissemination section. Within the first [the introductory section], there are two parts: first, stating the title of the chapter.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: "The Emergence from the Earth.

With teachers revered and the Way honored, they personally attend to the single command of the Tathāgata, surging forth from the four quarters. This is an explanation according to the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) perspective.
The transformative path of the three periods of time brings boundless benefit; like the single moon reflected in ten thousand waters, who could [fail to perceive it]?

To contemplate the past and manifest it to the present, thereby propagating the sutra for the benefit of the future—this is an explanation according to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint of benefiting people).
The void is serene, without "early" or "late"; yet those who are deluded cling to the traces and obscure the fundamental.
Therefore, by summoning the past to show the present, one shatters the near to reveal the far—this is an explanation according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment).
The "Elderly Father" at the site of enlightenment and the "Aged Child" in the realm of quiescent light manifest their medicinal power so that all may come to know it;
this is an explanation according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). Thus the text asks: "From where do they come? By what causes and conditions have they gathered?
Now, by explaining this chapter through various meanings, one reveals the understanding of the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*; therefore, it is called "Surging Forth."
The Presentation. Second, regarding the explanation of the scriptural text: from this point forward, it is extensively clarified that the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment long ago;

he has manifested his original state by setting aside his traces, revealing that the Tathāgata became a Buddha as far back as unspeakably unspeakable numbers of *rajas* (dust-motes) of kalpas, and not merely today at the royal city where he first realized the fruit of the Way. Why is this so?

That which has been accomplished for a long time is the "original essence" (honjitsu), while that which is accomplished now is the "manifest trace" (jaku). Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess Great Wisdom, they do not dwell in birth-and-death;

because they possess Great Compassion, they do not abide in Nirvana. To manifest from the original essence and establish traces to provide transformation and benefit sentient beings—this is precisely what is meant by this.
△ Second, explaining the scriptural text, in two parts: first, the emergence [of the assembly]; second, the inquiry. Regarding the first part, there is further...
2. First, the Bodhisattvas from other regions request that the sutra be propagated.

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from various lands in other regions—numbering more than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers—rose within the great assembly, joined their palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us, before the Buddha..."
After my parinirvāṇa, those who, within this Sahā world, diligently apply themselves with vigor to protect, uphold, read, recite, copy,
and make offerings to this sutra, shall extensively expound it in this land.

On the other hand, having heard that the merit of propagating the sutra through the Trace Gate is so great, the bodhisattvas from other directions all desired to make vows to dwell here and propagate it;
for this reason, they made their request. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s refusal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Stop, sons of good family! There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra. Why is this?
In my Sahā world, there are already bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers;
each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. All of them..."
That you, sirs, would be able to protect, uphold, recite, and widely expound this sutra after my parinirvāṇa—the Tathāgata restrains you for three reasons:
first, each of you has your own specific responsibilities; if you remain in this land, you will neglect those benefits [for others].
Second, the conditions for establishing karmic connections between that other region and this land are shallow; though you may wish to proclaim it...
Third, if he were permitted [to remain], he would not be able to summon those of the lowest grade;
if they did not come, his traces could not be destroyed and his distant [teachings] could not be manifested—these are the three reasons for which the Tathāgata stopped him.
There are likewise three reasons why he summoned those of the lower grades: first, they are my disciples and should propagate my Dharma; second, because their conditions are profound and vast.
It is able to bring benefit throughout this land, benefit throughout the lands of manifested bodies, and benefit throughout the lands of other directions—these are the three.
Furthermore, it attains the opening of the near to reveal the distant; therefore, it stops there and summons those below. △ Third, the emergence from below the earth, in two parts:
first, the narrator’s description of the signs, in five parts; first, the emergence.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the ground of this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds quaked and split open,
and from within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
△ Second, their physical marks:
The bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, possessing the thirty-two marks and immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, their dwelling place.
First, they all reside beneath this Sahā world, dwelling in the void of this realm.
Their place of residence is the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-raśmi*). "Eternal" is the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" is the virtue of bliss;
"light" is the virtue of purity and the virtue of self. This is called the secret treasury of the four virtues; it is their place of residence because it is non-abiding.
Regarding the phrase "the lower direction within the secret treasury of the Dharma": it refers to the abyssal depths of the *dharmatā* and the ultimate ground of the profound mystery;
thus it is called the "lower direction. Yet, being "below," it does not belong to this [world], and being "in space," it does not belong to that [realm].
Since it is neither that nor this, it is precisely the Middle Way. Departing from this, it is not above, nor is it here below. Since it is neither above nor below, it is the Middle.
That they are situated in mid-air is also the Middle Way. △ Fourth, hearing the command:
These bodhisattvas heard the sound uttered by Śākyamuni Buddha as it issued forth from below.

Those who come from below do so because they have heard the command, because they come to propagate the Dharma, because they come to shatter attachments, and because they come to reveal the fundamental;
all these matters are as explained above. △ Fifth, the Retinue.
Each and every bodhisattva was a leader of the great assembly, each leading a retinue as numerous as sixty thousand Ganges-sands;
how much more so those leading retinues of fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand Ganges-sands?
And how much more so those leading even down to a single Ganges-sand, half a Ganges-sand, a quarter, or even ten million Ganges-sands?
How much less those who have but one part in a hundred billion nayutas; how much less those with ten million billion nayutas of followers; how much less those with hundreds of millions of followers;
how much less those with ten million, one million, or even ten thousand; how much less those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten;
how much less those who lead only four, five, four, three, two, or one disciple; and how much less those who dwell alone, delighting in solitude?
Their practices are beyond measure, boundless, and cannot be known through calculation or analogy.

As for the retinues they lead, if one were to judge by human standards, leading sixty thousand or fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] would be considered many, while leading three, two, or one would be considered few;
"single" means being alone and solitary. If one follows the text to investigate, there are six... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Why is it that fifteen thousand is considered "few" while a single individual is considered "many"? The text states: "One who dwells alone and solitary, their number actually surpasses the former.
If one relies on the Dharma-gate, each and every one is a teacher whose virtue and power can lead the multitude to the place of treasure.
One should know that a single person is not truly solitary, and sixty thousand are not truly many; the "one" is precisely the one path of purity.
Two refers to concentration and wisdom; three refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom; four refers to the Four Noble Truths; five refers to the Five Eyes; six refers to the Six Perfections.
Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma-realms, and each realm likewise possesses ten aspects, making one hundred.
One hundred possesses one thousand, and the ten wholesome deeds possess ten thousand. Thus, each perfection possesses ten thousand, and the six perfections possess sixty thousand dharmas.
The gate is many, yet not many; it is one, yet not few; it is neither many nor few, yet both many and few.
△ Second, clarifying the inquiry of greeting (five sections): first, making offerings through the three karmas.
Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded through the air to the seven-jeweled, wondrous stupa where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located.
Upon reaching the two World-Honored Ones, they prostrated themselves at their feet;

likewise, they went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees, where they also paid homage, circumambulated them three times to the right, and joined their palms in reverent salutation.
With various methods of praise appropriate for bodhisattvas, they offered hymns of eulogy and stood to one side, joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had surged forth from the earth and praised the Buddha with various methods of praise appropriate for bodhisattvas.
During this time, fifty intermediate kalpas passed; at that moment, Śākyamuni—
The Muni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great multitude to perceive this duration as being like half a day.
At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the fourfold assembly also saw bodhisattvas filling the empty space of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.

Fifty minor kalpas are said to be like half a day; the fourfold assembly perceives this entirely because [the Buddha] conceals the long and manifests the short, employing his supernatural power to make the narrow appear broad—both of which are inconceivable. Prostrating and circumambulating are physical acts (*kāyakarman*);
praising the Dharma is verbal action (*vākkarman*); and gazing up with reverence is mental action (*manaskarman*). These fifty minor kalpas and...
Half a day—this is the inconceivable temporal measure perceived by the Tathāgata, who does not view things through dualistic characteristics.
Bodhisattvas from the lower realms constantly extol him face-to-face; the Tathāgata remains silent and constantly accepts their praise.
To those who understand, what is short is long, meaning fifty minor kalpas; to those who are deluded, what is long is short, meaning it is like half a day. This is how it is.
Why use the "original" (*hon*) and the "traced" (*shaku*) as an introductory lead? If the Tathāgata had not yet spoken, one would obscure the original and cling to the traced;
if he reveals and clarifies it, one awakens to the near and reaches the far. Thus, one knows that the inconceivable is one.
That the fourfold assembly sees everywhere, and even the Bodhisattvas do so, is also inconceivable. For what is seen by the fleshly eye or the divine eye does not extend far, yet now—
Seeing that all of space is filled, one knows from the heavy rain that the dragon is great; seeing the abundance of flowers, one knows the depth of the pond;
seeing that it should fill all of space, one then knows the true *maitrī* of the *dharmadhātu*. △ Second, setting forth the words of inquiry, in two parts:
first, designating the four guides.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders: the first was named Upariṣṭacārin, the second Anantacārin, the third Śuddhacārin, and the fourth Pratiṣṭhitacārin.
These four bodhisattvas were the foremost among the multitude, serving as their guiding teachers.
The Teacher mentions only these four individuals because he intends to reveal and enter the forty stages (*bhūmi*).
This is similar to how the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions Dharmamati, Guṇaratha, Suvarṇadhvaja, and Suvarṇagarbha to explain the forty stages; the meaning is the same. II.
The Statement of the Questions. A. Prose Exposition. 1. Questioning the Tathāgata’s Peaceful Bliss.
Before the great assembly, they each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after him, saying:
"World-Honored One, are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
This inquiry concerns the four aspects of peace and happiness: body, speech, mind, and intention. △ Second, the inquiry concerning the ease with which sentient beings may be delivered.
"Are those who are to be delivered easy to instruct, so as not to cause the World-Honored One fatigue?
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
△ Second, the verses in praise [of the Buddha's well-being], consisting of two parts: first, the verse praising the Tathāgata’s peace and happiness.
The World-Honored One is at ease, with little illness and little affliction, teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness.
△ Second, the verse on the question of whether sentient beings are easy to deliver:
Furthermore, are all sentient beings easy to transform so as not to cause the World-Honored One to experience fatigue?
△ Third, the Buddha’s response regarding his well-being, in two parts. First, the response regarding his well-being:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "So it is, so it is, sons of good family!
The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction."
This is the Tathāgata’s complete answer regarding the two matters of being "at ease" (*anurakṣa*) and "easy to deliver" (*sukha-vinaya*), which are mutually constitutive:

being easy to deliver means being at ease, and being at ease means being easy to deliver. △ Second, answering [the question on] being easy to deliver, part one: first, clarifying that their faculties are sharp and their virtues are profound.
All these sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered without any weariness. Why is this?

Because throughout successive lifetimes, these sentient beings have constantly received my transformation; they have also, under past Buddhas, paid respectful homage and planted various roots of goodness.
As soon as these sentient beings see my body and hear what I say, they immediately believe and accept it, entering into suchness.
"Come, O Wisdom!

This Buddha’s answer regarding those easy to deliver contains two meanings: first, those with sharp faculties and thick roots of virtue who have constantly received the great transformation throughout successive lifetimes;
upon first seeing my body, they immediately receive the *Avataṃsaka* and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata, for their fruit has already ripened and is easy to deliver."
Those who are "zero" [in merit] are easy to deliver. Second, regarding those of dull faculties and meager virtue:
except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle, I shall now likewise cause such persons to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
There are those whose two faculties are dull and whose virtue is thin, who from lifetime to lifetime have not received the great transformation.

For such people, it is necessary to open the way by teaching the gradual approach through the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras to bring them to maturity; this also enables these individuals to now hear the Lotus Sūtra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Although this is more difficult than before, it is very easy compared to [the previous state]. The Buddha recognizes what is appropriate for them and acts accordingly.

One then attains what was previously slighted; the application of ointment and cauterization and the realization of wisdom are identical. Now, ten points will be briefly raised to explain this: first, the initial vision and the present vision;

second, opening and closing versus not opening and not closing; third, vertical expansion and horizontal contraction; fourth, the one fundamental and the many traces, where traces share the fundamental while the fundamental remains solitary;

fifth, the addition of explanation versus the absence of explanation; sixth, the transformation of the land versus the non-transformation of the land; seventh, the manifold locations versus... [the text is incomplete].

In many places there are eight instances of "expelling and not expelling" (the nine [categories] of those who are not expelled). Ten: directly revealing the reality, opening up the provisional to reveal the reality.

Eleven: those with sharp faculties ripen first, while those with dull faculties ripen later; furthermore, regarding "first seeing" and "now seeing"—at the time of the initial attainment of the Way, it is called "first seeing," while at the long subsequent stage of true reality, it is called "now seeing. "The sun shines upon the high mountain" refers to the teaching of the Sudden [Dharma].

Neither opening nor closing, for those who have not yet entered, [the Buddha] opens [the path] by teaching the Sudden and the Gradual, using the five flavors to subdue them and lead them gradually toward the Sudden;

because the Sudden enters directly and vertically into the Dharma-realm, it is called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*). Because it does not pass through expedient means, it is called "horizontal" (*tiryak*) and "abbreviated.
Now, passing through the five flavors constitutes the "horizontal" and "extensive," while attaining entry into the Buddha-wisdom is the "vertical" and "extensive"—this is the single platform.

Therefore, because it originally consisted of one thousand leaves, it is called the "Original Text. Because its many traces largely coincide with those of other sutras, it is said to share the same root;

yet because it differs from other sutras, it is said to be uniquely augmented by the exposition of forty stages by four Bodhisattvas, rather than being taught through the opening, showing, awakening, and entering as spoken by the Buddha himself.
Because it is set in the Flower King World, it is said to be unchanging; yet because it transforms the three realms of the land, it is said to be changing.
The seven locations and eight assemblies on the earth constitute "many places"; because Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is far from the distant void, it is said not to be "many places.
The transformation city of Nirvāṇa is called "expelled" because it was a temporary fabrication; since there is no such matter here, it is not "expelled.
Practicing the great direct path is called "direct"; revealing the reality and definitively resolving the Śrāvaka Dharma is called "opening the provisional to reveal the real."
Those with sharp faculties whose conditions have matured enter the Buddha’s wisdom at the outset; those with dull faculties whose conditions mature later enter the Buddha’s wisdom now.

Since their conditions are not identical, there are briefly ten differences that must be understood. Because the seed-wisdom (*jñāna-bīja*) and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are without distinction, the text says:
"Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the Tathāgata’s wisdom," except for those who have practiced previously.
Those who have studied the Hīnayāna shall now enter the Buddha’s wisdom through this sutra; the clear exposition is here, so there is no need for doubt.
At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
△ Verses of Rejoicing (4):
"Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! These sentient beings are easily transformed and can inquire about the profound wisdom of the Buddhas;
having heard it, they believe and practice it—we rejoice in this."

This refers to the Bodhisattvas' understanding and sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), and their ability to inquire—namely, the four great beings in the *Avataṃsaka* and Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all of whom are capable of questioning. That which is questioned is the Buddha’s wisdom.
△ Fifth, the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the chief great bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent, sons of noble family!
You are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata."

This is precisely what the Tathāgata extols and praises; it differs greatly from the questions asked by ordinary questioners. Those who rejoice in the one capable of asking such questions are all bodhisattvas and those beings being transformed.

Having heard this, they practice with faith, and we likewise rejoice. As for the meaning of the Tathāgata’s extolling and praising the one capable of transforming others so that they give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*): how is this so? It is because those who are able to ask such questions are all ancient Buddhas. You [should understand] this.
The Tathāgata is able to rejoice in [the merit], and the Bodhisattvas rejoice in his traces;

the Tathāgata praises his fundamental source—this also secretly indicates the measure of his lifespan. △ Second, the doubts and questions, in two parts: first, the doubts of the Bodhisattvas in this land;
second, first, the long prose section on their doubting thoughts.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, all had this thought:

"Since long ago, we have never seen nor heard of such a great multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerging from the earth, standing before the World-Honored One with palms joined in worship and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being. At that moment, Maitreya Bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva knew the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, and likewise desired to resolve his own doubts.
This introduction to the inquiry spans from the time of the Śītavana [Jeta Grove] until the present assembly, wherein the Great Beings of the ten directions have gathered.
Although my unceasing [wisdom] cannot be limited, by the power of my knowledge as one in the position of succession (sāmantaka), I see and know all;

yet among this assembly, I do not recognize a single person. As I travel and transform throughout the ten directions, paying homage to the Buddhas, I am well known to the great assemblies of those Buddhas;
yet even in the places I have visited and traversed, I am not recognized, whether coming or going, or being such [a person].

When one investigates these matters, they are all beyond my knowledge. Furthermore, those great beings (mahāsattvas) are the pioneers and predecessors who have gone before, while Maitreya is a junior student of a later generation; because the latter does not know the former, he does not recognize them.

Moreover, those great beings fundamentally penetrate the depths of the true reality (bhūtatathatā) and manifest throughout the ten directions to teach and transform others individually; thus, the entirety of their true and provisional manifestations is not within the scope of Maitreya’s perception.
Because the realms [of existence] are such, they do not recognize [the Buddha]. Furthermore, the Buddha, entrusting the propagation of the sutra, summoned the great bodhisattvas;

hearing their master’s command, they gathered together. He secretly revealed his lifespan, as it was not something known by the assembly at that time; thus it is said they did not recognize him. This is an explanation of the "Introduction" section concerning doubts and questions, according to the four *siddhāntas*.
With palms joined toward the Buddha, he asked in verse:
[Section Two: Verses on the Proper Inquiry, Part Five] First, asking from where they have come:
"O World-Honored One of Two Feet, please explain: from where have these immeasurable thousands of millions of great assemblies of bodhisattvas come—beings whom we have never seen before?"
From where have they come? △ Second, asking for what reason they have come:
By what causes and conditions has this great body been assembled, with its great supernormal powers and inconceivable wisdom, and its resolve so firm and steadfast?
Possessing the power of great forbearance, they are a joy for sentient beings to behold; from where have they come?
△ Third, describing their number:
the retinues led by each of these bodhisattvas are immeasurable in number, like the sands of the Ganges River.
There may be great bodhisattvas who, together with a great assembly as numerous as sixty thousand Ganges-sands, single-mindedly seek the path of the Buddha;
these great masters, numbering sixty thousand Ganges-sands, all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra.
Others come numbering fifty thousand Ganges-sands—whose number exceeds that—or forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, down to ten thousand.
One thousand one hundred, and so on, up to as many as the sands of a *gaṅgā*;

half, a third, or a fourth part of a *koṭi-nayuta-bilakṣa* of disciples; even down to fifty million, their number further exceeding a million, reaching ten thousand, eleven hundred, one hundred and fifty, ten, and even down to three, two, or one.
Those who were solitary, without retinues, and delighted in dwelling alone all came to where the Buddha was; their number exceeded even that mentioned above.
If one were to count these great assemblies by casting tally-sticks, one would not be able to know them all even in more than *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Fourth, he asked whose teacher they were:
"Among this assembly of bodhisattvas of great majesty and diligence, who has preached the Dharma to them and transformed them?
From whom did they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment? Whose praise of the Buddha-dharma have they upheld, and whose sutras have they practiced and cultivated as the path of the Buddhas?"
△ Five: Maitreya’s Request in Five Parts. First, he offers praise for the supernatural power:
"Such is the great power of wisdom of the supernatural penetrations of these bodhisattvas.
△ Second, he requests an answer regarding their place of origin.
The earth in the four directions quaked and split open, and from within it the World-Honored One emerged. "I have never before seen such a thing since time immemorial;
I pray that you will tell me the name of the land from which he comes. I have constantly traveled through various lands, yet I have never seen such a phenomenon."
△ Third, the request for an explanation of the circumstances of his appearance:
"In this assembly, I do not recognize a single person; how is it that he has suddenly emerged from the earth? We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof.
△ Fourth, the joint request of the great assembly.

Now, in this great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas, all these bodhisattvas likewise desire to know the causes and conditions regarding the beginning and end of this matter.
△ 5. Request for the Master’s Reply:
"O World-Honored One of immeasurable virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
△ 2. Doubts of the Bodhisattvas from Other Lands.

At that time, the emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha who had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of other lands were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees in the eight directions.
Each of those Buddhas’ attendants saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas coming from the four quarters of the trichiliocosm.

Emerging from the earth and abiding in the void, each addressed his Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) assemblies of bodhisattvas come? At that time, each of those Buddhas spoke to their respective attendants:
"Good sons, wait but a moment; there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya Śākyamuni."
The Buddhas who were prophesied by the Bhikṣuṇī will all subsequently become Buddhas; having asked about this matter, the Buddha now answers it, so that you yourselves shall hear it through this.
Furthermore, those Bodhisattvas from other lands who have doubts—along with their manifested bodies and retinues scattered throughout the ten directions—are present together with Maitreya.
The doubt that both lands are unaware of the original ground arises from the desire to manifest that the attainment of the Way has been exceedingly long;

thus, each [assembly] presents their doubts to their own Buddha, and each Buddha suppresses them, awaiting Maitreya. △ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (Zhengzongfen), divided into two parts: First, the Admonition and Permission. Second, the Extended Prose (Changxing).
First, the Admonition, divided into two parts. First, the Description and Praise.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter.
△ Second, the formal admonition.
"You all should together with one mind don the armor of diligence and resolve upon a firm intention.
Admonish yourselves not to be distracted, not to be indolent, and not to retreat. △ Second, the granting of permission; first, the indication of the fruit-wisdom.
The Tathāgata now desires to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This promise has two meanings; first, it indicates the wisdom of the fruit, which is the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—the wondrous fruit of knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the teaching on conversion and transformation:
By the power of the Buddhas' sovereign supernormal faculties; by the power of the Buddhas' lion-like prowess; and by the power of the Buddhas' fierce and great majesty.

Next, regarding "opening and transforming through teaching," this refers to the proclamation [of the Dharma]. "Mastery of supernatural powers" (*vaśitā-ṛddhi*) signifies the benefiting of beings in the past.
"The lion’s vigorous leap" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) signifies the places where the emanated bodies manifest throughout the ten directions in the present.

Alternatively, it is said that "vigorous leap" represents the state of advancing forward; this symbolizes the aspect of the constant benefit of beings in the future. "Great Power and Majesty" (*mahāvega*)...
The "Valiant One" (Mingzhe) benefits sentient beings in the future; alternatively, this may refer to the present shaking of the ten directions according to the capacities of people's minds.
It is best to rely on the sequence of the text. Furthermore, Master Zhāng'ān privately comments:
"The Tathāgata’s sovereignty is 'I'; his supernatural powers (abhijñā) are 'Joy'; the lion’s boundless stride (siṃhavikrīḍita) is the vigor that removes defilements and attains purity."
Its power and majesty are fierce and formidable, and its future benefit for sentient beings is eternal; this is the intended meaning of the four virtues.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the two verses in praise [of the teaching]. First, the verse on the exhortation:
"One should practice with diligence and single-mindedness; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor doubt or regret.
These three lines praise the exhortation to encourage them to listen with a single mind and diligence as the Buddha proclaims this supreme Dharma-gate.
Do not harbor doubt or regret. △ Second, the verse on the granting of the two [powers]: First, the verse on the mark of the fruit of wisdom:
"The Buddha's wisdom is inconceivable.
△ Second, the verse on the transformative teachings of the three periods of time.
"By the power of your faith now emerging and abiding in the goodness of patience, you shall now hear all those dharmas never before heard.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue;
his wisdom is immeasurable, and the supreme dharma he has attained is profound and beyond conceptualization. Thus, I shall now speak it; listen with a single-minded focus."
The next three verses explain the intent of the teaching for transforming and guiding [beings] throughout the three periods of time.

II. The Main Exposition has three parts: 1. Briefly opening up the near to reveal the distant, thereby moving fixed attachments and giving rise to doubt; 2. Bestowing the prophecy of the Dharma-body in general; 3. Maitreya’s general expression of understanding and realization.

The first section (Briefly opening up the near to reveal the distant) further has two parts: A. Briefly opening up the near to reveal the distant, which moves fixed attachments and gives rise to doubt; B. Extensively opening up the near to reveal the distant, which severs [doubt].

Regarding the initial passage on the arising of faith from doubt, there are two parts; first, the brief opening, which has two sections. First, the prose explanation, which has two parts. First, the dual response, which has two sub-sections.
First, the response concerning the teacher and disciple:
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "I shall now proclaim this before this great assembly..."
I tell you, Ajita, that these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable—
who have emerged from the earth and whom you have never seen before,
were taught, guided, and disciplined by me after I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world.
Their minds were made to resolve upon the aspiration for enlightenment.
△ Second, the answer regarding their location:
These bodhisattvas all dwell beneath this Sahā world, in the space of this realm.
Regarding the statement "dwelling in the space below," as clarified in the *Śāstra*, there are four explanations concerning the *Adhas-citta-samādhi* (the samādhi of having a bottom).

First, "having" (*adhaḥ*) refers to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*); "bottom" (*citta*) refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is called the "bottom" because it is profound and supreme.
Second, "having" refers to names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*); "bottom" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is called the "bottom" because it is empty and quiescent. Furthermore...
"Yǒu" (existence) refers to the two extremes of the mundane world; "dǐ" (bottom/foundation) refers to the foundation because the wisdom of the ultimate limit is perfected.

In this sutra, the space below is taken as the bottom, which is not the same as the two realms of above and below. Here, the Middle Way is taken as the bottom. This is an analysis according to the teachings (*jiào*).
△ Second, the dual explanation of both [master and disciple]. First, the explanation of master and disciple. First, the dual cultivation of wisdom and cessation (*zhì-duàn*).
Regarding the various scriptures, one reads, recites, masters, contemplates, analyzes, and maintains correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
The teacher knows that the disciple cultivates the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); first, one cultivates both wisdom and abandonment:
analyzing the scriptures is the cultivation of wisdom, while correct mindfulness is the cultivation of abandonment. △ Second, the dual realization of wisdom and abandonment.
Ajita, these sons of good family do not delight in being among the multitude or in much speaking;
they always delight in quiet places, practicing with diligence and vigor without ever resting.
Next, the dual realization of wisdom and abandonment: not delighting in dwelling among the multitude is the realization of abandonment; diligent application of effort is the realization of wisdom.
△ Second, the explanation of the locus:
furthermore, one does not rely upon or dwell among humans or devas, but constantly delights in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and also constantly delights in...
The Dharma of all Buddhas is to seek supreme wisdom with single-minded diligence;
"not abiding in humans or devas" means not dwelling in or clinging to these two extremes.
"Profound, unimpeded wisdom" refers to relying on inconceivable wisdom. "Delighting in the Buddha-dharma" means delighting in the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, since the realm and wisdom are profoundly subtle, they are not for bodhisattvas of shallow practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses in Praise (Gāthā) A. First, verses praising the dual response. 1. First, the response regarding teacher and disciple.
Ajita, you should know that these great bodhisattvas have practiced the Buddha’s wisdom for incalculable eons;
they are all those whom I have transformed and inspired to resolve upon the Great Vehicle.

They are my sons who, relying on this world, constantly practice the dhūta austerities, delighting in secluded places, abandoning the clamor of the great assembly, and taking no pleasure in much speaking.
In this way, these sons of mine study my Way and Dharma, constantly exerting themselves day and night for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
△ Second, the answer regarding their location, which has two parts: first, the direct answer regarding the location.
He dwells in the space beneath this Sahā world.
△ Second, praising the virtues of the Bodhisattva:
His resolve and power of mindfulness are firm; he constantly and diligently seeks wisdom and expounds various sublime Dharmas, his mind free from all fear.
△ Second, the two verses explain both [the teacher and the disciples] together. First, the explanation of the teacher and disciples:

"When I sat beneath the Bodhi tree in the city of Gayā and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, I turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and thereby transformed them, causing them to first resolve upon the path. Now they all abide in non-retrogression and shall all attain Buddhahood."
I now speak these words of truth; you all should believe them with one mind.
△ Second, the explanation of the location:
"Since long ago, I have been teaching and transforming these multitudes."
△ Second, due to doubt, there is a further request, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections. First, the doubt:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas gave rise to doubt and wonder at what they had never before experienced, thinking:
"How is it that the World-Honored One, in such a short interval of time, has taught and transformed so many?"
He causes immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great bodhisattvas to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This doubt arises from hearing that he first brought them to maturity beneath the Bodhi tree; now they all abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Furthermore...
Having heard that I have been teaching these multitudes since time immemorial, and having heard these two statements, their attachments are shaken and doubts arise.

△ Second, the request [for clarification] has two parts; first, the explanation by way of Dharma, which has three parts. First, they doubt that the attainment of enlightenment was recent while the number of those transformed is vast; thus, clinging to the notion of proximity, they doubt the distance [of time].

He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From that time until now, only slightly more than forty years have passed. World-Honored One, how is it that within this short span of time you have performed such great deeds of a Buddha?"
By the power of the Buddha’s merit, he teaches and transforms such an immeasurable multitude of great Bodhisattvas so that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Second, since those transformed are numerous and their stages and positions are profound and subtle, they hold that what is distant is near, and thus harbor doubts.
“World-Honored One, even if someone were to spend thousands of millions of billions of kalpas counting this great assembly of bodhisattvas,
they could not exhaust them nor reach their limit. For a long time past, these beings have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas,
have accomplished the path of a bodhisattva, and have constantly practiced the pure conduct.”
△ 3. Triple Request for Confirmation:
"World-Honored One, such a matter as this is difficult for the world to believe.

△ 2. Explanation by Analogy (in two parts): First, the introduction of the analogy; third, the first part of the analogy, which illustrates the meaning of the proximity to attaining supreme enlightenment.
For example, suppose there is a person with a handsome appearance, black hair, and twenty-five years of age.
Second, as an analogy for the vast number of those being transformed:
one points to a hundred-year-old man, saying, "He is my son," and that hundred-year-old man likewise points to the youth, saying, "He is my father."
They gave birth to us.
△ Third, the conclusion of the meaning of the parable:
This matter is difficult to believe.

The various masters of the region north of the Huai River used analogies to explain this: when a father takes an elixir that reverses aging, his appearance becomes like that of a twenty-five-year-old, yet his son does not take the medicine and remains like a hundred-year-old.
If one knows the power of the medicine, one will not doubt the son’s age; those who do not know it find it strange.
Thus, the Tathāgata takes the "medicine" of manifesting traces and shows himself as newly born at Gayā, while the various Bodhisattvas are already direct [manifestations].

The treatise on the *Mūlabhūmi* states that although he has long since resolved his mind upon the Way and now dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, because the Buddha and those who possess the Buddha’s swift wisdom know this matter while others do not, they cannot help but harbor doubts;
therefore, it concludes by saying, "This matter is difficult to believe. △ Second, the explanation combining [the teaching] with the parable, in three parts:
first, combining the proximate parable.
The Buddha is also like this; since he attained the Way, it has actually not been long.
△ Second, the combined remote analogy:
yet these great assembly of bodhisattvas and others have already, for the sake of the Buddha-way, spent immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
Diligently practicing with vigor, he skillfully enters, emerges from, and abides in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis;

having attained great supernormal powers and long cultivated the pure life (brahmacarya), he is well-able to practice all wholesome dharmas in their proper sequence, is adept in questioning and answering, is a jewel among men,
and is exceedingly rare throughout all worlds.
Contemplating this Bodhisattva, one sees that he has long planted roots of goodness; it is not merely from his initial resolve at Gayā that he has attained such mastery.

"Skillfully entering, exiting, and abiding" refers to the nine successive concentrations as skillful entry, the lion’s bound (simha-vijṛmbhita) as skillful exit, and the *samādhi* of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*) as skillful abiding—this is the meaning according to the *Zhàngtōng* (Shared and Distinct) teachings. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth stage is called "skillful entry into the ten stages."
Entering the Gate of Profound Mystery and practicing the affairs of ordinary beings in reverse is called "skillfully emerging";

the pervasive fulfillment of wondrous enlightenment is called "skillfully abiding"—this is the distinct meaning. Completing the *dharmatā-samādhi* is "skillfully entering," and realizing the *śūraṃgama-samādhi* is "skillfully emerging";
the *rāja-samādhi* is "skillfully abiding"—this is the perfect meaning. Practicing various wholesome dharmas in succession is based on the cause.

One who has skillfully practiced and attained the fruit, who enters well into the teaching and provides excellent answers to difficult questions, is endowed with the two adornments and is the most honored among those of the seven stages of expedient means;
therefore, they are called "Jewel" (Ratna). △ Third, the combined request and response, in three parts: first, citing the Buddha’s words.
Today the World-Honored One has just said that when he first attained the Way of the Buddha, he first inspired their resolve to teach, transform,
and guide them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet not long after the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, he was already able to perform such a deed of great merit.
△ Second, the clarification of the intention for the request:

Although we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings given according to his suitability, and though we know that the words spoken by the Buddha are never false and that he has thoroughly mastered all that he knows,
there are newly resolved bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, might hear this...
Regarding the statement that some may not believe or accept [this teaching], it creates the causal conditions for the karmic offense of destroying the Dharma.
This passage has two intended meanings: first, for those in the present, it says, "Although I have not yet attained realization, I simply have faith";
second, for those of shallow practice in the future—beginners who easily give rise to slander—it means that those who slander [the teaching] will fall into ruin.
Those who do not regress from the evil paths, though they believe, do not slander [the teaching], yet they cannot increase their progress on the Path.

If one were to distinguish between them, those who slander give rise to faith, while those who already have faith increase their progress on the Path. △ Third, the formal request for an answer has two parts: first, the removal of our own doubts.
"Indeed, World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain this for us to remove our doubts.
△ Second, removing doubts regarding the future:
"And when the good sons of future ages hear this matter, they too shall not give rise to doubt. At that time, Maitreya...
The Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verses in Praise (Gāthā) A. First, the verses in praise of the Dharma-exposition (Dharmadeśanā). 1. First, the verses on the attachment to the recent [time].
In the past, the Buddha left the Śākya clan for homelessness and sat beneath the Bodhi tree near Gayā; since then, not much time has passed.
△ Second, a verse expressing doubt regarding their distance [from awakening]:
"These sons of the Buddha are immeasurable in number; they have long practiced the path of the Buddhas and abide in the power of supernormal knowledges.
They have skillfully trained in the bodhisattva path and are unstained by worldly dharmas, like lotuses in water. They have emerged from the earth."
All have given rise to a mind of reverence and stand before the World-Honored One; this matter is inconceivable.
△ Third, the verse concluding the request:
"How can it be believed? The Buddha’s attainment of the Way was so recent, yet that which he has accomplished is so vast. We pray you will dispel the doubts of the assembly."
Explaining through analysis according to reality.
△ Second, the verse on the parable, in two parts: first, the verse opening the parable.
For example, a person in the prime of youth, twenty-five years of age, shows people a hundred-year-old son with white hair and wrinkled face.
"These are my sons," he says, yet they call him their father; that the father is young while the son is old is something the whole world does not believe.
△ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the parable, in three parts: first, the verse on the synthesis of the proximate.
The World-Honored One is likewise; it has been but a very short time since he attained the Way.
△ Second, the verse on the convergence of the distant:
These bodhisattvas are firm in resolve and free from timidity, having practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable kalpas.
Skilled in answering difficult questions, his mind was free from fear; his resolve in patience was firm and upright, and he possessed majestic virtue praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He was well able to analyze and explain the teachings, taking no pleasure in the company of crowds and always delighting in meditative concentration.
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, he dwelt in the lower void.
△ Third, the combined request for a response in three verses:
"We have heard this matter from the Buddha and have no doubt; we pray that the Buddha will expound it for the sake of future generations so that they may attain understanding.
If there are those who harbor doubts regarding this sutra and do not believe it, they shall immediately fall into the evil realms; we pray that you will now provide an explanation."
How do these immeasurable bodhisattvas, in a short time, teach and transform others so that they resolve their minds for enlightenment and abide on the stage of non-retrogression?

△ Second, the extensive opening of the near to reveal the distant, thereby severing doubt and engendering faith. Part One: Stating the Title of the Chapter.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Sixteen: "The Life Span of the Tathāgata.

"Tathāgata" is a general term for all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—whether they be the two types of Buddhas (the Dharma-body and the transformation-body), the three types of Buddhas (the original Buddha, the trace Buddha, and the response Buddha), or the fundamental Buddha and the trace Buddha.

Regarding the title "The Life Span": "Life Span" (āyuṣ-pramāṇa) refers to the measurement of the merits of the two Buddhas and three Buddhas—namely, the Original Buddha and the Traces Buddhas—of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Since this chapter specifically measures the merits of the three Buddhas of the original ground, it is called the "Chapter on the Life Span of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, while the single title "Tathāgata" possesses many meanings, we shall now clarify two or three of them.

Other examples may be understood by extension. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because one comes to achieve perfect enlightenment by means of the vehicle of the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*), it is called the Tathāgata-vehicle.

Here, the "Dharma" refers to suchness (*tathatā*); "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the reality of that Dharma-suchness; and the "path" (*mārga*) is like the awakening, while the "fruit" (*phala*) is like suchness itself.
If one were to discuss the vehicle alone, suchness would have nothing to know; if one were to explain only reality, suchness would have no knower.

When object and wisdom are in union, there is cause and effect. When the illumination of objects has not yet reached its ultimate limit, it is called the "cause"; when the source is exhausted, it is called the "fruit.

Once the meaning of the realization of the Way is accomplished, one is a vehicle that comes via the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment; this is the Tathāgata of the True Body (*dharmakāya*).
It is by means of the wisdom of reality and the vehicle of the path of reality that one comes to be born within the three realms of existence and manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata. Regarding the three types of Tathāgatas, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because he understands according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and teaches according to the nature of phenomena, he is called Tathāgata.
'Tathā' (Thus) refers to the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*). This is the realm of suchness, which is neither cause nor fruit;
whether a Buddha appears or not, its intrinsic nature remains eternally as it is, pervading all places without variation. It is 'thus' because it is immovable, yet it 'arrives' [in manifestation]."

This refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata. Because the wisdom that accords with reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) mounts upon the path of the true suchness (tathatā) and comes to achieve wondrous enlightenment, its wisdom is called "accordance" (tathā), and following this principle it is termed "such" (tathā); following this wisdom it is termed "come" (āgata).
This is the Saṃbhogakāya Tathāgata. Therefore, the treatise says: "Because one understands according to the characteristics of phenomena, one is called Tathāgata."
Because the object and wisdom are in union with suchness (*tathatā*), one is able to manifest perfect enlightenment everywhere.

Just as mercury mixed with pure gold can be used to gild various images, so too the merit combined with the *dharmakāya* manifests in response everywhere, proceeding through the eight phases of enlightenment and turning the sublime wheel of Dharma;
this is the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata. Therefore, the treatise says: "It is called such because it is taught according to the characteristics of phenomena."
The Tathāgata of the Dharma-body is named Vairocana, which translates as "Pervading All Places.

The Tathāgata of the Reward-body is named Rocana, which translates as "Pure and Full. The Tathāgata of the Response-body is named Śākyamuni, which translates as "Crossing the Watōjō (the Scorching Sands).
These three Tathāgatas cannot be understood if taken individually; thus it is said in the Great Sūtra.
It is said that the Dharma-body is neither prajñā nor liberation, yet it is not separate from these three dharmas; their complete integration is termed the "Secret Treasury" and named Great Nirvāṇa.
It cannot be characterized as either identical to or different from them, nor can it be viewed through the dichotomies of vertical or horizontal, or as distinct or unified;

rather, it is the total encompassing of these three dharmas, designated by the provisional name "Tathāgata. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* concludes the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein the lotus pedestal is the root and the lotus petals are the branches.
This statement was made because the derivative and the fundamental were treated as a single condition; yet the derivative and the fundamental cannot be separated from one another.
The *Xiangfa jueyi jing* concludes with a passage on the *Nirvāṇa*, stating: "One may see Śākyamuni as Vairocana, or as Rocana.

Next, we shall discuss the five periods of the Dharma. What are the five? Regarding the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā*: the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is when the Buddha extensively expounded the teaching of emptiness to refute the attachments of sentient beings and to reveal the true nature of phenomena. Regarding the period of the *Nirvāṇa*: the period of the *Nirvāṇa* is when the Buddha, near the end of his life, taught the doctrine of the permanence of the Buddha-body and the eternity of the Dharma to console sentient beings and encourage their practice. Regarding the period of the *Lotus*: the period of the *Lotus* is when the Buddha finally revealed the true intent of the One Vehicle, uniting the provisional and the real, and returning all to the source. These five periods of the Dharma are established according to the sequence of the Buddha’s preaching and the gradual maturation of the capacities of sentient beings.
