Since bodhisattvas are subsumed within the three wholesome destinies of devas, humans, and asuras, while the remaining three evil destinies involve heavy karmic offenses, dull faculties, and meager wisdom such that they do not know how to engage in this practice, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* simply states that the Mahāyāna excels over the heavens.
Humans and asuras are also not included among the three miserable realms. There are three kinds of bodhisattvas:

those from the lower regions, those from other regions, and those who have long resided here. Those from the lower regions are those originally transformed by [the Buddha] himself; thus, they are free from attachment and do not dwell near [him].

As for those from other regions who have long resided here, there are two types: first, those who manifest from the Dharma-body; and second, those who in previous lives already attained non-arising (anutpāda).

Those who have previously heard the revelation of the manifested trace and the disclosure of the fundamental source, even if they have not yet attained the exhaustion of retribution and received the Dharma-nature body, will naturally hear this discourse on the long and distant [past] upon reaching the stage of the Dharma-body;

therefore, one should give rise to the thought that there are many Bodhisattvas who lack attachment and are near—meaning those who have now first attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) as well as those who have not yet attained it. All possess this.

It is said: △ Second, refuting the near to reveal the far, in two parts: first, revealing the far through both principle and parable; second, first, revealing the far through the teaching of the Dharma.
"However, good sons, since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of eons."
Regarding the phrase "In another kalpa;
since his attainment of Buddhahood has been for a very long time": the "near" refers to the [conventional] breaking [of the near], while the "breaking of the near" serves to reveal the far.
Briefly, there are ten meanings as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). This passage specifically employs the method of "breaking the near to reveal the far" to supersede [the conventional].
The two intentions of "negating the near to reveal the far" refer to the first, the negation of attachment to the near; this means setting aside the immediate teachings of today.
△ Second, citing analogies for comparative evaluation, in three parts: first, citing an analogy and posing a question.
Suppose, for example, that there were five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms, which someone were to grind into fine dust;
then, traveling eastward, he were to drop a single grain of dust after passing five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asaṃkhyeya* lands.
Continuing in this manner toward the east until all those grains of dust were exhausted—O sons of good family! [in that same measure...]
What do you think? Is it possible to contemplate, calculate, or know the number of all these worlds?
In other sutras, the number is sometimes explained as being beyond description, using metaphors such as motes of dust in the sands of the Ganges; yet compared to this, those are few.
Even the worlds where dust has already been marked are beyond description, so how could those where no dust has been marked possibly be described?
If even the realm of "dust-falling" or "non-dust-falling" cannot be described, how could "dust-falling" or "non-dust-falling" dust itself be described?
Furthermore, as the text below states, "it exceeds this even further," so how could it possibly be described? △ Second, the answer regarding not knowing.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others together addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;

they cannot be known through calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, even with their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), cannot contemplate or know their limits.
As for us, we abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) regarding this matter."
Furthermore, this is not something that can be fully comprehended; for the World-Honored One has stated that such worlds are immeasurable and boundless.
In this response, it is mentioned that even these three types of persons—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those like Maitreya who have attained awakening—do not know them.
△ Third, the combined explanation of the distant [kalpas].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: "O sons of good family, I shall now clearly declare to you:
take all those worlds—both those where atoms have been placed and those where they have not—and reduce them entirely to dust. Let one atom represent one kalpa."
Since I attained Buddhahood, more than hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed.
This is illustrated by the following analogy. △ Second, the suitability for benefiting beings in the past, in three parts: first, the places where beings were benefited.
Since that time, I have constantly been here in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and teaching and transforming beings,
and I have also guided and benefited sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya lands in other places.
Regarding "must manifest in a visible place": the analogy cited above implies a very long duration;

since he has resided there for so long, it is said that he constantly performs Buddha-work to guide and benefit sentient beings both in this land and in other lands. △ Second, clearing away the doubts regarding the preceding traces.
"O sons of good family, regarding this interval, I have spoken of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, and have further said that they entered parinirvāṇa;
all such statements were made through skillful means and analytical distinctions."

This refers to doubting the cause and doubting the result. Regarding what was taught in the past, practicing causes in various places and receiving predictions (vyākaraṇa) in various places constitutes the result.
Now, by dispelling these doubts—specifically by pointing to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, one dispels doubt regarding the cause;
and further, by stating that he has entered parinirvāṇa, one dispels doubt regarding the result. Thus, these matters of cause and result are not merely a single thread.
My expedient means are not literal statements; therefore, they are called "clearing away doubts.

Some may say that these are expedient teachings, asserting that Dīpaṃkara Buddha was my teacher, yet in reality, it was Śākyamuni manifesting as him. He does not arise through actual birth, nor does he perish through actual extinction;
thus he speaks in this way. Furthermore, regarding his statement about his parinirvāṇa, I say it is not so. One should simply adopt the previous explanation. What [is there to doubt]?
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, because his conditions were ripe, transformed himself into a Buddha-image to convert him;

whereas my own conditions were not yet ripe, I was merely a bodhisattva who, having received a prediction from the Buddha, attained the meaning of "fruit" (the result), and through the practice of various deeds, attained the meaning of "cause.
Such an interpretation of the text is sufficient. As for the word "that" (其), it refers to the person who was converted during the intermediate period of teaching; it does not mean otherwise.

This refers to the illumination by light. Furthermore, regarding the benefit of beings during the intermediate period, since there are both physical forms and sounds, if one speaks of encountering the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, this constitutes the benefit of physical form;

and if one further speaks of his entry into *nirvāṇa*, then after that Buddha’s passing, assisting the Buddha to propagate the transformation constitutes the benefit of sound. If this is so, both the benefits of form and sound belong to the intermediate period.
This is merely the cause for the interval. Since there is the arising of form and sound, there must also be death; once dead, one enters *nirvāṇa*, which is designated as the "fruit.
One cannot say that the fruit of Buddhahood has already been realized during the interval. Why? Because prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was not yet taught that he had attained Buddhahood;
how then could there be any doubt regarding the fruit of Buddhahood? Formerly, [the Buddha] took Dīpaṃkara as his own manifestation.

To act in this way is also not to understand the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Since the previous sutras did not discuss how [the Buddha] had already attained Buddhahood in the past, by what teaching was it said that Dīpaṃkara was my teacher?
It is precisely to dispel this doubt. △ Third, the correct elucidation of what is appropriate for benefiting sentient beings, in two parts:
first, the response and resonance.
"Good sons, if there are sentient beings who come to me, I observe their faculties, such as faith and the rest—
whether they are sharp or dull— and deliver them according to what is appropriate for their salvation.
Those who come to me are sentient beings of the past whose gradual and sudden capacities have silently struck resonance with my Dharma-body."
Regarding those who observe with the Buddha-eye: this is the function of one who has long since attained Buddhahood. Using the Buddha-eye to discern and illuminate, there is no omission or error.
When intending to manifest the two types of response—the superior and the inferior—to benefit sentient beings, there are two powers within their virtuous capacity:

first, to elicit the flowery retribution of humans and devas; second, to elicit the resultant retribution of the Buddha-way. Observing and knowing all conditions for myriad virtues through the Dharma-eye.

The gravity or lightness of these [actions] each receives a corresponding "flower-retribution" (hua-bao), yet one cannot ultimately know that they will finally result in the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā).
Only by using the Buddha-eye to perfectly illuminate all wholesome deeds can one know their beginning and end;

this sutra exclusively clarifies how the Buddha, through the observation of the Buddha-eye, knows that sentient beings' myriad wholesome deeds will ultimately lead to the Great Matter of the Buddha appearing in the world—this is its primary intent.

The "faculties such as faith" refers to the five faculties beginning with faith. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the cause of realization (*prativedha-hetu*), while the remaining faculties are the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*).
These two roots of goodness each have sharp and dull varieties, encompassing both sudden and gradual capacities and conditions.

The sharp and dull faculties of the sudden type correspond to the *Vimalakīrti* (Perfect/Complete) and *Bhadrakalpika* (Distinct) vehicles; the sharp and dull faculties of the gradual type correspond to the *Āgama* (Treasury) and *Vaipulya* (Penetrating) vehicles. Furthermore, there is the Small [Vehicle].
The faculties of those who ride the Great Vehicle are called "sharp," while those of the Small Vehicle are called "dull.

Furthermore, those of humans and devas are called "dull," whereas the sharpness or dullness of all the roots of goodness possessed by sentient beings within the ten dharma realms constitutes their "capacity" (*ki*).

Evil dharmas are not considered either the conditional cause (*en-in*) or the perfecting cause (*ryō-in*). The Tathāgata fully illuminates the capacities for goodness within the ten realms and acts according to what is required to deliver them.
Manifesting forms and sounds to provide benefit. △ Second, the bestowing of transformation [has two parts]: first, the benefit of form and sound; second, the benefit of form alone.
First, manifesting birth where there is no birth:
in various places, he himself declares different names and varying ages, whether great or small.
This correctly clarifies that the names of the various emanations (nirmāṇakāya) are distinct according to what is appropriate for them. Since they manifest their forms, they possess names;

because names are used to summon the essence [of the being], there are differences in the capacity of the recipients (the *adhikāra*). Thus, while forms may vary in excellence or inferiority, it is because the forms differ that the names are not the same.

Regarding the age—whether great or small—this refers to the excellence or inferiority of the form; "excellent" refers to those who are superior emanations (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇa*), and "inferior" refers to those who are less so.

The difference in the names of the Inferior Response-body and the [other] Buddhas corresponds precisely to the distinction between the limited and unlimited lifespans manifested by these two types of Buddhas.

Regarding "in every place": if discussed vertically, it refers to the various places where causes were cultivated in the past; if discussed horizontally, it refers to the various names of the lands throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, even regarding vertical locations, there are differences in the names of the teachings and the beings born therein.
When the present *nirmāṇakāya* is compared with past Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara, there are differences in terms of their respective lands,
modes of birth, dharmas, and names— just as the present *nirmāṇakāya* differs from its various emanations (*nirmāṇakāyas*),

as evidenced by the numerous distinct names of Śākyamuni listed among the ten titles in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, various sūtras distinguish that the Buddha possesses three bodies (*trikāya*).
The names by which they are invoked differ, and the dharmakāyas they summon are likewise distinct; some are called Vairocana, some Śākyamuni, and some the Dharmakāya Buddha.
Others are named Tathatā (Suchness), the Real Mark (Lakṣaṇa), the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha), Prajñā, or the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and so forth.
This refers to the differences in the names of the Buddha-dharmadhātu-body as it manifests; however, when it manifests as the bodies of the nine dharma-realms, the names are different.
Since their names differ, they are immeasurable and boundless, yet can be understood through the mind.

Regarding the magnitude of their lifespans, this clarifies that the length of life follows the manifested *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) appearing above: sometimes it is said that the lifespan is twenty thousand years, as in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha;

sometimes it is said that the lifespan is eighty thousand years, as in the time of Maitreya Buddha. These successive accounts mutually clarify the variations in magnitude, whether vertical or horizontal.
It should be understood that the size of the lifespans of the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas is as explained in the *Xuanyi* (Treatise on the Profound Meaning), etc.

Alternatively, one may distinguish between "great" and "small" by comparing the three bodies against one another; or, each of the three bodies is individually considered "small," while their collective exposition is termed "great.
This is generally illustrated by the analogy of the three dots, etc. All of these are merely manifestations of the body and the duration of life according to the specific needs of those to be saved.
△ Second, though not actually extinguished, he manifests extinction.
Furthermore, he manifests by saying, "I shall enter nirvana.
Moreover, for those who should be delivered through parinirvāṇa, he manifests that very state.
He brings about parinirvāṇa so that they may develop longing and reverence, thereby attaining liberation; this meaning is seen in the illustrative explanation below.
△ Second, the benefit of his voice:
Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Having a small body and a short lifespan refers to the teaching of the gradual approach; thus it is said that there are various skillful means.
Having a large body and a long lifespan refers to the teaching of the sudden approach; thus it is said that one preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma. △ Second, the joy of attaining benefit.
It is able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy;
although it begins gradually, it ultimately causes them to enter the Great [Vehicle], and for this reason it is said that it causes all to attain joy.

This very joy is itself the bestowing of transformation and the gaining of benefit. The Buddha, relying upon the four *siddhāntas*, bestows both physical and vocal benefits, whereby sentient beings obtain [them].

Regarding the four benefits, one rejoices when they accord with the capacities [of sentient beings] and is distressed when they do not; thus, the subsequent passage states, "All is real and not false," which refers precisely to this meaning.
△ Second, benefiting beings in the present, part one: first, clarifying the resonance of capacities.

"Sons of good family, when the Tathāgata perceives that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings, possess meager merit, and are heavily defiled—this is the present Lion’s Boundless Prowess for Benefiting Beings. This samādhi possesses ten merits:
first, it distinguishes whether the faculties of others are mature or immature, and whether they are pure or impure; second, by means of the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma..."
He teaches those not yet liberated so that they all enter the Dharma and Vinaya; his three great vows pervade the ten directions, and his voice is likewise.
Whether it be a single sound or hundreds of thousands of millions of sounds, they all pervade everywhere to universally instruct all classes of beings.
He turns the unsurpassed wheel of the four truths to transform and teach sentient beings, leading them all to attain nirvana. Others are unable to turn this wheel; only the Buddha can do so.
1. To manifest the turning of the five [aggregates] by demonstrating leaving home, shaving the head, and upholding the pure precepts, and also to enable others to take delight in them;

2. To harmonize the six modes of conduct with emptiness; 3. To emit light and demonstrate extinction—sometimes appearing to exist and sometimes appearing to perish—and to manifest physical marks or conceal them;
4. To subdue the four Māras; 5. To cause others to enter the ultimate essential and increase their *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; 6. To be endowed with the above.
The ten wholesome paths of action, the three bodies, and the four immeasurables (and so forth)—when the Tathāgata beholds these, it is the illumination of the Buddha-eye.
This is the capacity of those sentient beings who delight in the lesser Dharma. As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Though the great assembly is pure, there are others who delight in the lesser Dharma;
they may give rise to doubt and regret, suffering decline and affliction for a long night. Out of compassion for them..."

The verse states: "Others will not practice for long; their wisdom is not yet clear. Relying on consciousness rather than on wisdom, they will give rise to doubt and regret upon hearing [this teaching].
Fearing they will fall into evil realms, I do not speak [of it] out of compassion. According to that sutra, there are no śrāvakas or followers of the two vehicles mentioned;
it merely refers to those who practice for a short time as people who delight in the Small Vehicle. Nanyue said: "Delight..."

Those who are "small" are not necessarily followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); rather, they are called "small" because they delight in what is merely proximate. I shall now explain this comprehensively:
those who crave and love the twenty-five states of existence—that is, those with the capacity of humans and devas—who come to me, are said to be of the "Small Dharma.
Those who delight in Nirvana and seek their own liberation—that is, those with the capacity of the Two Vehicles—come to [the Great Dharma].

"Those who belong to me" are also called those who delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*). This refers to those with the capacity of Bodhisattvas of the three teachings who delight in the gradual and circuitous path to Buddhahood;

they come to me and are likewise called those who delight in the Lesser Dharma. Those of "meager virtue" are those whose functions regarding the two kinds of goodness—*paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected)—are weak and inferior, as the text below states:

"The children are young and immature," and "those with heavy defilements" refers to those whose *darśana-heya* (defilements abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (defilements abandoned by cultivation) have not yet been eliminated.

[The interlocutor] asks: "If those who practice the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) and so forth—which involve removing [delusions] and questioning [the truth], manifesting what is not yet born, and providing both gradual and sudden teachings—are indeed those who delight in the Small Dharma, while those for whom the Perfect and Sudden [teachings] meet their capacity are those who should delight in the Great Dharma, how can they all be collectively judged as 'delighting in the Small Dharma'?

Answer: The meaning was previously summarized; now it shall be explained in detail. There are generally four points regarding this: first, concerning... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "first, concerning...".)
In the past, although they had resolved upon the Great Mind, they were unable to apply themselves with single-minded diligence because they were deeply attached to base desires;
thus, they failed to attain the state beyond the world. These "base desires" are what is meant by "adhering to the Lesser Dharma. Second, regarding the present:

although gods and humans possess great spiritual capacity before the Buddha has appeared in the world, their minds are defiled by worldly pleasures and they cling to false views; therefore, this is called "delighting in the Lesser Dharma. This is the second point.
The two meanings are identical in intent to the following analogy of rolling upon the ground. Thirdly, regarding practice:

although one may not delight in the defiled desires of the triple world or in the minor dharmas, yet delighting in the three vehicles and the extinction of ashes (nirvāṇa) is also termed a "minor dharma.

Although one may not delight in the proximate fruits of the three vehicles, yet delighting in the gradual cultivation of the One Vehicle while being unable to achieve perfect integration within a single mind [is likewise so termed].
The "sudden and universal cultivation" is also called "delighting in externals"; these three meanings clarify the delight in inferior dharmas from the perspective of the cause.

Fourth, from the perspective of the fruit, they delight in hearing that the attainment of Bodhi began upon leaving the palace of the Śākyas—a minor realization achieved in the near term—and do not delight in hearing the long-term, great path of the distant future;
therefore, it is said they "delight in the small. Such a narrow-mindedness did not begin only today.

If one has previously delighted in the Great [Vehicle], then the Buddha does not speak of his initial attainment; those for whom he speaks of initial attainment are all those who delight in the Lesser Dharma.

△ Second, explaining the manifested transformation [body] has two parts: first, appearing to be born though not actually born; second, the actual explanation of appearing to be born. First, the actual appearance of birth.
For these people, I say that I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shortly after leaving home.
To those who perceive my traces as manifesting in birth, I say that from the time I first attained Bodhi, two types of capacities—sharp and dull—have come to evoke the Dharma-body;
I now manifest two corresponding responses, superior and inferior, wherein the inferior response corresponds to those of dull faculties.

The *Vijñānakāya* states that these two types of *saṃbhinna-śrotra* (the Victorious Response) correspond respectively to those of sharp faculties; both possess the two bodies of birth: the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).

Regarding the birth of the inferior response-body (*hīna-saṃbhinna-śrotra-janma-kāya*): it refers to being conceived through right wisdom, taking birth, and walking seven steps, as described by Kātyāyanīputra, up until the return from six years of ascetic practice;
this is called the birth of the birth-body. As for the birth of the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya-janma*): [it refers to...]
This refers to the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcadharmakāya) attained when the fetters and habitual tendencies have been completely severed through thirty-four moments of mind.
As for the "superior response-body" (*sambhogakāya*) and the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*), as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures:

while dwelling in the womb of Māyā together with the various bodhisattvas, he constantly expounds the Mahāyāna; furthermore, upon emerging from the womb, he takes seven steps in each of the ten directions—this is called the birth-body.

Regarding "birth," the birth of the *dharmakāya* occurs when, at the stage of the adamantine final mind (*vajrāntima-citta*) within the site of the tranquil extinction (*śānti-maṇḍala*), one cuts off ignorance entirely and attains the wisdom corresponding to wondrous enlightenment.
This wisdom exhaustively illuminates the *dharmatā*, and the various virtues and the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are perfectly clear and universally complete;

this is called the birth of the *dharmakāya*. As for "leaving home," the inferior response-body leaves the home of the segmented existence (*bhavāgra-vidyā*), while the superior response-body leaves the home of the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*).

Regarding those who attain *bodhi* within the household: for the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*), that which is called *bodhi* consists of the untainted knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) produced by the four noble truths with effort.
For the superior response-body (*praṇīta-nirmāṇakāya*), *bodhi* is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which illuminates the path of the three truths as one reality.
△ Second, [the section on] non-arising.

However, although it has indeed been this long since I truly attained Buddhahood, I have spoken thus by means of skillful expedients to teach and transform sentient beings, leading them to enter the Buddha-way.

This clarifies that my original nature is fundamentally unarisen; "unborn" does not mean that I was born only at the very beginning. It is simply that devas, humans, and asuras perceive me in this way.
Regarding these two kinds of birth, it is said that the two bodies (the Dharma-body and the Transformation-body) are "born at the beginning of words," but this is not so.
For I have long since attained these two bodies of the nature of birth; the birth today is not a real birth. Therefore, it is said, "for such a long time.
"Such a long time" refers to the great duration illustrated by the preceding analogies. However, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), [the text] clarifies below that [this birth] is not [real].

As for why he manifests birth when he is already truly born: it is for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to those who practice the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, and to enable those of meager virtue and heavy defilements to attain the Buddha-way.
Thus it is said, "He merely uses skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings," and speaks in this way because he does not undergo actual birth but manifests birth.
However, other sutras merely refute the inferior body of response-birth (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The "arising" and "non-arising" of the Dharma-body of the Inferior Response-Buddha (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) have not yet been refuted;

now, this sutra specifically refutes the "arising" and "non-arising" of the Dharma-body of the Superior Response-Buddha (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇa-kāya*). Why? Because I have truly attained Buddhahood for a period as long as this.

Therefore, we know that today both the inferior and superior Dharma-bodies—regarding their arising—are refuted. Thus, the "arising" and "non-arising" [of these bodies] are consistent with other sutras.
Forever distinct. △ Second, the benefits, in two parts: first, forms and sounds.
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of liberating sentient beings;
he may speak of his own person or speak of another’s person; he may manifest his own person or manifest another’s person; he may manifest his own affairs or manifest another’s affairs."
This clarifies that the augmentation of form and sound refers to teaching through sound and manifesting through form; yet form and sound do not emerge from either self or other.
To speak of the Dharma-body is to speak of one's own body; to speak of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is to speak of another's body.
To say "I encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara" is to speak of one's own body; to say "Dīpaṃkara was my teacher" is to speak of another's body. This demonstrates the correct [teaching].
"Recompense" refers to manifesting one's own affairs; "retribution" refers to manifesting the affairs of others. Speech that accords with the intentions of others describes the bodies of others;
speech that accords with one's own intentions describes one's own body. Manifesting one's own and others' affairs is likewise of this nature.
△ Second, clarifying that [the Buddha's words] are not false, in two parts: first, the heading stating they are not false.
All that is spoken is real and not false.
This [statement] specifically relies on the benefit of sound to explain "not false"; however, it simultaneously explains both [the reality of form and sound]. Regarding "not false" at the outset:

this refers to how the two types of capacities—gradual and sudden—receive these two kinds of forms and sounds, all of which provide benefit and are not false. The preceding chapter on the past has already clarified this.

Joy is like the benefit of the world; now it is clarified that all is not in vain. Whether superior or inferior, forms and sounds adapt to the two types of capacities, and the attainment of the four *siddhāntas* is also entirely not in vain.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the four *siddhāntas* are all real:

the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly) is real, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial) is real, the *pudgala-siddhānta* (for the person) is real, and the *dharma-siddhānta* (ultimate) is real. These three are the realities of the world.
In reality, even within the realm of empty conditions there are the three realities of the mundane world; yet from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these are empty.
If one applies this distinction between emptiness and reality to the two gates of the provisional trace and the fundamental source regarding the benefits of the gradual and sudden teachings:

the "emptiness" refers to the cause—the benefit of practicing past expedient means before attaining the benefit of the true path. This is because one clings to the immediate, provisional traces and has not yet attained the true reality of the fundamental stage.

The benefit of this is precisely that the fruit was previously empty; now, by opening the teaching of the Trace Gate, all enter the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), thereby attaining the actual benefit within the cause.
By opening the teaching of the Origin Gate, one eliminates the attachment to the near and attains the actual benefit of the far-reaching stage of fruition.
Thus, the two actualities attained now are contrasted with the two emptinesses of the past, specifically regarding the beings of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle] in relation to the Trace.

The two gates are fundamentally one real and one unreal; attaining the practice of the Middle Way is to obtain the real benefit within the cause, whereas clinging to a proximate fruit is to be unreal regarding the fruit.

Now, hearing the teaching on the cause no longer yields any separate real benefit, yet hearing the teaching on the distant fruit immediately yields the real benefit of the fruit. What was formerly unreal now becomes real.
Therefore it is said that all is real and not false. △ Second, explaining why it is not false, in two parts: first, the non-falsity of illuminating the principle. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death, neither retiring from nor emerging from it;
there is no one remaining in the world, nor anyone who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor false, neither suchness nor different; it is not as it appears.

The Tathāgata clearly perceives such matters within the three realms as they truly are, without any error. Below this, there is a general explanation that benefiting sentient beings is not in vain; first, the benefit of physical form is explained, followed by the benefit of speech. Herein, these six phrases reveal that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) does not depart from the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). The *dharmakāya* is formless and likewise without arising or ceasing. All beings possess the mechanism of arising and ceasing, which resonates with the power of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata’s vows to likewise arise and cease.
Since the perception of arising and ceasing originates from sentient beings, if one explains these phrases by way of the three realms, then the illumination of principle will not be in vain.
This means that when one realizes the principle and establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings to transform them, it will certainly not be in vain. Thus, one knows it as it truly is.
To see [this] is precisely true wisdom that illuminates the reality of the three realms according to principle. As for "reality," it means there are no causal marks of the three realms;

as for "no birth-and-death," it means there is no suffering of dualistic death. What is termed "arising and accumulation" is called "retrogression," and what is termed "the manifestation of impermanent results" is called "emergence.
Thus, there is neither abiding in the world of birth-and-death nor entering into the extinction of nirvana. This...
Because both [birth and death] have ceased, it is said that there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa.
This is not because of the reality of parinirvāṇa, nor because of the unreality of saṃsāra; thus it is said to be "neither real nor unreal.

This is not because of the separation and difference of the mundane world, nor because of the true suchness (tathatā) of the supramundane; thus it is said to be "neither suchness nor different. These four clarify the Middle Way.
It is not as [the view] of those within the three realms who perceive the three realms;

nor is it as the marks of the three realms perceived by the two kinds of sentient beings within the three realms. Only the Buddha alone thoroughly and truly illuminates the reality of the three realms.
Internally possessing the function of true wisdom, this is also speech according to his own intention, and it is also because he speaks of his own person; therefore, it is great.

The chapter states: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no conceptual differentiation. The Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom and knowledge-insight perceive the characteristics of the triple world exactly as they are;

that is, he perceives them just as the sentient beings of the triple world perceive them. There is no duality between death and [rebirth], yet he manifests the bodies of the two deaths in accordance with the intentions of others, and speaks of the existence of the two deaths in accordance with the intentions of others. There is neither falling back nor emergence, yet he [speaks of them] in accordance with the intentions of others."

I speak of falling back and emerging, yet there is neither one who remains in the world nor one who has entered extinction; nevertheless, according to the inclinations of others, I manifest birth in the world and manifest entry into nirvana.
I speak of those who remain in the world and those who have attained extinction, yet these are not real.

I speak of the reality of nirvana, which is not false, and the unreality of the triple world, which is not true. I speak of the existence of the three periods of time, though they are without distinction.
There is no such thing as a "true reality" apart from suchness, yet it is said that suchness exists;

this is seen within the three realms, and all [teachings] regarding the three realms are speech according to the intentions of others, termed "sometimes speaking of the affairs of another's body" or "indicating the affairs of another's body.
Because the Tathāgata’s two types of wisdom clearly examine the two truths, his verbal expressions provide dual benefit, both of which are real and not false. △ Second, responding to capacities.
The two initial responses are not in vain,
because sentient beings possess various natures, various desires, various conducts, and various recollections, thoughts, and discriminations.

This clarifies the responsive resonance between the capacity and the stimulus. Because the faculties of sentient beings differ—being either sharp or dull, gradual or sudden—and because their dispositions, desires, practices, and wisdoms vary in myriad ways, [the Buddha] taught the doctrines of both himself and others, as well as non-futile causes, conditions, and parables, so that each might increase their various roots of goodness.
Regarding "disposition" (*gotra*), there are various types of both gradual and sudden capacities.

One must employ the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint for benefiting people) to give rise to various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). These roots of goodness are themselves innate natures (*prakṛti*).

Since habitual desires form one's nature, why is it explained here that nature comes first and desire follows? [The answer is: Because there exists the fundamental nature of the faculties (*indriya-prakṛti*) from a previous day, one is able to give rise to the inclinations (*chanda*) of today.
It is like how the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arise because of afflictions (*kleśa*), and furthermore, because of the five aggregates, there is yet more [arising].
Afflictions do not arise before or after one another; sexual desire is likewise so. It must depend upon the practice of desire in order to become sexual desire.
Regarding those of gradual and sudden capacities, if their various inclinations and desires differ, this requires the use of the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint).

When a practitioner initiates karmic actions and cultivates various practices according to their inclinations and desires, this requires the use of the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the individual).
In the course of practice, there are many attachments that cause hindrances; these must be countered by means of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic teaching).
That which is "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is wisdom, which is a semblance of understanding; because one practices, this ability to generate understanding arises.

This is a skillful means (*upāya*), yet it has not yet accorded with principle; the path beyond words (*anabhilāpya-mārga*) is still a contemplation involving recollection and thought for those of both gradual and sudden capacities.

Abiding in the stages of ordinary beings, both internal and external, because they possess various roots of goodness and have a desire for [the truth], and because they practice through their longing, they attain a semblance of understanding.
This requires the use of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). According to the conceptual understanding they have attained, one further preaches the Dharma for them;
thus, they immediately achieve a clear awakening to the *paramārtha*, even reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), where they cultivate with longing.
When practicing on the second stage (*bhūmi*), to recollect and conceptualize the realm of the second stage is precisely *smṛti-saṃjñā* (recollection-thought).
If one gives rise to true understanding of the second stage, this is precisely *smṛti-saṃjñā-vipaśyanā* (recollection-thought-insight).

By eliminating all dharmas of verbal expression until reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one finally attains liberation from recollection and thought, obtaining constant, quiescent illumination. △ Second, the manifestation of transformation.
Desiring to cause the various roots of goodness to arise, he performs the Buddha-work of teaching the Dharma through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions,
never for a moment ceasing his activity.

This clarifies that he bestows the benefit of both self and others' voices precisely according to the capacities of sentient beings, enabling those with various gradual and sudden faculties to [attain realization].

In order to give rise to various roots of goodness, [the Buddha] manifests various matters concerning his own and others' bodies, various sounds and teachings for himself and others, and various causes, conditions, and parables.
For those with gradual capacities, he employs various causes, conditions, and parables within the four gates of the Tripiṭaka;
furthermore, within each gate, there are further variations. For example, for those who are indolent, he teaches suffering.
The patience of impermanence and so forth taught for those with the conceit of selfhood, as well as the four gates of the Shared Teaching, are likewise thus.
If one addresses those of sudden capacity, such as those of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, each also has its own four gates.

These various and manifold types, such as the thirty-two bodhisattvas each preaching the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality, and the various categories of practices and characteristics within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, are all for this purpose.

To teach the Dharma by employing various metaphors and expressions according to the diverse faculties and capacities [of sentient beings] means that the Buddha-works performed have never been abandoned for even a moment;

this is a summary concluding that [the teaching] is not in vain. As stated above, these various forms and sounds—whether one's own or others'—cause all sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
because they are not for the sake of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) or the limited goals of humans and devas, it is called "the Buddha-works performed."
If one person alone were to attain *nirvāṇa* while others did not, the work of a Buddha would be abandoned;
such abandonment would cause the multitude to fail to obtain true benefit. How then could it be said that "all is real and not false"? Furthermore, why was it previously said:
"While I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not obtain a single dharma as real," and that the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are not ultimate?
The extinction of the two [vehicles] into nirvāṇa is like an empty fist used as a skillful means; thus one knows that they are merely provisional and not yet the ultimate reality.
If those who were previously given the seven provisional teachings had ultimately failed to enter the single true reality, one might say they were truly empty.

However, since these provisional teachings lead them forth so that they do not remain in emptiness but enter the real, we know that what was formerly provisional serves as the real. Therefore, all are indeed real. Is this not so?
That "the Buddha-work of emptiness is never abandoned" is precisely this meaning. △ Second, [the section on] "not ceasing while manifesting cessation," in two parts: first, the direct clarification;
second, first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not cease; second, first, clarifying the permanence of the fruit-stage.
"In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, an extremely long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and I abide eternally without extinction.

This passage contains two meanings: first, it clarifies that the state of fruition is eternal, and because it is eternal, it is without extinction—this is indicated by the four characters [of the phrase].
It is clear that his great power in the future will be majestic and eternally abiding, benefiting all beings. Second, citing the cause to illustrate the result:
"O sons of good family, the lifespan I have achieved while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past is still not exhausted; it shall further double the aforementioned number."

Next, regarding the passage "Furthermore, when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path," this cites the cause to illustrate the result in order to clarify that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding.

Those who rely on this to prove impermanence—claiming that the period prior to the sands of the Ganges was surpassed by the subsequent doubling of that number, and that even the extension of life through supernatural powers is still impermanent—are taking a biased interpretation of the text's meaning and have lost much. The sutra cites the cause to illustrate the result; the result is not a numerical quantity.
Furthermore, a sutra states that the lifespan obtained through long-term cultivation over countless kalpas is not an extension of life through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Why? Because when a Buddha cultivates the perfect cause and attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), they have already attained eternal life;

since this eternal life is inexhaustible, it is already many times greater than the aforementioned number, let alone the state of fruition (*phala*). How can one discard such a fruition that serves as the object of comparison, while stubbornly clinging to the comparison itself?
Because this cause has already been established as being permanent and not impermanent—for example, when one is a crown prince, even the stipends of that time cannot be exhausted;
how much more so when one ascends to the supreme position of honor—how could the use of such stipends ever be exhausted? △ Second, clarifying the proclamation of extinction within the traces.
However, although there is no actual extinction at present, one proclaims that one shall attain extinction.

All three bodies exist simultaneously; thus, while there is no extinction, the meaning of proclaiming extinction is established. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The Dharma is originally unborn, and now it is unextinguished.
This refers to the Dharmakāya, which is non-extinguished. Furthermore, it says: "This is the meaning of quiescent extinction," which is the proclamation of extinction.
What is meant by this? If one has already fully realized [the truth], one does not proclaim extinction; it is only for those who have not yet realized it that one proclaims extinction.
If one says that "illumination is quiescence," this is proclaiming extinction; if one says that "quiescence is illumination," this is proclaiming arising.
As for the Dharmakāya, although it is neither arising nor ceasing, it nonetheless possesses arising and ceasing. If the deluded mind clings to it, then afflictions arise; yet wisdom...
When wisdom extinguishes [delusion] and understanding arises so that the mind is free from defilement, then wisdom is born and afflictions are extinguished;

this extinction of delusion and birth of understanding is what is termed "extinction through impermanence. If understanding arises and delusion is extinguished, this is "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirodha*).

Both of these modes of arising and extinction are distinguished in relation to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). If the two conditions of delusion and understanding were absent, one would not proclaim the existence of such arising and extinction as a retribution.
The body is not extinguished; who is it that proclaims its extinction? Who possesses wisdom, and who possesses afflictions, such that one could say that wisdom can destroy this?
This clarifies that light and darkness do not exclude one another; this is the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) being non-extinguished.

Because sentient beings have not yet realized this, upon hearing it they claim, "This is the Buddha," and thus give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, no longer practicing the Path. Therefore, he further proclaims:
The Way is able to extinguish delusion; when afflictions exist, there is no wisdom, and when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions.
Is it not, then, that wisdom is able to extinguish afflictions? The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not what is extinguished;

that which proclaims "extinction" must be the function of the response, reward, and reality-bodies (*dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, *svabhāvakāya*). Since their essence is without extinction, how could their function ever be exhausted? Thus, the response-body is not extinguished; it is merely—
If sentient beings were to see the Buddha constantly, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence; therefore, he proclaims, "Tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the benefits of manifesting extinction, in two parts: first, the harm that arises if he does not pass away; second, [the specific harms]. First, the harm of not passing away.

The Tathāgata employs these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness;
being poor, lowly, and base, they would become greedily attached to the five desires and fall into the net of discursive thought and false views.

There are those who suffer loss, such as the people previously mentioned who delight in inferior dharmas; because they see the Buddha as always present, they do not plant roots of goodness, remaining poor and lowly, and fail to give rise to the two kinds of goodness.
Thus, there is no benefit. Furthermore, if they do not sever the two evils of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), there is indeed loss.
Greedily clinging to the five desires, they enter into discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); this discursive thought is precisely the delusion of views, and the five desires are—
Because these sentient beings have heavy defilements of thought-afflictions (*vitarka-kleśa*), it is necessary to proclaim their cessation;

if one does not proclaim their cessation, then the two evils will arise and not be extinguished, while the two virtues will be impaired and fail to arise. △ Second, the detailed explanation of non-cessation.
If one perceives the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable, one will give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence,
and thus fail to conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter or a heart of reverence.
Because one gives rise to such arrogance and other such states of mind upon seeing the Tathāgata as eternally present, there is harm, and one cannot generate respect.
Because reverence brings no further benefit, arrogance and self-indulgence increase; because of weariness and indolence, afflictions of thought (*cetanā-kleśa*) arise;

and because the perception of the rarity [of the teaching] does not arise, the understanding of the truths (*satyadarśana*) cannot be produced. Furthermore, without reverence, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) cannot be produced.

For these reasons, it is appropriate that [the Buddhas] manifest their parinirvāṇa; for if one were to see or hear of the three Buddhas without them passing into extinction, all would possess arrogance and self-indulgence.
Yi then claimed that because sentient beings are like Maitreya, and like the one suchness (tathatā), and because this non-dual suchness is equality which is itself reality, pride arises from this;
he thought with arrogance: "All afflictions are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and now likewise do not cease;
what need is there to cultivate the path? He then gave himself over to indulgence and negligence, proclaiming: "This is the meaning of quiescence."
Furthermore, it is heard that all sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi, and the mark of bodhi is the very mark of afflictions;

light and darkness do not exclude one another, yet they manifest the Buddha’s bodhi. When sentient beings hear this, they again give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, no longer cultivating goodness, becoming indolent and negligent.
For the sake of such as these, it is proclaimed that the wisdom of the saṃbhogakāya can extinguish afflictions.

The power of ignorance is great; it can be extinguished by the wisdom of the Buddha’s Bodhi. While the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) does not actually perish, its appearance of perishing is easily understood.

If one proclaims that "the Dharma is fundamentally unborn and now likewise unextinguished," yet insists that one must first extinguish delusions before attaining quiescent extinction (*śānti*), the Sūtra says:
"Wisdom does not extinguish afflictions (*kleśa*); rather, when there is light, there is no darkness. You now possess afflictions in full measure.
How could affliction possibly possess wisdom? One should know that wisdom is able to extinguish obstructive delusions.

When sentient beings hear this proclamation of extinction, they give rise to the thought that the Three Buddhas are difficult to encounter and conceive a mind of reverence. △ Second, the proclamation of extinction is beneficial to all things.
Part one: Praising the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful means, saying that bhikṣus should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
It is difficult for the three Buddhas to appear simultaneously; sentient beings delight in and are attached to inferior dharmas, and their hindrances of views and afflictions are heavy.

If they hear that the three bodies do not perish, they will not cultivate the Path, and thus it is difficult for them to achieve union with the Dharma. △ Second, the explanation of "difficult to encounter."
Why is this? Because among those of little merit, after the passing of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, some may see the Buddha while others do not.
For this reason, I have said: "O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will surely conceive the thought that he is hard to meet, and their hearts will be filled with longing.
Because those who yearn for and thirst after the Buddha plant roots of goodness, the Tathāgata, although not truly extinguished, speaks of "extinction" (parinirvāṇa).
Among those of meager merit, some may see the Buddha and others may not, even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas; yet if they see him three times—
If a person has much goodness and little evil, the Buddha does not proclaim their extinction; such a person sees the Buddha as always residing on Mount Lingyan.

If a person’s karmic obstructions are heavy and their goodness is slight, they do not see the Buddha, for whom the Buddha explains the three bodies (trikāya), which are difficult for sentient beings to comprehend.
Upon hearing this, the person immediately thinks: "Although the three Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, one must nevertheless give rise to goodness."
To extinguish delusions and thereby attain realization is not an easy matter; thus it is said that such an encounter is difficult to find.

Those who harbor a heart of longing and yearning [for the Buddha] clarify that there is no loss in his manifesting birth and extinction. To extinguish the afflictions of views and thoughts is called "no loss," while planting roots of goodness is called "beneficial.
△ Second, the summary of non-futility in three parts: first, clarifying that the Buddhas appear in the five turbidities. Must...
First three, then one; first near, then far.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is thus.

From here below, the second major section is clarified: the conclusion that benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time results in actual benefit for those beings. △ Second, the clarification.
All of these are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings and delivering sentient beings.
△ Third, it clarifies that all are not false or deceptive.
All is real and not false.

△ Second, the explanation by way of parable, which has two parts: first, the opening of the parable; second, the application of the parable. The first part [the opening of the parable] further has two sections:

first, the parable of the skilled physician treating his sons, which illustrates the appropriateness of the responsive transformations throughout the three periods of time; second, the parable of the actual benefit in treating the sons, which illustrates the three periods of time.

The first section, "The Benefit is Not in Vain," is further divided into three parts. First, the analogy of the physician traveling afar illustrates the benefit to sentient beings in the past. This is divided into two parts: first, the analogy of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya);
second, the direct analogy of the response-body. Within the first, there is the leap-over analogy of the response-body.
For example, there is a skilled physician who is wise, discerning, and proficient in medicinal formulas, capable of effectively treating all manner of illnesses.
Now, such a physician may be of ten types: first, one who treats an illness but causes it to increase without alleviation, or even leads to death;

this is likened to the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), who act recklessly in evil and teach others to give rise to false views and sever their roots of goodness, thereby destroying the *dharmakāya*.
First, when both the life-force of wisdom and the physical body perish, this is the second type of illness. It neither increases nor diminishes;

it is like non-Buddhist ascetics who hold views of suffering, such as those who throw themselves from cliffs or leap into fire. Although they practice asceticism and perform virtuous deeds, they do not attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*);
thus, there is no decrease [in defilements], yet because they cannot sever even wholesome roots, there is no increase [in virtue]. Third, the illness diminishes but does not increase; however—

1. That which is treated by worldly physicians such that, once cured, the illness recurs; this corresponds to the non-Buddhists who cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), for they can cause a cure such that it does not recur, yet their treatment is not universal.

2. That which is treated by those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who can only treat one or two types of those with whom they have a karmic connection and cannot universally treat all;
this corresponds to the cessation (*śamatha*) [of suffering]. 5. Although one is able to treat both universally, there is no... [text incomplete]
The skillful arts used to treat pain and suffering are called "clumsy means" (*duṣprajñā*) in the *Śāstra*; this refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

The Bodhisattva’s great compassion extensively treats the six diseases through these marvelous arts. While these arts can treat those who suffer from illness, they cannot treat one who is destined for certain death.

This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), who, by means of the wisdom that realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-jñāna*), only treat those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who undergo cycles of rebirth, but cannot treat those who are not subject to such recurrence.
7. Capable of treating the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who are like scorched seeds;
although they can treat diseases that are difficult to cure, they cannot treat all diseases at once—this is the Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching (prātibheda-śāsana). 8.

Capable of treating all diseases at once, yet unable to restore them to their original state—this is the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Initial Mind in the Perfect Teaching (*vairocana-śāsana*). 9. Capable of universally treating [all diseases] within a single...

All [the other medicines] can also restore [the patient] to their original state, yet they cannot cause them to surpass that original state; this refers to the final stage of mind in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
At the eleventh stage, when treating all illnesses, one is able not only to restore them to their original state but also to cause them to surpass it;

this is the three types of physicians prior to the Tathāgata, which correspond to the "old physician" using milk medicine in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. The latter seven [stages] are all "guest physicians."
Those without skill merely employ dharmas such as impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, like using bitter, pungent, or sour medicines.
Those with skill, having come from afar, cause [the patient] to take milk again; they are ultimately excellent physicians. "Excellent" means "skillful.

Internally possessing the three types of penetration and the five eyes constitutes the eight skills. Having skillfully mastered the nature of the medicine and being adept at treatment, they externally identify the source of the disease.
One who can employ medicine is one whose wisdom consists of the two knowledges of the provisional and the real, deeply understanding the two truths.

One who is discerning and penetrating possesses the five eyes that examine the capacities of beings, distinguishing between sudden and gradual teachings without error. The principles and texts of the twelve divisions of the teaching are profoundly deep;
like clearly refining medicinal prescriptions, they treat the illnesses of sentient beings according to the four *siddhāntas*, just as one skillfully treats various ailments. This is immeasurable.

The commentary states: "The Great Physician, the King of Physicians, is called a 'skilled physician' because he is a great physician. Second, the analogy follows regarding the response of the faculties:
"That man has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even as many as a hundred."
Regarding those who have many children—whether ten śrāvakas, twenty pratyekabuddhas, or a hundred bodhisattvas—the "sons of the Bodhisattva" possess three meanings of "seed-nature.
First, with respect to all sentient beings, they all possess the three kinds of nature-virtue;
since the Buddha-nature is itself the son of the Buddha, it is said in this text: "All sentient beings therein are my sons."
It is said that there are many "sons," which refers approximately to the ten mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); these constitute the hundred "sons.

The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the true cause Buddha-nature (*tathāgata-garbha*), while wisdom (*prajñā*) is the revealing cause Buddha-nature. The remaining nine factors, supporting one another in their arising, belong to the conditional cause Buddha-nature.
When one factor arises, the other nine assist it; in this manner, the hundred are formed. These sons of the Buddha-nature’s virtues are not [merely] conditioned wholesome states.

Because they are not unwholesome and yet permeate both the wholesome and the unwholesome, these ten mental factors, together with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), constitute the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*).
Therefore, the three causes of the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) all belong to the "True Cause" of the Buddha's children. Second, regarding being a child of the Buddha through past connections:
for example, when the sixteen princes preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* again, those who heard the Dharma also gave rise to a slight understanding. This is [the meaning].
That which constitutes the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in the past through subtle cultivation is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*);

taking the True Nature as the foundation, these three causes together belong to the conditioning cause, which awakens the understanding of the single reality today. Therefore, the "karmic connection established in the past" serves as the conditioning cause;
"Buddha-sons" refers to the thirty children within the burning house, and this pertains to each of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

At the moment of arising, they already possess the remaining nine [stages] and, because they still possess the hundredfold faith (*śraddhā*), they are able to form a karmic connection as children of the Buddha.
Third, the children of the "enabling cause" (*pariniṣpattihetu*) are those who today hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and abide within true wisdom;
they have the firm resolve that "I shall certainly become a Buddha," and they understand that the Dharma of the Śrāvakas is the king of all sutras, having been born from the mouth of the Buddha.

Because they share in the Buddha-dharma, they are called true children; this also possesses three causal natures. Now that the Buddha-nature has been clearly revealed, it is seen that all belong to the *vidyā-hetu* (revealing cause).

Regarding the meaning of the "hundred sons of the Buddha," one takes the number ten and applies it to the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśala*), and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are entered into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
Therefore, the *tathatā-hetu* (original cause) pervades both the fundamental and the derivative; this is clarified in this text.

The hundred sons did not take [the medicine], yet they were saved because their father took it; since the father was among his subordinates, they did not fail to submit their hearts. This is clarified within the section on taking medicine.
△ Second, the analogy for manifesting extinction:
due to certain circumstances, he traveled far away to another country.
The analogy of departing for another land due to some business matter illustrates the manifestation of extinction within past responsive transformations.
△ Second, the analogy of returning and then departing again illustrates present responsive transformations, consisting of two parts: first, the analogy of the arousal of spiritual capacity.
Later, the sons drank another person's poisonous medicine; when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disoriented, rolling about on the ground.
The sons drinking poison later is a metaphor for those of superior capacity whose responses are interconnected with the teaching:

because they see that sentient beings have meager virtue and heavy defilements, and thus after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa delight in and become attached to the teachings of false teachers within the triple world, it is said they "drink another person's poisonous medicine."
This means that because one wanders to other lands, transmigrates through the various realms of existence, and falls within the triple world, it is said that "one wallows upon the ground.
△ Second, the analogy for the manifested transformation [body], in two parts: first, manifesting birth where there is no birth; second, first, the analogy for the benefit of form and sound;
first, the benefit of form.
At that time, their father returned home; those sons who had drunk the poison—whether they had lost their original minds or not—saw their father from afar and were all greatly delighted.
They bowed down, knelt, and inquired after his well-being, saying, "We have returned safely.
Out of our folly, we mistakenly took this poison; we pray you will save us and grant us life once more."
The father’s return is like my attaining *sambodhi* at a young age after leaving home;

the sons drinking poison and departing is like receiving the teachings of false teachers with increasing physical and mental conviction—this is called "drinking poison. Losing one's mind refers to those born with inferior faculties and conditions who lose their sanity;
gaining one's mind refers to those born with superior faculties and conditions who do not lose their sanity. Furthermore, there are those who lose their minds.

Those who are greedily attached to the three realms lose the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles previously planted. For the sake of such people, [the Buddha] does not teach extinction, yet speaks of extinction;
they do not lose their resolve. Although those who do not lose their resolve are attached to the five desires, they do not lose the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles.

For the sake of such people, [the Buddha] does not manifest birth, yet manifests birth. Because their goodness is strong and their evil is light, upon seeing the Buddha they are immediately able to cultivate the Way and sever their fetters.
It is like a son who sees his father; though he seeks medicine and his illness is cured, he treats the good lightly and the evil heavily.

Even if he has met the Buddha, he seeks only rescue and protection rather than practicing the Way. It is like a son who sees his father; though he can seek rescue, he is unwilling to take the medicine.
For this son’s sake, the father cries out, "He must die. Those who see from afar understand that when a Buddha appears in the world, sentient beings are likewise [in such a state].
Because seeing the physical body (rūpakāya) is obstructed by the barriers of views and afflictions, one cannot personally attend upon the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); thus it is said to be "remote.

Whenever one sees or hears of a Buddha’s appearance, there are matters of joy and reverence; examples such as the Brahma King’s invitation found in various sutras are all expressions of seeking salvation.
△ Second, the benefit of the voice (ghoṣa-anugraha), in two parts: first, the analogy of the Buddha accepting an invitation.
He turned the wheel of the Two Truths.

Seeing that his sons were suffering in such a manner, the father sought excellent medicinal herbs according to the methods of various scriptures— herbs that were fully endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor—
and having ground and sifted them together, he gave them to his sons to take as medicine.
The "scriptural formulas" (*sūtra*) are the teachings of the twelve divisions of the canon; the "medicinal herbs" are the eighty thousand dharma-gates elucidated by those teachings.
From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions, and from them even emerges *nirvāṇa*—this refers to the emergence of the gradual and sudden medicinal herbs.
To emerge directly from the Buddha as the twelve divisions refers to the emergence of the sudden medicinal herbs. From the Buddha emerges the *sūtra*.

In this context, the color of the gradually emerging medicinal herbs is a metaphor for *śīla* (precepts); the precepts prevent misconduct of body and speech, and their characteristics are clearly manifest.
The fragrance is a metaphor for the merit of *samādhi* (concentration), which perfumes all things. The flavor is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom), which is able to attain the flavor of principle.
These—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—are precisely the Eightfold Noble Path; by cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one can perceive the Buddha-nature. Furthermore, "color" is *prajñā*.
The color that illuminates and comprehends the *dharmatā* is distinct and unimpeded; fragrance is the liberation of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) which is free from foul odors;
and flavor is the principle-taste of the *dharmakāya*. These three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; they are called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*).

By practicing according to the teaching, one attains entry into this treasury. It is said that through the power of the emptiness-samādhi of the Three Vehicles, it is like pounding the formless and sifting the non-existent.

To act as in the compounding [of medicine]: each of the three samādhis—śīla, samādhi, and prajñā—is fully present. Furthermore, the contemplation of emptiness is like pounding, the contemplation of the provisional is like sifting, and the middle-way contemplation is like compounding. These three contemplations are each inseparable from śīla, samādhi, and prajñā.

Bestowing this Dharma upon sentient beings of both gradual and sudden capacities and causing them to practice it is called "making them take the medicine. △ Second, the parable of admonition and exhortation, in two parts. First, the exhortation.
[The Buddha] entered the gate and spoke these words: "This great medicinal herb is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor; you all should take it.
△ Second, the Gate of Admonition.
It swiftly eliminates suffering and affliction so that no further calamities remain;
it employs both the teachings of admonition and exhortation to cause all sentient beings to take the medicine of the Dharma. △ Second, the analogy for how the benefit is not in vain.
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds saw that this excellent medicine was both fine in color and fragrance, and they immediately took it;
their illnesses were completely eliminated and they were healed.

This is a metaphor for the fact that the benefit received by the superior [type of person] is not in vain. Regarding the "not in vain," there are two parts: first, the statement that it is not in vain; second, the explanation of why it is not in vain. Now, it is said:
Among those sons, those whose minds were not lost took the medicine and their illnesses were cured; this is an analogy for what was stated above as being entirely real and not false.
"Not false" and "not fabricated" serve as the analogy. △ Second, the manifestation of extinction where there is no actual extinction. Part one: the analogy of the imminent death.
Part two: the cause for proclaiming extinction.

The other sons, whose minds were deranged, though they rejoiced upon seeing their father arrive and inquired after him and sought treatment for their illness, would accept the medicine he gave them yet refused to take it.
Why was this? Because the toxic vapors had penetrated deeply and they had lost their original minds;
thus, they found that medicine of excellent color and fragrance to be unpleasant. The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable, having been struck by poison."
Their minds are entirely inverted; though they see me and rejoice, seeking a remedy, they are unwilling to take such excellent medicine.
The reason for proclaiming death is that the son does not take it; this is like those of inferior merit who see the Buddha as always present, yet only increase their arrogance and self-indulgence.

Regarding the manifestation of extinction, there are two points: first, that his fundamental reality does not extinguish; second, that although he is not extinguished, he manifests extinction and does not remain.
Regarding the reasons for manifesting parinirvāṇa: among the benefits of proclaiming parinirvāṇa, the primary reason is now explained through analogy.
It is precisely because sentient beings have meager merit that they see the Buddha as eternally present and fail to practice;
this is like being unwilling to take medicine. △ Second, the formal proclamation that he ought to die, in two parts: first, the consideration of whether to depart or remain.
I shall now employ skillful means to cause you to take this medicine.
It is like proclaiming "extinction" when there is no extinction. △ Second, proclaiming that one should die:
he then spoke these words: "You should all know that I am now old and decrepit, and the time for my death has arrived; this is a fine and excellent medicine."

"I remain here now; you may take [this medicine] and consume it, and do not worry that it will not cure you. Having given this instruction, he went again to another country and sent a messenger back to announce:
"Your father has already died"—this is an analogy for the manifestation of his passing away.
"The period of transformation is nearing its end; the time of death has arrived," means that he was about to enter *nirvāṇa* and left behind these scriptures.

Because the teaching remains, it is said that this is a "good medicine. To now remain here and subsequently go to another land is precisely the meaning of what was stated above: "I vow to see and protect you from afar while in another land.
This refers to the act of dispatching messengers, or taking the great voice that proclaims universally within *nirvāṇa* as one's messenger.
Alternatively, one may employ supernatural powers, or relics, or the teachings of the scriptures to lead sentient beings.

Now, by means of the four reliances, I speak to sentient beings, saying: "The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; he has left behind only this Dharma. I now proclaim and propagate it; you should receive and practice it.
If, in future times, sentient beings lacked these four reliances to transmit and expound the sutras and the Dharma, how could they possibly [attain liberation] on their own?
Knowing that the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa, [the disciples] employ the four reliances; these are the messengers. △ Second, the analogy of the sons being awakened, in two parts:
first, the benefit of manifesting extinction.
At that time, the sons heard that their father had passed away, and their hearts were filled with great grief and distress, thinking: "If our father were still alive..."
"Out of compassion for us, you were able to provide protection; yet now you have abandoned us to perish far away in another land.
△ Second, the response of future sentient beings:
"Reflecting upon myself, I am solitary and exposed, with no one left to rely upon; constantly harboring this grief, my mind was finally awakened, and I realized the nature of this medicine."
Upon taking it, its color, fragrance, taste, and aroma immediately cause all toxic illnesses to be cured.
Because sentient beings after my parinirvāṇa will awaken, take this medicine, and practice as a causal condition, they will be able to evoke future manifestations of my response-body;
as the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Teaching Left Behind) says: "For those not yet delivered, create the causal conditions for their deliverance," and there are also those who attain it in the present.
The *Guan Puxian Pusa Xingfa Jing* (Sutra on the Visualization of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra) states:

"Through diligent and arduous practice, one attains the vision of the emanations of Śākyamuni, the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, the Buddha Bhadra of the East, and the seven World-Honored Ones of the past Buddhas. Regarding those who are "solitary and exposed, having no one to rely upon," one who loses their father in childhood is called "solitary" (*gu*).
As the poem says: "Without a father, what can one rely upon? Without a mother, what can one depend on? This is like a child who has lost their kin.
They are impoverished and distressed, wandering long distances, eating in the wind and sleeping in the dew, appearing in a state of utter destitution.
