△ Third, the analogy of seeking and subsequently returning illustrates the future manifestations of transformation.
When the father heard that his son had fully recovered, he immediately returned and allowed him to see him all at once.

This is the power of majestic authority to benefit beings in the future; that the father heard of the son’s recovery and was moved by the circumstances to let him see him is the manifestation of future responsive transformations, which will subsequently provide dual benefit through both form and voice. △ Second, the treatment.
"Son of Good Family, this analogy further clarifies that the benefits of the three periods of time are not in vain.
What do you think, sons of good family? Is there anyone who could say that this skilled physician has committed the fault of falsehood?
No, World-Honored One."
This analogy of the non-empty cloth illustrates that the benefits [bestowed] throughout the three periods of time are not in vain. △ Second, combining the analogies into three parts;
first, combining the past benefit of sentient beings.
The Buddha said: "I, likewise, since attaining Buddhahood, have been for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of years..."
For the sake of sentient beings throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
△ Second, combining [past and future] to benefit beings in the present:
by the power of skillful means, he says that he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The text is abbreviated and does not accord with the future. △ Third, the benefit of beings is not in vain.
Furthermore, there is no one who can rightfully charge me with the fault of falsehood. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the two verses in verse form: first, the verse on the Dharma-exposition; second, the verse on the parable-exposition. The first section [of the Dharma-exposition] further has two parts:
first, benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time; second, [the specific benefits]. First, regarding the past: first, the verse on having long since attained enlightenment.
Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
△ Second, the verse on benefiting sentient beings in the interim:
Throughout these immeasurable kalpas since then, I have constantly preached the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
△ [The Buddha] dwells permanently in this place.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests parinirvāṇa through skillful means, yet in reality he does not pass away; he dwells permanently here preaching the Dharma.
I dwell permanently here, and by means of various supernormal powers, cause deluded sentient beings to fail to see me even though they are near.
△ Second, two verses concerning the present; the first verse concerns the non-arising yet manifest arising.
When the multitude sees my parinirvāṇa and makes extensive offerings to my relics, they all harbor longing and give rise to a heart of thirsty aspiration.
Once sentient beings have gained faith and submission, being upright in nature and gentle in mind, they desire with single-mindedness to see the Buddha, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain.
△ Second, the verse on non-extinction appearing as extinction:
At that time, I said to sentient beings, "I am always here and do not pass away; it is only through the power of skillful means that I appear to pass away, yet I do not truly pass away."
"In other lands, there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight in [the Dharma]; I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them.
You have not heard this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa."
△ The three verses concerning the future; the first verse concerns the response to the conditions of future sentient beings.
Because I see that sentient beings are submerged in suffering and affliction, I do not manifest my body to them so as to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning;
once their hearts are filled with devotion and admiration, I then appear and preach the Dharma for them.
The following ten and a half verses elaborate upon the four characters "eternally abiding and non-extinguished" mentioned above regarding the future.

This commentary contains four intended meanings; first, one and a half lines clarify the responsive conditions of sentient beings in the future. Second, [the remaining lines] eulogize the eternally abiding and non-extinguished nature.
By such supernormal powers, throughout incalculable eons, I shall always remain on Vulture Peak Mountain and in other dwelling places.
When sentient beings see this world-system being consumed by the great fires at the end of an eon, my own land will remain peaceful and secure, filled with devas and humans.
Its gardens, groves, halls, and pavilions will be adorned with various jewels; its precious trees will abound in flowers and fruits, providing a place of joy and recreation for all sentient beings.
The various devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform manifold musical offerings, raining down *māndārava* flowers upon the Buddha and the great assembly.

This [land] on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is called the Land of True Retribution (*sambhoga-kṣetra*), while the other various dwelling places are called the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-kṣetra*).
This is the meaning of the aforementioned "other lands. That it is filled with devas and humans refers to those at the stage of the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*).
The "Ten Stages of Man" refers to the celestial drum being struck by the gods, which is the unasked self-proclamation [of the Buddha].
The *mandārava* flowers represent the stages of the worthy and the sage. △ Third, the explanation of the non-perception of causes and conditions.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes perceive it as being utterly consumed by flames, filled with such sorrow, fear, and various afflictions;
these sentient beings of evil karma, due to the conditions of their misdeeds, shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem for incalculable kalpas.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the causes and conditions for being able to see [the Buddha].
All those who cultivate merit and are gentle, mild, and upright shall all see my body here preaching the Dharma.
At times, for this assembly, I speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan; for those who see the Buddha only after a long time, I speak of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of its insight illumines the immeasurable, and this lifespan of countless kalpas was obtained through long-cultivated practice.
II. The verses state that all is real and not false:
"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are real and not false."
△ Second, the two verses on the illustrative explanation. Part one: the first verse opens the analogy. 3. First, the verse on the past:
"Like a physician with skillful means.
△ Second, the verse on the present.
To discipline his wayward son, he spoke of death while actually remaining alive.
△ Third, the verse on non-falsity:
none are able to say it is false.
△ Second, combining the analogies into three parts: First, the verse combines the past:
"I am also the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer.
△ Second, the verse combines the present.

For the sake of ordinary beings who, due to their inversions, speak of actual extinction because they perceive a self through the view of permanence, and who thus give rise to a mind of arrogance and indulgence,
becoming heedless and attached to the five desires so as to fall into the evil realms— I always know whether sentient beings practice the Path or do not practice it,
and according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various dharmas for them.
△ The three verses combined show that [the teaching] is not in vain.
Each time he forms this thought: "By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter the unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?
By opening the three to reveal the one, and by opening the near to reveal the far, I desire to cause sentient beings to swiftly enter the Buddha-way; this matter must surely [be accomplished]."
It is not in vain that they have attained it.
△ Second, the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharma-body, in two parts.
First, the presentation of the chapter title: *The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Seventeen: The Analysis of Merit*.
The Buddha spoke of the lifespan because his disciples of the two periods attained various benefits; thus it is called "Merit.
Because the depth and shallowness within that merit differ, it is called the "Chapter on Distinctions. This text constitutes the second section, the bestowal of predictions, within the Root Teaching.
△ Second, the general exposition of the sūtra text by way of bestowing the prediction of the Dharma-body. Part one: The general introduction by the Sūtra-reciter.

At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan being so long and vast—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—and that immeasurable sentient beings had attained great benefit.
The "Sūtra-author" (jīngjiā) refers to the Venerable Ānanda, who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
"Preface" (xù) is synonymous with "narrative" (xù); it essentially recounts the events of that time. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s analysis.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya Ajita:

"When I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty million *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
furthermore, a thousand times more Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining."
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech;
again, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the immeasurable revolving dhāraṇī of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis;
and there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world-systems.
There were also two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a medium-sized world-system, who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
there were further bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a small thousand-world system, who would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight births;
and there were bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms of four sets of four-continent worlds.
Four hundred thousand *mahāsattvas* shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after four births;
furthermore, there are *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* numbering as many as the atoms in three sets of four continents who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after three births;
and there are *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* numbering as many as the atoms in two sets of four continents who shall attain it after two births.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within one four-continent world-system who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in their next life;
and there were sentient beings equal in number to the atoms within eight worlds who all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s discernment: because the Buddha’s words are perfect and subtle, they cannot be explained using provisional stages.

Therefore, while the preceding section revealed the opening, showing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this present chapter—wherein the path is increased and birth is diminished—all explanations are based on the perfect stages (*yuan-wei*).
As for those who resolve their minds in the eight worlds below, these are people of the six faculties’ purity who have first entered the stage of the ten faiths (*shixin*).

Therefore, the *Ratnarājasūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva of the Ten Wholesome Paths who gives rise to the Great Mind forever parts from the ocean of the suffering wheel of the triple world"—this is precisely that meaning.
Because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"In the first stage, the Abode of Initial Resolve, one generates all [resolves] by generating a single resolve; one attains the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body."
Manifesting in various forms is precisely this meaning: by hearing and retaining the *dhāraṇī*, one enters the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*);

by attaining the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), one enters the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*); by attaining the *dhāraṇī* of infinite revolution, one enters the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) and becomes non-regressive;
by attaining purity, one enters the Second Ground; and by [attaining] the eight births, one enters the Fourth Ground. (The Third Ground is reached through seven [births]).
One birth leads to the fifth stage; six births lead to the sixth stage; five births lead to the seventh stage; four births lead to the eighth stage;
three births lead to the ninth stage; two births lead to the tenth stage; and one birth leads to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the Vajra-mind.

This is discussed solely in terms of the increase of wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*). In terms of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), it is discussed as decrease. In terms of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is discussed as arising; in terms of the non-... [the text is incomplete].
The treatise on illumination explains the analogy of the moon in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: from the first day to the fifteenth day, the light and color gradually increase;
from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, the light and color gradually decrease.

While discussing the body of the moon as a whole, this increase and decrease serve as an analogy for the wisdom and abandonment (jñāna-prahāṇa) of the Dharmakāya. Alternatively, it may be understood that a single person possesses these eight qualities at one time.
The increase or decrease of [the number of] kalpas may be for one lifetime, eight lifetimes, or immeasurable lifetimes;
it may be for a single thought-moment, eight thought-moments, or immeasurable thought-moments; or it may be for as many people as there are atoms in a multitude of worlds—it is likewise so.
Therefore, one must not restrict this by means of the arising of causes or the arising of effects, nor can one be separated from the expansion of wisdom and the severance of ignorance.

To explain this: the number of those who attain the Way through the Root Gate is several times greater than that found in other sutras; it is not merely a matter of numbers, but because their cultivation has been long-standing.
From the original manifestation of the Trace, he has guided and drawn them in everywhere; having encountered him repeatedly during the intervening periods, they have reached maturity time and again.

Now, in this world of the five flavors, he tames them at every stage, gathering them together and bringing them back to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It is like a farming family in the springtime.
Sowing in summer, cultivating and weeding in spring, harvesting in autumn, and storing in winter—once the harvest is gathered, it is like picking up ears of grain after the main crop has been reaped;
from the *Lotus Sūtra* onward, those who attain the Way are like this. △ Third, the offerings of the assembly at the three times of day.
When the Buddha spoke thus of how these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained the great benefit of the Dharma, mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the void,
scattering over the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees,
as well as scattering over Śākyamuni seated upon the lion throne within the stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
The Buddha, as well as the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who has long since entered parinirvāṇa, also scattered [flowers] over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly;
furthermore, they rained down fine powdered sandalwood and aloeswood incense, while in the midst of space celestial drums resounded of their own accord with profound and far-reaching sounds,
and there fell thousands of kinds of celestial garments, hanging necklaces, pearl necklaces, and maṇi jewels.
Necklaces and wish-fulfilling jewel necklaces pervaded the nine directions;
precious incense burners burned priceless incense that spontaneously reached everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly.
Above each Buddha, various bodhisattvas held banners and canopies, ascending in succession as far as the Brahma Heaven. These bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses of praise.
He praised the Buddhas.
Those in the assembly who heard the profound and far-reaching Dharma during this time obtained great benefit; desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they made offerings.
This too was a symbolic act intended to manifest their realization and understanding of the superior traces of the Gate of the Trace. The Bodhisattvas likewise attained awakening.
Because the Great Matter was not yet complete, I did not present offerings;

now that the Root Chapter has concluded, Maitreya generally declares his understanding and realization, clarifying that the various bodhisattvas hold up banners and canopies, ascending in succession as far as the Brahma Heaven.

"Banner" (dhvaja) signifies the meaning of turning; "canopy" (chattra) signifies the meaning of covering; "earth" (bhūmi) signifies the meaning of the beginning; and "Brahma" (brahman) signifies the meaning of purity. Wisdom and severance proceed in successive stages.
The successive transformations of compassion cover both the high and the low, the deep and the shallow, without losing their proper order, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven;
they manifest the Bodhisattvas' increase in the Path and decrease in birth, approaching the stage of Subtle Enlightenment and culminating in Ultimate Purity.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses.
△ Third, Maitreya’s general expression of understanding and realization, in three parts: first, a verse on the assembly’s attainment of understanding.
The Buddha has preached this rare Dharma, never heard before; the World-Honored One possesses great power and an immeasurable, incalculable lifespan.
When the sons of the Buddha hear the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition, those who attain the benefit of the Dharma are filled with joy that pervades their entire bodies.
△ Second, the verses on the classification of the Tathāgatas:
Some abide in the stage of non-retrogression; some have attained dhāraṇīs; some possess the dharanis of ten billion revolutions of unimpeded eloquence;
and there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a great trichiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each of whom is capable of turning the pure wheel of Dharma;
there are Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, who will each attain Buddhahood after eight more births;
and there are Bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms in four, three, two, or one such world-system of four continents, who will attain Buddhahood after a corresponding number of births.
Or there were Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world-system, who had only one more birth remaining before they would attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
such beings, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan was so long, attained immeasurable, untainted, and pure karmic fruits.

Furthermore, there were beings as numerous as the atoms in eight world-systems who, upon hearing the Buddha speak of his lifespan, all resolved their minds upon supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The World-Honored One has taught immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas that bring great benefit, as boundless as space.
Those who attain the fruit of retribution—immeasurable, outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and pure—are distinguished from those of the two vehicles by being "immeasurable.

Because they are produced by wondrous causes, they are called "pure. Because they are unobstructed lands, they are called "fruit of retribution. Thus they differ [from the fruits of the two vehicles].
The two vehicles have no such retribution. △ Third, the verse on the offerings of the assembly at that time:

Heavenly Māndārava and Mahāmāndārava flowers rained down; Śakra and Brahmā came from as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges, raining sandalwood and aloeswood that fell in profusion and disorder, like birds flying through the air, descending to scatter as offerings before all the Buddhas.
In the midst of the void, celestial drums spontaneously produced wondrous sounds; ten million kinds of celestial garments whirled down from above;
and various exquisite incense burners made of precious jewels burned priceless incense, which naturally pervaded everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.

The assembly of great bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, of wondrous height and beauty numbering ten trillion varieties, which reached successively up to the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled banners were suspended with excellent pennants, and likewise, ten million verses were chanted in praise of the Tathāgatas.
Such various matters as these had never before occurred. Hearing that the lifespan of the Buddhas is immeasurable, all were filled with joy.
The names of the Buddhas resound throughout the ten directions, extensively benefiting sentient beings; all are endowed with roots of goodness to assist their unsurpassed resolve.
△ Section on the Propagation of the Teaching consists of eleven chapters and a half, divided into two parts:

first, from this point until the *Anuparīndanā* (Entrustment) chapter, three chapters and a half clarify the profound merit of propagating the sūtra and provide earnest exhortations for its circulation; second, from the *Rddhyabhisaṃskāra* (Supernatural Powers) chapter downward, eight chapters clarify the entrustment and propagation.
Within the first part, there are again three sections: first, this half-chapter together with the *Prasādapratilambha* (Attaining Joy) chapter clarify the beginning.

Section Two: Exhorting the Circulation by Way of the Merit of the Causes. This consists of two parts: 1. From the "Chapter on the Merit of the Dharma Master," clarifying the exhortation to circulate [the teaching] by way of the merit of the initial fruit; 2.
The "Chapter on Never-Despising," which cites the offenses of those who believe or slander and the blessings of those who have faith, thereby providing evidence for the exhortation to circulate.

The first of these [two parts] further divides into two: A. The four types of faith in the present; B. The five chapters following the extinction [of the Buddha]. The first of these [four] further divides into four, the first of which is a single thought-moment.
Regarding the first of the two [sections on] faith and understanding, the initial prose section has three parts.
First, the persons are introduced: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya Ajita:
"If there are sentient beings who, having heard that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are even able to give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding..."

"One who possesses faith and understanding in a single thought-moment" refers to one who, upon hearing the Dharma wherever it may be, attains sudden and clear illumination; who enters according to the words without any obstruction;
who believes that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; and who further believes that the Buddha-dharma is not separate from any dharma.
Such a person realizes that neither the Buddha-dharma nor any dharma can be grasped, yet they perceive all dharmas as the Buddha-dharma.
It is one yet three, and three yet one. It is also practicing non-ways to penetrate the Buddha-way;
practicing the Buddha-way to penetrate all ways; not attaining the Buddha-way while penetrating all ways;
and all ways being non-existent yet existent, and existent yet non-existent—neither existent nor non-existent.
Just as the road before a gate leads unimpededly to all directions—east, west, south, and north—so too are the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
whatever they encounter is likewise thus. To be without doubt is called faith (*śraddhā*);
to be clear and lucid is called understanding (*adhimukti*). This is the mind of single-minded faith and understanding. If one sits in contemplation accordingly, [it will be realized].
When one’s contemplation suddenly opens up and one attains penetration into the Three Truths, it is likewise so.
Such faith and understanding is called the stage of the Iron Wheel. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: this is not yet the full Iron Wheel, but rather the initial mind of the Ten Faiths;
because that person has not yet attained the purity of the six sense organs, it is not the formal position of the Iron Wheel. △ Second, the explanation.
Regarding the two types of merit, first is the general discussion of their immeasurability:
the merit obtained is without limit.
△ Second, the comparative measurement of their quantity has two parts; first, the five perfections (pāramitās) are cited as the basis for comparison.
If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
practice the five pāramitās— namely, the pāramitā of dāna, the pāramitā of śīla, the pāramitā of kṣānti, the pāramitā of vīrya,
and the pāramitā of dhyāna— excluding prajñā, for eighty million nayutas of kalpas;

Pāramitā. Since *prajñā* (wisdom) is the correct wisdom of the present, it is said that [the others] exclude *prajñā*. Question: If *prajñā* is excluded, then why are the five not called "crossings" (*pāra*)? Answer:
Because they are all practiced for the sake of seeking the Buddha-wisdom, even when they reach the limits of giving and precepts, they may also be called "crossings. This is because...
This is the meaning of the sequence. △ Second, the formal comparison:
compared with these merits, the former merits do not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, one hundred-thousandth, or one hundred-thousand-billionth part;
they are beyond reach even by calculation or analogy.
"Comparing" (*kalpa*) refers to analogy; "measuring" (*māna*) refers to measurement. It means that upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, one believes deeply without doubt;
furthermore, upon hearing this sutra, in a single thought one's afflictions are dissolved and the mind reaches its destination—this is the gateway of "tending toward.
Considering its benefits and merit, they are by no means small; neither ordinary wisdom nor the mundane mind can fathom them, so one must rely on parables and analogies to compare and measure them.
Only after such measurement can one understand its resemblance. △ Third, the stage of non-retrogression in practice:
If a son of good family possesses such merit, it is impossible for him to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Six of the [ten] minds are subject to regression, while seven are non-regressive. Upon reaching the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan chu zhu xin*), one is immediately non-regressive.
Hearing of the lifespan and merits [of the Buddha] provides external support, while the internal cultivation of perfect, compliant faith and understanding provides internal nourishment;

thus, one does not regress. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There are bodhisattvas who regress and those who do not; there are those with Māras and those without Māras"—this refers precisely to this principle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
II. Verses in Praise (of the preceding prose), Part Three: First, the verses praise the comparison of quantities.
If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, for eighty quadrillion nayutas of kalpas, they practice the five pāramitās.

Thereupon, throughout these kalpas, they made offerings of food, drink, exquisite garments, and bedding, as well as sandalwood monasteries adorned with gardens and groves, to the Buddhas, the disciples of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Having performed such various and sublime acts of giving for the duration of all these kalpas, they dedicated the merit toward the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if one maintains the prohibitive precepts with purity and without flaw while seeking the unsurpassed path, one is praised by all Buddhas.
If one practices patience and dwells in the stage of gentleness, even if various evils are inflicted upon them, their mind remains unshakable.
Even if those who have attained dharmas harbor arrogance and slight or harass them for this reason, they are likewise able to endure it.
Furthermore, if one applies diligent effort with a mind that is always firm and resolute, remaining single-mindedly without indolence for immeasurable billions of kalpas;
and if, throughout countless kalpas, one dwells in secluded places, whether sitting or walking, removing drowsiness and constantly gathering the mind— by these causes and conditions,
one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) and abide for eight billion million kalpas with a mind that is undisturbed.
Maintaining this single-minded merit and aspiration, they seek the unsurpassed path; may I attain all-knowledge and exhaust the limits of all meditative concentrations.
Such persons practice these various merits as described above throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
△ Second, the verse summarizing the characteristics of the person [who hears this]:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing my teaching on the lifespan, believe it for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that [of the former];
if a person is entirely free from all doubt and regret, and with a profound mind believes it for even a brief instant, their merit shall be as such."
△ The third verse concerns non-retrogression in the stages of practice:
"Those bodhisattvas who have practiced the path for immeasurable eons and hear me speak of this lifespan will be able to believe and accept it.
Such persons as these shall receive this sutra upon their heads. May I, in the future, possess long life to deliver sentient beings."
"Just as today the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, preaches the Dharma with the fearless lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment,
so too shall we preach our own lifespans in the same manner when we sit at the site of enlightenment in all future ages,
being honored by all. Those who possess a profound mind— pure, upright, learned, capable of upholding [the teachings], and able to interpret the Buddha’s words according to their meaning— "
Such persons as these have no doubt regarding this;

those who have practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas have long cultivated the various perfections (*pāramitās*). "May I [attain this] in the future" expresses the aspiration of compassion and mercy.
By virtue of having long practiced and made vows, they hear this sutra and attain faith and understanding; now, at the very beginning of this first chapter, they first hear this sutra.
The merit of mindfulness, faith, and understanding, even if practiced for a long time, surpasses that [of merely hearing]. △ Second, a brief explanation of the meaning of the words, in two parts:
first, indicating the characteristics of the person.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there be one who hears of the Buddha’s lifespan being long and far-reaching and understands its meaning and intent...
This is the second chapter. In the preceding [chapter], there was only faith and understanding, but one was not yet able to expound and explain;

since explaining involves names and numbers and requires proficiency in terminology, this present chapter possesses these qualities. Therefore, it is said that one "explains and elucidates for others," and based on this predominant activity, it is named the Second Chapter.
△ Second, the comparative evaluation.
The merit attained by this person is limitless and can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
By the power of their teaching, they can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of both themselves and others. △ Third, extensively explaining it for others, in two parts:
first, identifying the characteristics of such a person.
How much more so for those who extensively hear this sutra, whether they cause others to hear it, uphold it themselves, or cause others to uphold it;
whether they write it themselves, or cause others to write it; or if they make offerings to the scroll with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps.
This is the third chapter: hearing extensively, understanding extensively, explaining it extensively to others, and making extensive offerings.
△ Second, the evaluation:
the merit of this person is immeasurable and boundless, capable of generating all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By making offerings to external resources, one causes internal wisdom to enter swiftly; thus, one is able to give rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Fourth, the accomplishment of profound faith through contemplation:
"Ajita, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears me speak of the long duration of my lifespan and believes it with a deep heart..."
Upon understanding this, one sees that the Buddha is always present on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as he preaches the Dharma;
furthermore, one sees this Sahā world with its ground of lapis lazuli, level and even, with the Jambūnada gold marking the eightfold paths,
rows of jewel trees, and all the terraces and towers made entirely of precious gems— such is his awakening.

If all the assembly of bodhisattvas dwells within this, and if there are those capable of contemplating in such a manner, one should know that this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding.

This is the fourth stage; having fully prepared for the preceding three stages, one further cultivates contemplative practice, enters meditative absorption, and achieves the mental image through wisdom.

The appearance of the two lands—the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*) and the Land of True Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*)—where one sees the Buddha together with the assembly of bhikṣus constantly residing on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, is the mark of the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder. Furthermore, seeing the Sahā world consisting purely of bodhisattvas is the mark of the Land of True Retribution.

The first two chapters constitute the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); the extensive hearing and extensive exposition therein constitute the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).

The stage where the contemplative visualization is perfected is the stage of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); progressing from shallow to deep, it constitutes the six roots of purity and the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
△ Second, the extinction [of the five grades] after death. Part one: Listing the five grades and evaluating the merits of four grades. Part two:
Evaluating the merits of the first grade by means of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). The initial text further divides into two sections; the first is the long prose section (five).
First, one should immediately give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, if, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one hears this sutra and does not disparage it but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy,
you should know that this is already a sign of profound faith and understanding.
Now, first we shall set forth the five grades to measure the merits of the four grades, followed by the grade of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) to measure the merits of the first grade.
Question: Why is this so? Answer: The four grades are measured in a general way, while the first grade is measured in detail.

Once it has been measured in detail, the superiority of the others can be understood by implication; there would be no need for the Buddha to laboriously provide elaborate explanations in the text. Such is the case here.

Regarding these five grades: first, one simply gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; second, one further adds personal upholding, recitation, and chanting; third, one further adds exhorting others to uphold, recite, and chant;
fourth, one further adds the concurrent practice of the six pāramitās; and fifth, one further adds the correct practice of the six pāramitās.

These five types of persons, in general discussion, all practice for themselves and transform others, as the subsequent text states: "Fifty people [of these grades] successively [transform one another]."

The *Xiāngjiào* (Teaching on Characteristics) is correct in this regard: since both possess the general title of "disciple" for their own practice (*zìxíng*), they both possess the general title of "Dharma Master" (*fǎshī*) for transforming others (*huàtā*).

Discussing these two individuals separately, there are only those who practice for themselves; the three [other] types fully possess the method of transforming others and are thus called Dharma Masters.

As for the former, their names reside in the "three" but not in the "five. Since their own practice is universal, they are all collectively called disciples; this is indicated at the beginning of the first chapter.

As for "merely a person," the detailed evaluation will be discussed later. △ Second, adding the practice of personally upholding, reading, and reciting. Part one: indicating the characteristics of the person.
"How much more so for those who read, recite, uphold, and maintain [this sutra]?"
This second chapter illustrates those who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra]. △ Second, the comparison:

Such persons are as if they were bearing the Tathāgata Ajita upon their heads; these sons and daughters of good family need not further erect stupas and temples for me, nor build monasteries, nor provide the four requisites to the Saṃgha. Why is this?
What is it that a son or daughter of good family who upholds, reads, and recites this sutra has already performed?
It is as if they have erected a stupa for the Buddha, constructed monasteries, and made offerings to the Sangha;

it is as if they have raised a stupa of the seven precious jewels for the Buddha’s relics, vast and high, tapering gradually until reaching the Brahma-heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, various jeweled bells, flowers, incense, necklaces, and powdered incense.
By offering powdered incense, burning incense, various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all manner of dances and performances,
and by praising with sublime sounds through song and hymns, one has already performed such offerings for immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

A beginner fears that external conditions will cause agitation and obstruct the cultivation of the primary practice; therefore, by single-mindedly upholding this sutra, one makes the highest offering.

By setting aside worldly affairs to preserve the principle, the benefit is vast and manifold. Later, when mental contemplation has matured, engagement with external matters does not hinder internal cultivation;

rather, external affairs support the Way, just as abundant oil makes a fire fierce. It is like sailing with the current while raising the sails, further augmented by human effort. Its power is such that...
The momentum shifts rapidly; the scriptural text itself is the *dharmakāya* relic, so there is no need to enshrine relics of the physical body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The text is the signified, and [the commentary] is the signifier; this is the stūpa, so there is no need for ritual worship of a physical structure.

The scriptural text can accommodate the ultimate community (*paramārtha-saṃgha*), so it does not depend upon a community defined by outward signs. Question: If that is so, upholding the scripture is itself the ultimate precept (*paramārtha-śīla*). Why then...?
Furthermore, it is said that those who "are able to uphold the precepts" answer this by clarifying the meaning of the first chapter; one should not raise objections based on subsequent chapters.
If one wishes to explain this: upholding the sutra accords with principle, and the precepts are likewise maintained spontaneously.

Thus, while the first two chapters are now fulfilled, what is meant by "being able to uphold the precepts" is that there is no deficiency in the matters of the third chapter and beyond. △ Three: Addition.
Exhorting others to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra] has two parts;

first, the description of the person's characteristics: "Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it."
△ Second, the measurement:

He constructed monasteries, erecting thirty-two halls made of red sandalwood, eight *tāla* trees in height, magnificent in their height and breadth, wherein a hundred thousand bhikṣus resided; there were also groves and bathing ponds. Sūtra.
In these meditation caves, they are filled with all requisites for comfort—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal elixirs, and so forth.
Such monasteries, halls, and pavilions number in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, beyond measure.

By providing such offerings before my very eyes and those of the community of bhikṣus, I therefore say that if, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there should be anyone who receives, upholds, and recites [this teaching]...
If one recites it, explains it to others, writes it oneself, or teaches others to write it, and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls,
there is no further need to erect stupas or monasteries, or to build monastic dwellings to provide for the Sangha.
Regarding "eight *tāla* trees high," the *Xiyu ji* states that its appearance is like this: the tallest *zōnglǐ* (Caryota) trees in this region reach seven or eight *zhàng*;
when their fruit ripens, it is red in color and as large as a pomegranate, which many people eat.
Some say one *tāla* tree is seven *rèn* high; since one *rèn* is seven feet, this amounts to forty-nine feet. Thus, eight *tāla* trees would be...
It is three hundred and ninety-two feet high. The general purport of the current text suggests that if there were someone who,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, could exhort others to receive and uphold [the teachings], the merit thereof would be no different from initially establishing monasteries,
halls, pavilions, gardens, groves, food, drink, clothing, bedding, and seating for the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Therefore, it is said that there is no need to further construct stupas, temples, or monasteries. △ Fourth, the addition of practicing the six perfections concurrently:
First, the description of the person’s characteristics.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person who can uphold this sutra while concurrently practicing giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, and single-mindedness.
Wisdom. Second is the measure of its qualities,
which are most supreme, immeasurable, and boundless, like space in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
The merit of this person is likewise immeasurable and boundless, and they will swiftly attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Fifth, the addition of the six perfections as correct practice (2): First, the description of the person’s characteristics.
If a person reads, recites, accepts, and upholds this sutra and explains it to others; or if they write it themselves or instruct others to write it;

and furthermore, if they can erect stupas and construct monasteries to make offerings to and praise the assembly of śrāvakas, and also praise the merits of bodhisattvas by means of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of methods of praise; and moreover, for the sake of others, through various causes and conditions...
One who explains this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with its meaning is further able to dwell together with those who maintain pure precepts and are gentle;
they possess patience and freedom from anger, their resolve is firm, they always value sitting in meditation and attain various profound concentrations,
they are diligent and courageous in gathering all wholesome dharmas, and they possess sharp faculties and wisdom to skillfully answer difficult questions.
△ Second, the evaluation.
Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they shall possess such virtuous merits as these;
you should know that such persons have already set out for the site of enlightenment and are close to [Buddhahood].
Under the Bodhi tree where one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever this good man or good woman sits,
stands, or walks, a stūpa should be erected there; all devas and humans should make offerings to it just as they would to a Buddha-stūpa.

If these five grades are categorized according to their stages, the first three persons belong to the stage of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing); the next [grade] belongs to the stage of *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection), wherein one practices the six *pāramitās*;

and the final grade belongs to the stage of *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation), wherein one correctly practices the six *pāramitās*. All of these belong to the period prior to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Alternatively, it is said that the first grade, "Rejoicing" (*anumodanā*), constitutes the stage of entering the mind of faith, and this single grade is divided into two minds; thus, the five grades consist of...
The ten levels of faith correspond to the stage of the iron wheel and the purification of the six sense faculties.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Part Two: Verses in Praise, Section Four; First, the verses praising the second chapter.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who can uphold this sutra, the merit of such persons shall be immeasurable, as has been described above.

This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings: building stupas for the śarīras, adorned with the seven treasures, with spires exceedingly high and wide, reaching gradually up to the Brahma-heaven, where billions of jeweled bells produce wondrous sounds when stirred by the wind.
Furthermore, if one were to make offerings to this stūpa for immeasurable kalpas with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial garments, and manifold music,
and constantly illuminate it all around with lamps of fragrant oil and ghee; then, in the final age of the Dharma during the degenerate world,
one who is able to uphold this sūtra will have already completed all such offerings as described above.
△ Second, the verse on the third chapter:
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present in person;
one would build a monastic hall for offerings out of gośīrṣa-candana, thirty-two *tāla* trees high, fully equipped with exquisite food, fine garments, and bedding.
The dwellings of hundreds of thousands of beings, their gardens, bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves—all are variously adorned and magnificent.
△ Third, the verses on the fourth chapter:

If there is one with a mind of faith and understanding who receives, maintains, reads, recites, or transcribes [this sutra], or further teaches others to transcribe it, or makes offerings to the scroll of the sutra.

By scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense, and by constantly burning perfumed oils such as *sumana*, *campaka*, and *atimuktaka* to make offerings in this manner, one attains immeasurable merit; its virtue is as boundless as space.

How much more so for one who upholds this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, maintaining the precepts, enduring patience, delighting in meditative concentration, being free from anger, and refraining from harsh speech.
*Sumana* (須曼) is also called *sumanā*, which means "flower that well-gathers the mind. It is yellowish-white in color and fragrant;
the tree is three or four feet high and droops like a canopy. *Campaka* (薝蔔) is also called *campaka*, which means "yellow flower.
Its blossoms are small, yet their fragrance is exceedingly exquisite. △ Fourth, the verse on the fifth chapter.
One should revere the stupas and temples, show humility toward all bhikṣus, remain far removed from self-exalting pride, and constantly contemplate wisdom.
When questioned or challenged, one should not become angry, but should explain the teachings in accordance with the truth. If one can practice such conduct, their merit will be immeasurable.
If one sees this Dharma-preacher endowed with such virtues, one should scatter celestial flowers over them and cover their body with celestial robes.
One should perform the prostration by touching the head to the feet and give rise to the thought of regarding them as Buddhas; furthermore, one should reflect:
"Before long, they shall go to the tree of enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state to bring vast benefit to all devas and humans.

Whether it be their dwelling place, their walking path, or where they sit or lie down—even if it is merely where they have spoken a single verse—one should erect a stupa there, adorning it so that it is exquisite and making various kinds of offerings to it.
The Son of the Buddha dwelling in this stage is one whom the Buddhas enjoy; he constantly dwells therein, walking, sitting, and reclining.
Those who give rise to a mind like that of a Buddha are initially designated by the title "Tathāgata. Before long, they shall go to the Tree of Enlightenment;
their station is such that, though not yet having attained the Iron Wheel, they will soon enter the Copper Wheel and be able to manifest the eight phases of a Buddha. This is the [first] stage.
The five grades are identical to the fourth stage of faith; both belong to the level of wisdom cultivated through practice (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

If one discusses their entry into the stages, they are equally the level of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), differing only in that the former occurs during the lifetime of a Buddha while the latter occurs after his parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing (*Anumodanā-puṇya*). First, the title of the chapter:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eighteen, "The Merit of Rejoicing.

"Rejoicing" (*anumodanā*) means to accord with the non-duality and non-distinction of phenomena and principle; "rejoicing" (*modanā*) refers to celebrating for oneself and for others upon hearing the profound and deep [Dharma].
The Dharma that accords with principle possesses the merit of reality; the Dharma that accords with phenomena possesses the merit of skillful means. To rejoice in oneself is wisdom;
to rejoice in others is compassion. Because these—skillful means and reality, wisdom and abandonment—are explained in conjunction, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.

Furthermore, that which accords with principle means that upon hearing of the Buddha’s original ground as being profoundly deep and far-reaching, one believes and follows it without opposition, not missing even a single point.

Those who follow the affairs of the world with even a hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction, upon hearing that the Buddha benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—pervading all places both vertically and horizontally—will likewise find not a single hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.
Thus, they penetrate profound principle through extensive phenomena, and penetrate extensive phenomena through profound principle.
Though there is duality, it is non-dual; though there is distinction, it is undifferentiated. Yet, while being dual and distinct, there is neither duality nor distinction.
To have such faith and understanding is called "following the appearance of the Tathāgata. For more than forty years, he did not reveal the reality [to those of] the seven stages of skillful means;

he did not speak of the ultimate truth to them. Rejoicing for himself and for others, he uses the ordinary mind of a *pṛthagjana* to equalize it with what the Buddha knows, and uses the eye produced therein to see as the Tathāgata sees. With such knowledge and vision, one ultimately realizes the *dharmadhātu*.

Vast, boundless, peerless, equal to the unequaled, and unsurpassed—now that the Buddha has spoken this and I have heard it, this is called the Fiftieth Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. This is the beginning of the first chapter;
herein there is but a single thought of understanding and a single thought of rejoicing for oneself and others, yet no further deeds of practice or grace have occurred.
The merit obtained by others cannot compare to that of the Tathāgata’s skillful parables, which surpass even those of the Aśaikṣas;
how much more so for those who first heard this assembly, or those who have attained the second, third, fourth, or fifth stages,
or those who have entered the stages of the ten abidings and ten practices up to the final mind— whosoever hears such profound and wondrous merit, how could they not look upon it with admiration?
To explain why this teaching is so highly esteemed, the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit" is spoken.

Previously, when the merits of upholding this sutra were praised, the assembly all believed that such virtues could only be attained upon entering the stage of the true cause; they had suddenly conceived a notion of weakness and insignificance regarding the very first moment of the initial resolve.
Yet, they now hear of the *Hao-jian* (a tree name originating from the Tripitaka) which, though its sprout has only just emerged from the ground, already measures a hundred spans in circumference.
The sound of the letter *ga* surpasses that of all birds; it is rare and extraordinary, and because light doubts are thereby dispelled, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.

Those non-Buddhists who have attained the five supernatural powers can move mountains and dry up the oceans, yet they cannot subdue the views of craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*), which do not reach even the level of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).
Even the disciples of the Two Vehicles who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and are liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) are still bound by the fetters of *nirvāṇa*.

Knowing that their cause and effect are both provisional, those who follow the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) may be skillful in their cultivation of the cause, yet they do not recognize the five hundred *yojanas* when they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment;

their attainment of the fruit merely eliminates the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). Although these individuals are superior to the Two Vehicles, their cultivation of the cause is partial and their approach is clumsy;
thus, they are not praised by the Buddha, as they all fall short of the person who first rejoices in merit. The Buddha now cites the person of Arhatship...
This is used as an analogy because the subsequent Dharma-assembly surpasses all other teachings; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. Question:

How does this differ from the "Rejoicing" [chapter] in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? Answer: This refers to the Dharma, while that refers to the person; they are mentioned interchangeably. △ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text, in two parts: first, the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, experience sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), how much merit do they obtain? And he spoke in verse:
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?

The preceding chapters have already established the meaning of four chapters; as for why the first chapter was not explained, Maitreya, responding to the occasion, asks about this meaning, as the text states.
II. The Response, which has two parts: A. Prose Exposition; B. Verse Recitation. Part A (Prose Exposition) further has two sections: 1. The Response to the Internal [Question].
Regarding the five ways in which people rejoice with their hearts, the first is mutual instruction.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya Ajita:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other wise persons—whether old or young—hear this..."
Having rejoiced in the sutra, they depart from the Dharma assembly for other places— whether to monasteries, secluded spots,
cities, streets, villages, or rural fields— and according to what they have heard, they expound it to their parents, kinsmen, good friends,
and acquaintances to the best of their ability. When these people hear it, they likewise rejoice and further propagate the teaching to others.
Having heard it, they likewise rejoice and teach it to others; thus it is transmitted in succession until the fiftieth person.
△ Second, the comparison of the original merit:
"Ajita, I shall now describe the merit of rejoicing of that fiftieth son or daughter of good family."

Listen well to this: suppose there were sentient beings within four million *asamkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth, whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
whether legless, two-legged, four-legged, or many-legged—all such beings as are reckoned among the number of sentient beings.
Suppose there were a great donor who, whenever anyone sought merit, provided them with all the articles for their enjoyment according to their desires;
and suppose he gave to each and every sentient being gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber,

and all manner of exquisite treasures filling the entire Jambudvīpa, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems— such a person would be a great donor.
After eighty years of such giving, he thought to himself: "I have already provided these sentient beings with all manner of entertainments according to their every desire.
Yet, these beings are all in decline; they are over eighty years old, their hair is white, their faces are weathered, and death will soon come for them.
I should instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. He then gathered these sentient beings together and proclaimed:
He expounded the Dharma to transform and instruct them, benefiting and gladdening them; at that moment, they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna,
Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, exhausting all outflows and attaining mastery over profound meditative concentrations,
endowed with the eight liberations.
The number fifty is now explained through two perspectives: first, by cross-referencing the four assemblies across the various teachings;
second, by directly calculating according to the numbers of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding the first perspective: the Tripitaka has four gates, and each gate has four assemblies.
If one further distinguishes the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, they form six persons per gate; thus, across the four gates, there are twenty-four persons.

Regarding the practitioners of faith (*śraddhā-carita*) and those who practice by dharma (*dharma-carita*), there are forty-eight people; when the first and last are combined, there are fifty people in total.

This applies equally to the four gates of both the general and the specific. Furthermore, calculating directly according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the method of counting consists of seven small sevens and seven large sevens;
these seven times seven make forty-nine, all of whom—both teacher and disciples—are endowed with both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
The last individual among those of virtue merely possesses self-understanding and lacks the virtue of teaching others; thus, he is ranked below to highlight the superiority of the former.
Furthermore, the supplementary note states: "The six destinies" (*ṣad-gati*)—the number six refers to the six paths, and "destiny" (*gati*) refers to the process of going toward them;

that is, sentient beings proceed toward the six paths according to the karma they have performed. "The four modes of birth" (*catasro yonayaḥ*) are viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born, as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

The verse says: Humans and animals possess all four [modes of birth]; those in the hells and the various heavens, as well as intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*), are born exclusively by transformation (*upapāduka*).

Ghosts (*preta*) may be born either from a womb or by transformation. Regarding their forms and so forth, this demonstrates the essential characteristics and dwelling places of the four modes of birth.

"Having form" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); "formless" refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Possessing perception" refers to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). As for "without perception," it refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to that which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). It is not the "having perception" of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nor is it the "non-perception" of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
rather, it is the fourth heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The *Erya* states: "Those without feet are called *zhai*;
those with feet are called *chong*. By extension, one may know that this applies to those with two feet, four feet, and many feet.
Centipedes, and so forth. △ Third, the question:
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much or not?
△ Fourth, the answer.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, the merit of such a person is exceedingly great, immeasurable, and boundless.
If a donor were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure to sentient beings, his merit would already be immeasurable; how much more so if he causes them to attain the fruit of Arhatship?”
△ Fifth, the correct evaluation.

The Buddha told Maitreya: "I now speak to you clearly: suppose a person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the sentient beings of the six realms throughout four hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and furthermore cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship."
The merit obtained by those [preceding] is not like that of the fiftieth person who hears even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it;
their merit does not equal one hundredth part, one thousandth part, nor even one hundred-thousand-millionth part of it, and it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Ajita, such is the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices.
If even this merit is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), how much more so for those who, at the very beginning of the assembly, hear [this teaching] and rejoice in it;
their merit is even more supreme, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, beyond all comparison.

In this comparison, first one is granted worldly happiness to extract them from the suffering of the fruits [of karma], and later they are granted the bliss of nirvāṇa to extract them from the suffering of saṃsāra.
This is a brief enumeration of Brahma-merit; now it shall be further expanded.

The merit of all people filling Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī; the merit of all people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal that of a single person in Pūrvavideha.

The merit of all humans filling the three continents is not equal to the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru. The merit of all humans filling the four continents is not equal to that of one among the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*).
The merit of the Four Heavenly Kings is not equal to that of a single Śakra, and so on up to the sixth heaven, which is not equal to the merit of a single Brahmā.
Regarding the merit of Brahmā, there are two types: the fixed and the dispersed; the dispersed type refers to performing [meritorious acts] where no stūpa exists.
To repair a ruined stupa, to reconcile a divided Saṃgha, to request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and to reunite a dispersed assembly—these are the four merits.
Because they are equal to those of Brahmā, they are called "Brahma-merits. As for "Noble merits," this refers to Arhats dwelling in their final body who have attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, there are three types of merit regarding the realization of the Dharma (*dharmakāya*).
The practitioner on the vehicle shares the same realization of non-arising and exhausts the afflictions until they are completely consumed like wood turned to ash.

Furthermore, the *sattva* of noble merit practices for both self-benefit and the benefit of others; through the path of wordless speech, they sever the afflictions and enter the nirvana without remainder.
Moreover, the merit of the *sattva* refers to the successive transformation of beings from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until their entry into great parinirvāṇa—such is the comparison.
The merit of Brahmā is not equal to the merit of a noble one; the merit of a noble one is not equal to the merit of the essence of a noble one;
the merit of the essence of a noble one is not equal to the merit of a *kṣudrasattva*; the merit of a *kṣudrasattva* is not equal to the merit of a great bodhisattva;

and the merit of a great bodhisattva is not equal to the merit of the initial sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Why is this? Because that [other merit] is not the Buddha-dharma, it is not real, and it is not...
Because it is perfect, although one abides in the subsequent fruit, it does not equal my initial resolve; such is the meaning.
△ Second, directly clarifying those who listen as external recipients of the Dharma, part four: first, going personally to listen.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastic dwelling and listens to it for even a brief moment—
whether sitting or standing— by virtue of this merit, in their subsequent rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephant and horse carriages,
precious palanquins, and celestial palaces.
△ Sharing one's seat. If there is someone sitting at a place where the Dharma is being taught, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen by offering to share their seat,
the merit of that person will cause them to obtain the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin in their next rebirth.
The place where a Wheel-Turning Sage King sits.
△ Third, exhorting others to listen:
"Ajita, if there should be someone who says to another person, 'There is a sutra named the Lotus Sutra; we should go together to hear it.'"
He immediately accepted the instruction; and after a mere moment, having heard of this person’s merit, he was reborn in a future life to dwell together with bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs.

Possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, he would never be mute, his breath would never be foul, his tongue would always be free from ailment, and his mouth would likewise be free from disease; his teeth would not be stained black, nor yellow, nor sparse.
His lips are not deficient, nor uneven, nor crooked; they do not hang down, nor are they drawn back or shriveled;
they are neither coarse nor rough, nor are they scarred or cracked; they are neither cleft nor distorted, neither thick nor large, nor are they dark-brown;
they are free from all that is loathsome. His nose is not flat or bulbous, nor is it curved or twisted; his facial complexion is not black, nor is it narrow or long, nor is it sunken.
There was not a single feature of his form that was not pleasing; his lips, tongue, teeth, and gums were all perfectly refined and beautiful.
His nose was long, high, and straight; his countenance was full and round; his eyebrows were high and long; and his forehead was broad and level.
Endowed with these marks of a superior person, in every birth he took, he saw the Buddhas, heard the Dharma, and faithfully accepted their teachings.

Zhang’an says that from "exhorting others to listen to the Dharma" up to "being born in the same place as the *dhāraṇī*-possessing Bodhisattvas" and "the perfection of human marks," there are fifty merits in total.
Taking these merits as the standard for the person, they likewise constitute fifty [meritorious qualities].

However, while the previous fifty were discussed in terms of internal understanding of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), the present discussion concerns external matters as the point of distinction. Furthermore, this passage...
There are also six faculties: the merit of sharp faculties and wisdom is the merit of the mind; the merit of not being mute is the merit of the tongue;
the merit of a nose that is well-developed, high, and straight is the merit of the nose; the merit of seeing the Buddha is the merit of the eyes;

the merit of hearing the Dharma is the merit of the ears; and the remainder are merits of the body. The former [set] refers to the merits of the stage of semblance, whereas these refer to the merits prior to the stage of semblance.
△ Fourth, the practice of listening with full attention:
"Ajita, you should observe that the merit of exhorting even a single person to go and listen to the Dharma is such as this;
how much more so for one who listens to it with a single-minded focus, recites it, and, within the great assembly, analyzes it for others and practices according to what has been taught?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:

△ Second, the verses in praise [of the merit of rejoicing], divided into two parts; first, the praise for those who rejoice within [the assembly], further divided into three parts; first, the praise for the fifty people.
If a person, having heard this sutra at a Dharma assembly, even for a single verse, rejoices in it and speaks of it to others,
and thus transmits it in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person.
△ Second, the comparison by verse:
I shall now distinguish the merit obtained by the person of the final age. Suppose there were a great donor who provided immeasurable necessities for eighty years, fulfilling every desire at will;
yet, seeing that person’s signs of aging—hair white and face wrinkled—[he would still provide such gifts].
With teeth sparse and his form withered, he realized that his death would not be long in coming. "I should now instruct him so that he may attain the fruit of the Path.
He then employed skillful means to preach the true Dharma of Nirvana: "The world is entirely unstable, like foam, bubbles, or flames.
You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment. Upon hearing this teaching, all those people attained Arhatship.
They are fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the eight liberations.
△ Third, the verse on the correct calculation:
Finally, the fiftieth verse states that the merit of one who rejoices upon hearing a single verse surpasses the former [merit] beyond all comparison.
Thus, by successive transmission, the merit of even those who hear it is immeasurable; how much more so for those who hear it at the beginning of the Dharma assembly and rejoice accordingly.
△ Second, the verse on those who hear the Dharma externally (4): first, the transposed verse encouraging them to listen.
If there is one who exhorts another person, leading them to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, saying, "This sutra is profound and subtle;

it is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas," and that person follows the instruction and goes to listen—even if only for a brief moment—the merit and reward of this person shall now be explained in detail:

in every successive life, they will have no afflictions of the mouth; their teeth will not be sparse, yellow, or black; their lips will not be thick, curled, or cleft; and they will possess no loathsome features.
His tongue was not dry, black, or short; his nose was high, long, and straight; his forehead was broad and even;

his facial features were entirely dignified and handsome, such that he was pleasing to behold to all people. His breath was free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issued from his mouth.
△ Second, a verse summarizing the preceding section on his own journey:
"If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling desiring to hear the Lotus Sutra, and hears it even for a brief moment with joy, I shall now describe its merit:
in future lives among gods and humans, one shall obtain exquisite elephant and horse-drawn carriages, precious jeweled litters, and ride within celestial palaces."
△ Third, three verses on sharing one's seat:

If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras, through this causal condition of merit, one will obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King.
△ Fourth, four verses on listening and practicing.
How much more so for one who listens with a single mind, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to those teachings; their merit would be beyond measure.
△ Second, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" clarifies the merits resulting from the first chapter and exhorts the circulation [of the sutra]. Part One:
Stating the Chapter Title.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher.

Regarding the meaning of "Dharma-preacher," it is as explained in the "Chapter on the Dharma-preacher. As for "merits," those previously mentioned at the beginning of the first chapter were the merits of that initial stage;

these [merits] now refer to the superior stage of the five chapters, namely the purification of the six sense faculties and their internal and external adornment, including the purification of the five faculties.
The purity of the faculty of mind and its external adornments are called internal adornment.
Furthermore, the manifestation of all forms and images—from those in the hells up to and including the Buddhas—within one’s own body is called internal adornment.

The universal manifestation of all forms and images—from those in the hells up to and including the Buddhas—through the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation for the sake of external transformation is [also] called internal adornment.
This is called external adornment; as it is with the body-faculty, so it is with the other five faculties. As it is with recitation and study, so it is with the four types [of practice].
As it is with the first stage, so it is with the four stages. As it is with the semblance [attainment], so it is with the partial realization, which is twice as great.
When the practitioner hears of these merits and benefits, they rejoice beyond measure, seeking them with tireless diligence, and their faith and progress increase twofold.

It further clarifies that the Mahāyāna possesses great power and is free from the net of doubt; it resembles the initial stage of understanding, yet surpasses the ultimate limit of the Two Vehicles by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
It points to the beginning to reveal the end, providing a comprehensive liberation that culminates in the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because this chapter elucidates these four meanings in full, it is called "The Merit of the Dharma Master."

This is the section on the qualities of virtue. △ Second, the explanation of the scriptural text has two parts. First, a general listing of the numbers regarding the expansion and contraction of the merits of the six sense organs.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent:
"If a good man or a good woman receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or writes out this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, such a person shall obtain eight [thousand]..."
The merit of the hundred eyes is one thousand two hundred; the merit of the ears is eight hundred; the merit of the nose is one thousand two hundred;

the merit of the tongue is eight hundred; the merit of the body is one thousand two hundred; and the merit of the mind is eight hundred. Adorned with these merits, the six sense faculties are all rendered pure.
According to the *Three Kinds of Action and the Practice of Peaceful Bliss*, there are ten wholesome acts; each wholesome act has ten, making one hundred wholesome acts.

Within each of these, there are ten such as these, making one thousand wholesome acts. When calculated in terms of transforming others, this becomes two thousand. Based on the Tathāgata’s robe, seat, and chamber, this results in six thousand.
The five kinds of Dharma-preachers all possess the purity of the six sense faculties, and each individual faculty possesses [these qualities].
A thousand merits: furthermore, within a single mind, the ten dharma-realms are fully present; each realm possesses ten suchnesses, which together constitute one hundred.

When the six sense organs universally apprehend the six objects, there are six hundred. When these are combined with the two adornments of meditative concentration and wisdom, there are one thousand two hundred.
Thus, every single organ is fully endowed with the adornments of concentration and wisdom, totaling one thousand two hundred.
If one discusses the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), that purity is not described in terms of merit—whether it be small or great.
