If one speaks of adornment, it can be expanded, contracted, or made equal; as for these various adornments, each organ has six thousand [attributes].
If one speaks of twelve thousand, it manifests its capacity for expansion; if one speaks of eight hundred, it manifests its capacity for contraction; and if one speaks of purity, then...
There is no increase, no decrease, and no equality; the six sense organs function interchangeably because the faculties are sovereign and inconceivable.
To judge this unilaterally would be to lose the essential meaning. As for the stage of "semblance," if it is based on the four wheels, it is the stage of the iron wheel;
if based on the fifty-two stages, it is the ten levels of faith; if based on the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), it is the ten great wholesome deeds.
"The mind now facing the constant and diligent" refers to the third mind among the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Although the names and titles differ across various sutras, they are all identical to this stage of semblance-realization (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*). △ Second, the detailed explanation in six chapters:
First, the faculty of the eye; 2. First, the prose section.
These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, see all that exists within and without the three-thousandfold world-system—
from the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas down to the Avīci Hell, and up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra)— and they see all sentient beings therein,
as well as the places where they are born through the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of their deeds; they see them all.
[The Buddha] knew.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
△ Second, the verse summary.
If one preaches this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* within a great assembly with a mind free from fear, listen to its merits:
such a person shall obtain eight hundred kinds of supreme eyes. Because they are adorned by these, their eyes will be exceedingly pure;

with the eyes born of their parents, they shall see the entirety of the three thousandfold world-system, including both the interior and exterior of Mount Meru, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).

Furthermore, all other sentient beings within the mountains, forests, great oceans, rivers, and waters—reaching from the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above—all see [the Buddha] with their physical eyes, even though they have not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Such is the power of his physical eyes.

This chapter clarifies that what is produced by one's parents is called the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsacakṣus*). What it perceives surpasses that of the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*) obtained as a karmic reward by the Brahmā Kings.

While within their own realm, they see throughout the great trichiliocosm; however, beyond the great trichiliocosm there is a wind-wheel that acts as an obstruction to the eye, preventing them from seeing what lies outside.
If they were in another realm, they would not be able to see the great trichiliocosm everywhere, as it is not their domain.
Generally speaking, a Lesser Arhat sees a small chiliocosm, a Great Arhat sees a great trichiliocosm, and a Pratyekabuddha sees a hundred Buddha-worlds;

they are not obstructed by wind-circles, nor is there any separation between their own realm and others'. Now, according to this sutra and treatise, the eye is able to see both the interior and exterior of a great trichiliocosm.
This must be the divine eye (divyacakṣus); why then is it called the fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus)? This is the "semblance" [stage] of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

By virtue of the power of the sutras, one possesses the function of superior faculties; yet, as long as true reality has not been realized, it cannot be called the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus) and is still termed the "fleshly eye" (māṃsacakṣus).
For example, in the Hīnayāna, when one has not yet attained supernormal powers (abhijñā), one does not call it the divine eye, but rather the ear [of the flesh];
because it is still a body of segmented existence (paricchinna-deha), it is said to be "born of parents. Although it is called the fleshly eye, it nonetheless possesses the five eyes.
To see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm is the function of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

To see all sentient beings along with the causes and conditions of their karma is the function of the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). For its eyes to be exceedingly pure is the function of the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*).

To see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm all at once, seeing both karma and purity, and further to subdue the delusions above the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in perfect completeness, is the function of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "Though one possesses the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye; because it is the Buddha-eye, it is called pure.
Since it is endowed with the five eyes, it is said to be "adorned. Its ability to expand and contract is called the function of the supreme faculties, and is termed "mastery over the faculties.
How could this be understood merely as [the capacity for] eight hundred or twelve hundred *yojanas*? △ Second, the Chapter on the Ear-faculty (2): Part One.
The prose section continues:

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the ear. With these purified ears, they shall hear the three...
Within a trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, there are various internal and external sounds and voices:
the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots; the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and sighing;
the sounds of conch shells, drums, bells, and gongs; the sounds of laughter, speech, men, women, boys, and girls.
The sound of Dharma and the sound of non-Dharma; the sound of suffering and the sound of pleasure; the sound of ordinary beings and the sound of noble ones;
the sound of joy and the sound of lack of joy; the sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas;
the sounds of fire, water, wind, and the sounds of the hells and animals.
The sounds of hungry ghosts, the sounds of bhikṣus, the sounds of bhikṣuṇīs, the sounds of śrāvakas, the sounds of pratyekabuddhas,
the sounds of bodhisattvas, and the sounds of buddhas— in short, all internal and external sounds whatsoever within the trichiliocosm,
though he has not yet attained the divine ear, he hears and knows them all with his naturally born, pure, ordinary ears.
Thus, although he discriminates various sounds, his faculty of hearing is not impaired.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
II. Verses in Praise.
The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity or defilement; with these natural ears, one constantly hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system:
the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou*;
the sounds of flutes and pipes; and pure, beautiful songs. Hearing these and the voices of countless kinds of people, one is able to understand them all clearly without becoming attached.
Furthermore, they hear the subtle and wondrous singing voices of the devas, as well as the voices of men and women, boys and girls;
they hear the calls of the kalaviṅka birds and the jīvañjīvaka birds within the mountains, rivers, and steep valleys;
they hear the sounds of the various sufferings and manifold agonies of those in the hells; and they hear the cries of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, as they beg for food and drink.
When the various asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves, they produce a great sound;

likewise, when the birds and beasts in the worlds of the ten directions call out to one another, the person who expounds the Dharma hears all these sounds from this place without their faculty of hearing being impaired.
The sounds of speech from all the Brahma heavens, including the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
the Dharma Master dwelling here hears them all. Whether the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs recite the sūtras or preach the Dharma for others, the Dharma Master dwelling here hears them all.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who read and recite the sutras and dharmas, or explain them for others, or compile and interpret their meanings—

all such sounds they shall hear. Those Great Holy Buddhas who teach and transform sentient beings by expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma within great assemblies— all those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shall hear them all.

Throughout the inner and outer reaches of the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, one hears all sounds without the faculty of hearing being impaired;
because the ears are so sharp and keen, one is able to discern and comprehend them all.
Thus, for one who upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, although they have not yet attained the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), the merit of their natural ears is already such as this.
In this chapter on the faculty of hearing, one universally hears the sounds of the ten dharma-realms, both internal and external, throughout the great trichiliocosm.

Hearing those of the six paths is the fleshly ear; hearing those of the two vehicles is the heavenly ear; hearing those of the bodhisattvas is the wisdom ear; and hearing those of the Buddhas is the Buddha-ear.
Furthermore, the fleshly ears born of one's parents can hear both the internal and external, which is the function of the heavenly ear. It is not that [the other ears] do not hear.
Attachment is the ear of wisdom; non-delusion is the ear of Dharma; hearing simultaneously and reciprocally is the ear of the Buddha.
By analogy with the ear, the eye is likewise: seeing humans and devas is the fleshly eye; seeing the two vehicles is the wisdom eye;
seeing bodhisattvas is the Dharma eye; seeing the Buddha is the Buddha eye. △ Third, the Chapter on the Nose Faculty, Part Two: First, the Lengthening [of the Organ].
...practices.

Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family who constantly exerts diligence receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they will accomplish eight hundred merits of the nose; by means of this purified faculty of the nose, they shall hear...
Within the trichiliocosm, there are various kinds of fragrances—above, below, and throughout;
the fragrance of *sumanā* flowers, *jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, red lotuses, blue lotuses, white lotuses;
the fragrance of flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, sandalwood, and aloeswood.
Whether it be tagara incense, tamāla incense, karpūra incense, or ten million varieties of blended perfumes— whether in powder, pill, or ointment form—
the one who upholds this sūtra, while remaining in this very world, is able to distinguish them all; furthermore, they can specifically discern the scents of sentient beings,
the scents of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, as well as the scents of men, women, boys, and girls.
Whether near or far, all fragrances— those of incense, grasses, trees, and groves—
the holder of this sutra perceives them all without error. Although dwelling here, they also smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens,
as well as the fragrance of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, and the fragrance of the māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers.
He perceives and knows every fragrance produced from the blending of celestial incenses—such as the fragrance of *roca* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers;
the fragrances of sandalwood, aloeswood, and various powdered incenses; and the fragrances of diverse mixed flowers—as well as the bodily fragrances of the devas.
He also hears the fragrance of Śakra-devānām-indra as he enjoys the five desires within his magnificent palace.

Whether they are playing and sporting, or if the fragrance is in the Sudharmā Hall while preaching the Dharma to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, or if it is the fragrance when sporting in the various gardens, or the fragrances from the bodies of the men and women of the other devas—all these are smelled from afar.
In this manner, proceeding successively up to the Brahma world and even as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the fragrances from the bodies of all those devas are likewise smelled. And...
He smells from afar the incense burned by the devas, as well as the fragrance of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodily fragrance of the Buddhas;
he knows their locations upon smelling them. Yet, although he smells these fragrances, his faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded;
if he wishes to distinguish them and explain them to others, his recollection is unerring.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verse Recitation:
The nose of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul, he perceives all various kinds of odors.
The scents of *sumana*, *jāti*, *tamāla*, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon; the scents of various flowers and fruits;
the scents of sentient beings; and the scents of men and women—the preacher of the Dharma, staying at a distance, perceives these scents and knows their locations.
Great powerful wheel-turning kings, minor wheel-turning kings, their sons, ministers, and palace ladies—he perceives them by scent and knows their locations.

By smelling the fragrance, one knows the location of the precious jewels worn upon the body, as well as the treasures hidden in the earth; by smelling the fragrance, one knows the whereabouts of the precious women of the wheel-turning king.
By smelling the fragrance, one knows the various ornaments for adorning the bodies of people, their clothing, necklaces, and the various types of unguents applied to them.
If the devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing miraculous transformations, those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* can know them all by smelling the fragrance.
The fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as ghee and oil, are fully known by the holder of this sutra while dwelling here;
likewise, those sentient beings who dwell amidst the blossoming sandalwood trees in deep and perilous mountain regions can be known by their scent,
and the sentient beings within the Iron Ring Mountains and the great oceans can all be known by their location through the scent perceived by the holder of this sutra.
When the male and female asuras and their various retinues engage in combat or play, they are able to know [all things] by smelling fragrances.

In vast wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, they smell the scent of lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like, and by smelling their scent, they know their locations.
If there are those who are pregnant, they can discern whether it is male or female; they can also smell and fully know the presence of those without genitals or non-human beings.
By the power of smelling fragrances, one knows whether a woman who has recently conceived will achieve a successful pregnancy or not, and whether she will give birth in comfort to a blessed son;
by the power of smelling fragrances, one knows the thoughts of men and women—whether their minds are stained by desire, delusion, or anger—and likewise knows those who practice virtue.
One can also smell all the various treasures hidden underground, such as gold, silver, and precious gems contained within copper vessels, and know them all through the power of smelling fragrances.
There are various kinds of necklaces whose prices no one can appraise; yet by smelling their fragrance, one knows their value, their origin, and where they are located.
Regarding the various celestial flowers such as the *māndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *pāriyātraka* trees, by smelling their fragrance, one can fully know them.
Regarding the celestial palaces with their distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, adorned with various precious flowers, by smelling their fragrance, one can fully know them all.

In the celestial gardens, superior palaces, and various pavilions, with the Hall of the Sublime Dharma situated in their midst, he enjoys himself; by smelling their fragrance, he is able to know all the devas—
whether they are listening to the Dharma or indulging in the five desires— as they come and go, walk, stand, sit, or lie down, and by smelling their fragrance,
he is able to know everything when the celestial maidens wear fine garments and are adorned with excellent flowers and perfumes as they move about and sport.
Thus, proceeding upward through successive stages as far as the Brahma-world, he can perceive by means of their fragrance all those who enter and emerge from meditative absorption;
from the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), he can perceive by means of their fragrance all those who are newly born or passing away.
Furthermore, among the assembly of bhikṣus who are constantly diligent in the Dharma—whether sitting, walking, or reciting the sūtras—he can likewise perceive them all by means of their fragrance.
Or those who, beneath forest trees, sit with single-minded devotion in meditation or uphold the sutras—hearing their fragrance, he knows their locations.
Whether a bodhisattva’s resolve is firm as they sit in meditation, recite or chant, or preach the Dharma for others—hearing their fragrance, he is able to know them wherever they may be.
O World-Honored One, those who are revered by all and who preach the Dharma out of compassion for the masses—hearing their fragrance, he is able to know them all.
When sentient beings hear this sutra before the Buddha, they all rejoice and practice according to the Dharma. By smelling the fragrance, they are able to know everything;
although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) dharma, those who uphold this sutra first attain this mark of the nose.
In this chapter on the faculty of the nose: that which is born of one's parents is the fleshly nose; hearing within and without the great trichiliocosm is the celestial nose;
being unstained and unattached is the wisdom nose; discerning without error is the Dharma nose; and the simultaneous, mutual functioning of these is the Buddha nose.
This chapter clarifies their mutual functioning: the nose perceives the pleasant and the foul, distinguishes the noble from the base, and beholds the splendor of celestial palaces.
In the case of Śāriputra and others, the nose possesses the function of the eye when they recite and preach the Dharma, for they can discern [the presence of others] by smelling their fragrance;
the nose possesses the function of the ear; the nose possesses the function of the tongue when it perceives the fragrances of tree blossoms, fruits, and ghee;

the nose possesses the function of the body because entering and emerging from dhyāna involves the eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*), and the pleasures of the five desires are likewise tactile phenomena; the nose possesses the function of the mind through its attachment to desire and delusion.
One with a mind of anger also knows that those who cultivate goodness have a mental function regarding the nose; the sovereign and superior function of the nose-faculty is such as this.
△ Fourth, the Chapter on the Tongue-Faculty, in two parts: first, the prose exposition.
Furthermore, Nityodyukta, if a son or daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue. Whether things be pleasant or unpleasant, delicious or unpalatable,
or even bitter and astringent substances, when they come into contact with their tongue-root, all shall transform into the supreme flavor, like celestial ambrosia.

There is nothing that is not beautiful: if one uses the faculty of the tongue to proclaim teachings amidst the great assembly, producing profound and wondrous sounds that can enter their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and experience happiness;

furthermore, when the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas hear these profound and wondrous sounds as they proclaim and discourse in orderly succession, they all come to listen, as do others...
Nāgas and nāgīs, yakṣas and yakṣīs, gandharvas and gandharvīs, asuras and asurīs, garuḍas and garuḍīs, kiṃnaras and kiṃnarīs,
and mahoragas and mahoragīs all came to attend upon and reverently make offerings to the monks for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, retinues, minor wheel-turning kings, and great wheel-turning kings—
with their seven treasures, their thousand sons, and their inner and outer retinues— mounted their palaces and came together to hear the Dharma.
Because this bodhisattva was skilled in preaching the Dharma, the brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom [were fully inspired].
Throughout their lives, they will attend upon and make offerings to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas, who always delight in seeing them.
In whichever direction such a person may be, all the buddhas will turn toward that place and preach the Dharma for them;
they will be able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas and will further be able to produce profound and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verse Recitation:
The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure, and they shall never again experience unpleasant flavors; whatever they consume or eat shall all become nectar.

Using a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preaches the Dharma to the great assembly; through various causes, conditions, and parables, he guides the minds of sentient beings so that all who hear it rejoice.

They present various supreme offerings, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others all come together with reverent hearts to listen to this Dharma. If this preacher of the Dharma wishes to employ a wondrous voice—

Pervading the three thousandfold world system, they can reach it at will; the great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons, constantly come with palms joined in reverence to listen to and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas also constantly and joyfully come to make offerings. So too do Brahmā, the King Māra, Īśvara, and Maheśvara.

Thus, the hosts of devas constantly come to his abode; the Buddhas and their disciples, hearing the sound of his preaching the Dharma, always keep him in mind and protect him, and at times manifest themselves before him.
This chapter on the tongue faculty is also like this. That which is born of one's parents is the physical tongue, yet it is capable of producing the speech of the ten dharma realms;
by means of this, the meaning of the five tongues is clarified. Being able to produce the speech of the ten dharma realms is the celestial tongue;
being indestructible is the wisdom tongue; being unerring is the Dharma tongue; and the simultaneous, mutual functioning of these is the Buddha tongue. Question:

If bitter and foul tastes reach the tongue and all transform into supreme flavors, one must understand that all forms are identical to the Buddha’s form and all sounds are identical to the Buddha’s voice;
since they are equally pure, there is no contradiction in this principle. Thus, one universally knows all phenomena of form and sound without confusion or error.
Furthermore, there is no impediment to the faculty of mastery; why then do you conceive of it as something dull and obstructive? △ Section Five:
The Chapter on the Body-Faculty, Part Two:
Prose Exposition. Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, or recites this sutra...
If one explains or transcribes this, one shall obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli,
which all sentient beings will joyfully behold. Because that body is pure, the births and deaths, the high and low, the beautiful and the ugly,
and the rebirths in good or evil realms of all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm— including the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains— will all appear therein.
Mount Sumeru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other mountains, as well as the sentient beings dwelling within them, all appear therein;
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) above, everything and all sentient beings therein appear within it.
Furthermore, the preaching of the Dharma by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—all their forms and images appear within his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
II. Verse Recitation:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure, like that of clear lapis lazuli; all sentient beings will joyfully behold them."
Furthermore, just as a pure, bright mirror reflects all forms and images, so too does the Bodhisattva, within their pure body, perceive everything that exists in the world;
this alone is clearly understood by themselves, while others do not see it.
All the various beings within the trichiliocosm—gods, humans, asuras, those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—all such forms and images appear within their body.
The palaces of the various devas, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*), Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, and all the great oceans,
all appear within his body. Furthermore, the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas— the children of the Buddha—
whether teaching the Dharma alone or in assembly, all appear therein, even though he has not yet attained the wondrous body of the untainted nature of phenomena (*anāsrava-dharmatā*).
Because the pure, eternal essence manifests everything within it:
the function of the physical body is such that all things in the world appear within the body;
the function of the celestial body is such that everything up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) appears within the body; and for the followers of the Two Vehicles, wisdom appears within the body.
This is the function of the body: the Bodhisattva manifests the function of the Dharma-body within the body; the Buddha manifests the function of the Buddha-body within the body.
They are manifested simultaneously, they function reciprocally at once, they are without error at once, and they are without attachment at once.
△ Chapter Six: The Faculty of Mind. Part Two: Initial Prose Exposition.

Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty. By means of this purity...
With a purified mental faculty, from hearing even a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings;
having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for a month, four months, or even a year.
All the teachings thus spoken accord with their intended meaning and do not contradict the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), whether they concern worldly scriptures.
Whether it be writing, worldly discourse, or activities for sustaining life, all such things accord with the True Dharma.
He fully knows the mental activities, the movements of the mind, and the conceptual proliferations of all sentient beings throughout the six realms within the trichiliocosm.
Although he has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), his faculty of the mind is thus purified; such is the nature of this person’s contemplation.
All deliberations and discourses are the Buddha-dharma; none are not true, for they are also what was taught in the sutras of previous Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the verse:
This person’s mind is pure, clear, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement; with this wondrous faculty of the mind, they know the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas.
Even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and explain them in sequence according to the Dharma—from a month, four months, to a year.
All sentient beings within and without this world— whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, or others— who dwell within the six realms of existence,
shall at one time fully know the various kinds of thoughts they harbor; and regarding the marks of the countless Buddhas of the ten directions,
adorned with a hundred merits, who preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they shall hear it all and be able to receive and uphold it as the retribution for upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
Contemplating immeasurable meanings, they preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways; from beginning to end, they never forget or err because they uphold the Lotus Sutra.
Thus, they fully know the characteristics of all dharmas, recognize their sequence according to their meaning, and master names and language.
Whatever they expound is entirely the teaching of the Buddhas of the past; because they propagate this Dharma, they possess no fear among the assembly.
The faculty of mind of one who upholds the Lotus Sūtra is purified to such an extent that, although they have not yet attained the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*), they already possess such signs.
Because this person upholds this sūtra, they abide in a rare and marvelous stage;
they are joyful and beloved by all sentient beings, and because they uphold the Lotus Sūtra, they are able to analyze and expound it through thousands of millions of skillful modes of speech.
The chapter on the faculty of mind is also like this: all worldly livelihoods and industries accord with the Dharma;
that which the human mind purifies and the heavenly mind practices, and all that the heavens move and act, are fully known. When the heavenly mind is pure for four months, these are the Four Truths;
when it is for one year, these are the twelve months, which are the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. These do not contradict the true mark (dharmatā).
The purity of the mind of wisdom is like the full moon; this is the purity of the mind of the Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle.

Whatever is deliberated upon therein is all that was taught in the sūtras of the former Buddhas—that is, the purity of the Buddha-mind. At one time it is perfectly luminous; at one time its faculties function interdependently;
at one time it is untainted; at one time it is without error. Its faculties and functions are sovereign: it can expand and contract, it can equalize and purify. Thus it is complete.
The general explanation of the sixth fascicle is hereby completed.

△ Chapter Three: The Parable of Never-Disparaging. Section Two: Citing the Transgressions of Faith and Slander, and the Merit of Virtue, to Exhort the Circulation [of the Scripture].
First, the presentation of the chapter title: *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.
Internally harboring the realization of "Never-Disparaging," externally revering the objects of "Never-Disparaging," he established the practice of "Never-Disparaging" through his body and speech.
Regarding the teaching of not disparaging others, one should cultivate the eye of non-disparagement and the understanding of non-disparagement. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"This bodhisattva knows that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and therefore does not dare to disparage them. There are five aspects of Buddha-nature:
the fundamental cause (正因), the pervasive and original (通亘本), and the conditions for realization (緣了). These seeds are inherently present; they are not something acquired only now.
The nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-fruit will certainly be attained; this is never in vain. This is called the understanding of "Not Disparaging.
Applying this understanding to others, one treats them in the same way; this is called the sphere of "Respecting Not Disparaging.
Because one respects this sphere, it is called the practice of "Not Disparaging. Because one proclaims these words, it is called the teaching of "Not Disparaging. Those who previously disparaged him—

This refers to people; now, the Sūtra-compilers use this to title the chapter. The *Jian shi sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality) states that the Buddha spoke for his father, the King:
"The King asked, 'Are all sentient beings Buddhas? The Buddha replied, 'If one sees sentient beings according to reality, they are indeed Buddhas.
I have personally categorized this statement based on the principle that if one does not see according to reality, [they are not].
To see the Buddha as being within [the categories of] the ordinary and the holy is like a beginner at archery who misses the bullseye more often than he hits it;

yet if one takes the earth itself as the bullseye, there is nowhere he does not hit. If one discriminates between the worthy and the holy, asking who is right and who is wrong, and observes them according to reality, that is precisely the Buddha.

The former is an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); the latter is an explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). This chapter introduces people [to this truth].

To certify the profound merit of the five grades and the heavy retribution of the six sense organs, I formerly rejoiced in [this teaching] to obtain both present and future rewards, thereby encouraging its circulation.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse.
In the first part (the prose), there are three sections. First, a double reference to the offenses and blessings of the preceding chapter. First, the reference to offenses.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "You should now know that if any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka,
or upāsikā who upholds the Lotus Sūtra is reviled, abused, or slandered with harsh words,
they will receive a retribution for their great offense as previously described."
As explained in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. △ Second, pointing out the merit:
the merit obtained is as previously described regarding the purification of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as explained in the "Chapter on Merit.
△ Second, the dual opening of this chapter concerning faith and slander, first clarifying the basis of the matter in seven parts.
First, the time period:
In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
Second, the name.
There was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World,
Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
△ Third, the kalpa and the land:
the kalpa is named Free from Decline, and the land is named Great Achievement.
△ Fourth, the teaching of the Dharma.
That Buddha King of Majestic Sound, within that world, preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras;
for those seeking to become śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, and death to ultimate nirvāṇa;

for those seeking to become pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for all bodhisattvas, [he taught] by means of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The teaching on the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*) corresponds to the ultimate Buddha-wisdom through the Dharma of the six *pāramitās*.
△ Fifth, regarding lifespan:
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lifespan of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand eons.
△ Sixth, the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:

The number of kalpas that the True Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of dust motes in one Jambudvīpa; the number of kalpas that the Semblance Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of dust motes in the four continents.
After that Buddha has extensively benefited sentient beings, he subsequently enters parinirvāṇa.

△ After seventy-two trillion Buddhas had passed away and their True Dharma and Semblance Dharma were completely extinguished, a Buddha again appeared in this land, also named King of Majestic Sound Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer... [and so forth].
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, followed this same sequence for twenty trillion Buddhas, all of whom bore the same title.
△ Second, clarifying the past events (pūrvayoga), in three parts: first, a general clarification of the time period.
First, after the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had already entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, △ Second, the names of two individuals are presented together:
during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were monks of overweening pride who possessed great power; at that time, there was a bodhisattva...

The name of the Bhikṣu was Constantly Not Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). Those who reviled him were called "Arrogant" (*adhimāna*) at that time, while those who believed in him were called "Constantly Not Disparaging" at that time.
△ Third, a dual clarification of gain and loss, in two parts: first, discussing gain from the perspective of the believer.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, for what reason was that bhikṣu named Sadāparibhūta?
Whenever he saw anyone—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—he would always prostrate to them, praise them, and say:
"I deeply revere you all; I do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this? Because you are all practicing the bodhisattva path."
When he shall attain Buddhahood, that bhikṣu will not merely devote himself to reading and reciting the sūtras;
rather, he will practice prostrations even when seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, going to them to prostrate and praise them, saying:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become buddhas."
Attaining the grand principle of the correct teaching and gaining the wondrous benefit of its circulation—this is the "One" of Name, namely Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta).
This person’s every act of seeing [another] is the "One" of Principle; his universal prostrations are the "One" of Practice; and his speaking these words is the "One" of Teaching.
These constitute the fourfold "Ones" that reveal the provisional to manifest the real. From the passage beginning with "Even from afar he saw... onwards is...
Because the fundamental principle is one, going to pay homage is the oneness of practice; making these words is the oneness of teaching;

and being but a single person is the oneness of the individual—this meaning is easily understood. This constitutes the fourfold "oneness" that reveals the remote by opening up the near. As the text says:
"Those who do not specialize in the recitation and study of the scriptures, but merely practice prostration"—this is the stage of the first type of person who rejoices in others' merit.
I also rejoice that all dharmas possess the nature of peace and bliss, and that they are all of one true mark; I rejoice that all people possess the three Buddha-natures:

the capacity for awakening through study and recitation of the scriptures is the *nirvedhabhāga* (the cause of realization); the practice of the Bodhisattva path is the *ālambana* (the causal condition);
and not daring to treat others with contempt while instead maintaining deep reverence is the *mūla* (the fundamental cause). Thus, one respects others.
To revere the Dharma without giving rise to contention is the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). To not disparage [others] and to revere them deeply is the seat of the Tathāgata.
To endure being struck or reviled is the robe of the Tathāgata. To constantly practice with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion without ceasing is the hall of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, deep reverence is the mental action (*manas-karman*), and the teaching of "not disparaging" is the verbal action (*vāk-karman*); therefore, one should go to pay homage.
These three types of bodily action, when conjoined with compassion, constitute the vow for the practice of peaceful bliss.
Why would such [practices], whether three or four, not be of wondrous and beneficial circulation? △ Second, clarifying the faults of those who disparage them.
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to thoughts of anger and impurity, reviling him with harsh words, saying:
"This ignorant bhikṣu has come from where? He says of himself, 'I do not slight you; I bestow upon you the prediction that you shall become a Buddha.
We have no need for such a false prediction. Thus it continued for many years, and they were constantly...
Even when reviled, he did not give rise to anger, but always spoke these words: "You shall all become Buddhas.
When he said this, some among the multitude struck and pelted him with clubs, wood, tiles, and stones; yet even as they fled and stood at a distance, he still cried out in a loud voice:
"I dare not slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. Because he constantly spoke these words, [his merit] increased.
Arrogant bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās called him "Never-Disparaging.
There were those who gave rise to hearts of anger and impurity, refusing to accept even a single verse of the fourfold Dharma; they reviled him as one lacking wisdom.
Because he knew the principle through his wisdom, and since they called him "lacking wisdom," they would not accept his teachings. Thus, that bhikṣu did not receive [the offerings of] others.

First, as for "coming from nowhere," not accepting the practice of a single false prophecy, not accepting instruction, and having experienced many years of constant abuse—this is the first of the four [aspects] of "not accepting" that resolve provisional means to reveal the ultimate (*upāya-saṃdhāraṇa-vinivartana-tattva-prakāśana*).

Second, as for fleeing far away and dwelling at a distance while shouting aloud, this too is "not accepting"; it refers to the fundamental principle of "not accepting" the provisional to reveal the ultimate.
Regarding the first of the four points on the ground: because he constantly spoke these words, those who were bound by faith did not cease their deep belief.
Regarding the fourth point, that he gave the name "Never-Disparaging" to the fourfold assembly: this refers to those who were bound by disparagement and would not stop their slanders.
Question: When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he hesitated and did not speak; why did Never-Disparaging speak impulsively upon seeing him for the first time? Answer: Fundamentally...

Because they already possess roots of goodness, Śākyamuni protects them by means of the small; because they have not yet possessed roots of goodness, he does not treat them lightly by means of the great, but rather subjects them to strong toxicity.

It is only because their fundamental conditions differ that this is so. △ Third, the dual exhortation regarding the latter two [types of beings] in terms of contrariety and conformity, also called the dual clarification of the retributions for praise and slander. Part one: clarifying the retribution for those who believe. Part one: the initial section.
This clarifies the karmic retribution.
When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the void all twenty quadrillion verses of the Lotus Sūtra previously taught by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
he was able to receive and uphold them all, and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye.
Having purified the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and having attained this purity of the six faculties,
he further increased his lifespan by two hundred trillion nayutas of years and extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of arrogant monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen looked down upon and despised this person, treating him as follows:

Those who heard the name "Not Disparaging" saw that he had attained the power of great spiritual transformations, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great sublime tranquility;
they all believed, submitted, and followed his teachings. This bodhisattva further transformed thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After his life ended, he encountered two thousand koṭis of Buddhas, all of whom were named...

Under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, he preached this Lotus Sūtra within his Dharma; by these causes and conditions, he further encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Meghasvarendrarāja.
Within the Dharmas of these various Buddhas, he received, upheld, read, and recited this sūtra and expounded it for the fourfold assembly;
therefore, he obtained these constant eyes, as well as the purity of his ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
With his faculties purified, he preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear and attained great power.
This was the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Never Disparaging, who made offerings to, reverently honored, and praised such a multitude of Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness.
Thereafter, he again encountered thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and likewise preached this [Dharma] within the teachings of all those Buddhas.
Through the accomplishment of the merits of this sūtra, one shall attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the believer’s three types of retribution: first, they obtain the purification of the six sense faculties in the present life; second, they are born at a time when they encounter the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;

third, they subsequently encounter two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas. Their supernormal powers constitute the purity of bodily action (*kāyakarma*), and their power of eloquence in joyful exposition constitutes the purity of verbal action (*vākkarma*).

The power of great, sublime tranquility is the purity of mental action. △ Second, the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern, in two parts: first, the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? At that time, was the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging anyone other than myself?
It was indeed my own self.
The one who was formerly Never-Disparaging was the World-Honored One’s causal body; thus it is said, "I myself am he.
△ Second, citing faith to encourage compliance:
"If I had not, in past lives, upheld, recited, and read this sutra, nor explained it for others, I would not have been able to attain [enlightenment] so swiftly."
"Because I received, upheld, recited, and expounded this sutra for others under previous Buddhas, I have swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, explaining the retribution for those who disparage [the teaching]. This has two parts; first, explaining the attainment of the result:

"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, because at that time the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—disparaged me with minds of anger and contempt, they shall for two hundred billion kalpas never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṃgha."
After undergoing great suffering in the Avīci Hell for a thousand kalpas, once these karmic offenses were exhausted,
he again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught him the path to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Those who disparage [the Buddha-nature] obtain both good and evil fruits; because they slander it, they fall into the evil realms. Yet, hearing the name of the Buddha-nature possesses the power of a "poisonous drum" that protects one’s virtuous retribution.
This so-called slander also constitutes a seed. It is like a person who falls to the ground and must rely on that very ground to rise again;

if even through slander and disparagement one can still obtain such wondrous fruits, how much more so for those who do not give rise to such disparagement? They will surely be able to [attain liberation].
Is it those who praise and rejoice? △ Second, the conclusion connecting the ancient and the modern, in two parts: first, the formal connection.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Were those members of the fourfold assembly who constantly disparaged this Bodhisattva at that time anyone else?
They were none other than these five hundred Bodhisattvas in this assembly, such as Bhadrapāla and others, and Siṃhacandra and others."
These are the hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were formerly five hundred upāsakas, such as the Buddha’s father,
all of whom have become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Second, citing transgressions to manifest compliance, exhorting adherence to the precepts to prevent their destruction.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and enables them to reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and copy this sūtra.
The sūtra possesses great power and will ultimately bring about a great fruit; one must diligently practice the five kinds of conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
△ Second, the two verses in praise [of the preceding section]. First, the verses on the causes and effects of faith and slander. First, a general verse on the origin of the matter:
In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), whose divine wisdom was immeasurable and who led all devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, being venerated by them all.
△ Second, the specific verses on the original narrative (nidāna), in three parts: First, the initial verse jointly designating the two individuals.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at a time when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta; at that time, the fourfold assembly was attached to the Dharma.
△ Second, the two verses that clarify both gain and loss. First, the verse on gain:
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging went to where they were and spoke to them, saying, "I do not disparage you;
all of you who practice the Way shall surely become Buddhas."
△ Second, the verse on failure.
Having heard this, people disparaged, reviled, and abused him.
△ Third, the verse further clarifying success.
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging was able to endure this.
△ Third, the verses on the retribution and the correlation between the past and the present, in two parts: first, the retribution.
When his offenses were exhausted, at the time of his death, he was able to hear this sutra; by the power of his six sense organs being purified, [he attained supernatural faculties].

His lifespan was increased, and he further expounded this sutra extensively for all people. All those who were attached to dharmas received the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation, being brought to fulfillment and established in the Buddha-way. Not disparaged, at the end of his life he encountered countless Buddhas;
because he had preached this sutra, he obtained immeasurable merit, gradually perfected his virtues, and swiftly attained the Buddha-way.
The phrase "when their offenses were completed" refers specifically to the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
This was because the fourfold assembly reviled the Bodhisattva and even pelted him with tiles and stones; yet the Bodhisattva was able to endure all of it.

Consequently, all the karmic offenses related to birth and death were thereby extinguished, which is why it is said they were "completed. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a person receives and upholds this..."

The passage stating that "one who is treated with contempt by others was destined for the evil realms due to karmic offenses from previous lives, but because they are now treated with contempt by people in this life, their karmic offenses from previous lives are thereby extinguished" is precisely such an example. △ Second, the conclusion and correlation.
At that time, the one who was not disparaged was none other than myself. At that time, the fourfold assembly who were attached to the Dharma heard the words of the one who was not disparaged:
"You shall become a Buddha. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered countless Buddhas;

the five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, as well as the fourfold assembly of pure-faith laymen and laywomen who are now listening to the Dharma before me, were those very people in my previous lives.

I exhort these people to listen to and receive this sutra, the foremost Dharma; I instruct and reveal it to them so that they may abide in nirvana and uphold such a scripture from lifetime to lifetime.
Those who are attached to dharmas find that those dharmas cannot be demonstrated; if one definitively asserts that something exists, that is attachment to dharmas, and so forth...
"Samādhi" refers to that which is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is also termed "clinging to dharmas. As the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* states:
"The harm caused by a wheel of swords to the people of Jambudvīpa is still minor compared to the fault of those who preach the Mahāyāna with a mind of grasping at existence.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "To dispute with 'existence' and 'non-existence,' or even to dispute with 'neither existence nor non-existence' regarding existence and non-existence [is a grave error]."
Just as a cowhide and a dragon-rope both fail to escape their inherent defects, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"The Buddhas taught the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those attached to existence; those who become attached to emptiness cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. To definitively assert that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent is called the discourse of the ignorant.
If one loses the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, whether acting for oneself or transforming others, [all efforts will be in vain].

The title of the sutra is established such that, if one attains the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, both self and others will be free from attachment. △ Second, the verse on exhorting the upholding [of the Dharma]:
"Only after billions upon billions of kalpas, even unto an inconceivable time, shall one hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Only after billions upon billions of kalpas, even unto an inconceivable time, have the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, spoken this sutra. Therefore, practitioners, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."
Upon hearing this sutra, do not give rise to doubt; you should with single-minded devotion widely expound it. In every lifetime you shall meet a Buddha and swiftly attain the Way of Buddhahood.

It is encountered but rarely in hundreds of millions of births, and heard only with difficulty throughout vast kalpas. Those who are able to receive and uphold it will certainly achieve Buddhahood, as entrusted by the golden mouth [of the Buddha].

One might not believe this analogy; however, this single chapter concerns how, in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, the Tathāgata encountered a Buddha appearing in the world named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśravaṇarāja).

At that time, our World-Honored One was practicing the bodhisattva path under that Buddha, known by the name Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta), and he forcibly planted seeds of poison among the fourfold assembly. Yet, those members of the fourfold assembly possessed the roots [of goodness].
Their faculties were so feeble and inferior that they were incapable of receiving the Great Transformation; they instead struck and hurled tiles and stones at him.

Because of this transgression, they fell into the Niraya hell. Within that hell, they suddenly gave rise to three thoughts and said to one another, "By what causes and conditions have we now fallen into this place?
They further said to one another, "It is because in our previous lives we were foolish and ignorant..."
The object of knowledge was falsely reviled with harsh words by Wuliang (Not-Light), who further subjected him to the cruel infliction of wooden staves and torture;

it was because of these sinful deeds that he sank into the depths of saṃsāra. Subsequently, however, he immediately aroused goodness and reformed his evil ways, attaining the supreme fruit without even leaving the three miserable realms—just as withered wood sprouts in springtime and cold ashes flare up again into flame.
△ Second, the eight chapters from "The Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa-parivarta*) downward clarify the entrustment and circulation. This section has three parts:

first, the two chapters on supernatural powers and entrustment clarify the entrustment and circulation; second, the five chapters from "Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) downward exhort circulation by means of transforming others;
third, the single chapter on Samantabhadra exhorts circulation by means of one's own practice. Within the first part, there are again two sections; first is the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers."

The twenty-first chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, titled "The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers," clarifies the Bodhisattvas’ reception of the mandate to propagate the sutra. This section on entrustment has two parts:
first, the presentation of the chapter title.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma, Chapter Twenty-one: The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers* (Tathāgata-ṛddhi-bala-parivarta).
Regarding the term "Tathāgata," it has been explained above. As for "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*): "spiritual" (*ṛ*) means unfathomable, and "power" (*ddhi*) refers to efficacious function.
Being unfathomable signifies the profoundness of the natural body; being efficacious function signifies the greatness of the power of transformation.
Because ten kinds of great powers are manifested herein to entrust the profound Dharma, it is titled the "Chapter on Spiritual Power. II. Explanation of the Sūtra Text, Part Two.
The first part consists of the prose and two verses; the initial prose section is further divided into three parts. First, the Bodhisattvas receive their mandate.

Second, the introductory narrative by the sūtra-reciter describes their respectful demeanor: "At that time, all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth..."
Before the Buddha, they single-mindedly joined their palms and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
△ Second, the vow to propagate the sutra, in three parts: First, the time.
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, after the extinction of the Buddha..."
△ Second, the locations:
the lands and places of parinirvāṇa where the World-Honored One’s emanated bodies reside.
△ Third, the vows.

Why should this sutra be explained in detail? It is because we ourselves also desire to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it.

It is not merely that he fulfills his mandate to benefit others; he also personally aspires to this truly pure Great Dharma, so that both self and others may be simultaneously benefited and glorified.
△ Second, the Buddha manifests his supernatural powers, in two parts: first, the assembly addressed.

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
Before all assemblies, including humans and non-humans.
△ Second, the actual manifestation of supernormal powers in ten parts: First, the mark of the protruding tongue.
Manifesting great supernormal power, he extends his broad and long tongue until it reaches the Brahma world.

The teachings now expounded in this sutra open up the three to reveal the one; internally secret while externally manifesting, they set aside the near to reveal the distant, clarifying how the Buddhas benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—all of which is true and not false.
The tongues of those with merit reach the tip of their noses; the Buddha of the Tripitaka reaches his hairline;
now, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven, he transcends both the ordinary and the holy, culminating at the summit of the Pure Heavens. Such is his *uṣṇīṣa*.
This extraordinary teaching is all the more trustworthy. △ Second, the entire body emits light:
from every pore, immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors are emitted, universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Likewise, beneath the jeweled trees and upon the lion thrones, the Buddhas also similarly extend their broad and long tongues and emit [light].
When the Buddha Śākyamuni of Measured Light and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifest their spiritual powers, a full hundred thousand years pass;
light radiates from every pore of their entire bodies, illuminating the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not shine brightly— this symbolizes wisdom.

The realm is exhausted; the white tuft of hair above [the Buddha’s brow] emits radiance, first appearing in the east to symbolize the initial vision of the single principle through the seven stages of expedient means.

Now that the present Gate of the Essential Teaching has concluded, he emits all-encompassing light that illumines all lands, enabling those at the initial cause to reach the ultimate Buddha-wisdom at the stage of Equal Enlightenment. The manifested Buddhas are likewise so. △ Third, the clearing of the throat.
Thereupon, he withdrew his tongue-attribute and coughed once.
To cough is the prelude to speaking; it is also a sign of thorough penetration. For more than forty years, the truth was concealed and kept secret;
now that it has been fully extended and unfolded without any obstruction, this is the great matter of my appearance in the world to bring about complete penetration.
Therefore, he cleared his throat, wishing to entrust this Dharma to the bodhisattvas so that they might guide and benefit sentient beings in future ages;
it was for the purpose of speaking these matters that he cleared his throat. Furthermore, clearing the throat carries two meanings: first, clearing the throat to signal that the matter is concluded;
second, clearing the throat to signify the entrustment to others. △ Fourth, snapping the fingers.
Together they snapped their fingers.

To snap the fingers is to express sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). They expressed sympathetic joy that those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) would likewise enter the Perfect Path (*pariniṣpanna-mārga*).

They expressed sympathetic joy that the Perfect Path increases wisdom and diminishes birth. They expressed sympathetic joy that all Bodhisattvas uphold the Great Dharma of True Purity. They expressed sympathetic joy that future generations shall obtain [it].
This supreme jewel, with a single snap of the fingers, penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally across the ten directions.

△ At the fifth stage, there are six kinds of earth-movements; these two sounds reach everywhere throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and the earth in all those worlds trembles in six ways.
The sixfold movement of the earth signifies that from the initial mind to the final mind, there are six stages of movement;
through the cessation of ignorance, wisdom now moves all people’s six sense faculties, causing them to attain purity. △ Sixth, the Universal Vision of the Great Assembly.
Among them, the sentient beings— devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth— by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all beheld the Buddhas beneath the immeasurable,
boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of jewel-trees upon lion thrones in this Sahā world, and they saw [them].
They saw Śākyamuni Buddha sitting together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa;
they also saw immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly respectfully surrounding Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having seen this, they all rejoiced greatly, experiencing what they had never known before.
The universal vision of this great assembly signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is identical; from now on, it shall likewise be so.

As for the five thousand who rose and departed and were subsequently moved elsewhere by the three transformations—having lost their original resolve and being unable to manifest benefit—it is appropriate to treat their apparent extinction as non-extinction.
By following the various bodhisattvas who propagate the sutra and attain the Way, they shall enter the Buddha-wisdom, just as in this present assembly.
The difference also indicates that there is a single organic unity in the future. △ Seventh, the proclamation in the void:
At that moment, the devas in the midst of the void raised their voices and proclaimed:
"Beyond these immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā; therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
"O Bhikṣuṇī, you shall now preach for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*,
which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas. You all should, with deep resolve, rejoice in it, and you should also pay homage to and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha."
This indicates that there is one future informative act (vijñapti). △ Eighth, all together take refuge.
Having heard the voice from the midst of space, those sentient beings joined their palms toward the Sahā world and spoke these words:
"Namo Śākyamuni Buddha! Namo Śākyamuni Buddha!"
This indicates that in the future there will be those who offer even a single "Namo"—a Sanskrit term whose Chinese translation means "deliver me," "save me," or "take refuge and pay homage.
Tiantai remarked that "Namo" possesses great significance, which refers precisely to this.
It is because sentient beings have fallen into the seven realms of existence, sinking and circling in transmigration without ever ceasing, much like a young child caught in [danger].
Amidst water and fire, they cried out urgently for their parents, seeking rescue and deliverance;
those who were mindful of their lives all followed the words of their knocking and became disciples of the Buddha as a testament for the future—this is the first instance. △ Ninth:
Various objects were scattered from afar, and [the spirits] gathered like clouds.
With various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and all manner of ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite objects,
they all together scattered them from afar toward the Sahā world; these scattered items came from the ten directions like a gathering of clouds,
transforming into a jeweled canopy that completely covered the Buddhas here.
This indicates that there is one future practice. △ Tenth: The ten directions are universally identical as a single Buddha-field.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions are pervasively unobstructed, being as one Buddha-field.
This indicates that the principle is one. Question: How is it known that the ten characteristics manifest the intended meaning and further manifest the meaning for the future?
Answer: The text states: "By means of this spiritual power, even if I were to speak of the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment throughout immeasurable kalpas, I could not exhaust them.
This clearly manifests that the meaning is being conveyed. △ Third, the summary and exhortation to uphold.
Fourth, the initial praise and entrustment:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, such as Uṣṇīṣa-śikhi and others, saying, "The supernatural power of the Buddhas is thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
If, by means of this supernatural power, I were to [act] for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis..."
Even if one were to spend incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas speaking for the sake of entrustment, the merits of this sutra could not be fully exhausted.
△ Second, the summary and formal entrustment:
To state it in brief, all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata and all the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata—
The Tathāgata’s treasury of all essential secrets and all the Tathāgata’s most profound matters are all proclaimed and fully explained in this sutra.
That "all dharmas" refers to the fact that everything is the Buddha-dharma; this is the summary of the title "All-Wondrous. (1)
"All powers" refers to unimpeded penetration and the possession of the eight self-mastery powers; this is the wondrous function of this seal.
"All secret treasuries" refers to the fact that all places are the true mark (dharmatā); this is the wondrous essence of this seal.
"All profound matters" refers to cause and effect as profound matters; this is the wondrous thesis of this seal. All of these are proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra.
This concludes the entire sutra, which consists of only these four parts; having grasped its essential core, it is bestowed upon you so that it may be circulated.
△ Third, the exhortation and entrustment:
"Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe [this sutra]."
As it has been taught, in whatever land one practices accordingly, wherever there may be those who uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe [this sutra],
or wherever the scrolls of this sutra may reside— whether in a garden, a grove, beneath a tree, in a monastery,
in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in mountain valleys and wildernesses— in that place...
All should erect stupas to make offerings.
Regarding "exhorting and encouraging": "exhorting" means to urge them on, and "encouraging" means to praise and commend them, so that the fourfold assembly may admire this path.
Wherever it is, one should exhort and praise its circulation; in whatever region it reaches, one should always erect a stupa and make offerings.
The sincerity [of this] is such that this sutra is itself the true-body śarīra of the Tathāgata. △ Fourth, the explanation of the intent behind the entrustment. Why is this so?
One should know that this place is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for it is here that all Buddhas attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"In this [Dharma] is anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, and it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.
This passage explains the intent behind the entrustment. As stated above, "wherever these sūtra scrolls are located, one should erect a stūpa there. However—

The essential points taught in the sutra are contained within these four matters of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*): explaining the aforementioned profound matter as the attainment of *bodhi*;
explaining the aforementioned secret treasury as the turning of the wheel of Dharma; explaining all dharmas as entering *nirvāṇa*; and explaining the aforementioned supernatural powers.
Since these four essentials encompass the entirety of the sutra’s text, it is said that "stūpas should be erected for them all. As for what is meant by "essential":
Attaining Bodhi is the Dharmakāya; turning the Wheel of Dharma is Prajñā; entering Nirvāṇa is Vimukti.

These three dharmas constitute the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa), and for the Buddha to dwell within them is the meaning of a stūpa. The Āgamas state that when a Buddha appears in the world, stūpas are erected at only four locations:
the place of birth, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, and the place where he entered Nirvāṇa while sitting at the site of enlightenment.
The Place of Birth of the Dharma-body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
△ Second, the Verse Summary, Part Two: First, the summary of the ten kinds of spiritual powers.
The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers; for the sake of gladdening sentient beings, they manifest immeasurable spiritual powers.
Their tongue-reach extends to the Brahma-heaven, and from their bodies they emit countless rays of light. For those who seek the Buddha-way, they manifest these rare and marvelous events.
The sound of the Buddhas’ coughing and the snap of their fingers resounds throughout the lands of the ten directions, and the earth in every realm shakes in six ways.
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers.
△ Second, the verse summary of the essential points and the entrustment, in three parts: first, a general verse on the four dharmas.
Because I entrust this sutra, I praise those who receive and uphold it;

even throughout immeasurable kalpas, one could never exhaust the description of such a person’s merit, for it is boundless and inexhaustible, like the ten directions of empty space, whose limits cannot be found.
△ Second, the separate verses on the four dharmas. First, the verse on all dharmas:
"Those who can uphold this sutra have already seen me, as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his emanations;
they also see me today teaching and transforming the bodhisattvas."
To uphold this Dharma is to uphold the body of the Buddha. △ Second, the verse on sovereign spiritual powers:
"Those who can uphold this sutra cause me, as well as my emanations, the deceased Prabhūtaratna Buddha, and all others to rejoice.
They shall see and make offerings to the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions, as well as those of the past and future, and cause them all to attain joy."
Through his supernatural power, he exhorted the Buddha to rejoice. △ Third, the verses on the treasury of secret essentials:
"The secret essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when they sit at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long."
△ Four verses on the matter of profound depth:
Those who are able to uphold this sutra will possess inexhaustible eloquence in explaining the meanings, names, and phrases of all dharmas;
like the wind in space, they shall encounter no obstruction whatsoever, and after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, they shall understand the sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
Explaining causes, conditions, and the sequence according to their true meaning, just as the light of the sun and moon can dispel all darkness,
so too does this person, moving through the world, extinguish the darkness of sentient beings and teach immeasurable bodhisattvas to ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
△ Third, the summary verse concludes the meaning:
"Therefore, those with wisdom who hear these merits and benefits should, after my parinirvāṇa, uphold this sutra;
such persons will have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-way."
△ Second, the Entrustment Chapter (Parīndanā-parivarta), which clarifies the Tathāgata’s entrustment by stroking [the heads] of the assembly. Part One: Stating the Title of the Chapter.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Chapter Twenty-Two: The Entrustment (*parīndanā*).

"Entrustment" (*parīndanā*) refers to that which the Buddha has committed to others; "to hand over" (*parīndanā*) means to cause you to propagate it. This chapter derives its name from this sacred mandate.
Regarding the term "entrustment" (*parindanā*): "entrusting" refers to receiving the entrustment upon one's head; "that which is entrusted" refers to accepting it with joy and without weariness.

This is named according to the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance. Furthermore, "entrusting" refers to that which is entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, while "that which is entrusted" refers to the Bodhisattva’s sincere heart bearing it upon his head.
Since this is discussed in terms of both the bestowal and the reception, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment. Therefore, the Tathāgata...
The World-Honored One rose from his seat in person, extended his hand to stroke their heads, and bestowed upon them the Dharma that is difficult to encounter.

The great assembly bowed their bodies and joined their palms, pledging to carry out the World-Honored One’s instructions with full devotion. Because this was the earnest transmission and reception [of the teaching], it is titled the "Chapter on the Entrustment" (Zhūlèi Pǐn).
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text, in two parts. First, the actual entrustment, in three parts. First, the Tathāgata’s entrustment, in three parts.
First, the actual entrustment:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat, manifested great supernormal power, and with his right hand rubbed [the crown of] Ananda...
Touching the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, he spoke these words:
"I have cultivated this rare Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; I now entrust it to you.
You should, with a single mind, disseminate this Dharma and cause it to increase and flourish extensively."
The Tathāgata placed his hand upon the heads of all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and spoke these words:
"I have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so difficult to attain, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
I now entrust it to you; you should receive, uphold, read, recite, and widely proclaim this Dharma for the sake of all beings."
All sentient beings universally hear and know this.

As for the "True Entrustment," the Buddha, with the skillful hand of his single expedient wisdom, strokes the crowns of the heads of all the Bodhisattvas—who fill the void of three thousand three hundred nayutas of lands—with his true wisdom; thus does the Tathāgata confer the transformation of the Way.

Because it is the ground, it is called the Hand of Expedient Wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); because the Bodhisattva personally practices and receives the Way, it is called the Crown of Ultimate Wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
To extend the hand and touch the crown is the entrustment of the body; for Expedient Wisdom to approach Ultimate Wisdom is the entrustment of the mind;
