and to speak these words is the entrustment of the mouth. These texts contain the four *siddhānta* intentions. Regarding "I, at... [the text continues].
"This dharma, which has been cultivated through immeasurable kalpas and is difficult to obtain, was received and studied from previous Buddhas;
I now entrust it to you. You shall transmit it to others as the succession of the three periods of time, which is the world itself.
To disseminate it with a single mind is humanity; to cause it to increase extensively is the remedy; and to benefit others is the ultimate truth. △
Second, the explanation of entrustment.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess, and is without fear;
he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata-wisdom, and the self-arisen wisdom. The Tathāgata is the father of all sentient beings.
O Great Benefactors, you too should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and do not give rise to stinginess.
That which possesses great compassion is the chamber of the Tathāgata; that which is free from stinginess is the robe of the Tathāgata;
and that which is without fear is the seat of the Tathāgata. The wisdom of the Buddha is omniscience (sarvajñatā), [which is] the Tathāgata...
The wisdom of the modes of the path is the wisdom of the wise; the natural wisdom is the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Within the Tathāgata’s chamber, one can bestow these three kinds of wisdom upon sentient beings, and it is likewise so within his seat.
Because you are such donors—because you are free from stinginess and free from fear—you should train yourselves in this way according to the Tathāgata.
This Dharma is named "Expounding the Buddha’s Intent and Entrusting It. △ Third, the Admonition for Entrustment:

"In a future age, if there are good men or good women who believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them so that they may hear and know it, in order to cause those people to attain the Buddha-wisdom. If there are...
For those sentient beings who do not believe or accept [this], you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound teachings of the Tathāgata;
if you can act in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas.
Regarding the entrustment: if their roots are deep and their wisdom sharp, explain the Buddha-wisdom directly;

if they are not yet capable, then within other profound dharmas, provide instruction, benefit, and joy. You should know that the Buddha-wisdom is profound while the other six provisional means are not;
the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the gradual stage is both "other" and "profound. If you are able [to teach] these other profound dharmas...
To assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely to skillfully repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is called the "Instruction and Entrustment.
△ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ Acceptance:
At that time, having heard the Buddha speak these words, all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas were filled with great joy throughout their entire beings.
With even greater reverence, they bowed their bodies, lowered their heads, and joined their palms toward the Buddha, speaking with one voice:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out in full. So be it, World-Honored One; may you have no further concern.

The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas repeated these words three times, speaking with one voice: "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out in full. So be it, World-Honored One."
"May you have no further concern.
All were greatly rejoiced; this is mental acceptance. Bowing the body and lowering the head is physical acceptance.
Uttering words with one voice is verbal acceptance, which also implies mental acceptance. "As the World-Honored One has commanded"—this is acceptance.
The Great Donor should, with the intention of the Tathāgata’s chamber, fully practice and receive it; with the intention of the Tathāgata’s robe, he should receive it without stinginess;
with the intention of the Tathāgata’s seat, he should receive it without anxiety. Thus, the Buddha has made the three entrustments and the Bodhisattva has received the three;
all is as stated in the text. △ Having completed these three matters, the assembly is dismissed.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded all the Buddhas who had come from the ten directions as his emanations to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the various Buddhas each abide as they please, and may the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna return to its former state."
Because Prabhūtaratna came to bear witness to this sutra, the two gates of the present and the original have now been concluded; therefore, he must respectfully depart as before.
He divided his body in order to open the stupa, and now that the task of opening the stupa is finished, he causes the divided bodies to return to their original [abodes].
Since the stupa cannot be opened again, the divided bodies depart and do not appear; yet because the stupa still hears the Dharma, it remains closed and yet...
Question: When asking questions or listening to the Dharma, should one also keep the eyes closed? Answer: One closes them because they have already realized the truth;
they remain closed for the sake of listening so that the teaching may circulate. △ Second, the assembly rejoices.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who were seated upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees,
as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, the boundless assembly of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas such as Viśiṣṭacāritra,
the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas such as Śāriputra, and all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, heard what the Buddha had said.
It is said that all rejoice:
the Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice;
furthermore, it is said that people rejoice because they are pure—this refers to the Buddhas—and they rejoice because they have heard the pure Dharma—this refers to the wondrous sutra.

Because they hear the Dharma and attain realization, they rejoice; this refers to those who obtain benefit in the present and the future. Because these three matters are fully possessed, there is great joy.
△ Second, the five chapters from the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter downward concern exhorting others to circulate [the teaching]. Part one: The "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter.
Chapter Two: The Exquisite Sound; Chapter Three: Avalokiteśvara; Chapter Four: Dhāraṇī; Chapter Five: The Exquisite Adornments. The initial text is further divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of the chapter title.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Formerly known as Jyotīrasa, he heard the exposition of the Buddha’s wisdom from the Venerable Sūryagarbha.
He offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing: 'May I, in the future, be able to cure both the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings.
The entire world rejoiced and called him Bhaiṣajyarāja. This passage clarifies that Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly renounced one [of his two bodies].
Next, his body burns, followed by his two arms; he regards life lightly and the Dharma as weighty, so that though his life perishes, the Way remains.

To illustrate the past through the present, it is called the "Chapter on Past Deeds" (*Pūrvayoga*). If one were to infer this meaning, *Prabhāketu* should follow after *Priyadarśana*, for from the time he made his vow upon giving away his medicine, he was named "Medicine King. II. Explanation of the Sutra Text, Part Four: First, the Bodhisattva’s Request.

Question: The two Tathāgatas provide a definitive answer; there are three benefits and four praises by Prabhūtaratna. In the first section, there are again three parts. First, the general inquiry regarding his travels and transformations:
At that time, the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel?"
In the Sahā world. △ Second, the specific inquiry regarding ascetic practices:
"World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja has undergone hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, billions, nayutas of difficult and painful practices."
[He] proceeded.
△ Third, the request for the Buddha’s response and explanation:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will briefly explain [this] for the sake of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras."
The garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, as well as the bodhisattvas who had come from other lands and this assembly of śrāvakas, all heard it and rejoiced.

△ Second, the Tathāgata’s definitive response, which has two parts: first, the answer regarding ascetic practices; second, the praise of the sutra. The first section [the answer regarding ascetic practices] also has two parts:
first, clarifying the origin of the event; third, the duration of time.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Ratnottamaśrī): "In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
Second, there were the Śrāvakas and others of that Buddha.

There was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. That Buddha had eight [great assemblies].
There were ten billion great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and a great assembly of voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*) as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers;
the Buddha’s lifespan was forty-two thousand kalpas, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas were equal to his.
△ Third, the adornment of the land.
That land has no women, nor does it have the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras, nor any of the various difficulties;
its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, composed of lapis lazuli, adorned with jewel trees, and covered by hanging jeweled canopies and banners of precious flowers.
Jeweled incense burners and vases pervaded the entire realm, with pedestals made of the seven treasures;
for every tree there was a pedestal, and each tree stood at a distance from its pedestal equal to the range of an arrow-shot.
Beneath all these jeweled trees sat bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and upon each jeweled pedestal were ten billion devas performing celestial music and singing praises of the Buddha as an offering.

△ Second, explaining the original events (pūrvayoga), which has three parts: first, the Buddha preaching the Dharma; second, the performance of offerings; third, the conclusion and identification of the assembly. Now, for the first:
At that time, that Buddha was preaching the Lotus Sutra for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, as well as the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
However, since the Buddha universally acts for the sake of all beings, why is it that he alone rejoices at seeing this [disciple]?
It is because he must entrust [the teaching] to him for its circulation, as when Śāriputra was sent on a single mission. △ Second, the practice of making offerings, in two parts: first, the present;
second, first, practicing to attain the Dharma.
This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana delighted in practicing asceticism; within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī,
he practiced walking meditation with diligence and single-mindedly sought Buddhahood for twelve thousand years, after which he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
The attainment of the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies (*sarvarūpakāyasaṃdarśana-samādhi*) is precisely the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies;

this has three meanings: First, internal manifestation, as described in the sūtras: the body-faculty is purified such that the ten realms of both the primary and secondary supports appear within the body, just as various forms and images appear in a clear, bright mirror. Second, external manifestation, as described in the sūtras... [text continues]
Third, the universal manifestation according to capacities, wherein the forms of the ten realms differ: both internal and external appear together, as stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
One contemplates one’s own body, the bodies of sentient beings, and the bodies of all Buddhas, all of which manifest within one’s own body;

furthermore, one sees one’s own body and the bodies of sentient beings manifest within the bodies of the Buddhas, and likewise, the bodies of sentient beings [manifest within the bodies of the Buddhas].
For this reason, he is named "Universally Manifesting Ear. △ Second, the reflection on repaying the debt of gratitude, in two parts: first, by the power of samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately reflected:

"That I have attained the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* is entirely due to the power of having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. I shall now make offerings to the Tathāgata Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa."

The Buddha and the Lotus Sūtra immediately entered this samādhi, and from the midst of the void there rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and finely ground, hard black sandalwood, filling the void and descending like clouds.
Furthermore, there rained down the fragrance of *sāgara-cīrṇa* sandalwood; six *zhu* of this incense are worth as much as the entire Sahā world-system.
They made offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding "the shore of this side of the ocean," the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "Below Mount Sumeru is the shore of this side of the ocean;
'this side' refers to the southern shore. It is from there that this incense originates, hence it receives its name. As for the "six *zhū*," twenty [of these] constitute one...
Four *zhū* make one *liǎng*; thus, six *zhū* are merely one-fourth of that. △ Second, the power of the primary reward-body (*sambhogakāya*).
Part three: First, burning one's own body.
Having performed this offering, he arose from *samādhi* and thought to himself: "Although I have made this offering through my supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*),"
Not yet satisfied with making offerings to the Buddha with his body alone, he then consumed various fragrances— sandalwood, *kunkuma*, *turushka*, *pilikā*, aloeswood, and resin—
and drank the fragrant oils of *campaka* flowers for twelve hundred years. Having done so,
he anointed his body with these fragrant oils and wrapped himself in celestial jewel robes before the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Brightness (*Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa*).

Having poured various fragrant oils [upon him], by means of his supernormal powers and vows, his natural bodily radiance spontaneously illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of eight billion Ganges Rivers.
△ Second, the Buddha’s praise.
Therein, all the Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is true diligence;

this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. If one were to offer various such things as flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, unguents, celestial silks, banners, canopies, and the sandalwood from the other side of the sea—"
Even if one were to give away kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, it would still not equal it.
Noble son, this is called the foremost gift; among all gifts, it is the most honored and supreme.
Because they offer the Dharma to all Tathāgatas, having spoken these words, they each remained silent.

As for the true offering of Dharma, it refers to internally employing the contemplation of wisdom to observe that both the causes and effects of afflictions are all cleared away by the wisdom of emptiness;
therefore, it is called the "true Dharma. Furthermore, when one contemplates whether it is the body or the fire—the offerer or the object offered—all are the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Since neither the one who burns nor the fuel can be apprehended, and neither the offerer nor the object offered can be found, it is named the "true Dharma."
Furthermore: △ Third, the duration of time is long:
his body burns with fire for twelve hundred years, and only after this period has passed does his body finally perish.
△ Second, regarding the future [lives], first he will be born by transformation (*upapāduka*) into a royal family.
After the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed such a Dharma-offering and his life came to an end,
he was reborn by transformation, sitting cross-legged, in the household of King Śuddhayaśas within the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī.
△ Second, he himself recounts a past event.
He then spoke a verse for his father, saying:
"Great King, you should now know that as I was walking there, I immediately attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Bodies."
Exerting great diligence, he sacrificed his beloved body.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī is still present in the world today.
Having first made offerings to that Buddha, I attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings, and I further heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
"O Great King, after reciting eight hundred thousand million billion nayutas of *kankara*, *vimbara*, and *akṣobhya* verses,
I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha."
Regarding the attainment of the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, there is a samādhi named 'Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings,' which means that within a single syllable one explains all syllables, and understands all syllables to be identical to a single syllable.

As for *viṃśati*, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Viṃśati is [the same as] *viṃśaka*. (Note: The term *viṃśati* refers to twenty; the text here appears to be discussing phonetic or numerical equivalencies.)
Within the fifty-two numerical units, the sixteenth unit, *piṇḍa*, is the same as the eighteenth;
it is also called *piṇḍārbuda*, which is the twentieth unit. It is also called *akṣobhya*;
these differences arise from the discrepancies between the new and old translations. Some say that *nayuta* is one hundred million, while *kharva* is ten billion.
One *arbuda* is one hundred thousand *koṭis*. One *ahuva* is ten thousand *koṭis*, one hundred thousand *koṭis*, and one million *koṭis*.

Regarding the expression "eight hundred thousand *koṭis*," the *Fashijing yinyun* (Phonetics of the Dharma Master’s Sūtra) states that in the Western Regions there are four systems for the term *billion* (*koṭi*):
first, one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*; second, one million is called a *koṭi*; third, ten million is called a *koṭi*; [and fourth, one hundred million is called a *koṭi*].

Regarding "one hundred million" (*bì*): four ten-thousands make one hundred million; it is feared that in the current text, the number for "one hundred million" may actually refer to one hundred thousand.
△ Third, going to where the Buddha was.
Having made his announcement, he immediately sat upon a platform of the seven treasures, ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms with ten fingers together, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“Your countenance is most wondrous and sublime; your radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you, and now I come again to behold you in person.”
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world.
△ 4. The Tathāgata’s Entrustment.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Good son, the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived;
the moment of my final extinction has come. You should prepare a seat, for I shall enter parinirvāṇa this very night.
He further commanded the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Good son, by means of the Buddha-dharma..."
I entrust this to you and to all the bodhisattvas and great disciples, as well as the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, I also entrust to you the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system of seven-jeweled worlds, including all the jewel trees, jewel terraces, and the attendant devas;
and after my parinirvāṇa, all my relics shall likewise be entrusted to you, so that you may cause them—
After the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had thus exhorted the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and widely established offerings by enjoining the construction of several thousand stūpas,
he entered parinirvāṇa during the latter part of the night.
△ Five: Receiving the Command to Maintain [the Dharma]. First, the Erection of Stūpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, was overcome with grief and distress, longing for the Buddha.
He immediately used *candana* from this side of the ocean to construct a pyre as an offering for the Buddha’s body and cremated it with fire.
After his parinirvāṇa, his relics were collected and placed into eighty-four thousand precious jars, with which eighty-four thousand stupas were erected;
they reached the height of the three worlds, adorned with ornamental banners and poles, draped with various streamers and canopies, and hung with many precious bells.

Regarding "heaps of sandalwood," the character [卄/積] (ji) is fundamentally read as "accumulation" (*ji*). The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states that it refers to a "mound, embankment, or accumulation.
"Reaching a height equal to the three worlds" may mean that from the Desire Realm up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven constitutes one world;
thus, there are three such [worlds]. Others say it is, for example, like completely covering a trichiliocosm. This is why it is small.
A thousand [worlds] reach up to the First Dhyāna, a middle thousand reaches up to the Second Dhyāna, and a great thousand reaches up to the Third Dhyāna;

what is now called "high through the three periods" refers to reaching the Fourth Dhyāna. However, this height and breadth are the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas—a matter beyond the scope of ordinary sentiment.
One should simply believe with earnestness, for one will surely receive profound benefit. △ Second, burning the arms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana thought to himself again: "Although I have made these offerings, my mind is still not yet satisfied.

I shall now further offer worship to the relics. He then addressed the assembly of all bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others: "You all should concentrate your minds; I am now making an offering."
After the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Bright Virtue had spoken these words, he set his arm— adorned with the hundred blessings—
ablaze before eighty-four thousand stupas and made this offering for seventy-two thousand years.
△ Third, the benefit:
It causes countless seekers of the Śrāvaka vehicle— immeasurable asaṃkhyeya persons— to resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
and enables them all to dwell in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
△ Fourth, the present retribution.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and others, seeing that he was without arms, were distressed and grieved, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher and the one who has instructed us."
Now, having burned his arms so that his body was no longer complete, at that time the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana stood before the great assembly and made this vow:
"If I shall certainly attain the golden-colored body of a Buddha after casting away these two arms, and if this is true and not false, may my two arms be restored as they were before.
Having made this vow, they were naturally restored once again by virtue of this.
This was brought about by the profound thickness of the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom;
at that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers, such that all devas and humans experienced what they had never known before.
△ Third, the reconciliation of the two [sections]. First, the reconciliation:
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Ratnaprabha): "What do you think? Is the Bodhisattva 一切眾生喜見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) anyone else?
He is none other than the present Bodhisattva 藥王 (Bhaiṣajyarāja). His relinquishing of his body as an act of giving was thus without limit."
It measures hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
△ Second, the exhortation to practice:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there are those who resolve their minds and wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able..."

Nevertheless, making an offering to a Buddha stūpa with even a single finger of one’s hand— or even a single toe of one’s foot— is superior to making an offering with kingdoms, cities, wives, children,
and all the precious objects found within the mountains, forests, rivers, and lakes of a trichiliocosm.
To light a single finger-tip [of incense] is superior to giving away one's external body, because the external is light while the internal is heavy; thus, there is a difference in merit and virtue.

Regarding the text "wife and children," these refer to the external body; "kingdom, cities, and so forth" refers to external wealth. △ Second, praising the sutra, in three parts: first, praising those who can uphold it.
If there were another person who filled the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system with the seven treasures to make offerings to the Buddha,

as well as to the great bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal the merit of one who upholds even a single four-line verse of this Lotus Sūtra; the latter’s blessings are far greater.
Offering the seven treasures to the Four Noble Ones is not equal to upholding a single verse of the Dharma. This is because the Dharma is the Holy Teacher;
it can give birth, nourish, perfect, and bring glory. Since nothing surpasses the Dharma, people may be light while the Dharma is heavy.

In the sutras, it is said that the merit and blessings obtained from offering the seven treasures, filling a great trichiliocosm, to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats do not [equal those of upholding the Dharma].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one who upholds even a single four-line verse of this sutra," this uses the few to illustrate the many.
As for the "four lines," it refers to taking any four lines from within the sutra and upholding them. In the Western Regions (India), four lines constitute a single *gāthā* (verse);

however, one must not selectively pick out specific passages from the sutra to designate as such. If one were to select them arbitrarily, a mind of partiality would arise, leading to the perception of superiority and inferiority, or gravity and lightness.
Why is this so? For the beginning and end of this single scripture are all the holy words from the Buddha’s own mouth; how could they be subject to selection or rejection?
It is like a person eating honey, which is sweet both at the center and the edges; it is like a golden tally, which is gold from start to finish.
This is what is meant by the saying: "If one cuts through jade, every inch is treasure; if one splits sandalwood, every slice is fragrant. It is not merely this alone.
This sutra is like all other sutras. △ Second, praising the Dharma that is upheld, in two parts: first, praising the essence of the Dharma.
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, for example, among all the waters of streams, rivers, and great rivers, the ocean is foremost;
this Lotus Sutra is also like this, being the most profound and vast among all the sutras spoken by the Tathāgatas. Furthermore—
Just as Mount Sumeru is the foremost among all mountains— such as the Earth Mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains,
the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and the ten jewel mountains— so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* the most supreme among all sūtras.
Furthermore, just as the Moon Deity is the foremost among all the stars, so is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It is likewise so: among thousands of myriads of kotis of various sūtras and dharmas, it is the most illuminating;
just as the Sun Deity is able to dispel all darkness, this sūtra is also like this, being able to destroy all the darkness of unwholesomeness.
Just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost, this sūtra is also like this.
Among all the sūtras, this is the most honored, just as Śakra is the king among the thirty-three gods;
this sūtra is likewise the king among all sūtras. Furthermore, it is like Mahābrahmā, the father of all sentient beings;
this sūtra is likewise so for all noble ones—those in training and those beyond training—as well as for those who have resolved to attain the bodhicitta.
Just as among all ordinary worldlings, the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*,

and *pratyekabuddha* are the foremost, so too is this sutra the foremost among all the sūtras and dharmas spoken by all Tathāgatas, whether spoken by Bodhisattvas or by Śrāvakas. There is none that can...
It is likewise for those who receive and uphold this sutra: among all sentient beings they are the foremost;
among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost. This sutra is also like this:
among all sūtras and dharmas, it is the most supreme. Just as the Buddha is the King of all Dharmas, so too is this sutra.
Among all such sūtras, this is the king;
among all waters—streams, rivers, and great rivers—the ocean is the foremost. As stated in the *Anantavārṣika* (Infinite Meanings) Sūtra, the four waters serve as a metaphor for the teachings;
in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," it is said that a single cloud can rain down upon them. Now, we shall further discuss how all these waters collectively represent everything.

The reason other teachings specifically mention four [flavors] is merely as an analogy for the four tastes of milk, curd, raw [milk], and cooked [milk]. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaching is an analogy for the sea of *amṛta* (clarified butter).

It is "profound" because its exposition reaches the ultimate ground; it is "great" because it pervades all places; it is "purely bright" because it teaches only the Buddha-dharma and not other dharmas;
and it is "salty" [in its excellence] because it is the most profound and great. Such is the meaning of the names of the ten jewel mountains.
Because the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras state that the earth extends beyond the Black Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), it is not composed of jewels.

While the ten mountains may be made of jewels, they are inhabited by a mixture of deities and nāgas. In contrast, Mount Sumeru is composed of the four jewels and is the exclusive dwelling place of devas.

This serves as an analogy for the teachings of other schools, which speak of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and forty mental states (*citta*) as the "supported" (the faculties), whether they be ordinary beings, sages, or saints, while describing the [ten] earths as the "support. Or...
Whether mundane or supramundane, whether true or intermediate, these are considered inferior.

This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains the truth of reality—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—which serves as the basis for the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, much like that which is composed of the four jewels.
Therefore, this meaning is the most supreme. Although stars and the moon are both of the essence of darkness and both appear at night, the stars do not possess the phases of waning and waxing.
Furthermore, various sutras speak of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) as being unable to attain self-mastery;

this sutra clarifies that the provisional is itself the real and the real is itself the provisional, such that their fullness and deficiency refer to one another as non-dual yet dual—thus it is said that the wisdom of the provisional here surpasses that of other teachings.

The sun is the essence of yang and alone is able to dispel darkness; whereas the various sutras clarify that real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) dispels delusion, it does not even approach [the power of] this [wisdom].

Since the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the provisional (*upāya*) are not separate, and because one realizes the ultimate through the provisional, we know that this sutra clarifies that ultimate wisdom is the most supreme.
The wheel-turning king’s edicts reach only the four continents, whereas the Śakra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Brahmā’s edicts encompass both those above and below.
This serves as a metaphor for other sutras which teach the three truths and the three samādhis as being mutually exclusive and unable to contain one another.
In this sutra, it is taught that the entry into reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through the definitive understanding of the *śrāvaka* dharma is the king of all sutras;

the entry into reality through the conventional is not in contradiction with any livelihood or productive enterprise; and the entry into reality through the middle way is such that there is no phenomenon that is not the Buddha-dharma.
As the text says: "All those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who have resolved upon the bodhisattva mind..."
The meaning of "his father" is as follows: among all ordinary beings, those of the four fruits, and pratyekabuddhas, this [category] is the foremost;

this clarifies spontaneity and effortlessness (*anābhoga*). In other sutras, one must rely on effort to enter the stream, such as the persons of the four fruits who only attain awakening through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This sutra clarifies the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*asaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*), which are not mixed with such [gradual] methods.
They then naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), like a great white ox—plump, strong, and as swift as the wind;
these are the foremost among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. This clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] is foremost by reason of his cause (*hetu*).

While other sūtras clarify the cause through the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*), this sūtra clarifies that the cause lies outside of those skillful means; therefore, he is foremost by reason of his cause.

"The Tathāgata is the foremost" clarifies the fruit. While other sutras clarify the fruit as being proximate to the site of enlightenment at Vārāṇasī, this sutra clarifies the fruit by pointing distantly to the original ground;
therefore, it is the most supreme. △ Second, praising the function of the Dharma, in three parts: first, praising the function of uprooting suffering.
"O Rājādhyuṣita, this sutra can save all sentient beings; this sutra can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction.
△ Second, praising its function of bestowing happiness.
This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations: it is like a cool pond that satisfies all who are parched with thirst;
like fire for those who are cold; like clothing for those who are naked; like a master for merchants; like a mother for a child;
like a boat for those crossing over; like a physician for the sick; like a lamp for those in darkness; like wealth for the poor.
The treasure is like a commoner obtaining it, the king is like a merchant obtaining the sea, and the torch is like that which dispels darkness.
△ Third, the summary of bestowing and extracting:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise thus; it can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all ailments.
It can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
△ Third, the profound merit of upholding the sutra, in two parts: first, citing the merit of hearing the entire sutra.
If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it, the merit they obtain—
The wisdom of the Buddha cannot be measured in its extent; it has no limit.

If one were to write out this sutra scroll and offer it flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, banners, canopies, robes, and various kinds of lamps—such as ghee lamps, oil lamps, lamps of various fragrant oils, *campaka* oil lamps, *sumana* oil lamps, *pāṭala* oil lamps, and *vārṣika* oil lamps—[the merit would be immeasurable].
The merit obtained from making an offering of a *nāgavallī* oil lamp is likewise immeasurable.
△ Second, citing the merit of hearing this chapter, in two parts: first, the comparative measurement.
Ratnapuṣpa, if there be anyone who hears this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.

If there be women who hear this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" and are able to receive and uphold it, their female bodies will be exhausted at the end of this life, and they shall never again undergo such a form. Furthermore, during the final five hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if...

If there is a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings, upon the end of her life here, she will immediately go to the World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), to the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne;
she shall no longer be afflicted by desire, nor shall she be afflicted by hatred or delusion. Furthermore...
Untroubled by the defilements of pride and envy, they attain the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, their faculty of sight becomes pure. With this purified faculty of sight, they see seven million two thousand *koṭī-nayuta* Ganges-sand-like Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
At that time, all those Buddhas together praise them from afar, saying: "Excellent!"

Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and explain this sutra within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, the merit you thereby obtain is immeasurable and boundless; fire cannot burn it, nor can water wash it away.
The merits of yours could not be fully exhausted even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of them together. You have now indeed achieved this.
Having defeated all demonic marauders and shattered the army of birth and death, you have utterly crushed all other enemies.
Son of good family, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, shall together protect you;

among all the devas and humans in every world, there is none like you, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata. As for the wisdom of all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas— [...they do not equal yours.]
“Noble Wisdom, in meditative concentration, there is no one equal to you. Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this bodhisattva has accomplished such power of merit and wisdom.

If there is anyone who, upon hearing this ‘Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,’ can rejoice and praise it well, that person in the present life will constantly have the fragrance of blue lotuses issue from their mouth, and from the pores of their body, there will constantly [issue]...”
The merit obtained from emitting the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood is as described above.
That the mouth emits fragrance is a reward in the present life; the rest are rewards in future lives. △ Second, the entrustment.
Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this "Chapter on the Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" to you.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must propagate it widely throughout Jambudvīpa so that it does not become extinct, lest evil Māras, their followers, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others find an opportunity to cause harm. Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, you—
You should protect this sutra through the power of your supernormal faculties. Why is this?
Because this sutra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa. If anyone who is ill hears this sutra, their illness will immediately be extinguished;
they shall neither grow old nor die. Suvarnapuṣpa, if you see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, you should offer them blue lotuses.

Having scattered full measures of incense upon it, one should then form this thought: "This person shall before long surely take grass to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and shatter the armies of Māra;
they shall blow the Dharma conch and beat the great Dharma drum to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way, upon seeing one who upholds this sutra...
People should give rise to such a mind of reverence.
To hear this sutra and attain the state of neither aging nor dying requires contemplative understanding: "not aging" means bliss, and "not dying" means permanence.
This means that upon hearing this sutra, one attains the realization of permanence and bliss, which rests serenely within the heart, free from all fear.
[End of section] △ Third, the benefits:
While this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" was being expounded, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
△ Fourth, the praise by Prabhūtaratna.
From within the jeweled stupa, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised the Bodhisattva Rājādhiṣṭhānaguṇaviśuddhasvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Rājādhiṣṭhānaguṇaviśuddhasvara! You have accomplished inconceivable merit, that you are able to question Śākyamuni Buddha thus."
This matter benefits all sentient beings immeasurably.
△ Second, the "Chapter on Sublime Sound" (Miaoyin pin) clarifies the disciples who receive the mandate to propagate this sutra. Part one: Presenting the chapter title.
In the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," it is explained within the text itself:
[Gadgadasvara] formerly offered one hundred thousand kinds of music to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja;

now, as he travels through and transforms billions of lands, music follows him of its own accord. He formerly offered eighty-four thousand precious bowls; now, he possesses such a multitude of vessels for the Path.
Surrounded by his retinue, he had previously attained the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of all sentient beings;
now, manifesting his physical body everywhere with a wondrous voice that roars throughout the ten directions to widely proclaim this teaching, it is called the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound.
This chapter clarifies how the Bodhisattva, through inconceivable power, communicates the scriptures according to the various types of beings, such that all who behold his traces [are transformed].
To fathom its source, one simply savors its flavor without discriminating against its form;
one should humble oneself at that place and dam its own current—this is the second meaning within the section on transforming others. △ Second, the explanation of the scriptural text has six parts:

first, emitting light to summon from the east; second, receiving the command and coming from the west; third, propagating the sutra in the ten directions; fourth, the two lands obtaining benefits; fifth, the return.
In this country, the sixth chapter, "Advancing on the Path," begins now. At that time,
Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light from the *uṣṇīṣa*— the mark of a Great Man— and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between his eyebrows,
which shone everywhere throughout the east across as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in one hundred and eight million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.

Beyond this number of worlds, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*). In that land dwells a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalapuṣpa-nakṣatrarāja-jñāna*) Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men,
Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, who [is surrounded] by immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas.
Surrounded by a multitude who paid him respectful homage, Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma for them; the radiance from the white tuft between his eyebrows illuminated that land entirely.
As for the marks of a Great Man, they are an ocean of great signs; the merit of all the hairs on his body does not equal the merit of even a single secondary mark.
The merit of all the various secondary marks does not equal the merit of a single primary mark.

Each mark, from the lowest upward, successively surpasses the one below it, yet they do not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair). The merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* does not equal the merit of the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance);
therefore, these are called the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). This karma of the marks arises from filial obedience toward teachers and elders; now he emits this light.
He summoned his original disciples, those of great capacity who were to propagate the sutras of the Middle Way.
From the single path of pure origin, the white tuft of hair now emits this light to cause this Dharma to be propagated. [The disciples] asked:

"If each and every mark of the Buddha is the ocean of the Dharma-realm, why are there distinctions of superior and inferior? [The Buddha] replied: "In other sutras, it is appropriate to explain it in this way. [The disciples] asked: "Does the Buddha..."
Question: Since disciples fill the ten directions, why does he summon those from the east and speak of the west, rather than addressing all eight directions?
Answer: This has a symbolic significance. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "For what purpose do the sun and moon travel over Jambudvīpa?
It is to use their radiance to dispel the darkness of the masses. The east is the beginning of light, and the west is its end. To have a beginning and an end—this is the mark of the Sage alone.
As for humans, those who have not yet resolved their minds are caused to resolve them; those who have not yet reached the ultimate are caused to reach it.
As it is with one bodhisattva, so it is with all beings; as it is in one direction, so it is in all directions.
Since the Sages do not employ redundant phrasing—citing one instance to encompass all—they speak only of the east and west. II. Carrying out the Command to Come West. Part One.
Regarding the two sections on the arising of conditions for the first part of the initial text, there are again six subsections: first, the narrator’s account of the causes of merit;
second, the account of wisdom (which is "complete"); third, the account of the excellence of merit.

At that time, in the land of Sarvagandhasugandhā, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara who had long ago planted the roots of all virtues and had served and attended upon immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas.
He had fully accomplished profound wisdom and attained the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner, the Lotus Samādhi, the Samādhi of Pure Virtue, and the Samādhi of the Constellations and Kings.
The Play Samādhi, the Objectless Samādhi, the Wisdom Seal Samādhi, the Samādhi that Understands the Languages of All Sentient Beings,
the Samādhi that Accumulates All Merit, the Pure Samādhi, the Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers,
the Wisdom Torch Samādhi, the Ornamentation King Samādhi, the Pure Radiance Samādhi, the Pure Treasury Samādhi, the Unshared Samādhi, and the Sun Samādhi.
Through the *āvartana-samādhi*, one attains hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great *samādhis* equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River.

The cause for this accumulation of merit is the encounter with many previous Buddhas. Profound wisdom is the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-alaṃkāra*), while the sixteen *samādhis* are the adornment of merit (*puṇya-alaṃkāra*).
The Record states that these sixteen are all from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The various names for this state are explained according to their respective meanings; here, we shall describe the characteristics of the *dharmaparyāya-samādhi*.
△ Second, being illumined by light: Śākyamuni Buddha radiates light upon his body.
△ Third, he took leave of the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha Pure Lotus Flower Constellation King Wisdom, saying:
"World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, draw near to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and to see the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince."
The Bodhisattva Sarvauṣadhi-rāja, the Bodhisattva Sūradatta, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña,
the Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra, the Bodhisattva Vyūharāja, and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
△ Fourth, the exhortation to sincerity.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña said to the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara: "Do not disparage that land by conceiving thoughts of it as inferior.
Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with high and low ground, filled with mountains of earth and stone and all manner of impurities;
the bodies of the Buddhas there are small, and the forms of the bodhisattvas are likewise small, whereas your body is forty-two [yojanas]..."
"My body is one thousand yojanas in height, while yours is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas.

You are foremost in physical beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of merits and wondrous, sublime radiance; therefore, go there and do not disparage that land, nor conceive thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, or the realm."
The Buddha’s admonition is as follows: since Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, he achieves his purpose without the need for formal discipline;

yet, because those whom he leads may not yet have attained such realization, he relies upon that [external form] to provide a model for this [inner reality]. Indeed, the Buddha-body corresponds to the ultimate principle (*tathatā*);
one must not perceive its humble appearance and thereby forget its majesty. This is the admonition provided by means of the Tathāgata’s seat.

Now, when both teacher and disciple are fully endowed with wisdom and the power of cessation, yet the teacher employs skillful means while the disciple likewise conceals his true nature—this is a warning based on the Tathāgata’s robe.
For the land of the external environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) is entirely induced by the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*);

since the Tathāgata presides over the great trichiliocosm through his compassion, one must attend to both the high and the low. Do not merely behold the external environment and thereby neglect the primary retribution.
This is also a warning based on the Tathāgata’s chamber; this is the Buddha’s exhortation for the propagation of the sutra, also containing three points of instruction.
That Honored One’s warning is intended to show that the path of all Buddhas is the same. △ Fifth, receiving the Buddha’s mandate.

The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that I may now go to the Sahā world is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata, the playful mastery of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, and the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom."
The power of the Tathāgata is the power of this seat; the power of supernormal faculties is the power of this chamber; the power of adornment is the power of these robes.

Because this receives the great purport of the extensive sūtra and constitutes the essential core for benefiting sentient beings, one is able to travel and transform throughout the ten directions without moving from this assembly.
6. Manifesting the Signs of Arrival. Part One: Sending forth the Lotus.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered into samādhi. By the power of this samādhi,
not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak Mountain, he manifested eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels,
with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and *kiṃśuka* gems.
He used it to construct his terrace.
As for Jāmbūnada gold, there is a river in the Western Regions near a Jambu tree; the river was named after the tree, and this gold produced from the river was named after the river.
As for kiṃśuka, this is translated as "red-colored gem"; it is originally the name of a tree.
The flowers of those trees were red and resembled this jewel; therefore, they were so named. △ Second, Mañjuśrī’s inquiry:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen first appeared? There are many tens of millions of lotus flowers with stems of Jāmbūnada gold."
Its petals are made of white silver, its filaments of vajra, and its pedestal of karkarava gems.
Question: If Mañjuśrī’s rank were low, it would be inappropriate for him to seek an audience; if his rank were high, why did he suddenly fail to recognize [the Buddha] when they met?
Answer: Although they share the same rank, there are beginnings, middles, and ends. It is simply that he did not know this one particular instance.
Not wishing to disgrace his high station, and because he did not understand the origin of the auspicious sign seen among the assembly, he questioned the Buddha.
△ Third, Śākyamuni’s response:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara..."
Desiring to come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas,
to this Sahā world in order to make offerings to, draw near to, and pay homage to me, and also desiring to make offerings to and hear the Lotus Sūtra.
△ Fourth, the request to see the signs.

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted, and what merits has he cultivated, that he is able to possess such great supernormal powers?
What samādhi does he practice? We pray that you will explain this samādhi for our sake."
"We also wish to diligently practice this samādhi; only by practicing this samādhi can one behold the physical appearance, stature, and dignified deportment of that bodhisattva.
We pray that the World-Honored One, through your supernatural power, cause that bodhisattva to come so that we may behold him."
△ 5. Attributing the Merit.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has long since entered parinirvāṇa, shall manifest his form for you all."
△ Sixth, the arrival of the messenger.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas and sons of good family: "Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, wishes to see your body."
△ Second, the actual departure. Part one: The journey with the retinue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.
As they passed through various lands, the earth shook in six ways, and hundreds of thousands of celestial seven-jeweled lotuses rained down everywhere.
The musical instruments played without being struck.
△ Second, the description of his appearance as he ascends the platform:
This Bodhisattva’s eyes are like the petals of a vast blue lotus; even if a hundred thousand million moons were brought together, their light...

His countenance was upright and handsome, surpassing even this; his body was of a true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits, blazing with majestic power and radiant light, complete with all the primary marks.

Possessing a body as firm as that of Nārāyaṇa, he entered a pavilion of the seven treasures and ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground, where the assembly of bodhisattvas paid him reverent homage.
They surrounded him and came to this Sahā world, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Regarding the phrase "eyes like the broad petals of a great blue lotus," Master Zao’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states:

"In India there is a blue lotus whose petals are long and wide, with a distinct clarity of blue and white; because it possesses the marks of the eyes of a Great Man [Mahāpuruṣa], [the Buddha's eyes] are compared to it."
To illustrate this, Nārāyaṇa is here translated as "the Wielder of Might. △ Third, the inquiry and transmission of the message:

Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace, took a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was, prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet, presented the necklace, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom..."
The Buddha inquired after the World-Honored One: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are your four great elements in harmony? Can you endure worldly affairs? Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
Are they free from much greed, anger, delusion, envy, stinginess, and pride? Are they not unfilial toward their parents? Do they not disrespect śramaṇas or harbor wrong views and unwholesome minds?"
"Having restrained the five senses, the World-Honored One will soon subdue all demonic adversaries and enter parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, has the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna come from within his seven-jeweled stupa to hear the Dharma? And does he inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being, asking whether he is free from affliction, enduring, and dwelling in comfort?"
4. Requesting to See Prabhūtaratna:
"World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me so that I may see him.
5. The World-Honored One Opens the Way.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet you.
△ Sixth, the praise within the stupa:
Then the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You are able to make offerings to Śākyamuni..."
The bhikṣuṇīs, the Buddha, and those who have heard the Lotus Sūtra, as well as Mañjuśrī and others, have come here for this reason.
△ Second, the propagation of the sūtra in the thirty directions; first, the question and answer regarding the roots of goodness and spiritual powers; second, the initial question;
first, the question concerning what roots of goodness were planted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness did this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound plant?
This was his question concerning the past. △ Second, he asked about the existence of such supernormal powers.
"What merit has been cultivated to possess such supernatural power?"—this is the question now.
II. The Answer, in two parts: A. First, answering regarding the planting of roots of goodness.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King (Meghadundubhisvararāja) Tathāgata..."
In the land of the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvalokadarśana, during the kalpa named Priyadarśanasvarā,
the Bodhisattva offered one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments for twelve thousand years to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvara,
and presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious gems. By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution, he has now been born in this Pure Land.
In the buddha-field of the Buddha Padmashri-rāja-jñāna, there is such a supernatural power. Flower Virtue, what do you think?
Was the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara at that time—who offered music as an act of worship and presented precious vessels before the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja—anyone else?
It was none other than this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara. This is Flower Virtue; this is the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara. Thus it has been said.

Having made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas, he long ago planted the roots of virtue; furthermore, he encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

This answers the question regarding the planting of roots of goodness. In the past, he offered music and presented ritual vessels, yet he still brings together the ancient and the present, all of which is exactly as described.
[The Buddha] spoke. △ Second, the answer concerning the existence of this supernatural power:
"Huade, you see only that the body of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is here;

yet this Bodhisattva manifests various bodies everywhere to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings—sometimes manifesting as the body of Brahmā, sometimes manifesting as the body of Śakra..."
The body of Śākyamuni may manifest as the body of Īśvara, or manifest as the body of Maheśvara, or manifest as the body of Deva-senapati,
or manifest as the body of Vaiśravaṇa-rāja, or manifest as the body of a Cakravartin king, or manifest as the body of various minor kings,
or manifest as the body of a householder, or manifest as the body of a lay devotee, or manifest as the body of a high official, or manifest as...
He may manifest in the body of a brahmin, or manifest in the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
he may manifest in the bodies of elders, householders, or women; he may manifest in the bodies of wives of officials, or manifest in the bodies of brahmin women;
he may manifest in the bodies of boys or girls; or he may manifest as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras.
He preaches this sutra in the forms of rākṣasas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
he is able to rescue all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and other places of great suffering, even transforming into a female body within the royal harem to preach this sutra.
Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is able to provide protection and salvation.

These various sentient beings of the Sahā world are the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifesting such diverse transformations and appearing here in this Sahā land to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings;
yet there is no diminution whatsoever in his supernormal powers, transformations, or wisdom. This bodhisattva illuminates the Sahā world with manifold wisdom.
He causes all sentient beings to each attain what they know; it is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.
To those who should be liberated by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who should be liberated by appearing in the form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests in the form of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who should be liberated by appearing in the form of a bodhisattva...
To those who are to be saved by the form of a bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them;
to those who are to be saved by the form of a Buddha, he immediately manifests the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

In this way, through various manifestations according to what is appropriate for their salvation, he even displays the act of passing into parinirvāṇa for those who are to be saved by means of parinirvāṇa—such is the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue Wondrous Sound.
Such is the manner in which Mahāsattvas accomplish the power of great supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*) and wisdom.

This answer to the question regarding supernatural power demonstrates the thirty-four types of ordinary bodies and four types of noble bodies, thereby constituting the ten dharma-realms and the six paths of existence.
II. Question and Answer: "In what meditative concentration do you now abide? Part One: The Question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has deeply planted roots of goodness.
World-Honored One, in what samādhi does this Bodhisattva abide to be able to thus manifest transformations everywhere to deliver and liberate sentient beings?"
Question: Abiding now in which samādhi are you able to thus freely benefit others? △ Second, the answer:
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva, "Good son, the name of that samādhi is 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
When the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound abides in this samādhi, he is able to thus bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings."
The Buddha answered as written in the text. △ Fourth, the benefits gained by those in the two lands:

When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, the eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms; likewise, immeasurable bodhisattvas in this Sahā world also [attained it].
One attains these samādhis and dhāraṇīs. Regarding samādhi and dhāraṇī:
their essence is one while their functions differ; the function of quiescence is called samādhi, and the function of retention is named dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the form-body is called samādhi, while the eloquent exposition through voice is called dhāraṇī.
The *Dhāraṇī-śūramgama-sūtra*, in its superior section, states: "First, one attains the Samādhi of All Form-Bodies; by transforming the body, one attains the Dhāraṇī of All Languages.
One should know that sound is still a phenomenon of form (*rūpa-dharma*); therefore, it is said that their substance is one while their functions differ.

Furthermore, the purity of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is called a *dhāraṇī*, while the purity of the other faculties is called a *samādhi*; all of these pertain to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
This is the Dharma-door of Purity. △ Fifth, returning to his own land.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, having made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, returned to his own land;
as he passed through the various countries, the earth shook in six ways, and precious lotus flowers rained down, performing a hundred [miracles].

Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of various kinds of musical instruments, having arrived in his own land, he was surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas and went to the place where the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña was.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have gone to the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings;
I have seen Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and I have paid homage and made offerings to them. Furthermore—
Upon seeing the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja,
Vīryadatta, and Śūradatta, these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas also attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.

As for the shaking of the earth and the raining of flowers, if even a bodhisattva who has undergone such experiences can still provide incidental benefit, how much more so when the Buddha emits light before him that shines incidentally upon one hundred and eight million nayutas of lands in the eastern direction—this too is an incidental discussion of benefit. 6.
Advancing on the Path through Hearing the Chapter.

When this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
and the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa attained the Lotus Samādhi (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi).
The above concludes the text of the seventh fascicle.
