△ Third, covering them with supernatural power:
World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this dhāraṇī, they should know it is the supernatural power of Samantabhadra.
If the Lotus Sūtra circulates in Jambudvīpa and there are those who receive and uphold it, they should form this thought: "All of these are [the work of Samantabhadra]."
The power of the noble one’s majestic spiritual authority.
That which is covered by such spiritual power means that whether it be hearing or upholding [the teaching], none of these fail to be brought about by the spiritual power of Samantabhadra.
△ Fourth, showing the superior cause.
If there are those who uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and understand the meaning and intent [of this teaching], and practice according to what is taught,
you should know that such persons perform the conduct of Samantabhadra; they have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas,
and their heads are stroked by the hands of all Tathāgatas.

If one can cause the *Lotus Sūtra* to circulate for the sake of these five kinds of Dharma-preachers, then before the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one has planted, ripened, and attained liberation.
Because this person will attain liberation together with the future Buddhas, it is said that they share the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Because this person has already planted wholesome roots under previous Buddhas, it is said that they have deeply planted wholesome roots. This person acts as a manifestation...
Because he has been matured by the Buddha, the Buddha personally strokes his head with his hand. △ Fifth, showing the proximate fruit:
If one merely copies and writes [this sutra], at the end of that person's life, they shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

at that time, eighty-four thousand celestial maidens will come to welcome them with various musical performances, and that person will immediately don a crown of the seven treasures among the court ladies.
If even this brings such joy and happiness, how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and understand its meaning, and practice according to the teaching!
If there is anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, and understands its meaning, at the end of their life, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them,
ensuring they have no fear and do not fall into the evil realms, but shall immediately go to Tuṣita Heaven to meet Maitreya Bodhisattva.

Therein, Maitreya Bodhisattva—surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas endowed with the thirty-two marks—is accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial maidens as his retinue; within that realm, there are such merits and benefits as these.
One who is merely able to transcribe it will soon reach the Heaven of the Thirty-three and possess the five qualities of a Dharma Master; next, they will dwell in Tuṣita. △ Sixth, the summary:
Therefore, the wise person should with single-mindedness either transcribe it themselves or cause others to transcribe it, and then receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly contemplate it.
Reflect upon practicing according to what has been taught.
△ Second, protecting the Dharma:
"World-Honored One, by means of my supernormal powers, I shall now protect this sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa throughout Jambudvīpa."
To cause this to be widely circulated within [the realm] so that it shall never be severed—this is the vow to protect the Dharma.
△ Third, the account of its arousal, which has three parts. First, the transposed account of protecting the Dharma:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Samantabhadra, you are able to protect and assist this..."
The Sūtra has already brought peace, happiness, and benefit to many sentient beings;

you have accomplished inconceivable merit and profound great compassion, having long ago resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and are thus able to make such vows of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to protect this Sūtra. I, too, shall protect it with my own supernatural powers.
Regarding those who uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
the third [section] describes the arousal [of the mind]. This refers to the Tathāgata’s exaltation of the superior and his establishment of the inferior;
for those who practice with increasing vigor, he now first describes the protection of the Dharma, saying: "You are able to thus provide great benefit externally and internally."
Having accumulated compassion for a long time, I have provided such protection; by the spiritual power of the Buddha, I shall likewise protect this Dharma—how much more so you?
△ Second, the retrospective account of those who protected [the Dharma], in five parts: first, the description of the teachings manifested through the physical body.

Samantabhadra, you should know that if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, cultivate, and transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, such persons shall see Śākyamuni Buddha as if hearing this scripture directly from the Buddha’s own mouth;
you should know that such persons have made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; you should know that such persons are praised by the Buddha with the words, "Excellent! You should know.
One should know that such a person is one whose head has been stroked by the hand of Śākyamuni Buddha;
one should know that such a person is covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.
From this point downward, although the description of those whom he protects does not follow a sequential order, it should be understood that it serves to fulfill the intended meaning.
That people see Śākyamuni Buddha describes his manifestation of body and teaching of the Dharma; how much more so should they see my fruition-body endowed with ten thousand virtues?

Since even you, as a six-tusked white elephant during your causal stage, were able to hear the sutras in their entirety from the Buddha’s own mouth, how much more so should you, who have forgotten the chapters and verses of what was taught to you, receive the Buddha’s praise with his mouth and caress with his hand?
If even those covered by the Buddha’s robes [are protected], how much more so you, who are covered by the *dhāraṇī* of a human being? △ Second, skipping ahead to describe the superior causes:
such a person no longer clings to worldly pleasures, nor do they take pleasure in the scriptures or manuscripts of non-Buddhists; furthermore—
They take no pleasure in associating with such people or with those who are evil—such as butchers, those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, hunters, or those who traffic in female beauty.
Such persons are upright in mind and possess right mindfulness and the power of merit;
they are not afflicted by the three poisons, nor are they overcome by envy, pride, or arrogance.
A person afflicted by pride who possesses few desires and is content can cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra;

this extensively enumerates the causes, wherein the absence of all faults and evils, along with having few desires, being content, and cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra, constitute the description of the superior causes.
"Pride" (*māna*) refers to relying on oneself and looking down upon others; "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*) refers to falsely exalting oneself.

Furthermore, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) claim to have attained what they have not attained. As for the detailed explanation of the seven types of pride, this is fully contained in the preceding text.
Regarding "having few desires and being content," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Not seeking and not grasping is called having few desires;
when one obtains little, the mind feels no regret or resentment—this is called being content. △ Third, skipping ahead to describe the proximate fruit.
Samantabhadra, if after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there should be anyone who sees another receiving,
upholding, reading, or reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should form this thought: "This person shall before long proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*),
shatter the hosts of Māras, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, turn the wheel of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, blow the conch of Dharma, and rain down the Dharma."
"Vimalakīrti, you should sit upon the lion Dharma-seat amidst this great assembly of devas and humans.
Furthermore, if anyone in future ages upholds, receives, reads, and recites this sutra, that person shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food, drink, or the necessities of life;
their aspirations shall not be in vain, and they shall likewise obtain these meritorious rewards in the present life."
This describes the proximate fruits. Such a person shall proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and will certainly achieve the ultimate fruit; how much more so the proximate fruits?
Furthermore, they obtain these proximate fruits in the present life, not merely rebirth in heaven. △ Fourth, a retrospective account of warding off external calamities.
If there are those who speak with contempt, saying, "You are merely a madman; practicing such deeds in vain, you shall gain nothing," they will receive this retribution for their sin:
in every successive life, they shall be blind. Conversely, those who offer worship and praise shall obtain manifest rewards in this very life.
Furthermore, if one sees someone upholding this sutra and exposes their faults—whether real or imagined—[they too shall suffer].
If this person— who has not attained reality— contracts leprosy in the present life, those who mock them lightly shall, in every successive birth,
suffer from gaps and missing teeth, ugly lips, flat noses, contorted hands and feet, squinting eyes, a foul-smelling and filthy body, malignant sores with pus and blood,
abdominal dropsy, shortness of breath, and various other grievous illnesses.

This describes how it can ward off external calamities. The Tathāgata extensively reveals the offenses of those who disparage [this sutra] so that they may recognize their transgressions and surely reform them, rather than continuing to cause affliction and disorder.
It is not only that those who uphold the sutra obtain the extinction of such calamities, but also that blessings arise for even those who wish to disparage it.
Since there is neither disparagement nor calamity, both parties will enjoy peace and happiness; thus, its vast salvation is impartial and compassionate.
To provide further evidence for this, there was a monk from Mount Lu named Zu Ke, styled Zhengping, surnamed Su.

He was the son of Bo Gu of Guanghan in Western Sichuan and the younger brother of Yangzhi. Having studied under his family’s tradition from childhood, he joined the Jiangxi Poetry Society and formed close, unyielding friendships with the eminent scholars of the time.
His reputation was widespread, and he authored the *Baqian ji* (Collection of Waterfall Springs).

While publishing his works, he lived his daily life as if in ordinary times; though he had left the household life, his mind remained preoccupied with the "wind and moon" (the arts), constantly devoting himself to the refined elegance of poetry.
One day, he was suddenly awakened to a realization, thinking: "From my youth until now, as autumn approaches, I have focused exclusively on composing verses—all of this is merely flowery speech.
If the demon of death were suddenly to come for battle, how could I resist it? He immediately went to visit a venerable elder.

[The Master] said, "Furthermore, among the secret scriptures of the various vehicles (*yāna*), which is the most excellent? Suṅ replied, "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most excellent among all the sūtras.
Why is this? It can certainly be trusted that the Tathāgata himself proclaimed it the 'King of All Sūtras.
One may rely on the teaching and examine it thoroughly; after doing so, one will say: 'Though I have read through the entire scroll, the only thing worth taking from it is its fragrance.'"
The single couplet, "The wind blows away the withered flowers and rains down fresh and beautiful ones," is quite well-suited to the intent of the following passage.
Because his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were so thickly accumulated, the Buddhist scriptures (*pustaka*) could not enter him of their own accord;

yet, when he lightly uttered these words, he was immediately struck by *kāmalā* disease, his entire body becoming scorched and rotten—what the world calls the "great wind-disease" (*mahāvātavyādhi*). Its stench was initially unbearable to approach.
From that time until more than thirty years had passed, he finally died; thus, the monastic communities have to this day referred to him as "Lai-ke" (the Leper).

As the Sūtra says: "If one sees someone who receives and upholds this sūtra, and speaks of their faults—whether real or unreal—that person shall contract the disease of white leprosy in this very life.
This is the proof. How can we not take this as a warning? △ Five: An Account of Faith.
Such are the merits thereof.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, as if honoring a Buddha.
This describes the merit of those who have established faith; "as if honoring a Buddha" means that such reverence is ultimate. △
Fourth, the benefits of arousing [the aspiration for enlightenment]. First, the benefits of hearing the chapter:

When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being preached, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless, attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs*, and bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a trichiliocosm were fully endowed [with them].
The Path of Samantabhadra.

This concludes the benefit of the "Chapter on Hearing. The *dhāraṇī* of revolving is the stage of the first ground (*bhūmi*), while possessing the Path of Samantabhadra is the stage of the tenth ground.
△ Second, the benefit of hearing the sutra.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the entire great assembly— including Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas, Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas,
as well as the devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans— all rejoiced greatly, received and upheld the Buddha’s words,
prostrated, and departed.
This is the benefit of hearing the sutra, as previously explained regarding their joy. Question: Why is it still called "śrāvaka" (voice-hearer) here? Answer:
This is merely because the compiler of the sutra has preserved its original designation.

Furthermore, the compiler refers to them as "Mahāyāna śrāvakas," for since they cause all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, this meaning becomes even more manifest. This concludes the eighth section above.
The text of the fascicle is concluded. The Lotus Sutra, Fascicle Ten (End).
